specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I noted before in one of the responses to the questions, our plan will fix the problems in our energy system by securing affordable power, guaranteeing reliability, and restoring investor confidence.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods — affordable power, reliability, investor confidence — with no figure, mechanism, instrument or date attached to any of them. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is why those members opposite, who have colluded and collaborated with protesters targeting politicians’ homes, should be utterly ashamed of their hypocritical selves.
focus.explanation: A legislative measure is before the House, so there was substance available, but this sentence carries none of it: no clause, cost, effect or mechanism — it is entirely about what the other side is 'really like'.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: New Zealand is experiencing a renewable energy boom, which will bring prices down over time, but there is one barrier standing in our way: the energy system does not have enough back-up supply to keep the economy running when we can’t rely on hydro lakes and wind to generate electricity.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the current build-out of renewable generation will reduce electricity prices over time — an economic outcome, not a commitment to a government action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI electricity subindex and MBIE's quarterly retail electricity price series: true if the average real (CPI-adjusted) residential electricity price at the end of 2028 is below its October 2025 level; false if it is level or higher.

specificity.statement: Last week, the Government announced what we considered to be a risk-based, balanced system for earthquake-prone buildings that keeps life safety at its heart while saving $8.2 billion.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy change and attaches a concrete national savings figure ($8.2 billion), though the mechanism by which the saving arises is not given in this sentence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For Auckland, the savings will be monumental, with more than 1,300 buildings currently classified as earthquake-prone and an estimated $4.5 billion price tag for council, ratepayers, and owners.
specificity.explanation: Gives a building count, a cost figure and who bears the cost — checkable against the register and the costing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under the new system, unreinforced masonry or brick buildings under three storeys in small and rural towns will no longer require mandatory remediation or warning notices, as the risk from falling facades is lower in towns with fewer people.
specificity.explanation: Names the building type, a storey threshold, the settlement type and exactly which obligations are removed — someone could act on this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Dannevirke, Pahiatua, and Woodville will save, respectively, $68 million, $29 million, and $22 million.
specificity.explanation: Named towns matched to individual dollar figures; about as concrete and checkable as a claim gets.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s difficult to quantify the cost exactly, not least of all because the opportunity cost and the chilling effect of regulations that were well intended, admittedly, but have proven difficult to implement in the intervening eight years, have meant a focus on those particular risks, as opposed to other risks in the built environment.
specificity.explanation: Asked for a cost figure, he supplies none and gestures at 'opportunity cost' and a 'chilling effect' without quantifying either — a direction of argument with no checkable content, notable given how precise his other answers in the same session were.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The purpose of this bill is to contribute to the restoration of the health, the mauri, the wellbeing of the Hauraki Gulf and to acknowledge customary rights within various areas.
specificity.explanation: States an aim and the areas it touches, but no mechanism, protected area, figure or timeframe — the surrounding sentences add scene-setting rather than detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The current system has the best of intentions but has placed a heavy financial burden on property owners, leaving 5,800 buildings currently still awaiting either remediation or demolition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of buildings still on the earthquake-prone register awaiting remediation or demolition at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE's national earthquake-prone building register as at October 2025: true if approximately 5,800 buildings are recorded as earthquake-prone and not yet remediated or demolished; false if the register shows a materially different number.

veracity.statement: For Auckland, the savings will be monumental, with more than 1,300 buildings currently classified as earthquake-prone and an estimated $4.5 billion price tag for council, ratepayers, and owners.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both the number of Auckland buildings classified as earthquake-prone and the estimated remediation cost falling on council, ratepayers and owners.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE earthquake-prone building register count for Auckland and the MBIE/Auckland Council remediation cost estimate: true if the Auckland register holds more than 1,300 buildings and the published remediation cost estimate is around $4.5 billion; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: What costs has New Zealand incurred in the nine years since the earthquake-prone building rules came into place, and was ACT right, in hindsight, to be the only party opposed to the 2016 bill?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that ACT was the sole party to oppose the 2016 earthquake-prone buildings legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill in 2016: true if ACT is the only party recorded as voting against, false if it voted for, or if any other party also voted against.

rigor.statement: New Zealand’s known as the Shaky Isles for a good reason, but the latest science does indicate that seismic risk varies greatly across the country. That’s why the Government’s removing Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands from the earthquake-prone building system.
rigor.explanation: The inference from 'seismic risk varies greatly by region' to 'exclude the lowest-risk regions' tracks. The gap is an unnamed appeal to 'the latest science' as authority, and the premise supports differentiated treatment rather than specifically full exemption, so it is short of fully supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Under the new system, unreinforced masonry or brick buildings under three storeys in small and rural towns will no longer require mandatory remediation or warning notices, as the risk from falling facades is lower in towns with fewer people.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered and the conclusion follows from it: fewer people passing a facade means lower expected harm, so a lower regulatory requirement is warranted. Marked down slightly because population exposure alone does not establish the risk to those actually present, which the conclusion glosses over.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What costs has New Zealand incurred in the nine years since the earthquake-prone building rules came into place, and was ACT right, in hindsight, to be the only party opposed to the 2016 bill?
focus.explanation: The first half asks a real policy question about the cost of a named regulatory regime; the second half invites a verdict on which party was right, which is party positioning rather than policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In relation to political parties’ positions, I think, as I’ve acknowledged, the intent of all parties at the time following the tragedy that was the Canterbury earthquakes was right, but lived experience has indicated in the intervening period that it has been appropriate first to pause the enforcement of the current rules, as we’ve legislated, but also to take another look, which is what we’re pleased now to have done.
focus.explanation: Redirects a question about which party was right onto the named regulatory regime, the pause in enforcement and the review — policy content rather than party scoring.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In relation to political parties’ positions, I think, as I’ve acknowledged, the intent of all parties at the time following the tragedy that was the Canterbury earthquakes was right, but lived experience has indicated in the intervening period that it has been appropriate first to pause the enforcement of the current rules, as we’ve legislated, but also to take another look, which is what we’re pleased now to have done.
civility.explanation: Invited by a supplementary to say other parties were wrong in 2016, he credits the intent of all parties and stays on the substance. A genuine opportunity to attack, declined.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There is no doubt that the gulf is in trouble.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana is currently in poor ecological condition; the surrounding sentence names sedimentation, pollution and kina barrens as the drivers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hauraki Gulf Forum's triennial 'State of our Gulf' State of the Environment report, plus Fisheries NZ / NIWA assessments of the Gulf. True if those sources document continuing ecological decline (sediment loading, nutrient pollution, kina barrens) in Tīkapa Moana at the time of the statement; false if they record the Gulf as stable or in good ecological health.

veracity.statement: There are 19 marine protection areas that have been created and there is further investment of putea, time, effort, and energy that will be announced in short course.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count — 19 — of marine protection areas created in connection with this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill as reported back to the House, and the Department of Conservation / Ministry for the Environment description of it. True if the areas established (high protection areas, seafloor protection areas and extensions to existing reserves) total 19; false if the count is materially different.

veracity.statement: For example, removing the ability for the bill to regulate customary non-commercial fishing, something that other parties were willing to preserve.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that other parties wanted the bill to retain the power to regulate customary non-commercial fishing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Environment Committee report on the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill, including differing views recorded by non-government parties, and the parties' second-reading speeches. True if one or more other parties argued for retaining the bill's power to regulate customary non-commercial fishing; false if no party took that position on the record.

specificity.statement: There are 19 marine protection areas that have been created and there is further investment of putea, time, effort, and energy that will be announced in short course.
specificity.explanation: Carries one hard, checkable figure (19 areas), but the second half — 'further investment of putea, time, effort, and energy ... in short course' — commits to no amount, no mechanism and no date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For example, removing the ability for the bill to regulate customary non-commercial fishing, something that other parties were willing to preserve.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete mechanism — the removal of a regulatory power over customary non-commercial fishing — which someone could look up in the bill. No figures or timeframes, and the change is described rather than clause-referenced.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For example, removing the ability for the bill to regulate customary non-commercial fishing, something that other parties were willing to preserve.
focus.explanation: Names a specific amendment to a specific bill and what it does. The clause about 'other parties' is party framing, but the weight of the sentence is on the policy change itself, not on what the other parties are like.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
specificity.explanation: Names the income threshold, quantifies the gap ($33,000), and names the cost categories the test ignores. Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They can support their young person by encouraging them to get connected to employment, training, or work.
specificity.explanation: Asked what evidence supports the affordability threshold, the answer names no figure, mechanism or form of support — 'encouraging them' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re making sure they’ll get a job.
specificity.explanation: Answers a question about what measures will be put in place with no measure, no timeframe and no mechanism. A bare assurance.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I’d say to Carlos: actually, this is a Government that’s doing everything we can to try and create employment and opportunities for Carlos.
specificity.explanation: 'Doing everything we can' carries no programme, figure or timeframe; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, at just over 5 percent, our unemployment rate is actually below what it has been, on average, over the last 15 years or so.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rate, a comparator and a window — precise enough that someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What measures, if any, will the Prime Minister put in place to stop the 4,300 young people expected to lose jobseeker support next year from falling into poverty, homelessness, or leaving Aotearoa entirely?
specificity.explanation: A named cohort size, a timeframe, and the specific harms at issue. A precise question, as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re also introducing $1,000 bonus payment from October next year for a young person aged 18 to 24 who has worked with a community job coach, moved into employment, and stayed in a job for at least 12 months.
specificity.explanation: Amount, start date, age band and the qualifying conditions are all stated. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These changes are about fairness, opportunity, and personal responsibility.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues attached to the package; no figure, mechanism or step. Nothing here distinguishes this policy from any other.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Evidence shows us that if a young person goes on to welfare before the age of 25, they can spend, on average, another 18 years on benefit over their lifetime.
specificity.explanation: An age threshold and an average duration, presented as sourced from evidence — precise enough to be looked up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How many construction jobs were lost when the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes?
specificity.explanation: A named agency, a named figure and a defined quantity being asked for. A precise question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Kāinga Ora has delivered more new-build homes in the last 23 months under our Government than the entire three years under the last Labour Government.
specificity.explanation: A named agency, a defined 23-month window and an explicit comparator period. Checkable, though no absolute figure is given in this sentence.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we ask the private sector what stops them making those investments, they highlight two key factors: (1) high interest rates—that’s why it’s important we bring them down—and (2) consenting issues, which is why we have introduced the fast-track Act, which is already working to get major infrastructure developments off the ground.
specificity.explanation: Names two identified barriers and a named piece of legislation, but supplies no figures, no consenting timeframes and no measure of the effect claimed.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the parental income test — its threshold, and who it excludes. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy mechanism, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They can support their young person by encouraging them to get connected to employment, training, or work.
focus.explanation: Stays on the policy question (what parents are expected to do) rather than turning on the questioner's party. Vague but on-topic — the contrast with its Specificity score is the point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because there are opportunities for young people in those sectors in Australia but not here in New Zealand, because the Opposition opposes those.
focus.explanation: The sentence's whole weight is what the other side opposes rather than what the policy does; no mechanism, cost or outcome is named in it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can the Prime Minister justify cutting jobseeker access for our rangatahi when it is the Government, not our young people, that created the conditions of poverty and unemployment that they are now being punished for?
focus.explanation: Directed at a named policy change (restricting jobseeker access for 18–19-year-olds) and at the Government's record on unemployment, though the causal framing carries some of the weight in place of policy detail.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many construction jobs were lost when the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes?
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision and a specific number and asks for its measured effect. Textbook scrutiny of a named policy outcome, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
civility.explanation: Hard on the policy's evidential basis; no person is impugned. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’d say to Carlos: actually, this is a Government that’s doing everything we can to try and create employment and opportunities for Carlos.
civility.explanation: Addresses the case put to him without any slight to the questioner. Contested exchange, no personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is another attempt from that member to misrepresent a Minister.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate bad faith to the questioner — an accusation about her intent rather than about the accuracy of the quote. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m afraid this question highlights the importance of the work being done by my colleague Erica Stanford on structured literacy.
civility.explanation: A sneer implying the questioner cannot read. It engages nothing in the question and lands squarely on the member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She’s as bad at maths as she is at structured literacy.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the member's numeracy and literacy — her personal competence, not her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m grateful to the advice from my colleague Minister Stanford, who advises that some children require repeated instruction in order to grasp concepts.
civility.explanation: Condescension by comparison — the member is likened to a slow child. An attack on her comprehension rather than on her case.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If that member is so wrong-headed to think that every single construction job in New Zealand is dependent on public infrastructure, then perhaps she needs to get a little bit more reading done, because, as is actually the case, the construction sector relies heavily on private sector development—things like housing development, which tends to be funded also by the private sector, Member Andersen, and things like the Auckland Port development, which is being funded by that organisation.
civility.explanation: 'Wrong-headed' and 'needs to get a little bit more reading done' are aimed at the member's judgement and diligence, not at her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she accept that cutting almost $1 billion of Kāinga Ora’s building spend has contributed to the 20,000 jobs lost in the construction sector; if not, why not?
civility.explanation: Blunt about the spending decision and its consequences; nothing directed at the Minister personally.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What evidence does he have that whānau earning just over $65,000 a year can afford to support an 18- or 19-year-old, when two parents on minimum wage already exceed that threshold by $33,000, with no allowance for rent, other tamariki, or the rising cost of living?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two parents each earning the adult minimum wage full-time have a combined income about $33,000 above the parental income test threshold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE adult minimum wage rate in force October 2025, multiplied by 2 earners at 40 hrs/week × 52 weeks, minus the $65,529 parental income threshold. True if the resulting gap is approximately $33,000; false if it differs materially (say by more than $5,000).

veracity.statement: Well, at just over 5 percent, our unemployment rate is actually below what it has been, on average, over the last 15 years or so.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current unemployment rate, described as just over 5 percent, is below the 15-year average unemployment rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate for the most recent quarter as at October 2025, compared with the arithmetic mean of the quarterly HLFS unemployment rate over the preceding 15 years (2010–2025). True if the current rate is below that mean; false if it equals or exceeds it.

veracity.statement: What measures, if any, will the Prime Minister put in place to stop the 4,300 young people expected to lose jobseeker support next year from falling into poverty, homelessness, or leaving Aotearoa entirely?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that official forecasts expect 4,300 young people to lose jobseeker support in the coming year as a result of the change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MSD Regulatory Impact Statement and Cabinet papers for the Parental Assistance Test. True if official forecasts put the number of young people losing jobseeker support in the first year at approximately 4,300; false if the published forecast is materially different or if no such forecast exists.

veracity.statement: Evidence shows us that if a young person goes on to welfare before the age of 25, they can spend, on average, another 18 years on benefit over their lifetime.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an actuarial finding that entering welfare before 25 is associated with an average of a further 18 years on benefit across a lifetime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MSD benefit system actuarial valuation (Taylor Fry). True if the valuation reports an average of approximately 18 further years on benefit over the lifetime for people entering the benefit system before age 25; false if the published figure is materially different or if the valuation reports no such measure.

veracity.statement: How many construction jobs were lost when the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government cancelled 3,500 Kāinga Ora homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora build programme documents and Ministry of Housing and Urban Development advice covering the 2024 reset of the Kāinga Ora build programme. True if approximately 3,500 planned homes were removed from the programme; false if the number of homes withdrawn is materially different.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora has delivered more new-build homes in the last 23 months under our Government than the entire three years under the last Labour Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora new-build completions in the current Government's first 23 months exceed those over the previous Government's full three-year term.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora quarterly delivery reporting on new-build homes completed. True if completions in the 23 months to October 2025 exceed completions over the three years to November 2023; false if they do not.

veracity.statement: Does she accept that cutting almost $1 billion of Kāinga Ora’s building spend has contributed to the 20,000 jobs lost in the construction sector; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20,000 jobs have been lost in the construction sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction sector employment (HLFS/filled jobs by industry) from the sector's peak to the September 2025 quarter. True if the fall in construction employment is approximately 20,000; false if the decline is materially smaller or larger.

veracity.statement: Was Kāinga Ora wrong when they advised that $1 billion of building spend supports approximately 5,200 Kiwi jobs?
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim attributed to Kāinga Ora about the employment supported by $1 billion of building spend; the checkable fact is whether Kāinga Ora gave that advice in those terms.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora advice to Ministers released under the OIA or proactively published during 2024. True if a Kāinga Ora document states that $1 billion of building spend supports approximately 5,200 jobs; false if no such advice exists or the figure it gives is materially different.

rigor.statement: Because there are opportunities for young people in those sectors in Australia but not here in New Zealand, because the Opposition opposes those.
rigor.explanation: Non-sequitur: the conclusion that the opportunities do not exist in New Zealand is attributed to Opposition opposition, but an opposition party holds no power to block sector policy, and the Government has already legislated fast-track. The causal step is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When we ask the private sector what stops them making those investments, they highlight two key factors: (1) high interest rates—that’s why it’s important we bring them down—and (2) consenting issues, which is why we have introduced the fast-track Act, which is already working to get major infrastructure developments off the ground.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: two stated barriers are identified and each is matched to a policy response. The step from 'the sector cites consenting' to 'fast-track is therefore working' is asserted rather than evidenced, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If that member is so wrong-headed to think that every single construction job in New Zealand is dependent on public infrastructure, then perhaps she needs to get a little bit more reading done, because, as is actually the case, the construction sector relies heavily on private sector development—things like housing development, which tends to be funded also by the private sector, Member Andersen, and things like the Auckland Port development, which is being funded by that organisation.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: Andersen claimed a contribution to job losses from a $1 billion cut, not that every construction job depends on public infrastructure. The evidence offered rebuts a position nobody advanced, so it does not reach the actual claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she now regret slashing infrastructure projects when we can all see it has directly contributed to 20,000 job losses in the construction sector?
rigor.explanation: Appeal to obviousness: 'we can all see' is offered in place of any evidence for direct causation, and the leap from a spending cut to attributing 20,000 job losses to it is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Crayfish and scallops have become functionally extinct.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that crayfish and scallops in the Hauraki Gulf have declined to the point of functional extinction — i.e. present in numbers too low to play their ecological role.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NIWA / Fisheries New Zealand stock assessments for the Hauraki Gulf (CRA 2 rock lobster; SCA CS Coromandel scallops) and the Hauraki Gulf Forum 'State of our Gulf' report: true if those sources describe either species as functionally extinct or ecologically collapsed in the Gulf; false if either is assessed as at or above a sustainable biomass level.

veracity.statement: You actually can’t even kill Caulerpa or treat pests and other invasive species in a marine reserve.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the legal status of a marine reserve prohibits control of the invasive seaweed Caulerpa and other pest species within its boundaries.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Marine Reserves Act 1971 (in particular the Minister's and Director-General's powers to authorise activities within a reserve) and DOC's record of Caulerpa or pest-control operations conducted inside marine reserves: false if any lawful authorisation pathway exists or any such operation has been carried out in a marine reserve; true if no lawful mechanism permits pest treatment there.

veracity.statement: Now, the bill sets some time frames: 25 years will be the milestone where the first comprehensive assessment of biodiversity and improvement in the gulf will be carried out.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the bill provides: that the first comprehensive biodiversity assessment falls at a 25-year milestone.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill as passed: true if it requires a first comprehensive assessment of biodiversity at 25 years, false if the stated interval or the nature of the first assessment differs.

rigor.statement: They are a native species, but when nature goes rogue and kina do not have the natural predators and controls that they need, they destroy reefs. They turn reefs into kina barrens by eating all of the kelp and seaweed, leaving no ecosystem to sustain life.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain with each link stated: loss of predators removes control on kina, kina graze kelp, grazed reefs become barrens. The conclusion follows from the premises offered; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But, of course, here are the tough trade-offs: to continue to fish right over those places, those rocky reefs and other places which have been smashed and wiped out, they’re never going to recover. Fishers will only ever be fighting for scraps.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a stated premise (continued fishing over degraded reefs prevents recovery) to a conclusion about fishers' long-run catch. The inference tracks, though 'never' is asserted rather than supported and no evidence is offered for the recovery claim itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s very important that as soon as is practical, we establish a biodiversity baseline for these places we intend to protect in the gulf and that there is regular monitoring and reporting back, so all of those who doubt whether this is going to work can actually have their fears and concerns addressed.
rigor.explanation: Conclusion (establish a baseline and monitor regularly) is supported by a stated purpose — that without measurement, doubts about effectiveness cannot be settled. It leans partly on the management aphorism offered just before it rather than on evidence, which is a small gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, the bill sets some time frames: 25 years will be the milestone where the first comprehensive assessment of biodiversity and improvement in the gulf will be carried out.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument, the mechanism (a comprehensive biodiversity assessment) and a definite interval of 25 years. A reader could go to the bill and check it, or plan against it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s very important that as soon as is practical, we establish a biodiversity baseline for these places we intend to protect in the gulf and that there is regular monitoring and reporting back, so all of those who doubt whether this is going to work can actually have their fears and concerns addressed.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action — a biodiversity baseline plus regular monitoring and reporting — but supplies no measures, no cost, and no date beyond 'as soon as is practical'.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the bill sets some time frames: 25 years will be the milestone where the first comprehensive assessment of biodiversity and improvement in the gulf will be carried out.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the content of the measure before the House — its review mechanism and timing. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That is what we expect: abundance; that these structures, these protected areas, will actually allow the gulf to be restored to a place where if we do want to go for a fish, if we want to go and catch a crayfish or collect some scallops outside these areas, they’ll be available to all of us.
divination.explanation: Forecasts an ecological outcome from the new protected areas: recovered crayfish and scallop abundance in the Hauraki Gulf sufficient that recreational take outside the protected areas is available. Not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The statutory comprehensive biodiversity assessment of the Hauraki Gulf marine protection areas, together with Fisheries New Zealand stock assessments for Hauraki Gulf rock lobster and Coromandel scallops: true if crayfish and scallop abundance has risen materially above the 2025 baseline and recreational take outside the protected areas is open; false if abundance is flat or lower, or recreational take of either species remains closed.

specificity.statement: Overfishing, habitat loss, pollution, sedimentation, and the effects of poorly planned urban development have led to what we see today in the gulf: a 57 percent decline in key fish stocks in the Hauraki Gulf, a 67 percent decline in seabirds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
specificity.explanation: Three named indicators with percentage figures for a named area — directly checkable against the State of our Gulf reporting series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Delayed it to this point, passed eleventh-hour amendments that enable some commercial ring-net fishing in two of the high protection areas, which weakens the intent of this bill and has alarmed environmentalists and recreational fishers alike.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (commercial ring-net fishing), the count (two high protection areas) and the stage at which it happened — someone could go and check the amendment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So given that more than 30,000 people signed an open letter to the Prime Minister, urging this Government to reverse this particular change which allows ring-net fishing in the high protection areas, and more than 5,000 emails were sent by concerned members of the public to the relevant Ministers, and they—this Government—have chosen not to make those changes, Labour, in Government, will reverse the change that allows ring-net fishing in those HPAs.
specificity.explanation: Two figures (30,000 signatures, 5,000 emails) and a precisely bounded commitment — reversing the ring-net fishing provision in the HPAs. Checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just to take a step back and to reflect on the very core purpose ostensibly of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act, which is 20-odd years old now at this point, what that did was establish an entity that has the power to report on the health of the Hauraki every three years yet did not meaningfully give that entity the teeth to enforce the protections that communities so desperately wanted and deserved for our ocean, for our moana.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, its approximate age, and the specific mechanism (a three-yearly reporting duty without enforcement powers), but attaches no figures or proposed remedy.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: While we have ended up with a situation that is far better than the status quo, and we can and should celebrate the consensus that this House has come to with increasing protection to 6 percent, it is nowhere near the 30 percent that is necessary, that scientists tell us is necessary, but more so that our communities so desperately want, nor does it even touch the sides on the need to ban bottom trawling, for which we have so much evidence and which research tells us releases immense amounts of carbon and poses serious risks, therefore, for us with regard to climate changing emissions.
specificity.explanation: Gives the coverage the bill achieves (6 percent) against a named target (30 percent) and names a further concrete measure (banning bottom trawling). The carbon claim is left unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Overfishing, habitat loss, pollution, sedimentation, and the effects of poorly planned urban development have led to what we see today in the gulf: a 57 percent decline in key fish stocks in the Hauraki Gulf, a 67 percent decline in seabirds, and a 97 percent decline in whales and dolphins.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three quantified declines in the Hauraki Gulf — 57% in key fish stocks, 67% in seabirds, 97% in whales and dolphins — attributed to successive State of our Gulf reports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The State of our Gulf / Hauraki Gulf State of the Environment reports (Hauraki Gulf Forum) and the underlying NIWA/DOC series: true if those reports record declines of approximately 57% in key fish stocks, 67% in seabirds and 97% in whales and dolphins for the Hauraki Gulf; false if the reported declines are materially different or if no such figures exist.

veracity.statement: But sadly, despite the Environment Committee unanimously recommending to this House that the bill be passed with no substantive change, at the eleventh hour, because of some active lobbying of the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, we saw this Government cave to that pressure, and they have chosen to water-down the protections in the original bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Environment Committee's recommendation on the bill was unanimous and carried no substantive amendment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Environment Committee's report to the House on the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana marine protection bill: true if the committee recommended unanimously that the bill be passed with no substantive amendment; false if the report records a divided recommendation or recommends substantive amendments.

veracity.statement: In fact, the New Zealand Sport Fishing Council and the environmental group LegaSea wrote to Ministers Potaka and Jones, and they, basically, alluded to the fact, and said, that their behaviour—both those Ministers—is, quite frankly, embarrassing, that they are deeply disappointed in their lack of judgment, in permitting gillnetting within two of the HPAs in the gulf, and then went on to say that their lack of common sense and good judgment will be remembered.
veracity.explanation: The speaker is relaying a claim made by two named third-party organisations — that they wrote to the two Ministers describing their conduct on gillnetting in the HPAs as embarrassing and lacking judgment. What is checkable is the existence and content of that letter, not the Ministers' judgment.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The letter from the New Zealand Sport Fishing Council and LegaSea to Ministers Potaka and Jones, as published by those organisations or released under the OIA: true if such a letter exists and contains the quoted characterisations — 'embarrassing', 'deeply disappointed', 'lack of common sense and good judgment will be remembered' — regarding gillnetting in two HPAs; false if no such letter exists or its content is materially different.

veracity.statement: So given that more than 30,000 people signed an open letter to the Prime Minister, urging this Government to reverse this particular change which allows ring-net fishing in the high protection areas, and more than 5,000 emails were sent by concerned members of the public to the relevant Ministers, and they—this Government—have chosen not to make those changes, Labour, in Government, will reverse the change that allows ring-net fishing in those HPAs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two quantities of public correspondence on the ring-net change: an open letter to the Prime Minister with more than 30,000 signatures, and more than 5,000 emails to the relevant Ministers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records held by the campaign organisers and the Prime Minister's office, plus OIA responses from the offices of the Minister of Conservation and the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries: true if the open letter carried more than 30,000 signatures and more than 5,000 emails were received on the ring-net change; false if the counts are materially lower.

veracity.statement: His own Cabinet paper stated, quite clearly, that that fishing could occur elsewhere in the gulf, but he chose to ignore that, sadly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister's own Cabinet paper recorded that the ring-net fishing at issue could be carried out elsewhere in the gulf. Contested on the spot by Grant McCallum's interjection 'That is not true.'
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The proactively released Cabinet paper on the Hauraki Gulf marine protection amendments: true if it states that the ring-net fishing in question could occur elsewhere in the gulf; false if it contains no such statement or states the opposite.

veracity.statement: Here, I would just make the comparison that we have seen, when we have seen threats to our livestock, and we have seen Governments pour in close to a billion dollars to try and prevent the spread of Mycoplasma bovis but nowhere near the equivalent when it comes to eradicating the threat that is Caulerpa brachypus.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that government spending on the Mycoplasma bovis response approached $1 billion while spending on eradicating exotic Caulerpa is nowhere near that level.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury and MPI budget records for the Mycoplasma bovis eradication programme, and MPI/DOC appropriations for the exotic Caulerpa response: true if M. bovis funding approaches $1 billion and Caulerpa response funding is an order of magnitude smaller; false if M. bovis funding is materially below that figure or the two are comparable.

veracity.statement: We did not need New Zealand First’s support to pass this legislation. We could have passed it in its original format with members of the Opposition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a claim about parliamentary arithmetic: that the unamended bill commanded a majority from National plus the Opposition parties, so New Zealand First's votes were not required.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 54th Parliament's party seat counts and the recorded positions of National, Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori on the bill: true if the bill in its original form commanded a majority without New Zealand First's votes; false if it did not.

civility.statement: But sadly, despite the Environment Committee unanimously recommending to this House that the bill be passed with no substantive change, at the eleventh hour, because of some active lobbying of the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries, we saw this Government cave to that pressure, and they have chosen to water-down the protections in the original bill.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person — 'cave to that pressure' after 'active lobbying of the Minister' hints at a Minister swayed by interests — but the charge lands on the Government's decision rather than on the Minister's character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: While this bill is a step in the right direction, it is no thanks to the current Government, even though the Minister responsible—Minister Potaka—has, in the past, continuously tried to take credit for it.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to a named individual — that Minister Potaka has repeatedly claimed credit for work he did not do. Short of an insult, but it is about the person's conduct rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In fact, the New Zealand Sport Fishing Council and the environmental group LegaSea wrote to Ministers Potaka and Jones, and they, basically, alluded to the fact, and said, that their behaviour—both those Ministers—is, quite frankly, embarrassing, that they are deeply disappointed in their lack of judgment, in permitting gillnetting within two of the HPAs in the gulf, and then went on to say that their lack of common sense and good judgment will be remembered.
civility.explanation: The speaker relays, at length and approvingly, a third party's judgement on two named Ministers' 'lack of common sense and good judgment' — criticism aimed at the individuals' competence rather than at the merits of the carve-out.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We interrogated this abject ridiculousness at the committee of the whole House stage, and the Minister could not provide us with any evidence whatsoever for those fundamentally baseless assertions, nor was the Minister willing to engage in the many amendments that we put forward as members of the Opposition to try and actually work with—if we were to take in good faith—the rationale from the Minister to protect high-protected areas: to do what it says on the tin.
civility.explanation: Harsh language ('abject ridiculousness', 'fundamentally baseless') aimed at the justification rather than the man, but the aside 'if we were to take in good faith' edges into questioning the Minister's sincerity.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: While this bill is a step in the right direction, it is no thanks to the current Government, even though the Minister responsible—Minister Potaka—has, in the past, continuously tried to take credit for it.
focus.explanation: The bill is named, but the weight of the sentence is on who deserves credit rather than on any mechanism, cost or outcome of the legislation.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So given that more than 30,000 people signed an open letter to the Prime Minister, urging this Government to reverse this particular change which allows ring-net fishing in the high protection areas, and more than 5,000 emails were sent by concerned members of the public to the relevant Ministers, and they—this Government—have chosen not to make those changes, Labour, in Government, will reverse the change that allows ring-net fishing in those HPAs.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at a named provision of the bill and what the speaker's party would do about it; no party-character content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Just to take a step back and to reflect on the very core purpose ostensibly of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act, which is 20-odd years old now at this point, what that did was establish an entity that has the power to report on the health of the Hauraki every three years yet did not meaningfully give that entity the teeth to enforce the protections that communities so desperately wanted and deserved for our ocean, for our moana.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the design of a named statute — what powers it created and which it withheld. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We interrogated this abject ridiculousness at the committee of the whole House stage, and the Minister could not provide us with any evidence whatsoever for those fundamentally baseless assertions, nor was the Minister willing to engage in the many amendments that we put forward as members of the Opposition to try and actually work with—if we were to take in good faith—the rationale from the Minister to protect high-protected areas: to do what it says on the tin.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named legislative carve-out, the stated rationale for it, and the Opposition amendments moved against it — the accountability case, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Here, I would just make the comparison that we have seen, when we have seen threats to our livestock, and we have seen Governments pour in close to a billion dollars to try and prevent the spread of Mycoplasma bovis but nowhere near the equivalent when it comes to eradicating the threat that is Caulerpa brachypus.
rigor.explanation: A structured analogy: two biosecurity incursions, wildly different funding responses, therefore an inconsistency in how marine and terrestrial threats are treated. The inference holds, though it leans on the two cases being comparable in scale and tractability, which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: You’re kind of undermining those so-called high-protected areas if you are providing for, explicitly in legislation, carve-outs. That sets a seriously dangerous precedent.
rigor.explanation: The first inference is sound — a statutory exemption to a protection does by definition reduce that protection. The second step, that this 'sets a seriously dangerous precedent', is a mild slippery-slope extension offered without support.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’ll expand the protected area from currently 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures for a named change (current versus post-enactment protected proportion of the gulf); directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The two new marine reserves, the extensions to Cape Rodney-Okakari Point and to Whanga-nui-a-Hei Cathedral Cove will be managed under the Marine Reserves Act 1971.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific sites and the governing statute, and the management regime that follows; concrete enough to act on, though no figures or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If I just go back a few months to 11 May, 64 beaches were either black or red flagged for waste contamination.
specificity.explanation: A dated count with the exact flag categories used by the monitoring system — someone could go and check the record for that day.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They were normally around two per annum and they’re now up to 200 discharges that Watercare can make into the Mahurangi River.
specificity.explanation: Quantifies the change in permitted discharge frequency under a named consent variation — a checkable before/after figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
specificity.explanation: A day count, a volume and a named affected industry and waterway; precise enough to be audited against harvest-closure and overflow records.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’ll expand the protected area from currently 6.7 percent to over 18 percent of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill lifts the proportion of the Hauraki Gulf under marine protection from 6.7% to more than 18%.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC / Ministry for the Environment figures and the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill's regulatory impact statement on the share of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park under protection before and after enactment; true if the pre-bill figure is ~6.7% and the post-bill figure exceeds 18%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: So that has been done, and $15 million has already been put forward to deal with Caulerpa, which is that exotic invasive species which is causing a great concern right around the gulf and also up into Northland and down into the top of the Coromandel as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $15 million has already been committed by the Government to the exotic Caulerpa response.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget documents and Ministry for Primary Industries / Biosecurity New Zealand announcements of funding allocated to the exotic Caulerpa response as at October 2025; true if the cumulative committed figure is ~$15m, false if materially lower or higher.

veracity.statement: Today, eight of those beaches are currently closed due to waste-water overflows.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the day of the speech, eight of the named Auckland beaches (Orakei Basin, Hobson Bay, Judges Bay, Herne Bay, Home Bay, Island Bay, Milford Beach, Milford Beach South) were closed because of waste-water overflows.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council Safeswim records for 7 October 2025 for the named beaches; true if eight carried a no-swim / red or black status attributed to waste-water overflow, false if fewer did or the cause recorded was something else.

veracity.statement: If I just go back a few months to 11 May, 64 beaches were either black or red flagged for waste contamination.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on 11 May (2025), 64 beaches carried a black or red flag for waste contamination.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council Safeswim archive for 11 May 2025; true if 64 monitored sites were red or black flagged for faecal/waste contamination on that date, false if the count differs materially.

veracity.statement: They were normally around two per annum and they’re now up to 200 discharges that Watercare can make into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2022 Auckland Council alternative discharge frequency consent raised Watercare's permitted discharges into the Mahurangi River from about two a year to up to 200.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2022 Auckland Council resource consent / alternative discharge frequency approval for Watercare's Warkworth–Mahurangi waste-water network; true if the prior consent allowed ~2 discharges per annum and the new one allows up to ~200, false if the consented frequencies differ materially.

veracity.statement: That flows out into the ocean, into the harbour, the Mahurangi Harbour, and so far just this year alone, the Mahurangi oyster farmers have had closures for 158 days due to sewage contamination being spilled by Watercare—a total of 4 million litres of sewage contamination being spilled into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures for 2025 to date: 158 days of shellfish harvest closure for Mahurangi oyster farmers attributed to Watercare sewage spills, and 4 million litres of sewage discharged into the Mahurangi River.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI/NZ Food Safety commercial shellfish harvest closure notices for the Mahurangi growing area for January–October 2025, and Watercare's reported overflow volumes for the Mahurangi/Warkworth network over the same period; true if closures total ~158 days and reported spill volume is ~4 million litres, false if either is materially different or the closures are attributed to another cause (e.g. rainfall-only precautionary closures).

veracity.statement: During the committee of the whole House, Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments aimed at ensuring that there is a mandatory consultation process when giving permits, ensuring that the process requires consultation with mana whenua.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments at the committee of the whole House stage of this bill requiring mandatory consultation with mana whenua before permits are granted.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the committee of the whole House on the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill and the Supplementary Order Papers lodged against it; true if a Te Pāti Māori amendment or SOP proposing mandatory mana whenua consultation on permits was tabled, false if no such amendment appears in the record.

civility.statement: We need to take a look, and Watercare absolutely must take a look at their practices, because the degradation of the water quality due to Watercare’s infrastructure failures is unacceptable and totally objectionable, and it’s happening all around the Hauraki Gulf.
civility.explanation: Blunt condemnation — 'unacceptable and totally objectionable' — but aimed entirely at an organisation's infrastructure and practices. No individual's character, competence or motives are impugned. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism of a record sits at the top.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need to take a look, and Watercare absolutely must take a look at their practices, because the degradation of the water quality due to Watercare’s infrastructure failures is unacceptable and totally objectionable, and it’s happening all around the Hauraki Gulf.
focus.explanation: Names a specific operator, a specific failure (waste-water infrastructure and discharge practice) and its effect on the gulf. This is scrutiny of a concrete performance problem, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: During the committee of the whole House, Te Pāti Māori tabled amendments aimed at ensuring that there is a mandatory consultation process when giving permits, ensuring that the process requires consultation with mana whenua.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the legislative mechanism at issue — a named amendment to the permitting process in the bill before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Te Pāti Māori knows for a fact that whānau who go for a dive or fish to gather kai or kai moana for kai for tangihanga—they will be the ones who will be criminalised and fined, rather than the big corporate commercial fishing companies who exploit our taonga and kai.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that enforcement under the bill's new protection areas will fall on customary/recreational Māori gatherers rather than on commercial fishing operators.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: DOC and Fisheries New Zealand enforcement records for the Hauraki Gulf high protection areas and seafloor protection areas from commencement onward — infringement notices, fines and prosecutions broken down by offender type; true if customary or recreational gatherers make up the clear majority of enforcement actions and commercial operators few or none, false if commercial operators account for a comparable or larger share, or if no enforcement action of this kind occurs.

focus.statement: It's been a rare occurrence under this Government, unfortunately.
focus.explanation: A general swipe at the governing parties' legislative record with no policy, measure or figure named — party framing rather than scrutiny of a specific commitment. Not a Civility issue: no individual is insulted.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We know that we can protect 30 percent of our oceans. We know we can ban bottom trawling.
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy: names two concrete measures (a 30 percent marine protection target and a bottom-trawling ban) rather than talking about the other parties.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There's been a lot of talk about compromise, with this bill, and I do want to challenge that because, quite frankly, it's a load of fishmeal.
civility.explanation: Blunt, colourful dismissal aimed at the *argument* that the bill represents a compromise, not at any member. Robust but lands on the substance; the flourish edges slightly toward sneering at those making the argument, hence just short of the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
specificity.explanation: Carries two percentages and a named mechanism (commercial fishing permitted inside high-protection areas). Checkable against the Act's schedules regardless of whether the figures turn out to be right.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that we can protect 30 percent of our oceans. We know we can ban bottom trawling.
specificity.explanation: A figure and a named mechanism, but no how, no cost and no timeframe — a direction of travel rather than an actionable proposal. Deliberately scored well below Focus: the statement is about policy but carries little detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: Gives a multiplier (nearly tripling) and an absolute area (800 square kilometres of high-protection areas) — quantities someone could check against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When you have an ocean, any part of ocean that is 99 percent exploited, compromise does not look like protecting 6 percent and still allowing commercial fishing in the high-protection areas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three things: that the relevant ocean area is 99 percent open to exploitation, that the bill protects only about 6 percent, and that commercial fishing remains permitted inside the bill's high-protection areas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The final text and schedules of the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Act, plus DOC's published figures for protected area as a share of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park. True if the new protected area is around 6% of the gulf AND the Act as passed permits some commercial fishing method inside high-protection areas; false if commercial fishing is excluded from high-protection areas, or if the protected share is materially different from 6%.

veracity.statement: Everyone can be proud of the huge environmental achievement where we see this bill delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf, nearly tripling the protected area in the Hauraki Gulf, establishing high-protection areas for 800 square kilometres of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill delivers the highest level of marine protection the Hauraki Gulf has ever had, that it nearly triples the protected area, and that the high-protection areas it creates cover 800 square kilometres.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Act's schedules and DOC's published figures for marine protected area in the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park before and after commencement. True if the new high-protection areas total approximately 800 km² and total protected area rises to roughly three times its previous extent; false if the areas are materially smaller or the multiple is materially less than three. The "highest ever level of protection" limb resolves against whether high-protection areas restrict extraction more tightly than the gulf's existing marine reserves, which are no-take.

rigor.statement: As we all agree across this House, it's a very precious area that needs protecting for our future generations, and it does show a commitment by our Government to conservation.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to consensus ("as we all agree across this House") in place of a reason, and the concluding inference — that the bill demonstrates a general governmental commitment to conservation — is a non-sequitur from the premise that the gulf is precious. Nothing is offered to bridge the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I am sad to see some of the amendments to this legislation come in late. They don’t look very rational. They look like they may set us back again in those processes.
civility.explanation: Blunt criticism directed entirely at the amendments and their likely effect; no member is named, impugned or mocked. Under the re-anchored scale, hard criticism of a measure sits at the top.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I had to look up what ring-net fishing was and I was worried about what I saw in terms of catching a particular amount of fish and a particular type of fish and that it might not be a very good move.
specificity.explanation: She is trying to convey substance about a named practice (ring-net fishing) but supplies no quantity, species, threshold or mechanism — 'a particular amount' and 'a particular type' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So we have a situation where we know that the gulf was lined with mussels. We know that they fed the fish in that gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a historical ecological fact: that the Hauraki Gulf seabed formerly carried extensive green-lipped mussel (kūtai) beds, and that those beds supported the gulf's fish populations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed marine ecology and NIWA/MPI historical fisheries literature on the Hauraki Gulf mussel dredge fishery (c.1910–1960): true if the record shows extensive subtidal mussel beds across the gulf that were largely removed by dredging, and evidence that mussel reefs provided habitat/food supporting fish; false if no such extensive beds are documented or if the trophic link is not supported.

veracity.statement: There was already overflow from Warkworth and we didn’t do enough about it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wastewater was overflowing from Warkworth into the Mahurangi Harbour catchment roughly a decade before the statement (she dates her Scotts Landing bach to 'a decade or so ago').
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Watercare and Auckland Council consent-compliance and wastewater overflow records for the Warkworth wastewater treatment plant / network, c.2010–2016: true if recorded overflow or discharge events into the Mahurangi catchment exist in that period, false if the records show no such overflows.

rigor.statement: We’re creating a plan for protecting this area and we’re going to have to put our money where our mouth is, and I don’t know whether I accept that it’s all on Watercare. I think we stretch these services to the point of breaking and then we blame the organisations when things break.
rigor.explanation: A real inference is offered — infrastructure is under-resourced, therefore failures are not solely the operator's fault — and the conclusion tracks the premise. But the premise that the services have been 'stretched to the point of breaking' is asserted rather than supported, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’re creating a plan for protecting this area and we’re going to have to put our money where our mouth is, and I don’t know whether I accept that it’s all on Watercare. I think we stretch these services to the point of breaking and then we blame the organisations when things break.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question: who bears responsibility for wastewater infrastructure feeding into the gulf, and what funding role government should take. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We are going to have an Auckland that is growing. My area is going to grow more than most because a lot of the building is going to happen in those areas.
divination.explanation: Forecasts continued population growth in Auckland, and that the Mount Albert area will grow faster than most other parts of the city because a disproportionate share of new building will occur there.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates and Auckland Council building-consent data by local board / statistical area from 2025 onward: true if Auckland's population rises and the Albert-Eden / Mount Albert area records dwelling and population growth above the Auckland median; false if Auckland's population is flat or falling, or if Mount Albert's growth rate sits at or below the Auckland median.

veracity.statement: Now, those changes actually stipulated in the Minister of Conservation’s very own words, in his own Cabinet paper, that the ring-net fishers, who will still be able to fish in two of the high protection areas, could have fished in other parts, with minimal impact on them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister of Conservation's Cabinet paper on the late amendments states that ring-net fishers permitted to continue fishing in two high protection areas could have fished elsewhere with minimal impact on them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The proactively released Cabinet paper from the Minister of Conservation (Potaka) on the Supplementary Order Paper / amendments to the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill; true if the paper states that the affected ring-net fishers could fish in other areas with minimal or minor impact, false if the paper contains no such assessment or assesses the impact of exclusion as material.

veracity.statement: They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the Government publicly committed to accelerating the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill, and that the bill nonetheless remained on the Order Paper for roughly two years before this stage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill history for the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill (introduction date, first reading, select committee report-back, and dates of subsequent Order Paper stages), plus any Government or ministerial statement undertaking to accelerate or fast-track the bill; true if such an undertaking exists and the elapsed time between report-back/introduction and this debate is about two years, false if no acceleration commitment was made or the elapsed period is materially shorter.

specificity.statement: Now, those changes actually stipulated in the Minister of Conservation’s very own words, in his own Cabinet paper, that the ring-net fishers, who will still be able to fish in two of the high protection areas, could have fished in other parts, with minimal impact on them.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document (the Minister's Cabinet paper), the specific fishing method affected (ring-net), and the number of high protection areas involved (two) — someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But we will repeal those changes because they were the wrong thing to do—and we will continue to say that—so that we can protect the Hauraki Gulf for generations and years to come.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete action with an identifiable target (repealing the late ring-net amendments to this bill), but supplies no timeframe, no mechanism, and no indication of which provisions would be restored.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Despite the Minister’s own Cabinet paper saying that, unfortunately, the Government has chosen to proceed with amendments that will undermine and weaken this bill.
civility.explanation: Sharp criticism of the Government's decision and the amendments themselves; no imputation of bad faith, no attack on the Minister as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Despite the Minister’s own Cabinet paper saying that, unfortunately, the Government has chosen to proceed with amendments that will undermine and weaken this bill.
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks: if the Minister's own advice says the excluded fishers would face minimal impact, then permitting fishing inside the protection areas anyway removes protection without a countervailing justification, so 'weakens the bill' follows. The gap is that 'undermine and weaken' is asserted rather than quantified.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They promised to accelerate it; instead, it has sat here on the Order Paper for two years while eleventh hour changes were made.
focus.explanation: Names a specific commitment (to accelerate the bill) and a specific outcome (two years on the Order Paper). This is scrutiny of a government undertaking, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We will see the health of the ocean improve, and I’m looking forward to having visits in future years where we can actually point to real examples of where we are seeing fishery stocks grow back again in abundance.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that ocean health in the Hauraki Gulf will improve and that fishery stocks will visibly recover following the establishment of the high protection areas created by this bill.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Department of Conservation / Fisheries NZ / Hauraki Gulf Forum State of the Gulf monitoring of the new high protection areas; true if post-implementation surveys report a statistically significant increase in fish biomass or abundance inside the protected areas relative to the pre-protection baseline, false if surveys show no significant increase or a decline.

rigor.statement: We know what that sedimentation does: it stops the plant life in our oceans, and that plant life is so important as nurseries for our juvenile fish and other species, so we know that’s a problem as well.
rigor.explanation: A causal chain is offered — sediment smothers marine plant life, that plant life is nursery habitat for juvenile fish — and the conclusion that sedimentation is a problem follows from it. No fallacy; the only gap is that the mechanism is asserted rather than sourced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The answer was no, we can’t use either of those different tools, and that is, in part, because the Marine Reserves Act 1971 is very much about protection and being very, very focused on that protection only, and these reports had identified that there needed to be more than protection. There needed to be some use, but also a whole lot of different activities as well. And there were difficulties with the Resource Management Act because that would have involved a great number of regional councils working together for one plan, so the idea was: well, we’ll have this bespoke legislation.
rigor.explanation: Two premises are stated (the Marine Reserves Act 1971 permits only protection, while the Sea Change reports required use as well; the RMA route would require multiple regional councils to align on one plan) and the conclusion — bespoke legislation was needed — follows from them. Whether the premises are accurate is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That fisheries plan was looking at excluding from bottom trawling 74 percent to 89 percent of the gulf.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (the 2023 fisheries plan for the gulf), the mechanism (exclusion from bottom trawling) and a numeric range for the area covered. Someone could go and check the consultation document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to remind the House, while the Minister is here, that, as far as I am aware, the Gazette notices to finalise that South-East Marine Protection areas has not yet been undertaken, and, and I hope that it is very soon.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete administrative step (Gazette notices) and a specific programme (the South-East Marine Protection areas), which is checkable, but supplies no date, area or figure and is hedged with 'as far as I am aware'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a major win for the environment, a major win for Auckland, and it’s this Government that’s delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf.
specificity.explanation: Commendatory framing with no figure, mechanism or timeframe — 'major win' twice and a superlative. The only near-checkable element is 'highest ever level of protection', and even that is asserted without the area or instrument behind it.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That fisheries plan was looking at excluding from bottom trawling 74 percent to 89 percent of the gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fisheries plan announced alongside this bill in 2023 proposed excluding bottom trawling from between 74% and 89% of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 Fisheries New Zealand / MPI consultation document on bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf (the Hauraki Gulf Fisheries Plan and trawl-corridor options released with Revitalising the Gulf); true if the consultation options put the area closed to bottom trawling in the 74–89% range, false if the stated options cover a materially different proportion.
