veracity.statement: In May of this year, the current Minister for Oceans and Fisheries shelved those plans, and I want the other side of the House to really think about that, because we’ve heard in a number of these speeches and we see from all these reports that the Hauraki Gulf is protecting bits of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in May 2025 the sitting Minister for Oceans and Fisheries abandoned or set aside the 2023 proposals to exclude bottom trawling from most of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial announcements and Fisheries New Zealand decision documents from May 2025 on the Hauraki Gulf bottom-trawling exclusion proposals; true if the Minister announced in May 2025 that the proposed trawl exclusions would not proceed or were deferred indefinitely, false if the proposals were still live or were decided at another time.

veracity.statement: This has been a decade in the making—in fact, I would argue, at least 25 years in the making, when you reflect back on the landmark legislation that was the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000, which among other things created the Hauraki Gulf Forum, of course affectionately known as the “Guardians of the Gulf”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000 established the Hauraki Gulf Forum. The 'landmark' characterisation is opinion and is not part of the checkable claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park Act 2000 on the NZ legislation register; true if the Act constitutes the Hauraki Gulf Forum, false if the Forum was created by some other instrument or at another date.

veracity.statement: This is a major win for the environment, a major win for Auckland, and it’s this Government that’s delivering the highest ever level of protection for the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the protection this bill delivers for the Hauraki Gulf exceeds any previously in place — i.e. that the marine protection created by the Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill is the largest in the gulf's history.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC and Fisheries New Zealand figures on the area and strength of marine protection in the Hauraki Gulf before and after this bill (existing marine reserves and cable protection areas versus the high protection areas and seafloor protection areas the bill creates); true if the post-bill protected area and protection level exceed any prior configuration, false if earlier instruments protected as much or more.

civility.statement: That work needs to happen, and this Government seems to be washing the hands of those other pieces of work.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested criticism — she accuses the Government of walking away from sediment and bottom-trawling work — but it is aimed at the Government's conduct on the policy, not at any individual's character or competence. Pointed rather than personal.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In November 2020, the High Court ruled that regulations 26 and 27 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 and the associated minimum standards in the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 were unlawful and invalid.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific court decision: that the High Court, in November 2020, declared regulations 26 and 27 of the 2018 Regulations and the associated Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 minimum standards unlawful and invalid.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand High Court judgment in the November 2020 judicial review brought against the Attorney-General over pig welfare regulations (NZ Animal Law Association / SAFE proceedings). True if the judgment, dated in November 2020, declares regulations 26 and 27 of the Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations 2018 and the corresponding minimum standards of the Code of Welfare: Pigs 2018 unlawful and invalid; false if the date, the provisions named, or the finding differ materially.

veracity.statement: The new confinement period, totalling seven days, is a significant reduction from the current 33-day setting, and will be amongst the lowest in the world, with most countries we currently import pork from allowing their use for 33 days.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the wider world: that the new seven-day farrowing-crate limit will be among the lowest anywhere, and that most countries New Zealand currently imports pork from permit farrowing-crate confinement for 33 days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A comparison of farrowing-crate confinement limits in the jurisdictions supplying New Zealand's pork imports (Statistics NZ / MPI import-origin data for pork, cross-referenced against each country's animal welfare rules — e.g. EU Council Directive 2008/120/EC, Australian model codes, US and Canadian codes of practice). True if a majority of those source countries cap farrowing-crate use at approximately 33 days and no material set of jurisdictions has a limit at or below seven days; false if most source countries impose no duration cap at all (rather than a 33-day one), or if several jurisdictions already sit at or below seven days.

veracity.statement: There are fewer than 80 farms, with around 45 indoor piggeries.
veracity.explanation: A count of the New Zealand commercial pig farming sector: fewer than 80 farms in total, of which roughly 45 are indoor piggeries.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Pork / MPI figures on the number of commercial pig farms and indoor piggeries operating in New Zealand as at 2025. True if total commercial pig farms number under 80 and indoor piggeries are approximately 45; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: On some issues, there has been broad consensus—for example, the proposal to limit the use of mating stalls to a maximum of three hours is supported by the NZVA, the SPCA, New Zealand Pork, and MPI.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that four named bodies — the New Zealand Veterinary Association, SPCA, New Zealand Pork and the Ministry for Primary Industries — all supported the specific proposal to cap mating-stall confinement at three hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published submissions and MPI's summary of submissions from the public consultation on the pig welfare regulations. True if each of the NZVA, SPCA, New Zealand Pork and MPI recorded support for a three-hour mating-stall limit; false if any of the four opposed it or sought a materially different limit (for example, if SPCA's submission sought outright prohibition rather than a three-hour cap).

rigor.statement: The current regulations will expire on 18 December this year. The Animal Welfare Act does not permit an extension, and, unfortunately, that entire transition time was used when the industry had no idea what it was precisely supposed to transition towards. Without legislative action, there will be gaps in the law, gaps in particular about the requirements for how piglets and sows are managed during their most vulnerable stages of life.
rigor.explanation: A clean argument from stated premises: the regulations expire on a fixed date, the Act permits no further extension, therefore absent legislation there will be an unfilled regulatory gap. The conclusion follows directly from the premises offered; no fallacy or appeal is relied on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This bill provides a 10-year transition period. This aligns with international norms for changes of this scale and gives farmers time to plan, finance, and implement infrastructure changes.
rigor.explanation: Two supports are offered for the ten-year period: one is a genuine causal reason (farmers need lead time to plan, finance and rebuild infrastructure), the other is a bare appeal to unspecified 'international norms' with no norm identified. The conclusion is partly supported and partly leaning on an appeal to convention.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Firstly, regulation 25, which sets space requirements for grower pigs: this bill increases the k-value used to calculate minimum lying space from 0.03 to 0.034, a 13.3 percent increase.
specificity.explanation: Names the regulation being amended, the exact parameter changed, both the before and after values, and the resulting percentage change. Fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government is backing farmers, restoring balance, and making sure our regulations reflect both compassion and practicality.
specificity.explanation: A string of slogans — 'backing farmers', 'restoring balance', 'compassion and practicality' — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here is checkable or actionable, in contrast to the detailed passages earlier in the same speech.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The new confinement period, totalling seven days, is a significant reduction from the current 33-day setting, and will be amongst the lowest in the world, with most countries we currently import pork from allowing their use for 33 days.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure itself — the confinement period the bill sets, the setting it replaces, and how it compares internationally. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I acknowledge that these proposals will not be welcomed by all those with an interest in animal welfare. The proposed changes in this bill significantly strengthen animal welfare, are pragmatic, reflect available technologies, and have been informed by expert advice on the current science and good practice.
civility.explanation: Farrowing crates are the most contested issue in the speech and animal welfare advocates are the obvious target, yet the disagreement is acknowledged straightforwardly and the case is made on the substance — expert advice, available technology, the science. No bad faith imputed to anyone, no mockery of opponents.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Not all of these changes will take 10 years to implement, and I expect the sector to move faster where it can.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the behaviour of a third party — the pig farming sector — rather than promising the speaker's own action: that farms will adopt at least some of the new requirements ahead of the statutory 19 December 2035 commencement date.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: MPI/NZ Pork compliance and industry reporting on farrowing-crate, nurse-sow and mating-stall practice between 2026 and 2035. True if a substantial share of indoor piggeries is operating within the new seven-day farrowing, 36-hour nurse-sow or three-hour mating-stall limits before 19 December 2035; false if the sector as a whole continues at the pre-existing settings until the requirements take legal effect.

civility.statement: Now that we’ve heard nearly 10 minutes of spin, let’s put some facts on the record today about why this bill is such a shocker and a terrible indictment on this House, on this Government’s lack of commitment to animal welfare.
civility.explanation: Dismissing the preceding speech as "spin" imputes bad faith to the previous speaker rather than engaging its content, though it stops short of a direct personal insult. The criticism of the bill and of the Government itself is legitimate and costs nothing here.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister’s proposals, funnily enough, match the proposals from NZ Pork, who he has just admitted to having targeted consultation with.
civility.explanation: "Funnily enough" insinuates the Minister was captured by an industry lobby rather than arguing it. That is an imputation of bad faith directed at the person, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure — though a mild one, since no direct insult lands.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Here’s my genuine olive branch: I will happily work with the Minister to extend what is currently in law by one or two years so we can get this right, but not reduce standards from what was consulted on in 2022 by such a massive reduction, and definitely not 10 years before we get minimal improvements in animal welfare for pigs—tiny improvements that the Minister is trying to stand up and claim as being a good thing.
civility.explanation: Offers cooperation and confines the attack to the substance of the timetable and the standards. "Tiny improvements the Minister is trying to claim as good" is pointed about the argument, not the man.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He’s called the Minister of animal welfare, but, in fact, this legislation proves he should rightly be called the “Minister of animal cruelty”, because it is undeniable: the evidence from animal welfare experts across the world is that keeping pigs like this is inhumane, fundamentally.
civility.explanation: Renaming a named individual the "Minister of animal cruelty" is a personal epithet, not criticism of the legislation. The substantive point about expert evidence could have been made without attaching the label to the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Farrowing crates are terrible for pigs and their piglets. They cause significant animal welfare issues for sows and piglets. It leads to an increased risk of stillbirth, reduced growth rates, poorer maternal attention, and increased risk of mismothering—which is savaging of a piglet.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific set of welfare harms — stillbirth, growth, maternal attention, mismothering — as consequences of farrowing crate use. Note that the crushing/savaging direction is contested in the literature, which is what the criterion has to settle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed animal welfare literature and NAWAC's published advice on farrowing crate outcomes; true if the cited effects (increased stillbirth risk, reduced growth rates, poorer maternal attention, increased mismothering/savaging) are attributed to farrowing crate confinement in that evidence base, false if the literature finds crates neutral or protective on those specific measures.

veracity.statement: In 2018, the then Minister of Agriculture issued regulations and minimum standards, which allowed farrowing crates. There was a judicial review following that, which found it was a breach of the Animal Welfare Act. Following that, the Labour Government put in place regulations to phase out farrowing crates by 18 December 2025.
veracity.explanation: A three-part chronology: 2018 regulations permitting crates, a judicial review finding a breach of the Act, and a Labour-era phase-out deadline of 18 December 2025. Each element is documentary and independently checkable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2018 Animal Welfare (Care and Procedures) Regulations and the pigs code of welfare; the High Court judgment in the NZ Animal Law Association / SAFE judicial review; and the subsequent regulations setting the farrowing crate phase-out date. True if the 2018 instrument permitted farrowing crates, the court found it inconsistent with the Animal Welfare Act, and the replacement regulations set a phase-out on 18 December 2025; false if any of those three elements is materially wrong, including the date.

veracity.statement: He’s going to increase the minimum spacing requirements by 13.3 percent—the exact proposal from New Zealand Pork. Yet what Labour was proposing was either a 56 percent or 140 percent increase in space; not 13.3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Three linked numerical claims: the bill's space increase is 13.3%, that figure is NZ Pork's own proposal, and the 2022 consultation options were 56% and 140%.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The space allowance figures in the bill/regulations as introduced, NZ Pork's submission to the 2022 MPI consultation, and the options in that consultation document. True if the bill's grower pig space increase is 13.3% and matches NZ Pork's submitted figure, and the 2022 consultation offered 56% and 140% options; false if the percentages differ materially from any of those sources.

veracity.statement: That’s the fundamental thing that this bill does: it delays the legislated action to bring an end to the cruel use of farrowing crates by 10 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill's substantive effect is a ten-year deferral of an already-legislated phase-out. Checkable directly against the bill's transitional provisions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The commencement and transition provisions of the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill as introduced, compared against the 18 December 2025 phase-out date in the existing regulations. True if the bill pushes the end of farrowing crate use out by approximately a decade from that date; false if the delay is materially shorter or if the bill does not defer the phase-out.

veracity.statement: Guess who liked the idea of that! The pork industry. Guess who advised against that! The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, the very advisers to the Minister.
veracity.explanation: Claims the Minister's own statutory advisory committee opposed the settings the bill adopts, while the regulated industry supported them. NAWAC's advice is published, so the criterion resolves on a document.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NAWAC's published advice to the Minister on the pig welfare regulations, and NZ Pork's submissions. True if NAWAC recommended against the 13 percent space increase and/or the ten-year timeline that the bill adopts, and the pork industry supported it; false if NAWAC's advice supported the bill's settings or did not address them.

veracity.statement: It’s utterly unnecessary, because half of New Zealand pig farmers are already doing it like this, letting the pigs live a natural existence where they get to nurse their young and express their natural behaviours.
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim about current industry practice — that roughly half of NZ pig farmers already operate without farrowing crates. Note the ambiguity the resolver must settle: share of farmers is not share of sows, and the larger operations are the crate users.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Pork or MPI data on the proportion of New Zealand commercial pig producers using free farrowing rather than farrowing crates. True if approximately half or more of producers already farrow without crates; false if the share is materially below half.

veracity.statement: I stand to speak on the Animal Welfare (Regulations for Management of Pigs) Amendment Bill and I just want to point out that, actually, we’ve lost a large number of our pork producers over the last three or four decades.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a large long-run decline in the number of New Zealand pork producers over roughly thirty to forty years. Resolvable against registered producer counts.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Pork and MPI/Stats NZ counts of commercial pig producers in New Zealand from the mid-1980s to 2025. True if producer numbers have declined substantially over that period; false if numbers are broadly stable or have risen.

veracity.statement: We, at the moment, in New Zealand import 60 percent of all our pork products from Canada or from the US or from over in Europe.
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim about the imported share of New Zealand pork consumption and its origin countries. The resolver should note the distinction between all pork products and processed pork specifically, where the shares differ.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ trade data and NZ Pork figures on imported pork as a share of New Zealand pork consumption, and the source countries of those imports. True if imports are around 60 percent of pork consumed and are predominantly from Canada, the US and Europe; false if the import share is materially different or the sources are elsewhere.

specificity.statement: Farrowing crates are terrible for pigs and their piglets. They cause significant animal welfare issues for sows and piglets. It leads to an increased risk of stillbirth, reduced growth rates, poorer maternal attention, and increased risk of mismothering—which is savaging of a piglet.
specificity.explanation: Names four distinct, measurable welfare outcomes and defines the term used (mismothering as savaging), rather than asserting generalised cruelty. Falls short of 1.0 because no figures, magnitudes or sources are attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2018, the then Minister of Agriculture issued regulations and minimum standards, which allowed farrowing crates. There was a judicial review following that, which found it was a breach of the Animal Welfare Act. Following that, the Labour Government put in place regulations to phase out farrowing crates by 18 December 2025.
specificity.explanation: Dates, a named statute, a named legal process and an exact phase-out date. Someone could go and pull each document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: He’s going to increase the minimum spacing requirements by 13.3 percent—the exact proposal from New Zealand Pork. Yet what Labour was proposing was either a 56 percent or 140 percent increase in space; not 13.3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three precise percentages tied to a named policy option and a named industry body. Fully checkable against the consultation record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Here’s my genuine olive branch: I will happily work with the Minister to extend what is currently in law by one or two years so we can get this right, but not reduce standards from what was consulted on in 2022 by such a massive reduction, and definitely not 10 years before we get minimal improvements in animal welfare for pigs—tiny improvements that the Minister is trying to stand up and claim as being a good thing.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete counter-proposal with a timeframe (one or two years) and a named benchmark, but no detail on what standards would apply during the extension.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This transition will not occur overnight; instead it will be managed over a defined period, providing certainty, enabling farmers to secure resources and support the need for compliance.
specificity.explanation: The whole sentence is about a transition period without naming its length, its milestones, or what compliance requires — "a defined period" is precisely the detail withheld. The surrounding speech supplies no figures or dates either, so there is nothing nearby to credit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There needs to be a balance, and it needs to be realistic.
specificity.explanation: A bare directional statement about how the regulation should be pitched, with no indication of what is being balanced against what, or where the line should fall. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We, at the moment, in New Zealand import 60 percent of all our pork products from Canada or from the US or from over in Europe.
specificity.explanation: A figure and named source countries, offered in support of the regulatory-consistency argument. Checkable against trade statistics; loses a little for not distinguishing fresh from processed pork.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He’s going to increase the minimum spacing requirements by 13.3 percent—the exact proposal from New Zealand Pork. Yet what Labour was proposing was either a 56 percent or 140 percent increase in space; not 13.3 percent.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — the space requirement, its size, and its provenance. Comparing it to the prior consultation options is scrutiny of a specific policy figure, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here’s my genuine olive branch: I will happily work with the Minister to extend what is currently in law by one or two years so we can get this right, but not reduce standards from what was consulted on in 2022 by such a massive reduction, and definitely not 10 years before we get minimal improvements in animal welfare for pigs—tiny improvements that the Minister is trying to stand up and claim as being a good thing.
focus.explanation: Names an alternative mechanism (a one- to two-year extension of the existing law), the benchmark it should hold to (the 2022 consultation standards), and the timeframe objected to. Squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That’s the fundamental thing that this bill does: it delays the legislated action to bring an end to the cruel use of farrowing crates by 10 years.
focus.explanation: States what the measure before the House actually does and over what period. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, if anyone was in any doubt as to the essential animal cruelty of this Government, this bill proves the point.
focus.explanation: Anchored to a real bill, but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of the Government as a whole rather than of the measure. The policy serves as evidence for a claim about the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The Animal Law Association, who won a court case, and given that the Minister’s allowing this to run till February—we’ve got between December and February for another court case.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that fresh litigation will be brought in the gap between the 18 December 2025 expiry and the February date, on the strength of the same body having previously won a judicial review. The speaker supplies the window herself, so the resolve-by date follows directly.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand court records and public announcements from the NZ Animal Law Association or comparable animal welfare litigants. True if judicial review or other proceedings challenging the pig welfare regulations or the resulting legal gap are filed between 18 December 2025 and 28 February 2026; false if no such proceedings are filed in that window.

rigor.statement: Now, if anyone was in any doubt as to the essential animal cruelty of this Government, this bill proves the point.
rigor.explanation: A hasty generalisation bordering on circularity: one bill is offered as proof of a settled character trait ("essential animal cruelty") across a whole government, with the conclusion assumed in how the premise is framed. Nothing connects this single measure to the general claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He’s called the Minister of animal welfare, but, in fact, this legislation proves he should rightly be called the “Minister of animal cruelty”, because it is undeniable: the evidence from animal welfare experts across the world is that keeping pigs like this is inhumane, fundamentally.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered — international expert evidence that the confinement is inhumane — and the step from that to opposing the bill would hold. But the actual conclusion drawn is about what the Minister should be called, which the premise does not establish; "it is undeniable" also asserts consensus in place of showing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s utterly unnecessary, because half of New Zealand pig farmers are already doing it like this, letting the pigs live a natural existence where they get to nurse their young and express their natural behaviours.
rigor.explanation: The inference from "half already do it" to "a ten-year transition is unnecessary" is a real argument supported by a real premise, but there is a gap: existing adopters say nothing about the conversion cost facing the remaining half, which is the objection being answered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As we’ve seen, across the floor, around the farrowing crates, yes, that is an issue, but it’s also an issue if they’re not used and young piglets are squashed. This is the other thing: since we aren’t experts, we actually need to go delicately through this in select committee to actually understand what the right balance is going forward.
rigor.explanation: Sets out a genuine trade-off — confinement harms against piglet crushing risk — and concludes that non-experts should take evidence rather than settle it now, which follows from the premise. It leans on an appeal to expertise without engaging the evidence already tabled by the previous speakers, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just briefly to go back through history, the Animal Welfare Act was passed in 1999 by a visionary Government, a National Government actually, that saw the importance of animal welfare moving forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Animal Welfare Act was enacted in 1999 under a National-led Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Legislation record for the Animal Welfare Act 1999 (date of Royal assent) and the party composition of the government of the day; true if the Act was passed in 1999 while a National-led government held office, false if the year or the governing party differs.

veracity.statement: The National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee, which is an independent committee, came up with a code of practice, a code of welfare, for pigs in 2010, again under a National-led Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NAWAC issued a code of welfare for pigs in 2010, under a National-led government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The MPI register of codes of welfare issued under the Animal Welfare Act 1999; true if a Code of Welfare (Pigs) was issued in 2010 on NAWAC's recommendation while National led the government, false if the year or the issuing body differs.

veracity.statement: Of course, as has been said before, about 60 percent of the pork we consume comes from offshore.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 60 percent of pork consumed in New Zealand is imported.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ pork import volumes set against domestic pig-meat production for the relevant year (or NZ Pork's published market-share figures); true if imports are around 60% of consumption, false if materially different (e.g. below 50% or above 70%).

veracity.statement: Well, of course, if you are changing regulations—and I know the other side of the House will say, “Well, Parliament is sovereign, and we can use Parliament’s resources to do this.”—what happens is that there is no recourse to the courts for judicial review for those regulations, for that secondary legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that once regulatory content is enacted in primary legislation, it is no longer amenable to judicial review as secondary legislation would be.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand administrative law authority on the reviewability of primary versus secondary legislation (e.g. the Legislation Act 2019 and case law on ultra vires challenges to regulations); true if provisions enacted in an Act are not subject to judicial review on grounds available against regulations, false if such review remains available.

veracity.statement: But we’ve also heard that the SPCA—not known, you know, to be a hugely radical group—has not been consulted by this Minister.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the SPCA has not been consulted by the Minister for Animal Welfare on this matter.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: SPCA New Zealand's own statements or select committee submissions, and MPI's consultation record for the Bill and the pig welfare regulations; true if the SPCA confirms it was not consulted by the Minister, false if a consultation meeting or written consultation with the SPCA is on record.

veracity.statement: In fact, these new requirements in the bill will be among the highest animal welfare standards in the world.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the pig welfare requirements set by this bill rank among the strictest internationally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill's mating stall and farrowing crate requirements and their commencement dates, compared against comparable jurisdictions (EU Council Directive 2008/120/EC, the UK sow stall ban, and Swedish/Swiss farrowing rules); true if New Zealand's requirements are at least as strict and take effect no later, false if the permitted confinement periods or the timeline are more permissive than those jurisdictions.

specificity.statement: Of course, as has been said before, about 60 percent of the pork we consume comes from offshore.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete proportion for imported pork consumption that a reader could go and check against trade and consumption data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In New Zealand, we have extremely high animal welfare standards.
specificity.explanation: A generic assertion of quality with no figure, mechanism, comparison or named standard — nothing a listener could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The bizarre contradiction is that the pork industry has been lobbying the Government to say, “Don’t allow the importation of pork from lower-standard countries because we have higher standards.” Well, we’re moving to truly higher standards. This is going to dumb it down.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine inconsistency between the industry's import-standards argument and its opposition to raising domestic standards; the conclusion tracks the two positions set out, though the final step rests on the asserted premise that the bill lowers standards rather than on evidence offered here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I put it to the House and the Minister that this is not an accident; it is a cynical use of the parliamentary process to stop citizens who are concerned about legislation not being followed.
rigor.explanation: The mechanism she sets out (regulations changed by primary legislation remove judicial review) supports the effect, but nothing offered supports the leap from effect to deliberate intent; the conclusion about motive outruns the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Proposing this legislation might be giving them what they’re asking for, but it’s denying the reality of the direction of travel internationally.
focus.explanation: Directed at the named bill and its effect on the industry's international position; no party framing or tribal content.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It might be a short-term relief, but they’re still going to have to make the changes.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the pork industry will end up having to phase out farrowing crates and mating stalls regardless of the relief this bill provides.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand pig welfare regulation, or binding processor/major-retailer sourcing requirements, as at the resolve-by date; true if a phase-out of mating stalls and farrowing crates is in force or contractually required across most of the industry, false if the practices remain permitted and in widespread use with no such requirement.

civility.statement: I put it to the House and the Minister that this is not an accident; it is a cynical use of the parliamentary process to stop citizens who are concerned about legislation not being followed.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — a deliberate, cynical motive — to the Minister personally, rather than confining the criticism to the effect of the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The committee received 210 written submissions, a relatively modest number in comparison to when Te Pūkenga was set up—I believe, from memory, there were about 2,000 submissions back then.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two counts: 210 written submissions to the Education and Workforce Committee on this bill, and roughly 2,000 written submissions on the bill that established Te Pūkenga (the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill 2019).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill for the number of written submissions received, and the committee record for the 2019 vocational education reform bill for its submission count. True if the first is 210 and the second is of the order of 2,000; false if either is materially different (e.g. the earlier bill drew a few hundred, or many thousands).

veracity.statement: Without exception, they have all been pleased and relieved that they are getting their polytechnics back in their regions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every senior management team and community leader she met across the 10 institutes of technology and polytechnics standing up on 1 January 2026 was pleased and relieved at the disestablishment of Te Pūkenga — a universal claim ('without exception').
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, select committee submissions and media comment from the councils, chief executives and named community leaders of the 10 ITPs due to stand alone from 1 January 2026. True if none of them expressed opposition or reluctance about their institution returning to regional standalone status; false if any of those bodies or leaders publicly raised objections, or said the change left them financially unviable.

specificity.statement: They will be statutory standard-setting bodies with majority of industry governance: six of the eight on the board will be from industry, ensuring that vocational education and training remains responsive to both new and emerging industry developments, as well as current industry needs.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory function (standard setting) and gives a concrete governance composition — six of eight board members drawn from industry. Checkable against the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If there has been one thing that has come out of this adversity of Te Pūkenga, the one good thing has been that local communities have realised how important vocational education and training is, how important industry training is, and how important polytechnics are to their regions.
specificity.explanation: Beyond naming Te Pūkenga, the content is a string of generic assertions that things are 'important'. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or evidence of the claimed change in community attitudes.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They will be statutory standard-setting bodies with majority of industry governance: six of the eight on the board will be from industry, ensuring that vocational education and training remains responsive to both new and emerging industry developments, as well as current industry needs.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (that the system will remain responsive to current and emerging industry needs) is drawn from board composition alone; no mechanism is offered connecting a governance majority to responsiveness. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded, though the premise plainly bears on the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If there has been one thing that has come out of this adversity of Te Pūkenga, the one good thing has been that local communities have realised how important vocational education and training is, how important industry training is, and how important polytechnics are to their regions.
civility.explanation: Characterises the previous government's flagship reform as 'adversity' — a hard judgement on a contested policy — while attacking no individual. She could have turned this on the ministers who created Te Pūkenga and did not.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If there has been one thing that has come out of this adversity of Te Pūkenga, the one good thing has been that local communities have realised how important vocational education and training is, how important industry training is, and how important polytechnics are to their regions.
focus.explanation: Criticism is aimed at a named policy (Te Pūkenga) and its regional consequences rather than at the opposing party's character or record in general, so it stays on the policy question even while making a partisan point.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Tonight, in her speech, Minister Simmonds played down the number of submissions made to the Education and Workforce Committee, but she avoided sharing with this House what, in fact, they said.
civility.explanation: "Played down" and "avoided sharing" impute deliberate concealment to the Minister rather than engaging her argument. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes bad faith to the person, which is a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m unsure if she even listened to the recommendations in that report.
civility.explanation: An insinuation that the Minister did not bother to read or consider the select committee's recommendations. Framed as doubt rather than accusation, but it targets the person's conduct and attentiveness rather than the substance of the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The cuts to jobs, programmes, and campuses as a result of these reforms hurt our young people, our regions, and our economy.
civility.explanation: A harsh judgement, but entirely about the reforms and their consequences. No person is criticised, no bad faith imputed. This is the expected standard: fierce criticism of a policy is fully civil.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Only 11 percent of submitters supported this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific proportion — 11% — of submitters to the select committee expressed support for the bill. Note the speaker later restates it as 11% who "unconditionally backed" the reforms, so the resolver should check which measure the departmental report supports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's departmental report on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, which tabulates submitter positions; true if approximately 11% of submitters are recorded as supporting the bill, false if the recorded proportion is materially different (e.g. a different denominator or a substantially higher share of supportive submissions).

veracity.statement: The Minister repeatedly says that Te Pūkenga was not financially viable, despite it returning a $16.7 million surplus last year, as it was intended to do.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga returned a $16.7 million surplus in the most recent reported financial year. The claim about what the Minister repeatedly says is secondary; the checkable assertion is the surplus figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's audited annual report for the 2024 financial year; true if it records a net surplus of approximately $16.7 million, false if it records a deficit or a materially different surplus figure.

veracity.statement: We’ve already lost 19,000 construction workers, and last year, 3,700 fewer individuals enrolled in building apprenticeships and there were 9,000 overall fewer apprentice completions across all fields year on year under this National Government.
veracity.explanation: A compound claim of three separate quantities: construction workforce losses, a fall in building apprenticeship enrolments, and a fall in total apprentice completions, all attributed to the period of the current government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ employment data for the construction industry over the period since late 2023, plus Tertiary Education Commission / Ministry of Education industry training statistics on building apprenticeship enrolments and total apprenticeship completions year on year; true if all three figures (≈19,000 construction jobs lost, ≈3,700 fewer building apprenticeship enrolments, ≈9,000 fewer completions) are borne out within rounding, false if any is materially overstated or measured over a different period.

veracity.statement: We are losing specialist programmes that provide key skills for our economy—for example, the timber machining apprenticeship at Toi Ohomai in Rotorua, the only programme of its kind in the Southern Hemisphere, is set to be cut.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions bundled together: that the Toi Ohomai timber machining apprenticeship is set to be cut, and the superlative that it is the only such programme in the Southern Hemisphere. The superlative is the part most at risk of overstatement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Toi Ohomai's published programme review/disestablishment decisions for 2025, plus a check of Australian and other Southern Hemisphere providers for an equivalent timber machining apprenticeship; true if the programme is confirmed for cutting AND no comparable programme exists elsewhere in the Southern Hemisphere, false if the programme is being retained or if an equivalent qualification is offered by another Southern Hemisphere provider.

veracity.statement: This legislation has now removed the requirement for industry skills boards to act in a matter that contributes to an education system that honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific textual change made to the bill after select committee: the deletion of a Te Tiriti o Waitangi / Māori-Crown relations duty applying to industry skills boards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the bill as reported back from the Education and Workforce Committee against the bill as introduced; true if a clause requiring industry skills boards to contribute to an education system honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supporting Māori-Crown relations was present and has been deleted, false if no such requirement was removed.

rigor.statement: The Minister repeatedly says that Te Pūkenga was not financially viable, despite it returning a $16.7 million surplus last year, as it was intended to do.
rigor.explanation: Offers a concrete counter-example against the Minister's viability claim, and a surplus is genuinely relevant evidence about viability. Held back from the top because a single year's surplus does not by itself refute a claim about long-term financial viability — the inference has a real gap between the evidence and the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Consultants have indicated that $190 million may be needed to restart the 16 polytechnics, and yet there’s only a minimum of $177 million in Government funding set aside to support this. This legislation and these reforms do not set our polytechnics up for success. It puts them at greater risk and does not even provide them with enough funding to undertake the Government’s reforms.
rigor.explanation: A stated shortfall ($190m needed against $177m allocated) is offered as the reason the reforms are underfunded, and the conclusion tracks the premise. Docked because the speaker himself describes $177 million as a "minimum", which weakens the arithmetic gap the conclusion rests on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: ISBs don’t have the powers industry has asked for and they don’t have the funding that they need under this legislation—$30 million is not enough to do the same job that workforce development councils were doing for $60 million. That is half the funding and that is under-serving our workforce, our industry, and our communities.
rigor.explanation: The funding comparison ($30m against $60m) supports the conclusion of under-resourcing, but the inference assumes the industry skills boards are being asked to do exactly "the same job" as the workforce development councils — the very thing the reform disputes. A real point leaning on an unexamined premise about equivalent scope.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Consultants have indicated that $190 million may be needed to restart the 16 polytechnics, and yet there’s only a minimum of $177 million in Government funding set aside to support this. This legislation and these reforms do not set our polytechnics up for success. It puts them at greater risk and does not even provide them with enough funding to undertake the Government’s reforms.
specificity.explanation: Two named dollar figures, a named number of institutions, and an identified source (consultants) — someone could go and check the shortfall. Short of the top because neither the consultants nor the funding line is named precisely.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At the end of last year, it was indicated that the sector would lose up to 900 fulltime-equivalents, close 550 programmes, and close approximately 30 delivery sites.
specificity.explanation: Three concrete, countable quantities (900 FTEs, 550 programmes, 30 delivery sites) attached to a timeframe. Highly checkable and actionable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m hearing every week from the sector that these cuts and closures are only going to increase under this reform.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that job cuts, programme cuts and campus closures across the vocational sector will increase after the reform takes effect, rather than plateau or reverse.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Programme closure, campus closure and redundancy announcements from the polytechnics named in the debate (NorthTec, Toi Ohomai, Otago Polytechnic, WelTec, Wintec, Whitireia and others) through the first year of the new system; true if the count of announced job losses, programme closures or site closures during 2026 exceeds the 2025 baseline cited in this speech, false if it falls at or below that baseline.

focus.statement: This legislation has now removed the requirement for industry skills boards to act in a matter that contributes to an education system that honours Te Tiriti o Waitangi and supports Māori-Crown relations.
focus.explanation: Names a specific statutory provision and a specific change made to it. This is scrutiny of the legislative text itself, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we do see in the changes post select committee is a further reduction, though, of Māori representation, and some over the other side will be happy about this. This is what they voted for.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — a named change reducing Māori representation after select committee — but half the weight of the statement is a jab about what members opposite would be pleased by and what they voted for, which carries no policy content of its own.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the things that this bill has failed to do is it has failed to guarantee any kind of staff or student representation on the governing councils of the newly established institutes of technology and polytechnic (ITP) councils.
focus.explanation: Names a specific defect in a specific bill — the absence of a guaranteed staff/student representation provision on ITP governing councils. Entirely policy content, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Instead of fixing that issue, what the previous Government—the Labour Government—did was they decided to come up with this idea of a mega-merger. That was a complete distraction from the actual issues that needed to be dealt with.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy — the Te Pūkenga mega-merger — and criticises it against a stated objective, which is legitimate scrutiny. Marked down because 'a complete distraction' shifts the weight onto the previous Government's motives rather than the merger's effects.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, the Treasury analysis of this reform said that the newly established ITPs could expect financials that were the same, if not worse, than before Te Pūkenga was established.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury's analysis of the vocational education reform forecast that the disaggregated ITPs would face financial positions no better, and possibly worse, than the pre-Te Pūkenga polytechnics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treasury report / Regulatory Impact Statement on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if it states the new ITPs' expected financial position is the same or worse than pre-Te Pūkenga, false if it forecasts improved financials or makes no such comparison.

veracity.statement: There were 855 job losses last year and 1,000 are expected in this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 855 job losses across the ITP sector in 2024 and a further 1,000 expected during 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga / TEC workforce and restructuring reporting for 2024 and 2025, or the Tertiary Education Union's tally of ITP redundancies; true if 2024 losses are approximately 855, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: We do know that the Government has withdrawn from proposals to close the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses, thanks to the efforts made by communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that proposals to close the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses were formally dropped.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Toi Ohomai / NZIST change proposal documents and public announcements about the Tokoroa and Taupō campuses; true if the closure proposals were withdrawn before 7 October 2025, false if they remained live or proceeded.

veracity.statement: This Government has talked about how they want to reduce the amount of people—particularly young people—going on to be beneficiaries, but the free TAFE programme in Australia shows that when someone has gone through the free TAFE programme, they’re 37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit, and over half of those people who have gone through the free TAFE programme have actually seen their incomes increase.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two evaluation findings about Australia's Free TAFE programme: a 37 percent reduction in the likelihood of ending up on a benefit, and income increases for over half of participants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Australian Government (DEWR) Free TAFE evaluation and outcome reporting; true if it reports approximately a 37 percent lower rate of income-support receipt for Free TAFE completers and income increases for more than 50 percent of them, false if the published figures differ materially or no such finding exists.

veracity.statement: Look, the Minister talks about how this is an industry-centred reform, but, actually, of the around 38 industry submitters, only eight of them gave their full support to the changes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of roughly 38 industry submitters on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, only eight fully supported the changes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The submissions published on the Education and Workforce Committee's page for the Bill; true if approximately 38 submissions came from industry bodies/employers and about eight expressed full support, false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: But what I would say is that we know that New Zealand’s vocational education and training system has been in decline for some years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a multi-year decline in New Zealand's vocational education and training system prior to the reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC provider-based vocational enrolment, completion and financial-performance data for ITPs over the years preceding 2020; true if enrolments/completions and ITP financial results show a sustained decline, false if they were flat or rising.

specificity.statement: There were 855 job losses last year and 1,000 are expected in this year.
specificity.explanation: Two exact headcount figures tied to named years — directly checkable against sector workforce reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has talked about how they want to reduce the amount of people—particularly young people—going on to be beneficiaries, but the free TAFE programme in Australia shows that when someone has gone through the free TAFE programme, they’re 37 percent less likely to end up on the benefit, and over half of those people who have gone through the free TAFE programme have actually seen their incomes increase.
specificity.explanation: A named programme with two quantified outcome claims (37 percent lower benefit likelihood; over half seeing income increases) — concrete enough to look up and act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Look, the Minister talks about how this is an industry-centred reform, but, actually, of the around 38 industry submitters, only eight of them gave their full support to the changes.
specificity.explanation: Gives a submitter count and a support count, both drawn from a named process — precise and checkable, though the classification of 'industry submitter' is left undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would like to highlight two changes which ACT managed to get in this legislation: one is in new section 318, inserted by clause 22, which is about “Matters to be considered when appointing members of polytechnic’s council”.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact provision (new section 318) and the clause inserting it (clause 22), with its heading — anyone could open the bill and check the change.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Contrary to the Minister for Vocational Education’s rhetoric about how they’re overstaffed, for a sector that had only about 8,000 staff, losing about one-seventh of the staff is absolutely devastating to the capacity of these regions, and also the capacity of these institutions to remain as ongoing and viable concerns.
rigor.explanation: A stated base (about 8,000 staff) and a stated loss (about one-seventh) are offered, and the conclusion about lost institutional capacity follows from them. The arithmetic tracks the earlier figures; the inferential gap is only that 'devastating' is a judgement rather than a demonstrated effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But those members want to focus on gender. Those members want to focus on those people’s ethnicity. I think by just focusing on gender and ethnicity, we are not going to deliver what polytechs should be delivering. Because that is just empty virtue signalling, and we don’t believe in that.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy plus strawman: the removed subclauses listed gender and ethnicity among appointment considerations, not instead of merit, yet the argument is built on the premise that opposing members want to focus 'just' on those and abandon ability. The conclusion follows only from the misstated version of the position.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the offer that I’m going to make to the Minister—which I’m not going to make through some botched hit job through the media, like the Prime Minister did with the energy reform hit job, and the more successful hit job that Erica Stanford did—is that we do want to work with the Government on an actual cross-party tertiary strategy that will actually endure a change of Government, because when the election happens next year and, God willing, I end up as the tertiary education Minister, I don’t want to have to rip up what’s already been done before.
civility.explanation: The substantive offer is constructive, but it is framed by characterising named individuals — the Prime Minister and Erica Stanford — as having run 'hit jobs' through the media, one of them 'botched'. That imputes bad faith and disparages competence rather than engaging what they did.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But those members want to focus on gender. Those members want to focus on those people’s ethnicity. I think by just focusing on gender and ethnicity, we are not going to deliver what polytechs should be delivering. Because that is just empty virtue signalling, and we don’t believe in that.
civility.explanation: 'Empty virtue signalling' imputes insincere motive to the members opposite rather than engaging the drafting they supported. Short of a direct insult, but it targets their good faith, not their argument.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m not able to discuss it because it’s still in the middle of a media pitch, but when it does come out, it will reveal that, actually, this thing is not that financially viable.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that further, as-yet-unreleased Treasury advice on the vocational education reform will become public and will show the new ITP arrangement is not financially viable.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Subsequent Treasury advice on the vocational education reform released publicly (proactive release, OIA, or media reporting); true if released material concludes or shows the new ITPs are not financially viable, false if no such advice is released by the resolve-by date or if the released advice does not support that conclusion.

civility.statement: Now, Labour loved centralisation. I think that’s unarguable. I mean, we had that in health, we had that in the water sector, and we had that in education at the very least.
civility.explanation: A contested criticism of an opposing party's governing approach, aimed entirely at the policy pattern (health, water, education) and at no individual. Civil by the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, Labour loved centralisation. I think that’s unarguable. I mean, we had that in health, we had that in the water sector, and we had that in education at the very least.
focus.explanation: A generalisation about the other party's character ("Labour loved centralisation") but grounded in three named sectors where the restructuring actually happened, so it is party framing carrying a real policy point rather than pure tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New section 367, inserted by clause 23, sets out a range of important functions which, actually, if you look at them, are basically the same as the WDCs, but it also takes over the actual training process.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the bill before the House — a named clause and the function it transfers. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I hope, as we go through this process, that we actually allow those organisations not to have to go through the bureaucratic ISB process but can actually go and be established in their own right, straight away. That would be a much more efficient, much more effective way of doing things.
focus.explanation: A concrete implementation point about how the bill's transition provisions should apply to specific training organisations. Squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, the Green Party will probably say, “Well, just tax the living daylights out of everybody.” That’s a guaranteed way of making sure we’ll actually all end up poorer.
focus.explanation: Raised in a passage about sector funding, but the statement itself is about what the other party would supposedly say rather than any named tax, rate or spending measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We had a question today about why some people are leaving our country. Well, in some cases, it’s because we are driving them out of the country. That, I put on the previous Government—and we’re trying to fix that problem.
focus.explanation: Blame is placed on the previous government as a whole; no specific policy, decision or figure is named that would make this accountability rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Anyway, Labour established Te Pūkenga, as we know, by merging 16 polytechs and nine workplace training providers, and that only really started operating at the beginning of 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three things: that the previous Labour government created Te Pūkenga, that it was formed by merging 16 polytechnics and nine workplace training providers (industry training organisations), and that the merged body only began operating at the start of 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's establishing legislation (Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Act 2020), the Tertiary Education Commission record, and Te Pūkenga annual reports. True if 16 institutes of technology/polytechnics and nine industry training organisations were merged into it and the merged entity began operating as a single organisation at the beginning of 2023; false if either count differs or the operating start date is materially different.

specificity.statement: Anyway, Labour established Te Pūkenga, as we know, by merging 16 polytechs and nine workplace training providers, and that only really started operating at the beginning of 2023.
specificity.explanation: Carries two counts, a named institution and a start date — an assertion a listener could go and check without further information.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: New section 367, inserted by clause 23, sets out a range of important functions which, actually, if you look at them, are basically the same as the WDCs, but it also takes over the actual training process.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and inserted section and states what it does; loses a little for "basically the same", which is not operationalised.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to lift productivity. That’s been a long-term blight on our country. We need to stop getting in our own way. We need to reform our resource management and other bureaucratic processes.
specificity.explanation: A string of general imperatives with no figures, targets or timeframes. "Resource management" is the only named area, and even that comes with no indication of what reform is meant; "stop getting in our own way" commits to nothing.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I hope, as we go through this process, that we actually allow those organisations not to have to go through the bureaucratic ISB process but can actually go and be established in their own right, straight away. That would be a much more efficient, much more effective way of doing things.
rigor.explanation: The premise offered in the surrounding sentences — that some training organisations are ready now and would otherwise be moved into an ISB and out again within two years — does support avoiding the intermediate step. But the efficiency conclusion is asserted rather than shown; no cost or timeline is given for either route.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, the Green Party will probably say, “Well, just tax the living daylights out of everybody.” That’s a guaranteed way of making sure we’ll actually all end up poorer.
rigor.explanation: A strawman: he invents the opposing party's position in caricature and then rebuts the caricature. The rebuttal itself is a bare assertion — "guaranteed" to make everyone poorer, with no mechanism, threshold or evidence connecting taxation to the outcome.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We had a question today about why some people are leaving our country. Well, in some cases, it’s because we are driving them out of the country. That, I put on the previous Government—and we’re trying to fix that problem.
rigor.explanation: A causal attribution with nothing offered to support it: emigration is asserted to be caused by domestic conditions, and responsibility is assigned to the previous government, with no data, mechanism or comparison given. The conclusion does not follow from anything stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We need to take a whole-of-Government approach because, otherwise, what will happen is the drop-out rates, the inability to participate rates in those far-flung areas, will be much, much higher.
rigor.explanation: The premise set out just before — that uniform per-student funding does not suit sparsely served regions — is a genuine reason, so this is not a non-sequitur. But the step from that to "whole-of-Government approach" as the remedy is a gap: nothing links the proposed approach to lower drop-out rates.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It seems to be flip-flopping that’s based on vanity, and it’s vindictive and it’s full of lazy terms.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's motives — vanity, vindictiveness, laziness. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing here to check or engage with. This is the party-directed framing Focus exists to catch; note that Civility is untouched because no individual is insulted.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My point here is that we have heard over and over from the other side of the House that this is somehow all about local control. But I ask you, for Otago Polytechnic, how is it possibly about local control when it is not that anchor polytech?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill — the federation structure, the anchor polytechnic role, and a named institution. Testing a government's stated rationale against the text of its own clauses is exactly the accountability work that scores at the top of this scale.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wonder if that is just because of their general dark approach on Dunedin, whereby the hospital where they promised to build a bigger and better one than what Labour promised; they just put it on hold for over a year.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point buried here — a named commitment on the Dunedin hospital and a claimed delay — but the weight of the sentence is the 'general dark approach on Dunedin' framing, which is about the other side's disposition rather than about any measure.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now he’s informing the House that, in fact, he didn’t not say that they weren’t ideological. Work that sentence out, Hansard.
civility.explanation: Mockery of another member's self-correction, played to the gallery via the aside to Hansard. It targets the tangle of Andy Foster's denial rather than his character or competence, so it sits between 'pointed and robust' and the 0.5 mockery band rather than at a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is very interesting that you would put someone who has such strong desires to break up polytechs and to bring back SIT at any cost—that it is going to be difficult for that Minister to look at the evidence and make good decisions.
civility.explanation: Moves from the policy to the Minister's capacity to judge honestly, and 'at any cost' imputes a motive that overrides evidence. It is short of a direct insult and the speaker had just conceded 'good on her for being full of gusto', but attributing a personal interest that prevents good decisions lands on the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is a shameful bill and it’s terrible for Dunedin.
civility.explanation: The peroration of a heated speech, and the condemnation lands entirely on the bill and its regional effect. No member's character, competence or motive is touched. Harsh language about a measure is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So we know that the Labour Government had a problem, and it was before I was in Parliament, that there were many polytechs that were losing a lot of money, so the polytechs were put together in an effort to save the polytechs in the regions that were not making money and that were losing money.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts about the past: that many polytechnics were running significant losses before the merger, and that financial rescue of loss-making regional polytechnics was the reason they were amalgamated under the previous Labour government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission annual financial performance reports for the institutes of technology and polytechnics in the years preceding the 2020 Te Pūkenga merger, plus the Reform of Vocational Education Cabinet papers and regulatory impact statement. True if a substantial number of ITPs were recording operating deficits and if the stated rationale for the merger included their financial viability; false if most ITPs were in surplus or if the official rationale did not rest on financial distress.

veracity.statement: I know that because I recall her huge opposition to the mergers of the polytechs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the current Minister publicly and strongly opposed the amalgamation of polytechnics before entering Parliament. This is a claim about the past conduct of a named person, asserted by the speaker rather than relayed from someone else.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of Penny Simmonds' statements while chief executive of the Southern Institute of Technology and as a National MP — submissions on the Reform of Vocational Education, media interviews, and Hansard speeches from 2019 onward. True if there is documented, repeated public opposition by her to the polytechnic mergers; false if her recorded position was neutral or supportive.

veracity.statement: So it seems that this Government is down on Dunedin, it is down on jobs, and we’ve had reports in the Otago Daily Times that the polytech might have to decrease their land area by 60 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a specific figure — a possible 60 percent reduction in Otago Polytechnic's land area — has been reported in a named newspaper. What is checkable is whether the reporting says that, not whether the reduction will occur.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Daily Times reporting from 2025 on Otago Polytechnic's property footprint under the vocational education reforms. True if the ODT reported a prospective reduction in the polytechnic's land or campus area of around 60 percent; false if no such reporting exists or if the reported figure is materially different.

rigor.statement: This is very interesting that you would put someone who has such strong desires to break up polytechs and to bring back SIT at any cost—that it is going to be difficult for that Minister to look at the evidence and make good decisions.
rigor.explanation: A circumstantial ad hominem, but not a bare one: prior leadership of an affected institution and a recorded position against the merger is a genuine conflict-of-interest premise. The gap is that no evidence is offered that any specific decision actually departed from the evidence — the conclusion about the Minister's judgement is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My point here is that we have heard over and over from the other side of the House that this is somehow all about local control. But I ask you, for Otago Polytechnic, how is it possibly about local control when it is not that anchor polytech?
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises the speaker has just laid out from the bill: new sections 323 and 337 put a federation polytechnic under an anchor polytechnic that provides the services the Federation Committee requires, and Otago is a federation member rather than the anchor. If so, the 'local control' framing does not hold for Otago. Some slack remains because the anchor designation is asserted from outside the bill ('I'm told').
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I wonder if that is just because of their general dark approach on Dunedin, whereby the hospital where they promised to build a bigger and better one than what Labour promised; they just put it on hold for over a year.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the federation structure in the bill is explained by an imputed animus toward a city, evidenced only by an unrelated decision on a hospital build. Nothing connects the hospital timeline to the drafting of the polytechnic provisions, so the inference rests on motive attribution rather than on anything offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So it seems that this Government is down on Dunedin, it is down on jobs, and we’ve had reports in the Otago Daily Times that the polytech might have to decrease their land area by 60 percent.
specificity.explanation: Opens on two content-free clauses ('down on Dunedin', 'down on jobs') but closes with a named source, a named institution and a percentage figure that someone could go and check. The checkable half carries it above the midpoint without reaching the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is returning autonomy to the regions, as has been described, but also setting up a very useful system to allow for federation, which will keep long-term sustainability, it will enable cost-effective delivery, and it will be a very useful system.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — autonomy, sustainability, cost-effectiveness, 'a very useful system' twice — with no figures, no timeframes, no named institutions and no account of how federation delivers any of them. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Did you just arrive? Oh, sorry, have you been here the whole time?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic jibe at another member's attendance in the chamber — mockery directed at the person rather than anything they argued. Not a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You’re in the same party and you didn’t even have a meeting, and you have the nerve to attack me?
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal — 'you have the nerve' imputes gall to the member rather than engaging what they said, though it stops short of an insult to their character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Te Pūkenga was a failed Labour experiment. Big Brother. Centralisation. It resulted in $300 million going down the gurgler—$300 million down the Labour fiscal drain. It’s a bit like KiwiBuild, really.
civility.explanation: Brutal about a policy and about the Labour Party, but no individual is attacked. Under the re-anchored scale this is the expected standard — the tribalism is Focus's problem, not Civility's.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Minister has promised so much in terms of these reforms, but the information just isn’t even there. We can’t see the plan. We can’t see how they’re going to be financially viable.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the reform's substance — the absence of a plan and of financial viability information. Scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker
