focus.statement: Te Pūkenga was a failed Labour experiment. Big Brother. Centralisation. It resulted in $300 million going down the gurgler—$300 million down the Labour fiscal drain. It’s a bit like KiwiBuild, really.
focus.explanation: There is a policy referent (Te Pūkenga and a cost figure), but the weight of the passage is party framing — 'Labour experiment', 'Labour fiscal drain', an unrelated swipe at KiwiBuild.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you look at the West Coast of the South Island, the challenge here is the fact that these are programmes that take in so many of our young people who are transitioning out of school or are NEETs—not in education employment or training—coming into places like outdoor education where they find a future in the tourism industry or they find a future in rafting, but that is all in jeopardy because this Government is not managing the numbers, they’re not managing the books, and this doesn’t work.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — a named region, a named category of provision (outdoor education), and the cohort it serves — but it closes on general 'this Government can't manage the books' framing rather than the funding mechanism at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister has promised so much in terms of these reforms, but the information just isn’t even there. We can’t see the plan. We can’t see how they’re going to be financially viable.
specificity.explanation: Names the gap (plan, financial viability) but supplies no figures, no document, no mechanism — a direction with little checkable detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill brings polytechs back to the community, puts the “local” back in local, is community-led, focused on community needs, and enables viability into the future.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — 'community-led', 'community needs', 'viability into the future' — with no mechanism, funding figure, timeframe or named provision of the bill. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As Chris Penk has previously stated in the House, it is around 50 percent more expensive to build a stand-alone house in New Zealand than in Australia.
specificity.explanation: A figure, a defined comparison class (stand-alone house) and a named comparator country — precise enough that someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They know it is going to lead to job cuts, to cuts to courses, to the sale of land that we won’t be able to get back, and they’re just agreeing with their Minister and saying that this is going to be a great thing and promising.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the vocational education reforms will produce staff redundancies, course closures and disposal of polytechnic land — outcomes of a policy, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Public announcements and annual reports of the regional institutes of technology and polytechnics disestablished from Te Pūkenga, plus TEC reporting, for the two years following the Act's commencement. True if redundancies, programme/course closures and sales of polytechnic land are recorded across the sector; false if the sector's staffing, course offering and property holdings are broadly maintained.

divination.statement: This is one of the many polytechs that have failed in the past and are going to fail in the future.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that WITT — and regional polytechnics generally — will be financially unviable again after being re-established as stand-alone institutions under this bill.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: WITT's and other re-established regional institutes' audited annual reports and TEC monitoring for the three financial years after disestablishment of Te Pūkenga. True if WITT or a substantial number of regional institutes record operating deficits requiring Crown support or intervention; false if they operate without deficit-funding or Crown rescue over that period.

veracity.statement: Te Pūkenga was a failed Labour experiment. Big Brother. Centralisation. It resulted in $300 million going down the gurgler—$300 million down the Labour fiscal drain. It’s a bit like KiwiBuild, really.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga cost $300 million in wasted money. The checkable core is the dollar figure and what it is said to cover (accumulated deficits, establishment/transition costs, or both).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's audited annual reports 2020–2024 and Tertiary Education Commission/Ministry of Education figures for its establishment, transition and operating deficits. True if the total attributable losses/costs are approximately $300 million; false if the aggregate is materially lower (or if no defensible basis for the figure exists).

veracity.statement: Well, I’m assuming most of the members know that the head office for Te Pūkenga actually is in the Waikato, in Hamilton.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a matter of fact about where Te Pūkenga's head office is located, offered to rebut the charge that the merger centralised the sector in Wellington.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's annual report / official contact and registered office details and Companies Office or education-provider register listing. True if the head office address is in Hamilton; false if it is in Wellington or elsewhere.

veracity.statement: In fact, they’ve been bailed out twice by the Government over the last 20 years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Western Institute of Technology at Taranaki received Crown financial rescue on two occasions in roughly the two decades before 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission records and WITT annual reports 2005–2025 for Crown injections, deficit funding or Crown observer/commissioner interventions. True if two such bailouts are documented; false if there were none, one, or a materially different number.

veracity.statement: As Chris Penk has previously stated in the House, it is around 50 percent more expensive to build a stand-alone house in New Zealand than in Australia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified trans-Tasman comparison of stand-alone dwelling construction cost. Attributed to a colleague but advanced by the speaker as fact in his own argument. The checkable core is the ~50 percent premium for New Zealand over Australia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published comparative construction-cost studies for stand-alone dwellings (e.g. MBIE/Treasury analysis, NZ Initiative or Rider Levett Bucknall / CoreLogic per-square-metre comparisons, Australian Bureau of Statistics vs Stats NZ build-cost series) around 2023–2025. True if the New Zealand cost premium is approximately 50 percent on a comparable per-square-metre basis; false if the measured gap is materially smaller.

rigor.statement: It’s not about bringing everything back to Wellington, like we’ve been talking about; it’s actually about it being out in the regions.
rigor.explanation: The premise offered (the head office sits in Hamilton, not Wellington) does not support the conclusion drawn. Refuting the geography of the head office leaves the actual charge — consolidation of governance and decision-making away from regional polytechnics — untouched; the argument answers a narrower claim than the one made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They always talk about being the best managers of the numbers, but we can see, in this departmental report, that they are not.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is offered (the departmental report's concerns about missing financial modelling and cost-benefit analysis) and it does bear on the conclusion, but there is a real gap: officials' concerns about one bill's transition costings do not establish the general claim that the Government are not good fiscal managers. The inference generalises well beyond what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When you see that only 11 percent of submitters on this bill were in full favour, there are big questions that need to be asked.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that only 11 percent of written submitters on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill were fully in favour of it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's departmental report / summary of submissions on the bill: true if the share of submitters recorded as supporting the bill is approximately 11%, false if the recorded share is materially different.

veracity.statement: When we had countries, back in 2022 and 2023, such as China, who were coming out here saying, “What an amazing model. We are really interested in your model. We want to see it.” They signed memorandum of agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 2022–2023 Chinese parties praised the Te Pūkenga model and signed memoranda of agreement with it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga annual reports and international-partnership records for 2022–2023: true if one or more memoranda of understanding/agreement with Chinese institutions or agencies were signed in that period, false if no such agreements exist.

veracity.statement: The member for Northland said, in an RNZ article, that the Government has no intention whatsoever to close NorthTec, and he promises that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Grant McCallum was reported by RNZ saying the Government has no intention of closing NorthTec, and that he gave that as a promise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RNZ article referred to: true if McCallum is quoted stating the Government has no intention of closing NorthTec, false if no such quote appears or the reported statement is materially weaker.

veracity.statement: As of last year, some 900 fulltime-equivalents, 500 programmes, and approximately 30 delivery sites have been cut—cut, cut, cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific cumulative reductions across the vocational education sector as at 2024: about 900 FTE staff, 500 programmes and about 30 delivery sites.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga/NZIST and TEC reporting on staff FTE reductions, programme closures and delivery-site closures to end-2024: true if the three figures are approximately 900, 500 and 30, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: In fact, we saw in yet another article, the RNZ article, that there’s an estimate of about $190 million, more than the total amount allocated to the Government for transition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a reported estimate puts the cost of the vocational education transition at about $190 million, exceeding the total funding appropriated for the transition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RNZ report referred to plus the Budget appropriation for vocational education transition: true if a ~$190m cost estimate is reported and the appropriated transition funding is below it, false if the estimate or the appropriation figures do not bear that out.

veracity.statement: We have ISBs who are expected to do more work with half the funding of what the Workforce Development Councils had.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Industry Skills Boards are funded at roughly half the level of the Workforce Development Councils they replace, while carrying a wider remit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC funding allocations for the Workforce Development Councils in their final year against the appropriations for the Industry Skills Boards: true if ISB funding is approximately 50% of WDC funding, false if materially higher.

rigor.statement: The shortcomings or the limitations of planning is that it enables something, but it doesn’t necessarily make that thing a reality. There are still lots of other steps along the way that come after enabling things.

rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that’s a really important point because we don’t want to be creating risks and potentially creating little situations where there are lots of fires, because, just to plug the firefighters, they do not get enough support from Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ).
rigor.explanation: The chain from bad utility connections to 'lots of fires' to inadequate FENZ resourcing is asserted rather than supported — nothing is offered linking granny flats to an elevated fire rate. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded, though not a bare fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’re really happy that there are still some good safeguards within this bill that will require the dwelling to still meet the building code, for the work to be notified to council, and for those people that are building or constructing those granny flats to have the right authorisations, which is really important.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete mechanisms in the bill — building code compliance, notification to council, authorised builders — which someone could check against the text. No figures or timeframes, so short of full precision.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s time we started saying yes to innovative solutions to our housing challenges. It’s time we started saying yes to easing planning restrictions and unshackling ourselves from the bureaucracy of local planning laws.
specificity.explanation: Gestures at a direction ('easing planning restrictions') but commits to no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named rule. 'Innovative solutions' and 'unshackling ourselves from bureaucracy' are slogans with nothing to check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is it that people aren’t building? Is it because of council planning rules? Is it because the rules are too difficult to follow? Is it because of access to building materials? Is it because tradies can’t make a living on the work that’s available to them at the moment? Is it because major infrastructure projects have been cancelled, such as more than 3,000 State homes?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the policy problem — consenting rules, materials supply, trade viability, a named cancelled build programme with a figure. Scrutiny of a specific government decision rather than party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At 70 square metres, it could be a small three-bedroomed home with one bathroom. So not tiny, is my point on “small”.
rigor.explanation: Premise (70 m² would accommodate a three-bedroom, one-bathroom house) is offered and the conclusion drawn from it — that the dwellings are not 'tiny' — follows directly from it. No fallacy or appeal; the inference is a straightforward one from floor area to dwelling type.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So you can’t just say to councils, “Oh, it’s the vibe of the thing. We just want you to permit these things and we don’t want any paperwork or anything.” But then, “Council, if something goes wrong, you’re going to get sued and the ratepayers are going to have to pay for it.” That is not how the world works.
rigor.explanation: A coherent argument from stated premises: councils carry the liability when building work fails, therefore they cannot rationally be asked to consent loosely and without documentation. The conclusion tracks the incentive premise; no fallacy or appeal is relied on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My only point on these hazard provisions are that they do introduce an element of discretion that goes against the political rhetoric of “everybody is going to be able to build one of these 70 square metre houses.” There are some constraints and they are important constraints.
rigor.explanation: The premise — that the hazard provisions confer discretion to refuse — supports the conclusion that the universal 'everybody will be able to build one' framing overstates the bill's effect. The inference from discretionary gatekeeping to a qualified entitlement is valid; nothing rests on an appeal or an insult.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At 70 square metres, it could be a small three-bedroomed home with one bathroom. So not tiny, is my point on “small”.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure (70 square metres) and a checkable characterisation of what that area yields, but stops short of any mechanism, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: By simplifying the consenting process for small stand-alone dwellings, we are cutting red tape, supporting innovation, and enabling faster delivery of quality homes. It is a smart, balanced move to meet growing demand while maintaining safety and standards.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — cutting red tape, innovation, faster delivery, balance, safety — with no figure, threshold, timeframe or named mechanism from the bill. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But unfortunately the process was a bit shorter than the six-month process and we heard from some of the members of the Transport and Infrastructure Committee that it was rushed and that there are probably more rooms for improvement.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions: that the select committee's reporting period was shortened below the standard six months, and that committee members themselves described the process as rushed with room for improvement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill: the date of referral to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee and the reported-back date. True if the reporting period allotted was shorter than the standard six months; false if the committee had the full six-month period. The second limb is settled by the Hansard record of the same debate — true if committee members said the consideration was rushed.

veracity.statement: Councils, as was described by an ex-mayor of a council, are held liable for substandard building work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of current law that councils bear legal liability for substandard building work carried out under consents they issue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand building law and case law on territorial authority liability as a building consent authority — Building Act 2004 consenting/inspection duties and the leaky-homes line of authority (e.g. Body Corporate No 207624 v North Shore City Council [Spencer on Byron]). True if councils can be and have been held liable in negligence for building work they consented or inspected; false if no such liability attaches.

focus.statement: But unfortunately the process was a bit shorter than the six-month process and we heard from some of the members of the Transport and Infrastructure Committee that it was rushed and that there are probably more rooms for improvement.
focus.explanation: Directed at a named bill's select committee process and a specific procedural fact (the shortened reporting period). This is scrutiny of a specific measure, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But this bill is not a flip-flop, and that is to be commended. It’s very good to see this Government doing something that isn’t flip-flopping. So, well done.
focus.explanation: There is a thin policy hook (this particular bill is consistent), but the weight of the remark is a jab at the Government's general habit of reversing itself rather than at any named policy, measure or outcome. No individual is insulted, so this is a focus cost, not a civility one.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My only point on these hazard provisions are that they do introduce an element of discretion that goes against the political rhetoric of “everybody is going to be able to build one of these 70 square metre houses.” There are some constraints and they are important constraints.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific mechanism in the bill (the hazard-related conditions on the consent exemption) and what it means for who can actually build. Named provision, named consequence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By simplifying the consenting process for small stand-alone dwellings, we are cutting red tape, supporting innovation, and enabling faster delivery of quality homes. It is a smart, balanced move to meet growing demand while maintaining safety and standards.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and what it does to the consenting process, with no party framing or attack on opponents. On-policy despite carrying almost no detail — the two questions come apart here.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So you can’t just say to councils, “Oh, it’s the vibe of the thing. We just want you to permit these things and we don’t want any paperwork or anything.” But then, “Council, if something goes wrong, you’re going to get sued and the ratepayers are going to have to pay for it.” That is not how the world works.
civility.explanation: Mocking in tone ('it's the vibe of the thing'), but the mockery lands on the ACT member's position about council paperwork rather than on the member. Pointed rather than personal.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It is interesting that the commentary to the bill notes that the Resource Management Act component of allowing these small, stand-alone dwellings to not have to go through a consenting process is going to be done through a proposed National Environment Standards for Granny Flats that is expected to take effect by the end of 2025.
divination.explanation: Relays the select committee commentary's forecast that the Resource Management Act side of the exemption will be delivered by a National Environmental Standards for Granny Flats in force by the end of 2025. The speaker is reporting the commentary's timetable, not making her own commitment.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Gazette / Ministry for the Environment record for the National Environmental Standards for Granny Flats. True if that national environmental standard was made and came into force on or before 31 December 2025; false if it had not taken effect by that date.

specificity.statement: The building work must be carried out by those authorised professionals—that’s those registered builders and sparkies and plumbers who need that work—and councils must be notified that the work has been completed.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete mechanisms in the bill — the requirement for authorised trades and the council notification step — but carries no figures, thresholds or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I think it’s very important that it doesn’t come at the expense of creating warm, dry, and safe homes for New Zealanders, because every New Zealander deserves to have a warm, dry, and safe home.
specificity.explanation: A statement of a standard with no threshold, mechanism or measure attached — nothing here could be checked or acted on, and the surrounding text supplies no detail for this particular caveat.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The building work must be carried out by those authorised professionals—that’s those registered builders and sparkies and plumbers who need that work—and councils must be notified that the work has been completed.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanics of the measure before the House; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I think that’s a good thing for us to focus on here because so much of the records that we’ve seen kept over time, and historically, around things like construction and building projects, have been kept in formats that are very hard to access, very hard to compare, and very hard to contrast, and because this bill has moved at pace, it does need to be closely monitored in its implementation.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific implementation question — the record-keeping requirement and industry's submission on it — with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Principally, this bill shouldn’t become, essentially, a Trojan horse for lowering building standards, leading to what is quite patently riskier construction practices if not done right.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House and the specific risk of standards being relaxed by it. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National Government, as we’ve heard tonight, have made decisions that absolutely have caused a dramatic slowdown in new builds, and we’ve seen that manifest in various ways right across New Zealand.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim here — a slowdown in new builds — but no specific decision, figure, programme or target is named. The weight sits on 'the National Government' as an actor rather than on any identified policy, so it falls well short of the named-commitment scrutiny that would score high.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think that’s a good thing for us to focus on here because so much of the records that we’ve seen kept over time, and historically, around things like construction and building projects, have been kept in formats that are very hard to access, very hard to compare, and very hard to contrast, and because this bill has moved at pace, it does need to be closely monitored in its implementation.
rigor.explanation: A premise (historic building records are in inaccessible, non-comparable formats) offered in support of a conclusion (digital record-keeping is worth adopting, and the bill needs close monitoring). The inference tracks, though the leap from 'records were poor historically' to 'this bill specifically needs monitoring' leans on the added assertion that the bill moved at pace rather than showing it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I think it’s very important that it doesn’t come at the expense of creating warm, dry, and safe homes for New Zealanders, because every New Zealander deserves to have a warm, dry, and safe home.
rigor.explanation: The reason given is a restatement of the conclusion: homes should be warm, dry and safe because everyone deserves a warm, dry and safe home. Circular, with no independent support offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Principally, this bill shouldn’t become, essentially, a Trojan horse for lowering building standards, leading to what is quite patently riskier construction practices if not done right.
rigor.explanation: The conditional chain — removing consent requirements lowers standards, which raises construction risk — is plausible but is asserted, not shown; 'quite patently' does the work that an argument or evidence would. A real point with a genuine gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As Professor John Turkey pointed out, without building consents, authorities almost certainly will lose that robust oversight of how many new dwellings are being added and the pressure on local infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: A stated mechanism connects premise to conclusion — consents are the data-capture point, so removing them removes the record. Citing the expert is corroboration rather than a bare appeal to authority, since the causal step is spelled out.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As I said in my first reading speaking, I’m really looking forward to how this is going to help the over 50 percent of migrants in my community now that we’ve got the parent visa up and running.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 50 percent of the people in her electorate are migrants, and that the parent visa category is currently operating. The natural reading of the phrase is that migrants make up over half her community rather than that over half of migrants are affected; scored on that reading.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census 'birthplace' data for the Takanini general electorate (the speaker's seat): true if the overseas-born share of the usually resident population exceeds 50 percent, false if it is 50 percent or lower. Second limb: Immigration NZ published status of the parent visa category as at October 2025 — true if applications were open and being processed at that date, false if the category was closed or not yet open.

veracity.statement: The National Government, as we’ve heard tonight, have made decisions that absolutely have caused a dramatic slowdown in new builds, and we’ve seen that manifest in various ways right across New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that new build activity has slowed dramatically and that decisions of the current Government caused that slowdown. The causal limb is the substantive claim; the fall in activity is the observable limb.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ building consents issued for new dwellings and building activity series from Q4 2023 to Q3 2025 against the preceding period, plus published sector analysis (MBIE, RBNZ, BCITO/industry) on drivers: true if new dwelling consents fell materially over the period AND identified Government decisions are documented as a driver; false if consents did not fall materially, or if the decline is shown to predate the change of government and be attributable to interest rates and the credit cycle rather than Government decisions.

divination.statement: As Professor John Turkey pointed out, without building consents, authorities almost certainly will lose that robust oversight of how many new dwellings are being added and the pressure on local infrastructure.
divination.explanation: Relays a forecast that, once these dwellings are exempt from building consent, councils will lose their ability to track how many new dwellings are being added and the resulting infrastructure load. A forecast about a future consequence of the regime, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: other
divination.subject_name: John Turkey (academic cited by the speaker)
divination.falsification_criterion: Council and MBIE reporting on small stand-alone dwellings after the Act commences: true if councils cannot produce a reliable count of these dwellings or their infrastructure demand (i.e. the completion-notification requirement does not yield usable data), false if councils/MBIE publish counts and infrastructure-load data for these dwellings comparable to what consenting previously provided.

civility.statement: The National Government, as we’ve heard tonight, have made decisions that absolutely have caused a dramatic slowdown in new builds, and we’ve seen that manifest in various ways right across New Zealand.
civility.explanation: A hard criticism of the Government's decisions and their consequences that lands on the record, not on any individual. No imputation of bad faith or personal failing.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If we look at the statistics that are readily available for anybody to check in to, specific statistics that were released in April this year show that 33,595 new homes consented in the year to February this year—February 2025—and that was down 7.4 percent from the year before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific Stats NZ building-consent total (33,595 dwellings consented in the year to February 2025) and a specific annual change (-7.4 percent).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 'Building consents issued' release covering the year ended February 2025; true if the annual number of new dwellings consented is 33,595 (± rounding) and the change on the previous year is -7.4%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s the worst February for home consents since 2012.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the February 2025 monthly consent figure is the lowest of any February since 2012.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly new dwelling consent series for each February from 2012 onward; true if February 2025 is lower than every intervening February, false if any February between 2013 and 2024 was lower.

veracity.statement: The previous Labour Government had built more houses, more social houses, for instance, since the 1970s, and to sit on this side of the House and watch all of that momentum disappear through what I believe to be poor decisions from the current Government—you can’t turn that ship around lightly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017-2023 Labour Government added more social/public houses than any government since the 1970s. The rest of the sentence is flagged opinion and is not the checkable part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Housing and Urban Development / Kāinga Ora public housing stock and new-build figures by parliamentary term back to the 1970s; true if the 2017-2023 term's public housing builds exceed every term since the 1970s, false if any earlier term built more.

veracity.statement: This drop came straight after the Government stopped Kāinga Ora building houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public housing build and that maintenance fund as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two government actions: that Kāinga Ora was stopped from building houses, and that $1.5 billion was cut from the public housing build and maintenance funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 documents and Kāinga Ora's revised build programme / Vote Housing appropriations; true if a cut of approximately $1.5 billion to the public housing build and maintenance funding is recorded and the build programme was halted, false if the recorded reduction is materially different or no such halt occurred.

veracity.statement: Where I come from, there’s a single Kāinga Ora house in Lyttelton, for instance—one house, and they’re selling that, and the woman who’s lived there for 42 years has been unceremoniously told that, in her 70s, she has to leave.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Kāinga Ora holds exactly one property in Lyttelton, that it is being sold, and that the sitting tenant of 42 years has been told to leave.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora quarterly public housing stock figures by suburb for Lyttelton plus its property disposal listings; true if Kāinga Ora's Lyttelton stock is one dwelling and that dwelling is listed for sale with the tenancy ending, false if it holds more than one Lyttelton property or no such sale is recorded.

veracity.statement: When we think of the 20,000 construction jobs that have already been lost—which is 20,000 workers—we can only look at this particular bill, whilst we support it, being such a trivial, small step in the overall situation that we’re facing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20,000 construction jobs have already been lost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ employment data for the construction industry (HLFS industry employment or the monthly filled jobs series) over the period referenced; true if the fall in construction employment is approximately 20,000, false if materially smaller or larger.

specificity.statement: If we look at the statistics that are readily available for anybody to check in to, specific statistics that were released in April this year show that 33,595 new homes consented in the year to February this year—February 2025—and that was down 7.4 percent from the year before.
specificity.explanation: Carries a precise count, a named reference period and a percentage change — directly checkable against the official series.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This drop came straight after the Government stopped Kāinga Ora building houses and cut $1.5 billion from the public housing build and that maintenance fund as well.
rigor.explanation: Offers temporal sequence ('came straight after') as the explanation for the consent drop — a post hoc inference, with no mechanism or lag analysis connecting a public housing funding cut to total private and public consent volumes.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think if this Government is hell-bent on divesting from the public good, public housing, it would have been much more preferable for them to get their own house in order before considering selling this single house that is actually quite life-destroying for the individual involved.
civility.explanation: Pointed and imputes ideological motive ('hell-bent on divesting from the public good') to the Government collectively, but lands on no individual member and keeps the target on the housing divestment decision.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When we think of the 20,000 construction jobs that have already been lost—which is 20,000 workers—we can only look at this particular bill, whilst we support it, being such a trivial, small step in the overall situation that we’re facing.
focus.explanation: Engages the measure before the House directly — sets the bill's scope against a named sector outcome rather than against the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whilst the contributions from the other side tonight haven’t been very substantive and we haven’t gleaned much more information from that tonight, we now found ourselves at the end of this process.
focus.explanation: A blanket dismissal of the other side's debate contributions; names no policy, measure, figure or outcome, so it is about the opposing team rather than the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has the Prime Minister made statements in support of the America and Arab - led peace process, and how many letters has he received in support of that from members of the Opposition or their leaders?
focus.explanation: The first clause touches a real foreign-policy question, but the substance of the question is a letter-count aimed at embarrassing the Opposition rather than any named policy, measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I actually think we should be very proud of the efforts of President Trump and the Arab nations that actually are creating a pathway to peace, to stop the killing, and to create the ceasefire, but I have received zero letters that I am aware of.
focus.explanation: Half the answer engages the substance of the peace process; the other half takes up the invited jab about the Opposition's letters, which carries no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is her economic plan to talk about growth, hope interest rates come down, and house prices grow?
focus.explanation: Directed at the Government's economic plan, so not pure party-bashing, but it caricatures the plan rather than naming a measure, figure or outcome to test it against.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she agree with another business leader from the Mood of the Boardroom, who said, “The Government is ineffective. There is no compelling leadership and strategic plan evident that will turn New Zealand around.”?
focus.explanation: A general verdict on the Government's effectiveness and leadership, relayed second-hand. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing for the Minister to answer on the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is thanks to our Government’s Elective Boost, which has delivered more than 16,000 additional procedures, including hips, knees, and cataracts, between February and June by partnering with the private hospital sector.
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme, a delivery mechanism and a quantified outcome. Entirely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Opposition member wants talk about the wait-lists; I would just remind her that the number of people waiting more than four months for a first specialist assessment (FSA), under her watch, increased by over 6,000 percent while they were in Government.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure, a threshold and a quantified outcome rather than making a general 'they were hopeless' claim, though the framing is squarely about the other side's record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If his goal is to guarantee the rights of all New Zealanders, when will his Government be introducing legislation to address the 13,000 privately owned parcels of land that actually prevent people from accessing the foreshore and seabed?
focus.explanation: Names a specific quantified problem and asks for a specific legislative response, testing the Minister's stated principle against it. Squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he consider that his decision to arbitrarily limit Māori rights to only 5 percent of the coastline is an example of a fair and durable framework, as was intended in this Act when it was first passed?
focus.explanation: Names a specific figure, a specific ministerial decision and the statutory standard it is being measured against. Textbook scrutiny of a policy.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The economy is where it is now because harmful and painful inflation in 2021, in 2022, in 2023—fuelled by reckless Government spending—had to be brought down over time with high interest rates.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal chain is offered — inflation required monetary tightening, tightening suppressed activity — and the conclusion (the economy's current size is not attributable to her plan) does follow from it. The chain leans on an asserted rather than demonstrated link between fiscal spending and inflation, which is the gap; the truth of that premise is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she agree with another business leader from the Mood of the Boardroom, who said, “The Government is ineffective. There is no compelling leadership and strategic plan evident that will turn New Zealand around.”?
rigor.explanation: The implicit inference is an appeal to authority — a business leader says the Government is ineffective, therefore it is. No evidence connects the quoted opinion to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It has often been a reflection I have had that if some of the reforms that we are making had been made six years ago, how much better off our economy would be now.
rigor.explanation: Offered as rebuttal to the charge that growth is not evident, but it is a bare counterfactual: nothing is supplied to support the claim that earlier reform would have produced better outcomes, and even if true it would not show that growth is evident now. The conclusion does not follow from what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, I don’t, but I do agree with Mr Finlayson’s statement at the time when the bill did go in, in 2011, where he talked about a very high threshold for customary marine titles being granted. That, in essence, is what we are seeking to establish with this legislation.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered — the original Act set a high threshold, and the amendment is said to restore it — so the conclusion is supported in outline. But it sidesteps the actual inference in the question: that the Act's author says these amendments undermine rather than restore that intent. Appealing to the same person's 2011 words without addressing his present objection leaves a real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, anybody in a boat can access the foreshore and seabed, from any particular angle.
rigor.explanation: Non-sequitur. The question was about privately owned land blocking public access to the foreshore from the landward side; that the coast can be reached by boat has no bearing on whether that land-access barrier exists, so nothing offered supports the implied conclusion that there is no problem to legislate for.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I was asked for a figure, I proffered one. I point to the fact that the previous Minister the member quoted at the start offered a 10 percent figure at one point.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. That a previous Minister also named a percentage does nothing to show that this Minister's figure was not arbitrary — the conclusion rests entirely on the comparison rather than on any account of how the 5 percent was arrived at.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The economy is where it is now because harmful and painful inflation in 2021, in 2022, in 2023—fuelled by reckless Government spending—had to be brought down over time with high interest rates.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that inflation was elevated across 2021–2023, and that it was driven by the previous Government's spending.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the years ended December 2021, 2022 and 2023 — true if each was materially above the RBNZ 1–3 percent target band; and RBNZ/Treasury decompositions of inflation drivers over that period — the causal element is true if fiscal expenditure is identified as a material contributor, false if the analyses attribute the episode overwhelmingly to imported/supply-side and monetary factors.

veracity.statement: In our emergency departments, 73.9 percent of patients were admitted, treated, or discharged within six hours during that quarter, up from 71.2 percent during the same period last year, despite increased attendances.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the ED six-hour target result for the quarter, the prior-year comparator, and that attendance volumes rose over the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand published quarterly health target results for the April–June 2025 quarter, shorter stays in emergency departments measure: true if the result is 73.9 percent and the April–June 2024 comparator is 71.2 percent; false if either figure differs materially. The attendances element checks against ED presentation volumes for the two quarters.

veracity.statement: Well, 82 percent of children are now fully immunised by age two, up from 76.5 percent last year, representing the largest annual gain across all health targets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the immunisation target result and comparator, and that it was the largest annual gain of any health target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand quarterly health target results, childhood immunisation at 24 months, April–June 2025 quarter: true if the result is 82 percent against a 76.5 percent comparator a year earlier, and if that 5.5-point gain is the largest year-on-year movement of the five health targets in the same release; false if another target moved further.

veracity.statement: This is thanks to our Government’s Elective Boost, which has delivered more than 16,000 additional procedures, including hips, knees, and cataracts, between February and June by partnering with the private hospital sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a delivery volume for a named programme over a named period, attributed to outsourcing to private hospitals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health reporting on the Elective Boost programme: true if more than 16,000 additional elective procedures were delivered between February and June 2025 and were counted as additional to baseline planned volumes; false if the reported figure is materially lower or if the count includes procedures that would have been delivered anyway.

veracity.statement: The Opposition member wants talk about the wait-lists; I would just remind her that the number of people waiting more than four months for a first specialist assessment (FSA), under her watch, increased by over 6,000 percent while they were in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific magnitude of increase in the over-four-month FSA wait-list under the previous Government. The figure is large enough that it plausibly reflects growth from a very low base, which the criterion should test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health first specialist assessment wait-list series: true if the count of people waiting more than four months for an FSA rose more than sixty-fold between the start and end of the 2017–2023 Labour Government (or over the period the named member held the health portfolio); false if the increase was materially smaller or the series is not comparable across that period.

veracity.statement: No, I don’t, but I do agree with Mr Finlayson’s statement at the time when the bill did go in, in 2011, where he talked about a very high threshold for customary marine titles being granted. That, in essence, is what we are seeking to establish with this legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Act's sponsoring Minister said about the threshold when the bill was introduced in 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the 2011 debates on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill and contemporaneous statements by Christopher Finlayson: true if he characterised the customary marine title test as a very high threshold at introduction; false if the record shows no such characterisation.

veracity.statement: If his goal is to guarantee the rights of all New Zealanders, when will his Government be introducing legislation to address the 13,000 privately owned parcels of land that actually prevent people from accessing the foreshore and seabed?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of privately owned coastal land parcels that obstruct public access to the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Land Information New Zealand title data and Herenga ā Nuku (Outdoor Access Commission) analyses of freehold parcels abutting the coastal marine area without public access: true if approximately 13,000 privately owned parcels adjoin the foreshore in a way that blocks public access; false if the count is materially different or if the parcels identified do not in fact bar access.

veracity.statement: When I was asked for a figure, I proffered one. I point to the fact that the previous Minister the member quoted at the start offered a 10 percent figure at one point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister who introduced the 2011 Act publicly offered a 10 percent estimate of the coastline likely to be covered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements and interviews by Christopher Finlayson while Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations on the likely extent of coastline subject to customary marine title: true if he cited a figure of around 10 percent; false if no such statement exists or the figure he gave was materially different.

specificity.statement: Our approach, as a Government, is to address the underlying foundations for growth which includes low and stable inflation to create a lower interest rate environment; having responsibly managed books; driving reforms across the areas that have held New Zealand’s economy back for too long, including low rates of educational achievement, byzantine consenting processes, excessive regulatory burdens, and a dire approach to overseas investment.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete domains of reform (education, consenting, regulation, overseas investment), which is more than a slogan, but supplies no figures, mechanisms, thresholds or timeframes that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In our emergency departments, 73.9 percent of patients were admitted, treated, or discharged within six hours during that quarter, up from 71.2 percent during the same period last year, despite increased attendances.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages, a named target measure, a defined threshold (six hours) and a stated comparison period. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, 82 percent of children are now fully immunised by age two, up from 76.5 percent last year, representing the largest annual gain across all health targets.
specificity.explanation: Named target, age threshold, current figure and prior-year comparator, plus a rankable claim about the size of the gain.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Opposition member wants talk about the wait-lists; I would just remind her that the number of people waiting more than four months for a first specialist assessment (FSA), under her watch, increased by over 6,000 percent while they were in Government.
specificity.explanation: A named measure, a defined threshold and a numeric magnitude — checkable, even though the percentage is presented without the base it is calculated from.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are several cases that have been heard that will have to be re-heard in light of this legislation if it passes.
specificity.explanation: Asked directly how many customary marine titles would be exposed to re-litigation, the answer supplies 'several' — a direction with no number, no named cases and no timeframe, where a precise count was clearly available.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If his goal is to guarantee the rights of all New Zealanders, when will his Government be introducing legislation to address the 13,000 privately owned parcels of land that actually prevent people from accessing the foreshore and seabed?
specificity.explanation: A precise figure and a clearly identified category of land, though no mechanism or timeframe is proposed. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does he consider that his decision to arbitrarily limit Māori rights to only 5 percent of the coastline is an example of a fair and durable framework, as was intended in this Act when it was first passed?
civility.explanation: 'Arbitrarily' imputes caprice to the Minister's decision-making rather than only criticising the decision — pointed and edging toward the person, but it stops short of an attack on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We are going through a difficult recovery. As I’ve said, it’s two speed at the moment. In our provincial industries, in the South Island, and our rural communities, they are experiencing growth but certainly in our cities it’s been very difficult.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that provincial, South Island and rural parts of the economy are growing while the main cities are contracting or flat — a claim about the current regional distribution of growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ regional GDP and the regional economic indicators (Infometrics/ANZ) covering 2025: true if provincial/South Island/rural regions recorded output or income growth over the period while Auckland and Wellington were flat or contracting; false if the regional data show no such split.

veracity.statement: I’d just say for the 66 billion dollar man, who increased debt threefold, that we now write out a $10 billion interest bill each and every year, thanks to your mismanagement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that debt tripled under the previous Prime Minister and that the annual interest bill is now $10 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand: net core Crown debt in 2017 versus 2023, and core Crown finance costs for the 2024/25 year; true if debt roughly tripled and finance costs are around $10 billion a year, false if either figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Yeah, it’s difficult, unemployment has ticked up a bit, but it’s the same as what it has been over a 30-year average, it’s significantly below what it has been over the last 15 years, and—unlike that member—we’re just not happy to actually be the party of people who don’t work.
veracity.explanation: Two comparative claims about the current unemployment rate: that it equals the 30-year average, and that it is significantly below the level of the last 15 years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey unemployment rate for the quarter current at 8 October 2025, compared with the mean of that series over the preceding 30 years and over the preceding 15 years; true if the current rate is at or near the 30-year mean and materially below the 15-year mean, false if the 15-year mean is at or below the current rate.

veracity.statement: You put the country into the biggest recession in 35 years, you created the longest COVID hangover of any in the Western world, you actually made sure that you tripled the debt, for goodness’ sake, and we now have a $10 billion interest bill.
veracity.explanation: Two superlative claims: that the recession was the largest in 35 years, and that New Zealand's post-COVID slump was the longest in the Western world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP series on whether the 2023–24 contraction was the deepest peak-to-trough fall since 1990 excluding the 2020 lockdown quarters; and OECD quarterly GDP-per-capita data on how many quarters New Zealand stayed below its pre-COVID peak relative to other advanced economies. True if both hold; false if either is contradicted.

veracity.statement: If the dire current state of the New Zealand economy is all someone else’s fault, why is it that the New Zealand economy shrunk by almost 1 percent at a time when other economies around the world that have been hit harder by Donald Trump’s tariffs—many of whom had a higher rate of inflation at the peak of the global pandemic—have been growing faster than New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's economy contracted by almost 1 percent in the relevant quarter while economies facing higher US tariffs, and higher peak pandemic inflation, grew faster.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP release for the June 2025 quarter, and OECD quarterly GDP for the same quarter for economies subject to higher US tariff rates than New Zealand; true if New Zealand contracted by close to 1 percent while those comparator economies grew, false if the fall was materially smaller or the comparators also contracted.

veracity.statement: When he’s been out and about, why hasn’t he been talking to the businesses who say that hiring staff is not their primary constraint for growth—given that only 4 percent are saying that—whilst 63 percent of businesses, according to the NZ Institute of Economic Research, are saying their real problem is not enough customers?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in NZIER's survey about 4 percent of firms name labour as their main constraint and about 63 percent name insufficient demand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZIER Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion for the quarter current at 8 October 2025: true if roughly 4 percent of firms report finding labour as their main constraint and roughly 63 percent report sales/demand as their main constraint, false if either figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: The committee has decided to reduce the OCR by 50 basis points. This is the 8th OCR reduction since August last year. At that time, the OCR was 5.5 percent. It is now at 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the size of the cut, the level of the OCR before and after, and that this is the eighth reduction in the easing cycle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Monetary Policy Review of 8 October 2025 and the published OCR decision history; true if the OCR was cut 50 basis points to 2.50% and that was the eighth cut since August 2024, when the OCR was 5.50%; false if any of those differ.

veracity.statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that youth unemployment is 10,000 higher and filled jobs 36,000 lower than when the government took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey (15–24 unemployment) and the monthly Employment Indicators filled-jobs series, comparing November 2023 with the latest release before 8 October 2025; true if youth unemployment is about 10,000 higher and filled jobs about 36,000 lower, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that jobseeker recipient numbers rose by about 50 percent, or 60,000 people, over the previous government's term, at a time of 3.2–3.5 percent unemployment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets: jobseeker support recipient numbers for the December 2017 and December 2023 quarters, and the Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate over that period; true if the rise is about 50 percent and about 60,000 recipients, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This is a Government that is—I’ll tell you what the landlord cut did create: rents have gone down $5 a week, instead of up $180 a week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents have fallen by $5 a week following the restoration of interest deductibility for landlords, against a counterfactual of a $180 rise.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index and MBIE tenancy bond data on mean weekly rent for new tenancies, comparing the period before the interest-deductibility change with the latest available before 8 October 2025; true if average weekly rent fell by about $5, false if rents rose over that period.

rigor.statement: You cannot increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation, drive up interest rates, put the economy into recession, and raise unemployment. That is the consequence of your failed economic management.
rigor.explanation: A stated causal chain (spending → inflation → rate rises → recession → unemployment) that does support the conclusion drawn, but it is offered monocausally: nothing is offered to rule out the global inflation shock as the driver, so the conclusion outruns the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
rigor.explanation: The "if not because of" framing offers a single cause and treats it as the only available explanation — a false dilemma that also assumes causation from a before-and-after comparison. The figures are relevant but do not establish the attribution.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand, then, the basic maths that if there are four job seekers to every job that is available in this country, all of his cuts to jobseeker support couldn’t hope to possibly punish people into ghost jobs but will only deepen poverty and homelessness?
rigor.explanation: The seekers-to-vacancies ratio genuinely supports the first half — sanctions cannot create vacancies that do not exist. The leap to "will only deepen poverty and homelessness" is not carried by that ratio alone, leaving a real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are five immutable laws of economics. The first is about spending; that drives into creating inflation. When you have high inflation because spending went up 84 percent, you end up with 12 to 13 interest rate rises.
rigor.explanation: Asserted as "immutable laws" rather than argued — an appeal to authority standing in for the inference. The chain also treats domestic spending as the sole cause of an inflation episode that was worldwide, so the conclusion is not carried by what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just say for the 66 billion dollar man, who increased debt threefold, that we now write out a $10 billion interest bill each and every year, thanks to your mismanagement.
civility.explanation: A mocking personal epithet ("the 66 billion dollar man") aimed at the individual member, plus "your mismanagement" pinned on him personally. Short of direct abuse, but it lands on the person rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, unlike the member, I get out of Wellington most weeks and I actually get out and see the real economy and I see real businesses.
civility.explanation: Casts the questioner personally as insular and out of touch rather than answering the point about horticultural labour demand. Pointed at the person, though not a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: does he remember, with respect to the policies that he inherited, that the then former Prime Minister had had a huge sort of Guy Fawkes burn-up one night, and got rid of all those policies—how much more quickly could we have recovered if he had done that much earlier in his career?
civility.explanation: "A huge sort of Guy Fawkes burn-up" mocks the individual's decision-making and the closing clause needles his career. Ridicule directed at a person, not a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand, then, the basic maths that if there are four job seekers to every job that is available in this country, all of his cuts to jobseeker support couldn’t hope to possibly punish people into ghost jobs but will only deepen poverty and homelessness?
civility.explanation: Framing the question as whether the Prime Minister grasps "basic maths" is condescension aimed at the person's competence rather than at the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, unlike the member, I get out of Wellington most weeks and I actually get out and see the real economy and I see real businesses.
focus.explanation: The question named a specific sector claim and a named orchardist's contrary evidence; the reply is about the speaker's own travel habits and the other member's, with no policy mechanism, figure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If the dire current state of the New Zealand economy is all someone else’s fault, why is it that the New Zealand economy shrunk by almost 1 percent at a time when other economies around the world that have been hit harder by Donald Trump’s tariffs—many of whom had a higher rate of inflation at the peak of the global pandemic—have been growing faster than New Zealand?
focus.explanation: Names a specific outcome (quarterly GDP change), a figure, and an international comparison against a named cause. Scrutiny of the government's economic record, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Prime Minister: does he remember, with respect to the policies that he inherited, that the then former Prime Minister had had a huge sort of Guy Fawkes burn-up one night, and got rid of all those policies—how much more quickly could we have recovered if he had done that much earlier in his career?
focus.explanation: Invites speculation about a former Prime Minister's conduct. Beyond a mocking gesture at the 2023 policy reversals, no measure, cost, mechanism or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his cuts to jobseeker will impact over 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health, and, if so, how does he justify this?
focus.explanation: Names the specific policy change, the affected cohort and the number affected, and asks for the justification. Squarely on the measure, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why are there 10,000 more unemployed young people and 36,000 fewer jobs in this country since he took office, if not because of his Government’s billions of dollars of cuts to investment?
focus.explanation: Two named labour-market outcomes with figures, tied to a named category of government decision. Accountability for a specific record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our policy is designed for 18- and 19-year-olds that are on jobseeker benefit. When you go on a jobseeker benefit, you’re deemed able and capable of working.
focus.explanation: Engages the eligibility mechanism of the named benefit and the cohort the policy targets. On the substance of the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In the last administration, with 3.2 to 3.5 percent unemployment, the Labour-Greens Government drove a 50 percent increase and put 60,000 more people on jobseeker benefit.
focus.explanation: Names a specific benefit series and a specific outcome, which is a real record claim, but it is carried in party framing ("Labour-Greens Government") rather than tied to a policy mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It’s now growing again in quarter 3; the growth in quarter 4 will step up. The recovery is coming.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that quarterly GDP growth in the December 2025 quarter will be higher than in the September 2025 quarter.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP releases for the September 2025 and December 2025 quarters; true if December-quarter growth exceeds September-quarter growth, false if it is lower or negative.

divination.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand, then, the basic maths that if there are four job seekers to every job that is available in this country, all of his cuts to jobseeker support couldn’t hope to possibly punish people into ghost jobs but will only deepen poverty and homelessness?
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the jobseeker changes will increase poverty and homelessness.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ child poverty statistics (material hardship measure) and MSD/HUD housing register and emergency-housing data for the year following the jobseeker changes taking effect; true if both measures rise beyond sampling error, false if they are flat or fall.

specificity.statement: When he’s been out and about, why hasn’t he been talking to the businesses who say that hiring staff is not their primary constraint for growth—given that only 4 percent are saying that—whilst 63 percent of businesses, according to the NZ Institute of Economic Research, are saying their real problem is not enough customers?
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages attributed to a named survey source, framing a checkable claim about what firms report as their binding constraint.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The committee has decided to reduce the OCR by 50 basis points. This is the 8th OCR reduction since August last year. At that time, the OCR was 5.5 percent. It is now at 2.5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Exact figures, a count of prior decisions and start and end levels — fully checkable against the source announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Assuming today's reduction is passed on in full, a family with a 25-year $500,000 mortgage would have minimum repayments of $400 less a fortnight than they were in the middle of last year.
specificity.explanation: A worked example with loan size, term, a stated assumption and a dollar figure per fortnight against a named baseline period — someone could recompute it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the Prime Minister aware that his cuts to jobseeker will impact over 2,000 18- and 19-year-olds who may be disabled, sick, or experiencing severe mental ill health, and, if so, how does he justify this?
specificity.explanation: A named policy, a defined age group and a figure, though the "may be" qualifier leaves the health-condition share undefined.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is a Government that is—I’ll tell you what the landlord cut did create: rents have gone down $5 a week, instead of up $180 a week.
specificity.explanation: Names the policy change and gives a dollar-per-week figure with a stated counterfactual, though the period over which the change is measured is left unstated.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future. That compares with 84 percent of students from wealthier families.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two survey figures from the Education Review Office attendance research — 82% of students from poorer families and 84% from wealthier families agreeing school matters for their future.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education Review Office 2025 school attendance survey report: true if it reports approximately 82% (lower-decile/poorer) and 84% (higher-decile/wealthier) of students agreeing school is important for their future; false if the published figures differ materially or no such breakdown exists.

veracity.statement: Three years ago, it was four out of 10 parents who thought it was OK for their children to miss a week of school.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the comparable survey three years earlier, 40% of parents considered a week's absence acceptable, against three in 10 now.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2022 Education Review Office attendance survey of parents: true if approximately 40% of parents said it was acceptable for a child to miss a week or more of school; false if the earlier figure was materially different or the question was not asked.

veracity.statement: One of the key findings is that the expectations set by principals and teachers are critical, and yet there has been an enormous improvement in that, too: 93 percent of teachers and school leaders report that they set clear expectations with students, and 60 percent of students say that they have increased their efforts to set clear expectations for school attendance in their school community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 93% of teachers and school leaders report setting clear attendance expectations, and a further figure of 60% drawn from the same survey.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education Review Office 2025 attendance survey: true if it reports approximately 93% of teachers/school leaders setting clear expectations with students and a corresponding ~60% figure on increased effort around attendance expectations; false if those figures are absent or materially different.

veracity.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific meta-analytic result — a 14% higher piglet mortality risk in non-confinement farrowing systems, drawn from a review of 22 studies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The literature review supplied to the Minister on the animal welfare (pigs) code review: true if it covers ~22 studies and reports approximately 14% higher piglet mortality in free-farrowing versus confined systems; false if the review reports a materially different effect size or no such pooled figure.

veracity.statement: We are reducing the time from 33 days down to seven. Most of the rest of the world is at 33 days; we are reducing down to seven.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that most other jurisdictions permit confinement of sows for 33 days, against the seven days proposed for New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Comparative regulation of farrowing crate duration in the EU (Council Directive 2008/120/EC), the UK, USA, Canada and Australia: true if the prevailing permitted post-farrowing confinement period in most of those jurisdictions is around 28-33 days or longer; false if most permit materially shorter confinement or the 33-day figure has no counterpart abroad.

veracity.statement: How does he justify extending the use of cruel farrowing crates indefinitely when every animal welfare organisation in New Zealand, including the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee [NAWAC], and 73 percent of New Zealanders oppose the use of farrowing crates because of worse welfare outcomes for mother pigs and piglets?
veracity.explanation: Three factual assertions: that the extension is indefinite, that every New Zealand animal welfare organisation including NAWAC opposes farrowing crates, and that 73% of New Zealanders oppose them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) The Government's draft pig code/legislation: true if it sets no end date, false if it specifies a fixed transition (the Minister states 10 years). (b) NAWAC's published advice on the pig code: true if NAWAC's operative position opposes crating, false if its reconsidered advice accepts limited post-farrowing crating. (c) Published polling on New Zealanders' attitudes to farrowing crates: true if a reputable poll puts opposition at ~73%, false if no such poll exists or the figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20,000 jobs have been lost, and attributes the timing to the Government's decision to stop and pause infrastructure projects.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled jobs data for the construction sector between late 2023 and mid-2025: true if construction employment fell by approximately 20,000 over that period; false if the fall was materially smaller or the figure cannot be sourced.

veracity.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 761 private-sector construction employers closed in the past year and that construction firms are being liquidated at two per day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Companies Office liquidation notices and Centrix/MBIE insolvency data for the construction sector, October 2024 - September 2025: true if roughly 761 construction employers ceased operating and liquidations averaged about two per day; false if the counts are materially different.

veracity.statement: If the economy is recovering, then why are 200 New Zealanders leaving every day, including thousands of builders, heading to Australia instead of staying here to build in New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a departure rate of 200 New Zealanders a day, including thousands of construction workers, with Australia as the destination.
veracity.subject: speaker
