veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for the year to mid-2025: true if net or gross departures of New Zealand citizens run at approximately 200 per day (~73,000 a year) with Australia the main destination, and occupational data show construction workers in the thousands; false if the daily rate is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $61.8 billion budgeted for public infrastructure over the next four years, against $50.6 billion invested by the previous Government from 2019 to 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 documents and the National Infrastructure Pipeline / Treasury capital allowances: true if the four-year public infrastructure investment total is approximately $61.8 billion and the 2019-2023 comparator is approximately $50.6 billion on a like-for-like basis; false if the figures differ materially or rest on non-comparable definitions.

veracity.statement: It is a fact that I will repeat again: we have built more social homes in the past 23 months than the last Government did in its last three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more social homes were built in the Government's first 23 months than by the previous Government in its final three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD social housing register / public housing supply statistics: true if completions of public and community housing places between December 2023 and October 2025 exceed completions between late 2020 and late 2023; false if the comparison fails on completions, or if it holds only by switching between 'built', 'delivered' and 'contracted' measures.

specificity.statement: Critically, 82 percent of students from poorer families said that going to school is important for their future. That compares with 84 percent of students from wealthier families.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages with a named comparison group; a reader could go to the survey and check them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the key findings is that the expectations set by principals and teachers are critical, and yet there has been an enormous improvement in that, too: 93 percent of teachers and school leaders report that they set clear expectations with students, and 60 percent of students say that they have increased their efforts to set clear expectations for school attendance in their school community.
specificity.explanation: Names the finding and gives two figures tied to identified respondent groups, though the second clause is garbled enough that what the 60% measures is unclear.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With the other changes I’m proposing, an independent economic analysis estimated the cost of transition at more than $675,000 for the average indoor pig farm.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a dollar figure and a defined unit (the average indoor pig farm) — checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why is the Minister going against independent welfare experts who say farrowing crates cause significant suffering for mother pigs and piglets; they increase the risk of stillbirth; restrict normal nesting behaviour of mother pigs; and cause boredom, sores, pain, and distress due to prolonged confinement?
specificity.explanation: Enumerates four distinct, checkable welfare harms attributed to a named practice, though it cites 'independent welfare experts' without naming them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he know that, to build his infrastructure pipeline, he will need the 761 private sector construction employers who have shut their doors and laid off their people in the last year, and how does he plan to stop the liquidations of two construction firms every day on his watch?
specificity.explanation: An exact count of firms, a defined period and a rate of failure — precise enough to be checked against insolvency records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over the next four years, we have budgeted to invest a record $61.8 billion in public infrastructure, and this number is only set to grow with new capital earmarked for allocation and is a huge step up from the $50.6 billion the previous Government invested between 2019 and 2023.
specificity.explanation: Two dollar figures, both with defined periods, plus a named comparison. Directly checkable against the Budget.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Between now and Christmas, more than $7 billion worth of infrastructure projects will commence, including upgrades to Auckland City Hospital, Middlemore Hospital, Hawke’s Bay Hospital, the construction of a new acute mental health unit at Hutt Valley Hospital; over $5 billion worth of roading projects—the Ōtaki to north of Levin highway, Melling interchange, Waihoehoe Road, the Ōmanawa bridge; and more than $800 million in school property projects, which we’re building better and faster than ever before.
specificity.explanation: A timeframe, three dollar totals and nine individually named projects. About as checkable as a statement in the House gets.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: While education may not have done well for Duncan Webb, this Government thinks it's important.
civility.explanation: A jibe at a named member's education and, by implication, his intelligence. It engages nothing in the substance of the answer and lands squarely on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why was targeted consultation only undertaken with the pork industry across 2024 and 2025, while animal welfare organisations were blindsided on Friday with his plans to cancel the phase out of farrowing crates, and does he regard protecting animal welfare as his primary responsibility, or enacting the wishes of the pork industry?
civility.explanation: Goes beyond criticising the consultation process to impute motive to the Minister personally — that he is serving the industry rather than discharging his statutory duty. Short of an insult, but it attributes bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member seems to be labouring under the same misunderstanding her colleague Ginny Andersen had yesterday, in the last round of “Who’s got talent?”, in which she said that all changes in the construction sector are due to what public investment is happening in infrastructure.
civility.explanation: Mockery of two named members — the 'Who's got talent?' jibe frames a colleague's questioning as a talent-show audition. Condescending toward the person rather than the argument, which she addresses separately.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We just heard the Minister of Finance waxing and waning lyrical about some basic facts and basic maths, so let’s provide some of those basic facts and basic maths.
civility.explanation: Pointed and faintly mocking about the Minister's manner rather than her argument, but it stops short of imputing bad faith or attacking her character, and it moves straight to the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: An analysis of 22 scientific articles that are relevant shows that piglet mortality risk is 14 percent higher in systems that do not confine sows after farrowing.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (confinement after farrowing is justified) offered with a stated evidence base and effect size; the inference tracks what was presented, though it addresses only mortality and not the welfare harms put to him.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I have visited pig farms, where I have been there after piglets have been farrowed, and I saw absolutely no sign of any of that.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal anecdote: his own farm visits are offered to rebut a claim about pre-farrowing nesting behaviour, but he describes observations made after farrowing, so the anecdote does not bear on the point even if accurate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We needed to ensure that we had a system that was practical and affordable for them, otherwise we would not have a pig-farming industry in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: the choice is presented as this transition package or no pig-farming industry at all, with nothing offered to exclude the range of intermediate settings.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why was targeted consultation only undertaken with the pork industry across 2024 and 2025, while animal welfare organisations were blindsided on Friday with his plans to cancel the phase out of farrowing crates, and does he regard protecting animal welfare as his primary responsibility, or enacting the wishes of the pork industry?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy in the closing clause: protecting animal welfare and consulting the affected industry are presented as mutually exclusive, with nothing offered to establish that they are.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
rigor.explanation: Post hoc attribution: the job losses are dated after the pause and thereby credited to it, with nothing offered to separate the policy's effect from the wider construction downturn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let me explain: the statement of commitments does not indicate a drop in planned spending, it records, instead, at a particular point in time, where contracts have been signed that would involve the Crown spending money but the money hasn’t yet been paid or even owed.
rigor.explanation: Directly attacks the inference in the question by explaining what the cited accounting measure actually records, so the conclusion (no drop in planned spending is shown) follows from the definition offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, as has previously been traversed in this House, it is the case throughout New Zealand’s history that, as economies recover, fewer New Zealanders leave, and we expect that to be the case.
rigor.explanation: Rests on a general historical regularity without connecting it to the specific figure put to her; the inference from 'this has usually happened' to 'it will happen now' is offered with no supporting evidence about current conditions.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is the Minister going against independent welfare experts who say farrowing crates cause significant suffering for mother pigs and piglets; they increase the risk of stillbirth; restrict normal nesting behaviour of mother pigs; and cause boredom, sores, pain, and distress due to prolonged confinement?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the House — the named practice, the specific welfare harms alleged, and the expert advice against it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Isn’t the point that the damage is done, with 20,000 jobs gone after he decided to stop and pause infrastructure builds?
focus.explanation: Names a specific government decision and a specific claimed outcome. This is scrutiny of a policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Between now and Christmas, more than $7 billion worth of infrastructure projects will commence, including upgrades to Auckland City Hospital, Middlemore Hospital, Hawke’s Bay Hospital, the construction of a new acute mental health unit at Hutt Valley Hospital; over $5 billion worth of roading projects—the Ōtaki to north of Levin highway, Melling interchange, Waihoehoe Road, the Ōmanawa bridge; and more than $800 million in school property projects, which we’re building better and faster than ever before.
focus.explanation: Wholly about named public infrastructure projects and their cost, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Yes, it is the case that, as the economy recovers, we expect that more jobs will be created in the construction sector.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a recovery in construction sector employment; not a promise about the Government's own action but a prediction about a labour-market outcome.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / HLFS employment in the construction sector: true if construction employment is higher at the end of 2026 than at the September 2025 quarter; false if it is the same or lower.

divination.statement: Well, as has previously been traversed in this House, it is the case throughout New Zealand’s history that, as economies recover, fewer New Zealanders leave, and we expect that to be the case.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that departures of New Zealanders will fall as the economy recovers.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics: true if the annual number of New Zealand citizen departures for the year to December 2026 is materially lower than the year to September 2025; false if departures are flat or higher.

veracity.statement: Growing and strengthening the education workforce is exactly what this Government is doing, and, as I’ve already told the member on numerous occasions, the schooling teacher workforce grew by 2.5 percent in 2024, delivering 864 new teachers—the largest year-on-year increase since records began in 2009.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts about the 2024 schooling teacher workforce: a 2.5 percent growth rate, 864 additional teachers, and that this is the largest annual increase in the series since 2009.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education Teaching Workforce / Education Counts staffing series for 2024: true if headcount/FTE growth is ~2.5% and ~864 net additional teachers, and no year from 2009 onward shows a larger year-on-year increase; false if the growth figure or the 'largest since 2009' ranking is contradicted by that series.

veracity.statement: Why were teachers offered a pay rise of less than inflation when Crown board members are getting up to an 80 percent increase?
veracity.explanation: Two factual premises: that the teacher pay offer is below the inflation rate, and that Crown board members are receiving increases of up to 80 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZEI/PPTA collective agreement offer documents for the 2025 round compared against the Stats NZ CPI annual rate at the date of the offer, plus the Public Service Commission / Cabinet Fees Framework 2025 schedule of Crown entity board fees: true if the annualised offer is below CPI and some board fee rates rose by up to about 80 percent; false if either leg is not borne out.

veracity.statement: The 4.7 percent that is on the table at the moment is a fair and reasonable offer that we hope the New Zealand Educational Institute and Post Primary Teachers’ Association members will take seriously.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the offer currently before NZEI and PPTA members is 4.7 percent; read with the preceding sentence, that it meets the unions' call for an offer matching inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The offer documents tabled in the 2025 NZEI/PPTA collective bargaining round: true if the offer is 4.7 percent and, annualised over its term, is at or above the Stats NZ CPI annual rate at that date; false if the figure is not 4.7 percent or if annualising it over the term puts it below CPI.

veracity.statement: Does the Minister for the Public Service’s comments that people are striking just to have a long weekend increase or decrease the likelihood of strike action?
veracity.explanation: Embeds a factual claim that the Minister for the Public Service said striking workers were doing so merely to obtain a long weekend. The Minister disputed making the remark in the House immediately afterwards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A recorded, reported or Hansard-attributable statement by the Minister for the Public Service before 8 October 2025 characterising strikers as seeking a long weekend: true if such a statement exists in that form, false if no such remark is on the record and the attribution is a paraphrase of something materially different.

veracity.statement: Our Government has turned around the delivery of school property, we’ve halved the cost of building new classrooms, and children deserve to live in safe, warm, dry classrooms and we’re delivering just that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the per-classroom build cost has been reduced by half under this Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education published average per-classroom construction costs before and after the standardised/offsite classroom designs were introduced: true if the average cost is about 50 percent lower on a like-for-like basis, false if the reduction is materially smaller or is drawn from non-comparable classroom types.

veracity.statement: We are determined to reverse the trend we inherited, which saw people under the age of 25 on jobseeker spend an average of 18 more years on benefit. This has been 49 percent longer than in 2017.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an average projected 18 further years on benefit for under-25 jobseeker recipients, and that this is 49 percent longer than the equivalent 2017 figure. The Minister later gives the second figure as 47 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD Benefit System Performance Report / actuarial valuation figures for average future years on benefit for jobseeker recipients aged under 25, current year versus 2017: true if the average is about 18 years and the increase on 2017 is about 49 percent, false if either number is materially different.

veracity.statement: Why has she made it so that two parents who are both working 27 hours each on the minimum wage can now work 11 hours less a week and yet be financially better off?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the proposed parental income test a two-earner minimum-wage household at 27 hours each would be financially better off reducing to 16 hours each.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Modelling of the proposed parental income test threshold against the minimum wage and Working for Families abatement rates: true if net household income at 2 x 16 hours exceeds net household income at 2 x 27 hours once the 18/19-year-old's jobseeker entitlement is included, false if the household is worse off or no better off at the reduced hours.

veracity.statement: How can she claim that this change will incentivise young people when her Government has increased university fees, increased youth unemployment, cut the Apprenticeship Boost, and made life even harder for working Kiwi families struggling with the cost of living crisis?
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts about the Government's record: university fees have risen, youth unemployment has risen, and the Apprenticeship Boost has been cut.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission annual maximum fee movement settings since 2024; Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for 15–24 year olds, latest quarter versus late 2023; and Budget documents for the Apprenticeship Boost appropriation. True if fee maxima rose, the 15–24 unemployment rate is higher, and the Apprenticeship Boost's scope or funding was reduced; false if any of the three moved the other way.

veracity.statement: This survey follows an identical survey in 2022, and most critically, it shows that in nearly every single measure for nearly every type of person, attitudes to attendance are improving.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the ERO survey replicates a 2022 instrument and that attitudes to attendance improved on nearly every measure across nearly every respondent group.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ERO report 'Back to class: How are attitudes to attendance changing?' and its 2022 predecessor: true if the instrument is comparable and the great majority of measures show improvement across student, teacher and parent groups, false if the surveys are not comparable or if improvement is confined to a minority of measures or groups.

specificity.statement: We’ve strengthened the workforce by training 30,000 teachers in structured literacy, 20,000 in structured approaches to maths, and we’re delivering high-quality resources, professional learning and development, and, through Budget 2025, three-quarters of a billion dollars into learning support so that every single school has access to a learning support coordinator, along with 349 literacy intervention teachers for over 1,240 schools—exactly what the sector was asking for.
specificity.explanation: Carries counts of teachers trained, a named Budget, a dollar figure, a named role, and a count of intervention teachers and schools. Someone could go and check each element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has been backing teachers since the day that we took office with more professional learning and development, more resourcing, more moving of back-end resources to deliver to the front line, three-quarters of a billion dollars into learning support, and more intervention teachers in mathematics and literacy.
specificity.explanation: A direction with one real figure (three-quarters of a billion for learning support) but otherwise a list of 'more X' with no amounts, baselines or timeframes attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why were teachers offered a pay rise of less than inflation when Crown board members are getting up to an 80 percent increase?
specificity.explanation: Puts a numeric comparison on the table — an offer below the inflation rate against an increase of up to 80 percent — which is precise enough to be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The 4.7 percent that is on the table at the moment is a fair and reasonable offer that we hope the New Zealand Educational Institute and Post Primary Teachers’ Association members will take seriously.
specificity.explanation: Gives the actual percentage on the table and names both unions, though it does not say over what period the 4.7 percent applies.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The investment package includes $58 million for maintenance work for all schools, which is a 50 percent uplift in their school maintenance grant; $255 million for improvements for small, rural, and isolated schools; $100 million over five years to fund urgent and essential infrastructure work.
specificity.explanation: Three itemised dollar figures, the cohort each applies to, a percentage uplift, and a timeframe on the third tranche.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why has she made it so that two parents who are both working 27 hours each on the minimum wage can now work 11 hours less a week and yet be financially better off?
specificity.explanation: Names an exact household case — two minimum-wage earners at 27 hours each — and an exact behavioural margin of 11 fewer hours. Precise enough to be modelled and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve strengthened the workforce by training 30,000 teachers in structured literacy, 20,000 in structured approaches to maths, and we’re delivering high-quality resources, professional learning and development, and, through Budget 2025, three-quarters of a billion dollars into learning support so that every single school has access to a learning support coordinator, along with 349 literacy intervention teachers for over 1,240 schools—exactly what the sector was asking for.
focus.explanation: Entirely about named programmes and their resourcing; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why were teachers offered a pay rise of less than inflation when Crown board members are getting up to an 80 percent increase?
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision (the teacher pay offer) and a specific comparator (Crown board fees). This is scrutiny of a named outcome, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Will she accept responsibility for the anger that teachers, principals, and support staff are feeling, or will she continue to stick her head in the sand?
focus.explanation: A policy dispute is live, but the question names no policy, figure or outcome — it is about blame and how people feel, not about the offer's terms.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why has she made it so that two parents who are both working 27 hours each on the minimum wage can now work 11 hours less a week and yet be financially better off?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the parental income test and the incentive it creates at the threshold.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she claim that this change will incentivise young people when her Government has increased university fees, increased youth unemployment, cut the Apprenticeship Boost, and made life even harder for working Kiwi families struggling with the cost of living crisis?
focus.explanation: Names four specific things — fees, youth unemployment, the Apprenticeship Boost, cost of living — against the policy's own stated aim. Legitimate scrutiny of named commitments, though the closing clause is general framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could the Minister explain what giant leap in comprehension it takes for people to realise that the first responsibility for a family member lies with the family and not the taxpayer?
focus.explanation: Gestures at the principle behind the parental assistance test but names no part of the policy — a real policy point carried almost entirely by framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Will she accept responsibility for the anger that teachers, principals, and support staff are feeling, or will she continue to stick her head in the sand?
civility.explanation: 'Stick her head in the sand' lands on the Minister personally, imputing wilful avoidance rather than criticising the pay offer itself. Pointed criticism of the offer would have been costless here; this goes past it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Could the Minister explain what giant leap in comprehension it takes for people to realise that the first responsibility for a family member lies with the family and not the taxpayer?
civility.explanation: Frames disagreement as a failure of comprehension on the part of those who disagree — condescension aimed at people rather than at the argument for taxpayer support. Short of a direct insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This announcement is great for tradies, and what is great for tradies is great for our economy.
rigor.explanation: The economy-wide conclusion rests on a bare universal premise ('what is great for tradies is great for our economy') offered with no support — a sweeping generalisation standing in for an argument about the spending's net effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because what we don’t want to see is the welfare dependency that we saw blow out in the six years of the previous Government; as I said, a 47 percent increase in the length of time a young person under 25 would go on to spend on welfare.
rigor.explanation: The premise (long-term benefit duration rose under the previous Government) does not reach the conclusion that this particular abatement design is right — nothing offered connects the duration statistic to the threshold effect she was asked about. A real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I believe the most important number in New Zealand today is the number of children who go to school, because the amount of education that we pass from one generation to another more powerfully defines our future than anything else we can do on this day.
rigor.explanation: A superlative conclusion ('the most important number') rests on an equally sweeping unsupported premise about intergenerational education. Nothing is offered to rank it against any competing measure — assertion doing the work of an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
veracity.explanation: Two quantitative claims: that filled jobs/employment in New Zealand are down about 36,000, and that youth unemployment is up about 10,000, over the two years from the change of government in late 2023 to October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / Monthly Employment Indicator: compare total filled jobs (or total employment) for the September 2025 quarter against the September/December 2023 quarter, and the number of unemployed 15-24 year olds over the same period. True if the employment fall is approximately 36,000 and the rise in unemployed youth approximately 10,000; false if either differs materially (say by more than a third) or moves in the opposite direction.

veracity.statement: They have cut thousands of State home builds. They have scaled back infrastructure in hospitals, resulting in 15,000 fewer construction sector jobs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that construction sector employment has fallen by 15,000, and attributes that fall to reductions in State house building and hospital infrastructure. The checkable core is the 15,000 figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction-industry employment (HLFS by industry or Monthly Employment Indicator filled jobs, construction) between late 2023 and September 2025; plus Kāinga Ora build programme announcements and Health NZ capital deferrals. True if construction employment fell by roughly 15,000 over that period; false if the fall is materially smaller or employment rose.

veracity.statement: That probably explains why New Zealanders are, unfortunately, leaving in boatloads to the tune of approximately 200 every single day to Australia, because that is this Government’s policy on where the jobs are.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 200 New Zealanders per day are departing for Australia — i.e. of the order of 73,000 a year to that one destination.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the year to mid-2025: departures of New Zealand citizens with Australia stated as their destination (or net migration loss to Australia), divided by 365. True if approximately 200/day; false if materially lower (e.g. nearer 100/day, which would be the case if the ~200 figure covers all destinations rather than Australia alone).

veracity.statement: In his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Luxon described himself using the phrase 'wealthy and sorted'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media transcripts or recordings of Christopher Luxon's public remarks; true if he used that phrase about himself (widely reported around the 2023 election period), false if no such quotation exists or the phrase is materially misattributed or altered.

veracity.statement: When they stand up and they say, “Oh, the economy is turning a corner—turning a corner”, let’s be clear what that really means: it means thousands of people with no work; it means 200 Kiwis per day leaving Aotearoa New Zealand for Australia, for better opportunities; it means Kiwis here are unable to afford to see their GP.
veracity.explanation: The checkable assertion is that 200 New Zealanders per day are leaving for Australia — approximately 73,000 a year to that destination.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates for the year to mid/late 2025: departures of New Zealand citizens with Australia as destination (or net migration loss to Australia), divided by 365. True if approximately 200/day; false if materially lower, which would be the case if the ~200/day figure describes departures to all destinations rather than to Australia alone.

veracity.statement: It’s quite interesting to see, today, the Minister of Finance saying, “I didn’t take any credit for it”, despite, in the first question before that, saying the Government takes credit for it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in question time on 8 October 2025 the Minister of Finance disclaimed credit for falling interest rates having, in an earlier question the same day, claimed credit for them on the Government's behalf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of oral questions for 8 October 2025; true if the Minister of Finance's answers contain both the disclaimer and the earlier credit-claiming answer as characterised, false if either answer is absent or says materially otherwise.

specificity.statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
specificity.explanation: Two named figures attached to a named population and a defined time window; directly checkable against official statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Greens have spent the last 18 months outlining our solutions and our clear policies, which would see free early childhood education, free dentistry, and free GPs. We would create 40,000 good, green jobs because we used to make things in this country and we can do it again.
specificity.explanation: Three named policy commitments and a job-creation figure, which is well above a slogan — but no costings, no funding mechanism beyond 'a fairer tax system', and no timeframe for any of it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The next Labour Government won’t just be a Labour Government; it will be a Government for everybody in New Zealand, because when everybody thrives in New Zealand, our country thrives.
specificity.explanation: A slogan. No policy, mechanism, figure or timeframe — 'a Government for everybody' commits to nothing that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But, again, some of those basic facts: there are 36,000 fewer jobs and there are 10,000 more unemployed young people in the two years since this Government came to office and implemented their economic policies of firing up the shredder and cutting billions of dollars of investment in our economy and in our people.
focus.explanation: Names specific outcomes (jobs, youth unemployment) and ties them to the Government's economic policy. Legitimate scrutiny of a record, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Cuts are not how you build a country. Evidentially, it’s how you break one, and it is abundantly clear that this Government’s economic policy is to kill the golden goose: to whittle down our infrastructure to such an anaemic state and then to pass it off at bargain-bin prices to the private sector, and also then to exploit the very environment that we trade on on the international stage.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim here (infrastructure spending, privatisation, environmental standards), but no measure, figure or named programme is attached; the weight of the sentence is the 'kill the golden goose' framing of the other side's motives.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I really hope that New Zealanders understand just how much this Government laughs at the state of affairs which this Government is handing down to future generations, because this Government is choosing to intentionally make life harder for New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other team's conduct and character in the Chamber — that they laugh, and that they intend harm. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing here to hold the Government to account against.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Greens have spent the last 18 months outlining our solutions and our clear policies, which would see free early childhood education, free dentistry, and free GPs. We would create 40,000 good, green jobs because we used to make things in this country and we can do it again.
focus.explanation: Squarely about policy: what the party would do, in named areas. The only party-directed content is the closing aside.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The jeering from the other side of the House during the last speaker’s speech is exactly why that side of the House and the Government is so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders, because you can jeer and laugh at the teenagers who need jobs, you can jeer and laugh at the fact that we are doing nothing for climate change in this House because of that Government, and you can jeer and laugh at the fact that this economy is tanking because of their inaction, but they won’t think that’s funny, because they are so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: About the other side's behaviour and character in the House. Climate change and the economy are gestured at, but no policy, measure or figure is named — the content is that they laughed.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government isn’t on the side of ordinary New Zealanders; they’re on the side of tobacco companies, of property speculators, of the oil and gas industry.
focus.explanation: About whose side the other party is on. The three industries gesture at real policy areas (smokefree repeal, tax on property, oil and gas exploration), but no measure, figure or outcome is named, so the statement lands as a claim about allegiance rather than about policy.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That probably explains why New Zealanders are, unfortunately, leaving in boatloads to the tune of approximately 200 every single day to Australia, because that is this Government’s policy on where the jobs are.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the emigration figure is attributed to the Government's job cuts on the strength of the two things co-occurring. A premise was offered (jobs are down), so it is not a bare assertion, but nothing links the departures to that cause, and 'that is this Government's policy' converts an outcome into an intention without support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Cuts are not how you build a country. Evidentially, it’s how you break one, and it is abundantly clear that this Government’s economic policy is to kill the golden goose: to whittle down our infrastructure to such an anaemic state and then to pass it off at bargain-bin prices to the private sector, and also then to exploit the very environment that we trade on on the international stage.
rigor.explanation: Assertion dressed as demonstration: 'evidentially' and 'abundantly clear' stand in for evidence, none of which is offered. It also imputes intent from outcome — the claim that the Government's policy *is* to run infrastructure down in order to sell it cheaply does not follow from anything stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The jeering from the other side of the House during the last speaker’s speech is exactly why that side of the House and the Government is so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders, because you can jeer and laugh at the teenagers who need jobs, you can jeer and laugh at the fact that we are doing nothing for climate change in this House because of that Government, and you can jeer and laugh at the fact that this economy is tanking because of their inaction, but they won’t think that’s funny, because they are so disconnected from everyday New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Circular: 'they are disconnected' is both the conclusion and, restated at the end, the premise. The only evidence offered — jeering in the Chamber — is a non sequitur for the claim about being out of touch with the public.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Prime Minister is so out of touch that I bet you—and I’m willing to take a wager from anyone here in Parliament—that he hasn’t got a clue at all, because, in his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
rigor.explanation: An inference is offered (his own self-description supports the conclusion that he is out of touch), so it is not a bare insult, but the gap is large: a single soundbite about personal wealth is thin support for a general claim of not having 'a clue at all'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: According to the National Party MPs, they do not work hard.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The interjection being answered was 'He works hard; nothing wrong with working hard' — a claim about the Prime Minister. It is recast as National asserting that New Zealanders working two and three jobs do not work hard, which no one said.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We asked the Prime Minister at question time today if he could guarantee that there was a job available for every job seeker that he seems so intent on punishing, and he deflected from the question.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Prime Minister personally — that he is 'intent on punishing' jobseekers, i.e. that hardship is his aim rather than a consequence. Short of a direct insult, but it goes to motive rather than to the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Do you think Christopher Luxon has any idea what life is really like for everyday New Zealanders?
civility.explanation: A rhetorical question about the Prime Minister as a person — his understanding and life experience — rather than about any decision he has made. Aimed at the man, not the policy, though phrased as a question rather than an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Prime Minister is so out of touch that I bet you—and I’m willing to take a wager from anyone here in Parliament—that he hasn’t got a clue at all, because, in his own words, he is “wealthy and sorted”.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Prime Minister's personal competence and awareness — 'hasn't got a clue at all' — offered as a wager rather than as a criticism of any decision.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: After a period of consistent clarity about building, focusing on growth, focusing on investment, and giving confidence to the broader community, in our second and third terms the economy was growing well, and we managed to reverse the flow across the Tasman, and that’s going to happen again this time.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the net migration flow between New Zealand and Australia will reverse again under the current government, as he claims it did in National's second and third terms after 2008.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for NZ–Australia flows: true if a 12-month period on or before 2027-12-31 shows a net migration gain from Australia (arrivals exceeding departures); false if New Zealand records a continued net loss to Australia throughout.

focus.statement: It’s the Greens—it’s the sanctimonious “tofu wouldn’t melt in your mouth” Greens—who are the ones who are driving the division and acrimony within our body politic, aided and abetted by Labour.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the character of two other parties — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named. This is party framing rather than scrutiny of a specific commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My encouragement to all parties across the House is to just think twice about the approach that is taken around intimidation and, frankly, to support this legislation that we have before the House to ensure that no New Zealander has to suffer people intimidating them in their private home—in their castle—and to do the right thing by that.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at a measure before the House and what it is meant to do, rather than at the other parties' character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In addition to accusations and inquiries, the Government still attacks our people by continuing to keep te iwi Māori struggling: the cost of living crisis; the disestablishment of the Māori Health Authority; section 7AA, Oranga Tamariki; the Regulatory Standards Bill; Treaty principles bill; Marine and Coastal Area; removing tikanga Māori from justice systems; removing $30 million from Māori education.
focus.explanation: Names eight specific measures and a dollar figure — this is scrutiny of a government's programme, not content-free party-bashing, notwithstanding the adversarial framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is no place in this democracy for intimidation, and yet that is what we have been seeing over the last few weeks, months, and years. People are lining up, banging pots, using loud hailers, and intimidating politicians in their own homes. Chlöe Swarbrick and the Greens have been behind a lot of this, and the hypocrisy is, quite frankly, outrageous.
civility.explanation: Names an individual member and imputes bad faith to her personally ("the hypocrisy is, quite frankly, outrageous") rather than criticising a position or a policy. Short of direct abuse, but past the point of engaging the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This only further highlights that Māori will always be guilty by whakapapa, and that we will always be tried, convicted, and executed before the truth is revealed, whilst the wealthy get to hide behind name suppression and privilege. That’s how Māori are treated in this country’s media.
civility.explanation: A severe charge, but aimed at the media's conduct and at a systemic pattern — no individual is insulted or has their character, competence or motives attacked. Fierce criticism directed at conduct rather than a person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no place in this democracy for intimidation, and yet that is what we have been seeing over the last few weeks, months, and years. People are lining up, banging pots, using loud hailers, and intimidating politicians in their own homes. Chlöe Swarbrick and the Greens have been behind a lot of this, and the hypocrisy is, quite frankly, outrageous.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that a named MP is "behind" the intimidation rests on association rather than any link offered between her and the acts described; the hypocrisy charge is guilt by association across three different members' separate conduct.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When allegations were made against Manurewa Marae, Whānau Ora, Te Pou Matakana, and Te Pāti Māori, the headlines screamed corruption before a single fact was proven, and, when the truth came out—when the Police, Stats NZ, the Public Service Commission, and the Serious Fraud Office found no evidence, and when the successful Māori kaupapa were cleared—the media went quiet. That silence speaks volumes because, in this country, the presumption of guilt still has a whakapapa, and it’s brown.
rigor.explanation: The asymmetry premise (loud allegation coverage, quiet exoneration coverage) is offered with named instances and does support a claim of unequal treatment; the leap from those instances to a general racial presumption of guilt across the country is a hasty generalisation the evidence given does not carry.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: You look at a quote from Benjamin Doyle saying that “No person should have to avoid going to the supermarket or the letterbox because they’ve been advised that doing so would expose them to violence.”, and yet, at the same time, you’ve got Ricardo Menéndez March writing letters in support of people who vandalise MPs’ offices and, at the same time, you’ve got the leader of the Greens in press conferences with a peace-loving actor who hands out the private addresses of MPs for people to go and hassle them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Ricardo Menéndez March wrote letters in support of people who vandalised MPs' offices, and that the Green Party co-leader appeared at press conferences alongside a person who distributed MPs' private addresses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary news reporting and any court documents on letters of support or character references written by Ricardo Menéndez March for people charged with or convicted of vandalising MPs' offices, and reporting on Green co-leader press conferences and who appeared at them; true if such a letter and such an appearance are documented, false if no letter of support exists or the appearance did not occur.

veracity.statement: It’s interesting that we’ve seen Duncan Webb saying, “Well, no, actually, we’re going to stick to our guns. We think people should protest outside MPs’ houses.” and Mr Hipkins has said that they shouldn’t, but they both voted against the bill that we’ve got in the House that deals with it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Duncan Webb and Chris Hipkins both voted against the Government bill currently before the House dealing with intimidation at MPs' private residences, while taking publicly opposed positions on protest outside MPs' homes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the relevant reading of the Government bill on intimidation at private residences; true if Labour, including Webb and Hipkins, is recorded voting against it, false if they voted in favour or no such vote has been held. Webb's and Hipkins' quoted positions checkable against media reporting from the period.

veracity.statement: There have been 14 inquiries in the last 18 months into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori, and not a single allegation was upheld.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a count — 14 inquiries into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori between roughly April 2024 and October 2025 — and that none of them upheld any allegation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published reports of inquiries in that window by the Public Service Commission, Te Puni Kōkiri, the Electoral Commission, the Serious Fraud Office, Police and Stats NZ into Manurewa Marae, Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust, the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency and Te Pāti Māori; true if 14 such inquiries occurred and every one recorded no adverse finding, false if the count is materially different or any inquiry upheld an allegation (including adverse data-handling findings).

veracity.statement: When faced with the Treaty principles bill, over 100,000 people hikoi-ed and over 300,000 submissions were made—over 90 percent in opposition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three figures about opposition to the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill: over 100,000 participants in the hikoi, over 300,000 written submissions, and over 90 percent of those submissions opposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Principles of the Treaty of Waitangi Bill for the submission count and the proportion opposed, and Police/media crowd estimates for the November 2024 Hīkoi mō te Tiriti; true if submissions exceeded 300,000 with more than 90 percent opposed and credible estimates put hikoi participation above 100,000, false if any of the three is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: The latest Electoral Commission figures show that, since April 2023, almost 31,000 voters have switched to the Māori roll, and more than 25,000 first-time voters have gone for the Māori electoral option.
veracity.explanation: Attributes two specific enrolment figures to the Electoral Commission: nearly 31,000 switches to the Māori roll since April 2023, and over 25,000 first-time enrolees choosing the Māori roll.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electoral Commission published statistics on Māori electoral option roll changes since the option became continuous in April 2023; true if the switch figure is close to 31,000 and first-time Māori-roll enrolments exceed 25,000, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Over a billion people saw the haka led by Hana in Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than one billion people viewed the haka led by Hana-Rawhiti Maipi-Clarke in the House in November 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Aggregated platform view counts and contemporaneous reporting on the reach of the video; true if credible measurement supports viewership above one billion (distinguishing views from unique people), false if the best available estimates are an order of magnitude lower.

specificity.statement: My encouragement to all parties across the House is to just think twice about the approach that is taken around intimidation and, frankly, to support this legislation that we have before the House to ensure that no New Zealander has to suffer people intimidating them in their private home—in their castle—and to do the right thing by that.
specificity.explanation: Points at a purpose but names no bill, no provision, no threshold and no mechanism — "this legislation that we have before the House" leaves the reader unable to check or act on anything.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There have been 14 inquiries in the last 18 months into Māori organisations and Te Pāti Māori, and not a single allegation was upheld.
specificity.explanation: Carries a count and a timeframe and a defined class of subject, so a reader can go and enumerate the inquiries and their outcomes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The latest Electoral Commission figures show that, since April 2023, almost 31,000 voters have switched to the Māori roll, and more than 25,000 first-time voters have gone for the Māori electoral option.
specificity.explanation: Two figures, a named source and a start date — directly checkable against the Electoral Commission's published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Growth and more growth means jobs and more jobs, it means higher wages, and it means a better future for New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Opens with a chain of generic goods — growth, jobs, wages, a better future — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve slashed the red tape, we’ve got rid of the bureaucracy, and we’ve been out in the world hustling for trade deals so we have better markets to send our good products to, and, wow, is that making a difference.
specificity.explanation: Claims three categories of action but names no regulation removed, no agency or process cut, and no trade agreement or market. A listener could not check any part of it or identify what was actually done.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
specificity.explanation: A named sector, a dollar figure and a period — precise enough that anyone can look it up against the official export series.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So the news today of the official cash rate dropping another 50 basis points and decreasing mortgage rates is welcome news for families struggling with mortgage repayments, but it is also welcome news for our growers, farmers, and businesses across Hawke’s Bay because it gives confidence and certainty and more money to invest in growing our economy and creating jobs, and this lifts wages for everyone.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the day of the statement (8 October 2025) the Reserve Bank cut the Official Cash Rate by a further 50 basis points, and that mortgage rates are falling.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The RBNZ Monetary Policy Review/Statement dated 8 October 2025: true if the OCR was reduced by 50 basis points at that decision, false if the cut was a different size or there was no cut. Mortgage-rate direction checkable against RBNZ published new-lending mortgage interest rate series for the surrounding months.

veracity.statement: A highlight in the last few weeks was visiting the Hastings Stortford Lodge saleyards, and it was amazing to see the farmer confidence back again, with record highs in farmer confidence because finally they have a Government that is backing them and allowing our farmers to do what they do best, and that is farm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that measured farmer confidence is at record highs as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published farmer-confidence surveys covering mid-to-late 2025 — Federated Farmers Farm Confidence Survey and/or the Rabobank Rural Confidence Survey: true if the net confidence reading is the highest in the series' history, false if it is merely elevated or below earlier peaks in those series.

veracity.statement: For years, I sat on the board of New Zealand Apples and Pears, and under the Labour Government the apple industry could never meet the $1 billion export mark.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that apple export revenue never reached $1 billion in any year of the 2017–2023 Labour government, and (in the following sentences) that it has since exceeded that mark.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ / MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries apple (or apple and pear) export revenue by year: true if no year from 2017/18 to 2022/23 reached $1.0 billion and a year under the current Government did, false if any Labour-era year reached $1.0 billion.

veracity.statement: In fact, our horticulture exports have hit record highs: $8.5 billion this year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts total New Zealand horticulture export revenue of $8.5 billion in the current year, and that this is an all-time record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries horticulture export revenue series (year to 30 June 2025): true if revenue is approximately $8.5 billion and exceeds every prior year, false if materially different or below a previous year.

veracity.statement: Around 360,000 Kiwis are employed in our food and fibre sector, about 15 percent of the total workforce.
veracity.explanation: Two linked assertions: food and fibre sector employment of roughly 360,000, and that this is about 15 percent of the total New Zealand workforce.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries food and fibre employment estimate, divided by Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey total employment for the same period: true if employment is near 360,000 AND the share is near 15 percent, false if the share is materially lower (e.g. closer to 12–13 percent) even where the headcount is right.

veracity.statement: They have used the Investment Boost package of this Government, which enabled a 20 percent tax deduction along with depreciation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the design of the Government's Investment Boost policy: a 20 percent deduction on qualifying new asset spending, available in addition to ordinary depreciation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Inland Revenue / Budget 2025 documentation for Investment Boost: true if the scheme allows an immediate 20 percent deduction of a new asset's cost with normal depreciation applying to the remainder, false if the rate, the eligibility or the interaction with depreciation differs materially from that description.

rigor.statement: So the news today of the official cash rate dropping another 50 basis points and decreasing mortgage rates is welcome news for families struggling with mortgage repayments, but it is also welcome news for our growers, farmers, and businesses across Hawke’s Bay because it gives confidence and certainty and more money to invest in growing our economy and creating jobs, and this lifts wages for everyone.
rigor.explanation: The first step (a rate cut lowers repayments and eases business borrowing) follows, but the conclusion is stretched to "this lifts wages for everyone" with no connecting step offered between cheaper credit and universal wage growth. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A highlight in the last few weeks was visiting the Hastings Stortford Lodge saleyards, and it was amazing to see the farmer confidence back again, with record highs in farmer confidence because finally they have a Government that is backing them and allowing our farmers to do what they do best, and that is farm.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal attribution: the rise in confidence is credited to the current Government purely on the basis that it coincides with it. No mechanism or evidence links the two, and obvious alternative drivers (commodity prices, interest rates) are not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I love these stories. We need to keep creating jobs and opportunities, which is done by supporting our primary sector.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that job creation is achieved by supporting the primary sector — rests on a single anecdote about one worker in one packhouse. Appeal to anecdote; nothing is offered to show the case is representative or that the policy caused it.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In Hawke’s Bay alone, our region is set to add another thousand new jobs in agriculture and horticulture.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a future increase of about 1,000 agriculture and horticulture jobs in the Hawke's Bay region. It is an outcome forecast about the regional labour market, not a commitment to an action by the speaker or her Government.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled-jobs / Infometrics regional employment data for Hawke's Bay, agriculture and horticulture industries: true if employment in those industries rises by at least roughly 1,000 above the 2025 level, false if the increase is materially smaller or employment falls.

veracity.statement: That COVID hangover was caused by the previous Labour Government spending $66 billion of taxpayer money and raking up debt, over twice, to 44 percent of gross domestic product. That was the largest debt-fuelled spending binge in the developed world, according to the IMF.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable things: a $66 billion COVID spend by the 2017-23 Labour Government, net core Crown debt roughly doubling to 44 percent of GDP, and an IMF finding that this was the largest debt-funded fiscal response in the developed world.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury fiscal strategy/Budget documents for the COVID-19 Response and Recovery Fund total and the net core Crown debt-to-GDP series; and the IMF Fiscal Monitor database of above-the-line COVID fiscal support as a share of GDP. True if the fund is ~$66b, debt peaked near 44 percent of GDP, and the IMF series ranks New Zealand first among advanced economies; false if the IMF series places other advanced economies higher.

veracity.statement: That approval took place in 66 days, in record time—record time that would have never happened under the previous Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the fast-track consent for the Fergusson north berth extension at the Port of Auckland was granted in 66 days and that this was a record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Fast-track Approvals decision record for the Port of Auckland Fergusson north berth project: elapsed days between lodgement/referral and the panel decision, compared against the elapsed times of other fast-track approvals to date. True if 66 days and the shortest on record; false if the elapsed time differs materially or a shorter approval exists.

veracity.statement: Light rail to nowhere; the Skypath, $50 million of money spent and nothing delivered.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly $50 million was spent on the SkyPath/Northern Pathway with nothing delivered, and that Auckland light rail delivered nothing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA Waka Kotahi financial disclosures and Auckland Light Rail Ltd wind-up reporting on total expenditure and physical works delivered for each project. True if SkyPath spend was ~$50m with no constructed crossing; false if the spend figure is materially different or physical works were delivered.

veracity.statement: The National Party has dipped into the 20s, that psychological number that has every backbencher shaking in their boots, watching their majority disappear.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Curia poll released on this date put National's party vote below 30 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Curia/Taxpayers' Union poll published in the week of 8 October 2025: National's party-vote figure. True if below 30.0 percent, false if 30.0 percent or above.

veracity.statement: The gentailer’s share prices soared. That's how significant they were in reforming a broken market.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that gentailer share prices rose sharply on the day the Government announced its electricity market reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZX closing prices for the listed gentailers (Meridian, Mercury, Contact, Genesis) on the announcement day in the week to 8 October 2025 versus the prior close. True if they rose materially against the index; false if they fell or were flat.

veracity.statement: Simon Bridges, a former leader of the National Party, made it clear that the National Party had let the country down, that it had missed its opportunity and was not delivering what should be there.
veracity.explanation: The speaker is relaying a criticism she attributes to Simon Bridges; what is checkable is whether he said substantially this about the energy reform package.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, interviews or media reports by Simon Bridges on the Government's electricity market reform package in the fortnight to 8 October 2025. True if he criticised it as a missed opportunity or a failure to deliver; false if he made no such comment or endorsed the package.

veracity.statement: In the Manawatū, Canterbury, and Waikato under Plan Change 1, regional rules demand consents for what commons sense says should be permitted: growing food for people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Plan Change 1 rules in the named regions require resource consent for commercial vegetable growing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The operative text of Waikato Regional Plan Change 1 and the equivalent Canterbury and Horizons (Manawatū) plan provisions: the activity status assigned to commercial vegetable production. True if consent is required (discretionary or restricted discretionary) in the named regions; false if such growing is a permitted activity.

specificity.statement: That COVID hangover was caused by the previous Labour Government spending $66 billion of taxpayer money and raking up debt, over twice, to 44 percent of gross domestic product. That was the largest debt-fuelled spending binge in the developed world, according to the IMF.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a debt-to-GDP percentage and a named source; someone could go and check every element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve got Fulton Hogan Land Development, and they’re delivering around 1,100 housing units to the total of $595 million—again, under this Government’s fast-track approvals regime, which never would have happened under the previous Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the developer, the location, the number of dwellings, the total value and the consenting pathway.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s going to mean an estimated $4.5 billion does not need to be spent on strengthening buildings right across the Auckland division.
specificity.explanation: A single named consequence with a dollar estimate attached to a named regulatory change; checkable against the reform's impact statement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In a few months, this Government—and it's set out in the Government's quarter four plan—will introduce a new resource management system with two focused laws: a natural environment Act which sets clear environmental rules suited to each region, so we stop arguing over trivia and focus on the real environmental risks that we need to manage.
specificity.explanation: Names the replacement statutes, the mechanism (regional environmental limits), and a rough timeframe tied to a published Government work plan. Missing exact dates and thresholds, but well above a direction of travel.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Light rail to nowhere; the Skypath, $50 million of money spent and nothing delivered.
focus.explanation: Names two specific projects and a specific spend-versus-delivery outcome. This is scrutiny of a named policy record rather than content-free party-bashing, so it scores high even though it is aimed at the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are at least four job seekers sitting on that front bench queuing up for that job, and Christopher Luxon’s days are numbered.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal state — leadership ambitions on its front bench. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In the Manawatū, Canterbury, and Waikato under Plan Change 1, regional rules demand consents for what commons sense says should be permitted: growing food for people.
focus.explanation: Names a specific regional plan change, the regions affected, and the activity it regulates. Squarely about the policy instrument at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think the only person in Auckland that doesn’t want that to go ahead is Helen Clark, but that is going to provide real economic opportunity for this country.
civility.explanation: Singles out a named individual for mockery, casting her as the lone obstacle to a public good. Not abusive, but it lands on the person rather than her argument about stadium use.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is from the Government's own pollster, Curia, and I think this speaks very much to how weak and out of touch Christopher Luxon is showing New Zealanders he is.
civility.explanation: A direct attack on a named individual's personal qualities — weakness and being out of touch — rather than on any policy or decision.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If John Key was the “Teflon” Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon is showing himself to be the “Velcro” Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: A mocking label attached to a named individual. Pointed ridicule of the person rather than criticism of a decision, though short of abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: At best, Simon Watts stumbled to the cupboard and grabbed a Disprin—that's how far from a surgical set of reforms.
civility.explanation: Ridicule of a named Minister — the image is of the person bumbling, not of a defect in the reform package. Mockery, so a genuine failure, but not a character attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, unless trout grow legs and buy hiking boots, they’re not getting there. That’s not environmental protection; it’s performance art.
civility.explanation: Scathing about a regulatory decision and the consent condition behind it, but attacks no person — exactly the case where fierce criticism of a policy scores at the top of the scale.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There are at least four job seekers sitting on that front bench queuing up for that job, and Christopher Luxon’s days are numbered.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Christopher Luxon will lose the National Party leadership before his term as Prime Minister runs its course. It is a prediction about someone else's political fate, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The National Party leadership as recorded by the party and Parliament between 8 October 2025 and the 2026 general election. True if Luxon ceases to be leader of the National Party before that election; false if he leads the party into it.

divination.statement: What we have is a set of reforms that are not going to make energy cheaper for New Zealand households and businesses.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the announced electricity market reforms will not reduce energy costs for households and businesses. An outcome of someone else's policy, not a promise about her own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI electricity subindex and MBIE's Quarterly Survey of Domestic Electricity Prices, plus commercial electricity price series, from the reform's announcement to mid-2027. True (prediction correct) if real household and business electricity prices are flat or higher over that period; false if they fall in real terms.

rigor.statement: The gentailer’s share prices soared. That's how significant they were in reforming a broken market.
rigor.explanation: Offers a market signal as evidence that the reforms do not threaten incumbents — a real inference with supporting evidence, but a share-price move has other drivers and the conclusion is stated more strongly than the single data point supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These aren’t isolated tales; this is the Resource Management Act. The result is higher power bills, dearer groceries, slower housing investors who simply walk away.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: four unattributed anecdotes are declared representative of an entire statute by assertion, and then a chain of economy-wide effects is attributed to it with nothing offered to connect the anecdotes to the outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, there are 20,000 fewer construction jobs in New Zealander under his watch. There are 36,000 fewer people employed in New Zealand right now, over the past two years, under the watch of Christopher Luxon.
veracity.explanation: Two quantified employment claims: that construction employment has fallen by 20,000 and total employment by 36,000 over the two years since the change of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / filled-jobs series: construction industry employment and total employment, Q3 2023 compared with Q3 2025. True if construction is down by approximately 20,000 and total employment down by approximately 36,000; false if either differs materially in size or direction.

veracity.statement: Every single day, 200 New Zealanders leave our country.
veracity.explanation: A rate claim about departures of New Zealanders — roughly 73,000 a year — ambiguous between gross departures of NZ citizens and net migration loss.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for NZ citizens, latest annual period: true if gross departures (or net loss) of NZ citizens run at approximately 73,000 a year; false if materially below that on both the gross and net measures.

veracity.statement: They have increased youth unemployment—record levels of young people in New Zealand without employment or without any opportunities to retrain or focus on skills development.
veracity.explanation: Asserts youth unemployment is at record levels — i.e. the highest in the recorded series, not merely elevated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for 15–24 year olds (and the NEET rate) across the full series: true if the current print is the highest on record; false if any earlier period, such as the post-GFC years, was higher.

veracity.statement: A 2016 report confirmed the scheme contributes more than $100 million annually to the regional GDP and supports over 1,300 full-time job equivalents.
veracity.explanation: Attributes two specific economic figures for the Kerikeri irrigation scheme — over $100m annual regional GDP contribution and over 1,300 FTEs — to a named 2016 report.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2016 economic assessment of the Kerikeri irrigation scheme (Northland Regional Council / Kerikeri Irrigation Company commissioned work): true if it states an annual regional GDP contribution above $100 million and more than 1,300 FTEs; false if the report gives materially different figures or no such finding exists.

veracity.statement: Completed in May 2023, Matawii has a capacity of 750,000 cubic metres of water and serves two vital purposes: it acts as a crucial backup to Kaikohe township’s water supply, and also, most importantly, it has unlocked land for high-value development.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a completion date (May 2023) and a storage capacity (750,000 m³) for the Matawii reservoir, plus its function as backup supply for Kaikohe.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Tai Tokerau Water Trust and Kānoa/Provincial Growth Fund project records for Matawii reservoir: true if completion is dated to May 2023 and capacity is stated as approximately 750,000 cubic metres; false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: Our economy hasn’t grown; it’s gone backwards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand economy has contracted rather than grown over the period since the change of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ national accounts, real GDP and real GDP per capita, Q4 2023 through the most recent quarter to October 2025: true if the level is lower at the end of the period than at the start on at least the headline real GDP measure; false if real GDP is higher.

specificity.statement: At the Penrose mill in Auckland, 75 jobs gone. Smithfield meat works in Timaru shut its doors after 138 years of operating in New Zealand. Columbine Industries in Gisborne: 45 jobs gone there.
specificity.explanation: Named sites, named towns and exact job counts — every element is checkable against company announcements.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We believe in an economy that serves everybody, not the other way around. We believe that every person deserves a fair pay that pays a decent wage; good jobs that grow local economies and grow local communities.
specificity.explanation: A statement of values with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker
