specificity.statement: A 2016 report confirmed the scheme contributes more than $100 million annually to the regional GDP and supports over 1,300 full-time job equivalents.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a dollar figure and an employment figure — precise enough for anyone to go and verify.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealanders cannot go to the regions and look for a job, because there aren’t any jobs there.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: a list of individual plant closures is offered as grounds for the far stronger conclusion that no jobs exist anywhere in the regions. Nothing about regional vacancy levels is supplied to bridge that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The lesson of Kerikeri, reinforced by the rapid success of Matawii, is clear: water security is the foundation of economic growth in Northland.
rigor.explanation: Evidence was genuinely offered beforehand — GDP contribution, FTEs, land values, the T&G joint venture — so the inference is not bare. But it generalises from two schemes to water security being 'the foundation' of regional growth, which is a stronger conclusion than the two cases support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The answer is worse, because this Government is making it happen.
rigor.explanation: Causal conclusion drawn straight from a single anecdote (three children outside a Christchurch food bank) with no mechanism or evidence linking any government decision to that observation — post hoc reasoning resting on an appeal to emotion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government’s mismanagement and waste comes from cancelling new ferries and stopping and cancelling projects, contributing to 20,000 jobs—20,000 jobs—gone in construction; manufacturing closures in several regions across the country, costing vital, local jobs; and handing over hundreds of millions of dollars to tobacco companies, and billions of dollars to property speculators, to name just a few.
rigor.explanation: A list of decisions is asserted to have caused 20,000 construction job losses and nationwide manufacturing closures, with no accounting offered for how much of the fall those decisions explain. The tobacco and 'property speculators' items are loaded characterisations of tax changes substituted for argument rather than premises supporting the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When people are trying to find some sort of vision, some sort of hope in New Zealand, they’re being driven overseas, because the only green shoots going on here is for those members’ mates in those circles that they operate in.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith rather than engaging the substance: the suggestion is that Government members are steering benefits to personal associates. Short of a direct insult, but a sneer at motive rather than at policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Christopher Luxon made big promises on tackling the cost of living and fixing the economy, but, instead, he’s making things worse. He’s out of touch and he’s refusing to take responsibility.
civility.explanation: Moves off the record and onto the person: 'out of touch' and 'refusing to take responsibility' are claims about Luxon's character and judgement rather than about any policy.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In the last quarter alone, GDP fell 0.9 percent, and whilst Christopher Luxon, like that member, likes to talk about rights and responsibilities, you’ll never hear him—or her—take responsibility for the damage they are doing to our economy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that GDP fell 0.9 percent in the most recent quarter before October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure) for the quarter most recently published as at 8 October 2025 (the June 2025 quarter); true if the quarterly change is -0.9% to within rounding, false if materially different or of the opposite sign.

veracity.statement: Australia is up 0.6 percent, the United Kingdom is up 0.3 percent, the United States is up 0.8 percent, Japan is up 0.5 percent, and China is up 1.1 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the most recent quarterly GDP growth rates for Australia, the UK, the US, Japan and China as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Quarter-on-quarter real GDP growth for the June 2025 quarter from each national statistics agency (ABS, ONS, BEA, Japan Cabinet Office, China NBS) or the OECD quarterly GDP series; true if each of the five figures matches within rounding, false if any is materially different or of the wrong sign.

veracity.statement: Our first Māori MP was elected in 1867—James Carroll.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that New Zealand's first Māori MP entered Parliament in 1867 and that this person was James Carroll.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Parliament's register of members and the Māori Representation Act 1867; true if James Carroll was the first Māori MP and was elected in 1867, false if the first Māori members were elected at a different date or if Carroll was not the first Māori MP.

veracity.statement: There was also Peter Buck; Āpirana Ngata; Māui Pōmare; Iriaka Matiu Rātana, the first female Māori MP who served for 20 years; and Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan, the first female Minister, who, at the time she left Parliament, was the longest-serving female MP.
veracity.explanation: Three checkable claims: that Iriaka Rātana was the first Māori woman MP and served 20 years, that Whetu Tirikatene-Sullivan was New Zealand's first female Minister, and that she was the longest-serving female MP when she left Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Parliament's register of members and the official list of ministerial appointments; true if Rātana's service spans about 20 years and she was the first Māori woman MP, and if no woman held a ministerial warrant before Tirikatene-Sullivan and no woman had served longer than her at her departure; false if an earlier woman was appointed a Minister, or if either service claim does not match the record.

civility.statement: In the last quarter alone, GDP fell 0.9 percent, and whilst Christopher Luxon, like that member, likes to talk about rights and responsibilities, you’ll never hear him—or her—take responsibility for the damage they are doing to our economy.
civility.explanation: Names Christopher Luxon and another member personally and charges them with never taking responsibility. The criticism of the economic record itself would be fully civil; the added imputation that they personally always evade responsibility edges onto the people rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’re all going up, but the economic ineptitude on that side of the House is having real impacts on everyday Kiwis which looks like soaring unemployment, record homelessness, and children standing on the footpath in the rain outside food banks, instead of inside warm, dry homes or in their classrooms.
civility.explanation: 'Economic ineptitude on that side of the House' is aimed at the governing benches collectively, not at any individual, and the rest of the sentence is about outcomes. No person is attacked.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In the last moments of the House sitting before the recent two-week recess, we were forced to endure insult and indignity in this House by the dishonourable speech given by an MP for whom we had accommodated his desire to give a departing speech, an MP who had spent, in terms of the life of this Parliament, a matter of moments here.
civility.explanation: Calls a named colleague's speech 'dishonourable' and belittles them personally as an MP who was here 'a matter of moments' — the charge is against the departing member's character and worth rather than against anything they argued.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What an insult to our proud legacy, to the country that was the first to give women the vote in the world—the cowardice and ignorance of that passing shot by a member who did nothing to use the privilege afforded by being an MP in this Parliament and who threw passing shots and ran out the door, believing there would be no right of reply.
civility.explanation: Sustained attack on the person: cowardice, ignorance, 'did nothing', and running out the door. It is directed at the departing member's character and worth, not at the content of what they said.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Then, over the last days, the party that Benjamin Doyle represented has been associated with an attack on a Minister of the Crown’s home. Apparently, we are to believe it is a really long bow to draw to suggest there is a connection. Well, I think not.
civility.explanation: Imputes complicity in a violent act to a named former member's party without offering evidence — an insinuation of very bad faith rather than an engagement with anything the party said or did.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Australia is up 0.6 percent, the United Kingdom is up 0.3 percent, the United States is up 0.8 percent, Japan is up 0.5 percent, and China is up 1.1 percent.
specificity.explanation: Five named comparator economies each with a figure to one decimal place — anyone can look these up and check them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With a real long-term plan, we can build on these strengths to grow New Zealand, to create new, good jobs, better healthcare, affordable homes, and real action on the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: A list of generic goods — jobs, healthcare, homes, cost-of-living action — with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named policy. The 'real long-term plan' is asserted but never described.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They’re all going up, but the economic ineptitude on that side of the House is having real impacts on everyday Kiwis which looks like soaring unemployment, record homelessness, and children standing on the footpath in the rain outside food banks, instead of inside warm, dry homes or in their classrooms.
rigor.explanation: Comparator growth figures are genuinely offered as evidence, but the step from 'other economies grew and ours did not' to 'the Government is inept and is causing these harms' is left unmade — nothing rules out shared or domestic causes outside policy — and the conclusion is carried by an emotive image of children outside food banks rather than by the data.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member was an MP in a party led by two women, yet we were told this is a hostile and toxic place unless you’re a cis white man in a black suit and a briefcase.
rigor.explanation: A genuine counterexample argument: the composition of the member's own party leadership is offered as evidence against the claim they made. The inference is sound as far as it goes, though there is a gap — who leads a party does not by itself settle whether others experience the House as hostile.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Then, over the last days, the party that Benjamin Doyle represented has been associated with an attack on a Minister of the Crown’s home. Apparently, we are to believe it is a really long bow to draw to suggest there is a connection. Well, I think not.
rigor.explanation: Guilt by association. The conclusion that there is 'a connection' between a party and an attack on a Minister's home rests on nothing but proximity in time and the speaker's assertion; no link is offered, and the rhetorical 'I think not' substitutes for an argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Home to more than 1.7 million people, around one-third of the country’s population, Auckland's continued growth affects our national progress, but with that growth comes real and complex challenges: purchase of infrastructure, transportation, environmental concern, and the ongoing needs for sustainable investment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Auckland's resident population exceeds 1.7 million and that this is approximately one-third of New Zealand's total population.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland region and national population estimate at the nearest reference date to October 2025; true if Auckland exceeds 1.7 million and its share of the national total rounds to roughly one-third (30-35%), false if materially outside that.

veracity.statement: In December 2024, the board sold Auckland Council’s shares in Auckland International Airport Limited at $8.08 per share.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a date and a per-share sale price for Auckland Council's divestment of its Auckland International Airport shareholding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / Auckland Future Fund disclosures and NZX announcements for the December 2024 sell-down of the council's Auckland International Airport stake; true if the sale settled in December 2024 at approximately $8.08 per share, false if the date or price is materially different.

veracity.statement: In the 2024-25 financial year, the fund generated $38.4 million in distribution income compared to just $10.2 million in dividends that would have come from retaining the airport shares.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two figures: actual distribution income from the fund in FY2024-25, and the counterfactual dividend income the retained airport shareholding would have produced over the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Future Fund and Auckland Council FY2024-25 annual reports for the distribution income figure, and Auckland International Airport's declared dividends per share for that year multiplied by the council's former holding for the counterfactual; true if both figures match within rounding, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: We know that, in many of these measures, we are going backwards: prosperity, innovation, knowledge, culture, experience, place, connectivity is a big one, resilience, and sustainability.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland's benchmarked performance declined across the listed domains in the State of the City report referred to in the preceding sentences.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2025 State of the City benchmarking report for Auckland (Committee for Auckland / Deloitte); true if Auckland's ranking or score fell versus the prior edition across most of the named domains, false if it held or improved on most of them.

specificity.statement: This requires a 75 percent super majority of the council’s governing body to approve certain distribution resolutions.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact voting threshold and the class of decision it applies to — a mechanism a reader could check against the bill and act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In December 2024, the board sold Auckland Council’s shares in Auckland International Airport Limited at $8.08 per share.
specificity.explanation: A dated transaction with an exact price per share — fully checkable against market and council records.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s an investment in resilience, innovation, and the wellbeing of our communities.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named action — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is esteemed to return 7.24 percent per annum over the long term, with 5.2 percent returned to council as an annual cash distribution, and the rest protecting the real value of the fund.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages tied to a named mechanism (cash distribution versus capital retention) — checkable against the fund's reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: First, having a statutory protection gives Aucklanders lasting confidence in the fund’s purpose and governance, unlike council policy or trustees, which can be changed by future councils.
rigor.explanation: Premise (policy and trust deeds can be altered by a future council, statute cannot be) genuinely supports the conclusion (legislation is needed for durable confidence). No fallacy or appeal; the inference tracks the stated contrast.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Restricting them to Auckland alone would reduce this diversification, expose the fund to unnecessary regional risks, and could undermine long-term return and limited performance.
rigor.explanation: Standard portfolio reasoning: narrowing an investment universe to one region concentrates risk and reduces diversification, from which the return conclusion follows. The chain from premise to conclusion is intact.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Combining both the capital value and income, the council is currently around $100 million better off than it would have been without the fund.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion aggregates figures actually supplied earlier, so it is not a non-sequitur — but the capital component rests on a counterfactual priced at a single favourable comparison point (the August 2025 low), which is a selection gap between what was shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Restricting them to Auckland alone would reduce this diversification, expose the fund to unnecessary regional risks, and could undermine long-term return and limited performance.
focus.explanation: Directly engages a design question about the measure before the House — the geographic scope of the fund's investment mandate and its consequences. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The thing is, the promises that this Government made to Aucklanders haven’t been achieved.
focus.explanation: An accountability claim, but it names no specific promise, programme, figure or outcome — the weight falls on the other party's record in general rather than on any policy that could be checked.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I acknowledge Mayor Wayne Brown for the work that he’s done, along with his council, to move this Government to take one action—one action—to generate better outcomes for Aucklanders, because the Government has been woeful on real action on the cost of living for Aucklanders.
focus.explanation: Credits a named actor for a named legislative outcome, but the criticism attached to it ('woeful on real action on the cost of living') identifies no measure, figure or commitment; it is party framing around a thin policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This is esteemed to return 7.24 percent per annum over the long term, with 5.2 percent returned to council as an annual cash distribution, and the rest protecting the real value of the fund.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the fund's long-run annual return and the share of it paid out to council each year as a cash distribution.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Auckland Future Fund annual reports; true if the realised long-run annualised return is approximately 7.24% and the annual cash distribution to council runs at approximately 5.2% of fund value, false if either materially undershoots or overshoots.

civility.statement: I acknowledge Mayor Wayne Brown for the work that he’s done, along with his council, to move this Government to take one action—one action—to generate better outcomes for Aucklanders, because the Government has been woeful on real action on the cost of living for Aucklanders.
civility.explanation: Harsh about the Government's record — 'woeful' — but the target is the Government's action on cost of living, not any person's character or competence. Criticism of a record is civil under this scale.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: People are paying more for public transport in our city than they ever have in the last two decades.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland public transport fares are at their highest level in twenty years. The claim is about the present compared with a defined past window, so it is a factual assertion rather than a prediction or an opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport published adult AT HOP and cash fare schedules plus average fare paid per boarding, 2005-2025, deflated by Stats NZ CPI. True if the 2025 fare level is the highest of any year in that window; false if any earlier year in the period was higher.

veracity.statement: As a member of the Governance and Administration Committee that examined this bill, I can report that we've unanimously recommended that it be passed without amendment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific committee outcome: that the Governance and Administration Committee's report on the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill recommended passage unanimously and with no amendments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Governance and Administration Committee's report to the House on the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill. True if the report records a recommendation that the bill be passed without amendment and records no minority or differing view; false if the report recommends amendments or records a party dissent.

focus.statement: Where’s your investment in public transport? It’s gone backwards—there’s less.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a policy area — public transport investment — rather than about the other parties in general, but it is addressed at 'your' investment and names no programme, appropriation or figure to anchor the accountability claim.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The National Party members and the ACT Party members who are heckling across the other side, I challenge them to step up. Step up and invest in Auckland.
focus.explanation: Directed at the two governing parties as teams; 'invest in Auckland' gestures at a policy area but names no measure, sum or programme, so the weight of the remark is party framing rather than policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I am talking to the bill, because what you’ll understand about the Auckland Future Fund is that it’s about investment in our city—something that you have not done, Government members have not done.
focus.explanation: Names the specific measure before the House (the Auckland Future Fund) and its purpose, but the sentence turns to a general charge against 'Government members' without naming a commitment or outcome they missed. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Where’s your investment in public transport? It’s gone backwards—there’s less.
specificity.explanation: A direction of travel with no figure, no named fund or project, and no timeframe. 'There's less' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It requires public consultation through a long-term plan process and a resolution to be passed by at least 75 percent of council members.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism (long-term plan consultation) and the exact voting threshold (75 percent of council members) that gate a distribution from the fund. Someone could check this against the bill and act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The National Party members and the ACT Party members who are heckling across the other side, I challenge them to step up. Step up and invest in Auckland.
civility.explanation: Robust and directly addressed at opponents mid-heckle, but the challenge lands on their conduct as parties in the debate, not on any individual's character, competence or worth. No insult.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That unanimity reflects both the straightforward nature of this legislation and the quality of the process behind it.
rigor.explanation: Infers two causes — simplicity of the bill and quality of the select committee process — from the single fact of a unanimous recommendation. The inference is plausible but under-determined: unanimity is equally consistent with low salience or with the bill being a council request nobody wished to contest. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There have been far too many bills going through a curtailed process and it will not only have bad effects in the community but it will waste time in the next Parliament when we could be working constructively.
rigor.explanation: Offers a premise (curtailed legislative process) and draws two conclusions (harm in the community, wasted time in the next Parliament), but supplies no mechanism or instance linking truncated scrutiny to either outcome. The conclusion is asserted rather than derived — a gap between what was offered and what was claimed, though not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I just want to note that this bill’s probably unanimous passing should be a more frequent occurrence in this House.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill will pass its remaining stages without opposition. This is a prediction about the House's collective conduct, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division or voice-vote record for the third reading of the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill. True if the bill passes with no party voting against; false if any party or member is recorded opposing, or if the bill does not pass.

divination.statement: Your bill will succeed.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Carlos Cheung's Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill will be passed by the House — an outcome outside the speaker's sole control, and settled by the parliamentary record.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill: true if the bill passes its third reading and receives Royal assent; false if it is voted down, lapses, or is still not passed when the Parliament expires.

veracity.statement: That is why, in addition to all the other things that Auckland Council already has on its list—there’s a $4 billion shortfall between the infrastructure it knows it needs to fund and the amount of money it can get from ratepayers—it also is going to have to turn its mind to another million people coming, according to the Auckland plan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific $4 billion gap between Auckland Council's identified infrastructure need and its ratepayer-funded capacity, and attributes a further one million residents to the Auckland Plan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's Long-term Plan 2024–2034 and supporting infrastructure strategy: true if the documented gap between identified infrastructure need and funded capacity is approximately $4 billion, and the Auckland Plan projects roughly a further one million residents; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s projects like that that have cost half a billion dollars or more, wasting Auckland ratepayers’ money and that have led to the situation where Auckland’s run out of money for infrastructure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland Council's kerbside food-scraps collection (and comparable projects) cost half a billion dollars or more.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council budget and annual-report figures for the food scraps collection service — capital cost of the truck fleet and bins plus operating cost to date: true if the total reaches or exceeds $500 million; false if it is materially below that.

veracity.statement: Well, that was never planned or funded by the previous Labour Government or the previous ex-Labour mayor, Phil Goff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that grade separation of Auckland rail level crossings was neither planned nor funded under the 2017–2023 Labour Government or Phil Goff's mayoralty.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Transport / KiwiRail level crossing removal programme documents, ATAP packages and NLTP allocations for 2017–2023: false if any planning work or funding for level crossing grade separation was allocated in that period; true if no such planning or funding exists.

veracity.statement: Well, this Government has committed to the City Rail Link projects and put down around $200 million for the first stage of grade separation in some of those really important parts of the network out in South Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current-government commitment of approximately $200 million for the first stage of level crossing grade separation in South Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 / NZTA National Land Transport Programme and Ministry of Transport announcements on Auckland level crossing removal: true if a commitment of about $200 million for a first stage of South Auckland grade separation is recorded; false if no such allocation exists or the amount is materially different.

veracity.statement: Every day, 15,000 vehicles—including heavy trucks and freight and stock trucks—trundle down the main street of Kumeū and the neighbouring town of Huapai on their way to and from Auckland City.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a daily traffic volume of 15,000 vehicles through Kumeū and Huapai on SH16.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA / Auckland Transport traffic count (annual average daily traffic) for State Highway 16 through Kumeū–Huapai at the date of the statement: true if AADT is approximately 15,000; false if materially different.

specificity.statement: That is why, in addition to all the other things that Auckland Council already has on its list—there’s a $4 billion shortfall between the infrastructure it knows it needs to fund and the amount of money it can get from ratepayers—it also is going to have to turn its mind to another million people coming, according to the Auckland plan.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a named planning document and a population number — a listener could go and check both quantities.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Every day, 15,000 vehicles—including heavy trucks and freight and stock trucks—trundle down the main street of Kumeū and the neighbouring town of Huapai on their way to and from Auckland City.
specificity.explanation: A named location, a named vehicle mix and a daily count — precisely the kind of claim someone could verify against a traffic count.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The future elected members of Auckland Council will need to be courageous and take decisions that mobilise this fund into impactful investments, otherwise all this effort that proud Dr Carlos Cheung has put into it will be wasted.
specificity.explanation: Genuinely trying to say what the council must do, but supplies only virtues — 'courageous', 'impactful investments' — with no figure, threshold, mechanism or timeframe by which anyone could tell whether the council had met it.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That must sound like Armageddon to the Green Party.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how a rival party would react, not about the roading capacity question itself. No policy, measure or figure is named — the content is the other team's supposed temperament.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But we have an infrastructure deficit caused by an anti-growth council over many years, poor planning, and, of course, poor financial management.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy claim here (an infrastructure deficit and its causes), but it is carried by general characterisation of the council — 'anti-growth', 'poor planning', 'poor financial management' — with no named policy, decision or figure attached.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m sure that Julie Anne Genter would be having an absolute meltdown if she was here right now, but, in fact, growth demands infrastructure, and it’s not always the infrastructure that we like.
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named individual member — imputing an 'absolute meltdown' characterises her emotional self-control rather than her argument. Short of outright abuse, but past pointed and onto the person.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s projects like that that have cost half a billion dollars or more, wasting Auckland ratepayers’ money and that have led to the situation where Auckland’s run out of money for infrastructure.
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from one programme, plus an anecdotal claim that 'most households don't bother', to the conclusion that Auckland has run out of infrastructure money. Even granting the half-billion figure, that is a fraction of the $4 billion shortfall he cites — hasty generalisation from a single example to a system-wide cause.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Think of all of those towns that benefit from Transmission Gully and that are now able to grow. Kids can walk to school safely. All of these benefits are available if we put a bypass in.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy: growth and child pedestrian safety in Kāpiti towns after Transmission Gully are asserted, not evidenced, and then transferred wholesale to Kumeū with nothing offered to show the cases are alike. The conclusion that 'all of these benefits are available' outruns the single example given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Telling Aucklanders we’re going to take your golf course away and turn it into a wetland isn’t going to be the answer for everything.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: recasts blue-green / natural stormwater management as confiscating people's golf courses, then rebuts only the claim that it would 'be the answer for everything' — a position nobody advanced. The weakened target means the conclusion does no work against the actual proposal.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It was fascinating listening to Simon Court there. I think he probably spent the fund about a hundred times over!
civility.explanation: A named opponent is mocked, but the jab lands on the volume of spending proposals Court made rather than on his character or competence. Pointed and teasing, edging toward the person without an actual insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So it’s an example in Auckland—tale of one city—of how to do it right, and an example in Wellington—tale of another city—of how to do it completely wrong because you got your messaging and your ideas completely wrong, and probably misunderstood what you yourselves were trying to do.
civility.explanation: Harsh — it says a council did not understand its own plan — but the target is an institution and its handling of a decision, not any named person. No individual is insulted, so this passes Civility; it is the sort of blunt criticism of a record the re-anchored scale places near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It might make $40 million, $50 million a year, that’s going to be a significant benefit, but it’s not going to pay for all of those things—and certainly not all the things that Simon Court was talking about—in a short period of time.
rigor.explanation: A magnitude argument: the annual income of the fund is stated and the conclusion drawn is only that it cannot cover the listed uses quickly. The conclusion tracks the premise and is appropriately bounded; no fallacy. Whether the $40-50m figure is right is a Veracity matter.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The more that we sell, the more that we borrow, of course, the more that the balance of payments is undermined and we keep on paying for that.
rigor.explanation: A chained assertion offered as if self-evident. Selling assets and borrowing are treated as equivalent without argument, and the step to a damaged balance of payments is asserted rather than shown. Not a named fallacy so much as a bare causal chain with no supporting link at any joint.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Auckland Council: last year, 6.8 percent on the residential rates; this year, 5.8. They’re not tiny rate increases, but they are the smallest of the big metropolitan centres, and some of the smallest in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific Auckland residential rates increases and a comparative ranking of Auckland against the other large metropolitan councils over those two years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council's adopted annual plans / long-term plan for the 2024/25 and 2025/26 rating years, giving the average residential rates increase; and the equivalent adopted average residential increases for the other large metropolitan councils (Wellington, Christchurch, Hamilton, Tauranga, Dunedin) for the same two years. True if Auckland's figures are 6.8% and 5.8% (± rounding) and its increases are the lowest of that metropolitan group; false if the Auckland figures are materially different or another metro council had smaller increases.

veracity.statement: There was a special dividend from another asset of the Auckland Council, that is the Ports of Auckland. They declared not only their normal dividend but also special dividend of $45 million. That has gone also into the Auckland Future Fund, and that came from the sale of their shares in Marsden Maritime Holdings up in the Northport area.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $45 million special dividend from Ports of Auckland, funded by the sale of its Marsden Maritime Holdings shares, and paid into the Auckland Future Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ports of Auckland Ltd annual report / dividend declarations and Auckland Council financial reporting for 2024-25, plus NZX disclosures on the sale of Ports of Auckland's Marsden Maritime Holdings shareholding. True if a special dividend of $45 million was declared, was sourced from the Marsden Maritime Holdings share sale, and was paid into the Auckland Future Fund; false if the amount, the source or the destination differs materially.

veracity.statement: So, in the first place, they said they were going to sell; they then decided they weren’t going to sell; they then managed to be the only council in the country that that managed to torpedo their entire long-term plan; they then became the only council in the country which ended up an observer.
veracity.explanation: Two exclusivity claims about Wellington City Council: that it alone failed to carry through its long-term plan, and that it alone ended up with a Crown observer. The word 'only' is what carries the checkable content.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Wellington City Council's long-term plan (LTP) adoption record and the Department of Internal Affairs / Minister of Local Government records of Crown observer and Crown manager appointments to councils over the 2024-25 period. True if Wellington City Council was the only council in that period both to fail to complete its long-term plan and to have a Crown observer appointed; false if any other council also failed to adopt an LTP or also had an observer appointed in that period.

veracity.statement: New Zealand First has always been a very, very strong advocate for the retention of assets.
veracity.explanation: A claim about New Zealand First's own consistent historical position on retaining public assets. 'Always' is the load-bearing word and is what makes it falsifiable.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand First manifestos and its parliamentary voting record on state asset sales — in particular its votes on the Mixed Ownership Model Bill (2012) and its stated positions on partial privatisation across successive elections. True if the party has consistently campaigned and voted against asset sales; false if there are material periods or votes where it supported them.

veracity.statement: Unmet expectations: originally, in the first reading, Te Pāti Māori supported the intent of the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill, a bill that aims to protect whakapapa.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pāti Māori supported the bill at its first reading, which the division record settles directly. The characterisation of the bill as protecting whakapapa is her framing and is not part of the checkable claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the first reading of the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill. True if Te Pāti Māori's votes were cast in favour at first reading; false if the party voted against or abstained.

specificity.statement: Auckland Council: last year, 6.8 percent on the residential rates; this year, 5.8. They’re not tiny rate increases, but they are the smallest of the big metropolitan centres, and some of the smallest in the country.
specificity.explanation: Two numbered rates increases tied to named years and a named class of comparator councils. Someone could look this up and act on it. Marked down slightly because 'some of the smallest in the country' is left unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There was a special dividend from another asset of the Auckland Council, that is the Ports of Auckland. They declared not only their normal dividend but also special dividend of $45 million. That has gone also into the Auckland Future Fund, and that came from the sale of their shares in Marsden Maritime Holdings up in the Northport area.
specificity.explanation: A named entity, a named transaction, a named destination fund and a dollar figure. Fully checkable content, not a direction of travel.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So it’s an example in Auckland—tale of one city—of how to do it right, and an example in Wellington—tale of another city—of how to do it completely wrong because you got your messaging and your ideas completely wrong, and probably misunderstood what you yourselves were trying to do.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy comparison underneath (how two councils handled airport share sales and the resulting funds), but this passage itself weighs mostly on the competence and confusion of the other body rather than on the mechanism, the money or the outcome. Policy point wrapped in institutional framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No, this has to be in the long-term plan; it’s been publicly consulted on; it’s going to be publicly notified in accordance with the documents as set out in the Local Government Act; and then get the 75 percent majority. There are suitable protections.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete safeguards — inclusion in the long-term plan, public consultation, public notification under the Local Government Act, and a 75 percent supermajority threshold. Checkable against the bill; missing only the clause references.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, actually, what we have learned as we’ve teased out these ideas is that the protections that are coming through this bill mean you get the Local Government Act 2002 and the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009 legislation that have requirements for auditor-consolidated financial statements, for an auditor’s report, and Auditor-General reviews.
specificity.explanation: Two statutes named with their years and three named accountability mechanisms (consolidated financial statements, auditor's report, Auditor-General reviews). Someone could go and check whether those obligations follow from the local bill form.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The previous system would have, if it had been continued, cost an additional $1 million to administer that fund, so it is useful to have that system.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named comparison (previous system versus the fund under the bill) and a dollar figure for the administration cost. It lacks a period over which the $1 million falls, which is what keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, this has to be in the long-term plan; it’s been publicly consulted on; it’s going to be publicly notified in accordance with the documents as set out in the Local Government Act; and then get the 75 percent majority. There are suitable protections.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ("There are suitable protections") is drawn from an enumerated set of procedural requirements he has just listed. The inference is supported, though it asserts sufficiency without addressing what a supermajority could still permit.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It's a pleasure to rise in support of this bill, but how revealing that we had a National Party MP just stand up and tell us that he was half-hearted about Auckland—a third of New Zealand's population.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the member said he was half-hearted "about Te Atatū in particular, in this case", not about Auckland as a whole. The conclusion that this is "revealing" of an attitude to a third of the country's population rests on a broadened restatement of what was actually said.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, this has to be in the long-term plan; it’s been publicly consulted on; it’s going to be publicly notified in accordance with the documents as set out in the Local Government Act; and then get the 75 percent majority. There are suitable protections.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the measure before the House — the statutory tests and voting threshold. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It's a pleasure to rise in support of this bill, but how revealing that we had a National Party MP just stand up and tell us that he was half-hearted about Auckland—a third of New Zealand's population.
focus.explanation: The point is about a National MP's supposed attitude to a region rather than about any provision of the bill — no policy, figure or outcome is named. Some content survives in that it responds to a remark in the debate, but the weight is party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There were delays in terms of the appointment of the global investment manager, and while the distribution to the council measure was achieved, the gross return and net return for that third quarter weren't, so no doubt there will be things that we will need to continue to watch, but certainly this fund is placing Auckland in the right direction.
focus.explanation: Reports named performance measures from a specific report on the fund the bill concerns, including where it fell short, while supporting the bill. Entirely about the instrument's performance rather than about the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Maybe it’s a stadium or a sporting or community facility in town, so we can have more of those late-night concerts that Helen Clark loves!
civility.explanation: A light personal jibe at a named individual's concert-going rather than at any argument of hers. It carries no imputation of bad faith or incompetence, so it edges toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There are great things happening for Auckland aside from the investment, like the new City Rail Link, and, of course, the great news that members seem so disappointed about today, with those lowering interest rates saving them $400 a fortnight—great news.
civility.explanation: "the great news that members seem so disappointed about today" imputes bad faith to opposing members — that they are dismayed by good economic news for the public. It falls short of a direct insult but is no longer engaging only the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There are great things happening for Auckland aside from the investment, like the new City Rail Link, and, of course, the great news that members seem so disappointed about today, with those lowering interest rates saving them $400 a fortnight—great news.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that falling interest rates are saving mortgage holders $400 a fortnight as at October 2025. The claim is about the present, and the figure is a specific quantum attributable to the decline in mortgage rates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ published mortgage interest rate series (new residential lending / one-year fixed) from the 2023-24 peak to October 2025, applied to the average outstanding New Zealand mortgage as reported by RBNZ or the main banks: true if the resulting reduction in repayments for a typical mortgage holder is approximately $400 per fortnight ($10,400 per year), false if it is materially below or above that.

veracity.statement: The previous system would have, if it had been continued, cost an additional $1 million to administer that fund, so it is useful to have that system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific counterfactual administration cost: continuing the predecessor arrangement would have cost $1 million more to administer the fund than the arrangement provided for in the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland Council local bill's explanatory note, regulatory impact/financial analysis, and the Governance and Administration Committee report, plus Auckland Council's own papers on the predecessor Diversified Financial Asset Portfolio: true if those documents record an additional administration cost of approximately $1 million for retaining the previous system, false if no such figure appears or the documented figure differs materially.

veracity.statement: There were delays in terms of the appointment of the global investment manager, and while the distribution to the council measure was achieved, the gross return and net return for that third quarter weren't, so no doubt there will be things that we will need to continue to watch, but certainly this fund is placing Auckland in the right direction.
veracity.explanation: Three factual assertions about the fund's third-quarter report: that appointment of the global investment manager was delayed, that the distribution-to-council measure was met, and that the gross and net return measures were not.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland Future Fund's third-quarter report referred to: true if it records a delay in appointing the global investment manager and shows the distribution-to-council performance measure achieved while the gross return and net return measures were not achieved; false if any of those three is recorded otherwise.

civility.statement: This bill cannot deliver on its promise of equity or intergenerational wellbeing.
civility.explanation: A blunt, adverse judgement aimed entirely at the bill. No person is criticised, no bad faith imputed — this is the expected standard on a contested measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We also note that while we didn't support the decision from Auckland Council, what we have in front of us is the need to establish a framework in how the Auckland Future Fund will go ahead.
civility.explanation: Registers disagreement with a contested council decision while attacking nobody and imputing no bad faith — the expected standard, on a matter where he had a clear opening to go after the councillors or the previous speakers.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They can’t see the woods for the Woods on that side!
civility.explanation: A pun turning a named member's surname into a jibe about the opposition's inability to see clearly. It edges onto a person rather than an argument, though it is wordplay rather than an attack on character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But let's be realistic: expectations are not guarantees, and that remains an issue in this regard.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference from what she has just conceded: the bill sets out consultation requirements and Tiriti expectations, expectations are not enforceable guarantees, therefore the protection is not secured. No fallacy; the gap is only that she does not show the expectations have in fact failed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s why they’re bringing legislation—because, otherwise, under the legislation, you’d just need 51 percent. They’ve put in this clause, clause 11, which requires a supermajority of 75 percent—75 percent.
rigor.explanation: A valid explanatory inference: a bare council majority could otherwise undo the fund's terms, an entrenched higher threshold cannot be self-imposed by ordinary resolution, therefore the protection has to come by statute. Premises offered, conclusion tracks them.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The current mechanisms, including letters of expectation, statements of intent, and council policies, are weak tools for protecting Māori interests.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the governance mechanism at issue — named instruments and what they do or fail to do. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s important to note that this decision should shine a light on the importance for central government to adequately support our councils, from a financial point of view, to make sure that councils are able to—rather than having debates about selling assets—if anything, on how more assets can be owned by local communities, and devolved to Māori, as well.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question — council funding settings and public asset ownership — rather than on another party. It gestures at central government generally rather than naming a specific funding measure, which keeps it just short of the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They can’t see the woods for the Woods on that side!
focus.explanation: Purely about the other side of the House. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — content-free cross-chamber banter during a debate on a specific bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They might be a little protective, because their story was taking the OCR from 0.5 percent to 5.5 percent.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy datum here — the OCR track — but it is delivered as an account of what the other side's 'story' was, so the weight of the sentence is party attribution rather than the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The current mechanisms, including letters of expectation, statements of intent, and council policies, are weak tools for protecting Māori interests.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete instruments, which is checkable content, but 'weak tools' supplies no threshold, no figures and no proposed alternative mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If this fund is to protect intergenerational wealth, then Māori must have a say in what gets sold, how funds are invested, and who benefits from the returns.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete decision domains (disposal, investment, distribution) so it points at identifiable clauses, but supplies no mechanism, threshold or drafting for how the say would be given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s important to note that this decision should shine a light on the importance for central government to adequately support our councils, from a financial point of view, to make sure that councils are able to—rather than having debates about selling assets—if anything, on how more assets can be owned by local communities, and devolved to Māori, as well.
specificity.explanation: 'Adequately support our councils, from a financial point of view' names no funding tool, no quantum and no timeframe; 'more assets owned by local communities' is a direction without a mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But, make no mistake, there's more work that needs to be done to ensure that councils across the country—and certainly in our largest city—have the resources that they need to do well and to provide the basic essentials that people deserve, whether it's picking up the rubbish, whether it's clean drinking water, whether it's adequate public transport, and a thriving natural environment to protect us against extreme weather events.
specificity.explanation: A list of service areas rather than content: no funding figure, no mechanism for getting councils the resources, no timeframe. 'More work needs to be done' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To answer the question from that member, the official cash rate (OCR) has dropped from 5.5 percent to less than half of that, to 2.5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument and both endpoints as figures. Anyone can check it against the RBNZ series; only the dates are left implicit.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What that means is, when you refix the average mortgage, anywhere in New Zealand, you are saving $400 a fortnight.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure attached to a defined action (refixing) on a defined basis (the average mortgage). Falls short of 1.0 only because the mortgage size and rate assumptions behind the $400 are not stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why they’re bringing legislation—because, otherwise, under the legislation, you’d just need 51 percent. They’ve put in this clause, clause 11, which requires a supermajority of 75 percent—75 percent.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause number and both thresholds, so the account can be checked directly against the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: How can we talk about securing the future for generations to come when Māori, the fastest-growing population in Tāmaki Makaurau, over 250,000 strong, are not explicitly included in the governance of this fund?
veracity.explanation: Two embedded factual assertions about the present: that Māori are the fastest-growing population group in Auckland, and that the Auckland Māori population exceeds 250,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census usual resident population by ethnicity for the Auckland region, plus inter-censal (2018→2023) growth rates by ethnic group. True if the Auckland Māori count exceeds 250,000 AND Māori show the highest growth rate of any major ethnic group; false if the count is materially below 250,000 or another group (e.g. Asian ethnicities) grew faster.

veracity.statement: The Disabled Persons Assembly NZ has rightly called for amendments to ensure Māori, including whaikaha Māori, are directly consulted in decisions about the fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what a named submitter asked for: that the Disabled Persons Assembly NZ sought amendments requiring direct consultation with Māori, including disabled Māori, on fund decisions.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Disabled Persons Assembly NZ written/oral submission to the Governance and Administration Committee on the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill. True if the submission seeks amendments for direct Māori consultation on fund decisions; false if it made no such request.

veracity.statement: The Green Party, as our previous speaker noted, is voting in support of the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill which, as others have already described, comes through an unfortunate history of the selling of assets—in this case, airport shares—by Auckland Council.
veracity.explanation: Two present/past assertions: that the Green Party is voting for this bill at this stage, and that the fund arises from Auckland Council's sale of its Auckland Airport shareholding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The House's vote record for this stage of the Auckland Council (Auckland Future Fund) Bill (8 October 2025) for the Green Party's position, and Auckland Council's 2024 Long-term Plan decision documents on the disposal of its Auckland International Airport shares. True if the Greens voted in support and the airport shares were sold by the council; false on either count.

veracity.statement: To answer the question from that member, the official cash rate (OCR) has dropped from 5.5 percent to less than half of that, to 2.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the OCR's peak level and its level as at the date of the speech, and that the fall is more than half.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate series and Monetary Policy Review decisions. True if the OCR peaked at 5.50% and stood at 2.50% on 8 October 2025; false if either figure differs.

veracity.statement: What that means is, when you refix the average mortgage, anywhere in New Zealand, you are saving $400 a fortnight.
veracity.explanation: A quantified claim that refixing an average New Zealand mortgage now saves $400 per fortnight (about $10,400 a year), presented as holding anywhere in the country.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ average residential mortgage size and average new/existing fixed mortgage rates at the peak versus October 2025; compute the fortnightly repayment difference on refix. True if the saving on an average-sized mortgage is around $400 a fortnight; false if it is materially lower (e.g. under $300) once the actual fall in retail fixed rates rather than the fall in the OCR is used.

veracity.statement: They might be a little protective, because their story was taking the OCR from 0.5 percent to 5.5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous government's period was one in which the OCR rose from 0.5 percent to 5.5 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ Official Cash Rate history for 2020–2023. True if the tightening cycle began from 0.50% and ended at 5.50%; false if the starting point was materially different (e.g. 0.25%, the COVID-era low held from March 2020 until the first hike).

veracity.statement: People will be thinking of the “Takapuna Ice Cream Bill”, which this House has only just recently passed, which enabled the old boat club in Takapuna—on, as we all learned, Sir Peter Blake Drive—to sell ice creams.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the House recently passed a local bill concerning the Takapuna boating club premises on Sir Peter Blake Drive, the effect of which was to permit the sale of ice creams there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Parliament bills register for the local bill concerning the Takapuna Boating Club / Sir Peter Blake Drive land. True if it passed its third reading shortly before 8 October 2025 and its effect includes permitting food/ice cream sales from the premises; false if no such bill passed or its effect is materially different.

veracity.statement: It is growing at a rate of about 50,000 people per year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Auckland's annual population growth is roughly 50,000 people per year at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimates for the Auckland region, annual change for the years to June 2023-June 2025; true if annual growth is approximately 50,000 (say 45,000-55,000), false if materially below or above that (e.g. growth of ~30,000 or less).

veracity.statement: The sell-down of council’s final shareholding in the airport last year, as has been articulated, formed the basis for this $1.3 billion fund that now sits as the Auckland Future Fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Auckland Council's 2024 sale of its remaining Auckland International Airport shareholding provided the ~$1.3 billion seed capital of the Auckland Future Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council annual report / Auckland Future Fund establishment documents and NZX disclosures of the 2024 airport share sell-down; true if the fund was seeded from the airport share proceeds at approximately $1.3 billion, false if the seed amount or source differs materially (e.g. a partial rather than final shareholding, or a materially different sum).

veracity.statement: As has also been mentioned, there have been other contributions—one being in June, by the Port of Auckland, when they announced the special dividend of $45 million to be paid as a capital contribution into the Auckland Future Fund.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Port of Auckland announced a $45 million special dividend in June (2025) directed as a capital contribution into the Auckland Future Fund.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Port of Auckland Ltd's 2025 dividend announcement and Auckland Council/Auckland Future Fund records; true if a special dividend of approximately $45 million was announced in June 2025 and paid as capital into the fund, false if the amount, date or destination differs materially.

veracity.statement: Let’s not forget that it was a former National Government that delivered the amalgamated city, which has given it such clout to create a fund like this for the perpetuity of Auckland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the amalgamation of Auckland's local authorities into a single council was carried out by a previous National-led Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacting legislation and its date — the Local Government (Auckland Council) Act 2009 and associated reorganisation, with Auckland Council standing up on 1 November 2010; true if enacted under the Fifth National Government, false if enacted under a different administration.

divination.statement: In fact, Auckland could reach 2 million people by 2030, so that just gives you some indication of the challenges that lie ahead and the infrastructure need that is unrelenting.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Auckland region's population reaches 2 million by 2030.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ subnational population estimate for the Auckland region as at 30 June 2030; true if the estimated resident population is at or above 2,000,000, false if below.

divination.statement: Let’s not forget the City Rail Link that’s opening next year, guys, and that being a council and that being a former National Government that kicked that off and that will be there to cut the ribbon.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the City Rail Link opens in 2026, the year following the statement.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: City Rail Link Ltd / Auckland Transport service records; true if CRL commences passenger services at any point in calendar year 2026, false if the opening slips to 2027 or later.

specificity.statement: The sell-down of council’s final shareholding in the airport last year, as has been articulated, formed the basis for this $1.3 billion fund that now sits as the Auckland Future Fund.
specificity.explanation: Names the asset sold, the timing, the dollar figure and the fund it capitalised — someone could check every element.

rigor.statement: This Government is working very closely with this council, as you can see. focus.statement: I just want to see if the member can explain the purpose of inserting that phrase “or the alternative address” into section 159. rigor.statement: However, this bill has a different purpose. specificity.statement: I will draw the member’s attention to new section 360E, inserted by clause 5, where it talks about the requirements for an alternative address and it says what it must not be. It's not the company's registered office. It can't be a post centre or a document exchange.

focus.statement: How will the company's office ensure that an alternative is a real place so that when you turn up to undertake the activities that you might want to for those addresses, such as providing service, it is a physical location that you can drop something to? Who will be determining what qualifies and constitutes an alternative address?
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the bill — verification of the address and who administers it. No party framing at all; this is scrutiny of a named provision.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m assuming the member uses a smartphone and that, in fact, he could call up the Companies Act himself and have a look at it.
civility.explanation: A contested committee exchange where she had a real opportunity to engage plainly. Instead of simply citing section 189, she implies the member could have looked it up himself but has not bothered — condescension aimed at the person rather than at his argument. Short of a direct insult, so not lower.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ll wait with bated breath the answer from the member the Hon Dr Deborah Russell in the follow-up question from James Meager around the changes to potentially requiring it, as Minister Meager outlined.
civility.explanation: A light barb — 'bated breath' hints the answer has been slow in coming — but it stays on the exchange rather than the member, and names her respectfully. Pointed rather than uncivil.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m going to take it the member’s now moved on to discuss clause 4 because, in actual fact, if we look at it, clause 4 addresses exactly that privacy concern that the member was worried about.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: the concern raised was that a director's residential address stays discoverable in inspectable company records, and she answers it by identifying the specific provision that permits substitution. The conclusion follows from the premise she supplies immediately after. Not higher because it asserts the clause 'addresses exactly' the concern without engaging the residual case Meager is actually pressing (what happens when the company declines to update).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The director may well go to all extents to provide an alternative address, but if there’s no requirement to actually change it and make sure that the public record reflects that fact, wouldn’t that therefore defeat the intention of the bill in the first place?
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional argument: a permissive 'may' leaves the company free not to update, so the residential address can remain publicly visible despite the director having done everything the process asks — which would not deliver the privacy the bill states as its purpose. The conclusion tracks the premise; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m going to suggest further that a director who goes to the efforts to have an alternative address—and there is a process there—will also be similarly motivated to ensure that the company’s register is updated.
rigor.explanation: The inference — a director motivated to obtain an alternative address will also be motivated to have the register updated — is plausible but rests on assumed motivation, and it does not reach the conclusion the question requires. The objection was about what happens when the update does not occur; predicting that it usually will leaves a real gap between what is shown (a likely motive) and what is concluded (that no requirement is needed).
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How do the new subsections in 215(1A) and (1B), inserted by clause 4, interact with the main protections in new section 360D, which is if the Registrar removes public access to residential addresses, under new section 360D(2), why do companies also need the ability to replace addresses in their own records, under section 215(1A), and doesn’t that create potential inconsistencies between what are company records and the official register?
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference here: two independent mechanisms operating on two different records can produce divergent states, therefore an inconsistency is possible. But the argument is left implicit — he asserts the risk of discrepancy without setting out the case in which the two records would actually come apart, so the conclusion runs slightly ahead of what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m going to take it the member’s now moved on to discuss clause 4 because, in actual fact, if we look at it, clause 4 addresses exactly that privacy concern that the member was worried about.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the measure before the committee — names the clause and the privacy mechanism at issue. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The director may well go to all extents to provide an alternative address, but if there’s no requirement to actually change it and make sure that the public record reflects that fact, wouldn’t that therefore defeat the intention of the bill in the first place?
focus.explanation: Engages the drafting mechanism of the clause and its consequence for the public record. No party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How do the new subsections in 215(1A) and (1B), inserted by clause 4, interact with the main protections in new section 360D, which is if the Registrar removes public access to residential addresses, under new section 360D(2), why do companies also need the ability to replace addresses in their own records, under section 215(1A), and doesn’t that create potential inconsistencies between what are company records and the official register?

specificity.statement: If the clause applies, a company can replace a director’s residential address with an alternative address on the company’s records that are available for inspection.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is the harm caused by changing “may” to “shall” and actually saying to companies you have an obligation to do this rather than leave it up to a particular board of directors at a particular time?
specificity.explanation: Proposes an exact, actionable amendment — one named word replaced by another in an identified subsection — and states the obligation it would create. Precise enough for the Minister to accept or reject directly. Not 1.0 as it stops short of setting out how the obligation would be triggered or enforced.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How do the new subsections in 215(1A) and (1B), inserted by clause 4, interact with the main protections in new section 360D, which is if the Registrar removes public access to residential addresses, under new section 360D(2), why do companies also need the ability to replace addresses in their own records, under section 215(1A), and doesn’t that create potential inconsistencies between what are company records and the official register?

specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If the clause applies, a company can replace a director’s residential address with an alternative address on the company’s records that are available for inspection.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 4 of the companies amendment bill before the committee of the whole House on 8 October 2025, specifically the new section 215(1A) it inserts: true if that subsection permits a company to replace a director's residential address with an alternative address in records available for inspection; false if it does not, or if it applies only to the Registrar's register rather than the company's own records.

rigor.statement: A director has an incentive to get that address changed to an alternative address. I don't think we need to legislate that the director needs to do that, and it gives the company the capacity to act. That's why the word “may” is used.
rigor.explanation: A premise (directors are already motivated to substitute an alternative address) is offered and the conclusion (a permissive "may" suffices, no mandate needed) follows from it, with the added reason that the drafting preserves company capacity to act. No fallacy or appeal; the only gap is that the strength of the incentive is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If one wanted to expunge the e-record of an address from all of the documents that are available publicly, it would be quite an intensely manual process.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises she supplies immediately before it — company documents are verbose, addresses are scattered through them, and the register's holdings go back many years — so a full scrub would be manual. The inference is sound; the gap is that no evidence beyond her committee recollection is offered for the volume.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To the question from Tom Rutherford about inconsistencies between the company's records and the register of companies records, if the member cared to go to section 215 in the Companies Act, he would see that a company is required to keep records available for inspection by a person who serves written notice of intention to inspect on the company.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific legal proposition: that s 215 of the Companies Act 1993 requires a company to make records available for inspection to a person serving written notice of intention to inspect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 215 of the Companies Act 1993. True if s 215 provides for inspection of a company's records by a person who has served written notice of intention to inspect on the company; false if s 215 concerns some other subject matter or imposes no such requirement.

veracity.statement: The briefing materials indicate that there are over 650,000 directors currently on the Companies Register.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of directors currently recorded on the Companies Register, sourced to the bill's briefing materials.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / Companies Office published register statistics for 2025. True if the number of directors recorded on the New Zealand Companies Register exceeds 650,000; false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: The Institute of Directors survey found that privacy was the number one personal concern for directors, supported by 44 percent of directors generally and 61 directors who are on high profile NZX-listed companies.
veracity.explanation: Attributes two specific survey figures to the Institute of Directors on the ranking of privacy as a personal concern. "61 directors" reads as a spoken slip for 61 percent, given the parallel construction with the 44 percent figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Institute of Directors' published director sentiment survey. True if it reports privacy as directors' top personal concern with support at 44 percent among directors generally (and 61 percent among NZX-listed directors, the evident intent of "61 directors"); false if the survey reports different figures or a different top concern.

civility.statement: To the question from Tom Rutherford about inconsistencies between the company's records and the register of companies records, if the member cared to go to section 215 in the Companies Act, he would see that a company is required to keep records available for inspection by a person who serves written notice of intention to inspect on the company.
