civility.statement: About absolutely nothing. It’ll be just full of hot air—hot air.
civility.explanation: A direct jibe at a named member's contributions rather than at any argument — mockery of what he will say before he has said it. Short of sustained abuse, but plainly aimed at the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh, I look forward to you taking a call, Jan Tinetti, and contributing something to the committee.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm directed at a named member, implying she contributes nothing to the committee. A personal slight rather than engagement with anything she has argued.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: There is better legislation coming. The Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs has assured me that he’s working on his Companies Amendment Bill and that he anticipates having it in the House sometime soon.
divination.explanation: Relays the Minister's forecast that a government Companies Amendment Bill will be before the House shortly; the speaker ties the timeframe to the end of the year elsewhere in the same speech.
divination.subject: other
divination.subject_name: Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs
divination.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills register / Hansard. True if a Companies Amendment Bill introduced by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs is introduced and reaches its first reading by 31 December 2025; false if no such bill is before the House by that date.

specificity.statement: I’ve had a pretty upfront exchange with him as to what I intend to do with this bill, and my commitment to him has been that, if his bill has its first reading before the end of the year, I will withdraw this bill.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, checkable undertaking: a named trigger (first reading of the Minister's bill), a deadline (end of the year), and a named consequence (withdrawal of this member's bill). Anyone could verify whether it was honoured.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The briefing materials indicate that there are over 650,000 directors currently on the Companies Register.
specificity.explanation: A precise figure attached to a named register and a named source. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can the member, firstly, confirm how many directors currently have their residential address publicly available on the Companies Register and what volume of applications the Companies Office is expecting under new section 360D?
specificity.explanation: A precise ask: two named quantities, tied to a named register and a named new provision. A question this exact is as checkable as an answer would be.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If one wanted to expunge the e-record of an address from all of the documents that are available publicly, it would be quite an intensely manual process.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the operation of the measure itself — what removing an address from historical company records would actually require. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the member, firstly, confirm how many directors currently have their residential address publicly available on the Companies Register and what volume of applications the Companies Office is expecting under new section 360D?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill — implementation volume and resourcing under a named clause. Legitimate scrutiny with no party content.

focus.statement: About absolutely nothing. It’ll be just full of hot air—hot air.

focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, I note that the application has to be made in a particular form and there are some steps to it, including a statutory declaration. I doubt that there are going to be frivolous applications.
rigor.explanation: A premise (a prescribed form plus a statutory declaration is required) offered in support of a conclusion (few frivolous applications). The inference from procedural friction to low frivolity is reasonable but not tight — form requirements deter volume without ruling out frivolous intent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of whether or not it could be done in time: as we discussed earlier in this debate, officials assured us that they could do the work, and we have to take the officials’ word at that, and certainly I do as I am not a Minister; I am just a member. They assured us that they could do the work.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the work can be done in time rests entirely on an appeal to authority — officials' assurance — with no independent reason offered. She is candid that this is what she is doing, and officials are an appropriate authority here, but nothing beyond the assurance supports the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m sure we’ll understand a lot more about the implementation of any tax policy that that side comes up with, because, clearly, without any chartered accountants on that side, they don’t know.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur resting on a credentialist premise: the absence of a particular professional qualification in a caucus is offered as sufficient to conclude that the caucus does not understand tax policy implementation. Nothing connects the credential to the competence claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These are not mere frivolous applications for the sake of it. A person has to be able to say that they think they are at risk of physical or mental harm.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (applications will not be frivolous) is supported by the statutory test just cited — an applicant must attest to a risk of physical or mental harm. The premise does the work the conclusion needs; the only gap is that a declaration requirement constrains rather than eliminates weak applications.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I sincerely doubt that all 650,000 directors on the register of directors are going to turn up tomorrow the minute the bill is through asking for one of these, and I think it's not reasonable to engage in that kind of scaremongering.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. Bates's claim was that 'potentially up to 650,000' directors could apply; she rebuts the far stronger proposition that all of them will apply at once the day the bill passes. Refuting the exaggerated version leaves the original volume concern untouched.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Many Māori organisations’ trustees, Dr Russell, are listed as shareholders in their personal names, and not because they own the shares themselves but because they’re often holding them on behalf of iwi, hapū, and whānau. These trustees often aren’t directors, and yet they can face the serious risk and pressure and even the harassment from within their own communities, especially when decisions are contested.
rigor.explanation: A structured argument: trustees appear on the register as personal shareholders though they hold beneficially for others; they are exposed to the same harassment risk; but the bill's protection attaches to directors, so the gap is unprincipled. Each step supports the next, with no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Currently chartered accountants cannot sign a statutory declaration, so they’re going to have to deal with the large volumes that my colleague Tom Rutherford has referred to if potentially up to 650,000 directors who could apply go to their accountant as part of the annual reporting process, etc., and have these statutory declarations signed.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete legal restriction, a specific instrument (statutory declarations), a population figure (650,000 directors) and the process point at which the burden lands (annual reporting). Someone could check and act on it. Falls short of 1.0 only because no estimate of actual application volume or cost is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Currently chartered accountants cannot sign a statutory declaration, so they’re going to have to deal with the large volumes that my colleague Tom Rutherford has referred to if potentially up to 650,000 directors who could apply go to their accountant as part of the annual reporting process, etc., and have these statutory declarations signed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that chartered accountants are not currently among the persons legally authorised to take a statutory declaration in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of persons before whom a statutory declaration may be made under s 9 of the Oaths and Declarations Act 1957 (and any subsequent authorising instrument). True if chartered accountants are absent from that list; false if they are included by that Act or by other law.

veracity.statement: I understand that there aren’t any chartered accountants in the caucus on that side.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no member of the Labour caucus in this Parliament is a chartered accountant.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary biographies and CAANZ / former NZ Institute of Chartered Accountants membership records for sitting Labour MPs. False if at least one Labour MP has been admitted as a chartered accountant; true only if none has.

veracity.statement: I was, of course, admitted to the New Zealand Institute of Chartered Accountants myself in 1992.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a personal professional credential with a specific admitting body and year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZICA / CAANZ admission records and Russell's parliamentary and academic biographies. True if admission to the New Zealand Institute of Chartered Accountants in 1992 is recorded; false if she was never admitted or was admitted in a materially different year.

veracity.statement: Most justices of the peace run public desks in libraries or in malls and so on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a majority of New Zealand's justices of the peace staff publicly accessible service desks in community locations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Federation of New Zealand Justices' Associations service-desk register (number of rostered JP service desks and JPs staffing them) against the total number of appointed JPs. True if more than half of appointed JPs staff a public desk; false if the majority serve only by private appointment.

veracity.statement: Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa recommended that all shareholders should be able to apply to keep their residential address private; not just those connected to a director.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori Law Society made a specific recommendation — extension of the address-suppression right to all shareholders — in respect of this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The written submission of Te Hunga Rōia Māori o Aotearoa to the select committee on this bill, and the committee's report. True if that submission recommends extending address protection to all shareholders; false if it makes no such recommendation or recommends something materially different.

civility.statement: Not only is that an insult to myself as a chartered accountant but it’s also an insult to every chartered accountant in New Zealand.
civility.explanation: Responding to an interjection he regards as an insult, he characterises the remark rather than the member who made it — no attack on Webb's character, competence or motives. Pointed and heated, but it lands on what was said, not on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I sincerely doubt that all 650,000 directors on the register of directors are going to turn up tomorrow the minute the bill is through asking for one of these, and I think it's not reasonable to engage in that kind of scaremongering.
civility.explanation: Labelling the member's argument 'scaremongering' imputes bad faith — a deliberate attempt to frighten rather than an honest concern. Short of a personal insult, and it targets the argument's manner rather than the man, but it is no longer purely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m sure we’ll understand a lot more about the implementation of any tax policy that that side comes up with, because, clearly, without any chartered accountants on that side, they don’t know.
focus.explanation: Mentions 'tax policy' only as a category; the weight of the statement is a general claim about the other party's capability, with no measure, mechanism, figure or named policy engaged. This is party framing, not scrutiny of a commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And, Dr Russell, would you consider extending the protections under new section 360D to all shareholders, not just those linked to directors?
focus.explanation: Names the specific provision at issue and the precise change sought. Entirely about the mechanism of the bill and who it covers, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I appreciate the time to gather my thoughts after the shocking revelations from Dr Webb—rich coming from a lawyer, of course, which is one of the least trusted professions alongside politicians. Perhaps Dr Webb could start a podcast and get media and get the holy trinity?
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the member personally — impugning his trustworthiness by profession and a jibe about seeking media attention — rather than at anything he argued. Short of a direct insult, but it is sneering at the person, so it sits at the failure end rather than the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is the crux of that question around “may” or “shall”. If you change that term to “shall”, you then remove one of the uncertain criteria as to whether or not it is a reasonable step for the registrar to take.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: if the statute makes replacement of the address mandatory rather than optional, the registrar's obligation is no longer contingent on a company's discretion, so one source of uncertainty about 'reasonable steps' disappears. The conclusion tracks the premise; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I suppose it kind of comes down to: should we be actually extending this to all household members, not just who resides with the director? Bearing in mind that there are a lot of family-run businesses here in New Zealand which may have intergenerational shareholders.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered for the conclusion, but there is a real gap in it: the premise is about shareholding across generations, while the provision at issue turns on residence. Intergenerational shareholders are not necessarily household members, so the evidence offered does not reach the proposed extension to 'all household members'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A statutory declaration is—I know it seems like just signing a piece of paper, but it is actually a legal test. It does have legal standing. People can be prosecuted if they commit fraud, I suppose, when signing a statutory declaration, so there is that protection there as well.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the declaration requirement is itself a safeguard — follows from the premise that a false declaration is prosecutable. The step from 'prosecutable' to 'adequate protection' is asserted rather than shown, which is the gap, but there is no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That is the crux of that question around “may” or “shall”. If you change that term to “shall”, you then remove one of the uncertain criteria as to whether or not it is a reasonable step for the registrar to take.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the clause before the House — a named drafting choice ('may' versus 'shall') and its downstream legal effect. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, Winston Peters would have, I'm sure, really appreciated had that requirement not been in there and then wouldn't have had to necessarily declare his address being a director of a company, for example, and being publicly available—let alone people knowingly sharing it widely, which is just terrible, the harm that incited and the support that's been given from political parties in this House.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — a concrete illustration of how the harm-test requirement would have operated for a company director — but it is wrapped in an accusation about what other parties in the House have supported, which carries much of the weight and names no policy or measure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The question would be—really, there’s probably a couple of questions in there—how would “resides with” be defined in practice, and what proof will be needed to actually prove that a director resides with someone?
specificity.explanation: Pins down a named statutory term in a named provision and asks two checkable things — the definitional test and the evidential threshold. Precise about what is missing, though it proposes no definition or standard of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Then Dr Campbell also asked about “resides with”. It’s the ordinary meaning of the words, as often is the case in the law.
specificity.explanation: Names a real legal standard — the ordinary meaning of undefined statutory words — so it is not empty, but it supplies no test, no threshold and no worked criterion for the question asked. Nobody could apply this to a borderline living arrangement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill itself provides no definition of these terms in section 360D, so will this be addressed in regulations, or is the subjective assessment by the applicant intended to be the sole test?
specificity.explanation: Names the provision, identifies precisely what is absent from it, and offers two concrete, mutually exclusive alternatives — regulation-made criteria versus the applicant's own assessment as the sole test. Directly checkable against the bill and answerable as put.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is, unfortunately, a very narrow bill. It really does just deal with directors and people they live with.
veracity.explanation: An assertion about the scope of her own members' bill: that its protections extend only to company directors and persons residing with them, and to no wider class.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill as reported back from select committee, in particular new sections 360D and 360F inserted by clause 5: true if every address-suppression entitlement is keyed to a director or a person residing with a director; false if any provision extends to shareholders, employees or other persons independent of a director.

veracity.statement: A statutory declaration is—I know it seems like just signing a piece of paper, but it is actually a legal test. It does have legal standing. People can be prosecuted if they commit fraud, I suppose, when signing a statutory declaration, so there is that protection there as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a person who makes a false statutory declaration is exposed to criminal prosecution, and that this legal exposure is what gives the declaration standing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Crimes Act 1961 s 111 and the Oaths and Declarations Act 1957: true if making a false statement in a statutory declaration is a criminal offence carrying a penalty; false if a false statutory declaration attracts no criminal liability.

veracity.statement: Now, I note that Bell Gully's legal commentary noted that this standard appears to be subjective, with no guidance on actually what constitutes harm.
veracity.explanation: Relays a characterisation attributed to a third party: that Bell Gully's published commentary on this bill described the 'likely to result in physical or mental harm' standard as subjective and unaccompanied by guidance on what harm means.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Bell Gully's published commentary on the bill: true if it describes the harm standard in new section 360D(3)(b) as subjective and notes an absence of guidance on what constitutes harm; false if it makes no such comment or characterises the standard differently.

veracity.statement: Chapman Tripp, in their submission, recommended that the service address option should be available as a matter of preference without any need to establish safety risk.
veracity.explanation: Relays the content of a third party's select committee submission: that Chapman Tripp recommended making the service-address option available on request, with no requirement to demonstrate a safety risk.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Chapman Tripp's written submission to the select committee on this bill, as published on the Parliament website: true if it recommends the service address be available as of right or by preference without a safety-risk test; false if it makes no such recommendation or supports retaining the harm threshold.

divination.statement: I trust that the Minister's legislation that is promised will deal with that particular issue.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government bill promised by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs will, when it comes, extend address-privacy protection beyond directors and their cohabitants to the wider class of affected people raised in the debate.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Government's Companies Act amendment legislation as introduced by the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs: true if it contains provisions allowing suppression or substitution of residential addresses for persons beyond directors and those residing with them; false if it is introduced without such provisions, or if no such bill is introduced by the resolve-by date.

veracity.statement: Chapman Tripp's submission recommended that the service address option should be available as a matter of preference without any need to establish safety risk.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific content claim about what a named submitter (Chapman Tripp) recommended to the select committee on this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Chapman Tripp submission to the select committee on this bill, as published on the Parliament website; true if it recommends the service-address option be available as a matter of preference with no requirement to establish a safety risk, false if it makes no such recommendation or conditions the option on demonstrated risk.

veracity.statement: Given that there are 650-odd-thousand directors, I think part of the rationale for this, if I’m correct, was that we need to have some small barrier so that there isn’t an a tidal wave of requests that then aren’t able to be actioned and, then, in the volume itself, create a barrier to people having this actioned through the Registrar of Companies.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure for the number of company directors in New Zealand as the factual basis for the volume argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Companies Office / New Zealand Companies Register statistics on the number of registered company directors as at 2025; true if approximately 650,000 (within roughly 600,000–700,000), false if materially outside that range.

focus.statement: Why does section 360D(3)(b) limit eligibility to situations involving potential harm, both physical and mental, rather than allowing directors to protect their privacy for other legitimate reasons?
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at the mechanism of a named provision and the eligibility test it sets; no party framing at all.

specificity.explanation: A concrete conditional with a named trigger (first reading before year's end), a named consequence (holding off the third reading) and an implied deadline. Checkable against the Order Paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We have changes to the Children’s Act, the Crimes Act, the Oranga Tamariki Act, and also to the Public Records Act here.
specificity.explanation: Names the four statutes amended, so the scope of the bill is checkable; stops short of saying what each change does, which caps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that some of the other contributors to that horrendous abuse that took place in State care and in faith-based institutions was also a consequence of having untrained staff members, a lack of institutional safeguards, a lack of safe regulations, and also the location that some of these institutions were at—for example, Great Barrier Island or Aotea in the 1970s during the Whakapakari boot camp.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete contributing factors and a specific institution and location (Whakapakari, Great Barrier Island/Aotea), though the causal contributions themselves are listed rather than quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How do new sections 360D to 360G address the identification problem when multiple directors, such as the nearly 3,200 John Smiths in New Zealand, share the same names?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill — which provisions do what to director identification. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I guess to summarise what our inquiries will be about today, we’re really interested in the use of force and how that has been safeguarded, and we are wanting to ensure that that is a last resort and that all other options have been exhausted before we get to use of force.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at a specific provision of the bill — the use-of-force power and the last-resort threshold governing it. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The removal of residential addresses under these provisions, in my view, will make it even harder to distinguish between directors with 3,200 John Smiths currently registered.
rigor.explanation: The inference tracks: if address data is the field that currently separates identically-named directors, removing it makes them harder to tell apart. Premise supports conclusion directly; no fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That scrutiny is deserving because we know that one of the reasons why the scale of abuse of children, the scale of torture, the scale of violence that took place between the years of 1975 and 1999 is because of a lack of institutional safeguards, because of a lack of children’s safety and indeed, children’s rights being put at the forefront of legislation and of all of the rules and conditions around that State care.
rigor.explanation: An argument with a stated warrant: close scrutiny of safeguards is justified because absent safeguards were a cause of past abuse. The inference holds, though the causal premise is asserted rather than evidenced and the sentence is loosely built.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Minister concede that perhaps we can do better in the future iterations and changes to respond to this abuse inquiry?
civility.explanation: A pointed challenge on a genuinely contested failure of consultation, aimed entirely at the process rather than at the Minister personally. No imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We had a six-year process, which raised some of these issues.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission inquiry ran for six years, offered as the basis for the consultation claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's establishment date and the date of its final report (Whanaketia); true if the inquiry ran approximately six years, false if materially shorter or longer.

veracity.statement: There are hundreds of recommendations that need to be looked at, considered, and enacted, potentially, and we’re going through that work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Royal Commission produced hundreds of recommendations requiring action.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Count the recommendations in the Royal Commission's reports (Whanaketia final report, plus the He Purapura Ora redress report); true if the total the Government is working through numbers in the hundreds, false if it is well under 200.

veracity.statement: I also want to acknowledge that last night, in Parliament, we celebrated 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, and, I guess, the significance that that holds in the space we stand in today and as we talk about abuse in State and faith-based care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a parliamentary event on 7 October 2025 marking the Waitangi Tribunal's 50th anniversary.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975's enactment date and parliamentary records/media for the evening of 7 October 2025; true if the Tribunal was established in 1975 and an anniversary event was held at Parliament that night, false if either is wrong.

rigor.statement: We didn’t have many—hardly anyone, in fact, I believe—saying anything about this part of the bill that meant they were opposed to it. It’s a widely supported, relatively straightforward change that fills a known gap and responds to the royal commission report.
rigor.explanation: Infers wide support from the absence of opposing submissions. The inference tracks the evidence offered but leans on absence of comment as positive endorsement, which is a real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So this is not about survivors having appeal rights. This is about the core worker having an appeal right against not being able to work.
rigor.explanation: Identifies that the questioner's concern rests on a mistaken premise about who holds the appeal right, and the conclusion (the cost worry does not apply to survivors) follows directly from that correction.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We think it’s already clear, in this bill, that we are adding specified offences, as I mentioned in my opening speech. It’s very clear that, as things come up, we will consider adding them to the specified offences list, as we’ve done in this bill today.
specificity.explanation: Answering a precise question about whether a regulation-making power exists to add specified offences, this names no mechanism, no test for addition, no timeframe — only that additions 'will be considered'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just to be clear, this part already exists in the legislation for core workers who have a conviction in New Zealand. We’re just aligning the law so that people who have an overseas conviction and now fall under this piece of legislation also have an appeal right.
specificity.explanation: Names the existing provision, who it applies to (core workers with NZ convictions), and exactly what the change extends (appeal rights to overseas convictions). Concrete and checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m looking at new section 28C, in clause 5, in terms of the review process. It talks about going to the chief executive and the process of doing that, in terms of a survivor being able to ask questions, but I want to come through to new section 28D(2).
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact clause and new sections at issue and describes the review pathway they create — someone can go and check it against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of where we're sitting in this part of the legislation, you know, trust has been broken. The State and faith-based organisations have breached that trust for many, many years, and so my question to the Minister is: are you confident that we have landed, in this part of legislation—that survivors can trust that you have leaned in, that you've listened, and that you've taken on board what they want?
specificity.explanation: Asks about confidence and trust in general terms; names no provision, figure, mechanism or test that could settle the question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I can see that we talk about specified offences. I’d be really keen to know, from the Minister, with that kind of law change in the wind, which is really welcome, is that wide enough? Is it that there's a regulation where, in fact, specified offences can be added to and that that would mean that somebody involved in those kinds of activities, which in the past have not come into offences, would be captured?
specificity.explanation: Names the specified-offences provision and the coming trafficking law change and asks about a particular mechanism (regulation-making power), but supplies no clause reference, figures or timing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One of the main ones that we hear about is the request for an independent survivor-led redress system, but I understand that there were other recommendations that haven’t been followed through.
specificity.explanation: Names one concrete recommendation (an independent survivor-led redress system) but leaves 'other recommendations' unenumerated.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m looking at new section 28C, in clause 5, in terms of the review process. It talks about going to the chief executive and the process of doing that, in terms of a survivor being able to ask questions, but I want to come through to new section 28D(2).
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism in the legislation before the committee; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can see that we talk about specified offences. I’d be really keen to know, from the Minister, with that kind of law change in the wind, which is really welcome, is that wide enough? Is it that there's a regulation where, in fact, specified offences can be added to and that that would mean that somebody involved in those kinds of activities, which in the past have not come into offences, would be captured?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the bill's mechanism — whether the specified-offences list can be extended by regulation to capture forthcoming trafficking offences. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the main ones that we hear about is the request for an independent survivor-led redress system, but I understand that there were other recommendations that haven’t been followed through.
focus.explanation: Names a specific recommendation from the Whanaketia report and asks why it was not carried into the bill — scrutiny of a named commitment, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In terms of where we're sitting in this part of the legislation, you know, trust has been broken. The State and faith-based organisations have breached that trust for many, many years, and so my question to the Minister is: are you confident that we have landed, in this part of legislation—that survivors can trust that you have leaned in, that you've listened, and that you've taken on board what they want?
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested challenge — whether the Minister has actually listened to survivors — put without any imputation of bad faith or personal jab. Criticism is directed at the State's historical conduct, not at the Minister.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: His Government sold the Bank of New Zealand and then he was the inaugural chair of the new Government-owned *Kiwibank.
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions about the historical record: that the Bolger government sold the Bank of New Zealand, and that Bolger was the first chair of Kiwibank after its establishment as a state-owned bank.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury/NZ government records of the 1992 sale of the Bank of New Zealand and who was in government at the time; and Kiwibank/NZ Post company records naming its inaugural board chair. True if the BNZ was sold under the Bolger administration and Bolger is recorded as Kiwibank's first chair; false if either the sale fell outside his term or another person chaired Kiwibank first.

veracity.statement: His Government ushered in the *Employment Contracts Act and then subsequently he chaired a working group that led to the establishment of fair pay agreements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Employment Contracts Act was enacted under Bolger's government, and that Bolger later chaired the working group whose recommendations produced fair pay agreements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enactment date and governing party of the Employment Contracts Act 1991, and the MBIE/ministerial record of the membership and chair of the Fair Pay Agreements Working Group. True if the Act passed during Bolger's premiership and he is recorded as chair of that working group; false if either is not borne out by the record.

veracity.statement: He sacked *Winston Peters from his Cabinet and then formed New Zealand’s first MMP coalition with Winston Peters as his Deputy Prime Minister, a Government that transpired to be remarkably stable, much to the frustration of the then Labour Party Opposition.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger dismissed Winston Peters from Cabinet, and that Bolger subsequently formed New Zealand's first coalition government under MMP with Peters as Deputy Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial list records for Peters' dismissal from the Bolger Cabinet, and the 1996 post-election coalition agreement plus the ministerial warrants recording the Deputy Prime Minister. True if Peters was sacked from Cabinet by Bolger and later served as his Deputy Prime Minister in the first post-MMP coalition; false if the record shows otherwise (e.g. an earlier MMP coalition, or a different Deputy Prime Minister).

veracity.statement: He turned down a knighthood on leaving Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger was offered and declined a knighthood at the time he left Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary reporting and honours-system records (or Bolger's own published accounts/interviews) on whether a knighthood was offered to and declined by him around his departure from Parliament in 1998. True if a declined offer is documented; false if he is recorded as having received one or no offer is documented.

veracity.statement: I think it’s a huge tribute to him that he was nominated for New Zealand’s highest honour, the *Order of New Zealand, by a Government comprised of his former rivals.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger's appointment to the Order of New Zealand was made on the nomination of a government made up of his political opponents (i.e. not his own party).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The honours list recording Bolger's appointment to the Order of New Zealand, its date, and which party or parties were in government at that point. True if the appointment was made while a government of his political opponents held office; false if it was made under a National-led government or one otherwise containing his own party.

veracity.statement: The Rt Hon Jim Bolger served as Aotearoa’s Prime Minister between 1990 and 1997.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the dates of Bolger's tenure as Prime Minister: began 1990, ended 1997.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary/Cabinet Office record of Prime Ministers of New Zealand and their terms; true if Bolger was sworn in as PM in 1990 and ceased to hold the office in 1997, false if either date is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: He held several ministerial positions, being the first Minister of Fisheries*, the Minister of Immigration*, and the Minister of Labour*.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific portfolios held by Bolger, and that he was the first holder of the Fisheries portfolio.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial lists in the New Zealand Parliamentary Record / Cabinet Office ministerial appointment records; true if Bolger held Fisheries, Immigration and Labour and no earlier person held a Minister of Fisheries portfolio, false if he did not hold one of the three or if the Fisheries portfolio predates him.

veracity.statement: He also wasn’t afraid to work across political lines during Kiwibank and working on fair pay agreements, both under Labour-led Governments.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger, a former National PM, took roles in the establishment of Kiwibank and in the fair pay agreements work, in both cases under Labour-led governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kiwibank/NZ Post board records and the terms of reference and membership of the Fair Pay Agreements Working Group; true if Bolger held a role in each and both fell within a Labour-led government's term, false if he held neither role or the roles fell under National-led governments.

veracity.statement: He oversaw some significant reforms, including the introduction of the MMP* system—and acknowledging the Rt Hon Winston Peters from those times as well, and that Cabinet as well—the resource management, as well as the first major Treaty of Waitangi settlements in Tainui and Ngāi Tahu.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the introduction of MMP, resource management reform, and the first major Treaty settlements with Tainui and Ngāi Tahu all occurred during Bolger's premiership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Dates of the Electoral Act 1993 / 1996 general election, the Resource Management Act 1991, and the Tainui and Ngāi Tahu deeds of settlement, against Bolger's term as PM (1990–1997); true if each falls inside that term and no earlier settlement of comparable scale preceded them, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: He was, ironically, a republican serving his King Country electorate for 26 years, from 1972 until 1998.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Bolger held the King Country seat continuously for 26 years, entering Parliament in 1972 and leaving in 1998, and that he was a republican.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Parliamentary Record of members and electorates; true if Bolger was elected in 1972 and left the House in 1998 representing King Country (or its successor electorate) throughout, false if the dates or the electorate are materially wrong. Republicanism checkable against his public statements advocating a New Zealand republic.

veracity.statement: As you know, he served as Prime Minister for seven years, leading three terms of Government, which were markedly different to each other in their complexion and their output.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a seven-year premiership spanning three parliamentary terms of government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet Office record of Bolger's dates as PM and the 1990, 1993 and 1996 general elections; true if his tenure spans approximately seven years across three terms, false if it spans a materially different period or fewer terms.

veracity.statement: It’s true to say that, 29 years ago, in 1996, we formed the first MMP Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the first MMP government was formed in 1996, by a coalition including the speaker's party and Bolger's.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 1996 general election result and the National–New Zealand First coalition agreement; true if the first government formed under MMP dates from 1996 and included both parties, false if the first MMP government was formed in another year or without New Zealand First.

veracity.statement: Much has been covered of his career, but I would point out that his first election as Leader of the Opposition, in 1987, was a catastrophic loss, and yet he carried on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 1987 general election was Bolger's first as National's Leader of the Opposition and that National suffered a heavy defeat at it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Parliament / Electoral Commission records for the 1987 general election plus the date Bolger became National Party leader. True if Bolger led National into the 1987 election as its first election as leader and National lost seats/vote share by a wide margin; false if he was not leader at that election, or if National's result was not a substantial defeat.

veracity.statement: Remember he said, *“Bugger the pollsters.”, at the 1993 election, when they got back in by a whisker?
veracity.explanation: Attributes the phrase "bugger the pollsters" to Bolger on 1993 election night, and asserts National was returned with a very narrow majority.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous broadcast/press reporting of Bolger's 1993 election-night remarks, and the official 1993 general election result. True if the quoted phrase is recorded as his on that night and National's majority was one or two seats; false if the phrase is misattributed or belongs to a different occasion, or if National's 1993 margin was comfortable.

veracity.statement: Mr Bolger supported *Doug Graham in signing historic Treaty settlements with *Waikato-Tainui and *Ngāi Tahu.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waikato-Tainui and Ngāi Tahu Treaty settlements were signed by Doug Graham as Treaty Negotiations Minister while Bolger was Prime Minister and with his support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Deeds of settlement held by the Office for Māori Crown Relations – Te Arawhiti for Waikato-Tainui (Raupatu) and Ngāi Tahu: signing dates and Crown signatories. True if both deeds were signed by Doug Graham for the Crown during Bolger's premiership; false if either was signed under a different Prime Minister or by a different Minister.

veracity.statement: In 1995, the people of Parihaka also were met and included by this wonderful man.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Bolger, as Prime Minister, met the Parihaka community in 1995.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Prime Ministerial engagement records, Taranaki news archives and Parihaka/Taranaki iwi accounts for 1995. True if a documented visit or formal meeting between Bolger and Parihaka took place in 1995; false if no such engagement occurred, or occurred in a materially different year.

veracity.statement: He once remarked that his life was full of ironies, a reflection on his journey from privatising rail in the 1990s to later chairing its renationalised successor; and, as *Chris Hipkins had said, from selling the *Bank of New Zealand to later chairing *Kiwibank.
veracity.explanation: Asserts four matters of record about Jim Bolger: that his government privatised rail in the 1990s, that he later chaired the renationalised rail operator, that his government sold the Bank of New Zealand, and that he later chaired Kiwibank.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Companies Office / Treasury asset-sale records and KiwiRail and Kiwibank annual reports. True if (a) New Zealand Rail Ltd was sold under the Bolger government in the 1990s and Bolger is recorded as chair of the state-owned rail successor (KiwiRail) at some later date, and (b) the Bank of New Zealand was sold under the Bolger government and Bolger is recorded as chair of Kiwibank at some later date. False if any of the four is not borne out by those records — in particular if he chaired neither successor entity.

veracity.statement: Jim told me that he was nominated for the National Party candidacy in the King Country in 1972.
veracity.explanation: Relays Bolger's own account that he won the National Party candidate selection for the King Country electorate in 1972.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party candidate-selection records, contemporaneous newspaper reports, and the 1972 general election returns for King Country. True if Bolger was selected as National's King Country candidate in 1972; false if his selection was in a different year or a different electorate.

veracity.statement: He presided over the recognition of Te Wānanga o Raukawa* and Te Wānanga o Aotearoa* as wānanga under the relevant education legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that both Te Wānanga o Raukawa and Te Wānanga o Aotearoa were formally recognised as wānanga under the Education Act while Bolger was Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Gazette notices and NZQA/Ministry of Education records of establishment as wānanga under s 162 of the Education Act 1989. True if both institutions' formal recognition dates fall within Bolger's premiership (November 1990 – December 1997); false if either was recognised before or after that period.

veracity.statement: You saw the transition to MMP, as has been mentioned today, that has ushered in an era of our parliamentary story where there are more Māori MPs than ever before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of Māori MPs in the current Parliament is higher than in any Parliament before the introduction of MMP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Library counts of MPs of Māori descent by Parliament. True if the count for the current (54th) Parliament exceeds the count for every pre-MMP Parliament; false if any pre-MMP Parliament equalled or exceeded it.

veracity.statement: Who would have believed that someone who left school at 15 years old, with no qualifications, goes on to become the Prime Minister and the Leader of the National Party?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jim Bolger left school at age 15 without qualifications before later becoming Leader of the National Party and Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published biographies of Jim Bolger and the NZ Parliament / Te Ara biographical entries on his schooling — true if they record him leaving Ōpunake High School at 15 with no formal qualifications, false if they record him completing school or gaining qualifications, or leaving at a materially different age.

veracity.statement: There has been one member of Parliament between Jim Bolger and myself, and that was Shane Ardern.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an unbroken succession in the Taranaki-King Country / King Country seat: Bolger, then Shane Ardern, then Kuriger, with no other member in between.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Parliament's list of members for the King Country / Taranaki-King Country electorate from 1972 onward — true if Shane Ardern is the only member seated between Bolger's departure (1998) and Kuriger's election (2014), false if any other person held the seat in that interval, including in a by-election.

veracity.statement: Yes, I can, and what I can also confirm is that we’ve taken 21,000 people off welfare and into work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific cumulative figure for people moved from a benefit into employment under this Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit statistics / the Government's welfare target reporting on exits from main benefits into work since November 2023; true if the cumulative count is approximately 21,000 or more on the measure the Government publishes, false if materially lower or if the figure relies on a different denominator (e.g. all benefit exits, not exits into work).

veracity.statement: Today, I am pleased to announce we have not only achieved but surpassed the Government target of a 15 percent reduction in serious and persistent youth offending. We have done this more than four years ahead of the deadline, keeping communities safe by supporting young people to make better choices but also holding them to account when necessary.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable assertions: that the 15 percent reduction target for serious and persistent youth offending has been exceeded, and that this occurred more than four years before the target deadline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government Targets quarterly reporting for the serious and persistent youth offending target (baseline and current count of child and youth offenders meeting the definition) plus the published target deadline; true if the reduction exceeds 15 percent against the stated baseline and the deadline is more than four years away, false if the reduction is under 15 percent or the timing claim does not hold.

veracity.statement: Multiple and unplanned care arrangements have been associated with negative outcomes for children, and that’s why it’s great to see that, in the last year, 86 percent of children in out-of-home placements have had stable living arrangements with two or fewer caregivers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 86 percent of children in out-of-home placements had two or fewer caregivers over the last year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki quarterly/annual care statistics on placement stability (proportion of children in out-of-home placements with two or fewer caregivers in the relevant 12-month period); true if the published figure is approximately 86 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Oranga Tamariki has faced a sharp increase in reports of concern recently—up 44 percent overall.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 44 percent increase in reports of concern received by Oranga Tamariki over an unstated recent period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki published counts of reports of concern by year/quarter; true if the increase over the most recent comparable period is approximately 44 percent, false if materially different or if no comparison period yields that figure.

veracity.statement: The Mokopuna Ora initiative has seen 98 percent of children that they engage with successfully remain out of State care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 98 percent rate of children engaged by the Waikato-Tainui Mokopuna Ora initiative remaining out of State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki or Waikato-Tainui reporting on the Mokopuna Ora initiative's outcomes; true if approximately 98 percent of engaged children remained out of State care over the reported period, false if materially lower or if no such outcome measure is published.

veracity.statement: Why did she say last month that “We’ve got inflation under control” when inflation has increased over the last four quarters and is now at 3 percent?
veracity.explanation: The question asserts two checkable facts: that annual inflation has risen across each of the last four quarters, and that it currently sits at 3 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index annual inflation rate for the five most recent quarters up to September 2025; true if the annual rate rose in each successive quarter and the latest print is 3.0 percent, false if any quarter fell or the latest print differs materially.

veracity.statement: Well, I said that last month because three years ago inflation was 7.3 percent and now it’s 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual inflation was 7.3 percent three years earlier and is 3 percent now.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation series; true if a 2022 print of 7.3 percent and a current print of 3.0 percent both appear, false if either figure is materially different from the published series.

veracity.statement: Ultimately, the ultimate measure of affordability in the economy is whether wages are rising faster than inflation, which they are.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wage growth currently exceeds inflation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Labour Cost Index and/or average ordinary time hourly earnings annual growth compared with CPI annual inflation for the September 2025 quarter; true if wage growth exceeds 3.0 percent on the standard measures, false if it is at or below the inflation rate.

veracity.statement: Teachers are not getting a pay cut. They’ve been made a reasonable offer.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's offer to teachers does not constitute a pay cut — a claim that turns on whether 'cut' is read in nominal or real terms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Education's tabled collective agreement offer to NZEI/PPTA in October 2025: the nominal percentage change to base pay rates, and that change compared with CPI annual inflation over the offer's term. True in nominal terms if all rates rise; false in real terms if the annual increases fall below CPI inflation. Record which reading the evidence supports.

veracity.statement: The Government agrees, which is why in Budget 2025, we made the single largest investment in learning support in a generation of over $700 million for a range of incredibly important initiatives to provide better support for kids who need it most.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that Budget 2025 allocated over $700 million to learning support, and that this is the largest such investment in a generation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 documents (Vote Education summary and the learning support package announcement) for the headline figure, and prior Budget learning support allocations in real terms for the comparative claim; true if the package exceeds $700 million and no larger learning support allocation appears in roughly the preceding 25 years, false if the figure is lower or a larger prior allocation exists.

veracity.statement: And what, exactly, did that worker have to say about this Government’s, in real terms, under-inflation pay offers for those workers?
veracity.explanation: The question embeds a factual assertion: that the Government's current pay offers to teachers, nurses and firefighters are below inflation in real terms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The annual percentage increases in the Government's October 2025 offers to NZEI/PPTA, the nurses' collective and the firefighters' collective, compared with Stats NZ CPI annual inflation of 3.0 percent; true if each offer's annualised increase is below CPI, false if any of the named groups was offered at or above inflation.

veracity.statement: We’ve got 6,000 patients who are going to be disrupted, after Labour ran the wait-list up 30 times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the health waiting list grew thirty-fold under the previous Labour Government. He is asserting this himself, not relaying it, so it is his own claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Ministry of Health planned care waiting list series for 2017 to 2023 — specifically the count of patients waiting beyond the four-month target; true if that count rose by a factor of approximately 30 over the period, false if the growth factor is materially smaller or if no published series supports a thirty-fold increase.

veracity.statement: They got a 2.5 percent increase immediately. They get a 2.1 percent increase in October. Within 12 months, they’re up 4.7 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the specific terms of the primary principals' settlement: 2.5 percent immediately, 2.1 percent in October, 4.7 percent within twelve months.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The ratified Primary Principals Collective Bargaining Union settlement terms as published by the Ministry of Education; true if the two increases and their timing match, false if the percentages, dates or the twelve-month total differ materially.

veracity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that over 500 primary principals have settled with the Primary Principals Collective Bargaining Union (PPCBU) because they bargained in good faith, with openness and transparency, and that more principals are leaving the New Zealand Educational Institute and joining the PPCBU for that very reason?
veracity.explanation: Two checkable assertions: that over 500 primary principals settled via the PPCBU, and that principals are moving from NZEI membership to the PPCBU.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education settlement coverage figures for the primary principals' collective and PPCBU/NZEI reported membership numbers over 2025; true if more than 500 principals are covered by the PPCBU settlement and PPCBU membership rose while NZEI principal membership fell, false if the coverage count is lower or the membership movement is not evidenced. The causal 'for that very reason' is not separately checkable and should not decide the score.

specificity.statement: Today, I am pleased to announce we have not only achieved but surpassed the Government target of a 15 percent reduction in serious and persistent youth offending. We have done this more than four years ahead of the deadline, keeping communities safe by supporting young people to make better choices but also holding them to account when necessary.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific target, the percentage, and the timing against the deadline — a reader can go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In response to recent reviews, including the abuse in care inquiry, we have legislation progressing through the House this afternoon that will see changes to improve the safety for children and staff by repealing the ability to undertake strip searches of children and young people, allowing universal searches on entry to secure youth justice residences, and requiring search plans to be made with children and young people in all residences.
specificity.explanation: Names the driver (the abuse in care inquiry), the vehicle (a bill before the House today), and three concrete mechanisms — repeal of strip searches, universal entry searches, individual search plans.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: While this plan is implemented, Oranga Tamariki will be extending most contracts due to end this year through to March 2027.
specificity.explanation: A named action with an explicit end date, though 'most contracts' leaves the scope and the dollar value unstated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why did she say last month that “We’ve got inflation under control” when inflation has increased over the last four quarters and is now at 3 percent?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable question: it names the quoted statement, the trend period and the current figure. Scored high deliberately — a precise question carries as much checkable content as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They got a 2.5 percent increase immediately. They get a 2.1 percent increase in October. Within 12 months, they’re up 4.7 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two percentages, their timing, and the compounded twelve-month total — fully checkable against the settlement document.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In response to recent reviews, including the abuse in care inquiry, we have legislation progressing through the House this afternoon that will see changes to improve the safety for children and staff by repealing the ability to undertake strip searches of children and young people, allowing universal searches on entry to secure youth justice residences, and requiring search plans to be made with children and young people in all residences.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure and its mechanisms; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I encourage the Labour members to go fiscal literacy school; they need it.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party rather than the pay dispute under discussion — no policy, figure or mechanism is named. This is the party-directed jibe Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yes, including my statement that I put more effort into my Uber Eats order than that member put into her policy brain fart yesterday.
civility.explanation: A direct personal jibe at the questioner: mocks her effort and her thinking ('brain fart') rather than engaging any part of the policy. The target is the member, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I said that last month because three years ago inflation was 7.3 percent and now it’s 3 percent.
rigor.explanation: The question's premise was that inflation has risen for four consecutive quarters; the answer justifies 'under control' solely by comparison to a three-year-old peak. The chosen baseline is irrelevant to the trend put to him, so the conclusion does not engage the premise it purports to answer — a cherry-picked comparison rather than an inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re not backdating settlements, so every week that goes by, members are missing out from the unions by not settling and not being able to come with good-faith bargaining.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premise offered: if settlements are not backdated, delay does cost members money week by week. The inference is sound on its own terms; the tacked-on 'good-faith' characterisation is asserted rather than shown, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We’ve got 6,000 patients who are going to be disrupted, after Labour ran the wait-list up 30 times.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that 6,000 patients will have care disrupted by the strike scheduled for Thursday 23 October 2025. Not a promise about his own Government's action, so it is a prediction rather than a commitment.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora's post-strike reporting of deferred procedures, appointments and specialist assessments attributable to the 23 October 2025 strike; true if the reported total is approximately 6,000 or more, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: Yesterday, Stats New Zealand released the latest figures for the Consumers Price Index—the CPI—which showed annual CPI inflation increasing slightly, from 2.7 percent in the June quarter, to 3 percent in September, but remaining within the Reserve Bank’s target 1 to 3 percent band.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable data points from the September 2025 quarter CPI release: annual inflation of 3 percent, 2.7 percent in the June quarter, and that this sits inside the 1-3 percent target band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Consumers Price Index release for the September 2025 quarter: true if the annual rate is 3.0% and the June 2025 quarter annual rate was 2.7%; false if either figure is materially different or the September rate sits outside 1-3%.

veracity.statement: Let me remind members that inflation in the four quarters of 2022 was 6.9 percent in the March quarter, then 7.3 percent, then 7.2 percent, and then 7.2 percent in the December quarter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the four annual CPI prints for the 2022 calendar year quarters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual rate series for the March, June, September and December 2022 quarters; true if the four values are 6.9%, 7.3%, 7.2% and 7.2% (to rounding), false if any differs materially.

veracity.statement: Non-tradeables inflation—that is, for goods and services not exposed to international competition—fell to 3.5 percent, which is the lowest rate since mid-2021.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: the non-tradeables annual rate is 3.5 percent, and no quarter since mid-2021 has been lower.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI non-tradeables annual rate for the September 2025 quarter and the full series back to 2021; true if the print is 3.5% and every quarter from mid-2021 onward is higher, false otherwise.

veracity.statement: Local authority rates rose 8.8 percent in the year to September, and that’s why we are clear, in Government, in our call for councils to focus on the basics and to keep rates under control.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific annual increase in local authority rates for the year to September 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI local authority rates and payments subgroup, annual change to the September 2025 quarter; true if 8.8% to rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: What I can tell the member is that it’s not 7.3 percent, which is what it was under his Government because he had an 84 percent increase in Government spending, he drove inflation up to 7.3 percent, and then what he ended up doing was actually tripling our debt as well.
veracity.explanation: Three distinct factual assertions about the previous government's record: an 84 percent increase in government spending, a 7.3 percent inflation peak, and a tripling of debt.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenses and net core Crown debt series for the 2017-2023 Labour government, plus the Stats NZ CPI annual peak; true if spending rose ~84%, net debt roughly tripled and CPI peaked at 7.3%; false if any figure is materially overstated (e.g. debt less than doubled, or spending growth well under 84% on the standard measure).

veracity.statement: Is he still laser focused on the cost of living; if so, why do basic staples cost more than ever, with bread now 50 percent more expensive than it was just one year ago?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the price of bread has risen 50 percent in the year to September 2025.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ food price index / CPI bread subgroup, annual change to September 2025; true if bread prices rose ~50%, false if the rise is materially smaller (e.g. single digits).

veracity.statement: Why have rents increased by 2.6 percent over the last year, according to the Consumers Price Index figures released yesterday, when he said his $3 billion tax cut for landlords was going to lower rents?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2.6 percent annual rent increase in the latest CPI, and that the Prime Minister said the $3 billion interest deductibility change would lower rents.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI actual rentals for housing, annual change to the September 2025 quarter, plus the Hansard/press record for the Prime Minister's statements on the interest deductibility restoration; true if rents rose ~2.6% and he claimed the change would lower rents, false if either is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: One is, actually, for new rents prices have lowered, and for existing rents, prices have gone up slightly.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a divergence between the flow measure of rents (new tenancies) which has fallen, and the stock measure (existing tenancies) which has risen slightly.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE bond-data rental price series for new tenancies (flow) and Stats NZ CPI actual rentals (stock) over the year to September 2025; true if the flow measure fell while the stock measure rose slightly, false if both moved the same way.

veracity.statement: Can the Prime Minister confirm that inflation has been managed within the 1 to 3 percent target band for the last five quarters, after years of being out of control; if so, what steps has the Government taken that have helped make that possible?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual CPI inflation has been inside the 1-3 percent band for each of the last five quarters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual rates for the five quarters to September 2025; true if all five fall within 1-3%, false if any sits outside the band.

veracity.statement: But what was incredibly tragic was that in a period of low unemployment—about 3.2 percent—60,000 more people got consigned to benefits and jobseeker benefits; it increased by 50 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that jobseeker numbers rose by 60,000, a 50 percent increase, during a period when unemployment was around 3.2 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD benefit fact sheets, jobseeker support recipient counts for the 2017-2023 period, alongside the Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate; true if the count rose by roughly 60,000 (~50%) while unemployment was near 3.2%, false if the increase is materially smaller or occurred outside that period.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his claim from five months ago, that “Unemployment is just almost peaking and about to come down.”; if so, how does he explain the fact that it has continued to increase and is now at its highest number, in terms of job seekers, since 2012?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the jobseeker beneficiary count is now the highest since 2012, and that the Prime Minister made the quoted claim about five months earlier.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD jobseeker support recipient series back to 2012, plus the Hansard/media record for the quoted remark around May 2025; true if the September 2025 count exceeds every count since 2012 and the quote is accurate, false if either fails.

veracity.statement: Why should New Zealanders believe him now when he confidently predicted unemployment had peaked, yet it's still going up; he said, over a year ago, that the economy had “turned the corner”, when it's shrunk since then; he said his Government was going to increase infrastructure investment, but instead has cut it by $2.9 billion, putting thousands of people out of work?
veracity.explanation: Three assertions about the government's record: the economy has contracted since the 'turned the corner' remark, infrastructure investment has been cut by $2.9 billion against a promise to increase it, and unemployment has continued rising since the peak was called.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly real GDP series from mid-2024 to September 2025, Treasury/Budget capital allocation figures for infrastructure across the same period, and the HLFS unemployment series; true if GDP fell over that span and infrastructure spending fell by about $2.9 billion, false if GDP grew on balance or the infrastructure figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: We've had eight interest rate cuts, not 12 interest rate rises.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a count of eight official cash rate reductions under this government against twelve increases under the previous one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ official cash rate decision record; true if there have been eight OCR reductions since late 2023 and twelve increases during the 2021-2023 tightening cycle, false if either count is wrong.

specificity.statement: Yesterday, Stats New Zealand released the latest figures for the Consumers Price Index—the CPI—which showed annual CPI inflation increasing slightly, from 2.7 percent in the June quarter, to 3 percent in September, but remaining within the Reserve Bank’s target 1 to 3 percent band.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, both quarters, both figures and the target band. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Electricity prices are about 11 percent of the growth we’ve seen in the last quarter, and, actually, council rates are the other 9 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two numbered contributions to the quarter's inflation. Concrete enough to be checked against the CPI breakdown, though the phrasing leaves it ambiguous whether these are price rises or contributions to the total.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he still laser focused on the cost of living; if so, why do basic staples cost more than ever, with bread now 50 percent more expensive than it was just one year ago?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific staple, a specific percentage and a specific timeframe. A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, good economic management from this coalition Government; a senior team that actually understands economics and can deal with numbers, unlike what we’ve seen in the great New Zealand Future Fund documental pamphlet.
specificity.explanation: 'Good economic management' and 'a senior team that understands economics' commit to nothing checkable. A direct question about steps taken yields no step.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That's why you've seen the work that we've done on 18- to 19-year-olds being a parental responsibility. That's why you've seen the work that we've been doing on traffic lights and obligations that people have to look for work.
specificity.explanation: Names two actual measures — the parental assistance test for 18- and 19-year-olds, and the traffic light system of work obligations — but gives no numbers, thresholds or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Looking ahead, commodity export prices have levelled off, and so food inflation is expected to ease and inflation is expected to fall to somewhere near the mid-point target of 2 percent early next year, easing pressure on households and businesses.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that headline annual CPI inflation will fall to around the 2 percent mid-point of the target band in early 2026, driven by easing food inflation.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual rate for the March 2026 quarter; true if the annual rate is at or near 2% (roughly 1.8-2.4%), false if it remains at or above ~2.8% or falls well below 1.5%.

divination.statement: We expect that that will start to trend down, as the economy is growing.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that unemployment (and the jobseeker count under discussion) will begin falling from around late 2025 as growth resumes.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS unemployment rate for the quarters after September 2025; true if the rate declines from its late-2025 level over the following two to three quarters, false if it is flat or higher through mid-2026.

divination.statement: We have a projection for the next two years that we’ll grow faster than Australia.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand's economic growth will exceed Australia's over the following two years.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Annual real GDP growth for New Zealand (Stats NZ) and Australia (ABS) for 2026 and 2027; true if New Zealand's growth exceeds Australia's in both years, false if Australia matches or exceeds New Zealand.

rigor.statement: Clearly, the Reserve Bank is not concerned about lingering inflation, as it reduced the official cash rate by half a percent earlier this month, and financial markets are fully expecting the bank to make another 25 basis point reduction at the next opportunity in November.
rigor.explanation: A stated inference: a 50 basis point cut plus market pricing for a further cut implies the Reserve Bank is not worried about persistent inflation. The evidence genuinely supports the conclusion, though 'clearly' overstates what a single policy decision can establish about the bank's view.
rigor.subject: speaker
