rigor.statement: What I can tell the member is that it’s not 7.3 percent, which is what it was under his Government because he had an 84 percent increase in Government spending, he drove inflation up to 7.3 percent, and then what he ended up doing was actually tripling our debt as well.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal attribution: the spending increase is asserted to have caused the 7.3 percent inflation peak, with no mechanism offered and no acknowledgement of the global inflation shock of the same period. The conclusion does not follow from the correlation alone.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Actually, he could repeal the oil and gas ban and support that decision because, actually, that would help lower electricity prices.
rigor.explanation: A named action with a stated consequence, but the chain from repealing the exploration ban to lower electricity prices is asserted rather than shown, and skips the lead time between exploration and any generation effect. A real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What I can say is that isn’t it fantastic that this is a Government that, through excellent economic management and getting a grip on Government spending, has been able to lower domestic inflation from 3.7 percent to 3.5 percent?
rigor.explanation: Claims sole credit for a 0.2 percentage point move in non-tradeables inflation on the basis of its own asserted 'excellent economic management'. The causal step is bare assertion, and a change of that size is well within the range of ordinary quarterly variation.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Actually, he could repeal the oil and gas ban and support that decision because, actually, that would help lower electricity prices.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy — the oil and gas exploration ban — and a specific claimed outcome. Entirely about the policy question, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why have rents increased by 2.6 percent over the last year, according to the Consumers Price Index figures released yesterday, when he said his $3 billion tax cut for landlords was going to lower rents?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy, its cost, its stated purpose and the measured outcome. Textbook scrutiny of a government commitment, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, good economic management from this coalition Government; a senior team that actually understands economics and can deal with numbers, unlike what we’ve seen in the great New Zealand Future Fund documental pamphlet.
focus.explanation: Asked what steps the Government took, the answer is almost entirely a contrast with the other side's competence and their policy document. No mechanism, figure or named measure appears.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That's why you've seen the work that we've done on 18- to 19-year-olds being a parental responsibility. That's why you've seen the work that we've been doing on traffic lights and obligations that people have to look for work.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the government's own welfare policy settings, naming the mechanisms in question rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why should New Zealanders believe him now when he confidently predicted unemployment had peaked, yet it's still going up; he said, over a year ago, that the economy had “turned the corner”, when it's shrunk since then; he said his Government was going to increase infrastructure investment, but instead has cut it by $2.9 billion, putting thousands of people out of work?
focus.explanation: Every element names a specific commitment and a measured outcome against it — a forecast, a growth claim, an investment figure. Accountability for named commitments, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it's interesting, a day after their first policy launch and not a single question on this.
focus.explanation: Closes an answer about unemployment with a remark purely about the Opposition's conduct and the timing of their policy launch. No policy, measure or figure is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, good economic management from this coalition Government; a senior team that actually understands economics and can deal with numbers, unlike what we’ve seen in the great New Zealand Future Fund documental pamphlet.
civility.explanation: Sneering: 'actually understands economics and can deal with numbers' and 'documental pamphlet' mock the opponents' competence and their document rather than engaging what it proposes. Short of a direct personal insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is about unions who choose not to go to binding arbitration when the Minister offers to both Health New Zealand’s CEO and the senior doctors’ union to go to binding arbitration. They refuse. They’re not serious.
civility.explanation: Contested industrial dispute where there was a real opportunity to be uncivil. He criticises the bargaining conduct rather than any individual, but 'They're not serious' imputes bad faith rather than engaging the union's stated reasons. No individual is insulted, so this sits above a personal attack but below the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does the Prime Minister find it curious that a member would sit in this House, but question its right to make laws?
civility.explanation: A supplementary aimed at another member rather than at the substance — the sneer is that she is inconsistent for sitting in a House whose authority she supposedly denies. Short of a direct insult, but it targets the member's standing rather than her argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I assume all members are honourable.
civility.explanation: Invited by a colleague to attack another member's standing, he declines and affirms it instead. A genuine opportunity to be uncivil that was not taken.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, I’m not sure that that member has been listening, but we have seen a 29 percent increase in employment in the game development sector. We are performing better than Australia and actually have a better scheme than Australia, so why would they go when they get a better offer here?
civility.explanation: 'I'm not sure that that member has been listening' is a jab at the questioner's attentiveness rather than a response to the point about the rebate cap. Mild, but it lands on the person rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is about unions who choose not to go to binding arbitration when the Minister offers to both Health New Zealand’s CEO and the senior doctors’ union to go to binding arbitration. They refuse. They’re not serious.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Minister offered binding arbitration to both Health NZ's chief executive and the senior doctors' union, and that the union refused.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of the 2025 senior doctors' (ASMS) dispute — Health New Zealand and ministerial statements plus ASMS releases on whether binding arbitration was formally offered to both Health NZ's CEO and the senior doctors' union, and whether the union declined. True if such an offer was made and refused by the union; false if no binding arbitration offer was made, or if the union accepted it.

veracity.statement: Does the fact that two-thirds of rivers and half of groundwater bores are contaminated by E. coli, nitrogen, and other contaminants, while two-thirds of lakes are in poor or very poor condition demonstrates good Government stewardship?
veracity.explanation: Three separate quantified claims about the state of rivers, groundwater bores and lakes are asserted as established fact.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for the Environment / Stats NZ 'Our Freshwater' environmental reporting and LAWA monitoring data for the proportions of (a) monitored river sites exceeding E. coli/nitrogen guideline values, (b) monitored groundwater bores exceeding E. coli or nitrate limits, and (c) monitored lakes classed poor or very poor. True if each of the three stated proportions (two-thirds, one-half, two-thirds) matches the published figures within rounding; false if any is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: It’s not about Treaty settlements. This is about striking the right balance between the recognition of Māori customary rights and also the legitimate interests of all New Zealanders. In having had a lowering of the threshold under the courts, we’re bringing this back to what Parliament intended in 2011. It’s pretty simple.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the courts lowered the statutory threshold for customary marine title relative to what Parliament enacted in 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court judgments on customary marine title under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 (the Re Edwards line of cases), compared against the test as enacted in 2011. True if the courts' interpretation applied a lower threshold for customary marine title than the 2011 text and its legislative history indicate; false if the courts applied the test as enacted.

veracity.statement: As a result of the industry’s hard work, talent, and creativity and the Government’s continued support, the game development sector has seen strong growth, with a 38 percent increase in pre-tax income over the last financial year and a 29 percent increase in employment.
veracity.explanation: Two quantified growth claims about the game development sector over the last financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Game Developers Association annual industry survey for the financial year referenced. True if it reports a ~38% rise in pre-tax income and a ~29% rise in employment for the sector; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: How many game development jobs will end up overseas as a result of the decision not to increase the funding cap when 200 Kiwis a day are already leaving the country to find work overseas?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current rate of New Zealanders departing the country, and attributes the departures to seeking work overseas.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics for the year to the statement date: departures of New Zealand citizens. True if the figure supports roughly 200 New Zealanders per day (~73,000 a year) leaving; false if the relevant series is materially lower. The check should note whether the figure is net or gross departures, and whether 'to find work' is supported by any stated reason-for-travel data.

veracity.statement: Well, I’m not sure that that member has been listening, but we have seen a 29 percent increase in employment in the game development sector. We are performing better than Australia and actually have a better scheme than Australia, so why would they go when they get a better offer here?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's game development support scheme is better than Australia's equivalent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the New Zealand Game Development Sector Rebate (rebate rate and per-studio annual cap) with Australia's Digital Games Tax Offset (offset rate and cap) as published by NZTE/MBIE and the Australian Taxation Office. True if the New Zealand scheme offers a higher rate or a higher cap; false if Australia's offset rate and cap are more generous.

veracity.statement: I’m not sure that member has his ears on, because I have said that employment has grown 29 percent in the last year. The industry has earned $513 million in 2024 and is projected to surpass $750 million this year. It’s great news, the sector is in great heart, and we’re supporting them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific 2024 revenue figure for the New Zealand game development industry.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Game Developers Association annual survey reporting industry revenue for calendar/financial year 2024. True if it reports approximately $513 million; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: This Government has delivered on its promise to disestablish Te Pūkenga and rebuild a vocational education system that works for New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts in the past tense that the disestablishment of Te Pūkenga has already been delivered, on a date when the replacement structures are themselves described as taking effect on 1 January 2026.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Act and the New Zealand Gazette / TEC record of Te Pūkenga's legal status as at 21 October 2025. True if Te Pūkenga had been disestablished by that date; false if it remained a legal entity, with disestablishment scheduled for a later date.

focus.statement: Is the Prime Minister opposing iwi and hapū customary title over the foreshore and seabed because it limits his Government’s ability to approve seabed mining, bottom trawling, and deep-sea oil drilling?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy at issue — customary marine title under the MACA legislation — and names three specific activities said to be affected. Scrutiny of a named government position, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he think the closure, the ban on scalloping, the ban on crayfishing north of Auckland, and the state of the southern blue cod fishery demonstrates good Government stewardship of the coastal and marine environment?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of named fisheries decisions and outcomes. No party framing at all; it is entirely about the policy record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How many game development jobs will end up overseas as a result of the decision not to increase the funding cap when 200 Kiwis a day are already leaving the country to find work overseas?
focus.explanation: Names the specific decision at issue — not raising the rebate funding cap — and ties it to a stated outcome. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy, though the migration figure is broad framing rather than sector evidence.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister find it curious that a member would sit in this House, but question its right to make laws?
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The questioner had asked whether customary rights pre-dating the Treaty can be lawfully extinguished by legislation, which is a claim about the legal effect of Crown law, not a denial of Parliament's right to make laws. The implied inconsistency only follows from the misstated position.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yes, and I also believe that they see that the improvement in Māori literacy rates for new entrants is also giving them great trust in what this Government is doing, as well.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur. The proposition to be supported is public faith in the Government's stewardship of harbours and rivers; the reason offered — improved Māori literacy rates for new entrants — has no bearing on it. Nothing connects the premise to the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What’s more important to the Government: keeping well-paid, high-tech jobs in a growing sector in New Zealand, or giving hundreds of millions of dollars in tax cuts to tobacco companies?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy. The two options are presented as mutually exclusive when nothing offered establishes that the tobacco excise decision and the game development rebate trade off against each other.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he think the closure, the ban on scalloping, the ban on crayfishing north of Auckland, and the state of the southern blue cod fishery demonstrates good Government stewardship of the coastal and marine environment?
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete fisheries measures and conditions — the scallop closure, the crayfish ban north of Auckland, and the southern blue cod fishery — each of which can be looked up and checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does the fact that two-thirds of rivers and half of groundwater bores are contaminated by E. coli, nitrogen, and other contaminants, while two-thirds of lakes are in poor or very poor condition demonstrates good Government stewardship?
specificity.explanation: Carries three distinct proportions attached to named contaminants and named water bodies — precise enough that a reader could go and check each one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We want to make sure that we protect our natural environment but also this Government is unapologetically focused on economic growth, as well—as well as also lifting the immunisation rates for young Māori under the age of two.
specificity.explanation: A string of general commitments — protecting the environment, focusing on growth, lifting immunisation rates — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a result of the industry’s hard work, talent, and creativity and the Government’s continued support, the game development sector has seen strong growth, with a 38 percent increase in pre-tax income over the last financial year and a 29 percent increase in employment.
specificity.explanation: Two precise percentages tied to named measures (pre-tax income, employment) over a stated period. Directly checkable against the industry survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With the passing of the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, 10 regional polytechnics will be stood up by 1 January 2026, with four to be considered early next year, and eight industry skills boards will also be established on 1 January 2026.
specificity.explanation: Names the enabling legislation, the number of polytechnics and industry skills boards, and the commencement date. Every element is concrete and checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is about putting regions back in charge and unlocking the full potential of local economies, ensuring skills, jobs, and investment flow to support this Government’s Going for growth agenda.
specificity.explanation: A closing statement of generic benefits — regions in charge, full potential unlocked, skills and jobs and investment flowing — with no figure, mechanism or timeframe attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m not sure that member has his ears on, because I have said that employment has grown 29 percent in the last year. The industry has earned $513 million in 2024 and is projected to surpass $750 million this year. It’s great news, the sector is in great heart, and we’re supporting them.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that game development industry revenue will pass $750 million in the current year — an outcome of sector performance, not a commitment about the Government's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Game Developers Association annual industry survey covering 2025. True if reported industry revenue exceeds $750 million; false if it comes in at or below $750 million.

specificity.statement: Of this combined funding of $1.2 billion, $675 million is for consenting, design, route protection, site investigations, and some early works, and $515 million is for property acquisition, to get under way on these projects.
specificity.explanation: Breaks a headline figure into two named components with dollar amounts and states what each buys; someone could check it against the funding announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So far, we've delivered over $4 million in PLD for teachers to support students with complex needs using the Expanded New Zealand Curriculum, and nearly 3,000 teachers and countless students have benefited already.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure, a participant count and a named programme; checkable. 'Countless students' is the only slack in it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, that’s why I’d encourage the member to get in behind and support Fast-track, because there’s 25 renewable energy projects that will increase electricity generation in this country by 40 percent.
specificity.explanation: A count of projects, a named mechanism (the fast-track regime) and a quantified effect on generation.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How are nurses and teachers meant to shoulder rising costs, like household power bills, which have actually gone up 11.4 percent in the last year, when their pay hasn’t increased anywhere near as fast as inflation?
specificity.explanation: A precise, checkable figure attached to a named cost; a precise question, which counts as fully as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Are more than 36,000 nurses, 11,500 healthcare workers, and over 40,000 teachers all striking for political reasons?
specificity.explanation: Three separate workforce counts put to the Minister; the question is checkable against strike notices rather than a general complaint about industrial action.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Of this combined funding of $1.2 billion, $675 million is for consenting, design, route protection, site investigations, and some early works, and $515 million is for property acquisition, to get under way on these projects.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of nearly $1.2 billion approved, $675 million is allocated to pre-construction work and $515 million to property acquisition.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA board decision / Minister's 20 October 2025 roads of national significance funding announcement; true if the published allocation shows approximately $675m for consenting, design, route protection and early works and $515m for property acquisition, false if the split materially differs.

veracity.statement: It’s the 6,000 patients who are waiting for their surgeries, for their diagnoses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that around 6,000 patients have surgeries or diagnostic appointments affected by the announced strike action.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand's published estimate of planned-care procedures and specialist appointments deferred by the October 2025 health strikes; true if approximately 6,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: So far, we've delivered over $4 million in PLD for teachers to support students with complex needs using the Expanded New Zealand Curriculum, and nearly 3,000 teachers and countless students have benefited already.
veracity.explanation: Asserts over $4 million of professional learning and development spending on the extended curriculum, with close to 3,000 teachers having taken part to date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education figures on PLD expenditure and participant numbers for the Extended New Zealand Curriculum as at October 2025; true if spend exceeds $4m and participants approach 3,000, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Well, I think it’s a terrible tragedy that it’s going to impact kids who have missed out on a lot of schooling, kids who are about to go into NCEA exams; I think about the parents being mucked around, and I think about the 6,000 patients that are missing out on their surgeries because a Labour - Greens Government increased the wait-list by 30 times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the surgical wait-list grew thirty-fold under the previous Labour-led government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Ministry of Health planned care waiting-list series comparing 2017 with late 2023, on the measure of patients waiting longer than four months for surgery; true if the increase is of the order of thirty-fold on a stated measure, false if the increase is materially smaller or no measure supports it.

veracity.statement: Well, that’s why I’d encourage the member to get in behind and support Fast-track, because there’s 25 renewable energy projects that will increase electricity generation in this country by 40 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 25 renewable electricity generation projects sit in the fast-track pipeline and that together they represent a 40 percent increase in national electricity generation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 project schedule and subsequent referrals: count of renewable electricity generation projects, and their combined expected annual output as a share of current national generation per MBIE electricity statistics; true if the count is about 25 and the combined output is about 40 percent of present generation, false if either is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: How are nurses and teachers meant to shoulder rising costs, like household power bills, which have actually gone up 11.4 percent in the last year, when their pay hasn’t increased anywhere near as fast as inflation?
veracity.explanation: Asserts household electricity prices rose 11.4 percent over the year to the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ consumers price index, electricity subgroup, annual percentage change to the September 2025 quarter; true if approximately 11.4 percent, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: How are our teachers and healthcare workers meant to feed their whānau when pay offers continue to lag behind growing inflation while fruit and vegetable prices have increased by 7.4 percent in the last year?
veracity.explanation: Asserts fruit and vegetable prices rose 7.4 percent over the preceding year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ food price index, fruit and vegetables subgroup, annual percentage change to September 2025; true if approximately 7.4 percent, false if materially different.

focus.statement: Yeah, well, you guys didn’t build any, so don’t come at me about building roads.
focus.explanation: Abandons the transport programme entirely for a claim about the other side's record in general; no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yeah, well, you guys didn’t build any, so don’t come at me about building roads.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque — the criticism is dismissed on the ground that the critics have their own poor record, which does nothing to establish that the current programme is sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But this is a politically motivated move by unions; it’s unwarranted, it’s unfair, and they should just get back to the bargaining table and negotiate in good faith.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the action is unwarranted rests entirely on an asserted political motive; no evidence is offered for the motive, and the pay and staffing grounds raised in the question are not engaged at all.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Let’s not talk about Palestine as the No. 1 issue when you come to meet a Minister; actually care about educational outcomes and attendance.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: raising Palestine is treated as incompatible with caring about educational outcomes, with nothing offered to connect the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The NZTA board has now endorsed investment cases for all of the roads of national significance—most recently, in August, sections two and three of the Northland Expressway; the East-West Link, a critical project for congestion between State Highway 1 and State Highway 20; Hamilton Southern Links, which will unlock 17,000 new houses; Petone to Grenada and the Cross Valley Link, which is very important for Wellington; State Highway 1 Wellington improvements, which includes a second Mount Victoria and second Terrace tunnel, which we’re thinking about naming the Julie Anne Genter Memorial Tunnel; and the Hope Bypass.
civility.explanation: An otherwise substantive project list carries a jibe naming an individual former MP in a mock 'memorial' — mockery of a person rather than of a policy position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I understand a great many things, but one thing that I understand—that that member seems not to—is that in order to have a conversation with two parties negotiating, both parties need to be around a negotiating table.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at the questioner personally — the point is framed as something the member is too slow to grasp, rather than as a disagreement about bargaining.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Let’s not talk about Palestine as the No. 1 issue when you come to meet a Minister; actually care about educational outcomes and attendance.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the members opposite — that they do not actually care about educational outcomes — rather than contesting a position they hold.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: These reforms give learners stronger pathways from study to work, greater confidence in their qualifications, and better support from stable, accountable providers—all part of this Government’s Going for Growth agenda to deliver real skills for real jobs.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic benefits — 'stronger pathways', 'greater confidence', 'better support' — with no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named providers. The only named thing is the 'Going for Growth' agenda, which is a slogan rather than a checkable commitment. Nobody could act on or verify this.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So far, agencies have paid over $11 million in top-up payments to over 900 survivors, at an average amount of almost $12,000.
specificity.explanation: Three checkable quantities — total paid, number of recipients, and average payment — reported against a named mechanism (top-up payments). Anyone could go to agency reporting and verify or refute it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This includes 42 offences that are on the most serious end of the violent and sexual offending spectrum and that attract a maximum sentence of between seven and 20 years.
specificity.explanation: A precise count of offences and a stated maximum-sentence range, anchored to a named statutory schedule in the surrounding sentences. The scope of the regime is fully checkable against the Sentencing Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: These reforms give learners stronger pathways from study to work, greater confidence in their qualifications, and better support from stable, accountable providers—all part of this Government’s Going for Growth agenda to deliver real skills for real jobs.
focus.explanation: Squarely about her own reforms and their intended effect on learners and qualifications; no reference to another party at all. Low Specificity and high Focus is the correct pairing here — it is vague, but it is vague about the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does she agree with Civil Contractors New Zealand’s chief executive Alan Pollard, who said about her reforms, “It is not about training but about cutting costs.”; if not, why not?
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the vocational education reforms and an industry body's assessment of what they are actually for. Legitimate scrutiny of a named policy rather than party-bashing, though the critique he relays is itself framed broadly ('cutting costs') rather than pinned to a specific measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This includes 42 offences that are on the most serious end of the violent and sexual offending spectrum and that attract a maximum sentence of between seven and 20 years.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the bill before the House — which offences fall within scope and on what statutory basis. No party framing of any kind.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree with Civil Contractors New Zealand’s chief executive Alan Pollard, who said about her reforms, “It is not about training but about cutting costs.”; if not, why not?
civility.explanation: Question time on a contested reform is a real opportunity to be uncivil, and he takes none of it. The challenge is routed entirely through a named industry figure's criticism of the policy; nothing is said about the Minister's character, competence or motives.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does she agree with Civil Contractors New Zealand’s chief executive Alan Pollard, who said about her reforms, “It is not about training but about cutting costs.”; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Alan Pollard, chief executive of Civil Contractors New Zealand, publicly said of Simmonds' vocational education reforms that 'It is not about training but about cutting costs.' What is at issue is whether that attribution and wording are accurate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, media interviews or Civil Contractors New Zealand releases by chief executive Alan Pollard concerning the vocational education / ITO reforms, prior to 21 October 2025. True if Pollard made a statement to that effect in substantially those words; false if no such statement exists or the wording materially misrepresents what he said.

veracity.statement: I’m delighted to say that Alan Pollard has been very keen to be involved in the reforms and has made himself available to be a board member of the infrastructure industry skills board to help drive these reforms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Alan Pollard has made himself available to serve as a board member of the infrastructure industry skills board established under the vocational education reforms.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / Ministry of Education announcements of the membership of the Infrastructure Industry Skills Board, and Civil Contractors New Zealand statements about Pollard's role. True if Pollard was appointed to or publicly agreed to join that board on or before 21 October 2025; false if he holds no such role.

veracity.statement: In May, the Government announced a significant investment of $533 million to improve the current State redress system as quickly as possible for survivors of abuse in care, investing in changes that have a direct impact for them.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific figure — $533 million — announced in May 2025 as investment in improving the State redress system for survivors of abuse in care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 documents and the May 2025 Crown Response Unit / Government announcement on abuse in care redress. True if the announced redress package was $533 million; false if the announced figure was materially different or covered a different scope than the redress system.

veracity.statement: So far, agencies have paid over $11 million in top-up payments to over 900 survivors, at an average amount of almost $12,000.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that as at 21 October 2025 State agencies had paid more than $11 million in redress top-up payments to more than 900 survivors, averaging close to $12,000 each.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown Response Unit / redress agency (MSD, Oranga Tamariki, Education, Health) reporting on top-up payments made under the 2025 redress improvements as at October 2025. True if cumulative top-ups exceeded $11m across more than 900 survivors at an average near $12,000; false if the totals, recipient count or average are materially lower.

veracity.statement: This is modelled on very similar frameworks that apply to redress systems in Australia and Scotland.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the proposed presumption against financial redress for serious offenders, subject to review by an independent decision maker, is modelled on comparable provisions in the Australian and Scottish redress schemes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National Redress Scheme for Institutional Child Sexual Abuse Act 2018 (Cth) and the Redress for Survivors (Historical Child Abuse in Care) (Scotland) Act 2021. True if both schemes contain a provision restricting or specially assessing financial redress for applicants with serious criminal convictions; false if either scheme has no such provision or the mechanism differs materially from a presumption reviewable by an independent decision maker.

veracity.statement: The royal commission found that most survivors do not receive apologies that they feel are genuine or personal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific finding of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — that a majority of survivors did not experience the apologies they received as genuine or personal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, 2024) and its earlier redress report (He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu, 2021), sections on apologies. True if the Commission recorded that most survivors found apologies insincere or impersonal; false if the reports contain no such finding or found the opposite.

rigor.statement: However, this Government thinks it’s really important, to maintain public confidence in this scheme, that redress payments to serious offenders are considered through a separate and independent process.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion offered with a reason, so there is an inference to assess. But the premise — that public confidence in the scheme depends on serious offenders being routed separately — is asserted rather than supported; no polling, evidence or mechanism connects the two. It leans on an appeal to public opinion, and there is a real gap between 'public confidence matters' and 'therefore this specific separate process is required'. Not a non-sequitur, but not carried either.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While failing to declare or disclose relevant convictions is a serious matter, the availability of a defence and the maximum penalty of a fine, and not imprisonment, reflects the unique circumstances and vulnerability of many abuse survivors.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: two specific design features of the bill — a 'without reasonable excuse' defence and a fine-only penalty — are offered as evidence for the conclusion that the regime accommodates survivor vulnerability, and those features do support that reading. The gap is that proportionate penalties are consistent with reasons other than vulnerability, so the conclusion is well-motivated rather than compelled.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: The process will apply to all new claims made from 9 May 2025, and we expect that it will apply to around 100 claims a year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the annual caseload of the new serious-offender redress process at approximately 100 claims per year. This is a prediction about how many claimants will fall within scope, not a promise about the Government's own action, so it is a genuine forecast about an outcome outside the speaker's control.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Reporting by the State redress agencies or the redress officer on the number of claims referred into the serious-offender process in its first full year of operation. True if the figure falls broadly around 100 (roughly 50–150); false if it is materially outside that range, e.g. under 25 or over 250.

veracity.statement: It has been over a year now since the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care’s report was tabled in this House, and we will soon commemorate a year since the Crown apology last November.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two datable facts: that the Royal Commission's report was tabled more than a year before 21 October 2025, and that the Crown apology occurred in November of the previous year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary tabling record for the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's final report, and the date of the Crown apology delivered in the House; true if the tabling date is more than 12 months before 2025-10-21 and the apology falls in November 2024, false if either date is materially different.

veracity.statement: The royal commission explicitly recommended that all survivors be able to access redress, including those in prison or with a criminal record.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission's redress recommendations expressly extend to survivors who are imprisoned or have criminal convictions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's redress reports (He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu, 2021; Whanaketia, 2024); true if a recommendation states redress should be available to all survivors including those in prison or with criminal records, false if the reports are silent on that class or recommend exclusions.

veracity.statement: The much-trumpeted redress announcement in May, this year, ignored every recommendation the royal commission made about a redress system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a universal: that none of the royal commission's redress recommendations were reflected in the Government's May 2025 redress announcement. Note the speaker elsewhere in the same speech concedes a single entry point and a common assessment approach were promised.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's May 2025 redress announcement compared clause-by-clause against the royal commission's redress recommendations; false if any recommendation was adopted in whole or substantial part, true only if none were.

veracity.statement: The bill’s specifications of what a redress scheme does refers only to recognising abuse in care, with no mention of neglect, harm, or trauma, and it’s definition of abuse does not explicitly include racial or cultural abuse.
veracity.explanation: A textual claim about the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill as introduced: that its purpose/scope provision names only 'abuse' and that its definition of abuse omits racial and cultural abuse.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill as introduced; true if the purpose and interpretation clauses reference abuse without neglect, harm or trauma and the abuse definition contains no explicit racial or cultural limb, false if any of those terms appear.

veracity.statement: There are 200,000 survivors, and I bring to the House, again, the voice of another who was harmed in the system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a figure for the total number of survivors of abuse in State and faith-based care in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's estimate of the number of people abused in State and faith-based care between 1950 and 2019; true if the published estimate is approximately 200,000, false if it is materially higher or lower.

rigor.statement: We know that abuse, neglect, and trauma in care is connected with criminal behaviour and imprisonment. The royal commission made this connection clear throughout its reports. Experts tell us this, survivors tell us this, but the Government refuses to listen.
rigor.explanation: A causal premise is offered with a named evidentiary source (the royal commission's own findings), which supports the implicit conclusion that a prison-based exclusion screens out the very survivors most harmed. The tail leans on a bare appeal to authority — 'experts tell us this, survivors tell us this' — with no specific finding cited, which is what keeps it short of the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: These people who suffered in State care ended up in prison because of what they suffered, and yet now have legislation that is ignoring the call for creating a new, independent survivor-centred system as per the recommendations of the royal commission and, instead, uses a thing called “presumption” because the Government is worried about disrepute on its system that it has established, and that all we’re doing is entrenching the existing Crown-based system that protected itself.
rigor.explanation: The causal step — imprisonment 'because of what they suffered' — rests on the two individual accounts just recounted, which is argument from anecdote for a population-level claim. The imputed motive ('because the Government is worried about disrepute') is asserted rather than evidenced. The final link, that a presumption entrenches the existing Crown scheme, does follow from the bill's design, which keeps this above the floor.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We need to take responsibility as the Government on what has occurred and not try to change the deck chairs and retain the power within the Crown, and acknowledge that independence is required because how do you assess, how do you critique, and how do you improve a system when it’s yourself looking at yourself?
rigor.explanation: A genuine conflict-of-interest inference: if the assessing body is the body assessed, its findings are not independent, therefore independence is required. The conclusion follows from the premise. Delivered as a rhetorical question rather than shown, and no counter-case (e.g. statutory safeguards short of independence) is addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But it does not do the victims of those crimes any justice to know that, potentially, their abuser may now be getting financial compensation.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that redress should therefore be withheld — rests on how a third party would feel, not on any principle connecting the State's liability for its own abuse to a survivor's later offending against someone else. It is an appeal to sentiment across two unconnected obligations; the felt injustice is stipulated rather than shown to bear on eligibility.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Even if you were sodomised, does that give you the right to go and do that to another person? A hundred percent it doesn’t. Does that give you the right to go on and commit another violent crime? It 100 percent doesn’t.
rigor.explanation: A strawman: no member had argued that abuse confers a right to offend — the contested claim was about eligibility for State redress, which is a separate question from whether later offending is excusable. The proposition refuted is not the proposition advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We know that abuse, neglect, and trauma in care is connected with criminal behaviour and imprisonment. The royal commission made this connection clear throughout its reports. Experts tell us this, survivors tell us this, but the Government refuses to listen.
focus.explanation: Directed at the evidentiary basis of the bill's eligibility rule rather than at the governing parties; the closing 'the Government refuses to listen' is party framing but rides on a substantive point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill is morally bereft. It is cynical. It is a dog whistle to their base.
focus.explanation: A real objection to the bill, but this passage carries no mechanism, figure or provision — the weight sits on the other side's motives and their base rather than on what the bill does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s deeply concerning the way that this legislation has been pitched as if somehow it is fulfilling the recommendations of the royal commission of inquiry into abuse in State and faith-based care, when, actually, it betrays the intent and the mana of the inquiry’s findings.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the legislation measured against a named inquiry's recommendations — legitimate scrutiny of a specific commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Listening to the Opposition’s comments about the point around the bill about those that have committed serious violent offences, sexual violence offences, and done more than five years—look, I unreservedly accept the fact that those that suffered that kind of abuse may have gone on to commit crimes; 100 percent agree.
focus.explanation: Engages the exact eligibility provision at issue — the offence categories and the five-year sentence threshold — and concedes the opposing premise rather than pivoting to party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill’s specifications of what a redress scheme does refers only to recognising abuse in care, with no mention of neglect, harm, or trauma, and it’s definition of abuse does not explicitly include racial or cultural abuse.
specificity.explanation: Points to identified provisions of a named bill and lists the exact terms said to be missing — checkable against the text without further elaboration.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s deeply concerning the way that this legislation has been pitched as if somehow it is fulfilling the recommendations of the royal commission of inquiry into abuse in State and faith-based care, when, actually, it betrays the intent and the mana of the inquiry’s findings.
specificity.explanation: Names the inquiry and the claimed gap in general terms, but identifies no clause, recommendation number or mechanism that is said to be betrayed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need to take responsibility as the Government on what has occurred and not try to change the deck chairs and retain the power within the Crown, and acknowledge that independence is required because how do you assess, how do you critique, and how do you improve a system when it’s yourself looking at yourself?
specificity.explanation: A direction — independence — with no proposed structure, appointing body, funding or timeframe attached. 'Change the deck chairs' is metaphor rather than content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Listening to the Opposition’s comments about the point around the bill about those that have committed serious violent offences, sexual violence offences, and done more than five years—look, I unreservedly accept the fact that those that suffered that kind of abuse may have gone on to commit crimes; 100 percent agree.
specificity.explanation: Names the offence classes and the five-year threshold, which is checkable against the bill, but supplies no numbers on how many survivors the threshold would exclude.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill is morally bereft. It is cynical. It is a dog whistle to their base.
civility.explanation: Unsparing about the bill and the motive behind it, but no individual member is named, insulted or impugned. Under the re-anchored scale, ferocity aimed at a measure is not incivility; a small deduction only because 'cynical' and 'dog whistle' impute bad faith to the Government collectively.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Even if you were sodomised, does that give you the right to go and do that to another person? A hundred percent it doesn’t. Does that give you the right to go on and commit another violent crime? It 100 percent doesn’t.
civility.explanation: Blunt and confrontational, and it repeats an interjector's words back at them, but the target is the argument rather than any member's character or competence. No individual is disparaged.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m a member of the Social Services and Community Committee—a great committee—and I think this bill will be coming our way; I’m really interested to hear from those survivors and the public about their experiences.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill will be referred to the Social Services and Community Committee. Referral is a decision of the House, not an action of the speaker, so it is a prediction rather than a promise.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The House's referral motion recorded in Hansard at the conclusion of the bill's first reading; true if the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill is referred to the Social Services and Community Committee, false if it is referred to any other select committee or is not referred at all.

veracity.statement: This redress system, as it’s been characterised in this House, is not depriving anyone of redress.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill does not remove access to redress for anyone, only routes some claimants through a different process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill as introduced: true if every person otherwise eligible retains a pathway to financial redress (e.g. by application to the independent redress officer) with no absolute bar; false if any class is barred outright from redress.

veracity.statement: It undermines Aotearoa’s obligation under international human rights law, including the convention against torture and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, both of which require the State to provide redress to all victims of institutional abuse, without discrimination.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two named treaties impose an obligation to provide redress to all victims of institutional abuse without discrimination, and that the bill breaches it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of the Convention against Torture (esp. art. 14) and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (esp. art. 39), plus the relevant treaty-body general comments and NZ concluding observations: true if those instruments obligate redress to all victims of institutional abuse without distinction; false if the redress obligation is confined to torture/ill-treatment as defined and does not extend to all institutional abuse or bar such distinctions.

veracity.statement: One in three children placed in residential care by the State ends up in prison later in life. That number is 42 percent for mokopuna Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rate of later imprisonment among children placed in State residential care, and a higher rate for Māori children.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care (Whanaketia) final report and the underlying Oranga Tamariki / Corrections linked-data statistics: true if roughly one in three of those placed in State residential care are later imprisoned, and ~42% for Māori; false if the figures materially differ, or if the published statistic runs the other direction (the share of prisoners who were in State care).

veracity.statement: Māori account for 67 percent of the children in State care and 81 percent of those who were abused in those institutions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Māori share of children in State care and of those abused in care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki care-population statistics for the period referenced and the Royal Commission (Whanaketia) findings on the ethnic breakdown of those abused in care: true if the figures are 67% and 81% within rounding for a stated period; false if materially different or if no comparable figure exists for the abused population.

rigor.statement: It is a reality that when you are the victim of that serious violent and sexual offending, you will feel aggrieved if the State pays significant financial redress to your offender.
rigor.explanation: Offers a predicted emotional reaction as the justification for treating a class of survivors differently; an appeal to sentiment stands in for a reason why the differential treatment is warranted, though the point is coherent on its own terms.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Many of those convictions were born out of the trauma inflicted by the very institutions this bill now seeks to protect. To deny redress on that basis is to deny responsibility for the harm that the Crown and the Church caused in the first place.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: if the convictions are causally downstream of State-inflicted harm, then using them as a disqualifier does disclaim responsibility for that harm. The premise is unestablished, but that is a veracity matter; the step from premise to conclusion holds, with only a slight stretch in treating denial of payment as denial of responsibility.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is to ensure those payments to serious offenders do not bring the scheme into public disrepute, which is important because it’s important that we take the public with us on this challenging journey, to address this.
rigor.explanation: The justification loops back on itself ('important because it's important') and rests on an appeal to public opinion; nothing is offered to connect payments to serious offenders with loss of public support for the scheme.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I myself have worked in criminal courts and prisons around New Zealand, and I do know that the victims often become the victimisers.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to personal experience and authority: professional exposure is offered as the warrant for a general empirical claim, with no evidence supplied for the claim itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is a matter of trying to deliver a consistent approach that is easily accessible and survivor focused.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — consistent, accessible, survivor focused — with no mechanism, figure, threshold or timeframe attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It undermines Aotearoa’s obligation under international human rights law, including the convention against torture and the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, both of which require the State to provide redress to all victims of institutional abuse, without discrimination.
specificity.explanation: Names the two instruments and states the obligation claimed; stops short of citing the article or the specific provision the bill is said to breach.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: One in three children placed in residential care by the State ends up in prison later in life. That number is 42 percent for mokopuna Māori.
specificity.explanation: Two precise, sourced-style figures with a defined population; anyone could go and check them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We will implement the 81 of the 183 recommendations from the Whanaketia report.
specificity.explanation: Names the report and gives an exact count against a total, but does not identify which 81 recommendations or by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill does something else as well, which you’ve heard from some other speakers today: it also legislates that a survivor of abuse in State care, convicted of serious violent or sexual crimes and sentenced to five years or more in prison is not automatically eligible for a financial payment of the redress scheme.
specificity.explanation: States the exact eligibility mechanism, the offence class and the five-year sentence threshold that triggers it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the redress officer, it establishes that it must be an independent person, appointed by the Minister, who is either a retired judge, a King’s Counsel, or a lawyer with at least seven years’ experience, and who also understands the criminal justice system and the findings of the royal commission into historical abuse in State and faith-based care.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the appointing authority, the qualifying categories and the seven-year experience threshold — checkable directly against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think that when we drive emotive speeches that are suggesting that we are depriving anyone of their right to be heard, it is unfair to the victims and unfair to the work that has been done by a large group of people to develop a system that is trying to deliver a positive outcome.
civility.explanation: Pointed: characterises opposing speeches as 'emotive' and unfair to victims, which edges toward the motives of those making them, but stops short of naming or attacking any member.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I just think it’s really unfortunate that when we heckle in this House, when we hurl abuse at each other as we’re making speeches, we are not presenting this House in a proper light.
civility.explanation: In a heated debate where naming and attacking opponents was available, the criticism of heckling is framed inclusively ('we') and lands on no individual.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill is a betrayal of survivors, plain and simple.
civility.explanation: Brutal about the legislation, but the target is the bill, not any member; under the re-anchored scale fierce criticism of a policy is the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It discriminates against a class of survivor based on their criminal record, punishing them twice for a system that failed them first.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific mechanism of the bill — the eligibility bar tied to convictions — rather than the other party's general character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What’s more, the royal commission recommended that survivors who are in prison or have a criminal record should not be unduly penalised—clear as a bell—but, sadly, this bill penalises those people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care made a specific recommendation — that survivors who are imprisoned or have criminal records should not be unduly penalised — and that this bill contradicts it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The final report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions (Whanaketia, 2024), redress chapters: true if a recommendation states that survivors with convictions or in prison should not be excluded from or penalised in redress; false if no such recommendation appears.

veracity.statement: My mother, I think I've said before, spent 20 years, the longest serving Parole Board member in this country, appointed by the National Government—appointed by the Rt Hon Jim Bolger, actually, who we're going to honour on Thursday.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three checkable facts: a 20-year tenure on the New Zealand Parole Board, that this was the longest of any member, and that the appointment was made under Jim Bolger's National Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Parole Board / Department of Corrections annual reports and Gazette appointment notices for board members. True if the named person served approximately 20 years, appointed during Bolger's premiership (1990–1997), and no member is recorded with a longer tenure; false if the tenure, the appointing government, or the 'longest serving' claim does not hold.

veracity.statement: The bill implements the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State and Faith-Based Care to, firstly, recognise the experience as a person of abuse in care, and, secondly, to offer an alternative to litigation to be able to provide that redress.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill implements the Royal Commission's redress recommendations, and characterises those recommendations as recognition plus an alternative to litigation. This is the point directly contested by other speakers.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the Bill as introduced (and its explanatory note and regulatory impact statement) against the Royal Commission's redress recommendations. True if the Bill's provisions correspond to those recommendations; false if it departs from them on material points, such as eligibility of claimants with convictions.

veracity.statement: What’s being proposed here—and this is particularly for Minister Costello, who seems to be saying something quite different—is a presumption, a presumption that people in this situation have no right to redress.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Bill establishes a presumption that a defined group of claimants has no right to redress. Whether the Bill creates a presumption against redress, or only a different process with retained eligibility, is the factual question.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The clauses of the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill dealing with claimants convicted of serious offending. True if the Bill creates a presumption of ineligibility for redress for that group; false if eligibility is retained and only the assessment pathway differs.

veracity.statement: They save about $12,500 if the person stands by the presumption, and that is inappropriate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific per-claimant fiscal saving to the Crown of about $12,500 where the presumption is applied.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Bill's regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure statement and Crown Response Unit costings on average redress payments and forecast savings. True if the figure forgone per affected claimant is approximately $12,500; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Only 5 to 6 percent of claimants may even fall into this category, and most of them have not gone on to cause other victims in the system.
veracity.explanation: Two quantitative claims: that 5–6 percent of redress claimants fall within the affected category, and that a majority of those have not themselves caused other victims.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD / Crown Response Unit claimant data or the Bill's regulatory impact statement on the proportion of claimants with convictions engaging the presumption, and on how many have caused further victims. True if both the 5–6 percent share and the 'most have not' proportion match the official figures; false if either is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: They will still have the right to seek potential redress and so they still have that available.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that claimants in the affected category retain a right to seek redress under the Bill — the direct factual counter to the claim that the Bill removes that right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Bill's clauses on affected claimants and the independent process it establishes. True if such claimants may still apply and have their claim independently assessed; false if the Bill bars them from seeking redress.

focus.statement: What’s more, the royal commission recommended that survivors who are in prison or have a criminal record should not be unduly penalised—clear as a bell—but, sadly, this bill penalises those people.
focus.explanation: Names a specific recommendation of a named inquiry and a specific effect of the bill before the House — accountability on the policy, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What’s being proposed here—and this is particularly for Minister Costello, who seems to be saying something quite different—is a presumption, a presumption that people in this situation have no right to redress.
focus.explanation: Directed at the mechanism of the Bill itself — what the presumption is and whom it applies to — rather than at the other party's record or character.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know they're not being written off, but people who have been victims of the State are still being penalised by the State, and that's the problem with this bill.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the counter-point (claimants are not excluded outright) and still draws the conclusion from a stated premise — that the same institution which harmed them imposes a further penalty. The inference from 'penalised again' to 'that is the problem' holds, though the mechanism by which the bill penalises is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If I had seen a law here that suggested that all the money that was going to be set to the victim of some terrible abuse was going to be given to the victim of the victim, well then you might have an argument. We might be able to discuss that in a different way. But that’s not what’s being proposed here.
rigor.explanation: States the condition under which the opposing argument would succeed, then denies that condition obtains — a valid form of rebuttal rather than a mischaracterisation. The gap is that she asserts rather than demonstrates that the Bill does not do this.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: So, obviously, you're going to get an angry response from many of the victims out there.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that survivors of abuse in care will react angrily to this bill. Not a promise about his own action; a prediction about others' response.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Public record after the bill's first reading: submissions to the select committee on the Redress System for Abuse in Care Bill, and statements from survivor/advocacy groups reported in NZ media. True if multiple survivors or survivor groups publicly oppose or condemn the bill; false if survivor response is broadly supportive or absent.

specificity.statement: They save about $12,500 if the person stands by the presumption, and that is inappropriate.
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure tied to a named mechanism (the presumption), so the claim can be checked against the Bill's costings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Only 5 to 6 percent of claimants may even fall into this category, and most of them have not gone on to cause other victims in the system.
specificity.explanation: Supplies a numeric share of the claimant population attached to a defined category, which someone could check against departmental data.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The bill was introduced on 12 November 2024, and on the same day the Prime Minister apologised on behalf of the Crown to survivors of abuse and neglect in care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two dated facts: the introduction date of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, and that the Crown apology to survivors of abuse in care was delivered by the Prime Minister on that same date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bills database / legislation.govt.nz record for the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, plus the Hansard record of the Crown apology. True if the bill's first reading/introduction is dated 12 November 2024 and the Prime Minister delivered the Crown apology in the House on 12 November 2024; false if either date differs.

veracity.statement: There was widespread support for this change during the select committee process, and no person or organisation submitted against it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that of the submissions received by the Social Services and Community Committee on the children's workers safety regime change, none opposed it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Social Services and Community Committee's published submissions and departmental report on the bill. True if no submission opposes the Children's Act core-worker overseas-conviction change; false if at least one submitter opposed it.

veracity.statement: Currently, the Act provides that a child or young person must not be kept in secure care for more than 72 continuous hours, or more than three consecutive days, without judicial intervention.
veracity.explanation: A claim about the text of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 as it stood before this amendment — that it caps secure care without judicial oversight at both 72 continuous hours and three consecutive days.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The pre-amendment text of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 (secure care provisions, s 368/371 area) on legislation.govt.nz. True if it states both a 72-continuous-hour limit and a three-consecutive-day limit before judicial intervention; false if the limits stated differ.

specificity.statement: Under this bill, it will be unlawful to employ a core worker if they have an overseas conviction for an offence that is equivalent to a New Zealand offence specified in the Children’s Act, or a conviction for certain offences involving harm against minors in the Prostitution Reform Act 2003.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism (employment prohibition), the class of person (core workers), the triggering condition (equivalent overseas convictions) and the two statutes involved. Someone could check the clause and act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are committed to doing better for survivors, and I know these changes to our existing legislation will make a difference.
specificity.explanation: Asserts a commitment and an outcome with no figure, mechanism, threshold or timeframe — 'doing better' and 'make a difference' commit to nothing checkable, in a speech that elsewhere carries precise detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The bill removes the reference to the period of up to 72 hours. This means that the child or young person can only be held in secure care for the shorter of the time periods currently allowed.
rigor.explanation: A premise (the 72-hour reference is deleted) with a conclusion that tracks it (only the remaining, shorter-binding limit can apply). No fallacy or appeal; the inference holds given the stated content of the Act.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In their response to the royal commission, published in May this year, the Government declined to accept, or had not even started to consider, 85 of the royal commission’s 207 recommendations from across the two reports, Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu. The Government has fully accepted only 19 recommendations, and they claim to have completed a mere 13.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific counts from the Government's May 2025 response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care: 85 of 207 recommendations declined or not yet considered, 19 fully accepted, 13 recorded as completed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's May 2025 response to Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu (Crown Response Office publication), tallied by recommendation status: true if it shows 85 declined/not-yet-considered out of 207, 19 fully accepted and 13 completed; false if the counts differ materially.

veracity.statement: Further, we were concerned about the inclusion of the potential use of force during searches at youth justice facilities, and I submitted several amendments to include the use of proven de-escalation methods as an approach to avoiding the use of force—but these were not supported by the Minister and the Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the speaker lodged amendments to the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill requiring de-escalation methods, and that the Minister and Government did not support them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Amendment papers lodged in Prime's name against the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, plus the Hansard committee-of-the-whole record: true if such de-escalation amendments were lodged and were defeated or withdrawn without Government support; false if no such amendments exist or they were agreed to.

specificity.statement: In their response to the royal commission, published in May this year, the Government declined to accept, or had not even started to consider, 85 of the royal commission’s 207 recommendations from across the two reports, Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu. The Government has fully accepted only 19 recommendations, and they claim to have completed a mere 13.
specificity.explanation: Names the response document, its month of publication, both royal commission reports, and four exact figures (85, 207, 19, 13). Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Further, we were concerned about the inclusion of the potential use of force during searches at youth justice facilities, and I submitted several amendments to include the use of proven de-escalation methods as an approach to avoiding the use of force—but these were not supported by the Minister and the Government.
specificity.explanation: Names the provision (use of force during searches at youth justice facilities) and the remedy proposed (de-escalation methods via amendments), but gives no clause numbers, amendment numbers or content of the de-escalation requirement.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In their response to the royal commission, published in May this year, the Government declined to accept, or had not even started to consider, 85 of the royal commission’s 207 recommendations from across the two reports, Whanaketia and He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu. The Government has fully accepted only 19 recommendations, and they claim to have completed a mere 13.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny: names a specific government response and specific outcomes against a named commitment. No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government’s approach to Māori, Pacific, disabled people, people receiving income support, and young people in the youth justice system demonstrates that discrimination is alive and well in this country.
focus.explanation: Points at real policy domains (income support, youth justice) so it is not content-free tribalism, but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of the Government rather than any named measure or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We wholeheartedly welcome the removal of the use of strip searching for children and young people. This is entirely consistent with the royal commission’s recommendations and is a well-overdue change.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific provision of the bill (removal of strip searching for children and young people) and relates it to the royal commission's recommendations. Entirely on the policy, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And we have not seen a great deal of action from this Government, so perhaps they have been distracted—unless you call kicking the can down the road “action”.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic jab ("kicking the can down the road") aimed at the Government's record rather than at any individual. Pointed and mocking in tone but lands on the collective and its conduct, not on a person's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister was well-placed to consult properly or to remove this part of the bill, or to do further consultation, but she chose not to. That goes against the entire point of the royal commission.
