civility.explanation: Criticises a specific decision the Minister made and the options she had, not her character, competence or motives. "She chose not to" is a pointed attribution of responsibility that stays on the substance; it edges toward implying indifference without asserting bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The change to the Crimes Act to include disabled people as vulnerable adults was not supported by submitters. As a result, if passed, we will have something in legislation that is not supported by the people it is supposed to be there for. This result is wrong and should not have occurred.
rigor.explanation: Premise (submitters, including the affected group, opposed the clause) supports the stated conclusion (the enacted provision will lack the support of its intended beneficiaries). Valid given its assumptions; the only gap is treating submitters as representative of disabled people generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As we know so well, the children and young people who are in youth justice facilities have complex and often traumatic backgrounds; they need trauma-informed, specialist, wraparound approaches, not force.
rigor.explanation: The premise (traumatic backgrounds) does point toward the conclusion (trauma-informed rather than forceful responses), but the connecting step is asserted rather than shown, and "as we know so well" substitutes shared assumption for evidence — a mild appeal to common knowledge.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This Government’s approach to Māori, Pacific, disabled people, people receiving income support, and young people in the youth justice system demonstrates that discrimination is alive and well in this country.
rigor.explanation: "Demonstrates" claims a proof relation, but nothing in the statement is offered as the demonstrating evidence — no policy, decision or figure is identified. The conclusion rests on bare assertion about an unspecified "approach".
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This sits alongside the Government’s pilot boot camp legislation, to put these into law—no doubt soon—to be again considered in this House.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government's legislation putting the military-style academy (boot camp) pilot into law will come back before the House in the near future. A prediction about another party's action, not a promise about the speaker's own.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Order Paper and Hansard record for the Government bill legislating the military-style academy/boot camp pilot: true if that bill has a further reading or committee stage in the House on or before 30 June 2026; false if it has not been considered again by that date.

rigor.statement: The Green Party supports the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill because survivors deserve for us to support progress.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (support the bill) offered with a reason, so there is an inference to assess — but the reason is close to question-begging: it assumes the bill constitutes the progress survivors deserve rather than showing it. She concedes two sentences later that it falls well short of the recommendations, which undercuts the stated premise. Not a fallacy of the crude kind, but a real gap between what is offered and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings.
specificity.explanation: Names the precise legislative target — new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28 — and the substantive issue (permitted use of force in care settings). Anyone could go to the bill and check what that clause does. Short of 1.0 only because the nature of the concern is stated generically rather than with the mechanism or an alternative drafting.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
specificity.explanation: Two hard figures against a named body of recommendations — precise, checkable, and the reader knows exactly what is being measured. Held below the top only because the follow-on demand ("move a heck of a lot faster") carries no target or timeframe of its own.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are also still concerns from survivors over new section 384KB, inserted by clause 28, and the use of force that is still permitted in care settings.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: a named clause, a named section, and the policy effect it has. No party framing at all. This is the paradigm case of on-policy scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However, disabled people have been very clear that the proposed definition risks framing them through a lens of deficit and dependency rather than recognising autonomy, agency, and mana.
focus.explanation: Engages the substance of the bill — the definition of "vulnerable adult" and who it affects — and grounds the objection in the affected group's stated position. Nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
focus.explanation: Named commitment, named shortfall, and she explicitly extends it to "any Government of the day" rather than pinning it on one party. Textbook accountability rather than tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Surely we would all want for that, but in the former redress system bill, you are seeing some survivors’ abuse and violence undermined and minimised by creating a hierarchical structure that sees only some survivors being paid redress, what all survivors should be entitled to, and that to me is one of the biggest harms against the royal commission of inquiry, against the evidence, against the survivors, that the State is choosing to minimise and undermine the harm that it has caused only to some people, that it is saying that only some people’s harm deserves to be recognised, only some people deserve to be recognised for the violence that was inflicted upon them by the State.
focus.explanation: Names a specific companion bill and the specific mechanism objected to (a hierarchical eligibility structure limiting who is paid redress). The criticism is of a policy design, not of the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Has that bench seen this times nine [Holds up report] of the reports and the evidence and the harm and the lived experience of survivors to then stand up and demand us to not be emotive?
focus.explanation: A rhetorical challenge to the other side's conduct and attentiveness in the debate. It gestures at the inquiry reports, but names no clause, figure or policy outcome — the weight of the statement is on what that bench is like rather than on what the bill does. Note this is not a Civility item: it is aimed at a bench, not at any individual member.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side and how they spoke. No measure, figure, clause or outcome is named, even though a bill is before the House for her to engage with.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I note that only 28 of the 138 recommendations have been completed or have seen progress initiated, so we all have a responsibility to move a heck of a lot faster or more meaningfully than that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable figures about implementation of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's recommendations: that the inquiry made 138 recommendations, and that as at October 2025 only 28 of them were completed or had progress initiated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's final report Whanaketia (July 2024) recommendation count, and the Crown Response Office's published progress reporting on those recommendations as at October 2025. True if the report contains 138 recommendations and the official progress tracker records 28 (±rounding of category boundaries) as completed or with progress initiated; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: So back to this bill, because it was really important that I put that on record and I am proud of putting that on record—and I note some of your speakers stood up for about 10 seconds and also asked us to not be emotive.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Government speakers in this debate spoke for roughly ten seconds and that they asked opposition members not to be emotive. The "about 10 seconds" figure is the part most at risk of being overstatement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard transcript and Parliament TV timing for the third reading debate on the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, 21 October 2025. True if at least one Government speaker's contribution ran to roughly ten seconds and a Government speaker in that debate called on members not to be emotive; false if the shortest Government contribution was substantially longer or no such call was made.

civility.statement: Surely we would all want for that, but in the former redress system bill, you are seeing some survivors’ abuse and violence undermined and minimised by creating a hierarchical structure that sees only some survivors being paid redress, what all survivors should be entitled to, and that to me is one of the biggest harms against the royal commission of inquiry, against the evidence, against the survivors, that the State is choosing to minimise and undermine the harm that it has caused only to some people, that it is saying that only some people’s harm deserves to be recognised, only some people deserve to be recognised for the violence that was inflicted upon them by the State.
civility.explanation: About as fierce as criticism gets — accuses the State of choosing to minimise survivors' harm — and it lands entirely on the legislation and the institution, not on any member. Under the re-anchored scale this is the expected standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m really struggling to kind of even respond to some of the rubbish that has been spouted from the other side of the House.
civility.explanation: "Rubbish" and "spouted" are dismissal rather than engagement — the manner of the opposing speech is sneered at rather than any part of it answered. Short of a direct personal insult, and aimed at a bench rather than a named member, but it is no longer civil engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yeah, well, I’m actually one of those survivors, so can you just calm it down and allow people to have their own opinions without rubbishing everybody under one category, because at the end of the day, we can talk to multiple survivors who will all have a different version of how this has affected them, how this has traumatised them, and how they want us, as a Government, to respond to that.
civility.explanation: A sharp personal rebuke directed at another member ("can you just calm it down") and a charge of "rubbishing" people, but it stops short of attacking anyone's character or competence and moves immediately to the substantive point that survivors differ. Pointed and robust, edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Reasonable force is not about violence; reasonable force is done in good practice, with good training, to make sure that de-escalation does happen first, before reasonable force is used, and to say that that’s not going to happen is actually disingenuous.
civility.explanation: The bulk of the sentence engages the substance of the reasonable-force provisions, but it closes by calling opponents' argument "disingenuous" — an imputation of bad faith rather than error. That is a genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In the committee of the whole House, it was explained quite well to the Opposition that de-escalation training will happen, and so to say that that was not addressed is actually quite a joke—to say that we didn’t address that problem.
civility.explanation: Mockery of the Opposition's position ("quite a joke") combined with the suggestion they were told and did not take it in. It targets how opponents are behaving rather than their argument, but there is no direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has worked tirelessly in the background, changing practice across the youth justice system and professionalising the youth justice system to make sure that our young people are actually cared for in a way that is appropriate.
specificity.explanation: A claim of substantive activity with no checkable content: no named practice change, no figure, no timeframe, no mechanism. "Worked tirelessly", "professionalising" and "in a way that is appropriate" commit to nothing anyone could verify or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On top of the changes to the Public Records Act there is work going on in the background—particularly with Oranga Tamariki—around an upgrade to our front-line technology system, which will allow young people to have access to their lives in their own time and under their own rules on how they want to be able to access their information.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific statute, a specific agency and a specific class of action (a front-line technology upgrade enabling self-service records access), which is real detail. But there is no cost, no timeframe, no delivery date and no description of what the system will actually do — a direction with some detail, missing the how much and the by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill is a start. The bill is a process. Change needed to happen; more change will continue to need to happen.
specificity.explanation: Four clauses that convey no checkable content whatsoever — no provision, figure, mechanism, timeframe or named next step. "More change will continue to need to happen" commits to nothing that could be verified or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Look, we hear it quite a bit that these changes that are done have not been done in consultation with survivors, but what I would say is that there was six years of consultation with survivors: six years of an inquiry into the abuse in care, six years of listening to survivors, and six years of writing survivors’ stories, to be held and written for everybody to be able to read that going into the future.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the abuse-in-care royal commission constituted six years of consultation with survivors — a claim about the inquiry's duration and about survivor engagement being a sustained part of it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The establishment date and final-report date of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions, plus its published engagement record. True if the inquiry ran for approximately six years and included direct survivor consultation/testimony throughout; false if its duration was materially shorter or if survivor engagement did not span that period.

veracity.statement: The previous Government knew that this inquiry was happening, it knew of some of the recommendations well before we came into Government, and I think that we need to stop attacking each other and actually work together to move forward.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the previous Government was aware of the inquiry and had received some of its recommendations before the current Government took office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The publication dates of the royal commission's interim reports and recommendations (including the December 2021 redress report He Purapura Ora, he Māra Tipu) against the date the current Government took office in late 2023. True if recommendations were published and delivered to the previous Government before that date; false if all recommendations post-date the change of government.

veracity.statement: I think, to put some context into this bill, it was introduced at a time when the apology was being delivered and we wanted, as a Government, to ensure that there was a clear message that work had commenced, was under way, and was being prioritised.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a factual coincidence of timing between the bill's introduction to the House and the delivery of the Crown apology to survivors of abuse in care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliament's bill record for the introduction (first reading) date of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill, compared with the date of the Crown's formal apology to abuse-in-care survivors. True if the bill was introduced within days of the apology; false if the two are separated by months.

rigor.statement: What I don’t think we need to do is to constantly stop the work that we’re doing to have another talkfest when what survivors do want is for something to happen now, and that was the whole point of the recommendations.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (no further consultation is needed) rests on a premise the speaker herself contradicted earlier in the same speech — she argued survivors do not all want the same thing, then here attributes a single uniform preference to "survivors". Hasty generalisation from an assumed collective will, with the dismissive framing "talkfest" doing argumentative work in place of a reason.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I think that to say that there was no consultation is a little bit low, because there was six years of consultation.
rigor.explanation: Equivocation on "consultation": the criticism is about consultation on this bill's contents, while the rebuttal offers consultation conducted for the royal commission. The premise does not reach the conclusion because the two refer to different exercises.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whilst I appreciate that the Opposition is supporting these bills, what I would have appreciated more would be their speaking to the positive changes and speaking about how this will have a great effect on those who have fought for years to be heard and who have fought for years to have some of these changes made—and it was all made political.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the other side conducted itself in the debate — their tone and their alleged politicking — rather than about the measure. No policy, provision, figure or outcome is named; the complaint is about the Opposition's framing, which is the tribalism case this attribute exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What the bill misses is what the survivors asked for. They asked for the disestablishment of Oranga Tamariki.
focus.explanation: Names a specific institutional change survivors sought (disestablishing Oranga Tamariki) and measures the bill against it. This is scrutiny of a named policy question, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Unfortunately, some members of this House are very aware of that, and they are seeking to use this for political gain, which is unfortunate because this is a serious issue and a serious matter for many, many New Zealanders, both those directly affected, those indirectly affected, and for all of us.
focus.explanation: Concerns the motives and conduct of opposing members rather than any provision of the bill. No policy, figure or outcome is named in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What the bill misses is what the survivors asked for. They asked for the disestablishment of Oranga Tamariki.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific agency and a specific structural demand, but supplies no mechanism, timeframe or figures for what disestablishment would involve.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our solutions that we had were there, right in front of us all, to agree across every party in this House, and that was to adopt the 138 recommendations of the Whanaketia report—138 recommendations.
specificity.explanation: Names the report and the exact number of recommendations, and states a concrete course of action (adopt all of them); short of 1.0 because no individual recommendation, cost or timeframe is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This is not transformation—be very clear, w’ānau mā. This is business as usual. This is maintenance.
specificity.explanation: A characterisation of the bill offered entirely as labels — nothing in it identifies a clause, an agency function or a measurable outcome that would let anyone check the claim or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The research found that one-in-five within our prison system has been a victim of abuse in State care.
specificity.explanation: Gives a definite proportion and attributes it to research, so it can be looked up and checked; it stops short of naming the study, period or measure used.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are some changes to be made to the Oranga Tamariki Act, the Children's Act, the Crimes Act, and the Public Records Act—an omnibus bill, to make some changes to that.
specificity.explanation: Names the four statutes amended, which is checkable, but says only that 'some changes' are made — no clause, mechanism or effect is identified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Our solutions that we had were there, right in front of us all, to agree across every party in this House, and that was to adopt the 138 recommendations of the Whanaketia report—138 recommendations.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whanaketia report contains 138 recommendations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report, Whanaketia – Through pain and trauma, from darkness to light (July 2024); true if its recommendation list totals 138, false if it totals a materially different number.

veracity.statement: No; we’ve gone from apology to no action.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no action has followed the Crown's formal apology to survivors of abuse in care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of Crown measures enacted between the 12 November 2024 apology and 21 October 2025 — legislation, redress changes and agency reforms responding to the Royal Commission. True if no such measures were enacted; false if measures were (for example, the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill then at third reading, or changes to the redress process).

veracity.statement: The research found that one-in-five within our prison system has been a victim of abuse in State care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research — in context, the Royal Commission's evidence — found that one in five people in the New Zealand prison population were abused while in State care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care findings and the Department of Corrections prison-population research it drew on; true if a stated proportion of roughly 20 percent of prisoners are identified as having been abused in State care, false if the published proportion is materially different or if no such finding exists.

civility.statement: And I think the sad thing is that if we had a Prime Minister who truly supported this apology, then he would have proved it, and this Government would have proved it in everything they did.
civility.explanation: Moves from the bill to the Prime Minister personally, imputing that his support for the apology was not genuine. Short of a direct insult, but it is an attribution of bad faith to an individual rather than criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Unfortunately, some members of this House are very aware of that, and they are seeking to use this for political gain, which is unfortunate because this is a serious issue and a serious matter for many, many New Zealanders, both those directly affected, those indirectly affected, and for all of us.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to named-by-implication colleagues — that they are exploiting survivors' abuse for advantage. No individual is insulted outright, but motive-attribution of this kind is a civility failure rather than criticism of an argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And I think the sad thing is that if we had a Prime Minister who truly supported this apology, then he would have proved it, and this Government would have proved it in everything they did.
rigor.explanation: A no-true-Scotsman conditional: 'truly supported' is defined by the outcome the speaker wants, so no conduct could count as genuine support. The conclusion about the Prime Minister's sincerity is contained in the premise rather than derived from any evidence offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I don’t care what anyone who isn’t a survivor in this House has to say.
rigor.explanation: Genetic fallacy — the worth of an argument is settled by who is making it rather than by its content. It rules out the opposing case without engaging any part of it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are, unfortunately, many cases where people will use force against themselves or others, and reasonable force needs to be used to stop that, so let's have a responsible conversation as we continue this piece of work, ladies and gentlemen.
rigor.explanation: The support offered is a single anecdote about an adult prisoner assaulting a lawyer, generalised to justify use-of-force provisions for young people in Oranga Tamariki custody. Appeal to anecdote plus a disanalogy between the two settings: the conclusion about the bill's provisions does not follow from the case described.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is important the Government does well with this kaupapa, but when you have initiatives, like boot camps, that were clearly recommended against by experts in the community—absolutely adamant that that type of a strategy was not going to, and does not, benefit people who've been through the system—totally ignored by the Government, it does not help.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (boot camps) and a specific criticism (expert advice against it was disregarded). This is scrutiny of a named government initiative, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government needs to stop attacking communities, survivors, Māori.
focus.explanation: A general characterisation of the other side's disposition. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing here that could be held to account — only the claim that they are 'attacking' people.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is important the Government does well with this kaupapa, but when you have initiatives, like boot camps, that were clearly recommended against by experts in the community—absolutely adamant that that type of a strategy was not going to, and does not, benefit people who've been through the system—totally ignored by the Government, it does not help.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that community experts clearly and adamantly recommended against boot camps for people who have been through the care system, and that this advice was ignored by the Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official advice and submissions on the military-style academies — Oranga Tamariki/MSD departmental advice and regulatory impact statements, and expert and academic submissions on the youth offender military-style academy programme. True if officials and expert submitters advised against the boot-camp model and it proceeded anyway; false if the weight of expert advice supported it or no such advice exists.

veracity.statement: Just today—just today—in The Post, he criticises the manner in which the Government has gone about this process by limiting the involvement by survivors and by ignoring the call for a real, independent redress system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the day of the debate The Post published criticism from Ihorangi Reweti Peters that the Government limited survivor involvement in the process and ignored calls for an independent redress system.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Post's published output for 21 October 2025. True if an article that day carries Ihorangi Reweti Peters criticising the Government's abuse-in-care redress process on both grounds stated (limited survivor involvement; no independent redress system); false if no such article ran or its content differs materially.

veracity.statement: This is a legacy owed to the courageous nearly 2,400 survivors who provided their experience and shared their experience of abuse that has contributed to the commission’s work, which has now resulted in this additional step to improve the safety and wellbeing of children.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that close to 2,400 survivors provided their accounts of abuse to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission's final report Whanaketia and its published engagement statistics — the count of survivors who gave evidence or shared their experience with the inquiry. True if that figure is approximately 2,400; false if it is materially higher or lower.

civility.statement: I don’t come here to criticise or condemn any of the stories from the Government, from Minister Chhour. I do respect her story, her life story, and her position.
civility.explanation: In a contested third-reading debate where the Minister's own record was squarely available as a target, the speaker explicitly declines to attack her and directs his disagreement at the policy instead.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I’m trying to say, Mr Seymour, is that one of the calls from survivors was that the Treaty of Waitangi be respected and be part of this whole legislation, but Mr Seymour has got this weird sort of resentment to the Treaty and doesn’t understand that part of the Treaty process is that there is a special consultation process that has to be set up with Māori, that Mr Seymour disagrees with and refuses to be part of.
civility.explanation: Attributes a named member a 'weird sort of resentment' and a failure to understand — an attack on the person's motives and comprehension rather than on his stated position, though a policy point sits alongside it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, you are politicising it, because you’re not listening to what we’re saying.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to another member — that he is playing politics and wilfully not listening. Short of a direct insult, but it targets the person's conduct rather than the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I mean, how can we legitimately be against abuse in State care while still—and this is the point—allowing the State to use force, you know?
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument: opposing abuse in care while authorising State use of force is presented as contradictory. The inference is intelligible but rests on an unargued equivalence between abuse and any statutory use of force, which is the distinction the bill turns on — a real gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But the bill does not go far enough and, in many ways, is a missed opportunity.
specificity.explanation: Offers a substantive verdict on the bill but no figure, mechanism, clause or threshold — nothing that says how far the bill would have to go, or what the missed opportunity consisted of.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As other speakers have talked about, we are doing many things in the background. We cannot do it all at once.
specificity.explanation: Claims a programme of work exists but names none of it — no measure, no timeframe, no agency, nothing a listener could check or follow up on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Clearly, for some people, redress will mean they will get something; redress for others will mean they get nothing, no matter what the abuse they suffered.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the redress arrangements will produce payments for some survivors while leaving others who suffered abuse in care with nothing at all under the eligibility rules.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The eligibility criteria and first tranche of determinations of the redress system once operating (scheme rules and published decision statistics). True if applicants who suffered abuse in care are declared ineligible for any redress payment; false if every applicant found to have suffered abuse in care receives some form of redress.

veracity.statement: It wasn’t an easy one to remedy, and it hasn’t satisfied the Green Party, but it—this bill—actually has got the support of this House as a result.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two checkable things about the bill's passage: that the Green Party remained dissatisfied with the use-of-force provisions, and that the bill nonetheless carried the support of the House.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard record for the third reading of the Responding to Abuse in Care Legislation Amendment Bill on 21 October 2025, plus Green Party members' speeches on it. True if the bill was read a third time with the support of all parties (including the Greens voting for it) while Green speakers recorded dissatisfaction with the use-of-force provisions; false if the Greens voted against, or if any party opposed such that the bill lacked House-wide support.

veracity.statement: We’ve got way too high levels of domestic violence and sexual violence in this country, and sexual violence is actually on the rise.
veracity.explanation: The checkable component is that sexual violence in New Zealand was increasing as at October 2025. The 'way too high' clause is a value judgement and is not the part being assessed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey sexual-assault prevalence estimates and NZ Police recorded sexual assault and related offences, for the years up to 2025. True if either series shows a sustained increase over recent years beyond sampling error; false if the rate is flat or declining across both series.

veracity.statement: As a result of that, all three coalition parties campaigned on a concept, similar to what is in this bill, known as the rule of two.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that National, ACT and New Zealand First each campaigned at the 2023 general election on accepting medicines approved by two overseas regulators.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 general election health policy documents and manifestos of National, ACT and New Zealand First. True if all three published a policy to allow medicines consented by two overseas jurisdictions to be used in New Zealand; false if any one of the three had no such campaign policy (a post-election coalition agreement commitment does not satisfy 'campaigned on').

rigor.statement: That’s an incredibly important thing, because we know this is a place where violence grows—a relationship where somebody has no choice but to be there is a place where violence grows and there is predatory behaviour—so it’s really important that we make these amendments, and we change the system so that we’re checking overseas convictions.
rigor.explanation: An argument is offered: captive relationships create conditions for predatory behaviour, therefore vetting of those working with people in care should be strengthened. The inference from risk to vetting holds, but the key premise is asserted and then largely restated rather than supported, which is mildly circular.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s a definition of a vulnerable adult in the situation where a person is unable, by reason of those definitions—and that’s age, sickness, mental impairment, disability—to withdraw himself or herself because they are in the charge of another person.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual statutory test being debated and enumerates its elements (age, sickness, mental impairment, disability) and its condition (being in the charge of another). Someone could check the definition against the Crimes Act wording.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This engagement has to continue and it has to be a partnership, and I think it has to be a partnership with the people impacted.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no mechanism, no forum, no timeframe and no test for what would count as partnership. 'Partnership with the people impacted' commits to nothing checkable, and the surrounding sentences add process sentiment rather than detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It simply says that if two other jurisdictions have consented a medication for an indication, then it can be used in New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: States the operative mechanism of the bill precisely — the number of jurisdictions required, that the consent must be for the indication, and the consequence. Falls short of 1.0 only because it does not name which jurisdictions qualify or the timeframe, both of which are left to regulation.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t accept what Minister Chhour said when she said, “We have been engaging for six or seven years.” That is just not good enough.
civility.explanation: Directly rejects a Minister's account of consultation, but the target is the adequacy of the engagement, not the Minister as a person. No imputation of bad faith or personal capability.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I don’t accept what Minister Chhour said when she said, “We have been engaging for six or seven years.” That is just not good enough.
focus.explanation: Names a specific point of accountability — the Government's engagement with the abuse-in-care sector on this bill, and the Minister's stated justification for it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named process rather than party-bashing, though it stops short of detailing what adequate engagement would look like.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There are such things as magnanimity and grace, but they take time to earn in the House, and some members clearly have not spent that much time here just yet, but we have hope for them, just as we have hope for all people.
civility.explanation: Contested debate where a civil alternative was plainly available. No direct insult, but the remark is condescending toward unnamed other members — it implies they lack the standing to be magnanimous and adds a patronising 'we have hope for them'. Sneering/condescension short of a direct insult sits at the 0.5 failure band. Civility always attributes to the speaker even though the jibe is aimed at others.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Allowing all prescribers to prescribe will mean that people can get access to medications at critical times.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House — names the mechanism (extending prescribing rights) and the outcome it is meant to produce. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Allowing all prescribers to prescribe will mean that people can get access to medications at critical times.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism, but carries no figures, no timeframe and no definition of which prescribers or which medications, so the 'how much' and 'by when' are missing. Scored independently of Focus, which is high.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That means that there will be an estimated $90 million in economic benefit over the next decade from being able to have these conferences here.
specificity.explanation: A figure ($90 million), a timeframe (a decade) and a named source of the benefit (hosting medical conferences in New Zealand). Checkable and actionable regardless of whether it turns out to be accurate.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That means that there will be an estimated $90 million in economic benefit over the next decade from being able to have these conferences here.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a future economic outcome — that hosting medical conferences domestically, once the Amendment Paper legalises them, will generate about $90 million of economic benefit over the following ten years. Not a promise about the speaker's own action; the promise is the law change, the forecast is the economic consequence.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Regulation / MBIE evaluation or regulatory impact material on the medical-conference amendment, plus Stats NZ or Tourism NZ business-events expenditure data for medical conferences held in New Zealand between 2026 and 2035. True if the cumulative measured economic benefit over the decade is at least roughly $90 million; false if it is materially below that (e.g. under half), or if conferences of this kind are not held here at all.

veracity.statement: This is something that has come through the Ministry for Regulation’s red tape tip line and is a very good example of the Government listening and responding so that there can be more opportunities for New Zealanders to do well and to have greater opportunity to improve their lives through their own efforts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about provenance: that the medical-conference change originated from a submission to the Ministry for Regulation's red tape tip line, rather than from officials or the Minister's own initiative. The evaluative second half ('a very good example of the Government listening') is opinion and is not the claim being checked.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Regulation records or published summaries of red tape tip line submissions, and the departmental advice on the Amendment Paper. True if a tip line submission raising the medical-conference/unapproved-medicines marketing restriction is on record and is cited as the origin of the change; false if the change originated elsewhere and no such submission exists.

veracity.statement: We heard 185 submissions and oral evidence from 32 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific submission counts for the Health Committee's consideration of the Medicines Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Medicines Amendment Bill (2025) states the number of written submissions received and the number of submitters heard; true if 185 submissions and 32 oral submitters, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It doesn't include changes to existing drugs, new indications, formulations, or administration routes, and these actually make up a large share of the Medsafe applications.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a scope limitation of the bill (new medicines only) and that changed-medicine applications are a large share of Medsafe's application workload.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Medsafe's published application statistics / annual reporting on new medicine applications versus changed medicine applications (new indications, formulations, routes of administration); true if changed-medicine applications are a large share (roughly comparable to or greater than new medicine applications), false if they are a small minority. Scope limitation checkable against the Bill as reported back.

veracity.statement: Speaking of which, we know that, certainly under this Government's watch, it's become harder than ever to see a doctor or a nurse or a specialist.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that access to primary care and specialist care is now at its worst recorded level, and that this deterioration has occurred under the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey unmet need for primary care (adults reporting they could not see a GP when needed, due to cost or availability) plus Te Whatu Ora first specialist assessment wait-time data; true if the most recent figures are the highest/worst in the published series, false if earlier periods in the series were worse.

veracity.statement: I find it is my obligation to remind the House that this Government is putting more money into health than ever before—ever before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that current health expenditure is at an all-time high; ambiguous between nominal dollars and real or per-capita terms, so both readings need checking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health appropriations in the most recent Budget compared with prior years (Treasury Budget documents / Estimates of Appropriations); true if the figure is the highest on record in nominal terms, and separately check CPI-adjusted per-capita health spend — false if the latest year is not the highest on the measure claimed.

veracity.statement: They are extremely skilled, they are well trained—they have four years of training, they have 300 clinical hours—and they are good people to extend that part of the Act to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific training requirements for nurse practitioners and prescribers: four years of training and 300 clinical hours.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Nursing Council of New Zealand registration requirements for nurse practitioners (and Pharmacy Council requirements for pharmacist prescribers); true if the required programme amounts to about four years and includes a supervised clinical practicum of about 300 hours, false if the required hours or duration are materially different.

specificity.statement: It will allow the medicines to be approved for distribution in New Zealand when they've been approved by two other overseas jurisdictions.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism of the bill (approval contingent on two overseas jurisdictions) but supplies no timeframe, threshold list or figures in the statement itself.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that families are paying more, they're waiting longer, and they're getting less.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance about health access but carries no figure, service, timeframe or mechanism — a three-part slogan rather than a checkable claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: This will reduce the time it takes to get the medicines approved.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the rule-of-two pathway will shorten actual medicine approval times in New Zealand — an outcome, not merely a promise to pass the bill.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Medsafe published approval timeframes for new medicine applications: true if median/mean time to approval for applications under the recognised-jurisdiction pathway is shorter than the pre-Act baseline for comparable applications; false if approval times are unchanged or longer.

rigor.statement: It still requires a sponsor application. Companies need to see a commercial reason to apply in the first place, and the biggest barrier to that is going to be and will remain Pharmac funding, not necessarily Medsafe approval times. So unless Pharmac can fund the medicine, companies simply aren't going to bother making those applications and applying in the first place.
rigor.explanation: A genuine chain of inference: the scheme is sponsor-initiated, sponsors act on commercial incentive, funding drives that incentive, therefore approval-time reform alone will not generate applications. The conclusion tracks the premises offered; whether Pharmac funding really is the binding constraint is a separate (Veracity) question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If a country has a medicine approved by two of those countries, then clearly it is appropriate for approval here.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is asserted rather than supported — 'clearly' does the work of an argument. Nothing is offered to connect approval in two named jurisdictions to appropriateness in the New Zealand context (population differences, indications, supply). An appeal to obviousness.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s best practice that it goes through a select committee process, for a good reason. There are experts in this field, international lessons to be learnt, and we have a very powerful pharmaceutical industry across the world.
rigor.explanation: Reasons are offered for the conclusion — expert knowledge exists, comparable overseas failures exist, and the regulated industry is powerful — and each bears on why scrutiny of a late amendment matters. The link from the US opioid case to this particular amendment is analogical and left partly unargued, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, it is good for patients in need; it is good for the families of the patients. We are a Government that puts patients first; therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: The stated conclusion rests on a self-description rather than a premise: 'we are a Government that puts patients first; therefore, I commend the bill' is circular, and the benefit to patients is restated from the bill's purpose rather than shown to follow from anything.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can't help but reflect on the fact that National’s focus on cutting corners, on shifting control to Ministers rather than making the system work for patients, has been a step in the wrong direction.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point inside it — the bill's transfer of Classification Committee appointments to the Minister — but the weight of the sentence is party framing about National's motives rather than the measure itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We are opposed to this aspect and I think it is worth being very explicit about that. The Medicines Classification Committee, we think, should remain absolutely independent.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure: names the specific body and the specific provision of the bill being opposed, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's unfortunate that on something that has wide support of the House, the member who just resumed her seat, Tracey McLellan, couldn't but help herself to take the opportunity to spread misinformation about what this Government is doing in the health sector.
civility.explanation: Turns on a named individual rather than her argument: 'couldn't but help herself' is a jibe at her self-control and 'spread misinformation' imputes bad faith rather than error. A clear personal attack, though short of sustained abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Yes, it may be a great idea; however, it has come through the Ministry for Regulation, which, we know, is a creation from the ACT Party and is an interesting institution given that it's supposed to be about deregulating but is actually also being seen as a bit of an institution for fast tracking.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Ministry for Regulation was created by/for the ACT Party, and that it is functioning as a fast-tracking body rather than a deregulating one. The checkable core is the origin claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–ACT coalition agreement (November 2023) and the Cabinet papers/Order in Council establishing the Ministry for Regulation: true if the Ministry was established as an ACT coalition commitment with an ACT minister responsible; false if it originated independently of ACT or predates that agreement.

veracity.statement: I think nearly 200 submitters came before the select committee in writing and orally, and there were about 30-odd in terms of oral submissions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts approximate submission counts for the Health Committee's consideration of the Medicines Amendment Bill — roughly 200 submissions in total and around 30 heard orally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Health Committee's report on the Medicines Amendment Bill (and the committee's published submissions list) on parliament.nz: true if total submissions are close to 200 and oral submissions number around 30; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: In Kaitāia, there are some 3,000 whānau in Kaitāia that don’t have access to a GP right now.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that approximately 3,000 households/families in Kaitāia are currently without access to a general practitioner.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora primary care enrolment data for the Kaitāia/Far North area, or Te Hiku Hauora's reported unenrolled patient numbers for 2025: true if roughly 3,000 people or families are recorded as unenrolled/without GP access; false if the figure is materially lower.

veracity.statement: We see that strikes are coming up on 23 October, so clearly there are some issues within the health system.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that health-sector strike action was scheduled for 23 October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Union strike notices (NZNO / ASMS / APEX) and contemporaneous reporting for October 2025: true if health-sector strike action was formally notified for 23 October 2025; false if no such action was scheduled for that date.

focus.statement: Yes, it may be a great idea; however, it has come through the Ministry for Regulation, which, we know, is a creation from the ACT Party and is an interesting institution given that it's supposed to be about deregulating but is actually also being seen as a bit of an institution for fast tracking.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point here — the provenance and process of a late amendment — but the weight of the sentence is party framing about ACT and the character of the institution rather than the substance of the amendment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When we are now looking at the Medicines Classification Committee being a ministerial appointment, we don't think that is correct. It should be appointed by the director-general.
focus.explanation: Entirely about a named provision of the bill before the House, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We know that we want to get faster access to medicines, and it’s absolutely welcomed, but there also needs to be consideration around the wider pūnaha hauora, or the wider health system, in terms of both medication and the medicines but also access to those skilled clinicians that are needed in the community but also in secondary and tertiary care.
focus.explanation: Squarely directed at the policy question — whether the health system and its workforce can absorb what the bill enables. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We were given no warning, as far as I'm aware, and I think it does show, again, a bit of a lack of respect for due process by this Government.
civility.explanation: A pointed criticism of the Government's handling of the amendment. It targets a process failing by a collective body, not any individual member's character or competence, so it sits near the expected standard rather than being a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We were given no warning, as far as I'm aware, and I think it does show, again, a bit of a lack of respect for due process by this Government.
rigor.explanation: Premise (no warning of the amendment, so submitters could not be heard) supports the conclusion (disregard for due process). The inference tracks what was offered, though it leans somewhat on 'as far as I'm aware' and on a single instance to support 'again'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We also are happy that the medicines that are introduced will still need a sponsoring pharmaceutical company. That does provide a level of accountability that, we feel, will avoid New Zealand becoming a dumping-ground for inferior batches of drugs or drugs that could potentially be harmful.
rigor.explanation: An argument is advanced: a sponsor requirement creates accountability, therefore substandard product is deterred. The step is plausible but there is a real gap — nothing is offered connecting the existence of a commercial sponsor to the physical quality of batches, so the conclusion outruns the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We see that strikes are coming up on 23 October, so clearly there are some issues within the health system.
rigor.explanation: A short inference — scheduled strike action is offered as evidence of underlying problems in the system. It follows, but it is thin: the single fact is asked to carry a broad conclusion signalled by 'clearly'.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It does seem a little bit strange that when there's been other countries of the same ilk who have approved medicines that we would have to have a long, drawn-out procedure before they could be used here in New Zealand. This is about having new pathway to speed that up.
rigor.explanation: Advances an argument: comparable regulators have already assessed these medicines, so a full duplicate assessment here is unnecessary delay, and the bill's new pathway addresses it. The inference follows, but it rests on an unstated and unargued premise that 'countries of the same ilk' have equivalent standards.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we are now looking at the Medicines Classification Committee being a ministerial appointment, we don't think that is correct. It should be appointed by the director-general.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific body, the specific provision objected to, and the concrete alternative appointment mechanism proposed. Someone could act on this directly as an amendment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In Kaitāia, there are some 3,000 whānau in Kaitāia that don’t have access to a GP right now.
specificity.explanation: Gives a figure, a named place and a present timeframe — precise enough that someone could go and check it against enrolment data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We know that we want to get faster access to medicines, and it’s absolutely welcomed, but there also needs to be consideration around the wider pūnaha hauora, or the wider health system, in terms of both medication and the medicines but also access to those skilled clinicians that are needed in the community but also in secondary and tertiary care.
specificity.explanation: A direction rather than a proposal: it identifies workforce and system capacity as the gap but supplies no figures, mechanism, funding or timeframe. This is the paired case with focus — clearly about the policy, but carrying little checkable detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is about making it easier for New Zealanders to access medicines they need in a timely manner, because we know that some of these medicines can be the difference between life and death.
specificity.explanation: States the bill's general purpose in broad terms — no mechanism, no timeframe, no figures, nothing that could be checked or acted on. It is trying to convey substance, so it is eligible, but it commits to nothing concrete.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Much like Miss White, I am disappointed that that hasn't been brought to the committee at an earlier stage, because, as I've said, I think this is an area of huge public interest, and I suspect that there would have been submissions in terms of what is and isn't permissible at those medical conferences.
civility.explanation: Criticism of the Government's handling of the amendment is directed entirely at the process and its consequences for scrutiny; no member's motives, competence or character is impugned, though there was a clear opening to do so.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This bill's regulatory impact statement sites research comparing the registration of medicines across 20 OECD countries, which, in shocking news, between 2011 and 2020, New Zealand ranked last for the approval of modern medicines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that research cited in the Medicines Amendment Bill's regulatory impact statement compared medicine registration across 20 OECD countries over 2011-2020 and placed New Zealand last for approval of modern medicines.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement for the Medicines Amendment Bill and the study it cites (a 20-country OECD registration comparison covering 2011-2020): true if New Zealand is ranked 20th of 20 for approvals of new/modern medicines in that period; false if New Zealand is ranked higher, if the comparison covers a different country count or period, or if no such research is cited.

veracity.statement: This is, of course, something that the Labour Government introduced and that, in July this year, was removed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that free prescriptions (removal of the $5 prescription co-payment) were introduced by the previous Labour Government and were removed in July 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of the prescription co-payment policy: the Budget/legislative record for when the $5 co-payment was removed under the Labour Government, and the Ministry of Health / Pharmac notice of when the charge was reinstated. True if free prescriptions were a Labour Government measure and the charge returned in July 2025; false if either the originating government or the July-2025 reinstatement date is wrong.

veracity.statement: They have a new code of practice that was introduced in 2016, with updates in 2024, with a real understanding that for the public to trust these institutions, they need to know that they're independent, and they need to trust not only the individuals who are in those roles but the way in which they were appointed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the United Kingdom introduced a new code of practice governing public appointments in 2016 and updated it in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The UK Cabinet Office Governance Code on Public Appointments: true if a code was issued in 2016 and a revised version issued in 2024; false if the original code carries a different year or if no 2024 revision was published.

specificity.statement: This bill's regulatory impact statement sites research comparing the registration of medicines across 20 OECD countries, which, in shocking news, between 2011 and 2020, New Zealand ranked last for the approval of modern medicines.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, the number of countries, the exact date range and the ranking - all directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A couple of things that really excite me about this: firstly, the expansion of nurse practitioners to be able to prescribe unapproved medicines where that’s appropriate to their scope of practice.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a named provision - extending prescribing of unapproved medicines to nurse practitioners, bounded by scope of practice - so the change and who it affects are checkable. No figures or timeframe, which keeps it short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So while this certainly does address one of the issues, it doesn't address the second leg of the issues, and so there's, actually, a big question mark about whether this will go the whole way in resolving the issue of ensuring that there is access to medicines.
rigor.explanation: Premises are laid out immediately before (registration delay is one barrier; Pharmac non-funding deterring suppliers is a second, untouched by the bill) and the conclusion - that the bill will not fully resolve access - follows from them. No fallacy; it is short of 1.0 only because 'the whole way' is left loose enough that the conclusion is weaker than stated.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is, of course, something that the Labour Government introduced and that, in July this year, was removed.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (free prescriptions) and a specific change to it, tying it to the access-to-medicines argument at hand. Party framing is present but the content is a concrete measure, not general other-team commentary.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act was enacted by the National-led Government in 2011 following significant consultation and widespread dissatisfaction with Labour’s earlier Foreshore and Seabed Act.
focus.explanation: Names two specific Acts and the policy history that produced them; the reference to Labour carries some party framing, but the content is about the legislation rather than the other party's character.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The current wording of section 58 of the Act plainly states that in addition to holding the specified area in accordance with tikanga, the applicant groups need to have had exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the statutory test in s 58 currently requires — two limbs, tikanga plus exclusive use and occupation from 1840 without substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The enacted text of section 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 on legislation.govt.nz as at 21 October 2025. True if s 58 requires both (a) holding the specified area in accordance with tikanga and (b) exclusive use and occupation of it from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption; false if either limb is absent or materially differently worded.

veracity.statement: However, the Supreme Court’s own interpretation of the test has since been applied in the lower courts, with no apparent change to the outcomes, resulting in extensive awards of customary marine title, including the entire coast from Kāpiti to Manawatū and in southern Wairarapa.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that post-Re Edwards lower court decisions produced the same outcomes as before and granted CMT over entire named stretches of coastline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court customary marine title determinations issued after the Supreme Court's Re Edwards judgment (November 2024) and before 21 October 2025. True if those decisions awarded CMT covering the continuous coastline between Kāpiti and Manawatū and areas of southern Wairarapa; false if no such awards were made, or if the awards were materially narrower than the whole of those coastlines.

veracity.statement: During readings of this Act in the House back in 2011, the Hon Chris Finlayson and the Hon Tariana Turia both emphasised the Act was intended to recognise customary marine title in specific parts of the coastline.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about what two named Ministers said during the 2011 passage of the Act regarding the expected geographic extent of CMT.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the 2011 readings of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill. True if both Chris Finlayson and Tariana Turia stated that customary marine title was expected to be recognised only over particular or limited parts of the coast; false if neither did, or if their speeches indicated no such limitation.

veracity.statement: As I’ve said previously, the Government recognised the impact this has had on affected applicants and has provided $15 million to support costs for re-hearings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $15 million fund has been provided to cover applicants' costs of re-hearings caused by the changed test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial announcements and Budget/appropriation records for the takutai moana process. True if $15 million was allocated to meet applicant costs for re-hearings under the amended test; false if no such fund exists or the amount allocated differs materially.

specificity.statement: The current wording of section 58 of the Act plainly states that in addition to holding the specified area in accordance with tikanga, the applicant groups need to have had exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named section of a named Act, both limbs of the test and the 1840 baseline date — a listener could go and check the wording.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, the Supreme Court’s own interpretation of the test has since been applied in the lower courts, with no apparent change to the outcomes, resulting in extensive awards of customary marine title, including the entire coast from Kāpiti to Manawatū and in southern Wairarapa.
specificity.explanation: Names the deciding courts and two identifiable stretches of coastline; stops short of naming the individual judgments or the areas involved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I’ve said previously, the Government recognised the impact this has had on affected applicants and has provided $15 million to support costs for re-hearings.
specificity.explanation: Gives a dollar figure and states precisely what it is for; no timeframe or eligibility mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Retrospective provisions in legislation are reserved for exceptional circumstances and these are exceptional. The current approach to the test by the courts is damaging to the takutai moana process as a whole.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that these circumstances are exceptional is asserted rather than argued — the premise states the standard and the next sentence simply restates the claim in different words ('damaging to the process'). Circular: the exceptionality is established by assuming it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If the bill has prospective effect only, it would be unfair to those applicants who, by way of scheduling, would be subject to a stricter restored test, while others retain awards under what Parliament regards as an incorrect interpretation of the legislation.
rigor.explanation: A valid consistency argument: if the test changes prospectively, otherwise-identical applicants are treated differently purely by hearing date, which does support the unfairness conclusion. The gap is that it treats retrospectivity as the only cure without addressing the alternative of leaving the test alone.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The third reading of this bill continues a long legacy of this House, over many, many years, of treating Māori as second-class citizens.
civility.explanation: Fierce criticism of the bill and of the House's legislative record. No individual is attacked, no bad faith imputed to a person — under the re-anchored scale this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Yet, for whatever reason, this Government continues to say co-governance, co-management, or working alongside Māori, is not the thing to do, and would rather score political points instead of underscoring the good frameworks that are already in place that allow management of places like the marine and takutai moana—in this instance, the Ninety Mile Beach.
civility.explanation: Imputes a self-serving motive ('would rather score political points'), but to the Government collectively rather than to any individual member. Pointed and edging toward bad faith without landing on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The third reading of this bill continues a long legacy of this House, over many, many years, of treating Māori as second-class citizens.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House (the bill's third reading) and its named effect on customary and property rights, not about the other party's general character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Yet, for whatever reason, this Government continues to say co-governance, co-management, or working alongside Māori, is not the thing to do, and would rather score political points instead of underscoring the good frameworks that are already in place that allow management of places like the marine and takutai moana—in this instance, the Ninety Mile Beach.
focus.explanation: A genuine policy point — names co-governance/co-management frameworks and a specific instance, the Ninety Mile Beach arrangement — but a meaningful share of the weight is the motive attribution to the other side rather than the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The third reading of this bill continues a long legacy of this House, over many, many years, of treating Māori as second-class citizens.
rigor.explanation: There is an inference offered — the bill ignores historic, customary and property rights, therefore it treats Māori as second-class citizens — and the conclusion tracks the premise. But the step from 'ignores these rights' to 'second-class citizens' leans on characterisation rather than anything shown, so there is a real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yet, for whatever reason, this Government continues to say co-governance, co-management, or working alongside Māori, is not the thing to do, and would rather score political points instead of underscoring the good frameworks that are already in place that allow management of places like the marine and takutai moana—in this instance, the Ninety Mile Beach.
specificity.explanation: Names a governance mechanism and a specific place, which is more than a slogan, but supplies no figures, no description of how the existing framework works, and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have an arrangement there to look after the Ninety Mile Beach on behalf of all New Zealanders, which was agreed on by this House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a statutory arrangement exists under which Te Rarawa (with other Far North iwi) manage Ninety Mile Beach, and that Parliament enacted it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand statute book and Parliament's legislation record: true if an Act passed by the House establishes a body or arrangement giving Te Rarawa and/or neighbouring Far North iwi a management role over Ninety Mile Beach / Te Oneroa-a-Tōhē; false if no such enacted arrangement exists and any management role rests on a non-statutory or purely council instrument.

veracity.statement: She publicly apologised for that particular matter, and we continue to work on our relationship to build that bridge again and build that relationship with the Māori people.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Jacinda Ardern, as Prime Minister after the 2017 election, publicly apologised on Labour's behalf for the party's 2004 foreshore and seabed legislation — and, from the preceding sentence, that this was among the first things she did in office.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting and speech records from late 2017 to 2018 (Rātana, Waitangi, Hansard, party releases): true if Ardern publicly and explicitly apologised for the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 in that period; false if she only expressed regret in weaker terms, or if no such public apology by her can be located.

civility.statement: The Minister is more concerned with giving away seabed rights to Aussie miners and bottom trawlers than with recognising the customary rights of indigenous New Zealanders.
civility.explanation: Goes past the policy to impute a motive to the Minister personally — that he prefers offshore mining interests to Māori rights. That is an attack on the person's good faith, not on the bill's mechanism.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It's the worst kind of rubbish that has come before this House, and it will be undone by a future Government, and we will have to stand up and apologise, Minister, for this nasty piece of legislation to somehow try and restore the honour of the Crown that you are disdaining.
civility.explanation: 'Rubbish' and 'nasty' aimed at the legislation are fierce policy criticism and cost nothing under this scale, but 'the honour of the Crown that you are disdaining', addressed directly to the Minister, imputes bad faith to him personally.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Get thee hence, Satan—this is the worst pettiness and nastiness.
civility.explanation: Delivered across the Chamber at the Minister, it reads as sneering condemnation of the person; he then expressly disclaimed calling anyone Satan, saying the target was the idea. The disclaimer keeps it short of a direct insult but it remains mockery rather than engagement with the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: As such, this legislation has—and I said this in the first speech—a treasonous character, because its first service is not to New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: The stated premise (the bill's 'first service is not to New Zealanders') is asserted, not shown, and 'treasonous' does not follow from it even if granted — treason has a definite meaning that serving foreign commercial interests does not meet. Definitional leap layered on an unsupported premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises he laid out: old s 106(3) presumed non-extinguishment; new s 106(2) requires applicants to prove use without substantial interruption; substantial interruption can include extinguishment; therefore the burden has moved. Valid given those assumptions — whether they describe the sections accurately is a Veracity question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So we will be supporting this because it does restore what Parliament intended, it does restore an exacting test, and I commend this bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason for the vote, but the reason simply restates the bill's claimed purpose — that it restores Parliament's intent and an exacting test — without showing what the original intent was or how the new test achieves it. Assertion in the place of an inference; he defers the argument to the Minister rather than making it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Māori, like any New Zealander, have the opportunity to enjoy their coastline and enjoy the benefits.
