rigor.explanation: Equivocation: it answers the charge that the bill removes Māori rights by pointing to a different right — general public enjoyment and access to the coast — when the right at issue is customary marine title, which is by definition not held by any New Zealander equally. The conclusion that rights are not being removed does not follow from the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Section 106(3) of the MACA Act states that, unless there is evidence to the contrary, non-extinguishment of customary interest will be assumed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the presumption of non-extinguishment of customary interests is located in s 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, and that it operates unless contrary evidence is produced.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of section 106 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 as in force before this amendment (legislation.govt.nz). True if subsection (3) states a presumption that customary interests have not been extinguished in the absence of proof to the contrary; false if no such presumption exists or it sits in a different subsection with materially different effect.

veracity.statement: This bill fulfils a specific coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that amending the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act in this way is an express commitment in the New Zealand First–National coalition agreement.

veracity.statement: I think we go back to when the first claims were lodged under this Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, that every single centimetre of our coastline was subject to a claim.

divination.statement: It's the worst kind of rubbish that has come before this House, and it will be undone by a future Government, and we will have to stand up and apologise, Minister, for this nasty piece of legislation to somehow try and restore the honour of the Crown that you are disdaining.

specificity.statement: You know, there’s a big long list of our country’s desperate needs that the money could have been better spent on, like homelessness, poverty, or the cost of living.

civility.statement: You are scared of Māori asserting themselves in this world, and you have learned nothing, Mr Goldsmith, nothing, because Mr Potaka has been able to teach you nothing.

civility.explanation: Reports a former Minister's stated position on timing, and the electoral framing carries a faint implication of political calculation, but it names no character failing and is delivered without sneer — pointed at most, and immediately followed by the speaker including himself ('I'm guilty there as well').
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of a government funding decision and its consequences. No person is attacked, no bad faith imputed — this is the expected standard under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
focus.explanation: Names two specific policy levers (the walking and cycling budget, farebox recovery settings) and a specific consequence (higher fares). Legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I understand it, Waka Kotahi holds disproportionate weight in decision making, and while I really appreciate that the Wairarapa has separate councils from the metro Wellington, the idea of having three Wairarapa mayors and one capital mayor on a board fills me with a little dismay.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at a governance mechanism in the bill — the composition and voting weight of the scheme board. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The independent chair, I thought, was raised by a lot of submitters and will go some way to making sure that the scheme board makes decisions in an impartial manner for the benefit of people in the city.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a named change to the bill — the independent chair of the scheme board — and the reason for it. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This Government has made that cost of living crisis worse by halving the walking and cycling budget and increasing the public transport farebox recovery, which directly translates into higher bus and train fares.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two funding-policy facts: that the walking and cycling budget was halved, and that required farebox recovery for public transport was increased, with fares rising as a result.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA National Land Transport Programme 2024–27 walking and cycling activity class allocation compared with the 2021–24 NLTP, plus the farebox/private share expectations in the Government Policy Statement on land transport 2024. True if the walking and cycling allocation was roughly halved and the farebox recovery expectation was raised above the previous setting; false if either allocation was maintained or the farebox expectation was unchanged.

veracity.statement: Because congestion is only one negative impact of our car dependency, the health costs from air pollution actually exceeds the cost of congestion itself, and yet this bill ignores that evidence entirely, presumably because it’s an inconvenient truth that air pollution from motor vehicles—and this is the 53rd Parliament, so no doubt the costs have increased, like everything else—causes approximately $10 billion in social costs every year, including 13,000 cases of childhood asthma prevalence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that vehicle air pollution causes about $10 billion in social costs per year in New Zealand, including about 13,000 cases of childhood asthma, and that these health costs exceed the cost of congestion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The HAPINZ 3.0 (Health and Air Pollution in New Zealand) study's estimate of annual social costs of motor-vehicle air pollution and its childhood asthma prevalence count, compared against published NZ congestion cost estimates (e.g. NZIER/NZTA Auckland congestion cost studies). True if the social-cost figure is around $10 billion and the asthma count around 13,000, and the health figure exceeds the congestion figure; false if either figure is materially different or congestion costs are the larger of the two.

veracity.statement: Traffic reduction has fallen by 10 percent.
veracity.explanation: A spoken slip for 'traffic has fallen by 10 percent' — the intended claim is that vehicle traffic in the New York congestion pricing zone dropped by around 10 percent after the scheme began in January 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MTA congestion relief zone vehicle entry data for 2025 compared with the pre-implementation baseline. True if entries into the zone fell by roughly 10 percent; false if the reduction was materially smaller or larger, or if entries did not fall.

veracity.statement: The noise complaints in the city of Manhattan have fallen by 70 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that noise complaints in Manhattan fell by 70 percent following the introduction of congestion pricing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NYC 311 complaint records for 2025 versus the equivalent 2024 period, for noise complaints in Manhattan (and specifically the congestion relief zone). True if the fall is around 70 percent on the measure as stated — city-wide Manhattan noise complaints; false if the 70 percent figure applies only to a narrower category (e.g. honking complaints inside the zone) or if the overall fall is materially smaller.

veracity.statement: The city raises $50,000—or $50 million I should say—each month from the scheme that it can then plough back into public transport, and buses travel faster in Manhattan as a result.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New York's congestion pricing scheme raises about $50 million per month, that the revenue is directed to public transport, and that bus speeds in Manhattan have increased.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MTA published monthly congestion pricing revenue reports for 2025 and MTA bus speed data for Manhattan routes. True if monthly revenue averages around $50 million, is hypothecated to transit capital, and Manhattan bus speeds increased after January 2025; false if monthly revenue is materially different or bus speeds did not improve.

specificity.statement: Because congestion is only one negative impact of our car dependency, the health costs from air pollution actually exceeds the cost of congestion itself, and yet this bill ignores that evidence entirely, presumably because it’s an inconvenient truth that air pollution from motor vehicles—and this is the 53rd Parliament, so no doubt the costs have increased, like everything else—causes approximately $10 billion in social costs every year, including 13,000 cases of childhood asthma prevalence.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure ($10 billion annually), a named health outcome count (13,000 childhood asthma cases), and a stated comparison against congestion costs. Someone could go and check each element.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I understand it, Waka Kotahi holds disproportionate weight in decision making, and while I really appreciate that the Wairarapa has separate councils from the metro Wellington, the idea of having three Wairarapa mayors and one capital mayor on a board fills me with a little dismay.
specificity.explanation: Names the agency and gives the concrete board arithmetic (three Wairarapa mayors to one capital mayor), but leaves 'disproportionate weight' unquantified and proposes no alternative composition.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I am particularly amazed and delighted by new section 65Z(2)(c) in clause 4, because it mentions economic, social, cultural, and environmental impacts—long live the wellbeings, I say.
specificity.explanation: Cites the exact provision (new section 65Z(2)(c) in clause 4) and what it contains. Precisely checkable against the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The city raises $50,000—or $50 million I should say—each month from the scheme that it can then plough back into public transport, and buses travel faster in Manhattan as a result.
specificity.explanation: Gives a monthly revenue figure, states where the money goes, and names a measurable operational outcome (bus speeds). The self-correction from $50,000 to $50 million is a live-speech repair, not vagueness.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: For this scheme to be successful, fewer exemptions were considered, and, really, we’ve only allowed emergency vehicles, and public buses for particular schools as well.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual exemption categories allowed under the scheme (emergency vehicles, particular school buses), which is checkable against the bill, though it gives no threshold or coverage detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because congestion is only one negative impact of our car dependency, the health costs from air pollution actually exceeds the cost of congestion itself, and yet this bill ignores that evidence entirely, presumably because it’s an inconvenient truth that air pollution from motor vehicles—and this is the 53rd Parliament, so no doubt the costs have increased, like everything else—causes approximately $10 billion in social costs every year, including 13,000 cases of childhood asthma prevalence.
rigor.explanation: The inference from the quantified health cost to 'the bill should not ignore it' tracks the evidence offered. Marked down for the unsupported motive attribution — 'presumably because it's an inconvenient truth' — which is asserted rather than argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I was in the House for the previous debate on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, and it's hard to imagine a debate that could have had a more deeply felt and visceral opposition, from this side of the Chamber at least, and a kind of implacable difference, really, between the Government and the Opposition benches, by contrast.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested reference point (a bitterly divisive bill and the Government/Opposition split) where an uncivil turn was readily available. He characterises the disagreement itself, imputes no bad faith and attacks no member.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Good things often take time, and I'm very pleased to see that policy work that I started as transport Minister, probably seven or eight years ago, has finally found its way, through a succession of other Ministers, to this House in the form of this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the policy work underlying this time-of-use charging bill was begun under him as Minister of Transport roughly seven or eight years before October 2025, i.e. around 2017-18.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport records of when congestion/time-of-use charging policy work was commissioned (notably The Congestion Question project with Auckland Council) and the dates of Twyford's tenure as Minister of Transport; true if that work was initiated during his term around 2017-18, false if it began materially later or under a different Minister.

veracity.statement: We can say with certainty that it has the potential to reduce 10 percent or more of drivers at a particular time of day when the charging is in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the international evidence base from implemented congestion-charging schemes shows reductions of 10 percent or more in the number of drivers on the charged network at charged times.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluations of the London congestion charge, Stockholm congestion tax, Singapore ERP and Milan Area C reporting change in traffic volumes entering the charged zone during charging hours; true if those evaluations show reductions of at least 10 percent, false if the measured reductions are consistently below 10 percent.

rigor.statement: It is simply not possible, because when you have a growth in population, a growth in demand to move goods and people around, every time you expand the roads, in that context, you simply induce more demand.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise (population and travel-demand growth causes added capacity to induce further demand) that genuinely supports the conclusion that a growing city cannot build its way out of congestion. No fallacy or appeal; the inference tracks the mechanism offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Cities are basically labour markets, and if you stop people getting to the jobs that they might want to do, you dramatically reduce the efficiency of the labour market, because firms cannot get access to the choice of workers and the number of workers that they need to do their jobs.
rigor.explanation: Premise (cities function as labour markets) plus a stated causal channel (restricted access shrinks the effective pool of workers available to firms) supporting the conclusion about labour-market efficiency. The step from congestion to 'dramatically' is asserted rather than shown, which is the one gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: By adding a small charge to the use of that particular roading network at particular times of the day, it will incentivise people to change their transport behaviour, to take another mode, to get on the train or the bus or the ferry or to time their journey for a less expensive hour when they don't have to pay that extra fee.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual mechanism — a charge applied to a defined network at defined times, with the named behavioural responses (mode shift or retiming). No charge levels, zones or dates, so it stops short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We can say with certainty that it has the potential to reduce 10 percent or more of drivers at a particular time of day when the charging is in place.
specificity.explanation: Carries a numeric threshold (10 percent or more), a defined population (drivers on the charged network) and a defined condition (at the times charging applies) — precise enough that someone could go and check it against scheme evaluations.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: However, I made it clear in the select committee that I only support this bill with one clear condition: if any revenue is collected in the Mt Roskill electorate, I want it to return to Mt Roskill—for future transport infrastructure.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete condition with an identifiable geography and use of funds (revenue raised in Mt Roskill hypothecated to Mt Roskill transport infrastructure), but supplies no amounts, no mechanism for the ring-fencing and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: By adding a small charge to the use of that particular roading network at particular times of the day, it will incentivise people to change their transport behaviour, to take another mode, to get on the train or the bus or the ferry or to time their journey for a less expensive hour when they don't have to pay that extra fee.
focus.explanation: Entirely about how the measure before the House works; no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So this bill encourages travel outside the peak hours, which can ease congestion and improve travel reliability.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the measure before the House does and the outcome it is meant to produce; no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However, I made it clear in the select committee that I only support this bill with one clear condition: if any revenue is collected in the Mt Roskill electorate, I want it to return to Mt Roskill—for future transport infrastructure.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific design question about the bill — where charging revenue is spent — rather than the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We have to find other ways to fund our transport system and the technology that's in use here, and what will very likely be a shift to electronic GPS-based road-user charges for all vehicles—a technology that's already in place for a significant section of our trucking fleet—will mean that petrol excise can be phased out and replaced with a much more comprehensive way of raising revenue based on people's real-time use of the transport network.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand will move to electronic GPS-based road-user charging applied to all vehicles, and that fuel excise duty will consequently be phased out and replaced by that system.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: New Zealand legislation and NZTA implementation records; true if road user charges (electronically recorded) apply to all light vehicles and petrol excise duty has been repealed or wound down to a residual, false if petrol excise duty remains the principal charge on petrol vehicles.

rigor.statement: I am going to reject one of Dr Cheung’s claims that the money collected in Mount Roskill should be spent in Mount Roskill. Of course, the Auckland motorway and roading network is a network, and the spending needs to go across the network to ensure that the network functions effectively, which of course will, in turn, help people in Mount Roskill.
rigor.explanation: A real inference is offered — because the roading system is an interconnected network, revenue should be spent network-wide rather than hypothecated to the collection area. The step from 'it is a network' to 'therefore network-wide spending helps Mount Roskill' leans on the premise restating itself and no mechanism or evidence is supplied, so there is a gap between what is shown and what is concluded, but it is not fallacious.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We do spend a lot of time sitting in traffic, and so that’s a behaviour that clearly needs to change. We actually need to see if we can reduce the number of cars on the road.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that behaviour must change rests on the speaker's own commuting anecdote and that of a named colleague — an appeal to anecdote. The inference is not unreasonable, but nothing beyond personal experience is offered to establish either the scale of the problem or that fewer cars is the remedy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And there’s an interesting little supposition underlying that: that somehow school kids don’t deserve to be on the roads—they don’t deserve to use the roads because the roads are better when they’re not there.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. Using school-holiday traffic as a benchmark for uncongested flow carries no implication that children 'don't deserve' road access; the speaker attributes a moral claim about desert to an argument that made only an empirical comparison, then treats that invented claim as the position under discussion.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I am going to reject one of Dr Cheung’s claims that the money collected in Mount Roskill should be spent in Mount Roskill. Of course, the Auckland motorway and roading network is a network, and the spending needs to go across the network to ensure that the network functions effectively, which of course will, in turn, help people in Mount Roskill.
focus.explanation: Directly engages a specific policy question at issue in the bill — whether congestion charge revenue should be hypothecated to the area it was collected in. Names a place and a mechanism; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That’s a viable solution along State Highway 16 now that a busway is at last being retrofitted into State Highway 16.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that busway infrastructure is currently being retrofitted into the State Highway 16 corridor in west Auckland — i.e. that construction on a dedicated bus corridor there is under way as at October 2025, not merely planned or funded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Transport Agency (Waka Kotahi) / Auckland Transport project records for the Northwest / SH16 rapid transit and bus improvement programme as at October 2025. True if works to build dedicated busway or permanent bus lane infrastructure within the SH16 corridor were in construction at that date; false if the corridor works were still only at planning, consenting or business-case stage with no construction under way.

veracity.statement: London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific quantitative outcomes from existing overseas schemes: that the London congestion charge cut traffic by between 15 and 30 percent, and that Stockholm's congestion tax cut traffic by 20 to 25 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluations of the two schemes — Transport for London's Central London Congestion Charging impacts monitoring reports, and the Swedish Transport Administration / City of Stockholm evaluations of the Stockholm congestion tax. True if the measured reduction in traffic volumes attributable to each scheme falls inside the stated ranges (15–30% London, 20–25% Stockholm); false if the evaluated reductions fall materially outside those ranges.

specificity.statement: We must ensure that they have a choice to either pay the congestion charge, or to move along less congested routes, or to take—and this would be, I guess, the best solution—public transport.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete alternatives a charged commuter could take, which is more than a slogan, but attaches no threshold, funding figure, service level or timeframe to the requirement that viable alternatives exist. A direction with some detail, missing the how much and the by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are a number of reasons why congestion charging is a great idea: the environmental benefits, the revenue generation beyond what we already have, the sustainable infrastructure, improved cities, and, of course, economic efficiency, which is what we’re all about on this side of the House: economic growth and efficiency.
specificity.explanation: A list of generic virtues — 'environmental benefits', 'sustainable infrastructure', 'improved cities', 'economic efficiency' — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named measure attached to any of them. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: London and Stokholm are both great examples of congestion charging working where traffic reduced by 15 percent to 30 percent in London; 20 to 25 percent in Stokholm.
specificity.explanation: Names two identifiable schemes and gives numeric percentage ranges for each, so the claim is precise enough for anyone to go and check against the published evaluations. Marked slightly below the top only because no time period or measurement basis is given for the reductions.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We’ve got beautiful clear air, we don’t have a lot of congestion, and it takes about 25 minutes to do the 27 kilometres from my place to the airport, which I do quite frequently—it’s a beautiful drive, fantastic farmland on the way there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the drive from her home in South Dunedin to Dunedin Airport is about 27 kilometres and takes about 25 minutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Road distance and typical off-peak drive time from South Dunedin to Dunedin Airport (Momona) per NZTA road data or a standard mapping service; true if the route is ~27 km and ~25 minutes, false if materially different (e.g. under 20 km or over 40 minutes).

veracity.statement: The same distance—27 kilometres—from the airport in Jakarta and to the main city can take usually around an hour and a half.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the roughly 27 km trip from Jakarta's airport to the central city usually takes around 90 minutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published travel-time data for the Soekarno-Hatta Airport to central Jakarta route (e.g. TomTom/Google typical-time data, Indonesian transport authority figures); true if the typical journey is around 1.5 hours, false if the typical time is materially shorter (e.g. under an hour).

veracity.statement: We did have these half-price fares; the Government has removed them, so I’m keen to know what this Government is going to do to make sure the other side of the ledger of the congestion charge is about enabling people to get other forms of transport.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a half-price public transport fare scheme existed and that the current Government ended it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Transport / Waka Kotahi records and Budget decisions on the half-price public transport fares and Community Connect concessions; true if a half-price fare subsidy was in place and was discontinued by the current Government, false if it was never discontinued or was ended by a different administration.

veracity.statement: I was at a breakfast this morning where I heard the Hon Chris Bishop really lay into the councils, saying how useless they were, how they were rorting money from ratepayers to try to get infrastructure happening.
veracity.explanation: Relays what she says Chris Bishop said at a breakfast event on the morning of 21 October 2025 — that councils were useless and were rorting ratepayer money over infrastructure.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Recording, transcript or contemporaneous media reporting of Chris Bishop's address at the Auckland/Wellington business breakfast on 21 October 2025; true if he criticised councils in substantially those terms, false if no such remarks are on the record.

veracity.statement: The other thing, I suppose, is just really noting that former Minister of Transport Simeon Brown has said we want to make sure we’re not adding further cost to people using roads during a cost of living crisis.
veracity.explanation: Relays a statement attributed to Simeon Brown while Minister of Transport, that the Government wanted to avoid adding further cost to road users during a cost of living crisis.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Beehive press releases, Hansard, or media reporting of Simeon Brown's statements as Minister of Transport; true if he made a statement to that effect, false if no such statement is on the record.

veracity.statement: It’s a little bit like hearing Simeon Brown say that doctors have crossed an ethical line when they assert their right to stand up for their patients and talk about safer staffing and better pay and conditions to make sure that people receive adequate healthcare.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim that Simeon Brown said doctors had crossed an ethical line in the context of doctors advocating over staffing, pay and conditions.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Media reporting, interview transcripts or press releases of Simeon Brown's comments as Minister of Health about senior doctors' industrial action; true if he said doctors had crossed an ethical line (or used substantially those words), false if no such remark is on the record.

focus.statement: We did have these half-price fares; the Government has removed them, so I’m keen to know what this Government is going to do to make sure the other side of the ledger of the congestion charge is about enabling people to get other forms of transport.
focus.explanation: Names a specific transport policy (half-price fares) and ties it to the measure before the House, asking what the Government will do about the public transport side of the congestion charge. Squarely on policy, not party character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We need buses, we need trains, we need bus fares and train fares that take into account people’s circumstances and that also enable people like children, for example, to be able to attend sports games, to be able to attend training.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the public transport policy that should accompany congestion charging; no party framing at all. Vague but on-policy — the pair to keep apart from Specificity.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We also think that new section 65C(2), inserted by clause 4, allows too much ministerial control, and that’s about protecting local autonomy.
focus.explanation: A named clause of the bill before the House and its effect on local decision-making. Pure policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We need buses, we need trains, we need bus fares and train fares that take into account people’s circumstances and that also enable people like children, for example, to be able to attend sports games, to be able to attend training.
specificity.explanation: Names modes and a general fare principle but supplies no fare level, funding source, eligibility rule or timeframe — a direction of travel with nothing checkable attached.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We also think that new section 65C(2), inserted by clause 4, allows too much ministerial control, and that’s about protecting local autonomy.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact provision (new section 65C(2), inserted by clause 4) and the precise objection to it; anyone can go to the bill and check the claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we do need, though, is we need rail-enabled ferries and we need coastal shipping and we need a port and rail structure that makes sure that the South Island can operate independently of the North Island when all that congestion gets out of hand or when there’s another COVID epidemic or something else that happens that shuts down the country.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete assets (rail-enabled ferries, coastal shipping, port and rail infrastructure) and the resilience purpose, but carries no cost, route, capacity or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It seems to be a bit of a trend with this coalition Government, and now we see it again in a completely different area where once more the governance and the decision making is all vested in a Minister, where the democratic institutions of power really require that not to be so concentrated so that there is transparency and accountability and a firewall, if you like, between Ministers and those who might be making operational decisions.
rigor.explanation: The constitutional premise (concentrated ministerial control weakens transparency and the separation between ministers and operational decision-makers) does support the objection. But 'a trend' is generalised from two instances raised the same evening — a hasty generalisation propping up the wider inference about the Government's pattern.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Then, they moved to digital, but I’d never pay my bills on time, and I’d always get a snail mail $8 bill with a $5 admin fee, and I was just like, “If I knew about the bill, I wouldn’t have the admin fee.” So there’s definitely room to improve, I think, but I’m all for this process, so I commend it to the House.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that there is room to improve rests entirely on one personal anecdote about his own late payment of Tauranga toll bills — an appeal to anecdote, with nothing offered about how widespread the billing problem is or how the bill's scheme board provisions would address it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a shame that Minister Brown said that because it might come back to haunt him, especially if these other mechanisms that we’re discussing in the House tonight are not put into place.
civility.explanation: Contested ground with a real opportunity to turn on a named Minister. She stays on what he said and its consequences rather than attacking him; 'might come back to haunt him' is pointed and edges toward the person without landing on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: That’s the key part to this: because we know that for planning purposes, having the congestion charge is great—it is going to change behaviours—but it’s really difficult for some people if there are not other options available to them.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that introducing a congestion charge will change travel behaviour. Not a promise about her own action — the scheme is the Government's, and the forecast is about how road users will respond.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Post-implementation traffic data for New Zealand's first time-of-use charging scheme (Auckland), published by Auckland Transport/NZTA; true if peak-period vehicle volumes in the charged corridors fall materially against the pre-scheme baseline, false if volumes are essentially unchanged.

civility.statement: We respect the unions’ right to strike. We also encourage them to think about the impact they’re having on kids, parents, and patients.
civility.explanation: A contested exchange over strike rights where he could easily have gone after the unions or the questioner; instead the remark engages the issue and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Isn’t it great! We’re getting a question on the third Labour policy of this week, but we didn’t get one for one and two. This is really the big deal that’s going to move the needle from Labour!
civility.explanation: Sarcastic, but the target is Labour as a party rather than any individual, and it imputes no bad faith to a person. Party-bashing is Focus's business, not Civility's.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To take each of the three stupid assertions in that question in reverse order: the tobacco claim by the member is inaccurate and wrong; in relation to the board directors, if the last Government had not appointed boards that ran so many Crown companies—like, to take a random example, Kāinga Ora—so badly, we would not have been put in a position where we had to bring in some commercial expertise to get the books back on track; and, in relation to the first part of the question, I always agree with the Prime Minister.
civility.explanation: Labelling the member's assertions "stupid" is condescension toward the questioner rather than engagement with the figures. Short of a direct insult, but under the re-anchored scale that is a genuine failure — he could have said "inaccurate" and lost nothing.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We respect the unions’ right to strike. We also encourage them to think about the impact they’re having on kids, parents, and patients.
focus.explanation: A policy question is at issue (advice on limiting strike rights) but the answer names no policy, mechanism or figure — it redirects to how unions are behaving. Real topic, no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Asking teachers to consider whether they could do their professional development and their teacher only days in one of the 12 weeks of the school holidays is not an unreasonable request.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of what is actually being negotiated with the teachers' union, rather than on Labour or on the questioner.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Having a discussion about a Palestinian State from a teachers’ union is not a priority in improving attendance or education outcomes for New Zealanders.
focus.explanation: The question was about pay offers and workload; this pivots to an unrelated union remit motion. Attendance and education outcomes are gestured at, but no policy, figure or measure is engaged — the weight is on discrediting the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why isn’t he aware that the gaming sector has grown 86 percent in the last 2½ years since the gaming rebate was introduced by the previous Labour Government and that his Government, despite repeated requests from the sector, has not been willing to expand eligibility so that the budget that was set aside for it actually gets spent?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of a named scheme against a named outcome and an unspent appropriation — the constitutional job of an opposition MP, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Isn’t it great! We’re getting a question on the third Labour policy of this week, but we didn’t get one for one and two. This is really the big deal that’s going to move the needle from Labour!
focus.explanation: Answers a question about rebate eligibility with commentary on how many policies the Opposition has announced this week. No policy, mechanism, figure or outcome is engaged — it is entirely about the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can she stand by her statement that “Costs are under control, and inflation is under control” when there have been four consecutive increases in inflation?
focus.explanation: Holds a Minister to a specific quoted statement against a specific published series. Named claim, named outcome — accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: He said that, ultimately, we need to balance the right to strike and actually make sure we protect the interests of other New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Luxon is relaying what another Minister said about strike rights; the checkable content is whether Brown's actual words match this characterisation.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Locate Simeon Brown's public remarks on doctors' strike rights in the weeks before 2025-10-22 (media transcripts, press-conference audio, or Hansard). True if he said the right to strike must be balanced against protecting other New Zealanders' interests; false if his recorded words characterised the position differently — e.g. as a firm intention to restrict the right rather than a balancing consideration.

veracity.statement: Why didn’t the Government increase eligibility for the game development rebate given the current $40 million budget for the rebate isn’t being fully utilised?
veracity.explanation: Asserts both the size of the rebate budget and that it is not being fully spent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / NZ Film Commission appropriation and uptake figures for the Game Development Sector Rebate for the 2024/25 and 2025/26 years. True if the annual appropriation is approximately $40 million and actual rebate payments fell materially short of it; false if the appropriation is a different figure or the scheme was fully or near-fully drawn down.

veracity.statement: Why isn’t he aware that the gaming sector has grown 86 percent in the last 2½ years since the gaming rebate was introduced by the previous Labour Government and that his Government, despite repeated requests from the sector, has not been willing to expand eligibility so that the budget that was set aside for it actually gets spent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific growth rate for the games sector over a stated period, attributed to the period since the rebate began.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Game Developers Association annual industry survey revenue figures, comparing the year the rebate was introduced (2023) with the most recent survey before October 2025. True if total sector revenue grew by approximately 86% across that period; false if the compounded growth is materially different from 86%.

veracity.statement: When I looked at the numbers a few months ago—and don’t hold me to account—the 38 percent increase in the size of the gaming sector, I think it actually hit something like $780 million in the last year, which is fantastic.
veracity.explanation: Two specific claims about the games sector — a 38% annual increase and roughly $780 million in revenue — offered with an explicit hedge about recall.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Game Developers Association annual survey for the most recent year before October 2025. True if reported sector revenue is approximately $780 million and the year-on-year increase approximately 38%; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: It’s also why we’re backing farmers because, actually, dairy’s up 14 percent, red meat’s up about 9 percent, and horticulture’s up 19 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific year-on-year growth rates for three primary sectors.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for the Primary Industries export revenue figures for the year to June 2025 against the prior year. True if dairy is up approximately 14%, red meat approximately 9% and horticulture approximately 19%; false if any is materially different on the standard export-revenue measure.

veracity.statement: It shows that the super fund's total size was $85 billion at 30 June 2025, with average return since its inception of 10.1 percent per annum.
veracity.explanation: Two figures from the Super Fund's just-published annual report: fund size at balance date and since-inception annualised return.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Superannuation Fund annual report for the year ended 30 June 2025. True if total fund size at that date is approximately $85 billion and the since-inception average annual return is approximately 10.1%; false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The other 70 percent have been divested or liquidated as Temasek invested, divested, and grew their portfolio to $434 billion Singaporean.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current size of Temasek's portfolio in Singapore dollars, alongside the claim that the bulk of its original seed assets were disposed of.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Temasek's most recent published portfolio figure before October 2025 (Temasek Review). True if net portfolio value is approximately S$434 billion; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: How can she stand by her statement that “Costs are under control, and inflation is under control” when there have been four consecutive increases in inflation?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that annual inflation has risen in four consecutive quarters, against a quoted ministerial claim that inflation is under control.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation rate for each of the four quarters to the September 2025 quarter. True if the annual rate rose in each of four consecutive quarterly prints; false if any of those four prints was flat or lower than the one before.

veracity.statement: Well, inflation is within the target band. Three years ago, it was 7.3 percent. It is now 3 percent.
veracity.explanation: Three checkable assertions: the current rate, the rate three years earlier, and that the current rate sits inside the target band.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual inflation for the September 2025 quarter and for the corresponding quarter of 2022, plus the RBNZ 1–3% target band. True if the 2022 figure is approximately 7.3%, the current figure approximately 3%, and 3% falls within the band; false if any of the three is materially wrong.

veracity.statement: The Government has come to the table and put a record investment in Budget 2025 of over $700 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the size of the Budget 2025 learning support investment and that it is a record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 documents for the learning support package. True if the announced learning support investment exceeds $700 million on the measure implied (and is the largest such package on record); false if the headline figure is materially below $700 million or is not a record.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with the Prime Minister that “We would love to pay everyone more, but for that to happen, we’ve got to be a much wealthier economy.”; if so, would there have been more money for workers had she not handed out pay increases for board directors, $2.9 billion for landlords, and $300 million for the tobacco industry?
veracity.explanation: Asserts two specific fiscal costings for government tax measures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury fiscal costings for (a) the restoration of interest deductibility for residential landlords and (b) the heated tobacco products excise reduction, on the periods the figures are drawn from. True if the landlord measure costs approximately $2.9 billion and the tobacco measure approximately $300 million; false if either costing is materially different or the tobacco figure covers something other than the excise change.

specificity.statement: Asking teachers to consider whether they could do their professional development and their teacher only days in one of the 12 weeks of the school holidays is not an unreasonable request.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism (moving PD and teacher-only days into holiday weeks) and a figure (12 weeks), though it gives no number of days, no cost and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why didn’t the Government increase eligibility for the game development rebate given the current $40 million budget for the rebate isn’t being fully utilised?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific scheme (the game development rebate), a specific appropriation ($40 million) and a specific claimed failure (underspend). Someone could go and check it. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s also why we’re backing farmers because, actually, dairy’s up 14 percent, red meat’s up about 9 percent, and horticulture’s up 19 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three named sectors with three growth figures — concrete and checkable, though no base period or measure (revenue? volume?) is stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It shows that the super fund's total size was $85 billion at 30 June 2025, with average return since its inception of 10.1 percent per annum.
specificity.explanation: A named source, a dated figure and a stated return — fully checkable against a single published document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, inflation is within the target band. Three years ago, it was 7.3 percent. It is now 3 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two dated figures and a named policy benchmark — precise enough that anyone could verify it against the published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government has come to the table and put a record investment in Budget 2025 of over $700 million.
specificity.explanation: Names the Budget, the area of spending and a dollar figure, but not the period the money is spread over or what it buys.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she agree with the Prime Minister that “We would love to pay everyone more, but for that to happen, we’ve got to be a much wealthier economy.”; if so, would there have been more money for workers had she not handed out pay increases for board directors, $2.9 billion for landlords, and $300 million for the tobacco industry?
specificity.explanation: Three named recipients with two dollar figures attached, set against a directly quoted statement. Every element is checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: To take each of the three stupid assertions in that question in reverse order: the tobacco claim by the member is inaccurate and wrong; in relation to the board directors, if the last Government had not appointed boards that ran so many Crown companies—like, to take a random example, Kāinga Ora—so badly, we would not have been put in a position where we had to bring in some commercial expertise to get the books back on track; and, in relation to the first part of the question, I always agree with the Prime Minister.
rigor.explanation: The board-director limb is a real argument (bad appointments by the previous government forced the hiring of commercial expertise), but the causal chain to higher director fees is asserted rather than shown, and the tobacco limb is answered by bare denial — "inaccurate and wrong" with no reason offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As I outlined to the House yesterday, the Government’s spending $1.2 billion to move the next tranche of the roads of national significance to the next phase of development following the board’s approval of the investment cases.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure ($1.2 billion), a named programme (roads of national significance) and the triggering event (board approval of investment cases). Checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Ultimately, if the project is built completely between Auckland and Whangārei, it will reduce travel times by 38 minutes and of course reduce deaths and serious injury, which is something that many members are concerned about, by 66 percent.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures (38 minutes, 66 percent) tied to a named corridor and a stated condition. Someone could check it against the business case.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It will take 6,500 thousand vehicles off the most congested section of State Highway 1 and 2 and will reduce travel times between Lower Hutt and Porirua by 23 minutes at peak time.
specificity.explanation: Vehicle counts, a named corridor and a 23-minute peak saving. Precise enough to act on, though the '6,500 thousand' figure is a live-speech slip.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: After the previous Government did not advance the case for Let's Get Wellington Moving, we are committed to delivering meaningful improvements to State Highway 1 through Wellington, including a second Mount Victoria tunnel, a second Terrace tunnel, three-laning Vivian Street so you can no longer park on State Highway 1, Basin Reserve grade separation, and widening Ruahine Street and Wellington Road.
specificity.explanation: Six specifically named projects and one named mechanism (three-laning Vivian Street), but no costs, dates or sequencing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: State Highway 6 is a vital connection for people and goods, will boost economic growth in Nelson-Tasman, reduce peak journey times through Richmond by at least 10 minutes by 2034, and of course developments continue on the Belfast to Pegasus and Woodend Bypass road of national significance, with a fast-track application being worked through currently.
specificity.explanation: A named route, a named figure (10 minutes) and a date (2034), alongside two named projects and their current status.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, they’re not forced to do anything. I would like to just say that we have been listening to them, which is why we have delivered the biggest investment in learning support in a generation, more than they did in the last six years combined; which is why we have invested in paying for their teacher registration fees; which is why we’ve invested in an aspiring principal programme; which is why we’ve invested in a teacher bonding scheme, among many, many things we’ve done to back the sector.
specificity.explanation: Four named programmes (learning support, registration fees, aspiring principal programme, teacher bonding scheme) and one comparative claim, but no dollar figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, in response to our questions yesterday, that nurses have safe staffing conditions, when Te Whatu Ora’s own data showed that 50 percent of day shifts were understaffed in 16 districts over 10 months last year in our hospitals?
specificity.explanation: Names the source (Te Whatu Ora data), the measure (50 percent of day shifts understaffed), the scope (16 districts) and the period (10 months last year).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is he concerned that neonatal wards across Auckland, Whangārei, Christchurch, Palmerston North, and Tauranga hospitals were understaffed for more than a third of the shifts in the first half of this year, and, if so, what impacts does he think that these unsafe working conditions have on parents and newborns?
specificity.explanation: Five named hospitals, a named ward type, a stated threshold (more than a third of shifts) and a stated period (first half of this year).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The fact that, in less than two years, we’ve added 2,100 extra nurses into Health New Zealand is a really good thing, and the fact that we’ve made consistent efforts and investments in the healthcare system—$17 billion in our first Budget; up another 7 percent in our second Budget—is all good stuff.
specificity.explanation: A headcount figure, a timeframe, a dollar figure and a percentage increase, each attached to a named entity or Budget.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, I’m just very proud of the progress that we’ve taken since the departure of a Labour-Greens Government—that, clearly, we have put more money in, in the history of New Zealand; we have put more workforce into the healthcare system; we have good clarity on targets; and we now expect delivery from Health New Zealand to support patients.
specificity.explanation: 'More money', 'more workforce' and 'good clarity on targets' commit to nothing checkable — no figures, no named targets, no timeframes, and nothing about the neonatal staffing raised in the question.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As I outlined to the House yesterday, the Government’s spending $1.2 billion to move the next tranche of the roads of national significance to the next phase of development following the board’s approval of the investment cases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government has committed $1.2 billion to advance the next tranche of RoNS following NZTA board approval of the investment cases.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZTA board papers and the Government's October 2025 RoNS announcement; true if the announced allocation for moving the next RoNS tranche to the next development phase is $1.2 billion and follows board endorsement of the investment cases, false if the figure or the sequence is materially different.

veracity.statement: Ultimately, if the project is built completely between Auckland and Whangārei, it will reduce travel times by 38 minutes and of course reduce deaths and serious injury, which is something that many members are concerned about, by 66 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Northland Expressway investment case projects a 38-minute travel-time saving and a 66 percent reduction in deaths and serious injuries for the full Auckland–Whangārei build.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZTA Northland Expressway detailed business case / investment case; true if it states a ~38-minute travel-time reduction and a ~66 percent reduction in deaths and serious injuries for the complete Auckland–Whangārei route, false if it states materially different figures or no such figures.

veracity.statement: Why have over 40,000 educators been forced to take to the streets just to get their Minister to listen to their concerns?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than 40,000 educators took part in the strike action.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZEI Te Riu Roa and PPTA membership/participation figures for the 23 October 2025 education strike, and contemporaneous media counts; true if the number of educators taking strike action exceeds 40,000, false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: Well, they’re not forced to do anything. I would like to just say that we have been listening to them, which is why we have delivered the biggest investment in learning support in a generation, more than they did in the last six years combined; which is why we have invested in paying for their teacher registration fees; which is why we’ve invested in an aspiring principal programme; which is why we’ve invested in a teacher bonding scheme, among many, many things we’ve done to back the sector.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that this Government's learning support investment is the largest in a generation and exceeds the previous Government's learning support spending over six years combined.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024–2025 learning support appropriations compared with learning support appropriations in Budgets 2018–2023 (Treasury Vote Education estimates); true if the current package exceeds the six-year combined total on a like-for-like basis, false if it does not.

veracity.statement: Well, they do have a choice, and here is an example of a union that did have a choice: the Primary Principals’ Collective Bargaining Union, with over 500 members, chose not to strike; chose to be at the bargaining table with the Public Service Commission; chose to be open and transparent; chose to come to a settlement—a good, fair, and reasonable settlement. That is why more and more educators are joining their union, day by day: because they’re sick of the New Zealand Educational Institute.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Primary Principals' Collective Bargaining Union has over 500 members, did not strike, bargained with the Public Service Commission and reached a settlement, and that its membership is growing.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: PPCBU registered membership figures (MBIE union registration returns) and the Public Service Commission's record of the PPCBU collective settlement; true if membership exceeded 500 at the time and a settlement was reached without strike action, false if either is wrong.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, in response to our questions yesterday, that nurses have safe staffing conditions, when Te Whatu Ora’s own data showed that 50 percent of day shifts were understaffed in 16 districts over 10 months last year in our hospitals?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Whatu Ora's own staffing data recorded 50 percent of day shifts as understaffed across 16 districts over a 10-month period in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Whatu Ora / Health NZ shift-level staffing variance (CCDM) data for 2024 released under OIA; true if roughly half of day shifts across 16 districts over a 10-month period were recorded below required staffing, false if the recorded proportion or coverage is materially different.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned that neonatal wards across Auckland, Whangārei, Christchurch, Palmerston North, and Tauranga hospitals were understaffed for more than a third of the shifts in the first half of this year, and, if so, what impacts does he think that these unsafe working conditions have on parents and newborns?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that neonatal wards at five named hospitals were staffed below requirement for more than a third of shifts in January–June 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ neonatal unit shift-staffing records for Auckland, Whangārei, Christchurch, Palmerston North and Tauranga hospitals, January–June 2025; true if more than 33 percent of shifts were recorded below required staffing at those units, false if the recorded rate is materially lower.

veracity.statement: The fact that, in less than two years, we’ve added 2,100 extra nurses into Health New Zealand is a really good thing, and the fact that we’ve made consistent efforts and investments in the healthcare system—$17 billion in our first Budget; up another 7 percent in our second Budget—is all good stuff.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a net increase of 2,100 nurses at Health New Zealand within two years, $17 billion in the Government's first Budget for health, and a further 7 percent increase in its second.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ workforce reporting on nursing FTE from late 2023 to late 2025, and Treasury Vote Health appropriations for Budget 2024 and Budget 2025; true if the net nursing increase is approximately 2,100 and the Budget figures match, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, in answer to the first part of the question, there is no hiring freeze.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no hiring freeze is in effect in the health system at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ recruitment policy documents, vacancy-control instructions and internal communications in force during 2025; true if no freeze, pause or blanket vacancy control on clinical hiring applied, false if a freeze or equivalent hiring pause was in effect.

focus.statement: After the previous Government did not advance the case for Let's Get Wellington Moving, we are committed to delivering meaningful improvements to State Highway 1 through Wellington, including a second Mount Victoria tunnel, a second Terrace tunnel, three-laning Vivian Street so you can no longer park on State Highway 1, Basin Reserve grade separation, and widening Ruahine Street and Wellington Road.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the substance: six named works on a named corridor. The single clause about the previous Government is a factual reference point, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, it turns out I’ve got hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of friends, because that’s how many people are turning up to the Curriculum Roadshow to learn about the changes and the reform in education that is going to be raising achievement and closing the education gap in this country—which is more than those guys did in six years.
focus.explanation: There is genuine policy content — the Curriculum Roadshow and curriculum reform — but it is wrapped in wordplay and closes on a content-free comparison with the previous Government.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his statement, in response to our questions yesterday, that nurses have safe staffing conditions, when Te Whatu Ora’s own data showed that 50 percent of day shifts were understaffed in 16 districts over 10 months last year in our hospitals?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny with named evidence: a specific data source, a specific proportion, a specific number of districts and a specific period, tested against a stated Government position.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, I’m just very proud of the progress that we’ve taken since the departure of a Labour-Greens Government—that, clearly, we have put more money in, in the history of New Zealand; we have put more workforce into the healthcare system; we have good clarity on targets; and we now expect delivery from Health New Zealand to support patients.
focus.explanation: There is a policy frame (funding, workforce, targets), but the weight of the answer is a general contrast with the previous Government rather than the specific staffing question put to him.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: State Highway 6 is a vital connection for people and goods, will boost economic growth in Nelson-Tasman, reduce peak journey times through Richmond by at least 10 minutes by 2034, and of course developments continue on the Belfast to Pegasus and Woodend Bypass road of national significance, with a fast-track application being worked through currently.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that peak journey times through Richmond will be at least 10 minutes shorter by 2034 as a result of the Hope Bypass.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NZTA measured peak-period journey times through Richmond on State Highway 6 in 2034 compared with the pre-bypass baseline; true if the peak journey time has fallen by 10 minutes or more, false if the reduction is under 10 minutes or the bypass is not open.

civility.statement: Why have over 40,000 educators been forced to take to the streets just to get their Minister to listen to their concerns?
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person — it characterises the Minister as unwilling to listen — but the charge is about conduct in office rather than character, and no insult lands.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What message does she think she sends educators when she is willing to prioritise her roadshow with her friends over meeting with those who are striking?
civility.explanation: 'her roadshow with her friends' imputes that the Minister chooses friendly audiences over those she is accountable to — a sneer at motive rather than a criticism of the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she realise that educators have no choice but to strike when she has refused to listen to them despite open letters signed by hundreds of principals and petitions signed by thousands of concerned teachers and whānau?
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy: 'no choice but to strike' treats striking as the only available response, and the inference from unanswered letters and petitions to 'refused to listen' is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, they’re not forced to do anything. I would like to just say that we have been listening to them, which is why we have delivered the biggest investment in learning support in a generation, more than they did in the last six years combined; which is why we have invested in paying for their teacher registration fees; which is why we’ve invested in an aspiring principal programme; which is why we’ve invested in a teacher bonding scheme, among many, many things we’ve done to back the sector.
rigor.explanation: Spending is offered as proof of listening; the conclusion has a real gap, since funding decisions do not establish engagement with the concerns actually raised. The list of investments is relevant but does not carry the inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, they do have a choice, and here is an example of a union that did have a choice: the Primary Principals’ Collective Bargaining Union, with over 500 members, chose not to strike; chose to be at the bargaining table with the Public Service Commission; chose to be open and transparent; chose to come to a settlement—a good, fair, and reasonable settlement. That is why more and more educators are joining their union, day by day: because they’re sick of the New Zealand Educational Institute.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single union to the claim that all educators have a real choice, then asserts a cause for membership growth ('because they're sick of the NZEI') with nothing offered to establish the motive. Hasty generalisation plus an unsupported causal claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, it turns out I’ve got hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of friends, because that’s how many people are turning up to the Curriculum Roadshow to learn about the changes and the reform in education that is going to be raising achievement and closing the education gap in this country—which is more than those guys did in six years.
rigor.explanation: Turns on equivocating between two senses of 'friends' rather than engaging the inference; roadshow attendance is then offered as evidence of engagement with striking educators, which does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I could point to the progress made on our ambitious target to see 20,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime by 2029, and the most recent data released for the 12 months to May shows there were 29,000 fewer victims than when we came into Government; 9,000 ahead of our target.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the published victimisation data for the 12 months to May shows 29,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime than at the change of government, and that this is 9,000 ahead of the 20,000-by-2029 target.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZ Crime and Victims Survey / Government Target 2 quarterly reporting for the 12 months to May 2025, compared with the late-2023 baseline: true if the published reduction in victims of serious violent crime is about 29,000 (i.e. ~9,000 beyond the 20,000 target), false if the published figure is materially lower or if the comparison is drawn from a different measure.

veracity.statement: Well, our trial of clamping and seizing the cars of people who have not paid their court fines and reparations began in July and is set to expand, after it achieved more than $225,000 in fines and the seizure of 115 vehicles.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the fines-enforcement clamping trial started in July and has recovered more than $225,000 and seized 115 vehicles.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / court collections reporting on the vehicle clamping and seizure trial: true if the trial commenced July 2025 and recorded over $225,000 recovered and 115 vehicles seized by October 2025, false if the recovery or seizure counts are materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, alongside our target to reduce the number of victims of serious crime, we’ve also got a target led by Minister Chhour to reduce the number of children and young people with serious and persistent offending by 15 percent, which, the good news is, we have achieved as a Government already.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the government's target of a 15 percent reduction in children and young people with serious and persistent offending has already been met.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Government Target reporting on serious and persistent youth offending (Oranga Tamariki / Police measure): true if the reported reduction against the baseline is 15 percent or more at the date of the statement, false if the published reduction is below 15 percent or the target is reported as not yet met.

veracity.statement: In the last financial year, more than nine tonnes of illicit drugs were stopped from entering New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantity of illicit drugs intercepted at the border in the last financial year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Customs Service annual report and Police/Customs seizure statistics for the 2024/25 financial year: true if the combined weight of illicit drugs stopped at the border exceeds nine tonnes, false if the published total is materially below that.

veracity.statement: At the same time, $20 million to $25 million per year is being invested in new fire trucks. Currently, 78 are on order, including five aerial appliances.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an annual investment range in new fire appliances and a current order book of 78 appliances including five aerial.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Fire and Emergency New Zealand asset management plan, annual report and procurement records: true if annual fleet capital spend is $20–25 million and 78 appliances (five aerial) were on order as at October 2025, false if the spend or order numbers are materially different.

veracity.statement: Why should firefighters accept a pay offer that is a pay cut in real terms?
veracity.explanation: The question embeds an assertion that the offer on the table to firefighters amounts to a real-terms pay cut.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The nominal percentage increase in the FENZ offer to the Professional Firefighters Union as at October 2025, compared against Stats NZ CPI inflation over the same term of the offer: true if the nominal increase is below CPI over the offer period, false if it matches or exceeds it.

specificity.statement: I could point to the progress made on our ambitious target to see 20,000 fewer victims of serious violent crime by 2029, and the most recent data released for the 12 months to May shows there were 29,000 fewer victims than when we came into Government; 9,000 ahead of our target.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named target, a target date, a reporting period and three separate figures; anyone could go to the published series and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, our trial of clamping and seizing the cars of people who have not paid their court fines and reparations began in July and is set to expand, after it achieved more than $225,000 in fines and the seizure of 115 vehicles.
specificity.explanation: A named enforcement mechanism, a start month, a dollar figure and a vehicle count — concrete and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Before the end of the year, we will introduce legislation to strengthen consequences for crime in the Crimes Act, including new citizens arrest powers, a raft of coalition commitments, as well as to pass legislation to make stalking an illegal and jailable offence—a lot of talk about that over many years but this Government will do it before the end of the year.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, two identifiable measures (citizens arrest powers, a stalking offence) and a deadline. Short of full precision — 'a raft of coalition commitments' is unenumerated and no bill is named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the last financial year, more than nine tonnes of illicit drugs were stopped from entering New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A quantity, a commodity and a reporting period — checkable against published seizure statistics.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: At the same time, $20 million to $25 million per year is being invested in new fire trucks. Currently, 78 are on order, including five aerial appliances.
specificity.explanation: Dollar range, unit counts and appliance type — precise enough to be checked against FENZ procurement records.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is much more to do, but if you are a victim of crime—especially if you are victim of violent crime—it doesn’t matter how old the offender is, you and your family still suffer the consequences. That’s why it is so important that we deal more effectively with youth crime, which was out of control a couple of years ago.
rigor.explanation: The inference is sound on its own terms: if harm to the victim is independent of the offender's age, then youth offending warrants the same seriousness of response. Marked down slightly because the closing 'out of control a couple of years ago' is asserted rather than supported and does no work in the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No. Like many countries, we are not winning, but we certainly are not failing. As I stated in my response to the primary question, operational agencies like Police and Customs are doing great work, and we’re seeing the results of that excellence regularly.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion 'we are not failing' is supported only by agency effort and seizure volumes. There is a real gap: rising seizures are consistent with either better enforcement or a growing supply, so the evidence offered does not by itself settle the question asked.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is easy, in Opposition, to say that you think everybody should be paid more. However, it is also true that in these negotiations there are two sides that must be represented, and one of those are the New Zealanders who pay the cost.
rigor.explanation: The premise that levy and taxpayer funders are a party to the settlement genuinely bears on what can be offered, and the conclusion tracks it. It does not, however, establish anything about whether this particular offer is adequate — the question actually asked.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: None the less, it’s not true that money makes up for danger. We must take health and safety as a priority—perhaps above all else.
rigor.explanation: A strawman: the question asked whether the job has become more dangerous and whether FENZ should improve its offer, not whether pay compensates for danger. The rebuttal answers a proposition nobody advanced.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Before the end of the year, we will introduce legislation to strengthen consequences for crime in the Crimes Act, including new citizens arrest powers, a raft of coalition commitments, as well as to pass legislation to make stalking an illegal and jailable offence—a lot of talk about that over many years but this Government will do it before the end of the year.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the legislative programme — what will be introduced and when — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker
