veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of recreational-craft deaths notified to Maritime New Zealand in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Maritime New Zealand's recreational craft fatality notifications for the 2024 calendar year; true if the figure is 17, false if materially different.

specificity.statement: It makes the wearing of life jackets compulsory for anyone under 15 years of age while on board recreational vessels 6 metres or less in length.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact duty, the age threshold and the vessel-length threshold — anyone could check the bill against this or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My only query about this is the affordability for life jackets. A good quality life jacket is not cheap, and so we need to think about how we make those things accessible to whānau, because everybody's life is valuable and no price should be put on that.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a real implementation issue but supplies no prices, no funding mechanism and no proposal — 'we need to think about how we make those things accessible' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The 2024 numbers not wearing a life jacket have yet to be confirmed, given ongoing investigations, but what we do know is that life jackets would have saved several last year.
rigor.explanation: Self-defeating inference: the premise concedes the lifejacket-use data is unconfirmed and under investigation, then draws a confident causal conclusion that lifejackets 'would have saved several' from that same missing evidence. Nothing is offered to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In fact, most Kiwis already think they are already mandatory nationwide, reflected by the fact that most Kiwi kids are already in life jackets when out in the open water with family and friends.
rigor.explanation: Non-sequitur: observed behaviour (children wearing lifejackets) is offered as evidence of a belief (that the rule is already mandatory). People may wear them from prudence or bylaw rather than any belief about national law, so the stated premise does not support the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The current rules are inconsistent across every region in New Zealand, thanks to different unitary and regional by-laws. They are inconsistent, can be confusing, and hence ineffective.
rigor.explanation: The step from 'inconsistent and confusing' to 'ineffective' is asserted rather than shown — no evidence links bylaw variation to worse compliance or outcomes. The premise is plausible and the direction reasonable, but there is a real gap at the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We teach our kids to wear seatbelts in a car. We make them wear helmets on bikes. Wearing a life jacket on a small boat should just be as obvious.
rigor.explanation: Argument by analogy with two genuinely comparable mandatory child-safety rules. It is a reasonable inference but leans on the analogy alone — no disanalogy (cost, access, differing risk exposure) is addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My only query about this is the affordability for life jackets. A good quality life jacket is not cheap, and so we need to think about how we make those things accessible to whānau, because everybody's life is valuable and no price should be put on that.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: raises cost of compliance and who the mandate would burden. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now, just in the spirit of jest, while we do support this bill, I just want to say, oh, whānau, I hope you don't need to get your life jacket repaired, because that bill didn't get passed because the Nats didn't let it get heard tonight.
focus.explanation: Refers to a specific other member's bill and its fate on the same evening, so there is real policy content, but the weight of the remark is a jab at 'the Nats' rather than anything about lifejackets or the measure at hand.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, just in the spirit of jest, while we do support this bill, I just want to say, oh, whānau, I hope you don't need to get your life jacket repaired, because that bill didn't get passed because the Nats didn't let it get heard tonight.
civility.explanation: A partisan barb aimed at a party, not at any individual — no imputation of bad faith to a person, and explicitly framed as jest alongside support for the bill. Party-directed tribalism is Focus's business, not Civility's.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I agree with life jackets on small boats. It’s like seatbelts, and it’s regulation that will save lives.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy: life jackets are like seatbelts, therefore mandating them is justified regulation. The analogy is apt in kind but is asserted rather than supported — no evidence is offered that the seatbelt case transfers to the boating context, which is exactly the point later contested in the debate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yet the parties on the other side of the House, at the moment at least, think a 15-year-old can decide life or death, a 16-year-old can get married and can pay tax, but they can’t vote.
rigor.explanation: An inconsistency argument that treats differing statutory age thresholds as a contradiction. Nothing is offered to show the thresholds must align — legal systems routinely set different ages for different capacities — so the conclusion that the voting age position is incoherent does not follow from the premises given.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: At most it may have made a difference in one incident in 10 years, and even of that I'm very doubtful.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the evidence the speaker has just laid out: if only one covered drowning occurred in a decade, and in that case the conduct was already unlawful and other safety failures were present, then the bill's marginal effect is at most one incident. The inference follows from the premises offered; whether those premises are accurate is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Some will argue that such exemptions can be sorted out in select committee, but those exemptions already exist under the current law.
rigor.explanation: Anticipates and answers the obvious counter-argument on its own terms — if the flexibility already exists in current law, deferring it to select committee is not a gain. The rebuttal is directly responsive rather than a deflection, though the claim about current law is asserted rather than cited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It reflects a fundamental mistrust of parents and a disconnect from the lived experience of boating families.
rigor.explanation: Imputes a motive and an attitude to the bill from the mere fact that it sets a uniform rule. Nothing offered connects "this rule is inflexible" to "its authors fundamentally mistrust parents" — the conclusion overreaches the premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is why I just don't buy that example, and it's not consistent, really, with the type of culture that we wish to create in this country.
rigor.explanation: Rejects the counter-example not by showing it false but by appealing to the culture "we wish to create" — an appeal to a desired norm rather than a reason why calm-conditions exemptions are unsafe. The supporting anecdote (a relative's saying about short car trips) is also anecdotal rather than evidential.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: None of the five people on the 4.8-metre boat was wearing a life jacket when it was struck by two waves in short succession and capsized in Auckland’s Manukau Harbour a short time later.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the moment of capsize on 6 November 2022 at Clarks Beach, none of the five occupants of a 4.8-metre boat were wearing life jackets, and that the capsize followed two waves in quick succession in the Manukau Harbour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Coroner's findings and/or the Maritime New Zealand investigation report and court record for the Clarks Beach / Manukau Harbour capsize of 6 November 2022; true if those records show five people aboard a boat of about 4.8 metres, none wearing a life jacket at the time of capsize, and the capsize caused by successive waves; false if the number aboard, the boat length, or the life jacket finding materially differ.

veracity.statement: Even as our population grows, the overall trend in child drownings is falling.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number (or rate) of child drownings in New Zealand is on a declining trend despite population growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Water Safety New Zealand's DrownBase annual drowning statistics for under-15s over the last decade; true if the series shows a declining trend in child drownings over that period, false if the trend is flat or rising.

veracity.statement: Over the past decade, from 2014 to 2024, there has been only one such case.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that between 2014 and 2024 there was exactly one drowning of a child who would have been covered by this bill — that is, a child under 15 not wearing a life jacket on a recreational craft under six metres.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Maritime New Zealand official information response and Water Safety New Zealand breakdown the member offered to table, cross-checked against DrownBase records for 2014–2024; true if exactly one under-15 drowning in that period involved a recreational vessel under six metres with no life jacket worn, false if the count is zero or greater than one.

veracity.statement: The skipper was charged and pleaded guilty to manslaughter.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the skipper in the 2022 case was prosecuted and entered a guilty plea to a manslaughter charge.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The court record for the prosecution arising from the 2022 Clarks Beach / Manukau Harbour capsize; true if the skipper was charged with manslaughter and pleaded guilty to that charge, false if no manslaughter charge was laid, if the plea was not guilty, or if the conviction was for a different offence.

veracity.statement: Right now, we have very fragmented rules across New Zealand, based on the territorial authorities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that life jacket requirements currently vary by local authority area across New Zealand rather than being nationally uniform.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The navigation safety bylaws of New Zealand's regional councils and unitary authorities, and Maritime Rules Part 91; true if life jacket wearing requirements differ materially between council areas, false if a single national requirement applies uniformly.

specificity.statement: None of the five people on the 4.8-metre boat was wearing a life jacket when it was struck by two waves in short succession and capsized in Auckland’s Manukau Harbour a short time later.
specificity.explanation: Carries a date, a location, the number of people aboard, the vessel length and the mechanism of the capsize — every element is checkable against the coronial and investigation record.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, local government does a lot of work in water safety and pools and swimming, but please don’t make this another unfunded mandate that regional councils are required to enforce without any support from central government.
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete implementation issue and the actor it falls on, but supplies no figures, no estimate of enforcement cost, and no proposed funding mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Over the past decade, from 2014 to 2024, there has been only one such case.
specificity.explanation: A precise count over a named eleven-year window, tied to a defined population (children who would fall under the bill), and backed by documents the member offers to table. Directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is what this bill does; it seeks to mandate that every kid under 15 years of age wears a life jacket for vessels six metres or less.
specificity.explanation: States the operative rule precisely: the age threshold, the vessel length threshold, and the obligation created. Someone could check it against the bill or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I really am concerned that if this bill goes through with the title Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill, we will be advised that changing the age will not be within the scope of the bill.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, once the bill is at select committee, the committee will be advised that amending the age threshold falls outside the bill's scope. This is a forecast about advice the committee will receive, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Transport and Infrastructure Committee's proceedings and report on the Life Jackets for Children and Young Persons Bill; true if the committee is advised (by the Clerk or departmental advisers) that an amendment changing the age threshold is out of scope, false if the committee receives advice that the age may be amended or in fact reports back an amended age.

focus.statement: Yet the parties on the other side of the House, at the moment at least, think a 15-year-old can decide life or death, a 16-year-old can get married and can pay tax, but they can’t vote.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point (the age threshold in the bill), but it is used to pivot to an unrelated voting-age argument framed around what "the parties on the other side of the House" think, and the speaker herself immediately notes she should get back to the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of course, local government does a lot of work in water safety and pools and swimming, but please don’t make this another unfunded mandate that regional councils are required to enforce without any support from central government.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill: who enforces it and who pays. Names the affected body (regional councils) and the implementation problem (an unfunded mandate). No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill is a solution in search of a problem. Worse, it creates new problems of its own.
civility.explanation: A blunt dismissal of the bill that attacks nobody. The target is the measure, not its sponsor, and the speaker elsewhere commends the member personally. Harsh criticism of a policy is the standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I've listened intently to your speech, Cameron Luxton, and while I disagree, I really respect that within a coalition we can have these types of debate on principle and on policy.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested disagreement — a coalition partner has just opposed the bill — handled entirely on the level of principle and policy, with no imputation of bad faith or attack on the opposing member.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I just wanted to say, first off, in junior and youth sailing in this country, it is mandatory to wear life jackets.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that life jacket wear is compulsory in organised junior and youth sailing in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Yachting New Zealand's safety regulations and the sailing instructions for junior/youth class regattas; true if personal flotation device wear is mandatory (and inspected) at junior and youth events, false if it is left to competitor or race-officer discretion.

veracity.statement: In 2020, the rate is about 1.62 per 100,000 people. It’s higher than a comparable country like Australia, which is 1.1, and Canada, which is 1.3.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific 2020 drowning death rates per 100,000 population — New Zealand 1.62, Australia 1.1, Canada 1.3 — and that New Zealand's is the highest of the three.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National drowning statistics for 2020 (Water Safety New Zealand DrownBase, Royal Life Saving Society Australia National Drowning Report, Lifesaving Society Canada / WHO Global Health Estimates), expressed as deaths per 100,000 population; true if each figure matches to within rounding and the NZ rate exceeds both, false if any figure is materially different or the ordering reverses.

veracity.statement: In 2024 alone, 18 New Zealanders lost their lives in boat-related incidents. Of those, 17 were not wearing a life jacket.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 2024 boating fatality count of 18 and that all but one of those who died were not wearing a life jacket.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Maritime New Zealand recreational boating fatality data and Water Safety New Zealand's 2024 drowning report; true if the 2024 boating-related death toll is 18 with 17 recorded as not wearing a lifejacket, false if either number is materially different.

veracity.statement: Wearing a life jacket increases the chance of survival in a boating accident by up to 10 times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified survival benefit — up to a tenfold increase in the chance of surviving a boating accident — from wearing a life jacket.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Maritime New Zealand / Water Safety New Zealand published safety research and peer-reviewed studies comparing survival rates in boating incidents with and without a personal flotation device; true if a credible source supports an increase of around ten times, false if the best available estimate is materially lower.

veracity.statement: In Auckland, wearing life jackets on boats 6 meters or smaller is optional unless the skipper deems it’s unsafe. In Canterbury, children must wear life jackets, at all times, on boats 6 meters or smaller.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the substance of two regional navigation safety by-laws: Auckland leaves jacket wear on vessels 6m or under to the skipper's judgement, while Canterbury requires children to wear one at all times on such vessels.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Auckland Council Navigation Safety Bylaw and the Canterbury Regional Council Navigation Safety Bylaw as in force in October 2025; true if the Auckland bylaw makes wear discretionary for the skipper on vessels 6m and under while the Canterbury bylaw imposes an at-all-times requirement on children, false if either provision differs.

veracity.statement: I think we should, along with this piece of legislation, look forward to another National Party MP bringing forward a piece of legislation that says it is compulsory for all schools to teach kids to swim because, in fact, that has been squeezed out of the curriculum, out of school responsibilities. That’s part of the reason that we’re seeing too many people drown in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that swimming instruction has been squeezed out of the school curriculum and out of what schools are responsible for.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The New Zealand Curriculum Health and Physical Education learning area requirements on aquatics for years 1–8, plus Water Safety New Zealand / Education Review Office reporting on the proportion of schools providing swimming instruction over the last decade; true if the aquatics requirement has been removed or weakened, or provision has materially declined, false if the requirement stands and provision is stable.

veracity.statement: I think you were probably there with Mark Mitchell and the Prime Minister that Surf Life Saving New Zealand and Coastguard received a funding boost of $63.6 million over four years last year—over four years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Surf Life Saving New Zealand and Coastguard together received a $63.6 million funding increase spread over four years, announced in the year before this speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024/2025 documents and the Government's water-safety funding announcement; true if a package of $63.6 million over four years for Surf Life Saving New Zealand and Coastguard was announced in 2024, false if the figure, the period or the recipients differ.

rigor.statement: Why would we not support a bill that would make that rule consistent for all young people in this country? It just seems ludicrous when you think that even the best people can get caught out if they are not wearing those life jackets.
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from a single family anecdote (an experienced sailor who survived because of a jacket) to a national mandate. The anecdote genuinely supports the narrow point that skill does not remove risk, but generalising from one case is the only support offered, and the rhetorical question treats disagreement as unthinkable rather than answering it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They believe that personal responsibility or the burden is on the skippers, or they’re scared the Government is going to overreach, but I want to remind them that the cost of a life jacket is far less than the cost of a funeral.
rigor.explanation: The objection stated is about where legal responsibility should sit and about regulatory overreach; the reply answers it with a price comparison between a life jacket and a funeral. That is an appeal to emotion and a false equivalence — nobody argued the objection turned on the purchase price of a jacket — so the conclusion does not engage the premise it is offered against.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The idea that parents could look after their kids is complete idiocy when they’re in the water—and most of the time stepping on to a boat with the expectation that they will be safe, and for the most part, they are—but we have many, many pieces of legislation and regulation around this country for the small minority of people who might find themselves unfortunately in this situation, or harm themselves or harm us or whatever; it’s for the minority.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opposing position is that responsibility should rest with parents and skippers, not that parents can physically rescue a child in the water, and the reply refutes only the latter. The second half — that we already regulate for a small minority of cases — is a sound point, but it is bolted onto a misstated premise and the dismissal rests on calling the position idiocy rather than on the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We still go through some quite strict security regimes at the airport. The chances, thankfully, in our country of someone wanting to harm us on a plane is very, very small, but we’re prepared to do that for the greater good.
rigor.explanation: A parity-of-reasoning argument: we already accept a universal precaution against a low-probability harm in aviation, so the low probability of a given child drowning is not on its own a reason against a universal precaution on the water. The analogy is apt and the conclusion tracks it; the disanalogies (scale of harm, cost) are left unaddressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think we should, along with this piece of legislation, look forward to another National Party MP bringing forward a piece of legislation that says it is compulsory for all schools to teach kids to swim because, in fact, that has been squeezed out of the curriculum, out of school responsibilities. That’s part of the reason that we’re seeing too many people drown in this country.
rigor.explanation: The causal step — declining school swimming is part of the reason for the drowning toll — is plausible but nothing is offered to connect them: no trend in either series, no comparison. The conclusion outruns the single asserted premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why would we not support a bill that would make that rule consistent for all young people in this country? It just seems ludicrous when you think that even the best people can get caught out if they are not wearing those life jackets.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the House — the consistency of the life jacket rule for under-15s. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They believe that personal responsibility or the burden is on the skippers, or they’re scared the Government is going to overreach, but I want to remind them that the cost of a life jacket is far less than the cost of a funeral.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath — where the duty sits and what regulation costs — but the framing is largely a characterisation of what the other party believes and fears rather than engagement with their argument.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill introduces national consistency and a clear legal requirement that anyone under 15 years old on a boat 6 meters or smaller must wear a properly fitted life jacket—no excuse and no grey areas.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the measure before the House. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So this is about a consistent, nationwide rule that everyone understands, that kids under the age of 15 on vessels 6 metres or less will wear a life jacket—will wear a life jacket.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the content of the measure — what the rule would require and of whom.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2024 alone, 18 New Zealanders lost their lives in boat-related incidents. Of those, 17 were not wearing a life jacket.
specificity.explanation: Two exact counts tied to a named year and a named category of incident. Directly checkable against published fatality data.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In Auckland, wearing life jackets on boats 6 meters or smaller is optional unless the skipper deems it’s unsafe. In Canterbury, children must wear life jackets, at all times, on boats 6 meters or smaller.
specificity.explanation: Names two jurisdictions, a vessel-size threshold and the precise legal test applying in each. Someone could look up both by-laws and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill introduces national consistency and a clear legal requirement that anyone under 15 years old on a boat 6 meters or smaller must wear a properly fitted life jacket—no excuse and no grey areas.
specificity.explanation: States the operative rule exactly: the age threshold, the vessel-size threshold, and the fitting requirement. Someone could act on this description of the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I say this bill reflects who we are and who we want to be: a country that protects its young people, that learns from tragedy, and that learns about water safety.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic national virtues with no figure, mechanism, threshold or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this is about a consistent, nationwide rule that everyone understands, that kids under the age of 15 on vessels 6 metres or less will wear a life jacket—will wear a life jacket.
specificity.explanation: Gives the age threshold and the vessel-size threshold that define the rule. Precise enough to check against the bill, though it says nothing about enforcement or commencement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think you were probably there with Mark Mitchell and the Prime Minister that Surf Life Saving New Zealand and Coastguard received a funding boost of $63.6 million over four years last year—over four years.
specificity.explanation: Names the recipients, the exact dollar amount, the period it covers and roughly when it was announced — a checkable rebuttal rather than a general claim of adequate funding.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They believe that personal responsibility or the burden is on the skippers, or they’re scared the Government is going to overreach, but I want to remind them that the cost of a life jacket is far less than the cost of a funeral.
civility.explanation: Attributes fear and a mistaken belief to a party rather than to any individual, and no member is insulted. Pointed and slightly motive-imputing, but it stays off the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The idea that parents could look after their kids is complete idiocy when they’re in the water—and most of the time stepping on to a boat with the expectation that they will be safe, and for the most part, they are—but we have many, many pieces of legislation and regulation around this country for the small minority of people who might find themselves unfortunately in this situation, or harm themselves or harm us or whatever; it’s for the minority.
civility.explanation: "Complete idiocy" is aimed at a position rather than at any member, so it stays the right side of a personal attack, but the contempt carries over onto those holding the view. Robust and edging toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I went to a life jacket hub at Sport Waitākere, in West Auckland, where they, at nominal or no charge, give out life jackets to those groups and families that need them for occasions.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific organisation and location and describes the mechanism (free or nominal-charge distribution to families in need), but carries no figures, volumes or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It would strip mine an area the size of 1,700 rugby fields.
specificity.explanation: A concrete, quantified scale for the proposed mine footprint that someone could check against the fast-track application. Loses a little for using a rugby-field comparison rather than a stated area.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But we do—and I encourage the Transport and Infrastructure Committee to look at that genuine access, look at the affordability, look at communities, Grant McCallum, in the Far North, and their realistic access to life jackets, and on the East Coast, Dana Kirkpatrick.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the policy question — equity and affordability of access to life jackets in named regions — and at what the select committee should examine. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What this bill does is it draws that line in the sand: no new coal mines, no expansion of existing coal mines.
focus.explanation: States exactly what the measure before the House does. Purely about the policy mechanism, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I know that a certain Minister in this Government would laugh and brag about causing these species to become extinct—that’s how out of touch some of the Government members are.
focus.explanation: No policy, figure or measure is engaged in this passage — it is entirely a characterisation of what Government members are supposedly like.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: So there’s a lot to think about for the Transport and Infrastructure Committee to get their head around, but this is a bill that has the support of over 90 percent of New Zealanders—90 percent of New Zealanders want children in small boats to wear life jackets, and this will achieve that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over 90 percent of New Zealanders support requiring children in small boats to wear life jackets.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published survey evidence on New Zealanders' support for mandatory life jacket wear by children in small boats (e.g. Water Safety New Zealand or Maritime New Zealand public attitudes surveys, or polling cited in the bill's explanatory note / regulatory material). True if a reputable survey puts support at or above 90 percent; false if the best available polling puts it materially below 90 percent, or if no such polling exists to support the figure.

veracity.statement: The Department of Conservation ranks this plateau as one of the most valuable ecological sites on mainland New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Department of Conservation has itself rated the Denniston Plateau as among the most ecologically valuable sites on mainland New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: DOC's own published ecological assessments or conservation-value rankings covering the Denniston Plateau (e.g. DOC Sites of Special Wildlife Interest / ecological ranking documents, or DOC submissions on Denniston mining applications). True if DOC documentation places Denniston among the highest-value ecological sites on the mainland; false if DOC has published no such ranking or ranks it materially lower.

veracity.statement: It is the only home on Earth for the avatar moth and New Zealand’s very own endangered giant carnivorous snail.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Denniston Plateau is the sole global habitat of both the avatar moth and an endangered giant carnivorous (Powelliphanta) snail.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Distribution records for the avatar moth and for the relevant Powelliphanta land snail taxon (DOC threatened species listings, NZ Threat Classification System reports, and peer-reviewed taxonomic/distribution literature). True if both taxa are recorded only on the Denniston Plateau; false if either is recorded from any other locality (for example an adjacent plateau such as Stockton).

veracity.statement: It doesn’t pass the economic test. Indeed, the cost of the runoff from the acidified water, as a result of the open-cast coal mine, costs more for the Government to repair than the royalties they earn on the mining.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's cost of repairing acidified runoff from open-cast coal mining exceeds the royalties the Government earns from that mining.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown expenditure on acid mine drainage remediation attributable to the relevant West Coast open-cast coal operations (Treasury / DOC / MBIE remediation and Crown liability figures, e.g. the Stockton AMD provisions) compared against coal royalty receipts reported by NZ Petroleum & Minerals. True if documented remediation cost exceeds royalty revenue for the comparable mining operations; false if royalty revenue exceeds the Crown's remediation outlay.

veracity.statement: The Stockton mine, which is nearby—I don’t know if anyone’s visited the Stockton mine—has already cost taxpayers millions to clean up the mess.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that clean-up of environmental damage at the Stockton mine has already cost New Zealand taxpayers millions of dollars.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Records of public money spent on environmental remediation at the Stockton mine — Solid Energy legacy liabilities assumed by the Crown, Treasury/Crown accounts provisions, and DOC or MBIE reporting on acid mine drainage treatment at Stockton. True if documented taxpayer-funded clean-up expenditure at Stockton runs to millions of dollars or more; false if remediation has been borne by the operator with no material Crown cost.

civility.statement: We’ve known that for 10, 20, 30 years, and it saddens me that members in this House—who no doubt have children or grandchildren or other family members, and surely they care about the future world that those children and their children will inherit—are continuing to live in denial of the basic reality of what we need to do to have a livable future.
civility.explanation: Does not insult anyone directly, but characterises other members as 'living in denial' of reality — a slide from the policy disagreement onto the members' honesty with themselves rather than their arguments.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I know that a certain Minister in this Government would laugh and brag about causing these species to become extinct—that’s how out of touch some of the Government members are.
civility.explanation: Leaves the substance and turns on the people: imputes to a named-but-unnamed Minister a relish for driving species extinct, and labels Government members 'out of touch'. That is an attack on character, not on the mining policy.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It doesn’t pass the economic test. Indeed, the cost of the runoff from the acidified water, as a result of the open-cast coal mine, costs more for the Government to repair than the royalties they earn on the mining.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference with the premise supplied: if remediation of acid mine drainage costs the Crown more than the royalties received, the claim that the project fails an economic test does follow. Marked down only because the comparison ignores other economic effects (wages, company tax) that an 'economic test' would normally include.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The wholesale power price doubled overnight.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wholesale electricity prices doubled immediately following the previous Government's oil and gas exploration ban — a quantified claim about a past price movement, not a forecast or an opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electricity Authority / EMI wholesale spot price series for the period immediately surrounding the April 2018 announcement of the offshore oil and gas exploration ban. True if the wholesale price approximately doubled within days of the announcement; false if the price was broadly flat in that window, or if any doubling occurred gradually over months or years rather than 'overnight'.

veracity.statement: So consequently, suddenly, we became the only country in the world that instead of transitioning to renewables, we’re going away from gas to coal—to coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a superlative but operationalisable fact: that New Zealand is uniquely, among all countries, shifting from gas to coal rather than toward renewables.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IEA world energy statistics / Ember global electricity data for the years following 2018, comparing the change in coal's share of generation against gas's share, country by country. True only if no other country recorded a rise in coal share alongside a fall in gas share over the same period; false if any other country did.

veracity.statement: We have a huge pile of coal there that we’re importing from Indonesia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand is currently importing coal from Indonesia and holds a substantial stockpile of it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ merchandise trade import statistics for coal by country of origin, and Genesis Energy's public reporting on the Huntly Power Station coal stockpile. True if Indonesian coal imports are recorded and a stockpile of the order of hundreds of thousands of tonnes is held; false if imports are negligible or sourced elsewhere.

specificity.statement: The wholesale power price doubled overnight.
specificity.explanation: A quantified, checkable claim: a named quantity (wholesale power price), a stated magnitude (doubled) and a stated timeframe (overnight). Whether it is accurate is Veracity's question, not this one — a precise false claim still scores high here.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And there we go. There they go—they’re going again. Gee, they’re quite excited tonight, aren’t they?—quite excited.
civility.explanation: Mockery of the members opposite for reacting — sneering at their behaviour rather than engaging anything they said. It stops short of a direct insult to a named person, but it is derision rather than argument, which under the re-anchored scale is a genuine failure rather than merely robust.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In summary, this bill really is a typical idealistic, simplistic approach to a complex problem.
civility.explanation: Harsh, dismissive language aimed squarely at the bill itself. No person's character, competence or motives are impugned, and attacking a measure is exactly what a second-reading speech is for — under the re-anchored scale this is the expected standard, not a lapse.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And there we go. There they go—they’re going again. Gee, they’re quite excited tonight, aren’t they?—quite excited.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other side's demeanour in the Chamber. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — the passage carries no substantive content at all, and this is precisely the tribal-but-not-insulting case Focus was introduced to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because people on that side of the House, they think they have this idealistic view of the world that you could fix the world by ignoring the fact you actually need energy at an affordable price.
rigor.explanation: A strawman: it attributes to opponents a position nobody has advanced — that energy affordability can simply be ignored — and then treats that invented position as the reason their approach fails. The conclusion rests entirely on the misattributed premise, with nothing offered to show anyone actually holds it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It won’t reduce our impact on emissions in this country; it’ll make it worse because the coal’s got to be imported.
rigor.explanation: A real inference is offered — restricting domestic mining means the same coal is imported, and shipping it adds transport emissions — so this is not a bare assertion. But the conclusion outruns the premise: transport emissions are a small fraction of coal's combustion emissions, and the argument assumes without support that total coal burned is unchanged by the bill, which is the very thing at issue. A genuine gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The sad part about this, as I just heard the previous Government member talk about people laughing—and they are laughing: they are laughing at the lack of vision that this Government has and the absolute embarrassment that it has for the future generations who want to hear what is the solution.
focus.explanation: Directed at the Government's general character — its 'lack of vision' and being an 'absolute embarrassment' — with no policy, measure, figure or outcome named. This is the party-framing case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There hasn’t been much action, like many things under this Government in the past two years.
focus.explanation: Loosely anchored to the energy strategy mentioned just before, but the sentence itself generalises to 'many things under this Government' without naming a policy, target or outcome. Mostly party framing around a thin policy point.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The sad part about this, as I just heard the previous Government member talk about people laughing—and they are laughing: they are laughing at the lack of vision that this Government has and the absolute embarrassment that it has for the future generations who want to hear what is the solution.
civility.explanation: Harsh, but aimed at a collective ('this Government'), not at any individual member's character, competence or worth. Attacking a party rather than a person is a Focus problem, not a Civility one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because you’re comfortable sitting in the mud and the filth of what the sector does and brings to our whole nation.
civility.explanation: A direct personal attack on the members opposite — imputing that they are personally comfortable with 'mud and filth'. It goes to character, not to the coal policy being debated.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You have no idea at all of what it is that you’re proposing.
civility.explanation: An attack on the competence of the members opposite rather than on the substance of what they propose.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What we have here, and it’s not disputable, is that coalmining directly fuels the climate crisis and the issues that we have as a nation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as undisputed fact that coal mining is a direct driver of climate change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IPCC AR6 WGIII and IEA global emissions data on coal's share of anthropogenic CO2, plus MfE's NZ greenhouse gas inventory for coal's domestic share; true if coal extraction/combustion is a material and leading contributor to greenhouse gas emissions, false if the evidence shows it to be a negligible contributor.

veracity.statement: This bill prohibits new coal mines and any expansion of existing coal mines after the 1 January in 2025.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the scope and commencement date of the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill as introduced (legislation.govt.nz / the bill's explanatory note); true if it prohibits new coal mining permits and expansion of existing coal mining operations with effect from 1 January 2025, false if the scope or the date differ materially.

veracity.statement: The bill does not immediately shut down active mines, despite what Government members will say.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill leaves currently operating coal mines able to continue rather than closing them on commencement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The transitional and savings provisions of the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill; true if existing permit holders may continue operating under their current permitted activities after commencement, false if the bill revokes, terminates or forces cessation of existing coal mining permits.

rigor.statement: I mean, I’m hearing one over there that doesn’t agree that the mokopuna are the most important.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: an interjection during a debate about coal mining is converted into the conclusion that the member rejects the importance of grandchildren. The inference from heckle to stated value does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s a scare tactic, really, where they constantly use the line that we need more mines in order to keep the lights on when it comes to energy, and anyone who knows anything about the subject matter knows that that would only get us part of the way.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on an appeal to authority/common knowledge — 'anyone who knows anything about the subject matter knows' — with no evidence, modelling or figure offered to show that new coal supply would only partly meet electricity demand.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill prohibits new coal mines and any expansion of existing coal mines after the 1 January in 2025.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (prohibition on new mines and on expansion of existing ones) and a commencement date. Someone could check it against the bill as introduced.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think, after that standup comedy routine, I’d like to bring some serious analysis to this debate—some very serious analysis to this debate. Grant McCallum is a nice guy, but I’m going to overlook that rather facile analysis of the energy supply in this country.
civility.explanation: Dismisses another member's speech as a "standup comedy routine" and his analysis as "facile". The softener ("nice guy") keeps it short of a direct insult, but the mockery lands on the member rather than on the substance of the energy argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: She says it’s a climate plan; I say it’s a plan to manufacture energy scarcity, and that it’s frankly immoral.
civility.explanation: Goes past criticising the bill's effects to characterising it as deliberately "manufactur[ing]" scarcity and as "immoral" — an imputation of bad faith and bad motive to the member who lodged it, rather than an argument about the mechanism.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Willie Jackson: it’s an elite fantasy where other people pay your power bill.
civility.explanation: A direct address to a named member characterising his position as an "elite fantasy" funded by others — an attack on the member's character and detachment rather than on any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reason that power prices have been so high is because there are so many unbuilt but consented renewables available to us—wind farms that could have been built.
rigor.explanation: A single causal explanation is asserted for high power prices with nothing offered to connect the stock of consented-but-unbuilt renewables to the price outcome, and no account of why they went unbuilt. A real point, but the inference outruns what is shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: And when it comes to keeping the lights on, physics beats politics every day, because hydro needs rain, wind needs wind, solar needs sun, and when they don’t show up, New Zealand still needs reliable and affordable energy, and that is in the form of thermal coal.
rigor.explanation: The intermittency premise genuinely supports a need for firming, but the jump from "firming is needed" to "that is in the form of thermal coal" is a false dichotomy — gas, geothermal, hydro storage, demand response and batteries are simply not addressed.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Prohibiting modern, monitored higher standard mining, here, shifts demand to jurisdictions with lower environmental standards, longer shipping routes, and higher emissions.
rigor.explanation: A coherent leakage argument: if demand is unchanged and domestic supply is banned, supply moves offshore, and the stated consequences follow from the stated premises. The unexamined step is whether demand is in fact unchanged — a gap, not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The message to the Coast, to Southland, to the Waikato: “Thanks for your service, now shut up shop. Here’s a pink slip, with a pat on the head.” That’s what they call a transition.
rigor.explanation: A strawman: it substitutes an invented dismissal for the transition position actually advanced in the debate (worker protections, retraining, replacement jobs in the same regions) and argues against the invention rather than the position.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve already seen, from the Opposition’s gas and oil ban, how economic growth in this country was stifled under that announcement.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc causal attribution: a single policy is named as the cause of stifled growth with no evidence, magnitude or counterfactual offered, and the conclusion is simply asserted as already established ("we've already seen").
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We also don’t talk enough about the fact that 0.17 percent is our emissions—0.17 percent is the emissions that we are producing here in New Zealand. Why aren’t we talking about countries like China? Why aren’t we talking about the US? Why aren’t we talking about India, where all these other emissions are happening?
rigor.explanation: Relative privation: the small-share premise is used to argue against domestic action by pointing at larger emitters, which does not bear on whether the measure before the House reduces emissions or on New Zealand's per-capita position. The conclusion does not follow from the figure.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Opposition is shouting out, but you want to shut us down, you want to close our businesses down, and you want to skyrocket residential power prices just on an ideology that, for some reason, we are going to save the planet by not having some coal mines here in New Zealand. It’s absolutely farcical. People are laughing at that type of ideology that is coming from the Opposition parties.
rigor.explanation: Combines a strawman of the opposing case ("you want to close our businesses down") with an appeal to ridicule and popularity — "absolutely farcical", "people are laughing" — neither of which is an argument about what the ban would do.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The first is that, if we are to meet net zero emissions by 2050, we simply must have no new coal mines or extensions of existing ones.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the International Energy Agency has stated that meeting net zero by 2050 requires no new coal mines and no extensions to existing mines. The checkable content is whether the IEA in fact says this.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IEA report 'Net Zero by 2050: A Roadmap for the Global Energy Sector' (2021) and its subsequent updates: true if the roadmap states that no new coal mines or mine extensions are required/approved in the net zero pathway; false if it contains no such statement or states a materially weaker condition.

veracity.statement: And, Mr MacLeod, that does include coking coal.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the IEA's 'no new coal mines or extensions' condition covers metallurgical (coking) coal for steelmaking, not only thermal coal for power.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The coal-supply chapter of the IEA Net Zero by 2050 roadmap and IEA clarifications on metallurgical coal: true if the no-new-mines condition is stated for coal supply generally, including coking coal; false if the roadmap limits it to thermal coal or provides for new metallurgical coal supply.

veracity.statement: From 1 January this year, apparently, her bill would slam the door on any new coal mines and expansions on existing mines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content and commencement of the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill: a prohibition on new coal mining permits and on extensions of existing mines, operating from 1 January of the year of the debate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Crown Minerals (Prohibition on Coal Mining) Amendment Bill as introduced (bills.parliament.nz): true if it prohibits both new coal mining permits and extensions to existing permits with effect from 1 January 2025; false if the prohibition is narrower (e.g. thermal coal only, or excluding extensions) or carries a different commencement date.

veracity.statement: That’s why we export millions of tons of it to India, South Korea, and Japan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a volume (millions of tonnes) and the destination markets (India, South Korea, Japan) for New Zealand coking coal exports.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ overseas merchandise trade / MBIE coal export statistics by destination for recent years: true if annual coking coal exports run to two million tonnes or more and India, South Korea and Japan are all significant destinations; false if annual exports are materially under two million tonnes or the named destinations are not the actual markets.

veracity.statement: We’ve given coal- and gas-fired power stations the same one-year priority as renewables under the amended Resource Management Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's amendments to the Resource Management Act give thermal (coal and gas) generation the same one-year consent-processing priority previously afforded to renewable generation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The relevant RMA amendment Act and national direction instruments in force: true if they set the same one-year processing timeframe for consents for coal- and gas-fired generation as for renewable generation; false if the one-year timeframe applies only to renewables or if thermal generation sits under a different pathway.

veracity.statement: What I can’t understand is that we’re still bringing Indonesian coal into this country from—I just googled—over 750,000 kilometres away, nearly 800,000 kilometres away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, with a stated source (a search made during the debate), that Indonesian coal is shipped to New Zealand from over 750,000 and nearly 800,000 kilometres away. The figure is repeated twice rather than uttered once, so it is offered as the claim, not as an obvious slip.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Great-circle or shipping-route distance from Indonesian coal export ports (e.g. Kalimantan) to New Zealand ports: true if that distance exceeds 750,000 km, false if it is materially less (the Earth's circumference is about 40,000 km, so any figure in the hundreds of thousands of kilometres cannot describe a terrestrial shipping route).

veracity.statement: We also don’t talk enough about the fact that 0.17 percent is our emissions—0.17 percent is the emissions that we are producing here in New Zealand. Why aren’t we talking about countries like China? Why aren’t we talking about the US? Why aren’t we talking about India, where all these other emissions are happening?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand accounts for 0.17 percent of emissions — in context, New Zealand's share of global greenhouse gas emissions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand's gross greenhouse gas emissions (MfE Greenhouse Gas Inventory) as a share of global emissions (UNFCCC / Global Carbon Project / Our World in Data) for a recent year: true if the share is approximately 0.17 percent, false if it is materially different.

focus.statement: Now, people talk in terms of the “just transition”, but let’s cash out what that actually means: it means protections for workers; it means training for workers; it means ensuring that there are good, well-paying jobs that people who currently work in coal mines can transition to, very much preferably in the places where they already live.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question the bill raises — what happens to coal-mining employment — and attempts to define the contested term rather than characterising the other side.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a child doing homework in a cold house because Parliament decided to grandstand and that’s what we had from Labour and the Greens for six years.
focus.explanation: Starts from a genuine policy consequence (energy poverty) but the weight of the sentence is a general characterisation of two parties' six years in office, with no measure, figure or outcome named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Opposition is shouting out, but you want to shut us down, you want to close our businesses down, and you want to skyrocket residential power prices just on an ideology that, for some reason, we are going to save the planet by not having some coal mines here in New Zealand. It’s absolutely farcical. People are laughing at that type of ideology that is coming from the Opposition parties.
focus.explanation: Almost entirely a characterisation of the other parties' motives and "ideology". Coal mines are mentioned only as the object of that characterisation — no provision of the bill, cost, figure or outcome is engaged with.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, people talk in terms of the “just transition”, but let’s cash out what that actually means: it means protections for workers; it means training for workers; it means ensuring that there are good, well-paying jobs that people who currently work in coal mines can transition to, very much preferably in the places where they already live.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete components (worker protections, training, replacement jobs in the same locations), which is more than a slogan, but supplies no scheme, funding, numbers or timeframe for delivering any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve given coal- and gas-fired power stations the same one-year priority as renewables under the amended Resource Management Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the statute, the mechanism (consent processing priority), the timeframe (one year) and the generation types it applies to — someone could go and check the instrument.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We back building a million tonnes coal stockpile at Huntly to keep Auckland and the Waikato safe from blackouts and brownouts, and we back locally mined coal in Southland and the Waikato.
specificity.explanation: A named quantity (one million tonnes), a named site (Huntly), a named purpose (dry-year/peak security for Auckland and Waikato) and named supply regions. Missing only cost and timing.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What I can’t understand is that we’re still bringing Indonesian coal into this country from—I just googled—over 750,000 kilometres away, nearly 800,000 kilometres away.
specificity.explanation: Names the source country, gives a numeric distance twice, cites where the number came from, and sets it against a named domestic alternative — precise and checkable content, whatever its accuracy.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Unfortunately, it’s going to have a short life.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Julie Anne Genter's member's bill will be defeated rather than proceeding — an outcome of the House's vote, not a promise about the speaker's own action.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the first reading of the coal-mining prohibition member's bill debated on 22 October 2025; true if the bill was voted down at first reading, false if it proceeded to select committee.

civility.statement: He’s certainly got a more pragmatic future than you, Mr Abel, I think, because his feet are grounded, let’s put it that way.
civility.explanation: A direct reply to an interjector that turns on the person rather than the argument — the implication is that Steve Abel is not grounded, a mild slight on his judgement rather than on his case. Pointed and personal, but nowhere near abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What a load of nonsense from Ryan Hamilton. Have you got any mokopunas? It was just a very sad speech, but it sums up the other side very well.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the previous speaker rather than his argument — "a very sad speech" is sneering, and the rhetorical question about whether he has grandchildren goes to standing to speak rather than to the merits. Short of a direct insult, but past civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You’ve made such an impact on me that I forgot your last name!
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named member, on the theme of his insignificance. Aimed squarely at the person; no substance is engaged.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’re full of dingbats on the other side—I knew you’d find that funny, Madam Speaker.
civility.explanation: Straight name-calling directed at the members opposite — an attack on their intelligence, with no substance attached.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think James Meager should go up, because we want a Māori, and he’s one of those Māoris, you know?
civility.explanation: Condescending toward a named member — "one of those Māoris" reduces him to a category and the surrounding remark treats his advancement as a token. Personal rather than substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, I remember our Prime Minister acknowledging the departing of James Shaw and saying that, with James Shaw, there was the last true environmentalist.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Prime Minister, on James Shaw's departure from Parliament, described him as the last true environmentalist. A claim about what a named person said on a known occasion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for James Shaw's valedictory statement (early 2024) and contemporaneous reporting of the Prime Minister's remarks; true if the Prime Minister said something to that effect, false if no such remark is on record.

veracity.statement: Just by note, there’s something like 12 coal mining companies in New Zealand operating right now, and they’re employing people; they’re producing economic growth. This bill would just think to clip their wings and prevent them from expanding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of coal mining companies currently operating in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Petroleum and Minerals / MBIE coal mining permit register as at October 2025; true if roughly 12 distinct companies hold active coal mining permits, false if the number is materially different.

veracity.statement: It was a very, very weak speech because, as he well knows, his dear friend Matua Shane Jones was a huge supporter of the Labour Government and the ban on new oil and gas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Shane Jones supported the previous Labour-led Government and its ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ First and Cabinet records and contemporaneous reporting from April 2018 onward; true if Shane Jones publicly backed the offshore exploration ban as a minister in that government, false if he is on record opposing it at the time.

veracity.statement: Here’s the other thing: Winston Peters, the man who should still be Deputy Prime Minister, he supported the ban on oil and gas exploration in 2018.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Winston Peters supported the 2018 offshore oil and gas exploration ban.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet decisions and public statements from April 2018 when the ban was announced by the Labour-NZ First coalition; true if Peters publicly supported the ban at the time, false if he is on record opposing or distancing himself from it in 2018.

veracity.statement: The reality is you opposed the Paris Agreement, repealed the zero carbon Act, and abolished our Climate Change Commission.
veracity.explanation: Three distinct factual assertions about ACT's record: opposition to the Paris Agreement, repeal of the Zero Carbon Act, and abolition of the Climate Change Commission.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statute book and Hansard as at October 2025: whether the Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act has been repealed, whether He Pou a Rangi / the Climate Change Commission has been disestablished, and ACT's stated position and votes on the Paris Agreement. True only if all three occurred; false if the Act remains in force and the Commission still exists.

veracity.statement: We know there’s a move going on in terms of the leadership. Louise Upston is a candidate, and I congratulate Louise Upston. We also know that Erica Stanford is a candidate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a National Party leadership challenge is under way with two named declared candidates.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: National Party caucus records and contemporaneous reporting around October 2025; true if a leadership contest occurred or was publicly declared with Upston and Stanford as candidates, false if no contest or declared candidacies are on record.

veracity.statement: They certainly didn’t want to talk about the oil and gas ban when we had energy spot prices over $800, did they?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand electricity spot prices reached over $800 (per MWh).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Electricity Authority EMI wholesale spot price data; true if half-hourly spot prices exceeded $800/MWh at major nodes during the period referenced (the 2024 winter/dry-year peak), false if they did not.

rigor.statement: When all the ideology of the last administration talked about shutting coal down and shutting fossil fuels down, and then all of a sudden we were left with these rising power prices, who do we turn to in the time of need?
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the previous government's fossil fuel policy is placed next to rising power prices and the causal link is assumed rather than shown. No mechanism, no figures, and no consideration of the dry-year hydrology and gas-field decline usually offered as alternative explanations.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It was a very, very weak speech because, as he well knows, his dear friend Matua Shane Jones was a huge supporter of the Labour Government and the ban on new oil and gas.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the conclusion is that Hamilton's speech was weak, but the reason offered concerns what a different member did in 2018. Nothing about Jones's past position bears on the quality of the argument Hamilton just made.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The reality is that National back us, too, because the ACT Party, as we all know, are climate change deniers.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion does not follow from the premise at all — that ACT allegedly denies climate change gives no reason to think National supports Labour's position. The inference chain is missing entirely.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What it means is we’re going to keep importing that Indonesian coal, the same coal that members on that side of the House say that they hate and it’s a terrible thing and we shouldn’t have this. It doesn’t stop us using coal. It doesn’t lower our emissions. In fact, as a result our net emissions are worse as a result. It doesn’t fix the problem.
rigor.explanation: A genuine substitution argument: the bill restricts domestic extraction but not consumption, so demand is met by imports, and shipped Indonesian coal carries additional transport emissions. The conclusion tracks the premises; the weak point is that no import-emission figure is offered to establish the net worsening.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just by note, there’s something like 12 coal mining companies in New Zealand operating right now, and they’re employing people; they’re producing economic growth. This bill would just think to clip their wings and prevent them from expanding.
specificity.explanation: Carries a countable figure and a named effect on those firms, but no production volumes, employment numbers or economic value — a rough number attached to a general claim about growth.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The reality is you opposed the Paris Agreement, repealed the zero carbon Act, and abolished our Climate Change Commission.
specificity.explanation: Names three particular instruments and a particular international agreement — precise enough that anyone could go and check each one. Whether the claims hold up is a separate question.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They certainly didn’t want to talk about the oil and gas ban when we had energy spot prices over $800, did they?
specificity.explanation: Gives a named policy and a concrete price threshold that can be looked up, though without the date, node or duration that would pin it down fully.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We too care about our mokopuna, but we want to do it in a pragmatic way, not one that’s cooked up in ideology, where we burn papers in a bin on the steps of Parliament.
focus.explanation: A bill on coal mining is before the House, but this engages none of it: no mechanism, cost, timeframe or figure. The weight is on the opposing party's ideology and a protest stunt outside Parliament. "Pragmatic" is asserted, not described.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Tonight, I want to mihi to Julie Anne Genter and to my good friend Jacinda Ardern, because she was brave and she was courageous, unlike this useless lot on the other side, who keep embarrassing themselves and going down in the polls.
focus.explanation: A bill on coal mining is before the House and none of it appears here. The content is praise for two individuals set against the other side's general uselessness and polling position — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We know there’s a move going on in terms of the leadership. Louise Upston is a candidate, and I congratulate Louise Upston. We also know that Erica Stanford is a candidate.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other party's internal state during a debate on a coal mining bill. No policy content of any kind — this is the textbook case the attribute exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What it means is we’re going to keep importing that Indonesian coal, the same coal that members on that side of the House say that they hate and it’s a terrible thing and we shouldn’t have this. It doesn’t stop us using coal. It doesn’t lower our emissions. In fact, as a result our net emissions are worse as a result. It doesn’t fix the problem.
focus.explanation: Engages the bill's actual mechanism — what it bans, what it does not, and the consequence for supply and emissions. Squarely on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They’ve stuck with the green name because it sort of tries to work for their branding, but we never really hear from them. We don’t hear from them in question time asking about the environment.
focus.explanation: Leaves the bill entirely to characterise the other party's branding and general conduct. The question-time reference gestures at something checkable but names no policy, measure or outcome — the weight is on what the Greens are "really like".
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we’re going to have to burn coal, let’s at least burn New Zealand coal. Let’s at least create jobs.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy question before the House — domestic versus imported coal, and the employment consequence of the choice. No party-bashing content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No one wants to burn down the planet, but people on that side of the House seem to want to burn down our economy in the pursuit of it.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — it is a characterisation of what the other side of the House supposedly wants. Note this insults no individual, so Civility is untouched; the tribalism is what Focus catches.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: You're a bunch of dreamers. I'm sorry, the Government is a bunch of dreamers, but they're looking to the past. They're stuck in the past, and as of next year, this country has well and truly seen what a bunch of dinosaurs you are.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other parties are like. No policy, measure, figure or outcome appears anywhere in the passage.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, we could have, because my friends that have gone to Australia work in the mines. They dig the wealth out of the ground and they provide a better product than what they could import from overseas.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote: a general conclusion about New Zealand's capacity for well-paid mining jobs is rested entirely on the speaker's personal acquaintances working in Australian mines. No data or mechanism connects the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Banning coal would be like just banning petrol in New Zealand. Why don’t we do that? Why don’t we just ban petrol?
rigor.explanation: False analogy offered as a reductio. Nothing is supplied to establish that a ban on new coal mining is relevantly like a ban on petrol — different substitutability, different scale, different measure — so the absurdity of the second does not transfer to the first.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But, actually, if you know anything at all about how the energy market works in New Zealand, it's the coal price that is the most expensive. The coal is the most expensive kilowatt hours to generate electricity, and the overall price is all priced at the marginal price. So everybody's paying more for cheap hydroelectricity, for cheap wind power because of the coal peaking plants.
rigor.explanation: A real mechanism is supplied — marginal pricing means the most expensive dispatched generator sets the price for all generation — and the conclusion that consumers pay more for cheap hydro and wind follows from it. Whether the premise about coal being the marginal, most expensive source is factually right is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So the Government members, when they say things are ideological, they're talking about themselves.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. The charge of ideology is answered by turning it back on the accuser rather than by showing the Government's position is in fact ideology-driven or that the Greens' is not — the retort establishes nothing either way.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The reason that poor countries have higher emissions is because they can’t afford it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that lower-income countries emit more than wealthier ones, and attributes that to inability to afford alternatives.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: World Bank / Our World in Data CO2 emissions per capita cross-referenced against World Bank income-group classification: true if low-income countries show higher emissions per capita than high-income countries, false if lower. (If the intended measure is emissions intensity per unit of GDP rather than per capita, test that series instead — but as stated the claim is about emission levels.)

veracity.statement: The International Energy Agency concluded in 2021—so that was four years ago—that no new coal mines, mine extensions, or unabated coal plants should be developed in order for us to achieve net zero by 2050.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the IEA's 2021 net-zero work concluded no new coal mines, mine extensions or unabated coal plants should be developed on a path to net zero by 2050.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The IEA report 'Net Zero by 2050: A Roadmap for the Global Energy Sector' (May 2021): true if it states no new coal mines or mine extensions and no new unabated coal plants are required on the net-zero pathway, false if it contains no such conclusion or a materially weaker one.

veracity.statement: But, actually, if you know anything at all about how the energy market works in New Zealand, it's the coal price that is the most expensive. The coal is the most expensive kilowatt hours to generate electricity, and the overall price is all priced at the marginal price. So everybody's paying more for cheap hydroelectricity, for cheap wind power because of the coal peaking plants.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two factual premises: that coal-fired generation is the most expensive per kilowatt hour in New Zealand, and that the wholesale market clears at the marginal price so coal peakers set the price paid for all generation.
veracity.subject: speaker
