veracity.falsification_criterion: Electricity Authority wholesale market data and MBIE generation cost data for 2024-25: true if (a) the New Zealand wholesale market clears on a marginal-price basis and (b) coal-fired peaking generation shows the highest short-run marginal cost per MWh among dispatched sources; false if another source (e.g. diesel or peaking gas) is consistently the most expensive marginal unit or if the market does not clear at marginal price.

veracity.statement: We've got a whole lot of public servants and publicly funded roles: doctors, nurses, teachers, firefighters going on strike because they're not being paid sufficiently.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that doctors, nurses, teachers and firefighters in publicly funded roles were taking strike action at the time over pay.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Employment Relations Authority strike notices and union records (NZNO, ASMS, PPTA/NZEI, NZPFU) for 2025: true if industrial action over pay occurred in each of those four occupational groups during 2025, false if strikes in those groups did not occur or were not over pay.

divination.statement: They’re going to need a new one tomorrow, because this one’s not going to make it through.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the bill under debate will be defeated. Not a promise about the speaker's own action in the relevant sense — it is a prediction about the House's collective vote.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The division record for the next reading of the bill debated on 2025-10-22: true if the bill is voted down, false if it proceeds to the next stage.

divination.statement: Fast track is going to be used to destroy a living museum, a national treasure, the Denniston Plateau, because of this Government, in order for Bathurst to expand coal mining operations that will not be used, will not have anything to do with electricity generation, which will cost the country more than they will pay in royalties, more than we will earn in having those jobs.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the fast-track process will be used to approve an expansion of Bathurst's coal mining on the Denniston Plateau. The accompanying cost-versus-royalties claim is not separately operationalised; the approval is the checkable core.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Fast-track Approvals Act decision record for Bathurst Resources' Denniston/Escarpment coal project: true if a fast-track panel grants approval for an expansion of coal mining on the Denniston Plateau, false if the application is declined or the project does not proceed via fast track.

divination.statement: I'm sorry, you're going to get voted out.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the parties forming the Government at the time of the statement will lose office at the next general election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Official Electoral Commission results for the 2026 New Zealand general election and the government formed thereafter: true if the National/ACT/NZ First bloc does not command a majority and does not form the Government, false if it is returned to office.

specificity.statement: It kind of sounds nice, it doesn’t do what it says, and it creates more problems, and that’s why we’re not supporting the bill.
specificity.explanation: Announces the decisive reason for opposing the bill without naming a single clause, cost, mechanism or problem it would create. Nobody could check or act on 'it doesn't do what it says'.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The International Energy Agency concluded in 2021—so that was four years ago—that no new coal mines, mine extensions, or unabated coal plants should be developed in order for us to achieve net zero by 2050.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, the year, the precise scope of the recommendation (new mines, extensions, unabated plants) and the target it is tied to. Directly checkable against a published document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Fast track is going to be used to destroy a living museum, a national treasure, the Denniston Plateau, because of this Government, in order for Bathurst to expand coal mining operations that will not be used, will not have anything to do with electricity generation, which will cost the country more than they will pay in royalties, more than we will earn in having those jobs.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (fast-track approvals), the site (Denniston Plateau), the company (Bathurst) and the claimed cost-benefit failure. Missing figures for the royalty and jobs comparison, which is what holds it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So I'm sure many of the members opposite have never heard of the International Energy Agency, but it's a very mainstream body.
civility.explanation: Condescension directed at other members' ignorance rather than at their argument. Short of a direct insult, but it is about the people, not the position — a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The members in the National Party and the New Zealand First Party and the ACT Party have always said that the Greens were away with the fairies, because they're ignorant bullies. That's who those people are and they're making irresponsible decisions that are literally causing the country to be in an enormous amount of suffering right now.
civility.explanation: Members of three parties are called ignorant bullies and the House is told 'that's who those people are' — a sustained attack on the character of the people rather than on their policy. Aimed at others, but it is the speaker's own conduct being recorded.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: You're a bunch of dreamers. I'm sorry, the Government is a bunch of dreamers, but they're looking to the past. They're stuck in the past, and as of next year, this country has well and truly seen what a bunch of dinosaurs you are.
civility.explanation: Members are addressed directly as 'a bunch of dreamers' and 'a bunch of dinosaurs' — mockery of the people opposite rather than of anything they have proposed.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It takes too long, and it is too expensive to build in New Zealand. That is why the coalition Government, through the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement, committed to making it faster and more affordable to build granny flats.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the policy problem (cost and time to build) and a named commitment in the coalition agreement. No content about the other team at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It creates a new system for councils to be able to notify people of any risks associated with that, and that remains something that the Labour Party will continue to watch and determine whether that works because, as I have noted along the way in this process, there are systems in this which have been designed quickly; we do not know the full impact of them.
focus.explanation: Engages a specific mechanism in the bill — the council risk-notification system — and states a concrete concern about how quickly it was designed. Entirely about the measure, not about the governing parties.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wanted to highlight for the House, at this point—the third reading—just how important this is for New Zealand because, at a time when we are seeing more Government policy that makes it harder for people to afford their rents and harder for them to afford their housing cost, there should be some element of Government action on this.
focus.explanation: A real policy point — rents and housing costs, and the case for Government action on supply — but it is directed at 'Government policy' in the aggregate rather than naming a measure, figure or missed target, so it carries partisan framing alongside the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Removing barriers to building small simple houses is a common-sense change that will be an important step in helping address New Zealand’s housing crisis.
rigor.explanation: An argument is advanced — deregulate small dwellings, therefore the housing crisis is materially helped — but the only support offered is that it is 'common-sense'. That is an appeal to self-evidence; nothing is supplied connecting consent exemptions for 70m² dwellings to the scale of the housing shortage.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Before getting into the detail of the bill itself, it’s worth noting that this bill is widely supported by the public and across the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two present facts: that the bill enjoys broad public support, and that it is supported by parties across Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division/voice-vote record for the readings of the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill, plus the select committee submission tally and any published polling on granny-flat consent exemptions. True if the bill passed with support from both Government and Opposition parties and submissions/polling were predominantly supportive; false if a major party opposed it or the submission record was predominantly opposed.

veracity.statement: This is a change of the supply side which will make a small movement of the dial to make housing more affordable, at a time when rents continue to rise and when people in New Zealand are still facing a housing stock which has significant challenges of dampness, of thermal inefficiency, and—particularly for those more vulnerable communities—real issues in terms of affordability.
veracity.explanation: Contains a checkable present-tense factual assertion that rents in New Zealand were continuing to rise as at October 2025 (alongside unquantified claims about housing quality).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and MBIE bond-lodgement mean rent data) for the twelve months to October 2025. True if the national rent measure shows a positive annual increase over that period; false if annual rent growth was flat or negative.

specificity.statement: To ensure consent-exempt granny flats are simple, lower-risk buildings, the bill provides that they must be new, stand-alone, single-storey dwellings of 70 square metres or less.
specificity.explanation: A precise eligibility threshold — new, stand-alone, single-storey, 70 square metres — that a homeowner or council could apply directly. Fully checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill will make it easier to build, it will make it more simple, and it will make more lower-risk homes that many New Zealanders will be able to live in and benefit from.
specificity.explanation: Peroration with no figures, timeframes or mechanisms: 'easier', 'more simple', 'more lower-risk homes', 'many New Zealanders'. Nothing here is checkable or actionable, even though the earlier part of the speech was detailed.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wanted to highlight for the House, at this point—the third reading—just how important this is for New Zealand because, at a time when we are seeing more Government policy that makes it harder for people to afford their rents and harder for them to afford their housing cost, there should be some element of Government action on this.
civility.explanation: A pointed criticism of the Government's housing policy direction delivered on a genuinely contested point, with no person targeted, no imputation of bad faith and no mockery. Hard criticism of policy is the standard, not a failure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Successive Governments from the 1940s, those were Labour Governments, absolutely changed the picture for housing ownership. Rates rose over those two decades that were post-war years to increase housing ownership from about half to about two thirds.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that New Zealand home-ownership rates rose from roughly 50% to roughly 67% across the two post-war decades, and (b) that the governments responsible across that period were Labour Governments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Census/Stats NZ tenure series for dwelling ownership 1945-1966: true if the owner-occupied share rose from approximately one half to approximately two thirds over that span. Second limb: the record of which parties held office 1945-1966 — true if Labour governed for most of that period, false if National did.

veracity.statement: The big difference in housing policy arose in the 1990s when a National Government implemented a housing policy that involved slashing all controls around people's access, and increasing rents. Some people saw their rents of State houses go up 300 percent in six months.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 1990s National Government's move to market rents for State houses produced rent increases of up to 300 percent within a six-month period for some tenants.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Housing New Zealand / Housing Corporation rent records and contemporary official reporting on the 1991-1993 shift from income-related to market rents: true if any documented cohort of State tenants saw rents rise by around 300 percent within six months, false if the largest documented increases over six months were materially smaller.

veracity.statement: The legislation was developed quickly. The regulatory impact statement says it was rushed due to the coalition agreement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement accompanying this bill itself records that policy development was compressed because of a coalition agreement commitment.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement for the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill: true if it records constrained or truncated policy development attributed to a coalition agreement timeframe, false if it contains no such limitation.

veracity.statement: The previous Government built over 13,000 public homes, the most since the 1970s.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a delivery count of more than 13,000 public homes by the 2017-2023 Government, and that this is the largest public housing delivery of any comparable period since the 1970s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD Public Housing Quarterly Reports and Kāinga Ora delivery figures for 2017-2023: true if net new public homes delivered exceeded 13,000 and no comparable period since the 1970s delivered more; false if the count is below 13,000 or an intervening period delivered more. Note whether the figure counts net additions or gross builds.

veracity.statement: This Government has cancelled 3,479 homes, cut $1.5 billion from Kainga Ora, and is selling off existing stock.
veracity.explanation: Three distinct factual assertions: a specific count of cancelled public housing builds, a $1.5 billion reduction in Kāinga Ora funding, and an ongoing programme of selling existing public housing stock.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora board papers and HUD records of cancelled or paused developments since late 2023 (true if the cancelled dwelling count is approximately 3,479); Budget 2024 and 2025 appropriations and the Kāinga Ora review response (true if the reduction to Kāinga Ora's capital/operating funding totals approximately $1.5 billion); Kāinga Ora asset disposal records (true if existing stock is being sold).

veracity.statement: This Government was warned that their policy changes would increase homelessness, and it happened.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that officials gave the Government advance advice that its housing policy changes (notably emergency housing eligibility) would increase homelessness, and that homelessness subsequently increased.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MSD/HUD regulatory impact statements and briefings on the emergency housing eligibility changes: true if they warned of increased homelessness or rough sleeping. Second limb: the cross-agency homelessness insights reporting and rough-sleeping counts after the changes took effect — true if measured homelessness rose, false if it was flat or fell.

specificity.statement: Successive Governments from the 1940s, those were Labour Governments, absolutely changed the picture for housing ownership. Rates rose over those two decades that were post-war years to increase housing ownership from about half to about two thirds.
specificity.explanation: Gives a named era, a direction and rough start and end magnitudes for the ownership rate, but no precise figures or sources.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It increases our economic resilience; it increases resilience at the household and family level. It gives people something to be proud of and to hope for and a connection into their communities, which is unparalleled.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic benefits — resilience, pride, hope, connection — with no figures, mechanisms, timeframes or named measures. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This Government has cancelled 3,479 homes, cut $1.5 billion from Kainga Ora, and is selling off existing stock.
specificity.explanation: A precise dwelling count, a named agency, a named dollar figure and a named action. Every limb is checkable against public records.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The big difference in housing policy arose in the 1990s when a National Government implemented a housing policy that involved slashing all controls around people's access, and increasing rents. Some people saw their rents of State houses go up 300 percent in six months.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism of a previous government's housing policy and its consequences; no individual is attacked and no bad faith is imputed to any person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This Government was warned that their policy changes would increase homelessness, and it happened.
civility.explanation: A serious accusation about the Government's handling of warnings, made squarely against the decision rather than against any Minister's character or competence. She had an obvious opening to personalise it and did not.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That is, I think, the point here: that we are missing a trick if we think that these measures will make the difference that we need to radically increase not only home ownership but the quality of housing in New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion draws on the historical premise she has just laid out — that ownership and quality rose when supply measures were paired with demand-side State support — so a supply-only bill being insufficient does follow. The gap is that she establishes only what past governments believed, not that demand-side support is necessary, so the inference is supported but under-argued.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But, you know, we can't hold councils responsible on one hand and remove their oversight on the other.
rigor.explanation: Identifies a genuine inconsistency between two things the bill does — retaining council responsibility for infrastructure impacts while removing the consent process that gave them information and control. The conclusion follows directly from the premises she set out immediately before.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It also does little for productivity in the construction centre. One-off granny flats are not likely to be standardised. Productivity would come from more coordinated large-scale builds.
rigor.explanation: A clean premise-to-conclusion chain: productivity gains come from standardisation and scale, one-off dwellings offer neither, therefore the bill does little for construction productivity. The middle premise is asserted rather than evidenced, but the inference is valid.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: It's predicted that 13,000 of these small dwellings might be built because of this intervention.
divination.explanation: Relays an official forecast that the small stand-alone dwelling exemption will result in roughly 13,000 additional small dwellings being built. Other speakers in the same debate frame the same estimate as covering a ten-year horizon.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: MBIE building consent/exemption data and Stats NZ dwelling completion series for small stand-alone dwellings built under the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Act: true if approximately 13,000 or more such dwellings are recorded within ten years of commencement, false if the count is materially below that.

focus.statement: This Government has cancelled 3,479 homes, cut $1.5 billion from Kainga Ora, and is selling off existing stock.
focus.explanation: Names specific policy decisions, a specific agency and specific numbers to hold the Government to account for its housing record. This is scrutiny of policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We do not need any more demand-side intervention like KiwiBuild and other flops that did nothing but drive up the cost of housing in New Zealand and make the other side of the House ungovernable.
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy (KiwiBuild) and a real policy distinction (supply-side vs demand-side intervention), but the point is wrapped in party framing and closes on a jibe about the other side of the House rather than on the policy's effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, unfortunately, just about everything this Government has done has made things worse for Kiwis. We're seeing people sleeping on the streets.
focus.explanation: A sweeping verdict on the other team's record with no policy, measure, figure or named commitment attached — the generalised "everything this Government has done" is exactly the content-free framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we think about the State homes that have been cancelled, I think particularly about 2-12 Albertson Avenue in Port Chalmers.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny anchored to a named site and a specific decision about State housing. This holds the government to account for a concrete outcome rather than attacking the party in general, and is squarely on-policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we really wanted to make a difference, we would be amending the building code to make sure that we can build quickly to code from patterns and from component building.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the policy instrument and an alternative to it, with no party content. High Focus despite only moderate Specificity — the two are measuring different things here.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wish to apologise for the previous speaker, Scott Willis, because I think he’s a bit upset that we didn’t get to debate the Consumer Guarantees (Right to Repair) Amendment Bill yesterday—his party’s bill.
focus.explanation: No policy content whatsoever — wholly about another member and his party's unrelated bill, in a debate where the measure itself was available to engage with.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We do not need any more demand-side intervention like KiwiBuild and other flops that did nothing but drive up the cost of housing in New Zealand and make the other side of the House ungovernable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that KiwiBuild (and comparable demand-side programmes) produced no housing and raised the cost of housing in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD/Kāinga Ora KiwiBuild delivery records and independent evaluations (Treasury/MBIE) of KiwiBuild's effect on house prices. True if KiwiBuild delivered no homes and evidence links it to higher housing costs; false if the completions register shows a material number of delivered dwellings, or no evaluation attributes cost increases to it.

veracity.statement: We have seen many examples, during this process, for less than $250,000, which is well under the average building cost for New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that sub-$250,000 examples of these dwellings were presented during the select committee process, and that $250,000 is well below the average New Zealand build cost.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cost evidence presented to the Transport and Infrastructure Committee on this bill, compared with Stats NZ / MBIE average build cost per new dwelling. True if examples under $250,000 were put before the committee and that figure sits materially below the national average build cost; false if the submitted examples exceed that price or if $250,000 is at or above the national average.

veracity.statement: This bill’s regulatory impact statement tells us that there's going to be something like 7,800 new buildings in the next decade.
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific ten-year volume projection to the bill's regulatory impact statement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement published with the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill. True if it projects approximately 7,800 additional dwellings over roughly ten years; false if its projection is materially different or if it makes no such projection.

veracity.statement: Kāinga Ora was building 5,000 homes a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an annual new-build delivery rate of 5,000 homes for Kāinga Ora, used as the benchmark against which the bill's projection is judged small.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Kāinga Ora annual reports and HUD public housing supply statistics for new-build completions per year. True if annual new-build completions reached roughly 5,000 in a year; false if peak annual completions were materially below that figure.

civility.statement: It would have been good if the previous speaker Celia Wade-Brown had actually been on the committee, because a whole lot of the questions and issues that she raised were actually answered.
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging onto the named member — the repeated "actually" implies she has not done the work — but it stops short of impugning her character or competence directly.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, unfortunately, just about everything this Government has done has made things worse for Kiwis. We're seeing people sleeping on the streets.
civility.explanation: Attacks a government's record, not any individual. No person is insulted, so this passes Civility cleanly even though it is politically blunt.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I wish to apologise for the previous speaker, Scott Willis, because I think he’s a bit upset that we didn’t get to debate the Consumer Guarantees (Right to Repair) Amendment Bill yesterday—his party’s bill.
civility.explanation: Mockery of a named member: a sarcastic apology on his behalf plus an imputed personal motive ("a bit upset") that dismisses his argument as pique rather than engaging it.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I have one message for the member, which is: you’ve got to show up to this House on time.
civility.explanation: A direct personal rebuke of another member's conduct and diligence, addressed at him rather than at any argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It started with 60 square metres. Following consultation prior to the bill being lodged, it was raised to 70 square metres—another pragmatic change.
specificity.explanation: Concrete and checkable: two figures and the point in the process at which the threshold changed. Someone could verify it against the bill's drafting history.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What they are required to do is provide upfront the project information memorandum, as the Minister mentioned; identify any hazards; keep records of the finished dwelling; and levy any development contributions towards infrastructure, which addresses the Green Party member’s concerns earlier.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates the precise duties the bill leaves with councils — PIM, hazard identification, record-keeping, development contributions. Concrete enough to be checked against the bill or acted on by a council.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill’s regulatory impact statement tells us that there's going to be something like 7,800 new buildings in the next decade.
specificity.explanation: A named source document, a figure and a timeframe — precise enough that anyone could look it up.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we really wanted to make a difference, we would be amending the building code to make sure that we can build quickly to code from patterns and from component building.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete instrument (amending the building code) and two mechanisms (pattern-based and component building), but supplies no figures, no timeframe and no detail on what the amendment would say.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Getting more houses built faster creates jobs, creates housing where it’s of need, mostly, so we commend this bill to the Parliament.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion is drawn from a stated premise, but the load-bearing step is missing: nothing offered connects this bill to houses actually being built faster, and "where it's of need" is hedged with "mostly" without support.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is always going to be a section of the market that will not be met because the market solutions do not deliver what we need.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the conclusion (part of the market will not be served) is supported only by restating it (market solutions do not deliver what we need). No mechanism, evidence or independent premise is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It looks like an election slogan without a lot of work done, because we saw in the regulatory impact statement that it was done in a rushed manner because it’s part of the coalition agreement.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is offered for the conclusion — the RIS's own account of a rushed process — which genuinely supports "without a lot of work done". The step from "rushed process" to "election slogan" is a gap the reasoning does not close.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s always interesting to see my colleague Dan Bidois comment on other actions and showing up to the House on time, when, in fact, I think his own party has issues in getting votes right and practices in this House. But I’ll leave that for him to discuss with his own colleagues—foot-in-mouth syndrome, I think.
civility.explanation: Turns from the bill to a named member, ending on a personal jibe ("foot-in-mouth syndrome") aimed at Dan Bidois rather than at any argument he made. Short of sustained abuse, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member will, of course, know that Glenfield Salvation Army is reporting a homelessness list—as he moves around the House uncomfortably—of 150 people, who are sitting on that register in our own community. That’s the highest that Salvation Army Glenfield have ever reported.
civility.explanation: The substance is a service-provider statistic, but the parenthetical aside "as he moves around the House uncomfortably" comments on the member's physical demeanour rather than his argument. A mild sneer at the person, not an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s always interesting to see my colleague Dan Bidois comment on other actions and showing up to the House on time, when, in fact, I think his own party has issues in getting votes right and practices in this House. But I’ll leave that for him to discuss with his own colleagues—foot-in-mouth syndrome, I think.
focus.explanation: Opens a speech on a housing bill with the other party's voting mishaps and House practices. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — this is party-versus-party content only.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s not a solution to the housing crisis; let’s be very clear about that. The Government has taken us backwards in both building houses and also growing a skilled workforce for the construction sector—we have low number of apprentices graduating—but for the average Joe, in communities like mine, I think it’s a good thing.
focus.explanation: Squarely on policy: it names two specific outcomes the government is held to (houses built, apprentices graduating) and then assesses the bill on its merits for households. Legitimate scrutiny plus credit where due, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For many ethnic communities in New Zealand, including the Pacific and Asian families, multiple-generation living is not just practical; it is culture. These families value being close while also respecting each other's needs for privacy and independence. This bill allows the development of small stand-alone dwellings that support this way of living.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure and who it affects — it identifies a group of households and explains why the bill's dwelling type suits their living arrangements. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That member will, of course, know that Glenfield Salvation Army is reporting a homelessness list—as he moves around the House uncomfortably—of 150 people, who are sitting on that register in our own community. That’s the highest that Salvation Army Glenfield have ever reported.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two facts: that the Salvation Army's Glenfield centre currently has 150 people on its homelessness register, and that this is the highest figure that centre has ever reported.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Salvation Army Glenfield's own housing/homelessness register figures for October 2025, or the Salvation Army's reporting for that centre; true if the register stood at approximately 150 people and that is a record for the centre, false if the count is materially different or if higher counts have previously been reported there.

veracity.statement: He’ll be aware that De Paul House in Northcote are seeing the highest number of single kaumātua, kuia—seniors—accessing their support, so by no way is this a practical solution to our housing needs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that De Paul House in Northcote is currently seeing the highest number of single elderly Māori clients accessing its support that it has recorded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: De Paul House Northcote's published service statistics or annual report for 2024–25; true if its count of single senior/kaumātua clients is at a recorded high, false if the count is not a record or the provider reports no such breakdown.

veracity.statement: We know that under this Government, over the last two years, the construction sector has gone backwards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that New Zealand's construction sector contracted over the two years to October 2025, i.e. under the current government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ construction industry GDP and construction filled-jobs series for the two years to Q3 2025; true if construction output and/or employment declined over that period, false if both grew.

veracity.statement: As Labour’s tertiary spokesperson, I’m very clear that in the last two years, we’ve graduated 9,000 fewer apprentices in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific shortfall: 9,000 fewer apprenticeship completions in New Zealand over the two years to October 2025 than in the comparable earlier period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission / Ministry of Education apprenticeship completion statistics comparing 2024–2025 with 2022–2023; true if the drop in completions is approximately 9,000, false if the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The Labour Government, despite doing the largest public housing build since the 1970s, particularly, has been criticised for transitional housing options and using motels as an alternative.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2017–2023 Labour government delivered the largest public housing build since the 1970s.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: HUD / Kāinga Ora public housing supply data on net public housing places added by term; true if the 2017–2023 period added more public housing than any period since the 1970s, false if any intervening period added more.

veracity.statement: It is great to hear that this bill received unanimous support from the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Building and Construction (Small Stand-alone Dwellings) Amendment Bill was supported by every party in the House.

veracity.explanation: Two comparative claims about the tribunal's disposal rate and caseload relative to other New Zealand courts and tribunals.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice courts and tribunals statistics (case disposal times and volumes) for the most recent reporting year; true if the Disputes Tribunal ranks among the fastest on time-to-disposal and among the highest-volume civil forums, false if it sits mid-field or lower on either measure.

veracity.statement: The Government’s also separately progressing a proposal through the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill which will give the disputes referees the discretion to order the respondent to repay the cost of filing fees to a wholly or partially successful applicant.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a named separate bill before the House contains a provision empowering referees to order reimbursement of filing fees to a successful applicant. Directly relevant because Andersen later attributes the same provision to this bill instead.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill as introduced/reported back; true if it contains a clause conferring on Disputes Tribunal referees a discretion to order a respondent to repay filing fees to a wholly or partially successful applicant, false if no such clause exists in that bill.

veracity.statement: Around 11,000 people each year use the tribunal to sort out their issues.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual usage of the Disputes Tribunal at approximately 11,000 people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal application/claim statistics for the most recent full year; true if annual applications are approximately 11,000 (say 9,000–13,000), false if materially outside that range.

veracity.statement: This bill also allows referees to order that a losing party reimburse the successful applicant’s filing fee.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the filing-fee reimbursement power to the Disputes Tribunal Amendment Bill. The Minister stated earlier in the same debate that this provision sits in the separate Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, so the two accounts of which bill carries it cannot both be right.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Disputes Tribunal Amendment Bill as passed at third reading; true if it contains a clause empowering referees to order a losing party to reimburse a successful applicant's filing fee, false if that power appears only in the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill or in no bill currently before the House.

veracity.statement: Some have questioned whether increasing the tribunal’s cap will overburden it, but the evidence that we received is otherwise. The Ministry of Justice modelling shows that the system can absorb this change and that only a modest increase in the caseload is expected.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Ministry of Justice modelling produced for this bill shows about system capacity and expected caseload growth.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Justice departmental report and Regulatory Impact Statement for the Disputes Tribunal Amendment Bill; true if the modelling projects only a modest caseload increase absorbable within existing capacity, false if it projects a substantial increase or flags capacity risk.

veracity.statement: Labour also notes the recommendation of the Rules Committee last year, which suggested an even higher cap to $70,000 or even $100,000 by consent, along with clearer appeal rights.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Rules Committee recommended, in the year before the statement, a Disputes Tribunal jurisdiction of $70,000 or $100,000 by consent, plus clearer appeal rights.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Rules Committee's published report on improving access to civil justice; true if it recommends a Disputes Tribunal cap of $70,000 (or $100,000 by consent) and clearer appeal rights, false if the recommended figures differ materially. The 'last year' dating is also checkable against the report's publication date.

veracity.statement: There are legitimate reasons for a filing fee to cover the costs associated with a dispute resolution process; however, $468 is high to many New Zealanders right now—significantly higher than the $260 filing fees for the District Court and there is no associated fees waiver on the basis of hardship; there is such a waiver for the District Court.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable factual premises: that the comparable District Court filing fee is $260, and that a hardship-based fee waiver exists for the District Court but not for the new Disputes Tribunal fee tier.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The District Courts Fees Regulations 2009 (civil filing fee schedule and the waiver/hardship provision) and the Disputes Tribunal Rules 1989 as amended by this bill; true if the comparable District Court filing fee is approximately $260 and a hardship waiver exists there while none applies to the $468 tribunal tier, false if the District Court fee is materially different or a hardship waiver does apply to the tribunal fee.

veracity.statement: Sixty thousand exceeds the limit in which a no-asset insolvency is available.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that $60,000 is above the debt ceiling for entry to the no asset procedure, the effect being that a $60,000 tribunal award could not be discharged through that route.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Insolvency Act 2006 no asset procedure eligibility threshold in force at the date of the statement; true if the maximum total debt for entry is below $60,000, false if it is $60,000 or higher.

rigor.statement: In essence, we've got quite a good, efficient system that works for smaller claims up to $30,000, and for a long time that figure hasn't been adjusted. There has been a lot of inflation and we think it makes sense to extend that boundary further to $60,000—a practical, pragmatic thing that will make a difference to the many hard-working New Zealanders who just want to get on with their lives and get their disputes resolved in a timely fashion.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: an unadjusted nominal threshold plus inflation erodes the real coverage of the tribunal, therefore raise the threshold. The conclusion follows from the premises. The gap is that a doubling is not tied to any stated inflation measure, so the size of the adjustment is asserted rather than derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Whilst the new fee tier might seem a barrier to justice, it's a very small portion of the potential value of the claim. Disputes Tribunal proceedings remain significantly cheaper than bringing proceedings to the District Courts where court and legal costs are incurred throughout the case.
rigor.explanation: Anticipates the objection and offers two relevant reasons (fee-to-claim ratio, comparison with total District Court costs). But the objection is about the upfront cost to a claimant who may not have $468, and a ratio to the eventual claim value does not answer that; the argument partly addresses a different question than the one raised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We heard of some of these instances where a Master’s student was paid $9,000 for a full year’s work; she was owed $41,000 in total. But to bring her case to the tribunal, she had to forego more than a quarter of what she was owed.
rigor.explanation: The arithmetic holds: with a $30,000 cap, an $11,000 shortfall on a $41,000 claim is indeed more than a quarter, so the conclusion follows from the figures offered. Marked down because the general case for the reform rests here on a single submitted anecdote rather than on the distribution of affected claims — an appeal to anecdote propping up a structural argument, even though the mechanism it illustrates is real.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Some have questioned whether increasing the tribunal’s cap will overburden it, but the evidence that we received is otherwise. The Ministry of Justice modelling shows that the system can absorb this change and that only a modest increase in the caseload is expected.
rigor.explanation: States the counterargument fairly, then answers it with a cited source rather than assertion. The conclusion (the cap rise will not overburden the tribunal) follows from the premise (departmental modelling projects only a modest caseload increase), and no fallacy is relied on.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are legitimate reasons for a filing fee to cover the costs associated with a dispute resolution process; however, $468 is high to many New Zealanders right now—significantly higher than the $260 filing fees for the District Court and there is no associated fees waiver on the basis of hardship; there is such a waiver for the District Court.
rigor.explanation: Concedes the case for a fee before arguing against this one, and supports the 'barrier' conclusion with a like-for-like comparison plus the absence of a hardship waiver. The inference from 'higher fee, no waiver, lower-tier forum' to 'this may deter legitimate claims' is sound; it stops short of evidence that deterrence actually occurs at this price point.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill also amends the Disputes Tribunal Rules 1989 to introduce a new filing fee tier of $468 for claims of $30,001 or more to aid with cost recovery and reflect the higher private benefits of using the tribunal for higher value claims.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument amended, the exact fee, the exact claim threshold it applies from, and the stated rationale. Fully checkable against the bill as passed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government’s also separately progressing a proposal through the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill which will give the disputes referees the discretion to order the respondent to repay the cost of filing fees to a wholly or partially successful applicant.
specificity.explanation: Names the vehicle bill and states the precise mechanism (referee discretion, respondent repays filing fee, wholly or partially successful applicant). No timeframe given for when it will pass.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the justice space, we're focused on restoring law and order, but we're also focused on speeding up the wheels of justice so people can get on with their lives, get their disputes resolved, and continue prospering and doing well, like everybody aspires to do in this country.
specificity.explanation: A statement of general direction with no figures, mechanisms, named measures or timeframes. 'Restoring law and order' and 'speeding up the wheels of justice' commit to nothing checkable; the closing clause is pure sentiment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We heard of some of these instances where a Master’s student was paid $9,000 for a full year’s work; she was owed $41,000 in total. But to bring her case to the tribunal, she had to forego more than a quarter of what she was owed.
specificity.explanation: Concrete figures ($9,000 paid, $41,000 owed) and a named consequence tied to the existing cap. Checkable against the select committee submission it came from.

specificity.statement: Access to justice is the cornerstone of a fair society, and Labour has always believed that justice should not depend on the size of your wallet or your ability to hire a lawyer.
specificity.explanation: A statement of values with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named policy. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Labour also notes the recommendation of the Rules Committee last year, which suggested an even higher cap to $70,000 or even $100,000 by consent, along with clearer appeal rights.
specificity.explanation: Names the body, the two alternative figures, the consent mechanism and the accompanying appeal-rights recommendation. Directly checkable against the committee's report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There are legitimate reasons for a filing fee to cover the costs associated with a dispute resolution process; however, $468 is high to many New Zealanders right now—significantly higher than the $260 filing fees for the District Court and there is no associated fees waiver on the basis of hardship; there is such a waiver for the District Court.
specificity.explanation: Two exact fee figures, a named comparator court, and a named mechanism (hardship waiver) that is present in one forum and absent in the other. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is practical, it’s fair, and it’s overdue.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues offered as a summing-up. No figure, mechanism, provision or timeframe; nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: By raising the cap to $60,000, around 2,000 more claimants each year will be able to pursue the full value of their claims before the tribunal.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the annual number of additional claimants who will pursue full-value claims at the tribunal once the raised jurisdiction is in force. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — Labour is not in government and the outcome depends on claimant behaviour.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal statistics for the first full year after the $60,000 jurisdiction takes effect; true if claims filed with a value above $30,000 number approximately 2,000 (say 1,400–2,600) in that year, false if materially below or above that range.

focus.statement: Access to justice is the cornerstone of a fair society, and Labour has always believed that justice should not depend on the size of your wallet or your ability to hire a lawyer.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy principle here — cost as a barrier to civil justice, which is what the bill addresses — but the sentence is built around party branding ('Labour has always believed') rather than any named measure, figure or outcome. A real policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We feel that there has been a missed opportunity, that there have been a number of other improvements that could have been made to the Act.
civility.explanation: A direct criticism of the Government's legislative choices that attacks no one. No imputation of bad faith, no reflection on the Minister personally — the complaint is entirely about what the bill does and does not do. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It’s about 40 percent of the time in, say, the Ruahine wind farms and things like that, and the offshore wind farms can turn pretty much all of the time.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NZ onshore wind turbines (Ruahine-area farms) turn about 40 percent of the time while offshore turbines turn almost continuously.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / Transpower published capacity factors for Tararua–Ruahine range wind farms, and published capacity factors and availability figures for operating offshore wind farms (e.g. IEA / IRENA / UK DESNZ series). True if NZ onshore capacity factor is near 40% and offshore turbines operate at or near full availability; false if offshore capacity factors are materially below the implied near-100% figure and the claim is read as output rather than mere rotation.

veracity.statement: Those two uses are going to be particularly difficult to put together, but here we have reports from October 2024—so about this time a year ago—of wind power firm BlueFloat Energy cancelling its plan for wind farms in New Zealand, and the major reason was that a seabed mining firm wanted to mine offshore from the south coast of Taranaki.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that BlueFloat Energy cancelled its New Zealand offshore wind plans around October 2024, and that the principal stated reason was a competing seabed mining proposal off south Taranaki.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: BlueFloat Energy's own withdrawal statement and NZ media reporting (RNZ, BusinessDesk, Taranaki Daily News) from October 2024. True if BlueFloat announced withdrawal in that month AND the reason it or contemporaneous reporting gave as primary was conflict with the Trans-Tasman Resources seabed mining project; false if the withdrawal date is materially different or the stated primary reason was something else (e.g. global capital reallocation or regulatory uncertainty generally).

veracity.statement: However, we do have some things to say about this bill given that the Government is promoting fast track as a solution to everything, and we’ve seen what happens with fast track with Trans-Tasman Resources being written into the legislation and BlueFloat floating away.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Trans-Tasman Resources' seabed mining project was named in the fast-track legislation itself, and links that to BlueFloat's exit from New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The listed projects schedule of the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024. True if the Trans-Tasman Resources South Taranaki Bight ironsands project appears as a listed project in that schedule; false if it is absent or was only ever an applicant under the general referral pathway.

veracity.statement: We see in Scandinavia wooden wind turbine towers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that wooden wind turbine towers are in use in Scandinavia.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Company and trade-press records for Swedish manufacturer Modvion and any comparable Nordic producers. True if at least one commercial-scale wooden wind turbine tower has been erected and commissioned in a Scandinavian country; false if wooden towers exist only as prototypes or concepts with none installed.

specificity.statement: Those two uses are going to be particularly difficult to put together, but here we have reports from October 2024—so about this time a year ago—of wind power firm BlueFloat Energy cancelling its plan for wind farms in New Zealand, and the major reason was that a seabed mining firm wanted to mine offshore from the south coast of Taranaki.
specificity.explanation: Names the firm, the month and year, the competing use and the geographic location — someone could go and check it or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They are jobs where our sparkies can be employed, where our engineers can be employed, and where workers of all sorts can have work to do that actually really contributes to the country, that is well-paid, and that gives that sense of standing—the sense that when they get up and go to work in the morning, they are doing a job that is worth doing.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance about the employment case, but supplies only broad trade categories and a string of generic virtues — no job numbers, wage figures, timeframe or named programme.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It is time that we focused on the renewables transition we want rather than simply seeking to extract more minerals and destroy our reputation internationally.
specificity.explanation: A direction with no mechanism, figure, timeframe or named measure — it commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Those two uses are going to be particularly difficult to put together, but here we have reports from October 2024—so about this time a year ago—of wind power firm BlueFloat Energy cancelling its plan for wind farms in New Zealand, and the major reason was that a seabed mining firm wanted to mine offshore from the south coast of Taranaki.
focus.explanation: Entirely about a concrete policy conflict (competing seabed mining and offshore wind consents in a named area) rather than about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is part of the work that we must do to become an energy-independent nation, and that’s a great goal for us to have. Why? Because we do not want to be dependent on overseas fuel suppliers.
rigor.explanation: Circular reasoning: the reason offered for pursuing energy independence is that we do not want to be dependent on overseas suppliers, which restates the goal rather than supporting it. No cost, security or supply-risk premise is supplied to bridge the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is time that we focused on the renewables transition we want rather than simply seeking to extract more minerals and destroy our reputation internationally.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy — renewables development and mineral extraction are presented as mutually exclusive alternatives with nothing offered to show they cannot proceed together, and the reputational harm is asserted rather than evidenced.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Let’s be very clear, because what we are going to hear from Opposition parties is the challenging of the Government’s position in this space.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that Opposition parties, in the debate that follows, will challenge the Government's position on offshore renewable energy.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Hansard record of the second reading debate on the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill (22 October 2025 onwards); true if Opposition party speeches opposed or challenged the Government's position on the bill, false if Opposition parties spoke in support of it.

focus.statement: Let’s be very clear, because what we are going to hear from Opposition parties is the challenging of the Government’s position in this space.
focus.explanation: Frames the coming debate in terms of what 'Opposition parties' will do rather than any provision of the bill, though it is tethered to the Government's position in the energy space.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we do know is that, under the last Government, the issue was around consents; there was interest, but obviously people were waiting—it was reported publicly—eight years for consents.
focus.explanation: Criticism of the previous Government that names a specific policy problem (consenting duration) and a specific figure (eight years) rather than the other party's character — legitimate scrutiny on the substance.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This is something that we have spoken of not only in Government but, actually, in Opposition, when we stood on that policy of electrifying New Zealand, and that is the mandate we got in the last election—to bring bills like this through the House.
rigor.explanation: Premise (we campaigned on electrifying New Zealand and won the election) is offered in support of a conclusion (we hold a mandate for this particular bill). The inference is a recognisable appeal to mandate: a general election result does not by itself establish authority for a specific measure, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: International developers are exploring offshore wind projects in New Zealand, and this bill will give them certainty to invest.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that overseas developers are, at the time of speaking, actively investigating offshore wind projects in New Zealand waters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE offshore renewable energy programme documents and public announcements by offshore wind developers (e.g. feasibility or measurement work off Taranaki/South Taranaki Bight) as at October 2025; true if one or more international developers had publicly declared active offshore wind project work in New Zealand, false if no such developer activity is on record.

veracity.statement: What we do know is that, under the last Government, the issue was around consents; there was interest, but obviously people were waiting—it was reported publicly—eight years for consents.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that under the previous Government consent applications relevant to this sector took as long as eight years to process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: EPA/MBIE consenting records and contemporaneous reporting on marine and energy consent durations during the 2017–2023 Government; true if documented consent processes of about eight years exist, false if the longest documented waits are materially shorter than eight years.

veracity.statement: As it did at the first reading and as it did during the select committee process, the Labour Party supports this bill at the second reading.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour supported the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill at its first reading and through select committee, as well as now.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard division record for the first reading of the Offshore Renewable Energy Bill and the Transport and Infrastructure Committee's report; true if Labour voted in favour at first reading and did not oppose the bill in the committee report, false if Labour voted against or recorded opposition.

veracity.statement: It builds on work that was under way under the previous Government that was picked up and carried on with by the current Government, and it is much-needed legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that policy work on an offshore renewable energy regulatory regime was already under way before the change of government in 2023 and was continued rather than started afresh.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE publications on an offshore renewable energy regulatory regime dated before October 2023 (discussion documents, consultations, Cabinet papers); true if such work is documented pre-dating the current Government, false if the workstream only began after October 2023.

veracity.statement: Of course, we are experiencing, frankly, an over-abundance of wind today, and so I just want to recall in the House today that people in Canterbury, people in Kaikōura, people in Tasman-Nelson, and now people in Wellington are experiencing some pretty severe wind conditions today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that severe wind conditions were affecting Canterbury, Kaikōura, Tasman-Nelson and Wellington on the day of the speech.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MetService severe weather warnings and observed wind records for 22 October 2025; true if strong/severe wind warnings or damaging gusts were recorded for those regions that day, false if no such warnings or conditions were in place.

specificity.statement: Permits will be “use it or lose it”, which I think is important with the provisions, meaning that, if a project fails to start or progress, the area can be made available to other developers.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism in the bill and states its operative effect — what triggers it (a project failing to start or progress) and what follows (the area is reopened to other developers).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Shortly after the bill is passed, I intend to introduce feasibility permit and cost recovery regulations so that the regime is operational as soon as possible.
specificity.explanation: Names the specific secondary instruments to come (feasibility permit and cost recovery regulations), but the timing is 'shortly' and 'as soon as possible' — no date and no amounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In new section 28B(2), there is a reference to a chief executive receiving an application and the ability to hand that application for review on to another chief executive. I just have a question about the rationale for that and when it would be used.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision (new section 28B(2)) and the exact mechanism at issue — transfer of a review application between chief executives — so the question is fully checkable against the clause. Falls short of 1.0 only because it asks for a rationale rather than supplying figures or a test.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, yeah, I’m seeking to understand why we’ve specified that only core workers must not be engaged or employed in this business, and what safeguards are in place to make sure that every person that interacts—guides, teaches—in any way, small or big, with vulnerable children are not going to pose any danger or risk to their wellbeing and safety.
specificity.explanation: Anchored on a named statutory term ('core worker') and a specific coverage gap, but the second half ('every person that interacts—guides, teaches—in any way, small or big') is a broad category rather than a defined class, and no alternative threshold or wording is proposed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The key is that when people are working with children and have unsupervised access to children, they are teachers, learning support people, teacher-aides and those types of people who generally have unrestricted access to children that we need to protect children from.
specificity.explanation: Names the operative criterion (unsupervised/unrestricted access) and lists concrete role categories — teachers, learning support people, teacher-aides — but gives no clause reference, threshold or figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we are talking about here is Part 2, and we’re talking about the significance of the use of the words “vulnerable adult” and the potential replacement of those words with “adult at risk”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the Part, the exact words at issue and the exact substitute proposed — a checkable, actionable proposition. Not 1.0 because no drafting is put forward and no consequence of the change is quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: A comment on repeat was around the Limitations Act and whether consideration had been given in terms of that very key limitation on people being able to access their rights of complaint—which was six years, I understand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the limitation period constraining survivors' ability to bring a claim is six years. A factual claim about the statute book, not an opinion or a prediction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Limitation Act 2010 (NZ), primary period provisions (s 11); true if the general primary limitation period for a claim is six years from the act or omission, false if the applicable period is materially different (e.g. three years, or no fixed period for the claims at issue).

veracity.statement: What they wanted was a replacement of “vulnerable adult” with “adult at risk”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that submitters on the bill sought to have the term 'vulnerable adult' replaced with 'adult at risk'. A claim about what is on the record of the select committee process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published submissions and the select committee report on this bill (abuse-in-care / Crimes Act amendment, 2025); true if one or more submissions expressly propose substituting 'adult at risk' for 'vulnerable adult', false if no submission proposes that substitution.

veracity.statement: The select committee rejected the suggestion out of concern for what was seen as unintended consequences.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the committee's stated reason for declining the wording change was a concern about unintended consequences — a claim about the documented record of the committee, not an opinion on the merits.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee's report on the bill (commentary section on the 'vulnerable adult' terminology); true if the majority declined the change and cites unintended consequences or an equivalent concern, false if the report gives a different reason or does not address the proposal.

focus.statement: So, yeah, I’m seeking to understand why we’ve specified that only core workers must not be engaged or employed in this business, and what safeguards are in place to make sure that every person that interacts—guides, teaches—in any way, small or big, with vulnerable children are not going to pose any danger or risk to their wellbeing and safety.
focus.explanation: Entirely directed at the measure before the committee — the scope of the 'core worker' restriction in clause 4 and whether the safeguard covers other adults around children. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What we are talking about here is Part 2, and we’re talking about the significance of the use of the words “vulnerable adult” and the potential replacement of those words with “adult at risk”.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the text of the bill: a named Part and a specific wording change. Contains no reference to another party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The key is that when people are working with children and have unsupervised access to children, they are teachers, learning support people, teacher-aides and those types of people who generally have unrestricted access to children that we need to protect children from.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: unsupervised access is the risk factor, therefore the restriction attaches to the roles that carry it. The conclusion follows from the stated premise, but there is a gap — the premise does not establish that only those roles have such access, which is precisely what was asked, so the argument under-delivers on the question it answers.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Listening, in this case, and responding here today to this suggestion by altering the language or accommodating the worries of the people involved in this process would actually be its own step in terms of trust, rather than overriding it with something that can be seen as an institutional override.
rigor.explanation: There is a real inference — adopting submitters' wording would itself rebuild trust with survivors — and given the premise that trust is the scarce good, it holds. But the conclusion rests mainly on the submitters' preference (an appeal to the source of the request rather than to the merits of the term), and it does not engage the unintended-consequences objection she herself raises, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Listening, in this case, and responding here today to this suggestion by altering the language or accommodating the worries of the people involved in this process would actually be its own step in terms of trust, rather than overriding it with something that can be seen as an institutional override.
civility.explanation: Pointed criticism aimed at a process and an outcome — the select committee majority's decision, characterised as an 'institutional override'. No person is impugned and no bad faith is imputed to any individual; hard criticism of a decision is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are many people who live their lives and who have disabilities who we wouldn’t consider vulnerable; they’re completely independent, they’re capable of making their own choices, and they’re capable of moving around and exercising their own discretion and power in whichever way they see fit.
rigor.explanation: An actual inference: if many disabled people are independent and capable of exercising their own choices, then disability does not entail vulnerability, so the drafting choice that links the two is unsound. The premise supports the conclusion; the gap is that she treats 'many' as sufficient to reject a definition that only needs to cover some.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: FASD is very prevalent in our prison population, and I would assume, based on my one visit to a youth justice residence last year, Te Puna Wai in Christchurch, that foetal alcohol spectrum disorder is probably prevalent in a lot of the young people in there.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single site visit to the wider youth justice population — an argument from anecdote. It is not scored lower because she states the inference honestly ('I would assume, based on my one visit') rather than presenting it as established, so the reader can discount it appropriately.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you were to change “vulnerable adult” to another definition such as “at risk”, well, that obviously has consequences much more broadly than this particular instance because it would change that for everything that applies in that situation in the Crimes Act, with ramifications that may be unintended and not necessarily helpful to other elements of that regime.
rigor.explanation: Valid: the term is a defined term used across the Crimes Act, therefore redefining it for this purpose changes it everywhere, therefore there is spill-over risk. The conclusion tracks the premise. Short of full marks because the harm is asserted generically ('may be unintended') with no example of a provision that would actually be damaged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We understand that there will be a variety of views on this, but we do take some confidence in the process of the royal commission and the very extended process and significant amount of consultation that went into that in order to recognise that that was a sensible thing to recommend, and that’s why we’re carrying it through.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — the recommendation is sensible — rests on the authority and thoroughness of the body that made it, not on any reason why linking disability to 'vulnerable adult' is right. That is an appeal to authority/process. It is a defensible one (a royal commission's consultation is genuine evidence about what the affected community wants), which is why this sits mid-scale rather than at the bottom, but it does not engage the objection Paul actually raised.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This flexibility is needed to accommodate infrastructure differences between residences, which can affect where a scanner can be placed.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered and the conclusion follows from it: if buildings differ in where a scanner can physically sit, a definition of 'enter' fixed to one layout would not work everywhere, so the definition needs to be flexible. Not 1.0 because it does not address the obvious counter — that flexibility over where a search may occur also widens who gets searched.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are many people who live their lives and who have disabilities who we wouldn’t consider vulnerable; they’re completely independent, they’re capable of making their own choices, and they’re capable of moving around and exercising their own discretion and power in whichever way they see fit.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the drafting of the bill's definition of 'vulnerable adult' — a specific provision, no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If you were to change “vulnerable adult” to another definition such as “at risk”, well, that obviously has consequences much more broadly than this particular instance because it would change that for everything that applies in that situation in the Crimes Act, with ramifications that may be unintended and not necessarily helpful to other elements of that regime.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the legislative mechanism — how a defined term operates across the statute — with no reference to any party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This flexibility is needed to accommodate infrastructure differences between residences, which can affect where a scanner can be placed.
focus.explanation: Argues the operational merits of a specific amendment to a specific clause. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’d like a plain explanation of what this change is intended to do and what kinds of grey areas there have been in the past, and the concern over the previous way that this was written in the law and why we are now, in particular, moving to articulating that the commencement of the period is actually at the time when the person is first placed in secure care.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny directed at a named clause and a named change in the law. This is the opposition's job done on-policy; there is no party content in it at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: FASD is very prevalent in our prison population, and I would assume, based on my one visit to a youth justice residence last year, Te Puna Wai in Christchurch, that foetal alcohol spectrum disorder is probably prevalent in a lot of the young people in there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that foetal alcohol spectrum disorder occurs at high rates among people in New Zealand prisons. The second half is explicitly flagged as her own assumption and is not the checkable part.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed prevalence studies and Department of Corrections / Ministry of Health data on FASD among people in NZ prisons: true if estimated FASD prevalence in the NZ prison population is materially above the general-population estimate (commonly put at 1–3%), false if it is at or below the general-population rate.

veracity.statement: Ongoing Resource Scheme (ORS) funding, which gives that extra funding to kids in the education system with disabilities—if you’ve got FASD, you can’t even access that, and that’s not the only disability that is not recognised or funded or supported in this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a child with a foetal alcohol spectrum disorder diagnosis cannot access Ongoing Resourcing Scheme funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education ORS eligibility criteria and verification guidance: true if a child whose disability is FASD is ineligible for ORS on that basis, false if children with an FASD diagnosis can and do qualify for ORS (e.g. via the needs-based verification criteria rather than by diagnosis).
