veracity.statement: The royal commission’s conclusion and their recommendation to us was to acknowledge the concerns from the broader disability community about describing people as “vulnerable”, but they recommended changing the Crimes Act to strengthen the protections for disabled people in the current legislative framework.
veracity.explanation: A claim about the content of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care's recommendations: that it both registered disability-community objections to the word 'vulnerable' and nonetheless recommended amending the Crimes Act to extend protection to disabled people. He asserts this as fact rather than relaying it as the commission's own contention, so it is his claim to answer for.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report (Whanaketia, 2024) and its recommendations: true if a recommendation addressed to Government recommends amending the Crimes Act to strengthen protections for disabled people while noting disability-sector concern about the term 'vulnerable'; false if no such recommendation exists or if it recommended replacing the term instead.

veracity.statement: It clarifies the duration in secure care, which will be three days before court authority is required, and it also makes two changes to youth justice residences.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill sets the period a child or young person may be held in secure care at three days before court authority must be obtained.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Clause 16 of the bill (amending section 370 of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989) as reported back from select committee: true if the amended provision requires court authority after three days in secure care, false if the threshold is a different period.

specificity.statement: Ongoing Resource Scheme (ORS) funding, which gives that extra funding to kids in the education system with disabilities—if you’ve got FASD, you can’t even access that, and that’s not the only disability that is not recognised or funded or supported in this country.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific funding scheme, a specific condition and a specific consequence (exclusion from ORS). Someone could go and check the eligibility rules. Marked down because the closing clause — 'not the only disability' — names none of the others.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It clarifies the duration in secure care, which will be three days before court authority is required, and it also makes two changes to youth justice residences.
specificity.explanation: A figure and a mechanism: three days, then court authority. Directly checkable against the clause.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill is about making sure that we’re keeping our young people safe, keeping our staff safe, and bringing some professionalisation into these residences that hasn’t been there, to make sure that we have good oversight so that our young people can’t be hurt or harmed when they are in a residence.
specificity.explanation: A chain of generic goods — safety, professionalisation, good oversight — with no figure, mechanism, threshold or timeframe. Nothing here could be checked or acted on, in contrast to her clause-by-clause description a few sentences earlier.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d like a plain explanation of what this change is intended to do and what kinds of grey areas there have been in the past, and the concern over the previous way that this was written in the law and why we are now, in particular, moving to articulating that the commencement of the period is actually at the time when the person is first placed in secure care.
specificity.explanation: A precise question rather than a precise answer, but it isolates a named mechanism — the commencement point of the detention clock at first placement in secure care — and asks what defect it fixes. Marked down because 'grey areas' and 'the stories that we heard' are left unspecified.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It doesn’t always mean that you’d necessarily agree with the suggestions made, but that does not equate with ignoring.
civility.explanation: A live point of friction — he is rebutting an implied charge that the Government disregarded submitters — and he answers it on the substance without imputing bad faith or turning on either questioner. Eligible because the exchange was contested and a personal riposte was available.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So on the time limits on detention in secure care, we’ve got an Amendment Paper which reduces the 72 hours to three hours—mostly because we’re cognisant of the psychological and physical impacts that it can have on any human being who is detained in secure care for prolonged periods of time.
focus.explanation: Names the specific clause area, a specific Amendment Paper, and the exact change sought (72 hours to three hours). Entirely about the measure before the House; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are times when a young person may seek to abscond from youth justice residences; this is one of the reasons, which is one of the statutory grounds for placing a young person in secure care.
focus.explanation: Directly answers the policy question put to her — why the power is needed — by pointing to a statutory ground. No party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So on the time limits on detention in secure care, we’ve got an Amendment Paper which reduces the 72 hours to three hours—mostly because we’re cognisant of the psychological and physical impacts that it can have on any human being who is detained in secure care for prolonged periods of time.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named legislative instrument and two concrete figures — the current limit and the proposed one. The stated reason is general rather than quantified, which keeps it short of 1.0.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The problem is that when you have two separate definitions, if a child or young person was placed in secure care at 6 p.m. on the Tuesday, that is day one, so, when counting three days, they need to be out by midnight on the Thursday; in contrast to when counting 72 hours after 6 p.m. on a Tuesday, it is 6 p.m. on a Friday, 18 hours later than when counting three days.
specificity.explanation: Concrete throughout — named start time, named days, the resulting deadline under each definition, and the difference in hours. Anyone can check the calculation.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Obviously, at the extreme end, we see that quite a lot in the adult prison system, where you have reports like the report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit (PERU) at Auckland Prison, where there were people in there who spent 900 consecutive days in, essentially, solitary confinement.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the published report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit at Auckland Prison documents at least one person held for 900 consecutive days in conditions amounting to solitary confinement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Office of the Ombudsman / Chief Inspector of Corrections report into the Prisoners of Extreme Risk Unit at Auckland Prison. TRUE if the report records a prisoner held in the unit for approximately 900 consecutive days under conditions it characterises as, or equivalent to, solitary confinement. FALSE if the longest continuous period recorded is materially shorter than 900 days, or if the report does not describe the regime in those terms.

veracity.statement: I just want to clarify, because it’s been repeated a couple of times that we landed on a 72-hour time frame: actually, this legislation will be deleting the 72-hour time frame to make sure that we are very clear that it clarifies that three days in secure care before court authority is needed is what was landed upon; not 72 hours.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill under consideration removes the existing 72-hour limit on secure care and replaces it with a three-day period before court authority is required — i.e. that the 72-hour figure the questioner attributed to the bill is not in it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the clause of the Oranga Tamariki amendment bill before the Committee on 8 October 2025 dealing with time limits on secure care, as reported back. TRUE if the clause deletes the 72-hour reference and sets the pre-court-authority period as three days. FALSE if the clause retains a 72-hour limit, or if it does not change the existing time-limit wording.

veracity.statement: They don’t sit for three days with no contact with a person.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a factual matter that young people placed in secure care in a youth justice residence are not left without human contact for the duration of the placement — that staff contact is maintained throughout.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Independent monitoring reports on secure care in Oranga Tamariki youth justice residences — Office of the Ombudsman OPCAT inspections and Independent Children's Monitor reports covering 2023–2025 — plus Oranga Tamariki secure care records. TRUE if these show young people in secure care routinely retain staff contact and day-room access. FALSE if they document instances of young people confined alone in a locked room for all or most of a multi-day secure care placement.

rigor.statement: Because when people exit that secure care eventually, if they haven’t had any human or social interactions or contact for too long, it can cause even more adverse problems. It can mean that their emotions or their actions can become more aggressive or more hostile because they haven’t been around other human beings, so they have to kind of ease back into that.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal chain — prolonged isolation, then difficulty reintegrating, then heightened aggression — and the conclusion follows if the mechanism holds. But the mechanism itself rests on an appeal to anecdote ("having spoken to people who work in YJ residences") rather than evidence, and the hedged "it can" leaves the strength of the inference undefined.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The problem is that when you have two separate definitions, if a child or young person was placed in secure care at 6 p.m. on the Tuesday, that is day one, so, when counting three days, they need to be out by midnight on the Thursday; in contrast to when counting 72 hours after 6 p.m. on a Tuesday, it is 6 p.m. on a Friday, 18 hours later than when counting three days.
rigor.explanation: A worked example that actually carries the conclusion: the arithmetic is correct (midnight ending Thursday to 6 p.m. Friday is 18 hours), and it establishes the point that the three-day formulation is the shorter of the two. No fallacy or gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So this picture of sitting in a cell, with the door locked, dark and dank, and not being able to leave their room, and have no contact with people for three days, is absolutely untrue and overexaggerated.
civility.explanation: A blunt rejection aimed at the characterisation rather than at the member — no imputation of bad faith, no mockery, no comment on her competence. "Overexaggerated" edges toward suggesting the member misrepresented the position, which is what keeps it below a clean 1.0, but the target remains the description, not the person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: And I’ve tried to visit Korowai Manaaki as well but have been denied three times.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific past fact: that the speaker made requests to visit the Korowai Manaaki youth justice residence and was refused on three occasions.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki records/OIA response covering visit requests to Korowai Manaaki by MP Tamatha Paul before 8 October 2025: true if at least three requests were made and declined, false if no such requests or no declines are on record.

veracity.statement: So like I mentioned before with corrections officers, they have got body cameras and there’s CCTV everywhere.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as present fact that New Zealand corrections officers are equipped with body-worn cameras and that prisons have pervasive CCTV coverage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections policy and annual/rollout reporting as at October 2025 on body-worn camera issue to frontline corrections officers and on CCTV coverage in prisons: true if body cameras are generally issued to frontline officers and CCTV is installed across prison sites, false if body cameras are only trialled or limited to specific units.

focus.statement: So my questions are around the use of force, and I’m going to be talking specifically to our Amendment Paper No. 366, and this is an amendment that looks to remove all provisions for the use of force against youth justice residents.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the committee — a named amendment paper and the precise provision it would change. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my questions are around the use of force, and I’m going to be talking specifically to our Amendment Paper No. 366, and this is an amendment that looks to remove all provisions for the use of force against youth justice residents.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (Amendment Paper No. 366) and states exactly what it does (remove all use-of-force provisions for youth justice residents). Checkable and actionable, though it carries no figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In prisons, when there is a use of force, the best practice is that there’ll be a bit of a multidisciplinary team that come together. They look at the body camera footage, they look at the CCTV footage and they ask themselves, did we have to use force? Did we have to escalate this? Or could we have tried something else differently? And they bring in mental health professionals, kind of psychological experts, the officers themselves, and they kind of look at the situation to reassess. And that means that there is better practice because people are more aware of the different tools that they can utilise before resorting to force.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy with a stated mechanism: recorded incidents reviewed by a mixed panel raise awareness of alternatives, therefore practice improves. The conclusion tracks the premises and the causal link is spelled out rather than asserted. It leans on an unstated assumption that the prison setting transfers to youth residences, which is the gap that keeps it short of the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I guess the other point I’ll make in terms of the use of force is when weighing up whether to allow for the use of force and whether to expand that provision to other people as well, how did you strike a balance between professionalisation, which you talked about in your opening speech, Minister, versus institutionalisation?
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested provision the speaker opposes, put to the Minister as a question about the trade-off in the policy itself and referring to the Minister's own speech without any imputation of motive or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: When I was working at YouthLaw Aotearoa, I visited Whakatakapokai, and we used to go in to deliver sessions with educators, and there were times, on multiple occasions, when simple objects would go missing and that would restrict the provision of those legal services to those young people. I remember at one stage it was a pen that had gone missing and not been identified. So while I completely understand the Minister's explanation of it not being an isolated sort of cell that this young person is in, there are certainly large restrictions that are made around young people in care and a huge amount of discretion, so just one general point.
rigor.explanation: An argument is genuinely advanced: personal observation of residence practice is offered as a premise for the conclusion that restrictions and staff discretion are extensive. The inference leans on anecdote (a single missing pen, recalled from her own visits) to reach a general claim about the regime, which is a real gap. It is not a bare appeal, though — she had immediately before cited the statutory text authorising the search of 'any article' and of anything that 'could... be harmful', which independently supports the breadth conclusion. Mid-scale: a reasonable point resting more heavily on anecdote than the conclusion needs.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: A first question here would be what advice did the Minister seek regarding how the use of force is consistent with the royal commission's findings and recommendations that found that laws and regulations surrounding the use of force were often ignored when they were in place, and, in reality, legitimised the use of force, leading to severe harm, abuse, and trauma in far too many cases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as an embedded factual premise, a characterisation of what the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found about use of force in State care: that the laws and regulations governing it were often ignored where they existed, that in practice they legitimised the use of force, and that this led to severe harm, abuse and trauma in many cases. The claim is about the content of a published report, not about whether force is good or bad.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care in State and Faith-based Institutions final report (Whanaketia, July 2024) and its findings/recommendations on use of force and restraint in youth justice and State care residences. True if the report finds that use-of-force rules were frequently disregarded and that in practice the regulatory framework legitimised force causing serious harm; false if the report makes no such finding or finds the opposite (e.g. that the rules were generally observed and constrained force).

veracity.statement: In the explanatory note, it amends the current definition of a “pat down search” in section 384A to ensure that it covers not only the youth justice resident but those who enter a youth justice residence.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the Minister's Amendment Paper 354 does: that it widens the existing statutory definition of 'pat down search' in section 384A so that the power reaches visitors entering a youth justice residence, not only residents themselves.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text and explanatory note of Amendment Paper 354 to the bill before the Committee on 8 October 2025, as published on legislation.govt.nz / the Parliament website. True if the amendment extends the section 384A 'pat down search' definition to persons entering a youth justice residence; false if it leaves the definition confined to youth justice residents or alters it in some other respect.

civility.statement: I've just spoken to one of the roles I used to play entering a youth justice residence, and so I have just an observation that I think it would have been useful to consult with some of those entities that are regularly entering youth justice facilities to hear their views on the pat-down searches.
civility.explanation: This is a criticism of the Minister's process — that an amendment extending pat-down powers to visitors was brought without consulting the professionals who visit. It is contested ground with an obvious uncivil option available (imputing that the Minister could not be bothered, or does not care what visitors think). She takes none of it: the complaint lands entirely on the consultation step, and she grounds it in her own former role rather than in anyone's character or motives.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I think the point we're trying to make is that the discretion here is extremely broad and the question is whether there's consideration of how that could be drawn down.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the measure before the Committee — the breadth of the search discretion the new provisions confer, and whether it should be narrowed. It follows directly from her citation of new section 384A(2) and the 'anything that could... be harmful' limb, so a specific mechanism is at issue rather than the other party's record or character. Critical of the government's bill without a word of party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The amendment set out here requires reasonable modern de-escalation practices to be exhausted before any force is used in carrying out a search, and there’s a bit more to it but what I would say is I do not support this as legislating modern de-escalation practices in the context of searches would make the safeguards for searches different from safeguards for other contexts where force may be used, for example in self-defence or in defence of another person.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: premise that legislating de-escalation only for searches would create a safeguard regime inconsistent with self-defence and defence of another, conclusion that the amendment should not be supported. No fallacy; the gap is that consistency is asserted as decisive without addressing why searches on entry might warrant a different standard.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The existing time limit applies to the period before approval must be sought from the court for an extension. Reducing the period to three hours is not a practical time frame in which a court decision can be sought.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premise: if the statutory clock measures the window in which court approval must be obtained, then compressing it to three hours is defeated by court turnaround times. She also correctly identifies that the amendment would need redrafting if the intent were an absolute cap, rather than strawmanning it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would say, without this provision to use force in the context of a search on entry, Oranga Tamariki would have no authority to touch the child or young person who is not cooperating—for example, even to just guide them to a scanner.
rigor.explanation: A reductio: remove the force authorisation and even minimal physical contact becomes unauthorised. The inference is sound on its own terms but leans on the assumption that no lesser authority to guide a person exists elsewhere, which is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We allow adults to make those choices, but, in this situation, we’re kind of clamping down really hard—so you’ve got a child who’s coming in and they’re just stripped of all these things that have been used probably for comfort, etc., and they’re in an extremely challenging situation.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy — adults are trusted to weigh the harms of tobacco and vaping, so a blanket prohibition for young people entering a residence is disproportionate. The analogy leaves a real gap it never closes: the differing legal position of minors in state custody is precisely what the prohibition rests on. She does concede the harm, so this is a gap rather than a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The amendment set out here requires reasonable modern de-escalation practices to be exhausted before any force is used in carrying out a search, and there’s a bit more to it but what I would say is I do not support this as legislating modern de-escalation practices in the context of searches would make the safeguards for searches different from safeguards for other contexts where force may be used, for example in self-defence or in defence of another person.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of a named amendment paper and how it would interact with existing force safeguards. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We allow adults to make those choices, but, in this situation, we’re kind of clamping down really hard—so you’ve got a child who’s coming in and they’re just stripped of all these things that have been used probably for comfort, etc., and they’re in an extremely challenging situation.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of clause 17's harmful-item list and whether it admits proportionality. No party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I would say that this bill is clear that the scanner search images must be disposed of within 24 hours, meaning that they can be disposed of sooner if necessary.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill as it stands imposes a maximum 24-hour retention period on scanner search images, framed as an upper limit rather than a fixed period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill's clauses on scanner searches in youth justice residences (as reported back from select committee): true if it requires disposal of scanner search images no later than 24 hours after the search, false if it sets a different maximum, allows retention beyond 24 hours by default, or leaves the period to regulations.

veracity.statement: The Privacy Commissioner in his submission on this bill found the restriction on the retention of images was generally appropriate, so we won’t be supporting that amendment.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific characterisation of the Privacy Commissioner's select committee submission on this bill — that it judged the image-retention restriction generally appropriate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Privacy Commissioner's written submission to the select committee on this bill: true if it states the retention restriction is generally appropriate (or equivalent), false if it opposed the retention provisions, sought a shorter period, or made no such finding.

specificity.statement: The existing time limit applies to the period before approval must be sought from the court for an extension. Reducing the period to three hours is not a practical time frame in which a court decision can be sought.
specificity.explanation: Names the operative figure (three hours), the mechanism the existing limit governs (seeking court approval for an extension) and what would have to change for the amendment to work. Falls short of 1.0 in offering no actual figures for court response times.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wanted to ask the Minister to explain the process around how that decision would be made given what I have suggested, which is that we’ve got a fairly spare, a minimal principle of harm in the first clause.
specificity.explanation: Directed at a specific mechanism — the regulation-making power to declare new harmful items, read against the definition of harm earlier in the clause — but asks about 'the process' in the abstract, without naming a test, threshold or safeguard she would want applied.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I can certainly understand the thought behind this amendment. Further work is required to consider whether it’s practical to authorise contractors to carry out a search on entry, but to prevent them from using force if necessary to the purpose of the search.
civility.explanation: Rejecting an opposition amendment on a genuinely contested power to use force against children, with a real opportunity to be dismissive; instead engages the drafting problem and credits the intent. Attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Just in regard to the questions that have just been asked around harmful items: the harmful items are the same as the list in the Corrections Act, for starters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the list of harmful items to be prescribed under this bill is the same as the list already set out in the Corrections Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the proposed harmful-items list (departmental disclosure statement / officials' advice accompanying the Oranga Tamariki amendment bill) against the unauthorised items list in the Corrections Act 2004 and the Corrections Regulations 2005. True if the items correspond; false if the proposed list contains materially different or additional categories.

veracity.statement: The bill was also amended at select committee stage to include guiding criteria for this legislation-making power. This will require the Minister for Children to consult with the Minister of Justice and be satisfied on reasonable grounds that the harm that could be caused by the items justifies it being added to the list or even removed from the list if requested.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the select committee added a consult-and-be-satisfied test to the item-listing regulation power.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The select committee report and the reported-back version of the bill. True if the reported-back text adds a requirement that the Minister for Children consult the Minister of Justice and be satisfied on reasonable grounds as to harm before an item is listed or delisted; false if no such criteria were inserted at select committee.

veracity.statement: I do agree that in the past that hasn’t really been followed very well because there wasn’t a very good training programme in place when people came to work within youth justice.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the de-escalation-before-restraint procedure was historically not well followed, and that no adequate induction training programme existed for youth justice staff.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Oranga Tamariki internal practice reviews, Office of the Children's Commissioner / Independent Children's Monitor reports, and the Whanaketia report on training and restraint practice in youth justice residences before 2024. True if they find de-escalation training was absent or inadequate and restraint policy inconsistently applied; false if they record an established, followed training programme.

veracity.statement: Standard operating procedure is that physical intervention can only be used when verbal de-escalation techniques have failed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the content of Oranga Tamariki's current standard operating procedure on physical intervention.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Oranga Tamariki standard operating procedure / practice guidance on physical restraint in youth justice residences current at October 2025. True if it states physical intervention may be used only after verbal de-escalation has failed; false if it permits physical intervention on other grounds without that precondition.

veracity.statement: This bill’s not changing the existing time limits for secure care.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill leaves the statutory maximum periods for placement in secure care untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the bill as reported back against the existing secure care provisions of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. True if no clause alters the statutory time limits on a secure care placement; false if any clause extends, shortens or removes them.

veracity.statement: The Whanaketia report shows very clearly that they were not exaggerations; they were the horror that people lived through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Whanaketia report documents conditions in State care matching the 'dark and dank' descriptions, i.e. that those descriptions were not overstated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Whanaketia – Through Pain and Trauma, From Darkness to Light (Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care final report, 2024). True if the report's findings record conditions in residences of the kind described; false if it finds such descriptions unsupported or overstated.

veracity.statement: So this clause replaces the wording “must be carried out by a member of staff who is of the same sex as the child or young person being searched” with “must not be carried out in view of another child or young person in the residence”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what clause 23 of the bill does to the search restrictions in section 384G — replacing a same-sex-searcher requirement with an out-of-view requirement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 23 of the bill as reported back, amending s 384G of the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989. True if it substitutes the out-of-view wording for the same-sex-staff wording as quoted; false if the same-sex requirement is retained elsewhere or the replacement wording differs.

rigor.statement: It’s not just really up to discretion; there has to be a link between an item and harm. If the item is not likely to cause harm to a child or young person, there is no reason to add it to the list and regulations.
rigor.explanation: Answers a concern about arbitrary ministerial discretion with a constraint, but the inference has a real gap: 'there is no reason to add it' establishes only that adding a harmless item would be unmotivated, not that the power could not be used that way. The conclusion (discretion is bounded) is stronger than the premise offered supports.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So if you know you are going to be in a unit with young people that have weapons on them, that have the potential to stab you or kill you, you are not feeling safe. So what I would say is this is a valid response to making sure that young people in our care are safe.
rigor.explanation: The conditional premise (weapons present → residents do not feel safe) is reasonable, but the jump to 'this is a valid response' skips the step that matters: nothing is offered to show the item-listing power actually removes the weapons or is proportionate to the risk. Partly leaning on an emotive appeal to being stabbed rather than on the mechanism.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill was also amended at select committee stage to include guiding criteria for this legislation-making power. This will require the Minister for Children to consult with the Minister of Justice and be satisfied on reasonable grounds that the harm that could be caused by the items justifies it being added to the list or even removed from the list if requested.
specificity.explanation: Names the amending stage, the exact statutory mechanism (consultation with a named Minister) and the legal test ('satisfied on reasonable grounds'). Checkable and actionable; falls short of 1.0 only because no clause number or threshold is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, now, staff are trained in verbal de-escalation with restorative practice in addition to proactive prevention of events like fights. After the use of force, it will be reviewed by a team leader. It will also have a process to escalate internally to the Oranga Tamariki escalation team where any concerns about the appropriateness of the use of force can be investigated.
specificity.explanation: Names the training content, the reviewing role (team leader) and the named escalation body. Concrete enough to check or act on; no numbers, timeframes or coverage figures, which keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So spending three days in secure is one thing, but the 22 previous days is really where I’d want to understand in a more thorough way, Minister, as to what that actually does look like and what is the model of care.
specificity.explanation: Carries two concrete figures (three days, 22 previous days) that give the question a definite shape, but 'model of care' is left undefined — the direction is clear, the what and how are not.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So this clause replaces the wording “must be carried out by a member of staff who is of the same sex as the child or young person being searched” with “must not be carried out in view of another child or young person in the residence”.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the amended section, and quotes both the outgoing and incoming statutory wording exactly. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is not about taking away what young people enjoy. They are in an area where they are high risk; in a youth justice facility in particular, they are court-ordered to be there.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the policy question before the committee — the rationale for restricting items in a court-ordered residential setting. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So spending three days in secure is one thing, but the 22 previous days is really where I’d want to understand in a more thorough way, Minister, as to what that actually does look like and what is the model of care.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the regime: it directs attention past the secure-care episode itself to the care provided in the weeks around it. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question is, really: why wasn’t that explicit wording included in 384AC, and what was the intent of the removal of some of that language in section 384G, as well?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the drafting of two named sections and the inconsistency between them. Legitimate line-by-line scrutiny of the measure before the House, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What I would also like to say is, I just want to bring a little bit of balance to this, because we have some pretty amazing staff that take care of our young people, and whilst, at times, there are people that do skirt those lines of being responsible caregivers for our young people, most of our workers go to work every day to make our young people’s lives better.
civility.explanation: Responding to a genuinely contested line of questioning that implied staff abuse of secure care — a real opportunity to turn on the questioners. She rebuts on the substance, concedes that some staff do fall short, and attacks no one.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: From what I’m hearing this morning, I can hear intention, but I don’t hear deep conviction in that way, and I’d like to understand that better.
civility.explanation: Pointed and robust — it questions the depth of the Minister's commitment, which edges toward the person rather than the policy — but it stops short of imputing bad faith, and is framed as a request to be persuaded rather than an accusation.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Some of us might recall—a couple of years ago, I believe—there was this kind of big drama about police taking lots of images of young Māori on the street and not storing those images securely, and the Privacy Commissioner found that there were tens of thousands of unauthorised, unsecure photos of young Māori children just floating around and being stored on these devices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Privacy Commissioner inquiry a couple of years earlier found police held tens of thousands of unauthorised, insecurely stored photographs of young Māori, taken on the street on officers' devices.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2022 joint inquiry by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner and the Independent Police Conduct Authority into New Zealand Police photographing members of the public, and its published findings: true if that inquiry found Police unlawfully collected and insecurely held photographs of young people numbering in the tens of thousands, disproportionately Māori; false if it made no unlawful-collection finding, or if the volume of unauthorised images was materially smaller than 'tens of thousands'.

veracity.statement: It’s also justified in light of news stories—last year, I think—around Korowai Manaaki, where contraband was being brought in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that there was reporting in the previous year about contraband (including vapes) being brought into the Korowai Manaaki youth justice residence, and attributes related findings to the Children's Commissioner.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: News reporting from 2024 and monitoring reports on Korowai Manaaki by the Independent Children's Monitor / Children's Commissioner: true if they document contraband, including vapes, being brought into that residence; false if no such reporting or finding for Korowai Manaaki exists.

specificity.statement: Is it secure storage software or whatever it ends up being? How will we know and monitor that those images have been deleted within that 24-hour window? Who has access to those images? Does that include third-party contractors?
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete thing being asked about — the storage medium, the statutory 24-hour deletion window, the monitoring of that deletion, and named categories of access-holder including third-party contractors. A precise question, answerable point by point; short of 1.0 only because it does not name the clause or propose a mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If something is found, through either the scanning process or the pat-down process, if it is not an illegal item, then they will be given the option to take that back to their vehicle and then come back again.
specificity.explanation: A concrete operational rule: names both detection routes, the legal/illegal distinction that triggers it, and the actual remedy offered to the visitor. Checkable against the residence procedure; falls short of 1.0 with no timeframe or who exercises the discretion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d seek the Minister’s assurance that people would be given appropriate interventions in terms of things like nicotine patches, etc., because they’re undergoing huge amounts of stress and they’re being asked to, basically, detox at the same time, quite often.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete intervention (nicotine patches) and the substances at issue, which is more than a general call for support, but 'appropriate interventions ... etc.' carries no threshold, no coverage and no process — the how much and the by whom are missing.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One thing I have heard from rangatahi who have been in youth justice residences is that the family visits can make a big different to the care they’re being provided, or maybe the counselling they’re getting in there or the programmes they’re doing. Those family visits really reinforce the positive things that they’re learning.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (family visits reinforce rehabilitation, so search regimes that deter families carry a cost) does follow from the premise offered, and the premise is first-hand testimony from the affected group rather than a bare assertion. It is still an appeal to anecdote — no rate, study or monitoring finding is offered — so the inference is supported but not securely.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But what I would like to say is it's not as uncommon as we think. You walk through an airport; you get scanned at an airport, if you want to catch a flight. You often can come to these restrictions when going to court. There are multiple places where you walk through a scanner and nothing to see here and not a problem.
rigor.explanation: An appeal to common practice resting on a weak analogy: airport and court scanning is of adults who choose to enter, whereas the question raised was about whānau visiting detained children and, specifically, about how intimate images of those children are stored and who can see them. 'Nothing to see here' asserts the conclusion the analogy was meant to establish, and the analogy does not reach the storage and access concern at all.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: People would find things in the cars that were, perhaps, illegal. I remember I had a case where there was equipment for the use of marijuana and there was equipment for the use of P. In fact, it’s very hard to link that to the person who’s driving the car because so many people are in the car.
rigor.explanation: A genuine attribution argument: if a vehicle has many users, an item found in it cannot reliably be traced to the driver, so a vehicle search yields weaker evidence than a personal search. The conclusion follows from the premise; it leans on a single professional anecdote rather than any data on shared-vehicle use, which is what holds it below the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would like for people who are listening today to hear a little bit from the Minister about what kind of dogs are involved and whether there have been any instances where those dogs have got out of control, because it’s very hard to control a dog, actually. One the challenges that many of us who’ve had dogs face is they’re not, actually, entirely in our control.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from ordinary pet ownership ('many of us who've had dogs') to purpose-trained detector dogs — a weak inductive step across two quite different cases, and an appeal to shared personal experience. She partly flags the gap herself ('given the fact that these are trained dogs'), and the underlying request for safeguards does not depend on the generalisation holding, which keeps it off the floor.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So section 384G relates to searches inside residences. So the bill removes the current requirement that pat-down searches only be carried out by a person of the same sex as the child or young person. This is done because it would completely contradict the new section that it’s being replaced by, which would require search plans under new section 384AA, inserted by, clause 1, where a child or young person can express the gender or sex of the staff member they prefer to be searched by.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: premise is that new s384AA lets a young person nominate the sex or gender of the searcher; conclusion is that retaining the old same-sex-only requirement would contradict it. The conclusion follows directly from the premise. No fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s where contractors may come in through a back gate into the secure area. They might be bringing items in for kitchen, they might be bringing anything in, and it just gives us the ability to be able to make sure that contractors aren’t bringing in unauthorised items, because they will be skipping the process of going through the scanner in the initial entrance to residence.
rigor.explanation: Premise: contractors entering through a back gate bypass the entrance scanner. Conclusion: a separate vehicle-search power is needed to catch unauthorised items on that route. The conclusion tracks the premise and identifies the specific gap being closed; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Like, let’s be real. I don’t have a car, but if I did, like, I might have friends in that car, a vape might fall out of their pocket, and there might be, I don’t know, a vape on the ground or something like that—I guess I’m a bit nervous that that family might get searched and “Oh, you’ve got an unauthorised item in your vehicle.”—and then they’re not able to visit their kids or their niece or nephew or whatever it is.
rigor.explanation: The chain — minor item in a vehicle, therefore search, therefore visit refused, therefore families deterred — is offered entirely from an invented anecdote about herself rather than from the drafting or any evidence of practice, and each link is asserted rather than shown. It is not a non-sequitur (the steps are individually possible), but it leans on a hypothetical to carry the whole weight of the concern.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My concern on that one was more about whether we ought to make it explicit, given that in other sections we make it explicit that non-residents of the facilities can elect either someone of the same sex or the same gender. So it was just trying to work out why the language was different in that section versus new section 384AC, but I am assured that that remains a choice for the young people.
rigor.explanation: Argues from an internal inconsistency in the bill — other sections spell out the same-sex-or-same-gender election for non-residents, this one does not — to the conclusion that the omission may be significant and should be made explicit. The inference from differing statutory language to differing effect is a standard and valid one, and she concedes where the Minister's answer resolves it.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So section 384G relates to searches inside residences. So the bill removes the current requirement that pat-down searches only be carried out by a person of the same sex as the child or young person. This is done because it would completely contradict the new section that it’s being replaced by, which would require search plans under new section 384AA, inserted by, clause 1, where a child or young person can express the gender or sex of the staff member they prefer to be searched by.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, both sections, the exact requirement removed and the mechanism replacing it. Anyone could open the bill and check the drafting against this description.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In regards to new section 384KG, “Search of vehicles entering youth justice residence”, I just want to make it very clear that it’s vehicles that are brought within the secure perimeter of a youth justice residence. The vehicle may be searched by an authorised person for the purposes of detecting any unauthorised item. It’s the secure perimeter, so it wouldn’t be the car park that a visitor comes in to visit.
specificity.explanation: Names the section, the class of person who may search, the purpose of the search and the precise physical boundary it applies to, and states an explicit exclusion (the visitor car park).
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The use of dogs will be extremely limited. It would have to be quite a significant issue to use dogs. Maybe, if we found somebody coming into the secure area in a vehicle with cannabis—quite a fair bit of cannabis—we might call in to get that checked by dogs.
specificity.explanation: An assurance with an illustration but no operative content: “extremely limited” and “quite a significant issue” set no threshold, no authorisation step and no quantity, and “quite a fair bit of cannabis” is not a checkable trigger. The worked example lifts it above a bare platitude but there is nothing here anyone could hold the department to.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just also wanted to raise our Amendment Paper 371, which talks about, within Part 3, the amendments that specify that an authorised person is able to use force. We wanted to just question this a little bit and make sure we understand what the implications of this amendment are. Because we’re wondering if this means that contractors who may be running a programme or something within a youth justice residence—does this mean that they too are able to use force?
specificity.explanation: A precise question: the amendment paper is numbered, the Part identified and the ambiguity pinned to a named category (third-party contractors, including iwi social services). It stops short of proposing wording, which is what holds it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wondered whether it would be useful to prioritise obscuring the genitals as opposed to making it an alternative, and that way, saying that the preference by far is for that to be used as an option instead of making them not easily distinguishable, which feels to me quite invasive.
specificity.explanation: A concrete drafting change to an identified provision (new s384KF(5)(b)): make obscuring the genitals the primary requirement rather than one of two alternatives. Someone could act on this directly. The reason given for it — that the alternative “feels to me quite invasive” — is the imprecise part.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The next one is consequences of refusing a search because you failed to remove an outer item of clothing. Now, this includes head coverings, as well, and I just wonder whether the Minister had received advice on religious head coverings and the interaction with the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act and how that would be treated in terms of this instance?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named provision, a named category of item (religious head coverings) and a named legal instrument (the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act), and asks a checkable question — whether advice was received. Precise enough to be answered or refused on the record.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In regards to new section 384KG, “Search of vehicles entering youth justice residence”, I just want to make it very clear that it’s vehicles that are brought within the secure perimeter of a youth justice residence. The vehicle may be searched by an authorised person for the purposes of detecting any unauthorised item. It’s the secure perimeter, so it wouldn’t be the car park that a visitor comes in to visit.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the vehicle-search power in new s384KG is limited to the secure perimeter and does not extend to a visitor car park. This is a contested reading — Tamatha Paul had just described the power as covering vehicles entering the perimeter generally and worried about visiting families.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new section 384KG as it stands in the bill before the committee: true if the vehicle-search power is confined to vehicles brought within the secure perimeter of a youth justice residence, false if it also reaches vehicles parked in a visitor car park outside that secure perimeter.

focus.statement: I just also wanted to raise our Amendment Paper 371, which talks about, within Part 3, the amendments that specify that an authorised person is able to use force. We wanted to just question this a little bit and make sure we understand what the implications of this amendment are. Because we’re wondering if this means that contractors who may be running a programme or something within a youth justice residence—does this mean that they too are able to use force?
focus.explanation: Names a specific amendment paper, a specific Part, a specific power and a specific class of person it might extend to. This is scrutiny of a drafting consequence, with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It looks to me as if it’s balanced towards risk rather than benefit, and in most areas of the law we’ve moved to balancing those two things in our words as well, saying we need to actually look at the benefit as well as the risk when we decide whether to prohibit such an object.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy: other areas of law now weigh benefit against risk, therefore this regulation-making test should too. The inference is coherent and the earlier telephone example supplies a supporting instance, but the analogy to 'most areas of the law' is asserted rather than shown, leaving a gap between the premise and the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So I just need clarification that there is a description of what an authorised person is in order to make sure that they have the skills, because we know that we’re dealing with young people who have trauma and young people who are in escalated situations.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered and the conclusion tracks it: if the population is traumatised and situations escalate, the statutory definition of who may act needs to carry a skills requirement. The link leans on 'we know', an appeal to shared assumption rather than evidence about the effect of de-escalation training, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I can see why you may need to withhold possessions when they’re seized from residents of those facilities, but, certainly for visitors, they should have that property returned to them as swiftly as possible. In my view, given it is a search, it’s more appropriate for that to be set out in primary legislation as opposed for it to be delegated.
rigor.explanation: Draws a relevant distinction — residents and visitors are differently situated, so a retention power justified for one is not automatically justified for the other — and concludes that the visitor case belongs in primary legislation. The final step, from 'it is a search' to 'therefore primary rather than delegated', is asserted rather than argued, which is the remaining gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I questioned why we needed secondary powers to create other persons when we already had the wording of “an authorised person”. I couldn’t imagine circumstances where anyone but an authorised person would be the person who was there for a pat-down search.
rigor.explanation: The support for 'the regulation-making power is unnecessary' is that the speaker cannot imagine a case needing it — an appeal to personal incredulity. It carries some legitimate force in scrutiny, since the onus of justifying a delegated power sits with the Government, but nothing is offered beyond the speaker's own inability to conceive of an exception.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It looks to me as if it’s balanced towards risk rather than benefit, and in most areas of the law we’ve moved to balancing those two things in our words as well, saying we need to actually look at the benefit as well as the risk when we decide whether to prohibit such an object.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at the drafting of the regulation-making criteria for harmful items — the test the legislation applies — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: While I agree that there would be a disciplinary issue involved, there is also probably a role here for the Ombudsman in both situations where they would be looking at patterns of behaviour.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the oversight architecture for use of force and repeated searches under the bill; no reference to any party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: After a use of force, it’s reviewed by a team leader and would also be able to be escalated internally to Oranga Tamariki around any concerns of appropriateness of the use of force.
focus.explanation: Answers on the substance of the accountability mechanism for excessive force; nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It was about the amendment of the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, which was around the definition of “authorised person” and the request in our amendment around adding the words “a person who has received training in de-escalation methods appropriate for children and young people”.
focus.explanation: Entirely about a named clause and a specific drafting change; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I can see why you may need to withhold possessions when they’re seized from residents of those facilities, but, certainly for visitors, they should have that property returned to them as swiftly as possible. In my view, given it is a search, it’s more appropriate for that to be set out in primary legislation as opposed for it to be delegated.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism and the constitutional placement of a specific power in the bill; contains no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whilst this may seem like a small change, the change is to allow the chief archivist to audit an agency more frequently where required and allow the chief archivist to work with agencies to put in place action plans and to issue performance notices to improve practice.
focus.explanation: Describes what Part 4 of the bill actually does to the Public Records Act; entirely on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: While I agree that there would be a disciplinary issue involved, there is also probably a role here for the Ombudsman in both situations where they would be looking at patterns of behaviour.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific oversight body and the specific function it would perform (looking at patterns of behaviour across repeated searches), but supplies no statutory hook, mechanism or trigger threshold, so it is a direction with partial detail rather than something fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: After a use of force, it’s reviewed by a team leader and would also be able to be escalated internally to Oranga Tamariki around any concerns of appropriateness of the use of force.
specificity.explanation: Names the reviewer (team leader), the escalation path (internally to Oranga Tamariki) and what triggers it, so there is a real mechanism here — but no timeframe, no standard applied at review and no reporting requirement, so it stops short of something that could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It was about the amendment of the Hon Willow-Jean Prime, which was around the definition of “authorised person” and the request in our amendment around adding the words “a person who has received training in de-escalation methods appropriate for children and young people”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the amendment, whose it is, the defined term it alters and the exact words proposed to be inserted. Anyone could pick up the supplementary order paper and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Whilst this may seem like a small change, the change is to allow the chief archivist to audit an agency more frequently where required and allow the chief archivist to work with agencies to put in place action plans and to issue performance notices to improve practice.
specificity.explanation: Names the office (chief archivist) and three concrete new instruments — more frequent audits, action plans, performance notices — under a named statute. It stops short of the top because there is no audit frequency, no timeframe and no consequence attached to a performance notice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So anything that we can do to improve this, bring some more accountability into this space, speed up the process, and actually make sure that we’re doing the right thing to help people reflect on their history, heal in their present, and empower their future is a good thing.
specificity.explanation: A chain of generic goods — improve, bring accountability, speed up the process, do the right thing — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named step. Nothing here could be checked or acted on, in contrast to the same speaker's description of the chief archivist's new powers moments earlier.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If I have understood your questions around harmful objects, I actually think I’ve been very thorough in my explanations, a couple of times now, and have gone through the process of “It must go through a process to be added to the list or taken off the list”.
civility.explanation: Declines to re-answer with a note of impatience that edges toward the questioner — the implication is that the member was not listening the first two times — but it stops short of imputing bad faith, sneering or attacking her. Pointed rather than a genuine failure.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: When it comes to the oversight of a youth justice facility, the Ombudsman does have access to that information. Mana Mokopuna does regular reviews of our youth justice facilities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two present-tense facts about existing oversight arrangements: that the Ombudsman can access information held about youth justice facilities, and that Mana Mokopuna (the Children and Young People's Commission) carries out regular reviews of those facilities.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: True if (a) the Ombudsman's statutory powers to require information from Oranga Tamariki — Ombudsmen Act 1975 investigative powers plus the Ombudsman's designation as a National Preventive Mechanism for youth justice residences under the Crimes of Torture Act 1989 — cover youth justice residence records, and (b) Mana Mokopuna / the Children and Young People's Commission has a published monitoring function and published review reports on youth justice residences under the Children and Young People's Commission Act 2022 or the Oversight of Oranga Tamariki System Act 2022. False if either body lacks that access or has published no such reviews.

specificity.statement: The current section 33 of the Act, which is the “Independent audits of public offices”, requires that audits of the data kept “must be conducted at an interval of not less than five years and not more than 10 years”. The amendment removes that time period and changes the language so that it’s just “as directed by the Chief Archivist”. I am wondering what the rationale was for removing that time period?
specificity.explanation: Names the clause (34), the provision (s 33 Public Records Act), quotes the existing statutory interval and the replacement wording. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I know that at one stage a young person received what was their Child, Youth and Family information back in the day, but a lot of it was hard to understand. Is there any ability to ensure that plain language can be included in this piece of legislation?
specificity.explanation: Identifies a concrete concern (records released to a care-experienced young person being unintelligible) and a named remedy (a plain-language requirement in the Act), but offers no drafting, standard or mechanism for how it would be imposed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We support what the Ministers have presented and, as I say, we would have liked to see a few changes.
specificity.explanation: States a position on the bill without naming a single one of the changes the caucus wanted, despite this being the closing contribution where they could have been listed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The advice here is that this allows for faster re-audits to check up on agency record-keeping. The Chief Archivist is statutorily independent as to looking at those audits, and the budget available for the audits is not changing.
specificity.explanation: Gives a rationale (enabling faster re-audits) and two concrete assurances (statutory independence of the Chief Archivist, unchanged audit budget), but no figures, timeframe or the statutory basis for the independence claim.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill provides the necessary clarification because it goes further than the Supreme Court in crucial ways, including more tightly defining what “exclusive use and occupation” means, requiring the courts to base any inferences on firm physical evidence, not on cultural association alone, and placing the burden of proof more squarely on applicants.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete legal mechanisms — a tightened definition of exclusive use and occupation, an evidential restriction on inferences, and a shifted burden of proof — which can be checked against the bill's text. No figures or timeframes.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This will require rehearing seven cases, including four where customary marine title has already been recognised. In the Government’s view, retrospectively applying the amendment test is necessary to have as many applicants as possible decided under a test that appropriately captures Parliament’s original intent. Recognising the impact this will have for the affected applicants, the Government has approved $15 million to help meet their rehearing costs.
specificity.explanation: Gives the number of cases affected (seven), how many already have CMT recognised (four), the retrospective cut-off already stated (25 July 2024) and a dollar figure for rehearing costs ($15 million).
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The current section 33 of the Act, which is the “Independent audits of public offices”, requires that audits of the data kept “must be conducted at an interval of not less than five years and not more than 10 years”. The amendment removes that time period and changes the language so that it’s just “as directed by the Chief Archivist”. I am wondering what the rationale was for removing that time period?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill — what a named clause changes and why. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The bill provides the necessary clarification because it goes further than the Supreme Court in crucial ways, including more tightly defining what “exclusive use and occupation” means, requiring the courts to base any inferences on firm physical evidence, not on cultural association alone, and placing the burden of proof more squarely on applicants.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the measure does and how it differs from the current legal test. No reference to any other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The current section 33 of the Act, which is the “Independent audits of public offices”, requires that audits of the data kept “must be conducted at an interval of not less than five years and not more than 10 years”. The amendment removes that time period and changes the language so that it’s just “as directed by the Chief Archivist”. I am wondering what the rationale was for removing that time period?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that s 33 of the Public Records Act currently sets an audit interval of not less than five and not more than 10 years, and that the bill's clause 34 replaces that with 'as directed by the Chief Archivist'.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of s 33 of the Public Records Act 2005 as at 8 October 2025, and clause 34 of the bill as reported back; true if the current section contains the quoted 5-to-10-year interval and the clause removes it in favour of direction by the Chief Archivist, false if either wording differs materially.

veracity.statement: The advice here is that this allows for faster re-audits to check up on agency record-keeping. The Chief Archivist is statutorily independent as to looking at those audits, and the budget available for the audits is not changing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that the Chief Archivist is statutorily independent in respect of these audits and (b) that the funding available for audits under the Public Records Act is unchanged by the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Public Records Act 2005 provisions on the Chief Archivist's independence of function and on funding of s 33 audits, plus the bill's departmental disclosure statement and Vote Internal Affairs archives appropriations; true if the Act confers independence over audit functions and no appropriation change accompanies the amendment, false if the independence is not statutory or if the audit funding line is reduced.

veracity.statement: However, in 2023, the Court of Appeal interpreted the CMT test in a way that significantly reduced the need for continuity and exclusivity in the scope of what can constitute a substantial interruption.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Court of Appeal's 2023 decision lowered the continuity and exclusivity requirements in the s 58 customary marine title test, in particular by narrowing what counts as a substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal judgment in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) [2023] NZCA 504, compared against the High Court test it replaced; true if the Court of Appeal narrowed 'substantial interruption' and relaxed the continuity/exclusivity requirements, false if it left those requirements materially unchanged or tightened them.

veracity.statement: The Supreme Court confirmed that the Government was right to have concerns about how the 2023 Court of Appeal Re Edwards decision approached the customary marine title test.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court's December 2024 Re Edwards judgment vindicated the Government's stated concerns about the Court of Appeal's approach to the CMT test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) [2024] NZSC 164; true if the Court held the Court of Appeal erred in its formulation or application of the s 58 test in the respects the Government had identified, false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's approach to that test.

veracity.statement: This will require rehearing seven cases, including four where customary marine title has already been recognised. In the Government’s view, retrospectively applying the amendment test is necessary to have as many applicants as possible decided under a test that appropriately captures Parliament’s original intent. Recognising the impact this will have for the affected applicants, the Government has approved $15 million to help meet their rehearing costs.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the retrospective schedule will require seven cases to be reheard, that four of those have already had customary marine title recognised, and that Cabinet has approved $15 million towards the applicants' rehearing costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti advice and the bill's Schedule 1AA, the list of CMT determinations made since 25 July 2024, and the Cabinet paper or Budget appropriation for rehearing costs; true if seven proceedings fall within the schedule with four determinations already made and $15 million is appropriated, false if the counts or the figure differ materially.

rigor.statement: Section 33 in the current Act specifies that the archivist must carry the budget for those audits, and I wonder, if by making this change, we’re solving a budget problem but potentially not the independence issue, which the legislation, as it is currently drafted, protects.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise (the current Act requires independent commissioning and places the audit budget on the archivist) supports a conditional conclusion (allowing departmental employees to audit may relieve cost at the price of independence). The cost-motive step is inferred rather than shown, and is appropriately hedged as a question, so the inference is sound but incomplete.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Following the Supreme Court’s December judgment, the High Court issued a decision that has made extensive findings of CMT, illustrating that the Supreme Court’s test has not altered the approach of the courts in practice. Parliament, clearly, did not intend CMT would be available at that scale, so to resolve Parliament’s intent, legislative clarification is still required.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a single High Court decision to 'the approach of the courts in practice' — a hasty generalisation, since one judgment cannot show a test has had no effect. The second step asserts what Parliament 'clearly' intended without offering any evidence of intent, then treats that assertion as the premise for the conclusion that legislation is required.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I respect the role of the courts as one decisionmaker under this regime and the challenge in interpreting the CMT test in the context of the wider Act, but for this regime to work as Parliament intended, a rigorous test for CMT needs to be maintained.
civility.explanation: Legislating to override judicial decisions is precisely where judges get accused of activism or bad faith; the criticism here stays on the interpretation and on Parliament's intent, and explicitly acknowledges the difficulty of the courts' task.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If anyone knows where Waimahana is in the Far North, when you get to the ridge before you look down to the left on Waimahana, have a look to the right. There’s a place called Paradise Bay, where you can’t get to.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific location (Waimahana, Far North) and a specific inaccessible beach (Paradise Bay) with directions to it — a concrete, checkable instance of the access problem rather than a general assertion. Falls short of 1.0 because no figures, mechanism or extent of the blocked parcels is given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Labour opposes this bill, for the matters of retrospectivity, for the matters that the Minister has raised about their push and their policy to exploit the minerals at the Government’s will.
specificity.explanation: Names two grounds of opposition — the Bill's retrospectivity and the minerals policy — which is more than a bare statement of position, but neither is developed with a clause, figure, or mechanism.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Minister Finlayson—former Minister Finlayson, sorry—was very clear to this Government that what they’re doing to this bill is abhorrent, and it actually isn’t what he did when he passed this bill in 2011.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Finlayson, the Minister responsible for the 2011 Act, has publicly and clearly told this Government that the amendment is abhorrent and inconsistent with the 2011 legislation's intent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, media interviews or select committee submissions by Christopher Finlayson on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill; true if he publicly and unambiguously condemned the Bill as contrary to the 2011 Act's intent, false if he made no such statement or supported the Bill.

veracity.statement: I want to remind the House that that bill was carefully negotiated between the Māori Party and the National Party of the day.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 was the product of negotiation between the Māori Party and the then National Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2011 legislative record — the National–Māori Party confidence and supply arrangement, the Bill's select committee history and the third reading division for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011; true if the Act's terms were negotiated with the Māori Party and it voted for the Act, false if it was enacted without Māori Party involvement or over its opposition.

rigor.statement: Now we’re saying not only are we going to change the rules while everyone’s playing the game but we’re going to push you all back to the start line. Why does this sound familiar to our people in the House here? That’s what they did on pay equity—it’s the same thing.
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy: retrospective legislation resetting claims already in train is likened to the pay equity changes.
