The structural parallel (extinguishing claims mid-process) is real, so this is not a bare non-sequitur, but the analogy is asserted — "it's the same thing" — rather than shown, with no account of where the two cases correspond.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That member sits there and shakes his head, but he is incorrect when he thinks we are the ultimate lawmaker here. Yes, we are—however, the courts have the opportunity to define that.
rigor.explanation: Self-contradiction: the member is declared incorrect for thinking Parliament is the ultimate lawmaker, and in the next breath conceded to be right ("Yes, we are"). The point he is reaching for — that courts interpret what Parliament enacts — does not support the refutation he actually asserts.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is unjust and it is unfair—it is grossly unfair that the Government, at the will of their policies—at the will, dare I say it, of many of their backers—push a bill like this through the House simply because they are unhappy with a judgment from the court.
civility.explanation: Goes past criticising the policy to imputing a corrupt motive — that the Bill is being advanced at the will of the Government's financial backers. No individual is named, but attributing bad faith rather than error is a civility failure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member can chirp all he wants—and I look forward to hearing what he has to say when it comes to his party’s call on this bill, because I can tell that member that when the ACT Party get up in this House and talk about Treaty settlement bills, we’re all going to sit here and go: “Two-faced.”.
civility.explanation: "Chirp all he wants" is a belittling dismissal of the member, and the charge is of bad faith rather than error. Directed at a party more than at the individual, so short of a direct personal insult, but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That member doesn’t know what he’s talking about.
civility.explanation: A bare attack on the member's competence with no accompanying substance — it disparages the person rather than engaging the argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Now the Minister is saying that it’s going to pass again, it will still pass before Christmas, a year after it was first introduced in this House.
divination.explanation: Relays the Minister's forecast that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill will complete its passage before Christmas 2025, roughly a year after introduction.
divination.subject: other
divination.falsification_criterion: The NZ Parliament bill record for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill; true if the Bill passes its third reading on or before 25 December 2025, false if it has not passed third reading by that date.

focus.statement: That member can chirp all he wants—and I look forward to hearing what he has to say when it comes to his party’s call on this bill, because I can tell that member that when the ACT Party get up in this House and talk about Treaty settlement bills, we’re all going to sit here and go: “Two-faced.”.
focus.explanation: Carries no policy content at all: it is about the ACT Party's general character across Treaty settlement bills, not about any provision, cost or outcome of the bill before the House. Exactly the content-free party framing Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is a 700-year-old sailing waka found on a beach at the top of the South Island.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Anaweka waka, found on a beach in the northern South Island, is approximately 700 years old.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published radiocarbon dating and archaeological literature on the Anaweka waka (recovered from the Anaweka estuary, Tasman/Golden Bay); true if the hull is dated to roughly 700 years before present (c. 1300s AD), false if the accepted dating is materially different (e.g. 400 years or 1,200 years).

veracity.statement: The 2011 correction of the confiscation of the foreshore and seabed that was affected by the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, was achieved by agreement across the House.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 was passed with cross-party agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill in March 2011; true if it passed with support spanning government and opposition parties, false if major parties (e.g. Labour, Greens) voted against it.

veracity.statement: But this bill retrospectively cancels that right for all the claimants who’ve already been or are in the process of going to court.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's application provisions apply retrospectively to applicants who have already filed or completed customary marine title proceedings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The application/transitional provisions of the bill as reported back from the Justice Committee; true if the new test is applied to applications already filed or already determined, false if it applies only prospectively to new applications.

veracity.statement: Mr Christopher Finlayson, who wrote this bill, the former Attorney-General, put it plainly, “these amendments do not restore the original intent of Parliament, they undermine them”.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific quoted assessment attributed to Christopher Finlayson, the Attorney-General responsible for the 2011 Act, that the amendments undermine rather than restore Parliament's original intent.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, submissions or published commentary by Christopher Finlayson on the Customary Marine Title Amendment Bill during 2025; true if he stated in substance that the amendments undermine rather than restore Parliament's original intent, false if no such statement exists or he said the opposite.

veracity.statement: In fact, the Supreme Court agreed that the Court of Appeal got that wrong.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court held the Court of Appeal had erred in its interpretation of the customary marine title test.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment in the Whakatōhea/Edwards customary marine title appeal; true if the Court held the Court of Appeal's interpretation of the s 58 test was wrong, false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's approach.

veracity.statement: The Justice Committee—and I acknowledge the chair, the Hon James Meager—received and considered submissions from 6,692 interested groups and individuals and heard oral evidence from 69 submitters.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Justice Committee received 6,692 written submissions and heard 69 oral submitters on this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Justice Committee's report on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill; true if the submission figures match 6,692 written and 69 heard, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: A customary marine title cannot be sold, and public access is maintained.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two legal features of customary marine title under the 2011 Act: inalienability and preserved public access.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, ss 11, 26 and 60 and related provisions; true if the Act makes customary marine title inalienable and preserves rights of public access, false if either is not provided for.

veracity.statement: In 2023, the Court of Appeal interpreted provisions of the Act about the requirements for recognising customary marine title which materially reduced the threshold of the continuous exclusive use.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a 2023 Court of Appeal decision lowered the statutory threshold for exclusive use and occupation without substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal's 2023 judgment in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea); true if the Court adopted a reading of s 58(1)(b) less demanding than continuous exclusive use and occupation since 1840, false if it applied that requirement as written.

veracity.statement: This bill fulfils a coalition agreement between New Zealand First and National.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that legislating to restore the higher customary marine title test is a commitment in the National–NZ First coalition agreement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published National–New Zealand First coalition agreement of November 2023; true if it contains a commitment to amend the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act to restore the customary marine title test, false if no such commitment appears.

veracity.statement: My colleague the Hon Shane Jones has stated that recent court decisions have made the test for customary marine title too easy, and that rights creep—rights creep—could enable iwi to obstruct critical development projects such as ports.
veracity.explanation: Relays claims attributed to Shane Jones about court decisions lowering the test and 'rights creep' obstructing development projects such as ports.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements, speeches or media reports of Shane Jones on customary marine title; true if he made statements in substance that the test has become too easy and that rights creep could obstruct projects such as ports, false if no such statements exist.

civility.statement: Anyone who thinks there can be a cohesion, or a lasting contentment, in our nation, for any of us, without upholding and making good on the dignity and the intent of that founding agreement— Te Tiriti o Waitangi—is a fool, frankly.
civility.explanation: Not criticism of a policy — it labels every person holding the opposing view a fool. No individual is named, but the target is people rather than the argument, which is a real civility failure short of a direct personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The Minister resurrects the darkest tradition of Crown betrayal, evokes the tradition of colonial theft, and should we be surprised, because that particular Minister believes colonisation was a good thing for iwi Māori, so surely doing more colonisations would be good in his estimations?
civility.explanation: Turns from the bill to the Minister personally, sarcastically imputing to him a desire for 'more colonisations'. A clear personal attack on motive rather than on the measure.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Far worse than the Treaty principles bill, only because it will pass; it will affect confiscation.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill will be enacted, unlike the Treaty Principles Bill. Not a promise about the speaker's own action — he opposes the bill.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill; true if it passes third reading and receives Royal assent, false if it is defeated, withdrawn or lapses.

divination.statement: This wretched bill will be the first bill on the repeal list of things that we will do to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi when there is a change of Government in one year’s time.
divination.explanation: Embedded in the commitment is a forecast that the Government will change roughly a year from the statement — i.e. at the next general election.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The result of the next New Zealand general election and the government formed after it; true if a government is formed that excludes the incumbent National–ACT–NZ First parties, false if the incumbent coalition parties return to government.

rigor.statement: It has a constitutionally treasonous character because it betrays the intent of the mutual agreement which formerly brought the nation of New Zealand into existence.
rigor.explanation: Premise (the bill betrays the intent of Te Tiriti) is offered as support for the conclusion (the bill is constitutionally treasonous). The inference equivocates on 'treason', which has a definite legal meaning that departing from a treaty's intent does not meet; nothing is offered to bridge the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Minister resurrects the darkest tradition of Crown betrayal, evokes the tradition of colonial theft, and should we be surprised, because that particular Minister believes colonisation was a good thing for iwi Māori, so surely doing more colonisations would be good in his estimations?
rigor.explanation: The conclusion about the bill rests on an attributed belief of the Minister rather than on anything in the bill — an ad hominem, delivered as a sarcastic reductio that the speaker does not connect to the measure's actual effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: New Zealand First believes the court’s interpretation fails to give effect to the intended requirement that applicants for customary marine title must prove they have exclusively used and occupied the area from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the statutory wording she has just read into the record: if s 58(1)(b) requires exclusive use since 1840 without substantial interruption, and the court's reading relaxes that, the reading does not give effect to it. A real gap remains — she does not address the interpretive reasons the court gave — but the inference is sound on its own premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is the Parliament of New Zealand that sets the laws of this land, and this inserts a statutory declaration that overturns the court’s reasoning and ensures the intent of this House is clear.
rigor.explanation: Leans on an appeal to parliamentary sovereignty: that Parliament sets the law establishes it may override the courts, but nothing is offered to show that this reading is the House's original intent rather than a new one. The premise supports the power, not the claim being made with it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They don’t really believe in property rights. They believe in the right to accumulation of capital of those who would exploit nature.
focus.explanation: Names no policy, clause, figure or outcome — it is a characterisation of what the governing parties are 'really like' and what they secretly believe. Party framing with no policy content in the statement itself.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what we are simply doing is making sure it’s very clear what the customary title test should be.
specificity.explanation: Describes the bill's purpose without naming the clause, the wording being inserted, or what the restored test actually requires — a direction with almost no checkable content, despite the test itself being precisely stateable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Justice Committee—and I acknowledge the chair, the Hon James Meager—received and considered submissions from 6,692 interested groups and individuals and heard oral evidence from 69 submitters.
specificity.explanation: Exact submission and submitter counts attached to a named committee — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is cynical, and under your Government, you continue to kick Māori down.
civility.explanation: Directly addresses the Minister as "you" and imputes deliberate bad faith and a sustained intent to harm Māori. This lands on the person's motives rather than on the bill's mechanism, which is a genuine civility failure under the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It is cynical, it is mean-spirited, and it continues the punch-down of our indigenous people in this country.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith and mean-spiritedness to the Government's leadership. Aimed collectively rather than at a named individual, so short of a direct insult, but it characterises motive rather than argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: There is no reason for it, no reason other than keeping their crony mates happy so that they can get the consent they want to exploit coastal areas, whether it be for sandmining, for fishing, for wind farming—for whatever it might be.
civility.explanation: Imputes corrupt motive — legislating to favour "crony mates". Directed at the Government collectively rather than a named member, so short of a personal insult, but it attributes bad faith rather than engaging the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s a terrible bill, and I can’t believe Jenny Marcroft, who usually is so sensible on things affecting Māori, spoke in support of it, either.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal — it names a member and frames her position as a lapse from her usual judgement. The compliment softens it and it stops short of attacking her character or competence, but it edges onto the person rather than staying on the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: When we’re talking about cynical—someone from the other side of the House spoke about cynicism—it’s cynicism to work people up into a frenzy when they’re not saying what the actual truth is.
civility.explanation: Imputes deliberate dishonesty and inflammation to opposing members — not merely that they are wrong, but that they know they are and are stirring people up anyway. Aimed at an unnamed member rather than a named one, but it is an accusation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is cynical, it is mean-spirited, and it continues the punch-down of our indigenous people in this country.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is like — cynical, mean-spirited, punching down. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named at this point, so it is party characterisation rather than scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Every opportunity that I have in this House, I will remind Government members of the bad choices that they have made for our country and for Māori alike: repealing Te Aka Whai Ora, taking us backwards on Māori wards, removing Te Tiriti from legislation.
focus.explanation: Names three specific legislative actions rather than making a general claim about the other party. This is textbook opposition scrutiny of a named record and must score at the top.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As has been traversed by the Minister in charge and some of my colleagues already, the bill is amending the test for recognising customary marine titles, noting the decision of the Court of Appeal last year.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the Bill does — the test being amended and the court decision prompting it. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Every opportunity that I have in this House, I will remind Government members of the bad choices that they have made for our country and for Māori alike: repealing Te Aka Whai Ora, taking us backwards on Māori wards, removing Te Tiriti from legislation.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three specific things this Government has done: repealed Te Aka Whai Ora, changed the law on Māori wards, and removed Treaty references from legislation. "Taking us backwards" is evaluative, but each underlying legislative action is a matter of record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative record for the 54th Parliament: true if (a) the Māori Health Authority Te Aka Whai Ora was disestablished by statute, (b) legislation was passed altering the Māori wards regime in a way that reversed the previous settings, and (c) Treaty of Waitangi clauses were removed from existing statutes; false if any of these did not occur.

veracity.statement: And this Minister in the House today, he has not consulted adequately with Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a matter of process record that the responsible Minister did not adequately consult Māori before advancing this Bill. Operationalised via the Tribunal's findings and the Bill's own process documents.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry report into the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill, plus the Bill's regulatory impact statement and departmental disclosure statement: true if the Tribunal or those documents record that consultation with Māori was not undertaken or was found inadequate before the Bill was introduced; false if they record an adequate consultation process.

veracity.statement: The Minister, Paul Goldsmith, in one of his speeches said this legislation creates and confers property rights, and that’s not true.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that the Minister used the words "creates and confers" about property rights, and that this characterisation is legally wrong because the regime recognises pre-existing customary rights rather than creating new ones.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the Minister's speeches on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill: true if Paul Goldsmith characterised the legislation as creating or conferring property rights; false if he did not. The second limb turns on whether customary marine title under the 2011 Act is declaratory of pre-existing rights or constitutive of new ones, per the Act's scheme and the Supreme Court's treatment of it.

veracity.statement: Along comes a guy named John Key with the National Party—and the Māori Party; we worked together in 2011 to pass the Marine and Coastal Area Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act was passed in 2011 by National and the Māori Party working together under John Key's leadership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011: true if the Act passed in 2011 under a National-led government headed by John Key with Māori Party support, false if the date, the government of the day, or the Māori Party's support differs from that.

specificity.statement: They want unity, they want kotahitanga, they want access, they want fairness, and they want equality.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues offered as a description of what New Zealanders want. No figure, mechanism, timeframe or named policy — nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As has been traversed by the Minister in charge and some of my colleagues already, the bill is amending the test for recognising customary marine titles, noting the decision of the Court of Appeal last year.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the mechanism (amending the recognition test) and the trigger (a Court of Appeal decision), but gives no detail of what the test currently is, what it becomes, or which decision is meant.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Minister protests, but he doth protest too much, because he knows as much as anyone that the bill as it stood, the original piece of legislation, was carefully crafted, and it makes it very clear that, to establish customary title, the burden is high—that, in fact, you have to show that, across generations since 1840, you have exercised those rights, because customary rights can be lost through a failure to use them.
specificity.explanation: Sets out the actual statutory test with a date anchor (exercise of rights across generations since 1840) and the mechanism by which such rights lapse. Concrete enough that someone could check it against the Act.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yet, the ACT Party, for all of its pro-property rhetoric, doesn’t believe in protecting the property rights for Māori that are enshrined in customary title.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument with its premises laid out immediately beforehand: ACT promotes a bill protecting property rights from uncompensated impairment; customary marine title is a property right; ACT supports impairing it. Given those premises the inconsistency follows. The gap is that it slides from "supports this bill" to "doesn't believe in", which asserts a general belief from one instance.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There is no reason for it, no reason other than keeping their crony mates happy so that they can get the consent they want to exploit coastal areas, whether it be for sandmining, for fishing, for wind farming—for whatever it might be.
rigor.explanation: Asserts that no reason exists other than cronyism, and offers nothing to exclude the reasons the Government has actually advanced. The motive is inferred from the outcome — the conclusion is simply declared, not derived.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I do know, because, yes, I wasn’t here back then, but I actually do my research because I love this country.
rigor.explanation: Offers affection for the country as the ground for the reliability of her research, and that research as the ground for her knowledge. Loving a country is no evidence of having established a historical fact — a bare appeal to sentiment standing in for the evidence itself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: What’s happened since then is a court judgment has decided to go way above and beyond what the intention of this House was when we were restoring things in 2011; they went above and beyond what the intention was.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the court exceeded Parliament's intention — is asserted and then simply restated in the second clause. Nothing is offered about what the 2011 intention was or what the judgment held, so the claim rests on repetition rather than on any premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: All told, Government contracts are worth more than $50 billion a year.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the annual value of New Zealand government procurement exceeds $50 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE / New Zealand Government Procurement published estimates of total annual government spend on goods and services; true if the figure is at or above $50 billion a year, false if materially below.

veracity.statement: As a result, the number of rules is being reduced from 71 to 47—far, far simpler.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the procurement rules fall from 71 to 47 under the new settings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Count the numbered rules in the outgoing Government Procurement Rules (4th edition) against the new rules taking effect 1 December 2025; true if 71 becomes 47, false if either count differs materially.

veracity.statement: Business New Zealand has been campaigning for this sensible change for 10 years, and I'm glad our Government got it done.
veracity.explanation: Asserts BusinessNZ has publicly advocated an economic-benefit weighting in procurement for a decade.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: BusinessNZ submissions and public statements on government procurement from roughly 2015 onward; true if advocacy for this change is documented across that period, false if its advocacy is materially more recent.

veracity.statement: Is he concerned by Crown Law’s own assessment that altering the powers of the tribunal could breach the principle of separation powers and the principle of responsible Government?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Crown Law has produced an assessment warning that altering the Waitangi Tribunal's powers could breach separation of powers and responsible government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Crown Law advice on the Waitangi Tribunal review, as released under the Official Information Act or cited in the review's papers; true if such advice records that warning, false if no Crown Law assessment says this.

veracity.statement: Is an annual growth rate of negative 1.1 percent, three percentage points lower than forecast before the election, the result of her economic plan; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts an annual growth rate of -1.1 percent, three percentage points below the pre-election forecast.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ annual GDP growth for the most recent published year against the Treasury Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2023 forecast for the same year; true if the outturn is about -1.1% and roughly three points below forecast, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: The IMF’s latest world economic outlook shows that in 2023, out of all the world’s advanced economies, New Zealand had the largest positive output gap.
veracity.explanation: Attributes to the IMF WEO a specific ranking: New Zealand top of all advanced economies on 2023 output gap.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: IMF World Economic Outlook database, output gap (percent of potential GDP) for 2023 across the advanced-economy group; true if New Zealand's is the largest positive value, false if any advanced economy ranks above it.

veracity.statement: Inflation was far above the target band, and the Reserve Bank had to the raise the official cash rate (OCR) to 5.5 percent—the highest rate since 2008.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable assertions: the OCR peaked at 5.5 percent, and that was the highest level since 2008.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RBNZ official cash rate history; true if the OCR reached 5.5% and no higher rate was set between 2008 and that date, false if either fails.

veracity.statement: I’m pleased to report to the House that today’s Financial Statements of Government shows that debt, for the first time in five years, has not increased as a proportion of GDP.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the latest Financial Statements show net debt to GDP flat or falling for the first time in five years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2025, net core Crown debt as a percentage of GDP compared with the prior four years; true if this is the first year in five without an increase, false if any of the preceding four years also showed no increase or if the ratio rose.

veracity.statement: It’s approximately $8 billion that we are paying to service the interest on our debt.
veracity.explanation: Asserts annual core Crown finance costs of about $8 billion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand, core Crown finance costs for the year stated; true if approximately $8 billion, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Does she agree with Christopher Luxon that, “Nicola Willis and myself understand economics. We understand Budgets. We understand numbers.”; if so, is that why, under, even her own measure of OBEGALx, the deficit is higher now than it was it in 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that on the OBEGALx measure the deficit is larger now than in each of the four preceding years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: OBEGALx figures in the Financial Statements of the Government / Treasury fiscal time series for the 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025 years; true if the latest deficit exceeds all four, false if it is smaller than any of them.

veracity.statement: If she understands numbers, then does she understand that the Government reduction in capital asset spending of $2.9 billion less has played a role in the decline of the construction sector and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $2.9 billion reduction in Crown capital asset spending and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury capital allowance / capital spending figures across the relevant Budgets for the $2.9 billion, and Stats NZ HLFS construction industry employment for the change in jobs; true if both figures are approximately right, false if either is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: I’m proud that, unlike the last Government, we’re actually funding Dunedin Hospital, that we’re rebuilding Nelson Hospital, that we’re building more classrooms every year than they ever managed, and that we built more social homes in the past 23 months than they did in three years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two comparative delivery records against the previous Government: more classrooms built per year, and more social homes in 23 months than Labour built in three years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education classroom delivery figures per year and HUD/Kāinga Ora social housing net additions by period; true if this Government's per-year classroom count exceeds the previous Government's and its 23-month social housing delivery exceeds any comparable three-year Labour figure, false otherwise. Note the social-homes comparison turns on whether 'built' means gross new builds or net additions.

specificity.statement: When considering tender applications, Government agencies will now be required to give a weighting of at least 10 percent to benefits to New Zealand.
specificity.explanation: A named mechanism with a numeric threshold and an identified actor — the requirement can be checked against the published rules.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a result, the number of rules is being reduced from 71 to 47—far, far simpler.
specificity.explanation: Precise before-and-after counts for the rule set; directly checkable against the published procurement rules.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Can he confirm that the proposed name change would erode the independence of the tribunal, creating a system where Ministers decide what claims can be heard?
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (ministerial control over which claims are heard) but supplies no clause, document or figure underpinning it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government continues to be responsible in this space and is progressing the review announced, in a very timely manner.
specificity.explanation: Offered as substantive reassurance but carries no timeframe, milestone, scope or document — 'responsible' and 'timely manner' commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is an annual growth rate of negative 1.1 percent, three percentage points lower than forecast before the election, the result of her economic plan; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures — the growth rate and the gap against the pre-election forecast — both checkable against published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m pleased to report to the House that today’s Financial Statements of Government shows that debt, for the first time in five years, has not increased as a proportion of GDP.
specificity.explanation: Names the source document, the measure and the comparison window.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let me count the ways: tax relief for more than a million working New Zealanders; Investment Boost to encourage investment in our businesses so that they can grow; delivering fast-track infrastructure projects; investing in structured literacy in our schools; overhauling the Overseas Investment Act to welcome capital into this country.
specificity.explanation: Five named policies and one quantified reach, but no amounts, dates or delivery figures attached to any of them.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s approximately $8 billion that we are paying to service the interest on our debt.
specificity.explanation: A single figure answering the question asked, directly checkable in the Crown accounts.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she agree with Christopher Luxon that, “Nicola Willis and myself understand economics. We understand Budgets. We understand numbers.”; if so, is that why, under, even her own measure of OBEGALx, the deficit is higher now than it was it in 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024?
specificity.explanation: Names the specific fiscal indicator and four comparison years.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If she understands numbers, then does she understand that the Government reduction in capital asset spending of $2.9 billion less has played a role in the decline of the construction sector and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs?
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure for the spending reduction and a jobs figure for the claimed effect, both checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Well, in each of our Budgets, we have invested more funding in public infrastructure, and I can’t wait till we sign those contracts for the Northern Gateway road and for the many roads of national significance around the country.
specificity.explanation: Names one project and a programme, but attaches no amounts, no dates and no contract timing to either.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m proud that, unlike the last Government, we’re actually funding Dunedin Hospital, that we’re rebuilding Nelson Hospital, that we’re building more classrooms every year than they ever managed, and that we built more social homes in the past 23 months than they did in three years.
specificity.explanation: Names two hospital projects and gives a defined comparison window for the housing claim, but supplies no actual counts or dollar figures.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: When considering tender applications, Government agencies will now be required to give a weighting of at least 10 percent to benefits to New Zealand.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the content of the procurement rule change; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can he confirm that the proposed name change would erode the independence of the tribunal, creating a system where Ministers decide what claims can be heard?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a named institutional change and its stated constitutional consequence; no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is an annual growth rate of negative 1.1 percent, three percentage points lower than forecast before the election, the result of her economic plan; if not, why not?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny of the Government's economic record against a named forecast and a named measure — the constitutional job of an opposition finance spokesperson.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Let me count the ways: tax relief for more than a million working New Zealanders; Investment Boost to encourage investment in our businesses so that they can grow; delivering fast-track infrastructure projects; investing in structured literacy in our schools; overhauling the Overseas Investment Act to welcome capital into this country.
focus.explanation: Answers with named policy measures rather than party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How much of that deficit is interest repayments on debt that was built up by the previous Government?
focus.explanation: Asks for a specific fiscal quantum (debt-servicing share of the deficit), though the attribution clause carries party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is her idea of an economic plan to deliver more unemployment, a shrinking economy, an inflation that is on the rise, and to blame everyone else except Nicola Willis?
focus.explanation: Names real economic outcomes (unemployment, growth, inflation) but the weight of the question is the personal blame-shifting framing rather than a policy mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: All I’ve heard from that member is: lets borrow more, lets spend more, lets drive up the debt and inflation; and that is no prescription.
focus.explanation: Refers to fiscal settings in general terms but names no policy, figure or measure — it characterises the other side rather than engaging a proposal.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This provision does not breach international trade agreements, because overseas companies have the same opportunity to demonstrate wider value to New Zealand, and similar provisions exist in many of our trading partners’ procurement rules.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (no breach) supported by two stated reasons — non-discriminatory application, and precedent among trading partners — which, if accepted, do bear on the non-discrimination obligations at issue. Small gap in that precedent elsewhere does not itself establish legality.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That’s why the economy went into a long, painful downturn.
rigor.explanation: The causal chain offered — overheated economy, inflation above band, sharp tightening, downturn — is a standard and coherent inference from the premises she has just laid out, though it treats a single cause as sufficient.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The member might think that spending more, taxing more, and borrowing more is an alternative plan, but I disagree with it and so do most New Zealanders.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to popularity: the rebuttal rests on asserted majority agreement rather than on any argument against the alternative, and it is layered on a characterisation of the opponent's position she has supplied herself.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would also point out that those who are suddenly concerned about deficits might want to ask why they said that every time we made a spending reduction, whether it was pay equity, reducing the number of bureaucrats, reversing stupid programmes, that we shouldn’t be cutting spending—get consistent.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the charge of inconsistency is offered in place of any answer on the deficit itself, and opposing particular cuts is not logically inconsistent with concern about deficits.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If she understands numbers, then does she understand that the Government reduction in capital asset spending of $2.9 billion less has played a role in the decline of the construction sector and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs?
rigor.explanation: Offers a plausible mechanism (lower public capital spend feeding through to construction activity and employment) and claims only that it 'played a role' rather than caused the whole fall — a modest conclusion that the premises can carry.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, it is not, but I think that those who commit arson and then blame the firefighter should not repeat the same mistake.
rigor.explanation: False analogy standing in for an argument: the arson image asserts sole causation and bad faith without offering anything to connect the previous Government's decisions to the outcomes at issue.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: All I’ve heard from that member is: lets borrow more, lets spend more, lets drive up the debt and inflation; and that is no prescription.
rigor.explanation: Strawman: the opponent's position is restated in a form nobody advanced ('drive up the debt and inflation') and then dismissed, with no argument against the actual proposals.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would also point out that those who are suddenly concerned about deficits might want to ask why they said that every time we made a spending reduction, whether it was pay equity, reducing the number of bureaucrats, reversing stupid programmes, that we shouldn’t be cutting spending—get consistent.
civility.explanation: 'Suddenly concerned' imputes insincerity rather than engaging the fiscal point, and the closing instruction sneers, but it stops short of a personal insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she agree with Christopher Luxon that, “Nicola Willis and myself understand economics. We understand Budgets. We understand numbers.”; if so, is that why, under, even her own measure of OBEGALx, the deficit is higher now than it was it in 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024?
civility.explanation: Uses a quoted boast to set up a competence jibe at the Minister personally, though the substantive point is about a fiscal measure.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If she understands numbers, then does she understand that the Government reduction in capital asset spending of $2.9 billion less has played a role in the decline of the construction sector and a loss of 20,000 construction sector jobs?
civility.explanation: The 'if she understands numbers' opener is condescending toward the Minister personally, though the rest is on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is her idea of an economic plan to deliver more unemployment, a shrinking economy, an inflation that is on the rise, and to blame everyone else except Nicola Willis?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith — that the Minister's plan is to deflect blame — and mocks rather than engaging the substance of the fiscal argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, it is not, but I think that those who commit arson and then blame the firefighter should not repeat the same mistake.
civility.explanation: Casts opponents as arsonists blaming the rescuer — imputed bad faith and mockery aimed at the people rather than the policy, though it names no individual.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We announced a $5 million investment in a new centre court roof for Auckland's Manuka Doctor Arena. This is the first infrastructure project from our $70 million major events and tourism package.
specificity.explanation: Names the amount ($5m), the named facility, and locates it within a named $70m package — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In 2024, just this one event alone brought significant economic benefit to Auckland, resulting in 16,600 visitor nights to the region and injecting $3.4 million into the economy.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures (16,600 visitor nights, $3.4 million) tied to a named event and year.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: No. what our economic plan is directly responsible for is more than half a billion dollars having been committed to rebuilding Nelson Hospital and the fast tracking of a major housing development that on her watch would have been tied up in red tape for years.
specificity.explanation: Names a figure (over $500m) and a named project (Nelson Hospital rebuild), though the housing development is left unnamed and the fast-track timing unstated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why then are there 36,000 people who are not in work and liquidations are up 26 percent?
specificity.explanation: Two concrete, checkable figures put to the Minister — a jobs number and a percentage change in liquidations.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can she justify her plan when it has led to rising power and rent costs and a failing construction industry that has forced Auckland-based business Pipe Vision to go under and to cut 100 jobs?
specificity.explanation: Names a specific company, a specific job figure, and three named cost pressures — concrete enough to be checked.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Has Ikaroa-Rāwhiti been left out of her plan when the Hawke's Bay lost 837 jobs in just one quarter and Eastern Institute of Technology, Tairāwhiti lost 40 academic and support roles, who were there to help young people into work?
specificity.explanation: Precise job figures (837, 40), a named region, a named institution and a stated timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill introduces 19 new, expanded marine protection areas, and is the largest increase in marine protection in Aotearoa New Zealand in over a decade.
specificity.explanation: A count of protected areas and a comparative claim about scale, both checkable against the bill as passed.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: A 2023 NZ Institute of Economic Research report stated that the economic value of the Hauraki Gulf is $100 billion and produces over $5 billion of value each and every year, to this country.
specificity.explanation: Names the source, the year and two precise figures — someone could go and read the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What is his message to the 32,000 Kiwis who signed the World Wide Fund for Nature's petition urging his Government to remove the carve-out that allows commercial fishing in the Gulf's high protection areas due to the risk that it sets a dangerous precedent where industry lobbyists could weaken future marine protections?
specificity.explanation: Names the petition, its sponsoring organisation, the number of signatories and the exact provision at issue.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This investment will help New Zealand stay match fit on the international stage. If we want to continue to attract world-class events to New Zealand, we need to have world-class facilities to go along with it.
rigor.explanation: An argument is advanced (facilities are needed to attract events) but it is close to circular — 'world-class events need world-class facilities' restates the conclusion rather than supporting it, and no evidence links the roof to event attraction.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Higher unemployment is a result of an economic downturn driven by high interest rates—high interest rates needed to bring down inflation, fuelled by reckless and undisciplined Government spending.
rigor.explanation: A coherent causal chain (spending → inflation → interest rates → downturn → unemployment) is offered, but each link is asserted rather than evidenced, and it treats one contributor to inflation as the whole cause. A reasonable point with a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if that member's version of economics is that every Government should take responsibility for every firm that ever fails, then I invite her to have a chat with Barbara Edmonds.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The question was about one named firm and a specific set of cost pressures; the reply substitutes the far weaker position that government is responsible for every business failure ever, and defeats that instead.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, no. How could they possibly be left out when they are represented by Dana Kirkpatrick and Katie Nimon, two of the extraordinary members of Parliament in the National Party caucus?
rigor.explanation: Non-sequitur. Having National MPs representing an area does not bear on whether regional job losses were addressed by the economic plan; the conclusion has no connection to the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Why does she continue to refer to the pre-election forecasts for unemployment but not the GDP forecasts, which are three percentage points higher than what she has delivered?
rigor.explanation: A valid consistency argument: it identifies selective use of a single forecast document — citing it where it flatters and ignoring it where it does not — and offers the GDP gap as the supporting evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can she justify her plan when it has led to rising power and rent costs and a failing construction industry that has forced Auckland-based business Pipe Vision to go under and to cut 100 jobs?
rigor.explanation: Treats a single firm's failure as caused by the Government's economic plan, with no mechanism connecting the two — a hasty causal leap from one anecdote to a systemic conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We know that healthy marine environments can boost tourism by looking at the Goat Island Te Hāwere-a-Maki Marine Reserve, celebrating its 50th anniversary this week, which accommodates and hosts over 350,000 visitors per annum.
rigor.explanation: Genuine evidence is offered and it points the right way, but the conclusion generalises from a single reserve, and visitor numbers alone do not establish that the protection caused the tourism.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But isn't it ironic that the very member who asked that question today also, along with her party, voted for it yesterday.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque. Whether the questioner voted for the bill has no bearing on whether the commercial fishing carve-out will damage the Gulf, which is what was asked; the inconsistency is used in place of an answer.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The ASB Classic alone attracts thousands of visitors each year, and next year will be the 70th year of this event.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2026 ASB Classic will be the tournament's 70th year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tennis Auckland / ASB Classic tournament history: true if the 2026 edition is the 70th running (or 70th year) of the tournament, false if the tournament's founding year makes 2026 a materially different anniversary.

veracity.statement: In 2024, just this one event alone brought significant economic benefit to Auckland, resulting in 16,600 visitor nights to the region and injecting $3.4 million into the economy.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the 2024 ASB Classic generated 16,600 visitor nights and $3.4m of economic activity in Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The economic impact assessment for the 2024 ASB Classic (Tennis Auckland / Auckland Unlimited / MBIE major events reporting): true if it reports approximately 16,600 visitor nights and ~$3.4m economic injection to Auckland, false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: It is also the case, though—I would point out to members—that the number of unemployed New Zealanders at this point still remains lower than Grant Robertson was forecasting it would be at this point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the actual number of unemployed New Zealanders in late 2025 is lower than the level forecast for that date in the 2023 pre-election fiscal update prepared under the previous Minister of Finance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update 2023 unemployment forecast for the September 2025 quarter, compared with the Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey count of unemployed for that quarter: true if the actual number is below the PREFU-forecast number, false if it is at or above it.

veracity.statement: Because as the Treasury has previously acknowledged extensively on the record, they vastly overestimated their growth assumptions in the pre-election fiscal update, which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time but was inaccurate none the less.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury has itself acknowledged, on the record and repeatedly, that it substantially overestimated growth in the 2023 pre-election fiscal update.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published forecast performance reviews and subsequent Budget/HYEFU documents: true if Treasury has publicly acknowledged that its PREFU 2023 GDP growth assumptions were materially too high, false if no such acknowledgement exists or Treasury's growth forecasts were broadly accurate.

veracity.statement: But I would also point out that the assertion that rents have gone up under our Government is not correct.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that rents have not risen since the current Government took office in late 2023 — a claim about the level of rents, not about the rate of increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ rental price index (and MBIE tenancy bond median rent data) from the December 2023 quarter to the September 2025 quarter: true if the index/median is flat or lower over that period, false if rents rose over it.

veracity.statement: No. what our economic plan is directly responsible for is more than half a billion dollars having been committed to rebuilding Nelson Hospital and the fast tracking of a major housing development that on her watch would have been tied up in red tape for years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that more than half a billion dollars has been committed to rebuilding Nelson Hospital.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Budget documents for the Nelson Hospital redevelopment: true if the Government's committed capital for the rebuild exceeds $500 million, false if the committed figure is below that.

veracity.statement: Why then are there 36,000 people who are not in work and liquidations are up 26 percent?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 36,000 more people are out of work and that company liquidations have risen 26 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey for the change in the number of unemployed since the December 2023 quarter, and Companies Office / Centrix liquidation statistics for the year to September 2025 against the prior year: true if the unemployment increase is about 36,000 and liquidations rose about 26%, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: Has Ikaroa-Rāwhiti been left out of her plan when the Hawke's Bay lost 837 jobs in just one quarter and Eastern Institute of Technology, Tairāwhiti lost 40 academic and support roles, who were there to help young people into work?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a one-quarter loss of 837 jobs in Hawke's Bay and 40 roles cut at EIT Tairāwhiti.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ regional filled-jobs / employment indicator data for Hawke's Bay for the most recent quarter, and EIT | Te Pūkenga restructure announcements: true if Hawke's Bay employment fell by about 837 in one quarter and EIT Tairāwhiti disestablished around 40 academic and support roles, false if either figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: This bill introduces 19 new, expanded marine protection areas, and is the largest increase in marine protection in Aotearoa New Zealand in over a decade.
veracity.explanation: Asserts 19 new or expanded marine protection areas and that this is the biggest such increase in over ten years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hauraki Gulf / Tīkapa Moana Marine Protection Bill as passed: true if it creates 19 new or expanded marine protected areas and no larger marine protection increase has been enacted in New Zealand since 2015, false if the count differs or a larger increase occurred within the decade.

veracity.statement: A 2023 NZ Institute of Economic Research report stated that the economic value of the Hauraki Gulf is $100 billion and produces over $5 billion of value each and every year, to this country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what a named 2023 NZIER report concluded about the economic value of the Hauraki Gulf.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2023 NZIER report on the Hauraki Gulf: true if it states an asset value of approximately $100 billion and annual value of over $5 billion, false if the report gives materially different figures or no such report exists.

civility.statement: Is it just me or have I answered this question half a dozen times already?
civility.explanation: Dismisses the questioner rather than the question — a sneering aside implying the member is wasting the House's time. Short of a direct insult but no longer civil.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because as the Treasury has previously acknowledged extensively on the record, they vastly overestimated their growth assumptions in the pre-election fiscal update, which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time but was inaccurate none the less.
civility.explanation: The substantive answer is on the forecasts, but 'which may have been convenient for the Minister at the time' insinuates that the then-Minister benefited from — and by implication was untroubled by — an inaccurate forecast. That is an imputation of bad faith about a named person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No. As my mother once said to me, if you can't say anything nice, which I can't right now, don't say anything at all.
civility.explanation: Declines to insult in return, but the aside 'which I can't right now' openly conveys that the speaker holds the member in low regard. Restrained contempt rather than a direct attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Has she considered asking for help with her numeracy, considering that she considers negative growth to be a sign of recovery?
civility.explanation: A direct attack on the Minister's personal competence — suggesting she cannot do arithmetic — rather than on her economic argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But isn't it ironic that the very member who asked that question today also, along with her party, voted for it yesterday.
civility.explanation: Pointed and personal in direction — it turns on the questioner's own conduct rather than her argument — but it cites a voting record rather than attacking her character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why did he allow eleventh-hour lobbying to influence changes that now enable commercial fishing in high protection areas, when reports show that it will further damage the health of the Gulf?
civility.explanation: Frames the Minister as having yielded to late lobbying — an imputation of improper motive rather than a criticism of the provision itself. Short of a direct insult but not civil.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, these are the terrible human consequences of a down-turning economy which results when it is mismanaged as poorly as it was by the last Government.
focus.explanation: Answers a question about specific job losses with a general verdict on the previous Government's management. No policy, measure or figure is named — the weight is party framing rather than policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, no. How could they possibly be left out when they are represented by Dana Kirkpatrick and Katie Nimon, two of the extraordinary members of Parliament in the National Party caucus?
focus.explanation: A question about 837 lost jobs is answered entirely by praising two of the speaker's own party's MPs. No policy, programme, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why did he allow eleventh-hour lobbying to influence changes that now enable commercial fishing in high protection areas, when reports show that it will further damage the health of the Gulf?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: a named provision (commercial fishing in high protection areas), the change made to it, and the claimed environmental consequence.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What is his message to the 32,000 Kiwis who signed the World Wide Fund for Nature's petition urging his Government to remove the carve-out that allows commercial fishing in the Gulf's high protection areas due to the risk that it sets a dangerous precedent where industry lobbyists could weaken future marine protections?
focus.explanation: Entirely about a named provision of the bill and its consequences — legitimate scrutiny with no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can I ask the Minister as to where are the customers for those limited commercial fishing operations—are they New Zealand customers or overseas customers?
focus.explanation: A direct question about who the contested fishing carve-out actually serves. Entirely on the substance of the measure, with no party content at all, in a moment where a partisan intervention was available.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Yes, jobseeker support (health condition or disability) is a temporary support for people who are limited in their ability to work for two years because of a health condition, injury, or disability.
specificity.explanation: Names the benefit, the eligibility basis (health condition, injury, disability) and a duration (two years). Concrete enough to check against MSD's rules, though it gives no rates or thresholds.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it fair to subject 18- and 19-year-olds who are receiving jobseeker support (health condition or disability) to the new parental assistance test when they're suffering from severe ill mental health, recovering from a car accident, or undergoing cancer treatment as reported by 1News?
specificity.explanation: Named policy, named age bracket and named affected conditions, sourced to a 1News report; no figures on how many people are affected.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In August 2025, there were 135 more businesses in accommodation and food services than the previous month and that is trending up.
specificity.explanation: A named sector, a named month and an exact figure — directly checkable against the official series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does she consider the more than 2,500 hospitality closures and almost 300 liquidations in the past 12 months evidence that her Government is driving economic growth for the hospitality industry?
specificity.explanation: Two exact figures over a stated period, tied to a named sector. A precise question is as specific as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That's why I was pleased to see reports from the District Court's civil jurisdiction showing active cases down 20 percent in the year to July 2025 and the average age of active cases dropping by a remarkable 36 percent over the same period.
specificity.explanation: Named court and jurisdiction, two named measures, two percentages and a stated period — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Budget 2025 contained funding of $18.3 million over four years to fund two additional High Court judges and associated staff, as well as expand the number of community magistrates by three and appointing the Chief Community Magistrate.
specificity.explanation: An amount, a period, and an itemised list of what it buys — someone could check every element against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When will he accept responsibility and take action to help Pasifika into employment or training, when, in the last year alone, 6,100 more Pasifika people are now unemployed and 1,900 more Pasifika young people are not in education, employment, or training?
specificity.explanation: Two exact population counts over a stated period for a named group; checkable against the HLFS.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it fair to subject 18- and 19-year-olds who are receiving jobseeker support (health condition or disability) to the new parental assistance test when they're suffering from severe ill mental health, recovering from a car accident, or undergoing cancer treatment as reported by 1News?
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the parental assistance test), the specific group affected (18- and 19-year-olds on jobseeker HCD) and concrete circumstances. Scrutiny of a named policy, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he regret repeatedly cutting funding to the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, including cutting $22 million out of the Tupu Aotearoa work-ready programme at a time when Pacifica unemployment is 12.1 percent, more than double the national average?
focus.explanation: Names a specific programme, a specific funding cut and a specific labour-market outcome. Accountability for a named decision, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What I regret is the actions the previous Government took that put us in this position.
focus.explanation: Deflects a question about a specific funding cut into a blanket reference to the previous Government's 'actions'. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — it is entirely about the other team.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: That's exactly why there are programmes to support them. We don't think that it is acceptable in a country like ours to leave a whole generation of New Zealanders to rot on welfare.
rigor.explanation: The premise put to her — that some recipients cannot enter education because of their health condition — is answered with an unnamed 'programmes' assertion and then a false dichotomy between training and being left 'to rot on welfare'. The conclusion does not follow from anything offered; the work is done by an appeal to emotion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Recent closures in the hospitality sector are primarily driven by economic pressures, including high inflation and high interest rates, which were the legacy of the previous Government.
rigor.explanation: A two-step causal claim (closures caused by inflation and rates; those caused by the predecessor) asserted with no supporting evidence or mechanism. Not fallacious on its face — the chain is coherent — but the conclusion outruns what is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I disagree. If you look at another quote from Hospitality New Zealand, you can see that they are incredibly supportive of the Government’s major tourism and events boost and they know the enormous difference that that will make.
rigor.explanation: Answers a survey of 77 percent of business owners with a single supportive quote from an industry body — an appeal to authority plus a cherry-picked counter-example. Nothing offered engages the survey finding, so the conclusion ('I disagree') does not follow.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Our investments into tourism and hospitality will mean more international visitors, more full tables in our restaurants, more jobs being created across the country, and a stronger economy overall.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Government's tourism and hospitality investment will produce higher visitor numbers and higher employment in the sector. This is a forecast of outcomes in the wider economy, not a promise of an action the Government will take.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international visitor arrivals and Stats NZ filled jobs / HLFS employment in accommodation and food services for the year to December 2026 against the year to December 2025; true if both are materially higher, false if either is flat or lower.

divination.statement: This extra capacity will help relieve pressure across the justice system and improve timeliness, leading to a reduction in backlogs and the time that people do spend on remand.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the new judicial and magistrate capacity will reduce court backlogs and shorten remand times. The prediction is about system outcomes, not about the appointments themselves.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court timeliness statistics (active case volumes and average case age) and Department of Corrections remand population and average remand duration, for the year to June 2027 vs the year to June 2025; true if backlogs and average remand time both fall, false if either rises.

veracity.statement: In August 2025, there were 135 more businesses in accommodation and food services than the previous month and that is trending up.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a month-on-month net increase of 135 in the count of accommodation and food services businesses in August 2025, and that the series is rising.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly business counts (or MBIE's equivalent series) for accommodation and food services, July 2025 vs August 2025; true if the net change is +135 or close to it and recent months trend upward, false if the count fell or the increase is materially different.

veracity.statement: Does she consider the more than 2,500 hospitality closures and almost 300 liquidations in the past 12 months evidence that her Government is driving economic growth for the hospitality industry?
veracity.explanation: Asserts more than 2,500 hospitality business closures and close to 300 liquidations in the 12 months to October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Restaurant Association of NZ closure tallies and Companies Office / NZ Insolvency and Trustee Service liquidation records for hospitality (ANZSIC accommodation and food services) for the 12 months to October 2025; true if closures exceed 2,500 and liquidations are near 300, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: How can hospitality in Auckland’s CBD thrive when the Heart of the City survey showed that 77 percent of business owners say that the Government does not listen to their needs?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a Heart of the City survey found 77 percent of surveyed business owners say the Government does not listen to their needs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published Heart of the City member survey results; true if a question on Government responsiveness returned ~77 percent negative, false if no such figure appears or the number is materially different.

veracity.statement: Hospitality job advertisements are up 3.8 percent in July compared to last July.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 3.8 percent year-on-year rise in hospitality job advertisements for July 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MBIE Jobs Online (or Seek NZ) job advertisement index for accommodation and food services, July 2025 vs July 2024; true if the change is +3.8 percent or close, false if the series shows a fall or a materially different figure.

veracity.statement: That's why I was pleased to see reports from the District Court's civil jurisdiction showing active cases down 20 percent in the year to July 2025 and the average age of active cases dropping by a remarkable 36 percent over the same period.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two District Court civil jurisdiction statistics for the year to July 2025: active cases down 20 percent, and average age of active cases down 36 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice court statistics for the District Court civil jurisdiction, year to July 2025 vs year to July 2024; true if active case volume fell ~20 percent and mean case age fell ~36 percent, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: The Disputes Tribunal has had an outstanding year, completing more than 900 extra cases in the year to July 2025 compared to the year before.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the Disputes Tribunal completed over 900 more cases in the year to July 2025 than in the preceding year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice Disputes Tribunal disposal figures, year to July 2025 vs year to July 2024; true if the difference exceeds 900 completed cases, false if smaller or negative.

veracity.statement: Budget 2025 contained funding of $18.3 million over four years to fund two additional High Court judges and associated staff, as well as expand the number of community magistrates by three and appointing the Chief Community Magistrate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts Budget 2025 allocated $18.3 million over four years for two extra High Court judges plus staff, three extra community magistrates and a Chief Community Magistrate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 Vote Courts / Vote Justice appropriations and the accompanying Budget summary; true if the $18.3m over four years and the stated judicial and magistrate numbers appear, false if the figure or the items differ materially.

veracity.statement: Does he regret repeatedly cutting funding to the Ministry for Pacific Peoples, including cutting $22 million out of the Tupu Aotearoa work-ready programme at a time when Pacifica unemployment is 12.1 percent, more than double the national average?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a $22 million cut to the Tupu Aotearoa programme and a current Pasifika unemployment rate of 12.1 percent, more than double the national rate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024/2025 Vote Pacific Peoples appropriations for Tupu Aotearoa, and Stats NZ HLFS Pacific peoples unemployment rate for the most recent quarter before October 2025 against the all-groups rate; true if the appropriation fell by ~$22m and the Pacific rate is ~12.1 percent and more than twice the national rate, false if either is materially different.

veracity.statement: When will he accept responsibility and take action to help Pasifika into employment or training, when, in the last year alone, 6,100 more Pasifika people are now unemployed and 1,900 more Pasifika young people are not in education, employment, or training?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over the past year Pasifika unemployment rose by 6,100 people and the number of Pasifika youth not in education, employment or training rose by 1,900.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ HLFS Pacific peoples unemployment level and youth NEET level, most recent quarter before October 2025 vs the same quarter a year earlier; true if the increases are ~6,100 and ~1,900, false if materially different.

civility.statement: That member should have listened to the answer I gave to my first question, which was to say exactly that economic challenges from high inflation and high interest rates, which have led to an economic recession, have made it difficult for businesses to operate.
civility.explanation: Opens with a rebuke about the member's attentiveness before turning to substance. Condescending toward the person rather than the argument, though mild and short of an insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Thank you for that patsy question from the member across.
civility.explanation: Dismisses an Opposition member's question by mocking it rather than engaging it, imputing that the member is not asking seriously. Sneering at the person short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would highlight Alo Vaka, which, amongst other things, developed 14 micro-credentialing courses in the last financial year and more than 6,000 micro-credentials delivered to Pasifika, particularly Pasifika youth.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific programme (Alo Vaka), a count of courses (14), a delivery figure (6,000+) and a timeframe (last financial year). Someone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why this Government set a target of 80 percent of people being seen in primary mental health services within one week. We are meeting that target, with 83.8 percent being seen within one week.
specificity.explanation: A named target (80 percent within one week) and a precise performance figure (83.8 percent) against it — fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker
