specificity.statement: We’re also increasing the front-line mental health workforce, which has grown by 10 percent since coming into office, with the child and adolescent workforce growing by 19 percent and peer support lived experience by almost 100 percent.
specificity.explanation: Three separate growth figures against a stated baseline (since taking office), though no headcounts are given.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When we came in, there were 185,000 New Zealanders suffering violent offences; we've reduced that down to 156,000 in the latest stats.
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures against a defined baseline (on taking office versus the latest statistics); directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I would highlight Alo Vaka, which, amongst other things, developed 14 micro-credentialing courses in the last financial year and more than 6,000 micro-credentials delivered to Pasifika, particularly Pasifika youth.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Alo Vaka programme developed 14 micro-credentialing courses in the last financial year and delivered more than 6,000 micro-credentials to Pasifika people.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry for Pacific Peoples annual report / Alo Vaka programme reporting for the 2024/25 financial year; true if it records 14 micro-credentialing courses developed and more than 6,000 micro-credentials delivered, false if the figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: That’s why this Government set a target of 80 percent of people being seen in primary mental health services within one week. We are meeting that target, with 83.8 percent being seen within one week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the primary mental health and addiction access target is 80 percent seen within one week and that the latest (quarter four) national figure is 83.8 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand published quarter four mental health target data for the faster access to primary mental health and addiction target; true if the national figure is 83.8% against an 80% target, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: The Southern district went from being one of the worst-performing districts, at 66.4 percent, to one of the best, at 91 percent of Southern residents accessing services within one week.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a rise in the Southern district's primary mental health access rate from 66.4 percent to 91 percent seen within one week, and that this moved it from among the worst districts to among the best.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand quarterly mental health target data for the Southern district across quarter one and quarter four of the year referenced; true if the rate rose from 66.4% to 91% and the district's rank moved from bottom to top of the 20 districts, false if the figures or the ranking do not match.

veracity.statement: We’re also increasing the front-line mental health workforce, which has grown by 10 percent since coming into office, with the child and adolescent workforce growing by 19 percent and peer support lived experience by almost 100 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts front-line mental health workforce growth of 10 percent since November 2023, with child and adolescent workforce up 19 percent and peer support/lived experience up close to 100 percent.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand mental health and addiction workforce data comparing the November 2023 baseline with the latest published figures; true if the three growth rates are approximately 10%, 19% and ~100% respectively, false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: When we came in, there were 185,000 New Zealanders suffering violent offences; we've reduced that down to 156,000 in the latest stats.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the number of New Zealanders experiencing violent offences fell from 185,000 at the change of government to 156,000 in the most recent statistics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Crime and Victims Survey estimates of the number of adults who experienced violent interpersonal offences, comparing the cycle current at late 2023 with the most recently published cycle; true if the figures are approximately 185,000 and 156,000, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: I certainly can confirm that Corrections and the broader justice sector are very focused primarily on reducing the number of victims of crime, regardless of their ethnicity; unlike the previous Government, which had a focus on reducing the number of people in prison irrespective of what was going on in the community.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the previous Government's justice policy was oriented toward reducing the prison population, without regard to community conditions.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record of the previous Labour Government's stated justice objectives, in particular its target to reduce the prison population by 30 percent; true if such a prison-population reduction target was adopted government policy, false if no such target existed.

veracity.statement: Was Moana Jackson wrong when he said, “the majority of those behind bars are Māori, and the system itself reflects a punishing and very real racism.”, or does he accept that the overrepresentation of Māori in prisons is a reflection of structural racism?
veracity.explanation: Relays Moana Jackson's factual claim that Māori make up a majority of the prison population (the second half of the quoted sentence, about racism, is an interpretation rather than a checkable fact).
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: Department of Corrections prison population statistics by ethnicity; true if Māori are recorded as more than 50 percent of the prison population, false if 50 percent or less.

focus.statement: That’s why this Government set a target of 80 percent of people being seen in primary mental health services within one week. We are meeting that target, with 83.8 percent being seen within one week.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the policy: the target, the service, and the measured result. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I certainly can confirm that Corrections and the broader justice sector are very focused primarily on reducing the number of victims of crime, regardless of their ethnicity; unlike the previous Government, which had a focus on reducing the number of people in prison irrespective of what was going on in the community.
focus.explanation: Names a real policy contrast (a victims-of-crime target versus a prison-population target), but the second half is weighted toward characterising the previous Government rather than the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, I don't think that would be helpful to Māori victims of crime, and that certainly appears to be the Greens’ policy.
focus.explanation: Adopts a caricature of another party's position rather than engaging any named measure; the content is about what the Greens supposedly are, not about a policy mechanism or outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Minister think that defunding the police and letting offenders go without prosecution has any chance of helping innocent Māori victims?
focus.explanation: Frames an opposing party's position as "defunding the police and letting offenders go" with no named policy, figure or measure — the question is about the other team rather than about any policy at issue.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Could the Minister tell us exactly how many Māori accused did Moana Jackson ever defend at court?
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or outcome is engaged at all — the entire content is about one person's credentials.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can the Minister also confirm that Māori are disproportionately represented among the victims of crime, and would it help to go soft on the perpetrators for reasons of political correctness?
focus.explanation: The first half raises a real policy fact, but the second half swaps policy content for a "political correctness" caricature of the opposing position rather than naming any measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What evidence does he have that a higher prison population makes Māori safer?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: it asks for the evidence base behind the Government's imprisonment settings. Legitimate scrutiny, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, if you're wanting to reduce the number of victims of crime, a very good place to start is with that very, very small section of New Zealand society that creates multiple victims over and over again. The primary focus is effective rehabilitation of people who have been involved in violent crime, but there are some people that need to be kept out of society for a while so that the rest of society can be kept safe.
rigor.explanation: An incapacitation argument that does follow from its premise (a small group of repeat offenders creates many victims, so removing them reduces victims), but the question asked for evidence and none is offered — the premise about a concentrated offender group is asserted, not shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In regards to structural racism, I would say that that’s a very easy phrase for an academic to use, but I would say to the thousands of New Zealanders—Māori, Pākehā, and from a wide variety of ethnicities—who get up early every morning to work at Corrections or the courts or in many parts of the justice sector, the suggestion that they are just mere cogs in the wheel of a structurally racist regime is an insult to those people who work hard every day to do the right thing for this country and to keep New Zealanders safe.
rigor.explanation: Strawman plus appeal to emotion: a claim about structural racism is a claim about system-level outcomes, not an accusation that individual staff are racist, so rebutting the insult-to-workers version leaves the original claim untouched.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In regards to structural racism, I would say that that’s a very easy phrase for an academic to use, but I would say to the thousands of New Zealanders—Māori, Pākehā, and from a wide variety of ethnicities—who get up early every morning to work at Corrections or the courts or in many parts of the justice sector, the suggestion that they are just mere cogs in the wheel of a structurally racist regime is an insult to those people who work hard every day to do the right thing for this country and to keep New Zealanders safe.
civility.explanation: Dismisses the source rather than the argument — "a very easy phrase for an academic to use" belittles the speaker's standing rather than engaging the claim, though it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Could the Minister tell us exactly how many Māori accused did Moana Jackson ever defend at court?
civility.explanation: A personal jibe at a named individual, aimed at discrediting his standing to speak rather than addressing anything he said.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In 1970, Ngā Tamatoa and Ngā Kaiwhakapūmau i te Reo lobbied for the introduction of te reo Māori into all schools.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that two named organisations were both lobbying for te reo in schools in 1970 — a claim about the existence and activity of those groups at that date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Founding dates and campaign records of Ngā Tamatoa and Ngā Kaiwhakapūmau i te Reo (Te Ara / Ngā Taonga / Te Taura Whiri histories): true if both organisations existed and were lobbying for te reo in schools in 1970; false if either was not formed until later or did not campaign on schooling then.

veracity.statement: Two years later, the Māori language petition, signed by over 30,000 New Zealanders, was carried to the very steps of this Parliament; ordinary people, extraordinary in their vision, stood up to say that the language of our tīpuna and of this whenua will not die.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori language petition presented to Parliament in 1972 carried more than 30,000 signatures.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 1972 Māori language petition as recorded in the Journals of the House / Archives NZ petition record: true if the signature count exceeds 30,000 and it was presented at Parliament in 1972; false if the count was materially below 30,000 or the year differs.

veracity.statement: May I remind everyone in this House and out there that in 1975, just 5 percent of all Māori schoolchildren could speak and even understand their own mother tongue; 5 percent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific statistic: that as at 1975 only 5 percent of Māori schoolchildren could speak or understand Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The NZCER Māori language survey of the 1970s (Benton) or Te Taura Whiri's published historical figures: true if a survey of that period puts the proportion of Māori schoolchildren able to speak/understand Māori at about 5%; false if the published figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: They became the first bilingual school in the entire country in 1978.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Ruātoki was New Zealand's first bilingual school and that this status dates from 1978.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Te Ara records on the establishment of bilingual schooling: true if Ruātoki was the first officially bilingual school and the designation dates from 1978; false if another school was first or the year is materially different.

veracity.statement: That same year, the kōhanga reo movement was born in Ngāruawāhia.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the kōhanga reo movement originated at Ngāruawāhia in 1980 (the year named in the preceding sentence).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Kōhanga Reo National Trust and Te Ara accounts of the hui at which kōhanga reo was conceived: true if that founding hui was held at Ngāruawāhia in 1980; false if the hui was in a different year or place.

veracity.statement: Te Karere was born—and so was I—in 1983.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the te reo Māori news bulletin Te Karere first went to air in 1983.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ngā Taonga Sound & Vision / TVNZ broadcast records for the first Te Karere bulletin: true if the first broadcast was in 1983; false if it was in another year.

specificity.statement: May I remind everyone in this House and out there that in 1975, just 5 percent of all Māori schoolchildren could speak and even understand their own mother tongue; 5 percent.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named year and a precise percentage against a defined population — someone could go to the survey and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Aotearoa hou I aspire to is free from racism, from discrimination, from trauma, and from unnecessary suffering.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic goods with no mechanism, measure, figure or timeframe — nothing here could be checked or acted on, in a passage where she could have named what she intends to pursue.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One only has to turn to the Hansard to see in plain black and white how this Government and past Governments have perceived our people.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that successive governments have held a demonstrable view of Māori — rests entirely on a gesture at Hansard as a source, with no passage, period or instance offered. An appeal to a record rather than an argument from it, though the source named is at least the right kind of evidence.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The committee received 62 submissions, and several of them dealt with constitutional matters, as you would expect for a bill of this nature.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific count of submissions received by the Parliament Bill Committee on the Parliament Bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report to the House and the select committee submission record on the Parliament Bill; true if the number of submissions received is 62, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: All the committee’s recommendations are unanimous, and I thank the committee’s members for their approach and diligent work on the bill under the guidance of the chairperson, the Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that every recommendation in the Parliament Bill Committee's report was made unanimously, with no minority or differing views recorded.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report on the Parliament Bill; true if the commentary records no minority or differing views and all recommendations are agreed by the whole committee, false if any recommendation is recorded as split or accompanied by a differing view.

veracity.statement: It combines the four separate Acts that currently set out these arrangements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Parliament Bill consolidates exactly four existing Acts governing the operation of Parliament, its privileges, remuneration and support agencies.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill as reported back and its explanatory note / repeals schedule; true if exactly four existing Acts are consolidated and repealed, false if the number is other than four.

specificity.statement: Proposed new clause 190A requires officers to report to the chief executive within three working days when certain coercive powers are used, summarising the circumstances and reasons for their exercise.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, the reporting line, the trigger (use of specified coercive powers), the deadline (three working days) and the required content of the report. Fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Aside from this consolidation, the bill makes some policy changes to strengthen the independence of Parliament, setting out a funding model for the parliamentary agencies so their appropriations are commended by the House rather than determined by the executive, providing a statutory process for security arrangements in the parliamentary precincts, making the system for funding members’ work-related expenses clearer and more family friendly, and updating and aligning provisions relating to the functions and staffing of the parliamentary agencies.
specificity.explanation: Names four concrete mechanisms and one real institutional change (appropriations commended by the House rather than the executive), but carries no figures, dates or clause references, and 'clearer and more family friendly' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: There was unanimous agreement on the Standing Orders Committee that this was a matter which should be addressed.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Standing Orders Committee reached unanimous agreement that discriminatory electronic petitions needed addressing — a claim about a committee's recorded proceedings, not an opinion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Standing Orders Committee's report/minutes on the Petitions Committee submission regarding highly discriminatory petitions: true if the committee's report records agreement with no dissenting or minority view from any party; false if any member or party recorded dissent.

veracity.statement: In some cases, this has led to legislative policy changes in Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that petitions to Parliament have in some instances produced legislative or policy change by government — a claim about the past record of the petitions process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Petitions Committee reports and the corresponding Government responses on petitions.parliament.nz: true if at least one petition is documented as having led to a legislative amendment or announced policy change; false if no such case can be identified in the committee reports or Government responses.

rigor.statement: This sessional order now gives the Clerk the ability to not post those petitions on the website. In fact, those petitions could still occur on a paper form by doing the rounds in the kind of old-fashioned way. But that doesn't give it the appearance of this Parliament approving, as in any way legitimate, petitions which are outright offensive.
rigor.explanation: A valid argument answering the obvious free-speech objection: the order restricts hosting, not circulation, and the harm identified (implied parliamentary endorsement) attaches only to hosting. The conclusion tracks the premises with no fallacy or unstated leap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This will not prevent paper petitions of that nature from going out in the community; I don’t think, therefore, that anyone could argue that this is about restricting people’s ability to canvass petitions in their communities.
rigor.explanation: The inference from 'paper petitions are unaffected' to 'this does not restrict canvassing' largely holds, but overreaches in claiming nobody could argue otherwise — removing the platform is itself a restriction on one channel, a gap the argument does not address.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There is a reference in there to the prohibited grounds of discrimination under the Human Rights Act as a guiding light, but not the sole basis for refusing a petition, and this will be in place for six months, I suspect, that it will be seen as a useful innovation, and I hope will become a permanent feature of our Standing Orders, but that's not for today.
specificity.explanation: Names the governing statute (Human Rights Act 1993 prohibited grounds), its status as guiding rather than determinative, and the six-month duration — all checkable against the order's text. The back half is hedged aspiration carrying no content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When I think about the realities of some petitions that definitely have been highly discriminatory, and that are less about free speech and more about just causing genuine harm, I think this is an important step.
specificity.explanation: Offers the central justification for the measure without naming a single petition, category of content, or instance of harm; 'some petitions' and 'genuine harm' commit to nothing a reader could check.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would suggest that whenever we look at matters which strike to the constitution of our country, that is the approach that we should take, and, sadly, it hasn’t necessarily been the approach of this Government to date.
civility.explanation: A pointed criticism of how the Government has handled constitutional legislation. It targets a process and a record, not any individual, and imputes no bad faith beyond 'sadly'.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would suggest that whenever we look at matters which strike to the constitution of our country, that is the approach that we should take, and, sadly, it hasn’t necessarily been the approach of this Government to date.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine process point (constitutional bills should be prepared slowly and cross-party), but no specific bill, measure or outcome is named — the criticism lands as a general remark about 'this Government'.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But we have seen over the few years that risks to MPs have increased, and it is necessary to give powers to security staff, employees of Parliamentary Service and, in some cases, others to address those risks.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that security risks to New Zealand MPs have risen over recent years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service / Diplomatic Protection Service and Police reporting on threats and security incidents involving sitting MPs, plus the Parliament Bill Committee's departmental advice: true if the recorded number of threats or security incidents against MPs rose materially over roughly 2020–2025, false if the recorded series is flat or falling.

veracity.statement: Some of us in the House will know that the number of submissions being made on bills has increased and the work associated with it has increased as well and the amount of work that Governments are pushing through has increased.
veracity.explanation: Three linked factual claims: select committee submission volumes have risen, the associated workload has risen, and the volume of legislation Governments put through has risen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Office of the Clerk annual reports and select committee submission counts across the last several parliamentary terms, and the count of Acts passed per year: true if submission numbers and bills passed show a clear upward trend, false if the series are flat or declining.

veracity.statement: The reason why was actually well articulated by advisers—that is that it is the executive who is bound by the Treaty, not Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the advice given to the committee, that Treaty of Waitangi obligations bind the executive/Crown rather than Parliament as legislature.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report and the departmental/Crown Law advice to it, alongside settled NZ constitutional doctrine on who bears Treaty obligations: true if the advice and doctrine hold that Treaty obligations run to the Crown/executive and not to Parliament as legislature, false if the advice given was materially different or if the doctrine binds Parliament directly.

rigor.statement: But we have seen over the few years that risks to MPs have increased, and it is necessary to give powers to security staff, employees of Parliamentary Service and, in some cases, others to address those risks.
rigor.explanation: Premise (rising risk) to conclusion (new detention and removal powers are necessary) is a reasonable inference, but the step from 'risk increased' to 'these particular statutory powers are necessary' is asserted rather than shown — no alternative measure is considered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In my personal opinion, what I have observed is that with a growing population, with growing complex issues in our communities, the current mechanisms that are in place to ensure that parliamentary services and the Office of the Clerk are adequately resourced to, for example, ensure that we meet the needs of our communities at the select committee, are just insufficient.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (funding mechanisms are insufficient) is offered on the strength of population growth and 'growing complex issues' plus personal observation. The premises are consistent with the conclusion but nothing is supplied to bridge them — it rests substantially on an appeal to the speaker's own experience.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The change in the funding model, which essentially gives this House control over its own funding—in the same way as the Ombudsman is funded, and the like—is absolutely a step in the right direction.
specificity.explanation: Names the actual mechanism (House control over its own appropriation) and an existing analogue (the Ombudsman's funding arrangement), but supplies no figures, no timeframe and no description of how the appropriation would be set.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Those additional mechanisms include the requirement to report the uses of detention, force, and handcuffs to the Chief Executive of the Parliamentary Service within three days; the requirement for Parliamentary Service to report on the number of uses of detention, force, handcuffs, seizures, and removal of persons in Parliamentary Service’s annual report; the requirement for an approved training course for security officers, to be consulted on with Police and the Ministry of Justice; the requirement for identity cards held and presented by parliamentary security officers to include name, role, photograph, and unique ID number; and other measures.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates named statutory safeguards with the reporting recipient, a three-day deadline, the reporting vehicle (the annual report), the consultation parties for the training course, and the four required ID card fields. Every element is checkable against the bill as reported back.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The security, you guys are doing a great job, and I think we really did get some good wins in there for democracy.
specificity.explanation: Offered as the speaker's assessment of what the committee achieved in a substantive bill, but carries no content: no provision, safeguard, figure or change is named — 'good wins for democracy' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The committee made some amendments because we want to be very, very clear that there is additional training for those staff—because that was something that came through the submissions—and also, if there's an exercise of any of those powers, particularly issues where force is used or detention is used, the officer involved reports those within three days, and also—second tier—that the Chief Executive of the Parliamentary Service reports those in their annual report.
specificity.explanation: Names the concrete safeguards the committee added: additional staff training, a three-day officer reporting requirement triggered by use of force or detention, and a second-tier disclosure in the Parliamentary Service annual report. Mechanism, trigger and timeframe are all stated, so a reader could check the bill as reported back against this description.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: There have been a number of amendments that have soothed some of those issues, but I also reflect that the good outcomes and the improvements have come from being able to take the time. I think there’s a number of pieces of legislation that would hugely benefit from a more considered approach.
specificity.explanation: Gives a direction — more time on legislation — without naming any of the "number of pieces of legislation", any amendment, or any procedural change that would deliver the more considered approach. The surrounding text supplies no figures or named measures either.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I don't think they actually realised that they are published every quarter anyway, and, by crikey, I think we all know that the finance team are assiduous in pursuing every single receipt that we've got or haven't got.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that MPs' expenses are already published on a quarterly cycle, in response to submitters who wanted the bill to open them up.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Parliamentary Service members' expense disclosure releases: true if expense information for members is published on a quarterly schedule as at October 2025; false if the publication cycle is other than quarterly or if expenses are not routinely published.

veracity.statement: However, at the moment, the budget for the agencies of Parliament—the Office of the Clerk and Parliamentary Services—is set by the executive, not by Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that, prior to this bill, funding for the Office of the Clerk and the Parliamentary Service is determined through the executive's budget process rather than by Parliament itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The appropriation process for Vote Office of the Clerk and Vote Parliamentary Service as at October 2025, and the departmental disclosure statement / select committee report on the Parliament Bill: true if those appropriations are set through the Government's Estimates process rather than determined by Parliament; false if Parliament already sets them independently of the executive.

veracity.statement: We've only got to look at the incidents over the last week or so, particularly around our party leader’s home, and say that that is not something which we can take for granted and is something which we need to treasure and to look after.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that security incidents occurred in the week or so before 9 October 2025, including at the home of the New Zealand First leader.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous news reporting, police statements or parliamentary security advice covering late September to 9 October 2025: true if one or more security incidents at the residence of the New Zealand First leader are documented in that window; false if no such incident is recorded.

rigor.statement: There have been a number of amendments that have soothed some of those issues, but I also reflect that the good outcomes and the improvements have come from being able to take the time. I think there’s a number of pieces of legislation that would hugely benefit from a more considered approach.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a single worked case — this bill improved because the process was unhurried — to a general conclusion about other legislation. A modest generalisation from one instance, and no alternative explanation for the improvements is considered, but the speaker hedges the conclusion ("I'm not saying that everything would come out with cross-partisan support") rather than overclaiming, so it falls short of a bare appeal to anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Our committee services at the moment are under huge pressure, and again, this is one of the issues of ramming through legislation too fast.
civility.explanation: Harsh criticism ("ramming through") aimed squarely at the legislative process and the pressure on committee services. No person is named, impugned or mocked, so under the re-anchored scale this is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Our committee services at the moment are under huge pressure, and again, this is one of the issues of ramming through legislation too fast.
focus.explanation: Entirely about a process problem — select committee capacity and the pace of legislating. No party is named and no tribal framing is used; the complaint is about how the House handles bills.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I will support this bill on behalf of the Green Party, but unless there is some budget allocated for improvements to parliamentary services and the support of the staff, we will not, as a country, be as well served as we should be.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete lever (budget allocation for Parliamentary Service staffing) and a position on the bill, but supplies no amount, no mechanism and no timeframe — a direction rather than a checkable commitment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I reject that, and we've reported in our report exactly why. It is a very transparent process, what is being proposed—very similar to how Officers of Parliament operate as well—and so it would mean that all parties would be represented on a select committee to decide and to consider budget applications from the Office of the Clerk and from the Parliamentary Service, and would be scrutinised by, basically, all parties in Parliament.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (a select committee with all parties represented), the bodies whose budget applications it would consider (Office of the Clerk, Parliamentary Service), and the existing comparator. Missing the composition rules and any figures, which is what keeps it below the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I'll summarise the changes that we made in increasing reporting and increasing monitoring, because there were concerns that were raised around whether there was enough reporting and monitoring of what those officers will be doing: if they use their new powers, that must be reported to the CEO within three days, and the CEO must report those at least annually.
specificity.explanation: A concrete safeguard with a named trigger (use of the new powers), a named recipient (the CEO), a deadline (three days) and a reporting frequency (at least annually). Someone could check the bill against this description.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The special select committee received 62 submissions from some notable New Zealanders who had given some of the constitutional, weighty matters great thought and great consideration.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Parliament Bill Committee received exactly 62 submissions on the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report and the submissions list published on parliament.nz for the Parliament Bill; true if the recorded number of submissions received is 62, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Ultimately, the recommendations that the committee has made were unanimously agreed by members of Parliament representing every party in this current Parliament.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the committee's recommendations on the Parliament Bill were agreed unanimously, with every party in the 54th Parliament represented on the committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill Committee's report to the House; true if it records the recommendations as unanimous with no minority or differing views appended and lists members from every party, false if any party recorded a differing view or was unrepresented.

veracity.statement: Just a really short call from me this afternoon, to say this is a really collaborative and proactive approach to the legislation around how this place actually operates and how it works, bringing together four different Acts to enable a modern framework for Parliament to work as best as it possibly can, and the agencies that support this incredible place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Parliament Bill consolidates four existing Acts governing Parliament and its supporting agencies. The surrounding claims about collaboration are evaluative and not part of this item.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Parliament Bill as reported back and its explanatory note; true if it repeals and consolidates exactly four Acts, false if the number of Acts consolidated is other than four.

rigor.statement: Over the years, of the 150 or so years of unbroken, stable political democracy, participatory democracy, in New Zealand, society has changed, attitudes have changed, and so too must this institution of Parliament evolve, change, modify, and reform itself.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — society and attitudes have changed, therefore Parliament must change — but the conclusion outruns the premise. That an institution's surroundings have changed does not by itself establish that the institution must reform, and no link is offered between the two; it leans on the appeal of continuity rather than showing what specifically has fallen out of step.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I reject that, and we've reported in our report exactly why. It is a very transparent process, what is being proposed—very similar to how Officers of Parliament operate as well—and so it would mean that all parties would be represented on a select committee to decide and to consider budget applications from the Office of the Clerk and from the Parliamentary Service, and would be scrutinised by, basically, all parties in Parliament.
rigor.explanation: Answers the transparency objection with an actual reason: all-party representation on the deciding committee, plus an analogy to the existing Officers of Parliament process. The conclusion tracks the premise, though the analogy is asserted rather than demonstrated and the report is gestured at rather than quoted.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In terms of security, I encourage MPs to actually go and speak to some of our security officers around Parliament, and especially some of the ones that have been around for a little while, and they'll happily tell you why these changes are necessary.
rigor.explanation: The case for necessity is outsourced entirely — an appeal to authority and anecdote. Nothing is offered here about what incidents or gaps make the new powers necessary; the listener is told that someone else would find it convincing.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I did look to see if there had been complaints made or anything that was very obvious in the media space in this area, and I really couldn’t find anything, which says to me that the rules are set in a reasonable way.
rigor.explanation: Argument from absence of evidence: an informal personal scan of media coverage turning up nothing is offered as support for the conclusion that the rules are reasonable. Unreported complaints, complaints resolved internally, or simply low salience would all produce the same null result, so the premise does very little work for the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In the language itself, it’s quite restrained, but then we also have to remember that the common law continues to apply in these circumstances.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the search powers are restrained is drawn from the specific drafting language she has just quoted ('involves no physical contact', 'external examination of the person's clothes'), and she then adds an independent constraint — the continuing application of the common law and judicial supervision of reasonableness. Textual evidence plus a named backstop; the conclusion tracks what was offered, with no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I'm not suggesting that, but I think we're living in a world where things now happen that mean that the people who are at the front line—those are our security guards—need to be given appropriate powers.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that security staff need statutory powers rests on a single recalled incident (a banner dropped in the chamber) plus an unevidenced assertion that the world has changed. Generalising from one anecdote to a legislative need, with nothing offered on frequency or on whether existing powers were inadequate.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In April 2019, there was a decision taken to stretch those rules into a whole host of new tribunals, including the lawyers disciplinary tribunal and other tribunals as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in April 2019 the Courts Security Act regime was extended to cover a range of tribunals, including the lawyers disciplinary tribunal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ legislation website: commencement of the amendments extending Courts Security Act 1999 court security officer powers to tribunals (Tribunals Powers and Procedures Legislation Act 2018 and any associated Orders in Council). True if an extension covering the New Zealand Lawyers and Conveyancers Disciplinary Tribunal and other tribunals took effect in April 2019; false if no such extension occurred or it took effect at a materially different time or did not cover that tribunal.

veracity.statement: If you look at Australia, the UK, and Canada, there aren’t specific statutory powers or immunities as we’re writing them in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Australian, UK and Canadian jurisdictions have no statute conferring specific security powers or immunities on parliamentary security staff comparable to those in this bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The statute books of the three jurisdictions for parliamentary-precinct security: Australia's Parliamentary Precincts Act 1988 and Parliamentary Service Act 1999, the UK's Parliamentary Corporate Bodies/precinct provisions, and Canada's Parliament of Canada Act provisions creating the Parliamentary Protective Service. True if none of the three confers statutory search/screening powers or immunities on parliamentary security officers; false if any one of them does.

veracity.statement: Certainly to the Speaker directly, but there’s a useful case in Police v Beggs, which was a 1999 case where the courts were very clear that the Speaker must also have regard to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence of a 1999 decision, Police v Beggs, in which the court held that the Speaker's exercise of powers over the parliamentary precinct is subject to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The reported judgment in Police v Beggs (New Zealand, 1999). True if the case is from 1999 and holds that the Speaker must have regard to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990 when exercising powers over the precinct; false if the case does not exist, is from another year, or contains no such holding.

veracity.statement: I think, with 25 percent of our population identifying as having some sort of disability, there’s certainly a need for Parliament to consider whether it’s time for us to have that kind of review in place.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 25 percent of the New Zealand population identify as having some form of disability.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Disability Survey (most recent release at the date of the statement, and the earlier 2013 survey). True if the reported disabled share of the population is approximately 25%; false if it is materially lower or higher on the most recent official measure.

specificity.statement: Certainly to the Speaker directly, but there’s a useful case in Police v Beggs, which was a 1999 case where the courts were very clear that the Speaker must also have regard to the New Zealand Bill of Rights Act.
specificity.explanation: Names the case, the year, the deciding body and the specific legal proposition it stands for, so the listener can go and read it. She could have made the same point as a generality ('the courts have said the Speaker has to act reasonably'); she supplied the citation instead.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think that perhaps we should look at some other iterations of this later, things like perhaps a buddy system.
specificity.explanation: A proposal is being advanced, but only a label — 'a buddy system' — with no description of who would qualify, what access the person would have, what it would cost, or when it would be considered. Doubly hedged with 'perhaps'.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Something people haven’t yet mentioned is that the coverage of these new powers will extend to parliamentary meetings outside of the grounds and will also extend to electorate offices and community offices too.
focus.explanation: Wholly about the measure itself — identifies a specific extension of the bill's scope (off-precinct parliamentary meetings, electorate and community offices) that other speakers had not raised. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I wanted to touch on the fact that the bill makes the Parliamentary Library a standard business unit in the Parliamentary Service, and just acknowledge the role that the parliamentary librarians play in supporting us as MPs, particularly with our constituency work—the ability to engage and contact and get feedback that helps us answer constituents’ queries on a daily basis, for those of us who are hard-working constituent MPs like my colleagues on this side of the House.
focus.explanation: There is a genuine policy point — the bill's reclassification of the Parliamentary Library as a standard business unit — but it is closed with a partisan aside reserving 'hard-working constituent' status to his own side of the House, which carries no policy content and shifts the weight of the sentence to party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I remember in 2004, I was working for Tariana Turia at the time and she crossed the floor on the foreshore and seabed Act—well, bill then.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Tariana Turia crossed the floor against the Foreshore and Seabed Bill in 2004, and that the speaker worked for her at that time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The 2004 Hansard division records for the Foreshore and Seabed Bill and contemporaneous reporting: true if Turia voted against her own Labour Government on that bill in 2004, false if she did not; the employment claim checks against parliamentary staff records or her own accounts.

veracity.statement: This is the very reason why Hone Harawira actually left Te Pāti Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a causal fact about Hone Harawira's 2011 departure from Te Pāti Māori — that the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) legislation and the party's arrangement with National was the reason.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporaneous reporting of Harawira's departure from Te Pāti Māori and his own stated reasons: true if the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) legislation / the relationship with National is identified as the cause of the split, false if the break is attributable to unrelated causes.

veracity.statement: The current rules deprive local broadcasters of, they think, around $6 million annually in advertising revenue, and, of course, as we all know the pressure that the broader media sector is under, every dollar helps and every dollar counts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a quantified figure — roughly $6 million a year in advertising revenue foregone by broadcasters because of the section 81 restrictions — attributed to the broadcasters' own estimate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure for the Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Bill and broadcaster submissions to select committee: true if the foregone-revenue estimate is around $6 million annually, false if the documented estimate is materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: On 7 March 2024, TVNZ announces 68 job cuts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a dated, quantified event: that TVNZ announced 68 job cuts on 7 March 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TVNZ's own announcement and contemporaneous news reporting from March 2024: true if TVNZ announced approximately 68 role reductions on or about 7 March 2024, false if the date or the figure is materially different.

focus.statement: When the Helen Clark Labour Government passed the foreshore and seabed, that shouldn't have happened. The reaction of the National Party in addressing that, that shouldn't have happened. And I can tell you that this amendment shouldn't happen either.
focus.explanation: Names three specific pieces of legislation — the 2004 foreshore and seabed Act, the MACA response to it, and the amendment now before the House — and criticises his own party's past government alongside the other side. Directed at measures, not at party character.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This amendment bill restores clarity to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, ensuring Parliament’s original intention. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House; no party framing at all, despite a debate that invited it.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it is also a speech about broken promises, because this is from a Government that came in saying they were going to get things back on track, and from a Minister a year ago—over a year ago—who said he was going to take immediate action for our broadcasting and media sector.
focus.explanation: Scrutiny anchored to a named commitment — the Minister's promise of immediate action on the broadcasting and media sector — and to the delay in delivering it. Accountability for a specific undertaking, not content-free party-bashing, though the 'back on track' line adds some general framing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This amendment bill restores clarity to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, ensuring Parliament’s original intention. Therefore, I commend this bill to the House.
specificity.explanation: Names the Act, but supplies no mechanism, clause, test or effect — 'restores clarity' and 'original intention' are assertions nobody could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The bill repeals section 81 of the Broadcasting Act 1989, which restricts broadcast television and radio advertising on Sunday and Anzac Day mornings, and both television and radio advertising on Christmas Day, Good Friday, and Easter Sunday.
specificity.explanation: Names the section, the parent Act, the media affected and each restricted day — fully checkable against the statute.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Of course, online, all the various ways that people get their entertainment has changed dramatically, so the broadcasters, particularly the New Zealand - owned broadcasters, are at a competitive disadvantage in not having the ability to do something that their competitors can.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference: the premise that a restriction binds broadcasters but not the online platforms audiences have shifted to supports the conclusion of asymmetric competitive disadvantage. No fallacy or appeal; the conclusion tracks exactly what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And if this is immediate action, I think that was false advertising.
civility.explanation: Pointed and sarcastic, and it does edge toward suggesting the Minister misled — but the jibe lands on the promise rather than on the Minister's character or competence, and the pun keeps it within robust debate.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: If we look at the last five years of advertising revenue that has been spent on our local media, in 2019 the total industry revenue spent was $2.76 billion of advertising across our media. In 2024, it had increased by 30 percent, to $3.59 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts total New Zealand advertising industry revenue of $2.76 billion in 2019 rising 30 percent to $3.59 billion in 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Advertising Standards Authority / Think TV annual New Zealand advertising turnover series for calendar 2019 and 2024; true if the two totals are $2.76b and $3.59b (± rounding) and the growth is ~30%, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: However, television advertising revenue has gone down by 15 percent; radio has gone down by just 3 percent. The digital advertising, and this is the rub, has gone from $1.08 billion, in 2019, to $2.17 billion.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a 15% fall in television advertising revenue and a 3% fall in radio over 2019–2024, and a rise in digital advertising from $1.08b to $2.17b over the same period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Advertising Standards Authority annual turnover breakdown by medium for 2019 and 2024; true if television is down ~15%, radio down ~3%, and digital rises from ~$1.08b to ~$2.17b, false if any of the three differs materially.

veracity.statement: This broadcasting amendment bill will only increase advertising revenue by $6 million. That’s an assumption that’s been made: $4 million will go to television; $2 million will go to radio.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the estimated additional advertising revenue from repealing the restrictions is $6 million, split $4m television / $2m radio.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure statement for the Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Bill, or the select committee report; true if it estimates ~$6m additional revenue split ~$4m TV and ~$2m radio, false if it gives a materially different figure or split.

veracity.statement: They don’t even actually employ journalists, artists, photographers, or editors.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the offshore digital platforms displacing traditional media employ no journalists, artists, photographers or editors at all.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public staffing and role information for the major offshore platforms referred to (Google/YouTube, Meta) — e.g. published job listings and company disclosures for editorial, news-partnership and content roles; true if no such roles exist, false if the platforms demonstrably employ editors, content producers or journalists.

veracity.statement: Radio Rhema is able to advertise currently as a radio station on a Sunday. They choose not to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the existing advertising restrictions leave Radio Rhema legally free to carry advertising on Sundays, and that it abstains as a matter of choice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The restricted-hours provisions of the Broadcasting Act 1989 as they apply to radio on Sundays, plus Radio Rhema's own published advertising/sponsorship policy or rate card; true if radio is unrestricted on Sundays and Rhema carries no Sunday advertising, false if the Act restricts it or Rhema does advertise.

veracity.statement: I wanted to reiterate some of the points made around Government cuts to broadcasting, some of which are a $10 million cut to Whakaata Māori, our national Māori broadcasting channel; a forecast $18 million worth of cuts to Radio New Zealand, which is quite depressing given that they are also our kind of emergency national radio station, who have to communicate those really important messages to everybody; and the fact that TVNZ’s call for an extra $30 million worth of revenue has been ignored.
veracity.explanation: Three separate assertions: a $10m cut to Whakaata Māori, a forecast $18m of cuts to RNZ, and a rejected TVNZ request for an additional $30m.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 and 2025 appropriations — Vote Māori Development (Whakaata Māori) and Vote Arts, Culture and Heritage (RNZ) — plus TVNZ's published funding request/Ministerial response; true if the appropriations show reductions of ~$10m and ~$18m respectively and TVNZ's $30m request was declined, false if the figures or direction differ materially.

veracity.statement: Twenty percent of New Zealanders subscribe to some form of faith, and I’d assume that many of those include Sundays being protected and days of rest and days of worship as well.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 20 percent of New Zealanders have a religious affiliation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census religious affiliation results; true if the share reporting any religious affiliation is ~20%, false if materially higher or lower.

veracity.statement: But the reality of this one is, as with most of the New Zealand calendar, which was imported from England, it is the Christian tradition that we always commemorate. I don't see any broadcasting advertising being taken away for Eid or taken away for Ramadan or those kinds of things.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the statutory advertising restrictions cover only Christian observances and include no Islamic ones such as Eid or Ramadan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The list of restricted days and hours in the Broadcasting Act 1989 (Christmas Day, Good Friday, Easter Sunday, Anzac Day morning, Sunday mornings); true if no non-Christian religious observance appears in that list, false if any does.

specificity.statement: If we look at the last five years of advertising revenue that has been spent on our local media, in 2019 the total industry revenue spent was $2.76 billion of advertising across our media. In 2024, it had increased by 30 percent, to $3.59 billion.
specificity.explanation: Two dated totals, a growth rate and a named scope — directly checkable against the industry revenue series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This broadcasting amendment bill will only increase advertising revenue by $6 million. That’s an assumption that’s been made: $4 million will go to television; $2 million will go to radio.
specificity.explanation: A named bill, a total figure and a stated split between two media — someone could check it against the bill's impact statement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I wanted to reiterate some of the points made around Government cuts to broadcasting, some of which are a $10 million cut to Whakaata Māori, our national Māori broadcasting channel; a forecast $18 million worth of cuts to Radio New Zealand, which is quite depressing given that they are also our kind of emergency national radio station, who have to communicate those really important messages to everybody; and the fact that TVNZ’s call for an extra $30 million worth of revenue has been ignored.
specificity.explanation: Three named organisations each with a dollar figure attached and the direction of the change stated — checkable line by line against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Some of those ideas include long-term funding for public, Māori, Pasifika, and community media, strengthening NZ On Air and the Māori Television Service, supporting non-commercial spaces for children’s content, and protecting independent journalism and niche audiences.
specificity.explanation: Names real agencies and identifiable directions of policy, but carries no amounts, mechanisms or timeframes — a list of intentions rather than something anyone could cost or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: For radio, that’s a 0.73 percent increase. It’s very small amount. That’s an 0.81 percent increase—for the $4 million—to television. Now, we believe that this amount of money is not worth changing how we keep those special days sacred; carving out and protecting those days for special religious observance and for Anzac Day to commemorate all of those people who fought in the wars, as outlined by my colleague Hūhana Lyndon.
rigor.explanation: A clean cost-benefit inference: the quantified gain is under 1 percent of each sector's revenue, therefore it does not justify the cost to the protected days. The conclusion tracks the figures offered; the remaining step (that the days have value) is stated as the party's position rather than smuggled in.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we relax advertising standards at this point, it will be seen as a further dumbing down of our media space that we still do have control over.
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope. Nothing is offered to connect permitting advertising on a handful of days to a general degradation of the media, and 'will be seen as' substitutes anticipated perception for an argued consequence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In a time when people are quite suspicious of mainstream media and when people are getting a lot of their information from the internet, it’s probably quite important that we protect national broadcasting channels and platforms as a source of truth for people to get information and to learn things and to know what’s going on in the rest of the country and, indeed, the rest of the world.
rigor.explanation: A premise is offered and the conclusion is in its direction, but there is a real gap: that audiences are sceptical of mainstream media and get information online is asserted, not evidenced, and no step connects that state of affairs to national broadcasters being the reliable alternative.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’m sure that, along with myself and Mr Costley, other veterans have far better things to be doing on Anzac Day than watching television. It’s probably one of the busiest days of the year for us. Therefore, I commend the bill to the House.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur resting on anecdote. That the speaker and other veterans are busy on Anzac Day says nothing about whether the advertising restriction should be repealed for everyone else, yet 'therefore' presents it as the ground for supporting the bill.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the reality of this one is, as with most of the New Zealand calendar, which was imported from England, it is the Christian tradition that we always commemorate. I don't see any broadcasting advertising being taken away for Eid or taken away for Ramadan or those kinds of things.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument that does the work it claims: if the protection is defended as respect for sacred days but is extended only to Christian observances, the principle is being applied selectively. The example given supports the conclusion drawn.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It's about fairness when YouTube, when Facebook can make millions and billions of dollars and then little old TVNZ is unable to advertise on a Sunday morning. It just seems a bit unfair.
rigor.explanation: A genuine asymmetry is identified and the fairness conclusion follows from it, but the inference leans on the intuition that the two are like cases; nothing is offered to show that offshore platforms and a domestic free-to-air broadcaster should be regulated identically.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For radio, that’s a 0.73 percent increase. It’s very small amount. That’s an 0.81 percent increase—for the $4 million—to television. Now, we believe that this amount of money is not worth changing how we keep those special days sacred; carving out and protecting those days for special religious observance and for Anzac Day to commemorate all of those people who fought in the wars, as outlined by my colleague Hūhana Lyndon.
focus.explanation: Names the measure, the revenue effect and the specific days at issue — entirely engaged with what the bill does, with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This bill overlooks the cultural value of New Zealand’s commercial-free days as roadblocks to revenue and not foundations of our country’s character.
focus.explanation: Directed at what the bill does to the commercial-free days rather than at whoever is promoting it, though the point is made at the level of 'cultural value' rather than a named provision.
focus.subject: speaker

divination.statement: If this bill passes, they will not be taking advantage of advertising and will not conduct any advertising or seek any advertising revenue with this repeal.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, conditional on the bill's enactment, Radio Rhema will neither broadcast nor seek advertising revenue in the hours the repeal opens up.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Conditional on the Bill being enacted and commenced: Radio Rhema's broadcast output and published advertising/sponsorship offering in the twelve months after commencement; true if it carries no advertising in the previously restricted hours, false if it broadcasts or solicits advertising in them. Unresolvable if the Bill is not enacted.

civility.statement: This bill overlooks the cultural value of New Zealand’s commercial-free days as roadblocks to revenue and not foundations of our country’s character.
civility.explanation: A hard criticism of the bill's premise on a genuinely contested measure, aimed wholly at the legislation. No member, party or person is touched.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: On 9 April 2024, Newshub confirms their closure plans, and that is 200 job losses.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Newshub confirmed its closure plans on 9 April 2024 with 200 job losses.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Newshub / Warner Bros. Discovery public announcements and contemporaneous media reporting: the date Newshub's closure was confirmed and the number of roles disestablished. True if a confirmation occurred on or about 9 April 2024 involving roughly 200 jobs; false if the date or the headcount is materially different.

veracity.statement: My message is: say that to the hundreds of people losing their jobs in the media sector while you progress a 73-word bill that allows advertisements on linear broadcasters on Sunday mornings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the bill before the House is 73 words long and that its effect is to permit advertising on linear broadcasters on Sunday mornings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Bill as introduced: word count of its operative provisions, and which restricted periods it removes. True if the operative text is about 73 words and it lifts the Sunday-morning restriction; false if the count is materially different or the restricted periods removed are not as described.

veracity.statement: On 7 November 2024, TVNZ announced a further 50 jobs to be cut.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a TVNZ announcement of approximately 50 further role cuts on 7 November 2024.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TVNZ's public announcement and contemporaneous reporting for 7 November 2024. True if TVNZ announced or proposed roughly 50 further role reductions on that date; false if no such announcement was made then or the number differs materially.

veracity.statement: On 13 November 2024, one of the tools in the tool box, the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, was reported to be in limbo all of a sudden, and the next day, on 14 November, New Zealand Media and Entertainment (NZME) announces the closure of 14 regional community newspapers before Christmas, resulting in the loss of 30 more jobs in the broadcasting and media sector in New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts NZME announced on 14 November 2024 the closure of 14 regional community newspapers before Christmas, costing 30 jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZME's November 2024 announcement and contemporaneous reporting: the number of community newspapers closed, the timing, and the associated job losses. True if 14 titles were closed before Christmas 2024 with roughly 30 roles lost; false if the counts or timing differ materially.

veracity.statement: Minister Peters, on RNZ, when he didn’t like the tone of questions, said he’d simply turn the tap off, and Minister Seymour put out social media tiles celebrating the cuts to funding for Radio New Zealand, our State broadcaster, in this year’s Budget.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two things on the record: that Winston Peters threatened on RNZ to 'turn the tap off', and that David Seymour published social media graphics celebrating the Budget cut to RNZ funding.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The recording/transcript of the RNZ interview in which Peters is said to have made the 'turn the tap off' remark, and Seymour's published social media posts about RNZ funding in the most recent Budget. True if both are on the record substantially as described; false if either cannot be found or was materially different.

veracity.statement: I think that member ought to check the growth in the digital audience of RNZ, because I think you’ll see astronomical growth in the digital audiences and platforms of RNZ.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that RNZ's digital audience has grown very substantially, offered as a rebuttal to the claim that RNZ is losing its audience.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ annual reports and independent digital audience measurement (e.g. Nielsen online ratings) for RNZ's digital reach over the past several years. True if digital reach shows large sustained growth; false if it is flat or declining.

veracity.statement: To be fair, when we hear about the potential income that could be generated from allowing advertising on Sundays and public holidays, it’s just approximately $6 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the additional advertising revenue expected from the bill is about $6 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure statement for the Broadcasting (Repeal of Advertising Restrictions) Amendment Bill. True if the official estimate of additional advertising revenue is around $6 million; false if the estimate is materially different or no such estimate exists.

veracity.statement: Nothing’s open—none of the shops are open—so why should we allow advertising on such an important day for us in Aotearoa New Zealand?
veracity.explanation: Asserts, as the premise of the Anzac Day argument, that no shops are open on Anzac Day.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Shop Trading Hours Act 1990 and its Anzac Day provisions. True if shops are required to be closed for the whole of Anzac Day; false if the restriction covers only part of the day (e.g. until 1 p.m.) or if broad categories of shop are exempt and trade normally.

veracity.statement: They’re losing their audience.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that RNZ's audience is in decline.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: RNZ audience measurement — GfK/Nielsen radio survey share and RNZ annual report total reach across recent years. True if RNZ's overall audience has declined; false if total reach is flat or growing.

specificity.statement: On 9 April 2024, Newshub confirms their closure plans, and that is 200 job losses.
specificity.explanation: A named organisation, an exact date and a headcount — directly checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The other thing I’ve got here—I like lists; this is a list of dates, and on this list there are 49 dates during which Cabinet met and the Minister, in response to a question about what he took to that Cabinet meeting to help, what he took to those Cabinet meetings for immediate action for our broadcasting and media sector, the answer, for all of these 49 dates, is nothing—nothing taken; nothing offered; no immediate action.
specificity.explanation: A counted, sourced claim (49 dated Cabinet meetings, drawn from answers to a question) that someone could go and check.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In the biscuit tin, there is a bill for a stream of levies which ensures that the international streamers that sell us their content and charge New Zealanders to watch it would contribute a percentage of their profit back which could be invested in local content.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete mechanism — a levy on international streamers hypothecated to local content — but gives no rate, no revenue estimate and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Sustainable funding for public broadcasting is well overdue, and that’s what this bill does not address.
specificity.explanation: Names no mechanism, amount, source of funding or timeframe. A direction, not a proposal — high focus, low specificity.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I don’t know if you’re keeping count on the other side of the House; I don’t know if you care.
civility.explanation: Imputes indifference to job losses to opposing members. Short of a direct insult, but it attributes bad faith to people rather than criticising the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I can tell you, they run some of the best, tightest budgets I’ve ever seen, and they could teach Nicola Willis a thing or two about how to manage a decent budget.
civility.explanation: A jab at a named individual's personal competence rather than at any policy of hers. Light in tone, but it lands on the person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And I know there’s the obvious joke, and I’m not going to make it, about Minister Goldsmith being a clown, because I don’t think that would be fair, because, actually, Minister Goldsmith has been a mime: he’s moved around a whole lot and he’s waved his arms around, but he hasn’t said anything.
civility.explanation: Paralipsis — the 'clown' insult is delivered under cover of declining to make it — followed by sustained personal mockery of a named Minister. The target is the man, not the bill.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The ignorance from the other side of the House is astounding, and that’s why I’m not going to poke the bear any further, because we’ve actually got the solutions that the Minister needs, and the good news is they’re available for you, Minister: two of them sitting in the biscuit tin, and one of them is on your desk.
civility.explanation: Opens by calling opposing members ignorant — condescension aimed at people rather than at their argument — before pivoting to substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They’re losing their audience. Why would you fund losers?
civility.explanation: 'Losers' is a sneer at the broadcaster and the people who work there rather than an argument about the funding question. No individual is named, but the register is contemptuous rather than substantive.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: No, it’s State-sanctioned theft.
civility.explanation: Brutal about the proposed levy, but the target is entirely the policy — no person is attacked. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a proposal sits near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The other thing I’ve got here—I like lists; this is a list of dates, and on this list there are 49 dates during which Cabinet met and the Minister, in response to a question about what he took to that Cabinet meeting to help, what he took to those Cabinet meetings for immediate action for our broadcasting and media sector, the answer, for all of these 49 dates, is nothing—nothing taken; nothing offered; no immediate action.
focus.explanation: Named scrutiny of a specific ministerial commitment against a specific counted record (49 Cabinet meetings, nothing taken). Accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sustainable funding for public broadcasting is well overdue, and that’s what this bill does not address.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the policy gap in the measure before the House — what the bill does and does not do — with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If you have a business with a limited number of customers and you’re not making enough money and you’re trading six days a week, the solution is not just to open on Sundays, because you just have the same number of customers, but you have to be open more and you have to work harder.
rigor.explanation: A genuine argument by analogy with a reason attached, but the analogy has a real gap: the broadcast already goes out on Sunday, so the bill adds saleable inventory without the extra effort or cost the shop analogy turns on. Reasonable point, weak fit between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker
