rigor.statement: If you typed it out, you could fit it on a postage stamp, and it’s probably worth about the same to the industry, because no one believes it’s worth $6 million; it’s more broken promises from a Government that keeps making things worse.
rigor.explanation: The stated reason is an appeal to popularity — 'no one believes it' stands in for any costing — and the postage-stamp image treats the bill's brevity as evidence of its value, a non-sequitur.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: No, the shortfalls that we have in funding, if we’re being real about fixing the system, have got to be more than a $6 million lifeline, because that $6 million that might be raised isn’t going to fix the shortfalls that we have in TVNZ, fix Whakaata Māori, or fix Radio New Zealand also.
rigor.explanation: Circular: the 'because' clause restates the conclusion (the shortfalls exceed $6m) rather than supporting it. No figure for the actual shortfall is offered against which $6m could be shown inadequate.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Nothing’s open—none of the shops are open—so why should we allow advertising on such an important day for us in Aotearoa New Zealand?
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy — shops close, so advertising should too — but nothing is offered to connect retail trading restrictions to broadcast advertising, and the weight rests on the sentiment attached to the day.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But I also point out that another really good way for linear television broadcasters to increase their revenue is to produce products that people actually want to watch, and so if people watch it and then the advertisers get revenue, maybe that’s another way to fill the gap.
rigor.explanation: The stated chain (more viewers, therefore more advertising revenue) is close to definitional and does nothing to establish the conclusion at issue — that better content is an available remedy for the sector's revenue shortfall. The premise assumes away the problem it is offered to solve.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But the reality is—to finish off—the out of touch-ness of this Government.
focus.explanation: A bare characterisation of the governing parties as 'out of touch'. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named — it is party framing rather than scrutiny of a specific commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It is pretty much in the dark ages when we are having one set of rules for broadcast television, which I've heard referred to as linear television, and in exactly the same programmes provided by exactly the same entity, if you stream them, you're not subject to those rules. That's just irrational.
focus.explanation: Engages the regulatory mechanism directly — which content is caught by which rules and why. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Sadly, this Government just continues to let New Zealanders down.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the other team's record in general terms. No policy, target, figure or outcome is named, so there is nothing here that could be checked or held to account — this is the tribalism case, not scrutiny.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: This is $6 million; this is small change.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the additional advertising revenue the bill unlocks for broadcasters amounts to about $6 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement / departmental disclosure for the broadcasting advertising bill before the House on 9 October 2025, and any Ministry for Culture and Heritage estimate of additional broadcaster advertising revenue from lifting the restricted-day ban; true if the official estimate is approximately $6 million a year, false if materially different (e.g. an order of magnitude out).

veracity.statement: We heard today that funding for some of our Māori broadcasts like Te Karere is at risk.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as a present fact that funding for Māori-language broadcasts, Te Karere specifically, is under threat.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TVNZ and Te Māngai Pāho / NZ On Air public statements and select committee evidence current at 9 October 2025 on the funding status of the Te Karere news programme; true if a funding cut, review or contract lapse placing Te Karere at risk was on the public record at that date, false if its funding was secure and not under review.

veracity.statement: The New Zealand media sector has long called for these changes and this Government is responding.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that removing the restricted-day advertising prohibition is a change the broadcasting industry has been publicly requesting for a long time.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions to the select committee on the broadcasting advertising bill, and public statements by broadcasters and industry bodies (TVNZ, Warner Bros. Discovery/Three, NZME, MediaWorks, the Advertising Standards Authority); true if broadcasters or their industry bodies publicly sought removal of the restricted-day advertising ban over a period of years, false if such calls are recent only or cannot be found.

specificity.statement: We need to be sitting in this House, talking about bigger, more important things than a piece of legislation that just lets you put a bit of advertising on a Sunday morning or on Anzac morning, and I think we need to be reflective of that.
specificity.explanation: Describes the bill's actual effect concretely enough (advertising on Sunday and Anzac mornings), but the counter-proposal — the 'bigger, more important things' the House should address instead — is left entirely unnamed, with no measure, cost or timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: This bill really is about fairness. It’s about balance. It’s about bringing more revenue into broadcasting to make great content that New Zealanders love.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — fairness, balance, more revenue, great content — with no figure, mechanism, timeframe or named provision. Nothing here that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is pretty much in the dark ages when we are having one set of rules for broadcast television, which I've heard referred to as linear television, and in exactly the same programmes provided by exactly the same entity, if you stream them, you're not subject to those rules. That's just irrational.
rigor.explanation: A stated premise (identical programmes from an identical provider face different rules depending only on the delivery channel) supporting a stated conclusion (the distinction is irrational). No fallacy or appeal; the inference tracks the premise. Whether the premise is factually accurate is a separate question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So, look, yes, we're going to support this bill and quite right to observe that, particularly for religious days, it's a bit of an anachronism to have the Christian religious day as a preserve when we now live in a very multicultural society where other religious days come and go.
rigor.explanation: Premise (a multicultural society in which other faiths' observances carry no equivalent statutory protection) offered in support of the conclusion (singling out the Christian day is an anachronism). The inference holds, though it leaves a gap: it does not address why historical entrenchment alone might justify the distinction.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: He's miming the position of Minister of broadcasting, and frankly he seems to be somewhat stuck.
civility.explanation: Mockery aimed at the Minister personally — 'miming' the role portrays him as only pretending to hold the office. This lands on the person's competence rather than on any decision or policy. Subject is the speaker: the jibe is his own conduct, even though its target is someone else.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does he think that paragraph 2.68 of the Cabinet Manual has been upheld, where “Public perception is a very important factor. If a conflict arises in relation to the interests of family, whānau, or close associates, Ministers should take appropriate action”; and if so, what appropriate action did the Minister take to avoid public perception of a conflict of interest?
specificity.explanation: Names and quotes a specific paragraph of a specific document and asks for a specific action taken; entirely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Which thing is he most proud of: a shrinking economy, rising unemployment, more kids living in poverty, more homelessness, or record numbers of New Zealanders giving up and leaving the country?
specificity.explanation: A list of directions of travel with no figures, timeframes or named measures; nothing here could be checked as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m actually very proud that we’ve accelerated $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment that’s actually starting before Christmas.
specificity.explanation: A dollar figure and a deadline; someone could check both against the project list.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We’ve brought inflation down from a record high and pathetic 7.5 percent, from his economic management last time, to 2.7 percent. That’s lowered interest rates. Interest rates are down eight times under this Government; they were up 12 times under his.
specificity.explanation: Four separate figures with clear referents; every one is checkable against a published series.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: As a share of GDP, core Crown expenses fell from 33.1 percent in 2023-24 to 32.5 in 2024-25.
specificity.explanation: Named measure, two years, two figures to one decimal place, sourced to a released document.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is the record 73,900 New Zealand citizens leaving the country a sign that her economic plan is a success; if not, why not?
specificity.explanation: A precise figure tied to a named population, though the plan it is set against is not itself specified.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he think that paragraph 2.68 of the Cabinet Manual has been upheld, where “Public perception is a very important factor. If a conflict arises in relation to the interests of family, whānau, or close associates, Ministers should take appropriate action”; and if so, what appropriate action did the Minister take to avoid public perception of a conflict of interest?
focus.explanation: Scrutiny anchored to a named standard (Cabinet Manual 2.68) and a named process, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he think it's fair to the other farmers and water users in this catchment that his Minister may be risking the ecological health of the catchment by pressuring councils to grant consents for particular individuals?
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific consenting process and its effect on named classes of affected parties; policy content, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Of the Prime Minister, going from the questioner's original draft of the primary question, would he have confidence if any Minister couldn't spell “Ministers” properly?
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or outcome named at all; the entire content is a dig at an opponent.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “Economic growth is going to influence every decision I take this year.”; if so, why did he shrink the economy by almost 1 percent in the last quarter?
focus.explanation: Holds the Prime Minister to a specific quoted commitment and sets it against a specific measured outcome — accountability, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: He’s also a leader that actually says, “We’re not going to do oil and gas”, and what do a lot of New Zealanders do when they go to Australia? They go work in the oil and gas sector. He’s the member that says, “We’re not going to do mining”, but, actually, what do they do when they go to Australia? They go work in mining.
focus.explanation: Names real policy positions (oil and gas, mining) but frames them as the opponent's personal inconsistency rather than engaging the mechanism or numbers.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: On the topic of construction, does he agree with Christopher Luxon, “At the most basic level, the problem is not enough money being spent on new and existing infrastructure.”; if so, why did he slash nearly $3 billion in infrastructure investment in his first year as Prime Minister?
focus.explanation: Sets a quoted commitment against a specific spending figure — named policy, named outcome, the core of the accountability role.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “We’re determined to get the building and construction sector firing on all cylinders.”; if so, is 20,000 job losses in the construction sector the type of firing he was referring to?
focus.explanation: A quoted commitment tested against a specific sector employment outcome — named policy, named number.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Isn’t it funny, the great gaslighter forgets about something called interest rates, which he doesn’t take responsibility for creating. How on earth do you increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation over 7.5 percent, have 12 interest rate rises, and then ask some questions about how the construction industry works? Get back and understand some economics.
focus.explanation: Figures are cited, but they are deployed to disqualify the questioner rather than to address the construction employment question; the weight is on the opponent.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So why does he think billions of dollars of public money is better spent on tax cuts for landlords and tobacco companies instead of the infrastructure that he has cut spending on?
focus.explanation: Names identifiable policies — interest deductibility for landlords, the tobacco excise change, infrastructure spending — even though the framing is partisan.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Again, I’m proud of the fact that, actually, we lowered tax for low- and middle-income working New Zealanders—something the Labour-Greens opposed but that actually put more money into working New Zealanders. That’s a good thing.
focus.explanation: Names a specific tax change and who it applied to, though the opposition-voted-against framing carries part of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Well, it works because you have an economic philosophy that you’re going to spend more, you’re going to borrow more, you’re going to tax more, and it doesn’t matter whether it’s Labour, the Greens, or Te Pāti Māori, that’s what that uni-party is going to do. They’re going to continue with the track and the mess that put us in this position.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what three opposition parties are supposedly like in general — the 'uni-party' framing — with no measure, figure or policy named.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does he think it's fair to the other farmers and water users in this catchment that his Minister may be risking the ecological health of the catchment by pressuring councils to grant consents for particular individuals?
civility.explanation: Pointed scrutiny of a Minister's conduct that edges toward imputing improper favouritism, but is framed conditionally ('may be') and stays on the alleged action rather than the person's character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Of the Prime Minister, going from the questioner's original draft of the primary question, would he have confidence if any Minister couldn't spell “Ministers” properly?
civility.explanation: A jibe at another member's spelling — mockery aimed at the person's competence rather than at anything in the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Which thing is he most proud of: a shrinking economy, rising unemployment, more kids living in poverty, more homelessness, or record numbers of New Zealanders giving up and leaving the country?
civility.explanation: Sarcastic framing ('most proud of') is pointed and needling, but the target is the government's record rather than the Prime Minister as a person.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just say to the member: if you’re serious about it, rather than the crocodile tears why don’t you back it up with some proper action and get in behind backing oil and gas?
civility.explanation: 'Crocodile tears' imputes insincerity — bad faith attributed to the person rather than a criticism of the position.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, what I’d say to the member is that he has a problem with equity and debt—with understanding that—as we saw with the Chorus statement this week, but he also has a major problem understanding that, in construction, interest rates are the critical piece that enables developers to actually borrow money to go off and get things built.
civility.explanation: Twice frames the exchange around the member's failure to understand — an attack on his competence rather than on the argument he made.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Isn’t it funny, the great gaslighter forgets about something called interest rates, which he doesn’t take responsibility for creating. How on earth do you increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation over 7.5 percent, have 12 interest rate rises, and then ask some questions about how the construction industry works? Get back and understand some economics.
civility.explanation: 'The great gaslighter' is a direct attack on the member's honesty and 'Get back and understand some economics' on his competence; both are aimed at the person, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, it works because you have an economic philosophy that you’re going to spend more, you’re going to borrow more, you’re going to tax more, and it doesn’t matter whether it’s Labour, the Greens, or Te Pāti Māori, that’s what that uni-party is going to do. They’re going to continue with the track and the mess that put us in this position.
civility.explanation: Dismissive of parties collectively, but no individual is attacked; on the civility question alone this passes.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “Economic growth is going to influence every decision I take this year.”; if so, why did he shrink the economy by almost 1 percent in the last quarter?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the New Zealand economy contracted by almost 1 percent in the most recently reported quarter.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ quarterly GDP (production measure, seasonally adjusted) for the June 2025 quarter, the latest release before 14 October 2025; true if the fall is close to but under 1.0%, false if the economy grew or fell materially less.

veracity.statement: Well, because we had a very poor inheritance from the previous Government, which was Government spending that went up 84 percent, a lot of it very wasteful. That drove up inflation over 7 percent. That drove up interest rates—there were 12 interest rate rises under the member’s previous Government—and that put the country into recession and raised unemployment.
veracity.explanation: Three checkable claims about the 2017-2023 period: core Crown spending rose 84 percent, inflation exceeded 7 percent, and there were 12 official interest rate rises.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury core Crown expenditure series 2017-18 to 2023-24 for the 84% figure; Stats NZ CPI annual peak for the 'over 7 percent' figure; the RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision record from October 2021 to May 2023 for the count of rises. True if each figure matches within rounding, false if any is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: On the topic of construction, does he agree with Christopher Luxon, “At the most basic level, the problem is not enough money being spent on new and existing infrastructure.”; if so, why did he slash nearly $3 billion in infrastructure investment in his first year as Prime Minister?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that infrastructure investment was cut by nearly $3 billion in the government's first year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury Budget 2024 documents and the Financial Statements of the Government for 2023-24 and 2024-25: compare capital/infrastructure expenditure and the multi-year capital allowance against the previous forecast track. True if the reduction against the inherited track is close to $3 billion, false if the reduction is materially smaller or the figure relies on a measure not comparable year to year.

veracity.statement: I’m actually very proud that we’ve accelerated $7 billion worth of infrastructure investment that’s actually starting before Christmas.
veracity.explanation: Asserts $7 billion of infrastructure investment has been accelerated with construction commencing before December 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government/NZTA/Treasury infrastructure announcements for 2025 listing accelerated projects and their start dates; true if the projects named total about $7 billion with works commencing before 25 December 2025, false if the total is materially lower or the start dates fall later.

veracity.statement: We’ve brought inflation down from a record high and pathetic 7.5 percent, from his economic management last time, to 2.7 percent. That’s lowered interest rates. Interest rates are down eight times under this Government; they were up 12 times under his.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a peak annual inflation rate of 7.5 percent described as a record high, a current rate of 2.7 percent, and eight OCR reductions under this government against twelve rises under the previous one.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI annual series for the peak figure and the most recent quarter before 14 October 2025 for 2.7%; the RBNZ Official Cash Rate decision record for the counts of cuts (from August 2024) and rises (from October 2021). True if each matches, false if the peak was materially below 7.5% or was not a record, or if either count is wrong.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his statement, “We’re determined to get the building and construction sector firing on all cylinders.”; if so, is 20,000 job losses in the construction sector the type of firing he was referring to?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the construction sector has lost 20,000 jobs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ filled jobs / HLFS employment by industry for construction, comparing the latest 2025 release with the peak; true if the fall is about 20,000, false if materially smaller or if the figure requires a non-comparable base period.

veracity.statement: Again, I’m proud of the fact that, actually, we lowered tax for low- and middle-income working New Zealanders—something the Labour-Greens opposed but that actually put more money into working New Zealanders. That’s a good thing.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Labour and the Greens opposed the government's 2024 personal income tax reduction.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The division record for the Taxation (Budget Measures) Act 2024 and Labour/Green party votes on the personal income tax threshold changes; true if both parties voted against, false if either supported it or abstained.

veracity.statement: As a share of GDP, core Crown expenses fell from 33.1 percent in 2023-24 to 32.5 in 2024-25.
veracity.explanation: Asserts core Crown expenses as a share of GDP fell from 33.1 percent to 32.5 percent between the 2023-24 and 2024-25 fiscal years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the year ended 30 June 2025, core Crown expenses as a percentage of GDP; true if the two figures match to one decimal place, false if either differs materially.

veracity.statement: Is the record 73,900 New Zealand citizens leaving the country a sign that her economic plan is a success; if not, why not?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 73,900 New Zealand citizens departed in the period referenced and that this is a record.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration estimates, annual New Zealand-citizen departures for the year ended in the most recent release before 14 October 2025; true if the figure is about 73,900 and exceeds all prior annual totals in the series, false if the number is materially different or has been exceeded before.

veracity.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the cost of utilities are up 19.3 percent from a year earlier, including rates, water charges, and energy bills?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the combined cost of utilities — rates, water charges and energy — rose 19.3 percent in a year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ CPI subgroups for household energy and local authority rates and payments over the year to the most recent quarter before 14 October 2025; true if the combined or relevant index rose about 19.3%, false if the increase is materially lower or the 19.3% figure applies only to a narrower component.

rigor.statement: Well, because we had a very poor inheritance from the previous Government, which was Government spending that went up 84 percent, a lot of it very wasteful. That drove up inflation over 7 percent. That drove up interest rates—there were 12 interest rate rises under the member’s previous Government—and that put the country into recession and raised unemployment.
rigor.explanation: A stated causal chain (spending → inflation → rate rises → recession and unemployment) with figures offered at each step, but it treats domestic spending as the sole cause and ignores the global inflation shock, so the conclusion outruns what was shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: He’s also a leader that actually says, “We’re not going to do oil and gas”, and what do a lot of New Zealanders do when they go to Australia? They go work in the oil and gas sector. He’s the member that says, “We’re not going to do mining”, but, actually, what do they do when they go to Australia? They go work in mining.
rigor.explanation: The inference — that the member's resource policies drive emigration — rests on an unquantified generalisation about what emigrants do, and is a tu quoque aimed at the questioner rather than an account of the migration data.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, what I’d say to the member is that he has a problem with equity and debt—with understanding that—as we saw with the Chorus statement this week, but he also has a major problem understanding that, in construction, interest rates are the critical piece that enables developers to actually borrow money to go off and get things built.
rigor.explanation: There is a real mechanism offered (interest rates govern developers' borrowing costs), but it is asserted rather than evidenced and does not connect to the $3 billion cut that was asked about, so the conclusion is left unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Isn’t it funny, the great gaslighter forgets about something called interest rates, which he doesn’t take responsibility for creating. How on earth do you increase spending by 84 percent, drive up inflation over 7.5 percent, have 12 interest rate rises, and then ask some questions about how the construction industry works? Get back and understand some economics.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the conclusion is that the member has no standing to ask, which rests entirely on his record and the insult rather than on any answer to the 20,000 job losses put to him.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So why does he think billions of dollars of public money is better spent on tax cuts for landlords and tobacco companies instead of the infrastructure that he has cut spending on?
rigor.explanation: A false dichotomy: presents tax relief and infrastructure as the only two uses of the same money, and characterises the tax changes by their most unflattering beneficiaries without establishing the trade-off.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Is it possible to “Spend money on tax cuts”, or is a tax cut when people just keep more of the money that belongs to them in the first place? How does it work?
rigor.explanation: A genuine conceptual point — forgone revenue is not the same as expenditure — but it is loaded onto a contested premise (that the money 'belongs to them in the first place') asserted rather than argued, and it presents the two framings as exhaustive.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the cost of utilities are up 19.3 percent from a year earlier, including rates, water charges, and energy bills?
rigor.explanation: Asserts a causal link between utility price rises and emigration with nothing offered to connect them — a single correlate is presented as the explanation for a migration record.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would encourage that member and her party to reflect on the retrograde decision they have made to not support the repeal of the oil and gas ban.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure — the repeal of the oil and gas ban — and the Opposition's position on it. Policy-directed criticism, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Minister, are you saying that if one can phonetically pronounce “honesty” and “integrity”, then one would be better able to actually write those words properly, and, better still, possibly practice them?
focus.explanation: Hooks onto the literacy policy only as a vehicle for a jibe about opponents' honesty and integrity. No mechanism, cost, cohort or outcome is engaged.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did the Prime Minister give agricultural polluters a free ride instead of requiring them to do their fair share of emissions reductions, given that this means that households and businesses will have to shoulder more of the emissions reduction, increasing the cost of living for everyday New Zealanders?
focus.explanation: Squarely on a policy question — the allocation of emissions-reduction obligations between agriculture and everyone else — and names the consequence she is alleging. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Why is his Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations pushing a bill through this House today that the Waitangi Tribunal has described as a “gross breach” of Te Tiriti, which would, “significantly endanger the Māori-Crown relationship”?
focus.explanation: Names the bill before the House, the responsible Minister and a specific external finding against it. Scrutiny of a named measure, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I reject the characterisation of that question, but I just say to the member, as part of a Labour-Greens Government who wanted to shut down New Zealand farms and send production overseas, why don’t you come on board and actually support that policy too?
focus.explanation: Turns almost entirely on the other parties' past record and posture; the only policy referent is a characterisation of what they "wanted", with no target, figure or mechanism named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: No, I think farmers should be deeply valued and not treated like villains as they were under a Labour-Greens Government.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure or figure — a claim about how the other parties regarded farmers. Content-free party framing of the kind Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In the feedback coming through in her sojourn round the boardrooms of Auckland, she will know that some of the feedback coming from the business community and the energy sector has been to plead with the Opposition to support the Government’s move on energy security.
civility.explanation: "her sojourn round the boardrooms of Auckland" is a sneer at the member personally, implying a junket rather than work. Pointed and landing on the person, though short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: How can he claim that his targets are based on anything other than corporate interests when world-leading climate scientists have described his weakening of methane targets as “a great way of shooting yourself in the foot” and “New Zealand is setting a dangerous precedent that other governments must not follow”?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Prime Minister personally — that his targets are set to serve corporate interests. The framing forecloses any honest motive rather than contesting the target itself.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: She should start listening to the voices of reason in the business community that want bipartisanship on energy policy, because the best thing we could do for this country’s energy security is firm up the gas supply to make sure we keep the lights on.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered (gas firming underpins security), but the conclusion leans on an appeal to authority — the business community as "voices of reason" — rather than on evidence that gas supply is the binding constraint.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Do we have more work to do? Of course we do, but the facts are this: under that last Government’s epic mismanagement of the economy, people fled New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: Post hoc reasoning: the graph he cites establishes only that departures rose from 2020, and he converts coincidence in timing into a causal attribution to "mismanagement" without offering any mechanism or ruling out the obvious confounder of the border reopening.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand that weakening methane targets actually harms farmers’ livelihoods and increases their long-term cost of living as farmers are at the front line of climate-driven extreme weather events that threaten global food production and raise insurance premiums?
rigor.explanation: A real chain of inference is offered — weaker targets, more warming, more extreme weather, higher farm costs and premiums — but it skips the step connecting one country's methane target to a measurable change in the climate exposure of NZ farmers, which is the load-bearing link.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can he claim that his targets are based on anything other than corporate interests when world-leading climate scientists have described his weakening of methane targets as “a great way of shooting yourself in the foot” and “New Zealand is setting a dangerous precedent that other governments must not follow”?
rigor.explanation: A complex question: it presupposes what it purports to ask about, and the support offered is an appeal to authority — that scientists disapprove — which bears on whether the target is sound, not on whose interests set it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, I tell you, this Government is not going to shut down Kiwi farms and send that production to less carbon-efficient places, less productive places, and make global greenhouse gas emissions worse.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy built on a strawman: the question asked about the strength of methane targets, and the answer treats the only alternative to the Government's position as shutting farms down and exporting production.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I reject the characterisation of that question, but I just say to the member, as part of a Labour-Greens Government who wanted to shut down New Zealand farms and send production overseas, why don’t you come on board and actually support that policy too?
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the member's former government's alleged position is irrelevant to whether the current targets are set on corporate interests. No premise addressing the question is offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government’s intention is to put downward pressure on energy prices, which will come from a combination of Resource Management Act (RMA) reform, planning reform, sorting out the dysfunctionality of the energy market through the Electricity Authority, and the hard work being led by the Minister of Energy, and it will come from long-term stability when it comes to gas supply, which is why I repeat, again, that the Opposition should get on board with rational economic policy and realise that New Zealand’s energy security is underpinned by thermal electricity powered by gas.
specificity.explanation: Names real levers — RMA reform, the Electricity Authority, gas supply — but supplies no figures, no price target and no timeframe, so nothing here could be checked against an outcome.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We are putting in place the long-term structural reforms to sort out this economy: planning reform, infrastructure funding and financing, cutting red tape, sorting out the energy sector, boosting—as the Prime Minister said—our trade and services exports including by signing record free-trade deals.
specificity.explanation: A list of policy areas rather than policies: no amounts, no dates, no named instruments. "Cutting red tape" and "sorting out the energy sector" commit to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The latest report shows an incredible improvement in the number of students who are reaching 20 weeks at school at expected levels of phonics, up from 36 percent in term 1 to 58 percent in term 3.
specificity.explanation: Two figures, a named assessment point (the 20-week phonics check) and the terms compared. Directly checkable against the report.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We mandated structured literacy; we introduced a new English curriculum backing structured literacy; we trained over 33,000 teachers in structured literacy; we provided cash to schools for more structured literacy resources; and we provided 349 structured literacy intervention teachers to over 1,240 schools to support students who need help.
specificity.explanation: Named mechanisms plus hard counts — 33,000 teachers trained, 349 intervention teachers, 1,240 schools. Only "provided cash to schools" carries no figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Actually, the number of people leaving, on net, has flattened out.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that net departures from New Zealand have stopped rising and plateaued as at October 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics (monthly and annual net migration, and net migration of NZ citizens) up to September 2025: true if the net outflow has plateaued or declined over the preceding six to twelve months; false if it has continued to increase.

veracity.statement: Are a record number of New Zealanders leaving because the service sector has been contracting for every month since she took office?
veracity.explanation: Two factual assertions embedded in the question: that departures have hit a record, and that the services sector has contracted in every single month since the Government took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: (a) Stats NZ migration data on whether annual departures / net citizen outflow reached a record in the period referenced; (b) the BNZ–BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index for every month from November 2023 to September 2025 — true only if every print is below 50, false if any month printed at or above 50.

veracity.statement: Are a record number of Kiwis leaving because, as Christopher Luxon has said, “If you want a job, go where the jobs are.”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Christopher Luxon said these words, and that departures have reached a record level.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public record (media transcripts, press conference video) of Christopher Luxon's remarks: true if he said words to this effect about people going where the jobs are, false if the quotation is fabricated or materially altered; plus Stats NZ migration data for whether departures reached a record.

veracity.statement: The latest report shows an incredible improvement in the number of students who are reaching 20 weeks at school at expected levels of phonics, up from 36 percent in term 1 to 58 percent in term 3.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2025 phonics check data shows students at expected levels at the 20-week check rose from 36% in term 1 to 58% in term 3.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education phonics check reporting for 2025: true if the term 1 and term 3 proportions of students at expected level at the 20-week check are 36% and 58%; false if the published figures differ materially or the comparison is between non-comparable cohorts.

veracity.statement: For our tamariki Māori, I'm especially proud that 25 percent were at expectations in term 1 at their 20-week check, and this has risen to 43 percent in term 3 after two short terms.
veracity.explanation: Asserts specific ethnicity-disaggregated phonics check results for Māori students: 25% at expectation in term 1 rising to 43% in term 3.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education 2025 phonics check data disaggregated by ethnicity: true if Māori students at expectation at the 20-week check are reported at 25% (term 1) and 43% (term 3); false if the published figures differ materially.

veracity.statement: Why is his Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations pushing a bill through this House today that the Waitangi Tribunal has described as a “gross breach” of Te Tiriti, which would, “significantly endanger the Māori-Crown relationship”?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal characterised the bill in question as a "gross breach" of Te Tiriti and said it would "significantly endanger the Māori-Crown relationship".
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's report on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill: true if the report contains those phrases applied to this bill; false if the words are absent, or are drawn from a different inquiry or applied to a different proposal.

veracity.statement: Our farmers are the world’s most productive, best, and most carbon-efficient farmers in the world.
veracity.explanation: A superlative claim that New Zealand farmers rank first globally on both productivity and emissions efficiency.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Peer-reviewed emissions-intensity comparisons (e.g. AgResearch / FAO dairy and meat carbon-footprint studies) and OECD agricultural productivity data: true if New Zealand ranks first on emissions per unit of product and on productivity; false if any comparable country ranks ahead on either measure.

veracity.statement: The Court of Appeal lowered the threshold.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Court of Appeal reduced the legal test for recognition of customary marine title under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal's 2023 Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) decision on s 58 of the Act, compared with the High Court's approach: true if the Court of Appeal adopted a less stringent test for exclusive use and occupation; false if it applied or tightened the existing test.

specificity.statement: This is why the Government has set the methane target at a range of 14 to 24 percent below 2017 levels by 2050.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact target range, the baseline year and the deadline — fully checkable and actionable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What we need now to focus on is the achievement of a durable and sustainable peace, the disarmament and dissolution of Hamas, and the rapid development of Palestinian institutions capable of forming a legitimate and credible Government in both the West Bank and Gaza.
specificity.explanation: Names three concrete conditions and the territories they apply to, but supplies no mechanism, no New Zealand contribution and no timeframe by which any of them would be judged met.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: To back the new target, the Government is already investing more than $400 million with industry to speed up the development and roll-out of methane-cutting tools.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a present, committed co-investment of over $400 million with industry in methane-reduction technology.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget/MPI and AgriZeroNZ funding documents on public plus industry money committed to agricultural methane mitigation tools; true if the committed total exceeds $400 million and is already being spent, false if the figure is materially lower or is an aspiration rather than a commitment.

veracity.statement: Whilst the targets are extremely challenging, farmers have welcomed them and confirmed that they will meet these challenges head-on.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the farming sector's actual, recorded reaction to the new methane target was one of welcome and acceptance.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public statements from the major farming bodies (Federated Farmers, DairyNZ, Beef + Lamb NZ) in the weeks following the October 2025 announcement; true if their responses were predominantly supportive, false if they predominantly criticised or rejected the target range.

veracity.statement: Our primary sector earns nearly $60 billion in export revenue each year for New Zealand.
veracity.explanation: Asserts an annual export revenue figure for the primary sector.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: MPI Situation and Outlook for Primary Industries food and fibre export revenue for the year stated; true if annual export revenue is at or near $60 billion, false if materially below (e.g. under $55 billion).

veracity.statement: We note that while Hamas has released 20 hostages, Israel has released around 2,000 Palestinian prisoners.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the numbers on each side of the October 2025 hostage-for-prisoner exchange.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The exchange figures published by the ICRC, the Israeli Prison Service and major wire agencies for the October 2025 ceasefire exchange; true if 20 living hostages were released and the Palestinian prisoner release was of the order of 2,000, false if either count is materially different.

veracity.statement: We have seen not a press release, not a tweet, not a parliamentary question, and the question is: why this deafening silence?
veracity.explanation: Asserts a complete absence of public comment from pro-Palestinian advocates in New Zealand in the week following the ceasefire.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Public output of the main New Zealand pro-Palestinian campaign groups (e.g. PSNA) and of the Green/Te Pāti Māori MPs associated with them for the week of 7–14 October 2025 — press releases, social media posts and the parliamentary written-question register; false if any such release, post or question about the ceasefire exists in that window, true if none does.

rigor.statement: You can't solve climate change by shutting down the world's best farmers and sending that production overseas.
rigor.explanation: False dichotomy and strawman: the conclusion is drawn against an alternative (shutting farms down and offshoring production) that nobody in the debate proposed, and the leakage premise is asserted rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The evidence shows this is working, with the phonics data announced yesterday.
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation: a single indicator (phonics check data) is offered as proof of the far broader conclusion that the whole programme of "backing teachers" is working, with no link drawn between the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In 2023, there was a terrible strike action—tens of thousands of primary and area school and secondary principals and teachers participated in the historic walkout, followed by a further three days after that, and then rolling strikes for a whole term. So if she wants to know how long it takes, she should ask herself that.
rigor.explanation: Tu quoque: the question was how many strikers it would take before this Government acts, and the reply establishes only that strikes also occurred under the questioner's government. That premise does not bear on the conclusion invited.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How many teachers, principals, and support staff going on strike will it take before the Government finally takes them seriously?
rigor.explanation: Loaded (complex) question: it presupposes the contested conclusion that the Government is not taking the strikers seriously, offering no premise for it.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, that member should know, because she has a very short memory.
civility.explanation: Not a direct insult, but a jab at the questioner personally — imputing forgetfulness rather than engaging the question. Under the re-anchored scale this is a genuine failure of the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does she stand by her statement “I am not aware of any of those conversations or any of the details that may or may not have been talked about” in relation to the strikes; if so, does she think it’s acceptable for the Minister of Education to not be across the detail?
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the Minister's personal command of her portfolio, but framed as a question about ministerial responsibility rather than as an attack on her character.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: New Zealand commends the leadership of the United States, Donald Trump, Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, Indonesia, and other countries in bringing this deal together, and we view the events of the last 24 hours as providing momentum for peace and constituting a significant first step towards ending this devastating conflict—and not making stupid statements, like the people on my right.
civility.explanation: A clear personal jibe appended to an otherwise substantive statement — calling identified members opposite makers of "stupid statements" targets them rather than any argument they advanced.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: First of all, that they recognise that it was the US President and others from Muslim countries who brought this about and that anti-Americanism or any other sentiment is of no value when you’re concerned about peace, and particularly if you’re some arrogant twit that arrived here five minutes ago and doesn’t give a concern about this country’s initiative and its peace over the years.
civility.explanation: Contemptuous personal abuse — calling another member an "arrogant twit" and impugning both their standing in the country and their motives, wholly detached from any argument.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In 2023, there was a terrible strike action—tens of thousands of primary and area school and secondary principals and teachers participated in the historic walkout, followed by a further three days after that, and then rolling strikes for a whole term. So if she wants to know how long it takes, she should ask herself that.
focus.explanation: Names a specific past event, but the weight of the answer is on the opposing party's record rather than on the pay negotiation or any measure the Government is taking.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Because you’re all about performative politics.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the other side is "really like" — no policy, measure, figure or outcome is named.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand that Māori exercise kaitiakitanga and protection for the benefit of all of us here in Aotearoa—for example, when they veto applications for private companies to mine in our precious moana, and that by removing recognition of customary rights in the takutai moana, his Government has taken this away?
focus.explanation: Names a specific legislative change (removal of customary rights recognition in the takutai moana) and a specific consequence (loss of the power to refuse seabed mining applications). Squarely on the policy; no party-directed content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What good is capping fees when under-funded practices start charging for double consultations, leading to the pensioner who wrote to me saying, “I pay $91 for a 15-minute visit, and you’re only allowed to talk about one thing. If you want to talk about two things, you need to pay for another $91. I cannot afford to pay this.”?
focus.explanation: Names the government's fee-cap policy and identifies a specific claimed workaround (double-consultation charging) with a concrete outcome. This is scrutiny of a named measure, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As I say, you can’t trust Labour when it comes to GP fees.
focus.explanation: A general claim about an opposing party's trustworthiness. It gestures at a policy area but names no measure, figure or outcome — the content is the other team's character, not the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Does he stand by his decision to exclude Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the Regulatory Standards Bill, given that this bill defines the constitutional test for every future law?
focus.explanation: Names a specific bill and a specific drafting decision within it. Legitimate scrutiny of a named measure.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: How can he continue to deny the link between his tightening of the emergency housing entry criteria and the unprecedented increase in homelessness, when even pregnant women are now being denied access?
focus.explanation: Names a specific policy change (tightened emergency housing entry criteria) and the outcome it is said to have produced. Holding a minister to account for a named decision is on-policy scrutiny, not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Is it the case, like when MSD issued grants for homeless people to buy tents, or when women and children fleeing domestic violence were denied emergency housing, that the Minister knew there was an issue, but only acted when this was made public?
focus.explanation: Anchored in two named, specific incidents in the emergency housing system, but the weight of the question is on the Minister's conduct rather than on the policy mechanism or its remedy.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Does the Prime Minister understand that Māori exercise kaitiakitanga and protection for the benefit of all of us here in Aotearoa—for example, when they veto applications for private companies to mine in our precious moana, and that by removing recognition of customary rights in the takutai moana, his Government has taken this away?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the domain and the mechanism it says has been lost, but names no Act, section, threshold or case, and gives no figures — a direction with detail rather than something precisely checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Our Government has delivered the biggest ever funding boost for GPs—$175 million this year alone—and capped fee increases at 3 percent, keeping costs stable and predictable.
specificity.explanation: Carries a dollar figure, a period, and a named mechanism with a numeric cap. Someone could go and check the appropriation and the fee-review settings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What good is capping fees when under-funded practices start charging for double consultations, leading to the pensioner who wrote to me saying, “I pay $91 for a 15-minute visit, and you’re only allowed to talk about one thing. If you want to talk about two things, you need to pay for another $91. I cannot afford to pay this.”?
specificity.explanation: Gives a named mechanism, a dollar figure and a consultation length. Falls short of 1.0 because the scale of the practice — how many practices, how widespread — is not quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why is he proceeding with the Regulatory Standards Bill without a public mandate, when 99 percent of the 159,000 submitters opposed it?
specificity.explanation: Two precise figures attached to a named bill and a named process. Directly checkable against the select committee's submission analysis.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We, on this side of the House, are genuinely concerned by those who may be rough sleeping, and that’s why Minister Bishop and myself have taken direct action over the last six weeks to announce an additional 300 funded places for Housing First and additional support for transitional housing, and have also given some direction around both redirections and also the exercise of discretion by Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora—the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).
specificity.explanation: Names a programme, a number of places and a timeframe. The transitional housing support and the MSD 'direction' are left unquantified, which keeps it below the top of the scale.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: As a Government, we’re just returning what was a lowered threshold under the courts—we’re returning it back to what Parliament intended.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about the relationship between the courts' interpretation, the 2011 statute and Parliament's intent — specifically that judicial interpretation lowered the threshold and the amendment merely restores it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Compare the customary marine title test in s 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 as enacted, the parliamentary record of the 2011 debates/select committee report on the intended threshold, and the Court of Appeal (Re Edwards, 2023) and Supreme Court (Whakatōhea, 2024) rulings on that test. True if the courts' applied test is demonstrably less demanding than the statutory text and the recorded 2011 parliamentary intent, and the amendment restores that original test; false if the courts applied the test as enacted, or if the amendment sets a threshold higher than the 2011 provision.

veracity.statement: As the member will be aware, this follows a 30 percent increase in GP fees between 2017 and 2023.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific quantified change in general practice fees over a named six-year period.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ / Ministry of Health annual general practice fees data (the standard adult consultation fee series) for 2017 and 2023. True if the average or standard adult fee rose by approximately 30 percent across that period; false if the recorded increase is materially different.

veracity.statement: Today, 90 percent of adults without a community services card pay $70 or less to see their general practitioner.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a current distributional fact about what non-CSC adults pay for a GP visit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health NZ general practice fee schedule data for 2025 covering non-community-services-card adult patients. True if the share of such patients enrolled at practices charging $70 or less is around 90 percent; false if materially lower.

veracity.statement: Our Government has delivered the biggest ever funding boost for GPs—$175 million this year alone—and capped fee increases at 3 percent, keeping costs stable and predictable.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: a $175 million one-year funding figure, and the superlative that it is the largest GP funding boost ever made. The superlative is the part most at risk.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Vote Health appropriations and Budget 2025 primary care documents: the 2025/26 general practice capitation uplift, and the historical series of annual GP funding uplifts. Also the annual fee review settings for 2025. True if the 2025/26 uplift is approximately $175 million and is the largest single-year GP funding increase on record, and the fee increase cap was set at 3 percent; false if the figure is materially different or a larger prior uplift exists.

veracity.statement: Was a heart patient correct when they wrote to me, “On several occasions, I have avoided visiting the GP because I cannot afford the fees. Instead, I end up going to the emergency room and waiting for hours to be seen.”, or is this patient’s experience what the Minister meant when he said concern about fees was “misinformation put about by the Labour Party”?
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific quoted characterisation to the Minister. The checkable assertion is that he said it, not whether the patient's account is accurate.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The public record of Simeon Brown's statements as Minister of Health (Hansard, press releases, media interviews) in 2025. True if he characterised concern about GP fees as misinformation put about by the Labour Party in substantially those words; false if no such statement exists or the quoted words materially misrepresent what he said.

veracity.statement: Does he stand by his decision to exclude Te Tiriti o Waitangi from the Regulatory Standards Bill, given that this bill defines the constitutional test for every future law?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Regulatory Standards Bill sets the constitutional test for every future law — a claim about the bill's legal reach and bindingness.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Regulatory Standards Bill as introduced in 2025 and its explanatory note: whether it imposes a binding, generally applicable consistency requirement on all future legislation, or a non-binding set of principles with an advisory board and disclosure statements. True if the bill establishes a mandatory constitutional-style test governing every future law; false if compliance is advisory, non-justiciable, or does not apply to all future legislation.

veracity.statement: Why is he proceeding with the Regulatory Standards Bill without a public mandate, when 99 percent of the 159,000 submitters opposed it?
veracity.explanation: Asserts both a submission count and the proportion of submitters opposed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Finance and Expenditure Committee's submission tally and analysis for the Regulatory Standards Bill 2025. True if roughly 159,000 submissions were received and about 99 percent of those expressing a view opposed the bill; false if either the total or the opposition share is materially different.

veracity.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that the success of policies such as structured literacy and charter schools make the case that it is possible to uplift young Māori educational outcomes without making any reference to the Treaty whatsoever?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as established fact that structured literacy and charter schools have succeeded — the charter school reopening and the structured literacy rollout were both recent at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published evaluation evidence as at October 2025 on structured literacy (Ministry of Education implementation and achievement data since the 2024–25 rollout) and on charter schools reopened in 2025, specifically for Māori students. True if outcome data show measured gains for young Māori attributable to those policies; false if no outcome data yet exist or show no such gain.

veracity.statement: There are a number of people who may be declined emergency housing, but many—in fact, over half of them—are actually given some form of support.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific proportion — more than half — of those declined emergency housing nonetheless receive some form of support.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Social Development emergency housing special needs grant data for 2024–25: the number of applications declined and the share of declined applicants recorded as receiving some other form of housing or income support. True if over half of declined applicants received other support; false if the recorded share is at or below half.

veracity.statement: We, on this side of the House, are genuinely concerned by those who may be rough sleeping, and that’s why Minister Bishop and myself have taken direct action over the last six weeks to announce an additional 300 funded places for Housing First and additional support for transitional housing, and have also given some direction around both redirections and also the exercise of discretion by Te Manatū Whakahiato Ora—the Ministry of Social Development (MSD).
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific ministerial announcement of 300 additional funded Housing First places within the preceding six weeks.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Government announcements and Housing/HUD releases between late August and 14 October 2025. True if an additional 300 funded Housing First places were announced by Bishop and Potaka in that window; false if no such announcement exists, the number differs materially, or it predates the six-week window.

civility.statement: Was a heart patient correct when they wrote to me, “On several occasions, I have avoided visiting the GP because I cannot afford the fees. Instead, I end up going to the emergency room and waiting for hours to be seen.”, or is this patient’s experience what the Minister meant when he said concern about fees was “misinformation put about by the Labour Party”?
civility.explanation: Pointed: it uses the Minister's own words to imply he would dismiss a real patient. It engages what he said rather than attacking him personally, so it edges toward the person without landing on them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: But in my humble opinion, respectfully, I think it is potentially reckless and insensitive that the member would consider it appropriate for officialdom to ask women seeking emergency housing support, often in difficult circumstances, if they are hapū or not.
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy onto the member, calling his position reckless and insensitive toward vulnerable women. The politeness formula does not change that it is the member's judgement and decency being impugned, not the argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Is it the case, like when MSD issued grants for homeless people to buy tents, or when women and children fleeing domestic violence were denied emergency housing, that the Minister knew there was an issue, but only acted when this was made public?
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith to the Minister personally — that he knew of failures and deliberately sat on them until publicity forced his hand — and frames it as a pattern. Short of a direct insult, but it goes to his motives rather than the policy.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: We are focused on affordability and accessibility, including extending prescriptions to 12 months, where safe, which will save patients up to $105 per year in GP fees starting from early next year.
divination.explanation: Forecasts a dated economic outcome for patients — an annual saving of up to $105 in GP fees beginning early in 2026 — rather than merely promising the Government will legislate.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Whether the 12-month prescription regime is operative in New Zealand by mid-2026, and whether Health NZ / Ministry of Health or Pharmac assessment confirms annual GP-fee savings of up to $105 for patients on long-term medication. True if the regime is in force by that date and the stated saving is borne out for the patients described; false if it is not in force or the realised saving is materially below the stated figure.

rigor.statement: Does the Prime Minister agree that the success of policies such as structured literacy and charter schools make the case that it is possible to uplift young Māori educational outcomes without making any reference to the Treaty whatsoever?
rigor.explanation: The conclusion is loaded into the premise: the success of the two named policies is asserted rather than shown, and even granting it, two programmes operating without a Treaty reference would not establish the general proposition that Māori outcomes can be lifted without any such reference. A hasty generalisation resting on a presupposed premise.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But in my humble opinion, respectfully, I think it is potentially reckless and insensitive that the member would consider it appropriate for officialdom to ask women seeking emergency housing support, often in difficult circumstances, if they are hapū or not.
rigor.explanation: Strawman. The question asked how many pregnant women were refused emergency housing; it did not propose that officials interrogate applicants about pregnancy. The conclusion is drawn against a position the member did not take.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So could he just explain to me how it is that customary marine title rights are some kind of second-tier property rights compared with the rights of other New Zealanders?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the bill — the legal status the legislation gives customary marine title relative to other property rights. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Then the next one is whether he can give an example of where, in previous cases, a marine and coastal area, or a customary title, has been recognised, and what makes this particular one different to others that have been recognised in the past.
focus.explanation: A request for precedent on how customary title has previously been recognised — entirely about the operation of the legislation, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: In doing so, it recognised that customary rights of Māori are rights in respect of coastal and marine areas that have existed since at least 1840; that is to say that they are property rights.
rigor.explanation: A premise (rights existing since at least 1840) offered for a conclusion (they are property rights), but the step is asserted rather than shown — longevity of a right does not by itself make it proprietary. A real gap between what is offered and what is concluded, though not a fallacy.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is still the view of the Government that it still deviates from Parliament’s intention, because we’ve seen a couple of decisions that have been made since the Supreme Court decision and the Supreme Court test which have seen very large proportions of coastlines in the Wairarapa and Kāpiti that have been given customary marine title.
rigor.explanation: Evidence is offered (post-Supreme Court decisions granting title over large stretches of coast) and the conclusion tracks it, but it rests on an unstated premise that Parliament intended few or small grants. Outcome-based inference: the size of the awards is treated as proof the test is wrong, without independent evidence of the intended threshold.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, obviously enabling one group of New Zealanders who had received customary marine title to grant resource consents is a very significant deviation from normal expectations of New Zealanders living in this country in a democratic, modern democracy to have an equal say in decisions affecting their lives and their environment and what goes on around them.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion leans on "obviously" and an appeal to "normal expectations" rather than on anything offered. It also assumes without argument that a recognised property right held by particular owners is inconsistent with everyone having an equal say — an assumption that, if applied generally, would make all private property rights a deviation. The premise doing the work is unstated and unsupported.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: We have fishing rights to rivers for trout in the UK that have been recognised since medieval times, and you can't dam the river with the resource consent or their equivalent there.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that private river fishing rights in the UK are long-standing, medieval in origin, and strong enough to block damming of the river.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: English property/common law on private several fisheries and riparian fishing rights: true if such private fishing rights in rivers are recognised in English law with an origin traceable to the medieval period (pre-1500, e.g. rights predating Magna Carta 1215), and if English water-abstraction/impoundment law gives the holder of such a fishery a right to prevent damming that would destroy it; false if private river fishing rights in the UK are a modern statutory creation or carry no protection against impoundment.

veracity.statement: The Supreme Court agreed with the Government that the Court of Appeal had got that wrong, and indicated their own expression of what section 58 meant.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court accepted the Crown's position that the Court of Appeal misread s 58 and set out its own test. The question for the resolver is whether the Court in fact sided with the Crown on that point, or departed from the Court of Appeal on different grounds while rejecting the Crown's argument.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment on customary marine title under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 (the Whakatōhea / Re Edwards appeal): true if the Court held that the Court of Appeal erred in its interpretation of the s 58 test — in particular the "exclusively used and occupied … without substantial interruption" limb — and substituted its own interpretation; false if it upheld the Court of Appeal's approach on that limb, or if it did not accept the Crown's argument that the Court of Appeal had erred.

veracity.statement: It is still the view of the Government that it still deviates from Parliament’s intention, because we’ve seen a couple of decisions that have been made since the Supreme Court decision and the Supreme Court test which have seen very large proportions of coastlines in the Wairarapa and Kāpiti that have been given customary marine title.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that since the Supreme Court ruling, courts applying its test have awarded customary marine title over very large proportions of the Wairarapa and Kāpiti coastlines.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court customary marine title judgments issued after the Supreme Court decision covering the Wairarapa and Kāpiti coasts: true if those decisions granted customary marine title over a large share of the coastline in each area; false if the awards covered only limited stretches, or if no such post-Supreme Court decisions for those coasts exist.

veracity.statement: When this was done, this was an arrangement between the National Party of the time and the Māori Party, and it was an agreement in response to changing the previous Labour Government’s Foreshore and Seabed Act, which claimed title for the Crown, with the exception of areas where there was landholdings abutting that piece of the land.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the political provenance of the 2011 Act (a National–Māori Party deal replacing Labour's 2004 legislation) and characterises what the 2004 Act did to title in the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 (which parties negotiated and voted for it) and the text of the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004: true if the 2011 Act was an agreement between National and the Māori Party repealing the 2004 Act, and the 2004 Act vested ownership of the public foreshore and seabed in the Crown while leaving existing private titles intact; false if the 2011 Act was not a National–Māori Party arrangement, or if the 2004 Act did not vest title in the Crown on those terms.

specificity.statement: I’ll be bringing in Amendment Paper 380, which has an amended preamble, and it’s required because the Supreme Court and the High Court have issued relevant judgments since the original bill was introduced, and so they’ve been added into Part 1, clause 4 and the preamble, and different parts of the legislation, and also to give effect to Cabinet’s decision that the bill won’t apply to Ngā Rohe Moana o Ngā Hapū o Ngāti Porou.
specificity.explanation: Names the instrument (Amendment Paper 380), the exact provisions amended (Part 1, clause 4 and the preamble), the reason, and the named area carved out. Someone could go and check every element.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Now, the member is quite within his rights to say that “That’s not the right threshold”, “It should be a different threshold”, “There should be no threshold”—that’s fine.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested committee-stage exchange where the Minister is being directly challenged, so incivility was available. He concedes the opponent's entitlement to disagree and engages the disagreement as a question of thresholds rather than attacking Steve Abel.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That was the goal and that’s how it was always explained: that you had to achieve two legs, the first being to recognise it through tikanga, and the second requiring applicants to have held a specified area and “exclusively used and occupied the area from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption”.
specificity.explanation: Names both statutory limbs of the test, quotes the operative statutory wording, and fixes the date (1840). Anyone could go to the Act and check or act on this; it is not a direction-of-travel statement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: On page 15 of that analysis, point 44: “If the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the Crown, it could mean the additional time and resource on progressing amendments would not be required”, and the Supreme Court did rule in favour of the Crown.
specificity.explanation: Cites a named document, a page number and a numbered paragraph, and quotes it directly. Maximally checkable — a reader can go straight to the source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Canadian case law that the Minister was talking about there were cases like Calder v Attorney-General of British Columbia that was decided in 1973, which sets out a framework that is used all around the world in common law jurisdictions to determine both the extinguishment of title by radical title of the Crown and customary rights and interests that exist in land after that has occurred, and also Guerin v the Queen in 1984.
