specificity.explanation: Names two specific authorities with their years and states what doctrinal work each is said to do. Precise enough that another member could look the cases up and dispute the characterisation.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That was the goal and that’s how it was always explained: that you had to achieve two legs, the first being to recognise it through tikanga, and the second requiring applicants to have held a specified area and “exclusively used and occupied the area from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption”.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the 2011 Act's test for customary marine title has two limbs — holding the area in accordance with tikanga, and exclusive use and occupation from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of s 58 of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 on the New Zealand Legislation website. True if s 58 sets out both limbs and uses the quoted 'exclusively used and occupied ... from 1840 to the present day without substantial interruption' wording; false if the section contains no such two-limb test or materially different wording.

veracity.statement: On page 15 of that analysis, point 44: “If the Supreme Court ruled in favour of the Crown, it could mean the additional time and resource on progressing amendments would not be required”, and the Supreme Court did rule in favour of the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Asserts (a) that the supplementary analysis at page 15, paragraph 44, says progressing amendments might not be required if the Crown won, and (b) that the Supreme Court did in fact rule in the Crown's favour.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Page 15, point 44 of the supplementary regulatory impact analysis for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill, plus the Supreme Court's judgment of 2 December 2024 in the Te Whakatōhea (Edwards) customary marine title appeals. True if the quoted paragraph appears substantially as given and the Court allowed the Attorney-General's/Crown appeal on the s 58 test; false if the paragraph is not there or the Crown's appeal was dismissed.

veracity.statement: Te Arawhiti’s view was that consideration of the appeals by the Supreme Court could have resolved the issue, and they advised the Minister against these amendments being made until such a time as the Supreme Court finding came in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the responsible agency, Te Arawhiti, formally advised the Minister to hold off on the amendments pending the Supreme Court's judgment, on the view that the appeal could resolve the issue.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary regulatory impact analysis / departmental advice for the Bill, particularly page 14 as cited. True if the agency's stated preference was retaining the status quo and awaiting the Supreme Court judgment; false if the advice records no such preference or recommends proceeding with the amendments regardless.

veracity.statement: The Canadian case law that the Minister was talking about there were cases like Calder v Attorney-General of British Columbia that was decided in 1973, which sets out a framework that is used all around the world in common law jurisdictions to determine both the extinguishment of title by radical title of the Crown and customary rights and interests that exist in land after that has occurred, and also Guerin v the Queen in 1984.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Calder v Attorney-General of British Columbia was decided in 1973 and Guerin v The Queen in 1984, and that Calder supplies a widely-used common law framework on extinguishment of title and surviving customary interests.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Supreme Court of Canada law reports for both cases. True if Calder was decided in 1973 and Guerin in 1984 and Calder is standardly cited for the recognition/extinguishment of aboriginal title at common law; false if the years are wrong or the cases do not deal with that subject matter.

focus.statement: That’s not what the Parliament passed in 2011, and so there have been different interpretations of what that threshold should be, and that’s what we’re seeking to establish clearly with this amendment bill.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — the 2011 statutory threshold, the divergence in its interpretation, and what the amendment bill is meant to do. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That preamble would say that, essentially, this House has a disagreement with the interpretation of the law by our court system, and not only are we going to change the way that they would reinterpret future cases but that there would be a retrospective element of rehearing cases which have already passed.
focus.explanation: Engages the specific mechanism of the bill — the use of a preamble, its prospective effect on interpretation, and its retrospective effect on decided cases. No party content whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I will make a final analogy before seeking a response from the Minister: it is as if the Supreme Court banged the nail into the wall upon which we can hang the picture of Māori customary rights as a principle—a core principle—that upholds Te Tiriti o Waitangi. They clarified what the intention was from 2011, and through this amendment, the Minister is coming along with a sledgehammer and smashing that nail into the wall, destroying the actual intention of 2011, which was clarified by the Supreme Court finding.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — that the amendment destroys rather than restores the 2011 intention — is carried here by an extended metaphor rather than by any offered inference; the nail-and-sledgehammer image assumes the very thing in dispute (that the Court's reading is the 2011 intention). He gets partial credit because he cited the Finlayson statement and the Te Arawhiti advice earlier in the same speech, so the assumption is not wholly unsupported in context.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s fine for him to have a new policy direction, but why would we pass in legislation that the courts have made the wrong call, when, in 2011, that certainly seems to have been the intent.
rigor.explanation: A valid conditional argument given its premises: she has set out the responsible Minister's September 2010 statement of policy intent and the case law he pointed to, and concludes that legislating a finding of judicial error is unwarranted if the courts tracked that intent. The gap is that a Minister's public explanation is evidence of, but not identical to, the intention of Parliament — the inference leans on that equation without defending it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: However, what smarts even more and rubs salt in the wound is the fact that there was consultation with commercial fishing interests, which have already got statutory protections.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Crown consulted commercial fishing interests before finalising the proposed amendments, and that those interests already hold statutory protections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Waitangi Tribunal's report on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill and the Crown's own consultation record (Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti officials' advice and Cabinet papers): true if the record shows the fishing industry was consulted prior to the amendments being finalised; false if no such consultation is recorded. The second limb is settled by whether the Fisheries Act 1996 and Māori Fisheries settlement legislation confer statutory protections on commercial fishing interests.

veracity.statement: I think it’s also important to note that they found that the Crown breached its principles of active protection, as well as good government, by proposing those amendments.
veracity.explanation: Relays a specific finding attributed to the Waitangi Tribunal: that the Crown breached the Treaty principles of active protection and of good government by proposing the takutai moana amendments.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Waitangi Tribunal's urgent inquiry report into the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill: true if the report expressly finds breaches of both the principle of active protection and the principle of good government; false if it finds neither, or names different principles.

veracity.statement: What we've seen in recent cases, based on the Supreme Court test, is entire coastlines being granted CMT.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that courts applying the Supreme Court's test have granted customary marine title over entire coastlines, rather than over discrete stretches. The checkable content is the geographic extent of CMT orders made since that decision.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The CMT orders and judgments issued by the High Court and Court of Appeal following the Supreme Court's decision in the Whakatōhea (Edwards) litigation: true if the awarded areas cover the whole of the coastlines within the application areas; false if the orders are confined to specific bays, stretches or hapū rohe within those coastlines.

divination.statement: As a result, applicants will be forced to have their cases reheard, burdening them further, financially and emotionally as well.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that, once the amendments are in force, customary marine title applicants whose cases have already been through the courts will have to litigate them again.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: High Court and Court of Appeal records for Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act customary marine title applications: true if applicants whose applications were already heard or determined before the amendment are required to have those cases reheard or re-argued under the amended tests; false if determined applications are preserved and no rehearings are required.

civility.statement: It’s well and good that we have National Ministers turning up to celebrate 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, but, surely, if their research and their findings are valued enough, they should be reflected in the preamble of this bill.
civility.explanation: Imputes a degree of tokenism to National Ministers — attending a celebration while ignoring the findings — but it is aimed at a group rather than an individual and stops short of a personal attack.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To an earlier point the Minister made about the problem of customary marine title interfering with other users’ rights—and acknowledging the well-made point of my colleague Hūhana Lyndon that it seems that, frequently, it is the rights of non-Māori that are preferenced time and again over the rights of iwi Māori: for a Minister that purports to believe in property rights, I wonder that he can’t recognise the first property rights of this country, customary marine title, with a greater confidence and certainty.
civility.explanation: "Purports to believe" imputes insincerity to the Minister personally rather than testing the position on its merits — a bad-faith imputation, though delivered without abuse or mockery.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s well and good that we have National Ministers turning up to celebrate 50 years of the Waitangi Tribunal, but, surely, if their research and their findings are valued enough, they should be reflected in the preamble of this bill.
focus.explanation: Carries a concrete policy ask (that Tribunal findings be written into the bill's preamble), but the weight of the sentence is a jab at how National Ministers behave rather than at the mechanism itself.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So that is why we believe this legislation is required: to restore the parliamentary intent, which was a high threshold, and specific parts of the coastline, not entire coastline.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the measure before the House — the threshold, the intended scope, and why the amendment is being brought. No party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Did the Minister speak to Whakatōhea? Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Wairarapa? Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Aotea Harbour?
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at the process by which the amendment was developed and at the specific groups affected; no party-directed content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that is why we believe this legislation is required: to restore the parliamentary intent, which was a high threshold, and specific parts of the coastline, not entire coastline.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the premises he laid out: if the 2011 Act was intended to apply a high threshold to specific parts of the coastline, and courts are now awarding title far more broadly, amending legislation to restore that threshold follows. The gap is that original ministerial expectations about extent are treated as equivalent to the statutory test, which is a real but not fatal step.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Did the Minister speak to Whakatōhea? Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Wairarapa? Did the Minister speak to the tribes of Aotea Harbour?
specificity.explanation: Names three particular iwi and rohe rather than asking generally about consultation, so the answer is checkable one group at a time. It stops short of dates or documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: With respect to its application to other pieces of legislation, my question to the Minister on this part is: in recognising customary take of seafood and the issuing of permits as such, does that come under the customary title and occupation piece that the Minister is proposing here?
specificity.explanation: Ties a named clause of the bill to a named existing regime — customary seafood take and permitting — so the Minister can answer yes or no about a defined interaction. Falls short of 1.0 because the permitting regime is not identified by its own statute or regulation.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would like to know from the Minister: are there other factors, such as he didn’t want to have to pay for the funding for legal representation through the courts for claimants, because that was causing the Crown’s books some concern, and he had quite a bit of pressure to bring things into line and there was no other foreseeable way to stop those costs?
civility.explanation: Framed as a question, but it imputes a self-interested motive to the Minister personally — that he legislated over the courts to avoid paying claimants' legal costs. That is an imputation of bad faith rather than criticism of the policy, though softened by the invitation to rebut it.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would like to know from the Minister: are there other factors, such as he didn’t want to have to pay for the funding for legal representation through the courts for claimants, because that was causing the Crown’s books some concern, and he had quite a bit of pressure to bring things into line and there was no other foreseeable way to stop those costs?
rigor.explanation: The inference runs from a budget pressure to a motive with nothing offered to connect them — no document, decision or statement linking the funding costs to the drafting choice. Suggestive questioning in place of evidence; the conclusion is insinuated rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There hadn’t been an Act of Parliament passed between 1854 and 2004 that actively extinguished the Māori right to the takutai moana, so it stands that it was still there in 2004.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: if a right exists and no statute has extinguished it, it survives. The conclusion follows directly from the stated premise, and the premise is the operative legal test rather than an appeal or an anecdote.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’ve already been told there’s cuts everywhere—cut, cut, cut—and yet we see this Government bringing legislation in, just in the preamble itself, changing the nature by which we have to prove our connection and provide evidence of physical use and occupation, which is inconsistent with the test based on tikanga.
rigor.explanation: The core inference is sound — a heavier evidential burden requires resourcing, and resourcing is being cut, so the change is unfunded. But the final clause, that a physical use and occupation test is inconsistent with a tikanga-based test, is asserted as a conclusion with nothing offered to establish it.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would like to know from the Minister: are there other factors, such as he didn’t want to have to pay for the funding for legal representation through the courts for claimants, because that was causing the Crown’s books some concern, and he had quite a bit of pressure to bring things into line and there was no other foreseeable way to stop those costs?
focus.explanation: Names a specific mechanism (Crown funding of claimant legal representation) and a specific legislative act, so there is real policy content, though the framing is directed at the Minister's motive rather than the provision's effect.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In terms of whose rights we are talking about who would be potentially interfered with by the resource consent right, we’re talking about somebody who wanted to start new aquaculture, for example, somebody wanting to put in a jetty on their property, or somebody wanting to renew a consent for a jetty that they’ve had for generations.
focus.explanation: Answers squarely on the mechanism at issue — which third parties the resource consent right would affect — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The question is, are those two sets of constitutional rights, as set out in Te Tiriti o Waitangi, equally and adequately recognised on the basis of the bicultural constitutional framework of Te Tiriti o Waitangi?
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the amendment's balancing test — whether the two classes of right it weighs are given equal recognition — rather than at the other party. No tribal framing, though it argues at the level of constitutional principle rather than a named provision.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve already been told there’s cuts everywhere—cut, cut, cut—and yet we see this Government bringing legislation in, just in the preamble itself, changing the nature by which we have to prove our connection and provide evidence of physical use and occupation, which is inconsistent with the test based on tikanga.
focus.explanation: Identifies a specific provision (recital (7)(b), the physical use and occupation requirement) and a specific consequence for claimants. The 'cut, cut, cut' framing is party-directed, but the weight of the statement is on the mechanism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Thinking about the implications for decision makers, including the courts, to be based on evidence of physical use and occupation now and into the future, who is going to be financing the implementation of this?
focus.explanation: A direct implementation question about who bears the cost of the evidential standard the amendment creates — entirely on the measure before the House, with no reference to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In particular, I would like to know whether the cost pressures of claimant funding proceeding through the court process, which, in the year prior to this legislation being brought to the House and enacted, there was a substantial blowout—according to the scrutiny week that I sat on, as part of that—in terms of the court costs that the Crown was required to pay for.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Crown spending on claimant funding for takutai moana court proceedings substantially exceeded budget in the year before this legislation was introduced, sourced to select committee scrutiny week evidence.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Takutai Moana / Marine and Coastal Area claimant funding appropriation in Vote Treaty Negotiations (Te Arawhiti / Te Tari Whakatau) and Vote Courts for the year to 30 June 2025 — annual report actual spend against budgeted appropriation, plus the 2025 scrutiny week transcript she cites. True if actual spend materially exceeded the appropriation or supplementary funding was sought; false if spend was at or below the budgeted figure.

veracity.statement: I have met with a number, including Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Te Whānau-a-Apanui, Ngāti Kauwhata, and Ngāti Porou.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that he personally met with four named applicant groups during the development of the amendment and the legislation.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister's published ministerial diary releases for the period of the Bill's and Amendment Paper's development, and any OIA or select committee record of consultation meetings. True if meetings with each of the four named groups are recorded; false if the named groups are absent or the groups themselves state no meeting occurred.

veracity.statement: There hadn’t been an Act of Parliament passed between 1854 and 2004 that actively extinguished the Māori right to the takutai moana, so it stands that it was still there in 2004.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no statute enacted between 1854 and 2004 actively extinguished Māori customary rights in the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Court of Appeal's reasoning in Ngati Apa v Attorney-General [2003] 3 NZLR 643 and the statutory survey it relied on, plus subsequent legal analysis of pre-2004 statutes (e.g. the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zone Act 1965, Harbours Act provisions). True if no statute of general application in that period is identified as extinguishing customary title in the takutai moana; false if such a statute is identified.

specificity.statement: I have met with a number, including Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Te Whānau-a-Apanui, Ngāti Kauwhata, and Ngāti Porou.
specificity.explanation: Names four particular iwi and hapū groups rather than claiming vague 'consultation', so the answer is checkable — but supplies no dates, no count, and nothing about what was discussed or what changed as a result.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of whose rights we are talking about who would be potentially interfered with by the resource consent right, we’re talking about somebody who wanted to start new aquaculture, for example, somebody wanting to put in a jetty on their property, or somebody wanting to renew a consent for a jetty that they’ve had for generations.
specificity.explanation: Gives concrete categories of affected activity (new aquaculture, a new jetty, renewal of an existing consent) rather than abstractions, but offers no numbers of affected consents, no thresholds and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It leaves the courts in the position—or any decision maker, in fact, when they’re considering customary marine title—where, at some point, they need to hear evidence about physical use, but there’s no indication of whether that should be the only evidence, whether that should be the most heavily weighted evidence, or whether it must be one of a hundred things that they heard evidence on.
rigor.explanation: A premise (the amendment specifies no evidential weight) is offered and the conclusion (decision makers are left without workable direction) tracks it directly. The three enumerated possibilities show the gap rather than merely asserting it. No fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Having to prove physical use for somewhere like Ruapuke Island, where customary marine title has been granted to the whānau of Ruapuke, but where the sea between it and Rakiura or Invercargill might be used infrequently, is difficult and nonsensical, especially when you haven’t set out how that is intended to work for a court.
rigor.explanation: Argues from a concrete counterexample to the conclusion that the physical-use test is unworkable. The inference holds given the assumption that infrequent use of that stretch of sea is genuine customary use; the qualifier 'especially when you haven't set out how that is intended to work' supplies the connecting reason rather than leaving a leap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now we're all debating about where that threshold should be, and three different courts have had three different interpretations of that threshold. That’s why this Parliament is considering this Amendment Paper, which sets for Parliament to assert what it believes the threshold should be.
rigor.explanation: A clean inference: if successive courts have read the same statutory threshold differently, the legislature restating its intended threshold follows as a response. No fallacy; the premise about three divergent interpretations does the work, and its truth is Veracity's question, not this one.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Whilst an historian might be interested in the fact that there was a Court of Appeal decision, it’s actually really verbose to have in the preamble to the main Act a recitation of the Court of Appeal’s decisions which were, in fact, overruled by the Supreme Court.
rigor.explanation: Premise (the recited decisions were overruled) supports the conclusion (reciting them in the preamble adds length without legal effect). The concession to historical interest is handled rather than ignored. Whether the overruling claim is accurate is Veracity's question.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we’re going to give a genuine historical account of why we’ve got here, we should probably recognise that it’s really part of the Government’s approach to Māori and Māori interests, which is, basically, to roll back the progress that we’ve made over the past, I don’t know, 150 years or so.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion — a 150-year rollback characterising the Government's whole approach to Māori interests — rests on nothing offered in support. Sweeping generalisation from a single drafting dispute; the hedge 'I don't know, 150 years or so' underlines that no evidence is being adduced.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It leaves the courts in the position—or any decision maker, in fact, when they’re considering customary marine title—where, at some point, they need to hear evidence about physical use, but there’s no indication of whether that should be the only evidence, whether that should be the most heavily weighted evidence, or whether it must be one of a hundred things that they heard evidence on.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the proposed provision — what a decision maker would have to do with evidence of physical use. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This is unfair. It is gobbledygook. It is getting around a problem the Government has with a populist commitment that doesn’t make sense in law.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath (the drafting does not achieve in law what is claimed for it), but this passage carries it almost entirely as political characterisation — 'unfair', 'gobbledygook', 'populist commitment' — with no named measure, figure or outcome in the sentences themselves.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question to the Minister is: were the words that are in this preamble now and that have some really serious concerns, including the word “physical” and how you are determining occupation, predetermined because the Minister simply directed officials to choose which option best suited the Government’s desire for an outcome and best suited the minimisation of costs to the Crown?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy process: a named word in the preamble, a named agency's advice, and a specific paragraph of the regulatory impact statement. This is scrutiny of how a specific decision was reached, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Now we're all debating about where that threshold should be, and three different courts have had three different interpretations of that threshold. That’s why this Parliament is considering this Amendment Paper, which sets for Parliament to assert what it believes the threshold should be.
focus.explanation: About the measure before the House and the specific legal question it addresses — where the threshold sits and who should settle it. No content about the other side's character or record.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Whilst an historian might be interested in the fact that there was a Court of Appeal decision, it’s actually really verbose to have in the preamble to the main Act a recitation of the Court of Appeal’s decisions which were, in fact, overruled by the Supreme Court.
focus.explanation: Directed at a specific drafting choice in a specific clause — what the amended preamble should recite. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we’re going to give a genuine historical account of why we’ve got here, we should probably recognise that it’s really part of the Government’s approach to Māori and Māori interests, which is, basically, to roll back the progress that we’ve made over the past, I don’t know, 150 years or so.
focus.explanation: Framed as a comment on the preamble but the substance is a general characterisation of the other side's programme rather than a named policy, measure or outcome. Some policy anchoring survives (it is about what this preamble should record), which keeps it above zero.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Having to prove physical use for somewhere like Ruapuke Island, where customary marine title has been granted to the whānau of Ruapuke, but where the sea between it and Rakiura or Invercargill might be used infrequently, is difficult and nonsensical, especially when you haven’t set out how that is intended to work for a court.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific location, a specific existing recognition order, and the specific statutory test at issue. Falls short of 1.0 because no figures, timeframe or drafting alternative is supplied.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This is unfair. It is gobbledygook. It is getting around a problem the Government has with a populist commitment that doesn’t make sense in law.
civility.explanation: Blunt about the drafting, which costs nothing on the re-anchored scale, but it imputes a motive — legislating to manage a political commitment rather than to make workable law. That is directed at the Government rather than at any individual, so it sits between the standard and a genuine failure rather than at either.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: My question to the Minister is: were the words that are in this preamble now and that have some really serious concerns, including the word “physical” and how you are determining occupation, predetermined because the Minister simply directed officials to choose which option best suited the Government’s desire for an outcome and best suited the minimisation of costs to the Crown?
civility.explanation: Pointed and edging toward the person: it puts to the Minister that he steered officials toward a predetermined answer to save the Crown money. It stops short of an insult and is anchored to the regulatory impact statement she has just quoted, but the suggestion of a motive-driven process is more than criticism of the decision itself.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That's why the legislation was passed with the support of the National Party and the Māori Party at the time, and was set to strike a balance there with what was described, at the time, as a high threshold.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the original Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) legislation was enacted with the votes of both the National Party and the Māori Party, and that the test it created was characterised at enactment as a high threshold.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard division record for the third reading of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill (2011): true if both National and the Māori Party are recorded voting in favour, false if either voted against or abstained. The 'high threshold' characterisation is checkable against the 2011 third-reading debate and the Bill's explanatory note.

veracity.statement: So, in terms of the references to the Court of Appeal case, it’s entirely unnecessary because they’re gone, they’ve been overruled, and the Supreme Court case itself is the one which prevails.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Court of Appeal's decision on the customary marine title test no longer has legal effect because the Supreme Court overruled it, leaving the Supreme Court's judgment as the governing authority.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court's judgment in the Whakatōhea/Edwards customary marine title appeal and the Court of Appeal decision it reviewed: true if the Supreme Court set aside or displaced the Court of Appeal's interpretation of section 58 so that the Supreme Court's test now governs; false if the Court of Appeal's interpretation was upheld, or if material parts of it were left standing as binding authority.

veracity.statement: When we were doing this, the opponents said that this was terrible and appalling; then, lo and behold, the Supreme Court agreed that it was a misreading.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Supreme Court held the Court of Appeal had misread the second limb of the section 58 test by effectively reading out the word "exclusive" — i.e. that the Government's stated reason for the original bill was vindicated on appeal.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Supreme Court judgment in Re Edwards (Whakatōhea) on the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 s58(1)(b): true if the Court held the Court of Appeal erred in its interpretation of "exclusive use and occupation" and set that interpretation aside; false if the Supreme Court upheld the Court of Appeal's reading of that limb.

veracity.statement: For instance, the rights of Ngāi Tahu and Rakiura Māori in the Tītī Islands was recognised through a pathway of negotiation with the ground to recognise those special rights and have nothing to do with these concepts around physical use or adverse position.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Tītī (muttonbird) Islands rights of Ngāi Tahu and Rakiura Māori were recognised by negotiated settlement with the Crown, not through any physical-use or adverse-possession test. ("With the ground" is plainly a transcription slip for "with the Crown" and is not part of the claim.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ngāi Tahu Claims Settlement Act 1998 and the Titi (Muttonbird) Islands Regulations: true if the Rakiura/Beneficial Tītī Islands rights were vested or confirmed through the negotiated Ngāi Tahu settlement and contain no physical-use or adverse-possession test; false if those rights were established by a judicial test of physical use or possession.

civility.statement: When we were doing this, the opponents said that this was terrible and appalling; then, lo and behold, the Supreme Court agreed that it was a misreading.
civility.explanation: Contested ground with a real chance to attack opponents personally. "Lo and behold" is a mild sneer at the critics collectively, but no individual's character or competence is impugned and the point stays on the legal substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The point was around onus, and I’m loath to say that the member as elegant as Steve Abel didn’t quite capture, I think, what he perhaps intended, because there are two concepts: one is establishing marine title, and then another is to say that it’s been extinguished.
civility.explanation: Corrects another member's framing in a contested debate — an easy place to be dismissive — and instead flags the correction courteously and moves straight to the distinction itself. Attacks nobody.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The approach of the bill is to say that applicants must prove all the elements of the section 58 test now.
specificity.explanation: Names the statutory provision and states the precise legal change — where the burden sits and over which elements. Someone could check it against the clause. Missing only detail of the standard of proof.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Is it the Minister’s opinion that the original intent of the legislation was to place the burden of proof not on iwi Māori but on those who wished to disprove that iwi Māori had exclusive use and therefore a right of customary title?
specificity.explanation: A precise, answerable question: it identifies the exact contested element (onus of proof on the exclusivity limb) and states the two rival allocations of it. A precise question counts as fully as a precise answer, though it carries no figures or clause references.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I'll take the Minister to page 3 of the amendment bill. I'm asking him about his clause 5 that amends section 9 of the Act.
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints the page, the clause and the section of the principal Act being amended — maximally checkable and actionable for the Minister answering.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We don't expect Mr Andy Foster to get out every day and patrol the border of his house and dig something in the lawn out every six months to prove that he is physically using his lawn, do we? We don't expect Te Whakatōhea to patrol their borders, get out and swim in the moana and erect the jetty to show physical use. We don't expect those things.
rigor.explanation: An argument from analogy, drawn to a reductio: ordinary land ownership demands no continuing physical demonstration, so a physical-use requirement here is anomalous and needs definition. The analogy is apt for the burden it carries, though it glides over the possibility that customary title is a different species of right for which a different test could be justified — a real but modest gap between premise and conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think it’s quite separate from the question of establishing the coastal and marine title kind of prima facie, because it’s essentially a defence to say that, yes, all that’s true but there’s been an extinguishment through these series of events, because if the onus lies the other way, and the hapū or iwi have to prove on the balance of probabilities—and I’m assuming that that didn’t occur—that would seem entirely unfair.
rigor.explanation: Valid reasoning from a stated legal premise: extinguishment is pleaded as a defence, defences are ordinarily proved by the party raising them, therefore the onus on extinguishment should not sit with the applicant. The conclusion tracks the premises; the closing "entirely unfair" leans on a fairness appeal rather than the doctrinal point that carries the argument.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That key date that is missing from those series of events is the Cabinet decision on 28 November 2023, and that is clearly before the decisions of Whakatōhea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) v Te Kāhui Takutai Moana o Ngā Whānau me Ngā Hāpū o Te Whakatōhea.
specificity.explanation: Names an exact date, a specific Cabinet decision and the specific court proceeding it is said to predate — a reader could go and check the preamble against that timeline.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That clause, if we look at it, requires the claimant group to provide evidence based on physical activity or use of natural resources in the area of claim, and that spiritual or cultural association to that area is not relevant unless it is manifested in physical activity or use of natural resources.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism of a named subclause — what evidence a claimant must produce and the precise condition under which spiritual or cultural association counts. Checkable against the clause text, though no figures or timeframes are involved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Again, my point is a relatively short one, I think, and it’s about new section 9B, in particular, subclause (3)(b), which says that “This section prevails over—(b) section 7”—of the principle Act—“(Treaty of Waitangi (te Tiriti o Waitangi));”.
specificity.explanation: Names the new section, the exact subclause and quotes its operative words, and identifies the provision of the principal Act it displaces. Fully checkable against the Amendment Paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: That key date that is missing from those series of events is the Cabinet decision on 28 November 2023, and that is clearly before the decisions of Whakatōhea Kotahitanga Waka (Edwards) v Te Kāhui Takutai Moana o Ngā Whānau me Ngā Hāpū o Te Whakatōhea.
focus.explanation: Directed at the drafting of the Part 1 preamble and a specific omitted document. Although it points at a deal between two parties, it names a concrete instrument and a concrete date rather than generalised party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: What occurs on 28 November 2023 is that Cabinet endorses the coalition agreement between the parties as the basis on which the coalition Government will operate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Cabinet formally endorsed the coalition agreement as the operating basis of the Government on 28 November 2023, and that a Cabinet circular instructed chief executives to implement it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Cabinet Office circular / Cabinet minutes from the incoming coalition Government (DPMC Cabinet Office circular series, November 2023); true if a Cabinet decision dated 28 November 2023 endorses the coalition agreements as the basis on which the Government operates, false if no such decision exists or it is dated otherwise.

veracity.statement: I raise that as an issue in my kāinga, Whangārei-terenga-parāoa, where the claimants stood in hearings and are waiting for a judgment right now, knowing that very few parcels of land around Whangārei-terenga-parāoa remain within Māori hands.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions of present fact: that Whangārei Harbour takutai moana applicants have completed hearings and are awaiting judgment as at October 2025, and that very little land adjoining that harbour is still in Māori ownership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act application records for Whangārei Harbour (hearing completed, judgment reserved as at 14 October 2025), and Māori land tenure records (Māori Land Court / Te Puni Kōkiri Māori freehold land data) for parcels adjoining Whangārei Harbour; true if hearings are concluded with judgment outstanding and Māori-owned parcels adjoining the harbour are a small minority, false if judgment had already issued or if a substantial share of the abutting land remains Māori-owned.

veracity.statement: The only thing I'd say in relation to that member's speech, of course, is that nothing in this legislation impacts on the ability of Māori or non-Māori to go and collect shellfish and have a connection with a piece of coastline that continues, and there's all sorts of arrangements in place in relation to customary fishing rights and shellfish-gathering rights and tītī gathering rights.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the amending legislation leaves untouched the ability of anyone to gather shellfish and the existing customary fishing, shellfish-gathering and tītī-gathering arrangements.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill as reported back, checked against the Fisheries Act 1996 customary fishing regulations (Kaimoana Customary Fishing Regulations 1998 / South Island regulations), the Titi (Muttonbird) Islands regulations, and the public access and fishing provisions of the 2011 Act; true if no provision of the Bill amends or limits those rights, false if any provision does.

veracity.statement: Where the rubber meets the road in relation to this legislation, though, is the valuable rights that come with the recognition of customary marine title as outlined in this legislation, which, as we've heard, was an agreement between the Māori Party and the National Party back in 2011, which sought to balance the rights of New Zealanders alongside the desire to be able to assert customary marine title by particular groups, whānau or iwi.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the customary marine title regime in the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 was the product of an agreement between the Māori Party and the National Party.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The parliamentary record for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill 2010–11 — third reading division record and the National–Māori Party relationship/confidence-and-supply arrangements of that Parliament; true if the Māori Party negotiated and voted for the Act with National, false if it was passed over Māori Party opposition or without any such agreement.

rigor.statement: It is unfair on tangata whenua to have to show that somehow we’ve got a physical manifestation of connection to that space, when we may not own by Western law the whenua abutting that part of the takutai moana.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (the evidential test is unfair) supported by a stated premise (loss of title to the abutting land under general law) that she then illustrates with the Whangārei public works takings and continued cultural practice. The inference holds; the gap is that she does not address whether the clause admits other proof of use, which stops it short of the top.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that is why. With those valuable rights, part of the balancing act that was achieved by this legislation was a high threshold, which is what we're trying to establish through this legislation.
rigor.explanation: The premise he offers — that customary marine title carries consequential rights, including an effective say over resource consents — does support the conclusion that some threshold is warranted. But nothing offered connects it to the particular threshold in the Bill, so the inference from 'the rights are valuable' to 'this high threshold' has a real gap. He also does not engage the question actually put to him about extinguishment.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Yet you’re saying here that this piece of legislation will override the Treaty of Waitangi. That’s exactly what this says.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion overshoots the premise. What the clause says is that it prevails over section 7 of the 2011 Act — a statutory provision directing how that Act accounts for the Treaty. Treating 'prevails over the Act's Treaty clause' as identical to 'overrides the Treaty' equivocates between a statute and the Treaty itself, and he asserts the identity ('that's exactly what this says') rather than arguing for it. The underlying concern about the effect on Treaty-consistent interpretation is a real one, which keeps this above the bottom.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Well, you can scoff, Minister, but that’s what the words of the Treaty of Waitangi say.
civility.explanation: Pointed, and it characterises the Minister's reaction dismissively, but it lands on the argument rather than the man — no imputation of bad faith or attack on his character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So purporting to say that these rights had arisen in the agreement reached by the National Party and the Māori Party in 2011 and were then enshrined in that legislation is wrong and is an interpretation of the law which doesn't recognise that those rights were something that existed, that there were a bundle of property rights held by people in accordance with the legal system which was operative.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the premise that customary rights pre-existed 1840 under tikanga supports the conclusion that they cannot have 'arisen' in a 2011 political agreement. The step is valid given its premises; it leans slightly on assertion rather than authority for the pre-existence claim.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Can we expect a National Government to now insert a preamble into every other piece of legislation for which they don't like decisions from the courts, like setting out perhaps their political campaign documents in the Crimes Act and asking judges to comply with that, or else!
rigor.explanation: Slippery slope: nothing is offered to connect a single interpretive clause in this bill to a general practice of writing campaign documents into the Crimes Act. The extrapolation does no argumentative work beyond rhetorical escalation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We’re replacing the specific comments in the legislation over the broad comments in section 7, but we are not seeking to override the Treaty of Waitangi, or Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion tracks the distinction offered: if the clause operates on a named section of a statute, it does not by itself displace the Treaty. Valid given its premise about what the clause targets; it does not address whether displacing section 7 has Treaty consequences in practice.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Narrowing the things that the court can consider is particularly unhelpful for that court, because that very particular story that a member of this House was able to tell, that showed the relationship of her father’s iwi to the marine coastal environment would be exceedingly useful and informative for a court.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference — restricting admissible categories of evidence removes material a court would find probative — but the support offered is a single illustrative anecdote from the debate rather than anything about how courts weigh such evidence generally.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Surely, Minister, giving our courts that breadth of consideration to take into account all of these useful sources of information and evidence in order to give absolute confidence of the proof of customary marine title would be beneficial in upholding the principle of customary marine title and, indeed, Te Tiriti o Waitangi.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion rests on 'surely' — an appeal to the self-evident. Nothing is offered to show that a broader evidential base yields 'absolute confidence' rather than simply more contested material, so there is a gap between what was shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So purporting to say that these rights had arisen in the agreement reached by the National Party and the Māori Party in 2011 and were then enshrined in that legislation is wrong and is an interpretation of the law which doesn't recognise that those rights were something that existed, that there were a bundle of property rights held by people in accordance with the legal system which was operative.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the legal question before the committee — the source and character of customary rights and how the CMT amendments treat them. The reference to the National/Māori Party agreement is descriptive of the 2011 legislative history, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Can we expect a National Government to now insert a preamble into every other piece of legislation for which they don't like decisions from the courts, like setting out perhaps their political campaign documents in the Crimes Act and asking judges to comply with that, or else!
focus.explanation: There is a real drafting point underneath (interpretive clauses directing decision makers), but the weight of the sentence is a characterisation of what 'a National Government' would do rather than the mechanism or its effects.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Narrowing the things that the court can consider is particularly unhelpful for that court, because that very particular story that a member of this House was able to tell, that showed the relationship of her father’s iwi to the marine coastal environment would be exceedingly useful and informative for a court.
focus.explanation: Entirely on the mechanism of the amendment: what evidence the court may consider under the section 58 test and the consequence of narrowing it. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Inserting a preamble into a document is usually used in the context of Treaty settlements.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a fact about New Zealand legislative drafting practice — that preambles are predominantly a feature of Treaty settlement legislation rather than ordinary statutes.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: A survey of New Zealand statutes enacted in the modern era that contain a preamble (searchable on legislation.govt.nz): true if the clear majority of such Acts are Treaty of Waitangi settlement Acts; false if preambles are routinely used across general legislation of other kinds.

veracity.statement: As he well knows, what the section refers to is that it prevails over section 7 of the legislation, which has the title “Treaty of Waitangi”; it’s not the Treaty of Waitangi itself.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the override in the amendment operates on section 7 of the 2011 Act (a section bearing the heading 'Treaty of Waitangi') rather than on the Treaty itself.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 and of the amendment before the committee: true if section 7 of the 2011 Act is headed 'Treaty of Waitangi' and the overriding provision is expressed to prevail over that section; false if the provision is expressed to prevail over the Treaty or its principles more broadly.

veracity.statement: Just in terms of the burden of proof question that’s been raised by a number of people, the 2011 Act says, in section 106, “Burden of proof”, in subsection (3), that “In the case of every application for a recognition order, it is presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished”, and the bill does not change that.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: that section 106(3) of the 2011 Act contains the quoted non-extinguishment presumption, and that the bill leaves it untouched.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Section 106(3) of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 as quoted, plus the amending bill and Amendment Paper as before the committee: true if the quoted words are accurate and no provision of the bill amends or displaces section 106(3); false if the wording differs materially or the bill alters that presumption.

veracity.statement: That’s new section 58(1A)(a) in clause 8, but new section 58(1A)(b) is that it “is not based on a spiritual or cultural association”—it explicitly articulates that it must not be based on that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the proposed new section 58(1A)(b) says — that the exclusivity limb of the customary marine title test must not rest on spiritual or cultural association.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of clause 8 of the bill as amended by the Minister's Amendment Paper: true if proposed new section 58(1A)(b) states that exclusivity of use and occupation is not based on a spiritual or cultural association; false if no such paragraph exists or its effect is materially different.

civility.statement: As he well knows, what the section refers to is that it prevails over section 7 of the legislation, which has the title “Treaty of Waitangi”; it’s not the Treaty of Waitangi itself.
civility.explanation: 'As he well knows' implies the previous speaker mischaracterised the clause knowingly — a light imputation of bad faith directed at the member, though the substance of the reply stays on the clause.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Just in terms of the burden of proof question that’s been raised by a number of people, the 2011 Act says, in section 106, “Burden of proof”, in subsection (3), that “In the case of every application for a recognition order, it is presumed, in the absence of proof to the contrary, that a customary interest has not been extinguished”, and the bill does not change that.
specificity.explanation: Cites the Act, the section, the subsection heading and the operative words verbatim, and states precisely what the bill does not do to it. Fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So, in my amendment, I propose that in determining whether an applicant group has exclusively used and occupied a specified area, the court may consider the following types of evidence—and the purpose of this is to recognise the value of physical evidence.
specificity.explanation: Names the legal test being modified and, in the sentences immediately following, enumerates the categories of evidence proposed (kaitiakitanga practices, oral histories, whakapapa, recognition by other iwi and hapū, exercise of mana and tikanga). Credited in context; short of full precision only because it sets no threshold or weighting.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: They’ve done that recently and they won’t be doing it for a long time to come, I imagine, but you never know, they might, and that is the system that we have, and we’re accountable for that.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that New Zealand voters will not turn out the current government at the coming election. Hedged, but the substantive prediction is that the incumbent government survives the next electoral test.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The official result of the next New Zealand general election (due by late 2026), as declared by the Electoral Commission: true if the incumbent National-led government is returned to office; false if the election produces a change of government.

rigor.statement: It’s important that we appreciate that in paragraph (b), what is being extinguished here is the ability of that evidence to make a difference to these decisions; in fact, it’s a prohibition on someone hearing the evidence on which they would draw inferences about that.
rigor.explanation: She reads the wording of new section 58(1A)(b) and derives its operative effect from that text — a prohibition on drawing inferences means the evidence cannot bear on the decision. The conclusion tracks the premise she offers; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My question is really about whether the Minister is happy to stand up and do what he will be expected to do under the Regulatory Standards Bill when it’s passed and explain why he is not compensating, under this legislation, owners of property rights whose property rights are being significantly impaired by this.
rigor.explanation: A consistency argument: the Government's own Regulatory Standards Bill sets a test for impairing property rights; this bill impairs part-heard customary rights; therefore the Minister owes the same justification. The inference follows given its premise that the recognition process confers property rights — a premise the Minister may contest, but the reasoning itself is valid.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This whole House relies on testimony—oral testimonies—that we may question or test, but why would you deny something as powerful as the likes of the articulation of the relationship in a physical sense that an iwi produces on a regular basis in interaction, in telling their history with the land and the water?
rigor.explanation: An argument by analogy: the House accepted the Minister's unevidenced oral account of his family history, therefore iwi oral testimony should be admissible as evidence of use. The analogy is offered rather than established — parliamentary courtesy toward an anecdote is not the same standard as evidence in a title proceeding, and nothing is supplied to bridge that gap. A real point, but the conclusion outruns the comparison.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s important that we appreciate that in paragraph (b), what is being extinguished here is the ability of that evidence to make a difference to these decisions; in fact, it’s a prohibition on someone hearing the evidence on which they would draw inferences about that.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a named provision of the bill and what it does to the evidential process. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My question is really about whether the Minister is happy to stand up and do what he will be expected to do under the Regulatory Standards Bill when it’s passed and explain why he is not compensating, under this legislation, owners of property rights whose property rights are being significantly impaired by this.
focus.explanation: Names new clause 6, a named companion bill, and a specific consequence for iwi part-way through the recognition process. Scrutiny of a government measure, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The change is that cultural or spiritual evidence needs supporting evidence of physical use, but tikanga and oral evidence remain important.
focus.explanation: Answers on the mechanism of the clause under discussion — what the amendment changes about how evidence is treated. Entirely policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This whole House relies on testimony—oral testimonies—that we may question or test, but why would you deny something as powerful as the likes of the articulation of the relationship in a physical sense that an iwi produces on a regular basis in interaction, in telling their history with the land and the water?
focus.explanation: Directed at new section 58(1A) and what does or does not count as evidence of physical use — the substance of the clause, though put as a general appeal rather than to the wording.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Watch out, New Zealand, you’re getting the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and Labour.
focus.explanation: Names three parties and nothing else — no policy, measure, figure or outcome. Pure party framing thrown across a clause-by-clause debate on the evidential test in section 58.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: That was not a service that existed in the decades leading up to the 1990s, because the Waitangi Tribunal did not operate.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Waitangi Tribunal was not operating during the decades before the 1990s, and so no comparable oral-history recording work was being done then.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975 and the Tribunal's own record of inquiries and reports: true if the Tribunal was not constituted or heard no claims in the 1970s and 1980s; false if it was established in 1975 and issued reports across those decades (the 1985 retrospective-jurisdiction amendment is the relevant qualifier to weigh).

veracity.statement: The Government has set aside $15 million towards the extra cost.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a $15 million provision has been made by the Government to meet the extra cost of rehearing the customary marine title cases affected by the bill.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 / Vote Courts and Vote Justice appropriations and Ministry of Justice announcements relating to the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill: true if an allocation of approximately $15 million for rehearing costs is recorded, false if no such allocation exists or the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: I don’t have the exact figure, but more than $65 million has been spent by the people of New Zealand in support of claims that have been taken so far over the—what is it?—nearly 14 years since the legislation has passed, in support of claimants.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that cumulative Crown funding to claimants under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 exceeds $65 million since the Act passed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Justice / Te Arawhiti reporting on Takutai Moana applicant funding (the Crown's contribution to applicant costs under the 2011 Act): true if cumulative funding since 2011 exceeds $65 million, false if the reported total is materially below that.

specificity.statement: Does new clause 6 mean that courts cannot award costs against the Government in marine and coastal area claims?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact provision and the exact legal effect at issue, in a form the Minister can answer yes or no and anyone can check against the clause. A precise question, not an announcement.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Government has set aside $15 million towards the extra cost.
specificity.explanation: A named figure attached to a named purpose. Checkable against the appropriations.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The change is that cultural or spiritual evidence needs supporting evidence of physical use, but tikanga and oral evidence remain important.
specificity.explanation: States the mechanism (cultural evidence must be supported by physical-use evidence) but gives no detail on what counts as sufficient supporting evidence or how a decision maker is to weigh it.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I think the member knows the answer to that question, which is, no, it doesn’t.
civility.explanation: Implies the member asked a question he already knew the answer to — a mild imputation of rhetorical bad faith. Pointed and slightly condescending, but it lands on the question rather than on Webb himself, and the substantive answer follows immediately.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Watch out, New Zealand, you’re getting the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and Labour.
civility.explanation: Tribal, but it insults no individual and imputes no bad faith to any person. Under the re-anchored scale that is civil; the failure here is Focus, not Civility.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I want to underscore this point to you: that decision found from the expert evidence that the applicant group had held this specified area in accordance with tikanga and that they had whakapapa connections to that area, but they also had exercise control in that area through mahinga kai, through kaitiakitanga, through rāhui that they exercised, and through protection of biodiversity—regular use, physical use, use in a customary sense, use of land rights, and the use of British land rights, and that is something which meets all of the tests which the Minister has talked about today.
veracity.explanation: Asserts what the High Court found in the Ruapuke Island customary marine title decision: that the applicant group held the area according to tikanga, had whakapapa connections, and exercised control through mahinga kai, kaitiakitanga, rāhui and biodiversity protection — and that these findings satisfy the test the Bill's amendments impose.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published High Court judgment on the Ruapuke Island CMT application under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011. True if the judgment records findings of whakapapa connection, holding in accordance with tikanga, and exercise of control via the practices named; false if the judgment made no such findings or granted title on a materially different basis. The further claim that these findings meet the amended test is checked against the amended s58 criteria as set out in the Bill as reported back.

veracity.statement: Why must they go back—using taxpayers’ money, the $15 million, or a portion of that—to be reheard?
veracity.explanation: Presupposes as fact that $15 million of public money is attached to the reconsideration/rehearing of customary marine title applications under the amended regime.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Vote Justice / Te Arawhiti appropriation and any Budget or Cabinet paper covering funding for Takutai Moana customary marine title applications at the time of the Bill. True if approximately $15 million is appropriated for CMT application processing or rehearing; false if the appropriation is materially different or no such figure exists.

focus.statement: Why won’t you preserve the rights that exist now when the High Court has recognised them under the old test but will clearly meet your new test?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: it asks about a specific transitional effect of the Bill on a named, already-decided case, naming the old and new statutory tests. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: There are a number of questions there, but in terms of where the date of taking effect came from—and this is in relation to the date that we had in June last year—I mean, in essence, the goal was to ensure that we had as much consistency with the rest of the vast majority of cases that haven't yet come forward, to have a consistent test, but to recognise that those that had been concluded and granted before the date, we didn't want to unscramble.
focus.explanation: Engages the mechanism directly — why the commencement date sits where it does and which classes of case it separates. Entirely about the measure, with no reference to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Why won’t you preserve the rights that exist now when the High Court has recognised them under the old test but will clearly meet your new test?
civility.explanation: Contested committee-stage debate where the speaker had ample opportunity to attack the Minister personally; instead the challenge is entirely directed at the policy choice. This is the expected standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Given that there are a limited number of cases that fall in here, what is the massive policy objection to saying “Well, you got in under the law as it was”, which is how it works, we generally like to think that this is the concept of the rule of law; the Minister may not be familiar with it, but the idea is that you apply the law as it stands and you don’t pull the legal rug from under people and change legal history, but that seems to be exactly what’s going on here.
civility.explanation: "the Minister may not be familiar with it" is a sarcastic aside imputing that the Minister does not understand the rule of law. Short of a direct insult but clearly condescending about the person rather than the policy, which is a genuine failure on the re-anchored scale.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why must they go back—using taxpayers’ money, the $15 million, or a portion of that—to be reheard?
specificity.explanation: Carries a concrete figure ($15 million) and a named consequence (rehearing of a decided application), but the figure is dropped in as an aside without stating what it funds or over what period, so it is checkable rather than fully worked through.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of having to go back to the start, no, it's not our expectation that the cases that have been heard have to go right back to day one and start the whole process again, merely that they would presumably need to reconsider or hear any extra evidence that's required in relation to the amended test or the clarified test.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete operational position — prior procedural steps stand, only additional evidence relevant to the amended test is required — but hedges with "presumably" and supplies no provision reference, timeframe or account of which steps survive.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Given that there are a limited number of cases that fall in here, what is the massive policy objection to saying “Well, you got in under the law as it was”, which is how it works, we generally like to think that this is the concept of the rule of law; the Minister may not be familiar with it, but the idea is that you apply the law as it stands and you don’t pull the legal rug from under people and change legal history, but that seems to be exactly what’s going on here.
rigor.explanation: A real inference: few cases fall in the affected band, retrospective legislation offends the rule-of-law principle that law is applied as it stood, therefore grandfathering those cases carries little policy cost. Premises support the conclusion; it loses some ground by asserting rather than establishing that the number of cases is small. The jibe at the Minister does not carry the conclusion, so it is not scored here.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: There are a number of questions there, but in terms of where the date of taking effect came from—and this is in relation to the date that we had in June last year—I mean, in essence, the goal was to ensure that we had as much consistency with the rest of the vast majority of cases that haven't yet come forward, to have a consistent test, but to recognise that those that had been concluded and granted before the date, we didn't want to unscramble.
rigor.explanation: Offers a reason for the cut-off date — consistency of test across the bulk of undecided cases, balanced against not unscrambling concluded grants. The reasoning holds for the cut-off itself, but there is a gap: it does not connect the consistency goal to voiding decisions made in the interim period, which was the objection actually put.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In fact, they note in the regulatory impact statement that they sometimes only had days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the regulatory impact statement for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill records that Te Arawhiti was at times given only days to turn around policy advice.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published regulatory impact statement / supplementary analysis report for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill, limitations and constraints section; true if it states advice was turned around in a matter of days, false if it records no such timeframe constraint.

veracity.statement: Cabinet made policy decisions without a regulatory impact analysis actually being provided to them, and I would like to understand why that happened.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that Cabinet took the broad policy decisions on this bill before any regulatory impact analysis was supplied, with the supplementary analysis produced only afterwards.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Dates on the relevant Cabinet papers and minutes against the date of the regulatory impact statement / supplementary analysis report for this bill; true if the RIA post-dates the Cabinet policy decisions (or the RIS itself records that no RIA accompanied them), false if an RIA accompanied the Cabinet paper.

focus.statement: Cabinet made policy decisions without a regulatory impact analysis actually being provided to them, and I would like to understand why that happened.
focus.explanation: Names a specific decision-making step on a specific bill and asks the Minister to account for it — textbook scrutiny with concrete policy content, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The first question is whether or not the Minister will support the Amendment Paper tabled by my colleague, which I think is a reasonable one.
focus.explanation: Directed squarely at a specific amendment before the committee and the Minister's position on it; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Because it’s looking like all arrows are pointing towards this being simply a provision within the coalition agreement that was enacted without proper due analysis.
civility.explanation: A hard charge, but aimed entirely at the process and the coalition agreement rather than at the Minister's character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Because it’s looking like all arrows are pointing towards this being simply a provision within the coalition agreement that was enacted without proper due analysis.
rigor.explanation: The premises offered (compressed timeframes, RIA after Cabinet, no financial forecasting) do support a conclusion that analysis was thin, but the leap to a motive — that it was done 'simply' to deliver a coalition agreement provision — is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s quite conceivable that there are customary rights which occur only once every few months or only once a year or conceivably once a generation, or even longer than that, but that doesn’t make them any less customary rights.
rigor.explanation: Valid inference: if a right's frequency is irrelevant to its existence, then an interruption test keyed to continuous use will misclassify infrequent rights. No fallacy or appeal; the conclusion tracks the premise offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The financial forecasting was not undertaken before Cabinet policy decisions on the cost of re-hearings for the six live High Court cases that my colleagues, both Duncan Webb and Arena Williams, have referred to.
specificity.explanation: Names the missing analysis (financial forecasting), the decision point (before Cabinet policy decisions), and the countable subject matter (re-hearing costs for six live High Court cases) — checkable as stated.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I'm speaking to, in particular, the burial of bones, tupuna bones, sites of significance, many of which are already classified through either the Department of Conservation or through Treaty settlements with the Government, whether or not that actually meets the threshold of “occupation”, if you will, and in particular, undisturbed for those iwi or hapū or whānau during that time.
specificity.explanation: Gives a concrete category of use (urupā/tupuna bones and sites of significance) and an existing legal classification (DOC, Treaty settlements) and ties it to the statutory 'occupation' threshold, but leaves the test itself as an open question rather than proposing a defined criterion.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So if you have, I don’t know, dragon boats going up and down for a dragon boat festival; entirely unrelated to tikanga but it is wholly or partly in the area, by a person or persons who don’t belong to the group, and it is a lawful activity.
specificity.explanation: A worked example mapped element-by-element onto the three limbs of new section 57B(c), so the Minister could answer it directly; it is illustrative rather than drawn from a real case.
specificity.subject: speaker
