specificity.statement: But it does not mean interruptions caused by confiscation of adjacent land by the Crown; it does not mean legislation, including the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004; it does not mean the Crown's policies that prevented or restricted Māori access; it does not mean interruptions caused by the establishment of ports, harbours, or other infrastructure without the group's consent; and it does not mean commercial activities licensed by the Crown.
specificity.explanation: Enumerates five concrete categories of excluded interruption and names a specific statute (Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004); a drafter could act on it directly. No figures or dates, which is why it is not at the ceiling.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
specificity.explanation: Names a real mechanism (customary marine title plus the power to grant or withhold resource consents) but the asserted consequence is left as unquantified 'difficulties' — no example port, no figure, no process described.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The Amendment Paper—and I mentioned the use of occupation amendment, there's another Amendment Paper in my colleague Arena Williams’ name which refers directly to Part 1, clause 7, and it looks towards the removal of, under Part 1, clause 7 new 57B: replace every instance of “and occupation” with “stewardship”.
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact provision (Part 1, clause 7, new section 57B) and the precise textual change proposed — every instance of 'and occupation' becomes 'stewardship'. Fully checkable against the Amendment Paper.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I'm on page 14, and they're about the new Schedule 1AA and the transitional provisions that apply to cases that were—I'm going to ask him about the cases that have been heard and will need to be reheard since consideration of these changes began.
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a page, a named schedule (new Schedule 1AA) and a defined class of affected cases. The self-correction mid-sentence costs a little precision but the target is unambiguous.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But it does not mean interruptions caused by confiscation of adjacent land by the Crown; it does not mean legislation, including the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004; it does not mean the Crown's policies that prevented or restricted Māori access; it does not mean interruptions caused by the establishment of ports, harbours, or other infrastructure without the group's consent; and it does not mean commercial activities licensed by the Crown.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of a named clause in the bill before the committee — what 'substantial interruption' should and should not cover. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: The Amendment Paper—and I mentioned the use of occupation amendment, there's another Amendment Paper in my colleague Arena Williams’ name which refers directly to Part 1, clause 7, and it looks towards the removal of, under Part 1, clause 7 new 57B: replace every instance of “and occupation” with “stewardship”.
focus.explanation: Directed at the drafting of a named clause and a specific proposed wording change; no party framing whatsoever.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I'm on page 14, and they're about the new Schedule 1AA and the transitional provisions that apply to cases that were—I'm going to ask him about the cases that have been heard and will need to be reheard since consideration of these changes began.
focus.explanation: A transitional-provisions question about the Minister's own Amendment Paper — squarely on the measure before the House.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: A marine farm should not be a thing that interrupts customary title. It is a commercial activity that may be permitted and may be consistent with it so long as it is by the consent of the iwi, but it is not an interruption.
rigor.explanation: An argument is offered — a licensed commercial activity operating with iwi consent is not evidence of severed connection — but the conclusion ('it is not an interruption') largely restates the premise rather than being derived from it, and no reason is given why permitting plus consent is sufficient. A real gap between what is shown and what is concluded, edging toward circularity.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
rigor.explanation: The inference rests on an invitation to imagine and on what 'most New Zealanders could understand' — an appeal to common sense and popularity in place of a stated mechanism. Nothing is offered to show that CMT consenting rights would in fact impede port operation, so the conclusion outruns the premise, though the conditional structure is coherent.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So any arrangements that have been entered into would have been done in the knowledge that there was a risk that this legislation would pass and that the legislation would require those examples to be heard again under the new test, so I think everybody would have gone into it with eyes wide open.
rigor.explanation: The inference from 'the change was signalled' to 'parties were on notice' is valid for arrangements entered into after the announcement. But the conclusion is stated universally ('any arrangements', 'everybody'), which does not follow for arrangements or court decisions predating July 2024 — the very cases the question was about. A real gap between what the premise supports and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’d just invite people to imagine that if you have customary marine title in a spot where a port is and the ability to pass resource consents or not, then I think most New Zealanders could understand the difficulties that could pose for actually operating ports in this country, and so I won’t be supporting that.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested point — rejecting a Green amendment on customary title — answered wholly on the substance of the amendment's effect. No imputation of motive and no remark about Mr Abel personally.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: For example, in Treaty settlements, it is well understood the process for how taonga that are discovered in an area will then be notified to, and then a process worked through with, the Ministry for Culture and Heritage—those people who have rights in those areas to determine, in fact, what iwi or hapū has a relationship to that taonga because of their occupation of the land.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that an established process exists whereby newly discovered taonga are notified to the Ministry for Culture and Heritage and the iwi or hapū with a relationship to the taonga is then determined, and that Treaty settlements engage this process.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Protected Objects Act 1975 (taonga tūturu provisions) and Manatū Taonga / Ministry for Culture and Heritage published procedure for newly found taonga tūturu, plus the taonga tūturu clauses of representative Treaty settlement deeds. True if found taonga must be notified to the Ministry and a determination of the iwi/hapū relationship follows; false if no such notification or determination process exists in statute or settlement practice.

veracity.statement: Just in relation to that question, when this policy to overturn the Court of Appeal decision was announced originally in July 2024, the Government signalled, of course, right at that point that we would seek to have the legislation take effect from that point.
veracity.explanation: Asserts both that the policy to overturn the Court of Appeal's customary marine title decision was announced in July 2024, and that at the time of that announcement the Government stated it intended the legislation to take effect from that date.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's July 2024 announcement of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act amendments — beehive.govt.nz press release, Cabinet paper and contemporaneous reporting. True if the announcement is dated July 2024 and states an intention that the new test apply from the date of announcement; false if the announcement is dated otherwise, or if it contained no statement about the effective date.

rigor.statement: So the new section 106(2), in effect, mandates that the applicants prove that their customary interests have never been extinguished, as to amount to a substantial interruption; therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
rigor.explanation: A genuine inference: from the amendment's requirement to prove uninterrupted exclusive use, and from 'substantial interruption' encompassing extinguishment, he concludes the presumption of non-extinguishment is effectively reversed. The middle step (that extinguishment counts as substantial interruption) is asserted rather than shown, which is the one real gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So the new section 106(2), in effect, mandates that the applicants prove that their customary interests have never been extinguished, as to amount to a substantial interruption; therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the exact subsection (new s 106(2)) and the specific legal mechanism being altered; a reader could go to the amendment paper and check the reading.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But I simply want to put to the Minister that for the clarification of the burden of proof requirements, this amendment would, if it is genuinely the intent of the Government, ensure the default is non-extinguishment of customary interests, make that vastly clearer and put the burden of proof on the Crown to prove extinguishment rather than on iwi to prove customary title.
specificity.explanation: States a concrete effect of his amendment — burden of proof on the Crown to prove extinguishment rather than on iwi to prove title — but at the level of the mechanism only, with no drafting detail, threshold or figures in this sentence.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So the new section 106(2), in effect, mandates that the applicants prove that their customary interests have never been extinguished, as to amount to a substantial interruption; therefore, the practical effect of this amendment is that non-extinguishment is no longer presumed and is something applicants must now prove.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the text and operation of the measure before the committee; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But I simply want to put to the Minister that for the clarification of the burden of proof requirements, this amendment would, if it is genuinely the intent of the Government, ensure the default is non-extinguishment of customary interests, make that vastly clearer and put the burden of proof on the Crown to prove extinguishment rather than on iwi to prove customary title.
focus.explanation: Directed at the substance of the burden-of-proof provision and his proposed alternative; nothing about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Also, to the announcement that the Minister said they are setting aside $15 million—to do exactly what?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named commitment attached to the bill: a specific sum announced by the Minister, and what it is for. Naming the figure and the announcement makes this accountability, not party attack.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: To simply say, “Oh, for example, here’s a few we found” is actually either lazy or misleading.
civility.explanation: Nominally aimed at the drafting, but 'lazy or misleading' imputes either carelessness or bad faith to whoever produced it rather than staying on the defect itself. Short of a personal insult, but past the point of purely substantive criticism.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: So is this, you know, his own idea or is this his officials? Because I’m pretty sure that a good parliamentary counsel—and we have excellent parliamentary counsel in this Parliament—would not have advised this messy, duplicate, verbose, and largely redundant drafting.
civility.explanation: Robust and pointed: the adjectives are all aimed at the drafting, but the framing invites the inference that the Minister personally overrode competent advice. It edges toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But my question here is, where you see examples in legislation, it’s a kind of interpretive convention that examples are not the rules themselves.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a claim about New Zealand statutory interpretation: that an example included in legislation is illustrative only and does not itself operate as the rule.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Legislation Act 2019, s 13 (Examples) and the leading NZ interpretation texts/case law on the status of statutory examples. True if the law provides that an example is only illustrative of the provision it relates to, does not limit it, and yields to the provision where they conflict; false if examples are treated as independently operative rules capable of doing the legislative work themselves.

veracity.statement: Also, to the announcement that the Minister said they are setting aside $15 million—to do exactly what?
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Minister announced $15 million being set aside in connection with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) amendments.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations' public announcement/press release and Budget or Cabinet papers accompanying the Takutai Moana amendment bill in 2025. True if a $15 million allocation was announced in connection with these amendments; false if no such allocation was announced or the announced figure was materially different.

rigor.statement: If we are to have a seriously plural legal system, one that takes account of the fact that we have, over the course of time and jurisprudence, got a blending of tikanga and common law as the foundation of our legal system in this country, then we need to enshrine and recognise that tikanga has, at least, the same standing as common law, and that it must not meet the test of common law.
rigor.explanation: A conditional argument with a stated premise (tikanga and common law are already blended in NZ jurisprudence) and a conclusion (tikanga must be given equal standing and not be tested against common law). The first half of the conclusion tracks the premise; the stronger claim that tikanga 'must not meet the test of common law' is not derived from the blending premise and rests on an appeal to Te Tiriti asserted rather than argued. A real gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If we are to have a seriously plural legal system, one that takes account of the fact that we have, over the course of time and jurisprudence, got a blending of tikanga and common law as the foundation of our legal system in this country, then we need to enshrine and recognise that tikanga has, at least, the same standing as common law, and that it must not meet the test of common law.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the legal mechanism his amendment would create and the doctrinal principle behind it. No party framing, no reference to opponents.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We could, of course, call it the “Hobson’s Pledge Memorial Bill” because that’s really where these politics come from: the politics of attacking Māori simply for looking for the recognition of the rights that they have historically exercised.
focus.explanation: There is a residual policy referent (the Bill's treatment of historically exercised rights), but the weight of the statement is about where the politics 'come from' and the motives behind them rather than any clause, threshold or outcome. Attributing the measure to a lobby group's agenda is party framing, not the named-outcome scrutiny that scores high.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It does not break any deals; it is set out in its goal to find that balance between enabling Māori to establish customary marine rights and title, while also recognising the wide interests that all New Zealanders have in the marine and coastal space.
focus.explanation: Squarely about what the Bill is for and what it does, responding to the substance of the criticism. No reference to the other party's record or character. Low specificity and high focus is the intended pairing here.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I propose a name amendment of the “No Entitlement to Compensation for Māori Act”, because, ultimately, our people will not be eligible for compensation for the lost time, for the opportunity cost, for the years of preparation and going through the hearings.
focus.explanation: Framed as a rhetorical naming amendment, but the reason given identifies a specific gap in the measure — the absence of any compensation mechanism for applicants whose completed hearings are nullified. That is a named policy consequence, not content-free party-bashing. Marked down slightly because the naming device carries some of the weight.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It requires the court to recognise tikanga as evidence and sets out the nature and forms of the evidence that may take.
specificity.explanation: Names an actor (the court), a duty (must recognise tikanga as evidence) and a drafting location (new section 59A of Amendment Paper No. 380), which he quotes nearby. But the operative content is a list of categories rather than a threshold, test or figure — a direction with detail, missing the how much and the by when.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It does not break any deals; it is set out in its goal to find that balance between enabling Māori to establish customary marine rights and title, while also recognising the wide interests that all New Zealanders have in the marine and coastal space.
specificity.explanation: Offered as a substantive defence of the Bill, but supplies no test, threshold, clause or figure — 'find that balance' between two named interests is a statement of purpose with nothing in it that could be checked or acted on. This is where the Bill's actual test change would have been the specific content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Wairarapa have customary marine title (CMT) granted in interim judgment in December 2024.
specificity.explanation: Names the applicant area, the precise legal instrument (customary marine title), the form of the decision (interim judgment) and the month and year. Directly checkable against the court record.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The law has been changed not just to make it harder for future litigants, but to strip people who have had their day in court and won their case.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Bill operates retrospectively on applicants who have already obtained a favourable customary marine title determination, removing what those determinations gave them, rather than only altering the test for applications yet to be heard.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The application, transitional and commencement provisions of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Bill as reported back and as enacted: true if the new customary marine title test applies to applications already determined in the applicants' favour — including interim judgments not yet sealed — so that those recognitions are set aside or must be redetermined; false if determinations already made are preserved and only undetermined applications are affected.

veracity.statement: It seeks not to take away rights—nobody will wake up tomorrow with less ability to enjoy the coastal area or have a connection with it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Bill removes no existing legal entitlement — that no person's recognised rights or access to the common marine and coastal area are diminished when it takes effect.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Bill as enacted, read against orders already made under the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011: true if no customary marine title order or recognition already granted is extinguished, set aside or required to be redetermined, and no statutory right of access or use is narrowed; false if any granted recognition ceases to have effect or must be re-litigated on commencement.

veracity.statement: Wairarapa have customary marine title (CMT) granted in interim judgment in December 2024.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a High Court interim judgment issued in December 2024 granted customary marine title to Wairarapa applicant groups.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: High Court judgments on Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 applications for the Wairarapa coast: true if an interim judgment dated in December 2024 granted customary marine title to one or more Wairarapa applicant groups; false if no such judgment exists in that month, or if it declined customary marine title.

civility.statement: It’s a shameful day for the rule of law when we let people go to court and win, and then when we don’t like what they’ve won, we take it off them.
civility.explanation: Severe condemnation, but aimed wholly at the legislative action and its constitutional character. No individual's character, competence or motive is impugned. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a decision sits at the top.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: All of these groups, as well as other whānau, who have very important rights will have their judgments null and void, so they will not be entitled to any compensation for the loss of time, for the loss of opportunity, and for the sweat and tears that they have put into their hearings.
divination.explanation: Forecasts the effect of the legislation once in force: that the named northern applicant groups' judgments will cease to have effect and that no compensation will be payable to them for the cost of the hearings process.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) (Customary Marine Title) Amendment Act as enacted, plus any Crown compensation or ex gratia scheme announced for affected applicants: true if applicant groups whose customary marine title determinations are set aside receive no statutory or administrative compensation for hearing costs, preparation time or opportunity cost; false if a compensation or reimbursement mechanism is provided for them.

veracity.statement: Just another reminder to the members in this committee that today marks the 50-year anniversary since our tupuna Dame Whina Cooper led the march from the Far North here to Wellington.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 14 October 2025 is the 50th anniversary of the 1975 Māori land march led by Whina Cooper from the Far North to Parliament.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Contemporary records of the 1975 Māori land march (hīkoi) — the date it departed Te Hāpua and the date it reached Parliament. True if the march's arrival at Parliament fell on 14 October 1975; false if it departed or arrived on a materially different date.

veracity.statement: This month also recognises the 190-year commemoration of the signing of the declaration of independence on 28 October.
veracity.explanation: Asserts He Whakaputanga / the Declaration of Independence was signed on 28 October and that October 2025 marks 190 years since.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text and signing record of He Whakaputanga o te Rangatiratanga o Nu Tireni held by Archives NZ. True if signed 28 October 1835 (1835 + 190 = 2025); false if the signing date or year differs.

veracity.statement: Well, I’d like to thank the member for his history lesson, and I’ll give him another date, which is it is now coming up to 21 years since the Labour Government, in 2004, passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that took the coastal area for the Crown.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Foreshore and Seabed legislation was passed by the Labour Government in 2004 (about 21 years before the statement) and that it took the coastal area for the Crown.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 — its date of enactment, the government in office, and whether its vesting provision placed the public foreshore and seabed in Crown ownership. True if enacted in 2004 under a Labour-led government with Crown vesting; false if the year, government, or effect differs.

veracity.statement: This Act that we’re amending at the moment—the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act—was an agreement between the National Party and the Māori Party in 2011, to come up with a process by which Māori could establish their customary rights to the foreshore and seabed area—a significant advance.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the 2011 MACA Act arose from a National–Māori Party agreement and created a process for Māori to establish customary rights over the foreshore and seabed.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The National–Māori Party confidence and supply agreement of the 2008–2011 term and the enactment record of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011, including its customary marine title provisions. True if the Act was enacted in 2011 pursuant to that agreement and establishes a customary rights recognition process; false if either element is absent.

veracity.statement: There is no evidence that has been brought to this House in this committee stage or at any stage of the select committee that confirms what the Minister keeps saying: that he’s restoring the intent.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that no evidence of the 2011 Parliament's intent was placed before the House or the select committee at any stage of the bill's passage.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for every stage of the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill, the select committee report, and the departmental advice and regulatory impact material published with the bill. True if none of these cites 2011 legislative-history material for the intent claimed; false if the Minister or officials tabled or cited 2011 debates, committee reports or drafting material.

veracity.statement: It certainly moves away from it in so far as it puts the burden of proof on iwi Māori and the onus on iwi Māori, rather than the onus being on the Crown to prove extinguishment, which was clearly articulated by the Minister at the time, Chris Finlayson, in that the onus had to be borne by the Crown to prove extinguishment; not that iwi Māori had to prove customary title.
veracity.explanation: Two checkable assertions: that the amendment bill shifts the burden of proof onto iwi Māori, and that Chris Finlayson as the responsible Minister in 2011 stated the onus of proving extinguishment lay with the Crown.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the 2011 Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill debates and Finlayson's statements as Minister, plus the proof provisions of the current amendment bill compared with s 58 of the 2011 Act. True if Finlayson stated the Crown bore the onus of proving extinguishment and the amendment places the proof burden on applicants; false if either is not borne out by the record.

veracity.statement: I want to call back to what the officials told us in the supplementary analysis report, where Te Arawhiti said in their overall analysis—Te Arawhiti considered this reform was unlikely to address the primary concerns Māori have with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, as identified through the Waitangi Tribunal 266O inquiry, and any amendments proposed to address the coalition commitments only make it harder under the current law to prove customary marine title.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The supplementary analysis report / regulatory impact material published by Te Arawhiti for the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Amendment Bill. veracity.statement: Nobody’s bloody been successful in direct negotiations.

civility.statement: When I look towards the commencement of this particular bill, let it be another stain on the record of this committee and the treatment of the Māori people.

civility.statement: Well, I’d like to thank the member for his history lesson, and I’ll give him another date, which is it is now coming up to 21 years since the Labour Government, in 2004, passed the Foreshore and Seabed legislation that took the coastal area for the Crown.

civility.statement: I suggest another name for the bill could be the “Invention of Imaginary Intent Bill” because the Minister has created an intent from a previous Parliament for which there is no evidence.

specificity.statement: This Act that we’re amending at the moment—the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act—was an agreement between the National Party and the Māori Party in 2011, to come up with a process by which Māori could establish their customary rights to the foreshore and seabed area—a significant advance.

specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So I propose, as I did in my earlier kauwhau, October 2026 as a commencement date, to allow the system to catch up—allow the system to catch up—unless I’m missing something.
specificity.explanation: Names a concrete alternative commencement date that could be moved as an amendment. Marked down because "allow the system to catch up" supplies no measure of what readiness would look like.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want to call back to what the officials told us in the supplementary analysis report, where Te Arawhiti said in their overall analysis—Te Arawhiti considered this reform was unlikely to address the primary concerns Māori have with the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act, as identified through the Waitangi Tribunal 266O inquiry, and any amendments proposed to address the coalition commitments only make it harder under the current law to prove customary marine title.

specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: One of the things the Minister has set out as the argument for this bill is that it is resuming the intent or clarifying the intent of Parliament, but we have heard over and again from people who were directly involved in the actual creation of that Act in 2011 that this does not correct the intent.
rigor.explanation: States the Minister's position accurately and rebuts it with the testimony of those who drafted and passed the 2011 Act — relevant evidence for a claim about intent. It leans on authority rather than the enacted text, which is a real gap, but the inference is otherwise sound.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can we ever have any faith in a House and a system who apologises one day—gives redress one day—and then the next day does the same thing?
rigor.explanation: A genuine consistency argument: if the Crown apologises for historic breaches while repeating the conduct, trust is unwarranted. The inference holds, but the key premise — that this bill amounts to "the same thing" as the breaches apologised for — is asserted rather than shown.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: We need to allow the officials time and the court system to catch up, because they’re already significantly behind, it’s already a stretched workforce, and we already know there are budget cuts everywhere.
rigor.explanation: Three stated reasons — existing backlog, workforce capacity, funding reductions — each of which bears on the conclusion that commencement should be delayed. The conclusion tracks the premises offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: One of the things the Minister has set out as the argument for this bill is that it is resuming the intent or clarifying the intent of Parliament, but we have heard over and again from people who were directly involved in the actual creation of that Act in 2011 that this does not correct the intent.
focus.explanation: Directly engages the Minister's stated justification for the bill and the question of what the 2011 Parliament intended. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This Minister’s Government is taking us backwards as a country, taking us back to the worst attitudes towards respectful relations with iwi Māori on the part of the Crown.
focus.explanation: A judgement about the Government's attitudes in general rather than about any provision, figure or outcome. The surrounding passage does name the 2011 settlement, which keeps it off the floor, but this sentence itself carries no policy content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So I propose, as I did in my earlier kauwhau, October 2026 as a commencement date, to allow the system to catch up—allow the system to catch up—unless I’m missing something.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the clause before the committee — the commencement date — and the operational reason for changing it.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The member did refer to a lot of numbers, and I can assure the member that the Government has received advice and allocated up to $15 million to the rehearing of cases.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that the Government has received advice and allocated up to $15 million for the rehearing of cases — a checkable appropriation claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 / Estimates and Supplementary Estimates appropriations and Ministry of Justice advice on funding for the rehearing of cases; true if an allocation of up to $15 million for rehearings is recorded, false if no such allocation exists or the figure is materially different.

veracity.statement: However, there is currently no clause that enables anchor polytechnics to be removed from the designation as an anchor polytechnic in this amendment legislation.

veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill as reported back from select committee, in particular new sections 315, 337 and 338 inserted by clause 22; true if no provision permits removal of anchor polytechnic designation, false if any clause provides for it.

veracity.statement: The Minister has publicly stated and pledged to my local polytechnic, the Otago Polytechnic, and also to the Otago Daily Times, that if they meet the road to viability, which they’re on track to do, they will be able to exit the federation and exit their anchor polytechnic status.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister made a specific public commitment to Otago Polytechnic, reported in a named newspaper, that meeting viability would allow exit from the federation and from anchor status.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Daily Times reporting and Penny Simmonds' public statements during 2025 on Otago Polytechnic; true if she publicly said Otago Polytechnic could exit the federation and its anchor designation on meeting viability, false if no such statement exists or her stated position was materially different.

specificity.statement: The member did refer to a lot of numbers, and I can assure the member that the Government has received advice and allocated up to $15 million to the rehearing of cases.
specificity.explanation: Carries a named figure ($15 million) tied to a named purpose, though 'up to' and the absence of any timeframe or breakdown leave it short of fully checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So what I have done is I have drafted an Amendment Paper, Amendment Paper 388, explicitly modelled after new section 339—the same section around federation polytechnics—that will enable anchor polytechnics to be designated and removed from the designation of anchor polytechnics, using the exact same language and the exact same processes that the Minister has outlined for federations.
specificity.explanation: Names the amendment paper by number, the section it is modelled on, and the exact mechanism it would create. Someone could pick this up and check or act on it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: To ensure that a polytechnic is successful, it must be very engaged with their community, must be very integrated with their community, and must understand their community.
specificity.explanation: A string of generic virtues — engaged, integrated, understanding — with no figure, mechanism, threshold or named requirement. Nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Of course, all Opposition amendments to this bill have been, and are, made in good faith, but I just wanted to highlight my Amendment Paper now, at the start of the debate, to give the Minister time to seek advice from her advisers and consider adopting my amendment or incorporating the principles behind it into the legislation.
civility.explanation: On a bill he is vigorously opposing — a real opportunity to be uncivil — he attacks no one, extends good faith and offers the Minister time to consider. Entirely on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: However, there is currently no clause that enables anchor polytechnics to be removed from the designation as an anchor polytechnic in this amendment legislation.
focus.explanation: Names a specific gap in a specific piece of legislation before the House. Pure policy content with no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m interested, Minister, in understanding how Māori will be represented on the ITP councils.
focus.explanation: A question squarely about a mechanism in the bill — the composition of ITP councils — with no party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, one could argue that new section 315, inserted by clause 22, which replaces Subpart 4 of Part 4, gives the powers to designate the polytechnic by Orders in Council. But that is under the heading of “Establishment of polytechnics”. I would argue that the section is clearly for newly established polytechnics—so if you’re starting a polytech at the start, not intending to designate polytechs that already exist and are currently in existence and have been established.
rigor.explanation: States the strongest counter-argument against his own position, then answers it with a reason drawn from where the provision sits in the Act. The inference from a Part heading to the scope of a section is a recognised interpretive argument and the conclusion tracks it, though a heading is not conclusive as to scope.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: However, the anchor polytechnic is exactly that: the anchor polytechnic; the one that is going to generally provide the services and programmes for the other federation polytechnic. So the anticipation is that there would be a lot more movement of federation polytechnics than there would be of anchor polytechnics.
rigor.explanation: The premise is largely a restatement of the term being defined ('the anchor polytechnic is exactly that: the anchor polytechnic'), and the conclusion — that anchors will move less often — does not bear on the question actually put, which was whether any mechanism to move them exists. Expected frequency of use is not an argument that a power is unnecessary.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Therefore, if a polytechnic was operating in a community which was predominantly Māori, you would expect that polytechnic’s council to be predominantly Māori.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion follows cleanly from the stated premise that a council should reflect the make-up of its community. The premise is asserted rather than supported, and the inference gives an expectation rather than the mechanism that was asked about, but the reasoning itself is valid.
rigor.subject: speaker

divination.statement: However, the anchor polytechnic is exactly that: the anchor polytechnic; the one that is going to generally provide the services and programmes for the other federation polytechnic. So the anticipation is that there would be a lot more movement of federation polytechnics than there would be of anchor polytechnics.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that federation polytechnics will change designation more often than anchor polytechnics do, once the new system is in operation.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Orders in Council and NZ Gazette notices designating or removing federation and anchor polytechnic status from the Act's commencement to the resolve-by date; true if the count of federation designation changes exceeds the count of anchor designation changes, false if anchor changes equal or exceed federation changes.

rigor.statement: It’s not financially viable. I haven’t seen any information, nor has anyone ever told me that this puts the sector in a more financially viable position than it was prior to Te Pūkenga, and I still encourage the Minister to share that information with the House.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion ('it's not financially viable') is drawn from the absence of information rather than from evidence of unviability — an argument from ignorance. It is tempered slightly by the fact that he is placing an evidential burden on the Minister rather than asserting a positive finding, but as stated the inference does not carry.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think the challenges across this, and coming back to the financial viability piece, is that stability is not achieved by cutting hundreds of jobs, stability is not achieved by closing down campuses, and it’s certainly not achieved by shutting and cancelling courses from across the country that meet the needs of learners, particularly those more vulnerable than others, but particularly those that sit in our regional communities.
rigor.explanation: Assertion by rhetorical repetition: three parallel 'stability is not achieved by X' claims are stated but nothing is offered connecting job cuts, campus closures or course cancellations to instability. The conclusion is restated rather than supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s not financially viable. I haven’t seen any information, nor has anyone ever told me that this puts the sector in a more financially viable position than it was prior to Te Pūkenga, and I still encourage the Minister to share that information with the House.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the policy: the financial sustainability of the vocational education sector before and after Te Pūkenga, with a named demand for information. Legitimate scrutiny of a specific measure, no party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We’ve had the takutai moana bill that shafted Māoris, and so here we are doing it again.
focus.explanation: Names a specific other bill but only to assert a general pattern of Government behaviour toward Māori. No mechanism, clause, figure or outcome of the bill under debate is engaged — the weight is on characterising the other side rather than on the policy.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So if I turn to clause 4(2), in “Section 9 amended (Te Tiriti o Waitangi)”, which replaces section 9(2)(e) with section 314(d), the question for the Minister is: in her view, why has this wording been changed?
focus.explanation: Entirely about the text of the measure before the House — a drafting change and the advice behind it. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I think the challenges across this, and coming back to the financial viability piece, is that stability is not achieved by cutting hundreds of jobs, stability is not achieved by closing down campuses, and it’s certainly not achieved by shutting and cancelling courses from across the country that meet the needs of learners, particularly those more vulnerable than others, but particularly those that sit in our regional communities.
specificity.explanation: Names concrete categories of consequence — job cuts, campus closures, cancelled courses — but supplies no counts beyond 'hundreds', no campuses, no courses and no timeframe. A direction with partial detail.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So if I turn to clause 4(2), in “Section 9 amended (Te Tiriti o Waitangi)”, which replaces section 9(2)(e) with section 314(d), the question for the Minister is: in her view, why has this wording been changed?
specificity.explanation: Names the exact clause, the section being amended and the provisions being substituted, so anyone could look up precisely what is being asked about. A precise question, which is as specific as a precise answer; it stops short of 1.0 only because the question itself is open-ended rather than pinned to a figure or date.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In terms of the financial information, I’m very, very pleased to tell the member that for the last 18 months the Tertiary Education Commission has assigned financial advisers to each individual polytechnic to go through a pathway to financial sustainability—work that should have happened the day Te Pūkenga came into being.
specificity.explanation: Names the responsible agency, the mechanism (financial advisers assigned per institution), the coverage (each polytechnic) and a duration (18 months). Missing any cost, milestone or target that would make the 'pathway to financial sustainability' checkable, so short of the top.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I reflect back on 2018 when $20 million had to be injected into Whitireia and WelTec to keep the lights on so that they could continue to pay their staff and their bills.
specificity.explanation: A year, a dollar figure and two named institutions — fully checkable against public funding records.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: We’ve had the takutai moana bill that shafted Māoris, and so here we are doing it again.
civility.explanation: Blunt and aggressive, but the target is legislation and the Government's programme, not any individual member. Under the re-anchored scale harsh criticism of a bill sits near the top; it edges down only because 'doing it again' imputes a deliberate pattern of intent.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I look at Government members from across the House that at the eighth hour submitted amendments to the select committee report, obviously to accommodate the Government’s wishes and this Minister.

That is an attribution of bad faith rather than an argument about the amendments, so it falls short of the civil standard.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The fact that no work was done in five years to address their financial situation was absolutely appalling.
civility.explanation: Strongly worded condemnation, but of an institutional record rather than any individual. Under the re-anchored scale, brutal criticism of a decision or a record is civil; nothing here turns on a person.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: I look at Government members from across the House that at the eighth hour submitted amendments to the select committee report, obviously to accommodate the Government’s wishes and this Minister.

veracity.falsification_criterion: The Education and Workforce Committee's report on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill and the associated departmental report / committee proceedings records: true if amendments proposed by Government members were tabled in the final stage of the committee's consideration shortly before report-back; false if the recorded amendments were tabled in the ordinary course of consideration rather than at the end.

veracity.statement: In terms of the financial information, I’m very, very pleased to tell the member that for the last 18 months the Tertiary Education Commission has assigned financial advisers to each individual polytechnic to go through a pathway to financial sustainability—work that should have happened the day Te Pūkenga came into being.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that for the past 18 months the Tertiary Education Commission has had financial advisers assigned to every individual polytechnic to work through a financial sustainability pathway.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission records, annual report or ministerial/OIA statements on ITP financial sustainability support: true if TEC-assigned financial advisers were in place at all ITPs for roughly the 18 months to October 2025; false if advisers covered only some institutions or were engaged for a materially shorter period.

veracity.statement: I reflect back on 2018 when $20 million had to be injected into Whitireia and WelTec to keep the lights on so that they could continue to pay their staff and their bills.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in 2018 approximately $20 million of funding was injected into Whitireia and WelTec to cover their operating costs.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission funding records, Budget appropriations and the two institutions' annual reports: true if a bailout or capital injection of about $20 million was made to Whitireia and WelTec around 2018; false if no such injection occurred or the amount and year are materially different.

veracity.statement: The fact that no work was done in five years to address their financial situation was absolutely appalling.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that over a five-year period no work was undertaken to address the financial position of the institutions concerned under Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga and Tertiary Education Commission records for 2020–2024 — financial recovery or sustainability plans, board papers, annual reports and TEC monitoring correspondence: false if any documented financial sustainability programme, recovery plan or restructuring aimed at the institutions' finances existed in that period; true only if no such work is recorded.

veracity.statement: I understand from the first Budget bid that was leaked in October 2022 that that was to be $940 million – odd over 10 years. It was scaled back and scaled back and eventually got to a $200 million loan.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the first Te Pūkenga Budget bid, leaked in October 2022, sought approximately $940 million over ten years, and that it was progressively reduced until it became a $200 million loan.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The leaked October 2022 Te Pūkenga Budget bid and associated Ministry of Education / Treasury Budget papers: true if the initial bid was for roughly $940m over 10 years and the final decision was a loan of about $200m; false if the initial figure or the final instrument differs materially.

veracity.statement: Yes, you will see in a number of the papers that are released that I was constantly getting advice that there was no pathway to viability.

veracity.falsification_criterion: Proactively released Ministry of Education / Tertiary Education Commission advice to the Minister on NorthTec, 2024–2025: true if those papers repeatedly advise no pathway to viability; false if the released advice does not say this.

veracity.statement: You will be very pleased to know that out of the strategic investment fund, NorthTec have got the most of any polytechnic for the next two years.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NorthTec's allocation from the strategic investment fund for the coming two years is the largest of any polytechnic.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission strategic investment fund allocations by institution for the two years following October 2025: true if NorthTec's allocation is the largest single ITP allocation; false if another polytechnic received more.

veracity.statement: They weren’t able to do that once the pastoral care code came in, which the Green Party brought in.
veracity.explanation: Attributes the tertiary pastoral care code — and the resulting inability of mature students to stay on a marae during study blocks — to legislation brought in by the Green Party.

veracity.statement: NorthTec’s qualification completion rate for Māori was fourth out of 16 ITPs. For Māori, it was fourth out of 16. Now, in terms of the overarching retention of Māori learners at NorthTec, it was second out of 16 ITPs.

specificity.statement: So I’m happy with the work we have done over the last 18 months to ensure that individual polytechnics have got a pathway to sustainability, and I’m happy with the work that has been done in securing additional funding off $20 million a year over the next two years to ensure that strategically important areas, regions—geographic areas—are not put in jeopardy, and that strategically important disciplines such as agriculture or forestry are not going to be put in jeopardy while we work through what sort of funding changes might be needed in a long-term perspective of that.

specificity.statement: NorthTec’s qualification completion rate for Māori was fourth out of 16 ITPs. For Māori, it was fourth out of 16. Now, in terms of the overarching retention of Māori learners at NorthTec, it was second out of 16 ITPs.
specificity.explanation: Names the measure, the comparator set (16 ITPs), the sub-population and exact rank positions — anyone could pull the TEC performance tables and check it.

specificity.statement: We need to think of a plan whereby people are put at the centre of decision making instead of a balance sheet, because not all regions are the same, e tātou mā.

specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: I’m hoping that they will be able to grow that again, and I consider that we are not going to be faced with the sort of question of additional $930 million – odd being needed over the following nine years.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that no further large-scale bailout of the order of $930 million will be required for the polytechnic sector over the following nine years.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: Vote Tertiary Education appropriations and Budget decisions for the polytechnic/ITP sector from 2025/26 through 2034: true if cumulative additional Crown funding or loans to the sector beyond current baselines stays well below ~$930m; false if additional appropriations of that order are sought or granted.

rigor.statement: That is a decision that should be made by the council of that polytechnic because they should be engaged with their community, they should know what is needed in their community.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion (campus decisions belong to the polytechnic council, not a Minister) supported by a stated reason (councils are community-engaged and know local needs). The inference tracks, though it rests on an unexamined assumption that councils are in fact so engaged.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It’s not always about financial viability; it can actually be for public good, because what’s good for Northland is good for all of Aotearoa New Zealand.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion (fund NorthTec for public good rather than viability) rests on a bare part-to-whole generalisation — 'what's good for Northland is good for all of Aotearoa' — offered without any mechanism or evidence connecting the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If we ignore the people workforce, there ain’t no kaimahi. You’re going to be importing them from overseas or outside of the rohe, because, in Tai Tokerau, let’s get that clear, we are young, we are brown, and we are fertile.

civility.statement: So I would like the Green Party to have a wee look at the unintended consequences that have made it very difficult for a number of mature women in the Far North who want to undertake their nursing degree.

civility.statement: Of course Grant agrees; of course our Northland MP agrees. It would be great to see him come to our meetings; they’re well advertised.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic response to an interjection that turns on the named member personally, implying he does not show up for his own region's meetings. Short of a direct insult, but the mockery and imputation of neglect put it below the civil standard.

specificity.statement: Six of the governing positions will be by industry and will be put there by industry; two will be put by the Minister, but the Minister can only appoint people that industry have nominated.
