specificity.statement: Our hospital is only at 63 percent staffing capacity.
specificity.explanation: A single checkable figure about a named institution, offered in place of a general claim that staffing is short.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But even worse than this, and I hope the member listens very carefully to this—this is one of the reasons why redundancies have had to be made there—under the previous Government, $6.5 million was clawed back by the Tertiary Education Commission because under the closure of their campus from the cyclone, they didn’t meet their targeted numbers.
specificity.explanation: Names the amount, the agency, the mechanism (target under-delivery), and the consequence for the institution's base funding.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: The member will be delighted to know—absolutely delighted to know, I am sure—that EIT will be getting $1.559 million under the strategic fund in the next two years.
specificity.explanation: An exact figure, a named fund and a timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Six of the governing positions will be by industry and will be put there by industry; two will be put by the Minister, but the Minister can only appoint people that industry have nominated.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific membership structure for the industry skills boards under the bill before the committee.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The membership provisions of the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill as reported back (new sections inserted by clause 23): true if the boards have six industry-appointed and two ministerially-appointed members with the Minister confined to industry nominations; false if the numbers or the nomination constraint differ.

veracity.statement: How can this be ensured when areas like Tairāwhiti and EIT Tairāwhiti, who have a Māori population of 56 percent and a rangatahi population of 70.4 percent, have lost 40 academic and support roles?
veracity.explanation: Asserts that EIT Tairāwhiti serves a population that is 56 percent Māori with a 70.4 percent rangatahi share, and that 40 academic and support roles have been lost there.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census ethnicity and age data for the Tairāwhiti/Gisborne region for the two percentages, and EIT/Te Pūkenga disestablishment records or reporting on the EIT Tairāwhiti campus for the role count; true if the figures match within rounding, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Our hospital is only at 63 percent staffing capacity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a precise current staffing level at the hospital serving her electorate, offered as evidence that graduates are needed locally.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand / Te Whatu Ora staffing and vacancy reporting for Gisborne Hospital around October 2025; true if filled positions are approximately 63 percent of the funded establishment, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: But even worse than this, and I hope the member listens very carefully to this—this is one of the reasons why redundancies have had to be made there—under the previous Government, $6.5 million was clawed back by the Tertiary Education Commission because under the closure of their campus from the cyclone, they didn’t meet their targeted numbers.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Tertiary Education Commission recovered $6.5 million from EIT under the previous Government because enrolment targets were missed while the campus was closed after Cyclone Gabrielle.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC funding-recovery decisions and EIT/Te Pūkenga annual reports for 2023 and 2024; true if a recovery of approximately $6.5 million from EIT for under-delivery in the post-Gabrielle period is recorded, false if no such recovery occurred or the amount or cause differs materially.

veracity.statement: I will stand corrected if someone will give me a different figure, but I believe that the polytech sector trains more Māori than any other part of the tertiary education sector—something that I am incredibly proud of.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the polytechnic sub-sector enrols or trains more Māori learners than any other part of tertiary education (universities, wānanga, PTEs).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education / TEC tertiary participation statistics by sub-sector and ethnicity for the most recent year: true if ITP Māori enrolments exceed those of every other sub-sector, false if universities, wānanga or PTEs enrol more.

veracity.statement: I will correct the member that Māori and Pasifika trades training still exists—is still going—and I am absolutely looking forward to that growing as the economy takes off again, because construction is doing so well in the South.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Māori and Pasifika Trades Training programme is still operating at the time of speaking.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: TEC funding allocations and programme listings for Māori and Pasifika Trades Training for 2025/26: true if the programme is still funded and delivering, false if it was disestablished or defunded.

veracity.statement: Last night, I did ask a series of questions relevant to replacement section 314(d), inserted by clause 22, in particular that the Minister didn’t respond to.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that he put questions on replacement section 314(d) during the previous evening's committee stage and that the Minister did not answer them.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Hansard record of the committee stage on the evening of 13 October 2025: true if Halbert's contributions raise section 314(d) and no subsequent ministerial reply addresses it, false if he did not raise it or the Minister answered it.

focus.statement: The industry skills boards will set the standards, will develop the qualifications, will undertake the moderation, will give endorsement to those entities that can run the programmes, and will give advice to the Tertiary Education Commission about where funding should go, so it’s in the right place at the right time.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of the measure before the committee — the functions the new boards will hold. No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: For example, in an area like Tairāwhiti, where 56 percent of the population are Māori, does that mean 56 percent of the council will be Māori?
focus.explanation: Presses the Minister on how a specific drafting change (replacing an obligation to include Māori with 'regard to') will operate in a named region. Squarely on the policy, not the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: This clause enables the local community, not the Minister sitting in Wellington but the local community, to decide what the make-up of that board, of that council, should be for EIT.
focus.explanation: Answers on the mechanism of the clause itself — who holds the appointment power — rather than on the questioner's party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Last night, I did ask a series of questions relevant to replacement section 314(d), inserted by clause 22, in particular that the Minister didn’t respond to.
focus.explanation: Names the exact provision at issue and holds the Minister to a specific unanswered line of questioning on it. Scrutiny of a named clause, not party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: How can this be ensured when areas like Tairāwhiti and EIT Tairāwhiti, who have a Māori population of 56 percent and a rangatahi population of 70.4 percent, have lost 40 academic and support roles?
rigor.explanation: A real inference: the statute requires improved outcomes for Māori students, staffing at the relevant campus has been cut, so the requirement is in tension with what has happened. The gap is that role losses are not shown to translate into worse student outcomes — the link is asserted rather than demonstrated.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: This clause enables the local community, not the Minister sitting in Wellington but the local community, to decide what the make-up of that board, of that council, should be for EIT.
rigor.explanation: The premise (local rather than ministerial appointment) is offered in answer to a question about guaranteeing Māori representation, but local control does not entail proportional representation; the conclusion that the community's Māori share will therefore be well represented does not follow from the premise supplied.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But even worse than this, and I hope the member listens very carefully to this—this is one of the reasons why redundancies have had to be made there—under the previous Government, $6.5 million was clawed back by the Tertiary Education Commission because under the closure of their campus from the cyclone, they didn’t meet their targeted numbers.
rigor.explanation: A causal argument with a supporting comparison (the Christchurch earthquake precedent, where numbers were held): funding was recovered, the base dropped, so redundancies followed. The conclusion tracks the evidence, though 'one of the reasons' is not quantified against other causes.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: What was that, expert on Māori representation? Nothing, kia ora.
civility.explanation: Sarcastic mockery directed at the interjecting member personally — the 'expert' tag and the dismissive 'Nothing' target the person rather than anything he argued. Short of a direct insult, but plainly a jibe.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The member will be delighted to know—absolutely delighted to know, I am sure—that EIT will be getting $1.559 million under the strategic fund in the next two years.
civility.explanation: The repeated 'absolutely delighted to know, I am sure' is needling directed at the questioner, but it stops well short of impugning her character or competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m delighted to be talking about Nelson Marlborough Institute of Technology (NMIT) in particular, where the member had 15 years’ experience—of course, I had 30 years’ experience, but it’s great that there are others who have got experience in this sector.
civility.explanation: A one-up on the member's credentials with a faintly patronising coda ('it's great that there are others'). Pointed and slightly condescending, but it does not attack his competence or character outright.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They talked in their submission about how 38 percent of disabled people aged 15 years and over who were not currently in post-secondary education or training would like to do so in the future but face numerous barriers in accessing it.
veracity.explanation: Relays a statistic attributed to the joint DPA/NDSA submission: that 38% of disabled people aged 15+ not in post-secondary education or training would like to be, but face access barriers.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.subject_name: Disabled Persons Assembly and National Disabled Students' Association
veracity.falsification_criterion: The joint Disabled Persons Assembly / National Disabled Students' Association submission on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, and the Stats NZ Household Disability Survey figure it draws on. True if the submission states that figure for that population and the underlying survey supports it; false if the figure, the age band, or the population base is materially different.

veracity.statement: It started recovering in 2023 and there’s been a continuation and acceleration of that trend during this Government.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that international student numbers began recovering in 2023 and that the growth both continued and accelerated under the current Government.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education New Zealand / Immigration New Zealand international student enrolment and visa counts for 2022–2025. True if enrolments rose in 2023 and the year-on-year growth rate in 2024–2025 was at least as high as 2023's; false if enrolments fell in any of those years or if growth decelerated after 2023.

veracity.statement: I appreciate that very constructive start to his question, where he offered to review the unintended consequences that have come from the pastoral code that the Green Party brought in.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the tertiary pastoral care code was brought in by the Green Party.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The legislative history of the Education (Pastoral Care) Amendment Act 2019 and the Education (Pastoral Care of Tertiary and International Learners) Code of Practice 2021 — which Minister issued the code and under which government. True if the Green Party introduced or led the measure; false if it was introduced by a Labour Minister of Education under the Labour-led government, with the Greens as a supporting party rather than the originator.

veracity.statement: It’s a pity that the previous Government spent a billion dollars trying to solve a problem that was only about a few million at the time and didn’t create an enduring solution.
veracity.explanation: Two quantitative assertions: that the previous Government spent about a billion dollars on the vocational education reforms, and that the underlying problem was worth only a few million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury, Tertiary Education Commission and Auditor-General figures on the total cost of the Reform of Vocational Education and Te Pūkenga's establishment and deficits, set against the audited ITP sector deficits immediately before the 2019 merger. True if total spend approaches $1 billion and the pre-reform sector shortfall was of the order of single-digit millions; false if the spend was materially below that or the pre-reform deficit ran to tens of millions or more.

focus.statement: We would like to see the disability services potentially included in the list of relevant services as well as pastoral care services.
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the committee — proposes two named additions to the shared 'relevant services' list in clause 5(5). No party content at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In terms of this particular section, I think it’s very important to ensure that a piece of legislation like this can be enduring, and to put exhaustive lists in really constrains things to the moment now.
focus.explanation: Answers the question with a drafting rationale about the named section — exhaustive lists versus enduring legislation. Entirely about the measure, with no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Given the centrality of the Treaty in our country’s public life and matters of public policy, the importance of Māori being at the table and fully engaged in decision making and so on, including in the governance of our country’s institutions, why would the Government deliberately exclude the reference to including Māori in the governance of polytechs?
focus.explanation: Names a specific deletion in a specific provision (the removal of 'include Māori' from the council composition requirement) and asks the Government to justify it. Textbook scrutiny of a named measure, not party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It’s a pity that the previous Government spent a billion dollars trying to solve a problem that was only about a few million at the time and didn’t create an enduring solution.
focus.explanation: Carries a figure and a claimed outcome about a real policy, which is genuine accountability content, but it names no policy or measure and its function here is to praise the Minister by contrast with the other side. A policy point wrapped in party framing.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Specifically, given the conversation we’ve just had, how will Māori be represented on those industry skills boards?
focus.explanation: A direct question about the composition of a specific body created by the bill, picking up the substantive thread of the preceding exchange. Wholly on the measure.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: We would like to see the disability services potentially included in the list of relevant services as well as pastoral care services.
specificity.explanation: Names the mechanism (the relevant-services list) and the two services to add, but supplies no drafting, threshold or cost. A direction with real detail, short of something you could enact as written.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’ve said this on multiple occasions: a successful polytechnic is one that is engaged with their community, that is integrated with their community, that takes notice of their community, and that works with their community.
specificity.explanation: Four restatements of the same generic virtue. No figure, mechanism, threshold or test by which 'engaged with their community' could be checked — which is the precise point being contested about the replacement wording.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I think including disability services in the relevant services that could be shared across the different services could be a way that we get a cohesive approach on this, because I do think that it is something we need to make sure is not lost with Te Pūkenga.
rigor.explanation: A conclusion offered with a reason: Te Pūkenga's equity focus risks being lost, therefore share disability services across the federation. The reason supports doing something, but there is a real gap between 'don't lose the focus' and 'put it in the shared-services list' — nothing offered connects the mechanism to the outcome. Not fallacious, just under-supported.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I would expect that there would be virtually no community in this country that would not have a significant proportion of Māori in it, and therefore I would expect that that would be reflected in the council.
rigor.explanation: An explicit 'therefore' whose conclusion does not follow: the demographic composition of a community does not entail the composition of a council appointed to serve it. The inference quietly assumes the representation mechanism that the amendment under discussion deletes, which makes it close to circular — the premise only supports the conclusion if the removed requirement were still in force.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does it mean the people on the board should live in the same place? Does it mean they should have brown hair or blue eyes? It could literally mean anything to say “reflect the communities”.
rigor.explanation: A reductio: if the phrase sets no criterion, absurd readings satisfy it. The underlying point is supported — the replacement wording does name no group — but 'could literally mean anything' overstates what was shown, since 'reflect the communities in the region' does constrain to regional composition. A real gap between the demonstration and the conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Does it mean the people on the board should live in the same place? Does it mean they should have brown hair or blue eyes? It could literally mean anything to say “reflect the communities”.
civility.explanation: Mockery, but aimed at the drafting of a phrase rather than at the Minister. Nobody's character, competence or good faith is impugned; the ridicule lands on the words in the bill. Pointed and derisive about the text, still on the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It does dilute Māori representation and therefore will directly impact on achieving Māori outcomes.
rigor.explanation: A premise-plus-conclusion inference: diluted representation "therefore" causes worse outcomes. Nothing is offered to connect governance representation to educational outcomes, and the premise (that the amendments dilute representation) is asserted rather than shown, so the causal step is a real gap rather than a supported inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Now, let me give her the opposite situation in SIT, who went into Te Pūkenga with $40 million in reserves. Only $15 million of that will be ring-fenced, so they will not come out with the full amount that they went in with.
rigor.explanation: A directly responsive counter-argument to the favouritism charge: if SIT entered with $40m and retains only $15m, it is not being advantaged by the recapitalisation. The inference from the figures to the conclusion holds. It does not fully dispose of the conflict-of-interest question (which concerns her prior role rather than the reserve treatment), which is why it is not higher.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It is easy for members of her party to say to people, “Don’t take things personally.”, but I would like her to consider how personal it is to the people in Dunedin when our whole economy is predicated on health and education through the tertiary sector.
rigor.explanation: A real inference — a local economy concentrated in health and education means tertiary decisions land personally — and the premise is offered rather than assumed. But the weight rests on an appeal to the audience's feelings, and "our whole economy is predicated on" overstates the premise the conclusion needs, leaving a gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: It does dilute Māori representation and therefore will directly impact on achieving Māori outcomes.
focus.explanation: Squarely about the content of the bill's governance provisions and their effect, not about the other party. Names the mechanism (representation) and the outcome at issue; it is scrutiny of a specific legislative change.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: We had the wonderful example that Eastern Institute of Technology is in a community with 56 percent of the population Māori, and that is exactly what we expect to see reflected in the council of that entity.
focus.explanation: Directly on the policy question at issue — how the council-composition provision in clause 22 would operate for a named institution — rather than on the opposing party. Names an institution, a figure and the governance mechanism it bears on.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I would just point to the regulatory impact statement (RIS), page 3, which talks about the lack of consultation and the lack of being able to assess the risks, so one of my questions is: who bears those risks, particularly when there is active competition between polytechs in the way this has been set up?
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny anchored to a named official document and page, asking who carries an identified risk of a specific design choice. Entirely about the policy and its mechanism, with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Time and time again, we have seen from this Government a kneecapping of our lifeblood in Dunedin, and a disregard.
focus.explanation: A generalised charge against the Government's overall attitude to a region. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named in the statement — it is a characterisation of the other team's disposition rather than accountability for a specific commitment.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I appreciate Stuart Smith really has an interest around better French representation around council—you know, all over to you.
civility.explanation: Sarcasm directed at a named member in response to his interjection. It is a light jibe about the member's supposed interest rather than an attack on his character or competence — pointed and edging toward the person without landing on him.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Oh Madam Chair, am I pleased to be able to straighten out some of that misinformation that has just been put by that member.
civility.explanation: Characterising an opponent's questions as "misinformation" imputes bad faith to the member personally rather than disputing the claims. Short of a direct insult, but it is a charge about how the member is behaving, not about the substance.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I’m going to spell this out very clearly because I know that financial matters can be quite challenging for some members of the Labour Party, but let me make it very clear to you: there was no conflict of interest there.
civility.explanation: Condescension aimed at the intellectual competence of named individuals — that financial matters are beyond "some members of the Labour Party". That is an attack on people's capability rather than on their argument, and it sits at the personal-attack end of the scale.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I would like to ask the Minister about an elephant in the room in the lower South, in terms of why she is tearing apart our region when it comes to tertiary education.
civility.explanation: Loaded framing ("tearing apart our region") that presupposes the answer, but it targets the Minister's decisions and their regional effect rather than her character or competence. Pointed and robust, edging toward the person without landing on her.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: They were mostly themed around the removal of explicit Te Tiriti obligations for the vocational education sector, such as the obligations under section 9(1)(g) of the principal Act, the absence of effective engagement with Māori throughout the drafting process, and the potential lack of ongoing accountability to Māori and Māori representation through governance settings.
specificity.explanation: Names the source (the departmental report), the specific statutory provision (section 9(1)(g) of the principal Act) and three enumerated submission themes. Someone could go to the report and check each. Falls short of 1.0 only because no counts or proportions are given for "mostly".
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Now, let me give her the opposite situation in SIT, who went into Te Pūkenga with $40 million in reserves. Only $15 million of that will be ring-fenced, so they will not come out with the full amount that they went in with.
specificity.explanation: Two concrete figures and a named mechanism (ring-fencing of reserves under the recapitalisation exercise) attached to a named institution. Checkable against the recapitalisation settings.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I would just point to the regulatory impact statement (RIS), page 3, which talks about the lack of consultation and the lack of being able to assess the risks, so one of my questions is: who bears those risks, particularly when there is active competition between polytechs in the way this has been set up?
specificity.explanation: Cites a named document and page and identifies the two specific deficiencies it records. Not 1.0 because the risks themselves and who bears them are left as an open question rather than quantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They were mostly themed around the removal of explicit Te Tiriti obligations for the vocational education sector, such as the obligations under section 9(1)(g) of the principal Act, the absence of effective engagement with Māori throughout the drafting process, and the potential lack of ongoing accountability to Māori and Māori representation through governance settings.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that submissions on the bill were predominantly themed around removal of explicit Te Tiriti obligations including section 9(1)(g), inadequate engagement with Māori during drafting, and weakened accountability/representation through governance settings.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental report to the Education and Workforce Committee on the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if its summary of submissions on Te Tiriti obligations lists these three themes as the predominant ones, false if the report characterises the submission themes materially differently or the section reference is wrong.

veracity.statement: We had the wonderful example that Eastern Institute of Technology is in a community with 56 percent of the population Māori, and that is exactly what we expect to see reflected in the council of that entity.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the community served by the Eastern Institute of Technology has a population that is 56 percent Māori.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census ethnicity data for the territorial authorities/region EIT serves (Hawke's Bay and Tairāwhiti); true if the Māori share of the population of the stated catchment is approximately 56 percent, false if it is materially different (e.g. Hawke's Bay region as a whole, which is well under half).

veracity.statement: Otago Polytechnic sadly have a debt of $16 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Otago Polytechnic currently carries debt of $16 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Polytechnic's / Te Pūkenga's most recent audited financial statements and the Tertiary Education Commission's published financial position for the institution; true if reported debt (or accumulated deficit, as the Minister frames it) is approximately $16 million, false if materially different.

veracity.statement: My questions then, really, are around batting away the very strong perception of conflict of interest that exists for us locally; understanding from the Minister who she thinks bears the risk of her decisions, given that the RIS, on page 3, makes it very clear that there was not time to adequately assess Option 2.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that page 3 of the regulatory impact statement for this bill states there was insufficient time to adequately assess Option 2.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The regulatory impact statement published for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill, page 3; true if it records a constraint on the time available to assess Option 2, false if no such limitation is recorded there or the option numbering does not match.

veracity.statement: What can she say to claims locally that there is a privatisation agenda in tertiary education, because we have seen a mental health programme cut from Otago Polytechnic that is now suddenly appearing via a private provider in Dunedin.
veracity.explanation: Asserts as fact that a mental health programme was cut from Otago Polytechnic and that an equivalent programme has since begun being offered by a private provider in Dunedin.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Polytechnic's programme discontinuation records / NZQA programme approvals; true if a mental health programme was withdrawn by Otago Polytechnic and a private training establishment in Dunedin subsequently gained approval for a comparable programme, false if no such cut occurred or no private provider took up an equivalent programme.

veracity.statement: I would also say, for context, it does seem personal when this is the same Minister who, at the eleventh hour, in a different capacity, overturned a local government decision where local ratepayers had paid $18 million to get a decision made locally, in local democracy, around freshwater—it was this Minister who led the charge against that.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Penny Simmonds, acting in a portfolio other than tertiary education, overturned a local government freshwater planning decision on which local ratepayers had spent $18 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Otago Regional Council's published expenditure on its Land and Water Regional Plan and the ministerial direction/legislative change requiring its withdrawal; true if the recorded ratepayer spend is approximately $18 million and Simmonds, as Minister for the Environment, drove the withdrawal, false if the spend is materially different or another Minister was responsible.

focus.statement: Why would you take out from the charter a vital piece of the machinery, like the industry skills boards, the obligation that a Treaty clause conveys to engage fully with Māori leadership and with mana whenua to ensure that the right services are being delivered?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the measure before the House: names the charter, the industry skills boards and the Treaty clause being removed, and asks what the removal does. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I want to go to the pastoral support code that the Minister did speak to and that the Green Party did support, because that code is the anchor and maybe we need to review it—maybe we need to review it—because I’ve heard from Student Voice in particular that they want to strengthen it.
focus.explanation: Names a specific instrument (the pastoral care code) and proposes a specific action on it. Entirely policy-directed; no reference to the other party at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: They have been thrown under the bus by their leader, because remember, this mess was set up by the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins and followed on from the mess in the police and in health and in COVID.
focus.explanation: Drags in police, health and COVID — none of which is before the committee — to characterise the other party's leader. Almost no policy content survives; the weight of the sentence is who Labour chose as leader.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: She has not explained why she chose to disestablish Te Pūkenga as opposed to tweaking some of the challenges that the structure and the sector still faced.
focus.explanation: Names the specific decision (disestablishment) and the specific alternative not taken, and asks for the reasoning. This is scrutiny of a named policy choice, which is the job — not tribalism.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: As one example, as the Government loads an attack on young people at the moment, if we look at level 1 and 2 foundation learning, there’s simply not enough places for young people to access those particular programmes in Auckland, which is one example, even if the Government wanted them to.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point here — level 1 and 2 foundation learning provision in Auckland — but it is wrapped in the generalised 'the Government loads an attack on young people' framing, which carries a good share of the sentence's weight.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: In this debate, so far, we’ve had a number of calls on this question, but I haven’t yet heard from the Minister a clear explanation why she’s determined to strip the Treaty clause out, and I invite her to give us that.
civility.explanation: A genuinely contested point where he had every opportunity to impute motive. He criticises the absence of an explanation and invites one, attacking neither the Minister's character nor her competence.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Te Pūkenga: what a failed experiment, what a dreadful example of going with form before function, what a dreadful way to try to solve a few specific problems in the sector by creating far, far more.
civility.explanation: Brutal, but every word of it lands on the institution and the policy design, not on any individual. Under the re-anchored scale, fierce criticism of a policy belongs near the top.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They have been thrown under the bus by their leader, because remember, this mess was set up by the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins and followed on from the mess in the police and in health and in COVID.
civility.explanation: Turns from the policy to the person: a sweeping attack on Chris Hipkins' competence across four unrelated portfolios, plus the charge that he abandoned his own colleagues. That is character and competence, not argument.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Submissions noted in the Ministry of Education departmental report that there were alternative options—these were not adequately considered because of the ideological agenda of this Government and the Minister.
civility.explanation: Imputes bad faith: the options were not considered not through oversight or disagreement but because of an 'ideological agenda'. Short of a direct insult, but it ascribes motive rather than contesting reasoning.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Now, if I think about the Māori community, in the communities that I represent in West Auckland, probably one in five of our people in the communities I serve are Māori.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that roughly 20% of the population of the West Auckland communities he represents is Māori. Hedged with 'probably', but the underlying share is a published census figure.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ 2023 Census Māori ethnicity share for the Te Atatū electorate / West Auckland (Waitākere) local board areas. True if the Māori share is approximately 20% (one in five); false if materially lower (e.g. nearer 13-15%).

veracity.statement: Of course, this has nothing to do with the bill that we are currently looking at, but I can give the member assurance that total funding of approximately $18.5 million has been allocated to Māori and Pasifika trades training, and the funding was fully allocated in 2024-25.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions: an MPTT funding total of about $18.5m, and that it was fully allocated in the 2024-25 year.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission funding allocations / Vote Tertiary Education appropriations for Māori and Pasifika Trades Training in the 2024/25 year. True if the allocated total is approximately $18.5 million and was fully allocated in that year; false if the figure or the 'fully allocated' status is materially different.

veracity.statement: Let me see, perhaps the issue that it was going to take nearly a billion dollars over the next 10 years to have the IT systems operational is a good place to start.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a documented estimate existed putting the cost of getting Te Pūkenga's IT systems operational at close to $1 billion across ten years.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga / TEC business case and Ministry of Education advice on the cost of the Te Pūkenga IT and digital systems programme over ten years. True if the documented estimate is close to $1 billion; false if the official estimate is materially lower.

veracity.statement: Perhaps it’s the fact that the polytech sector, under Te Pūkenga, did not get back to pre-COVID numbers, with internationals sitting at only a third, when the universities and the schools and the private training establishments were getting back.
veracity.explanation: A comparative claim: polytechnic international enrolments stuck at about a third of pre-COVID volumes while universities, schools and PTEs recovered.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Education Counts / Immigration NZ international enrolment data comparing ITP-sector enrolments during the Te Pūkenga years against 2019 levels, and the same comparison for universities, schools and PTEs. True if polytechnic international enrolments sat at roughly one third of pre-COVID levels while the other three sectors recovered substantially; false if the polytechnic share was materially higher or the other sectors had not recovered.

veracity.statement: Submissions noted in the Ministry of Education departmental report that there were alternative options—these were not adequately considered because of the ideological agenda of this Government and the Minister.
veracity.explanation: The checkable part is the first clause — that the departmental report records submitters putting forward alternative options. (The motive attributed in the second clause is not a checkable fact and is not part of this claim.)
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministry of Education departmental report on the Bill. True if the report records submissions raising alternative options to full disestablishment and re-establishment; false if no such submissions are recorded there.

veracity.statement: She’s only got $20 million in that—she can’t afford it.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the strategic fund the Minister has been citing holds only about $20 million.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 / Vote Tertiary Education appropriation for the vocational education strategic (transition) fund the Minister refers to. True if the fund is approximately $20 million; false if materially larger or smaller.

veracity.statement: But that question remains: why did you disestablish and go against advice that you received to reestablish something that you don’t have a cost-benefit analysis of.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions embedded in the question: that the Minister acted against the advice she received, and that no cost-benefit analysis of the replacement model exists.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministry of Education advice papers and the Regulatory Impact Statement for the Bill, plus any Official Information Act releases on the disestablishment decision. True if officials advised against disestablishment/re-establishment and no cost-benefit analysis of the new model was produced; false if the advice supported the decision or a cost-benefit analysis exists.

specificity.statement: I want to go to the pastoral support code that the Minister did speak to and that the Green Party did support, because that code is the anchor and maybe we need to review it—maybe we need to review it—because I’ve heard from Student Voice in particular that they want to strengthen it.
specificity.explanation: Names the code and the stakeholder, but 'maybe we need to review it' and 'strengthen it' carry no mechanism, no provision, no timeframe. The pair with Focus above is the point: on-policy but thin on checkable content.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Of course, this has nothing to do with the bill that we are currently looking at, but I can give the member assurance that total funding of approximately $18.5 million has been allocated to Māori and Pasifika trades training, and the funding was fully allocated in 2024-25.
specificity.explanation: A named programme, a dollar figure and a fiscal year — someone could go and check the allocation. Docked slightly because 'approximately' and no breakdown of what the money buys.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Te Pūkenga: what a failed experiment, what a dreadful example of going with form before function, what a dreadful way to try to solve a few specific problems in the sector by creating far, far more.
specificity.explanation: Trying to convey substance about why the merger failed, but delivers only a string of pejorative characterisations — 'failed experiment', 'form before function' — with no figure, mechanism or named problem.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Let me see, perhaps the issue that it was going to take nearly a billion dollars over the next 10 years to have the IT systems operational is a good place to start.
specificity.explanation: A cost, a timeframe and the specific system being costed. Checkable against the business case; short of 1.0 only because 'nearly a billion' is a rounded figure with no source named.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Across this piece of legislation, it is the emperor without clothes, if anyone knows those stories, because the Minister has been building this plane as it flies, because there is a lack of information.
specificity.explanation: An attempt at substance about how the Bill was developed, delivered entirely through two stacked metaphors. No provision, document, decision or gap in the information is named, so there is nothing here to check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Despite the best advocacy of students to Northland Regional Council to change the bus timetable, they wouldn’t, and so students would have to start way earlier, get their kids off to school way earlier, in order to catch a bus.
rigor.explanation: A modest but valid inference: given a fixed, unsuitable timetable, earlier departures follow directly. The conclusion is proportionate to the premise; no fallacy or appeal, though nothing is offered to quantify the effect.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Across this piece of legislation, it is the emperor without clothes, if anyone knows those stories, because the Minister has been building this plane as it flies, because there is a lack of information.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the legislation is hollow rests on the metaphors themselves rather than on anything offered: 'there is a lack of information' is asserted as the supporting premise without a single instance of missing information being produced.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: She’s only got $20 million in that—she can’t afford it.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion 'she can't afford it' is drawn from the size of the fund alone. Without a figure for what the transition will cost, the gap between premise and conclusion is unbridged — the argument needs both sides of the comparison and supplies one.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: But for the polytech sector, which is governed by section 317, polytechs can have between six to eight members.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that section 317 of the Education and Training Act 2020 sets ITP council membership at six to eight members.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Text of section 317 of the Education and Training Act 2020 (as amended and in force on 14 October 2025); true if it prescribes a council membership range of six to eight, false if it prescribes any other range or no range.

veracity.statement: The first nursing degrees were brought about through collaboration.
veracity.explanation: Historical claim that New Zealand's first nursing degree programmes were established through collaboration between polytechnics.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Documented history of the establishment of the first nursing degree programmes in New Zealand polytechnics (NZQA/TEC programme approval records, institutional histories); true if the founding programmes were jointly developed by more than one institution, false if they were established by a single institution alone.

veracity.statement: I also note that we are only on clause 7 of 39 of Part 1, about 41 pages, so there’s a number of very specific provisions which have not been discussed at all in this committee stage, that cover the substantive part of this bill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Part 1 of the bill has 39 clauses across about 41 pages and that the committee stage had reached only clause 7, leaving most substantive provisions undebated.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The bill as reported back from the Education and Workforce Committee (clause count and page extent of Part 1) together with the Hansard record of this committee stage; true if Part 1 contains 39 clauses over roughly 41 pages and debate had covered only up to clause 7 at this point, false if the counts differ materially or later clauses had already been traversed.

veracity.statement: They said to the Education and Workforce Committee in their submission that at no point was anyone able to articulate the problem that the reforms solved.
veracity.explanation: Relays a claim made by a submitter about what its submission to the select committee said. What is checkable is whether the submission contains that statement.
veracity.subject: other
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Civil Contractors New Zealand written submission to the Education and Workforce Committee on this bill, as published on the Parliament website; true if it states that no one was able to articulate the problem the reforms are trying to solve, false if it contains no such statement.

rigor.statement: We know that some universities will be smaller than some polytechnics, so I don’t think it’s necessarily to do in size.
rigor.explanation: Premise (institutional sizes overlap across the two sectors) genuinely bears on the conclusion (that size does not explain the differing council-size ranges). The inference is sound but modest — overlap at the margins does not fully rule out size as a rationale, so it falls short of a clean conclusion.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anywhere between six and eight is generally accepted as a good working board or council that will be able to represent the community but also be agile and nimble.
rigor.explanation: Bare appeal to unattributed consensus ("generally accepted") standing in for a reason; the desirable properties are asserted of the range rather than derived from anything offered. No evidence or mechanism connects the number six-to-eight to the claimed outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: So my question is: how did that number of six to eight get arrived at as opposed to the membership of university councils which can be eight to twelve?
specificity.explanation: Names two statutory membership ranges and puts a checkable, answerable question about how one of them was set. Concrete enough that the answer could be verified against the policy advice.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I just want to ask—and I won't take a full call—a very specific question around clause 7 amending section 267, which looks at amending the main Education and Training Act 2020 in relation to the clause on academic freedom.
specificity.explanation: Names the clause, the section it amends, the parent Act and the subject matter — anyone could locate exactly what is being asked about.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I also note that we are only on clause 7 of 39 of Part 1, about 41 pages, so there’s a number of very specific provisions which have not been discussed at all in this committee stage, that cover the substantive part of this bill.
specificity.explanation: Carries exact counts — clause 7 of 39, about 41 pages — rather than a general complaint about rushed scrutiny.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I’m keen to know, in relation to section 314, why there is nothing in there, in the description of the characteristics, about the role that polytechs play in alleviating skills and workforce shortages.
specificity.explanation: Names the section, the part of it at issue (the characteristics) and the precise thing said to be missing; the Minister could answer it directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So my question is: how did that number of six to eight get arrived at as opposed to the membership of university councils which can be eight to twelve?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the mechanism of the bill — a named clause and a named figure. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: If that’s good enough for the polytech sector, why not require it also for the university sector to work in a collaborative manner?
focus.explanation: Engages the substantive design of the duty imposed by the bill and asks why it is not extended. Entirely policy content, no reference to the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I just want to ask—and I won't take a full call—a very specific question around clause 7 amending section 267, which looks at amending the main Education and Training Act 2020 in relation to the clause on academic freedom.
focus.explanation: Directed entirely at a named provision of the bill and its effect on academic freedom; no party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: I’m keen to know, in relation to section 314, why there is nothing in there, in the description of the characteristics, about the role that polytechs play in alleviating skills and workforce shortages.
focus.explanation: Legitimate scrutiny of a named provision and a specific omission from it. Entirely about the content of the bill, not about the other party.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Polytechnics, I think, are known for being collaborative, nimble, and agile. I don’t think university councils have ever been accused of being that but it’s important for the polytechnics that they are.
civility.explanation: A pointed dig, but aimed at a class of institutions rather than any person, in an exchange where she was being challenged and could have turned on the questioner. Attacks nobody.
civility.subject: speaker

divination.statement: In the past they have formed statutes and they have been different for each institution, and I would expect that, again, they will be different, so they won’t exclude any of the representation from staff or from students or from iwi.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the councils of the re-established polytechnics will adopt differing statutes and that none of those statutes will exclude staff, student or iwi representation.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The council statutes adopted by the re-established ITPs once constituted under this Act; true if the statutes vary between institutions and none excludes staff, student or iwi representation, false if statutes are uniform or if any institution's statute excludes one of those groups.

divination.statement: It will see courses cancelled in the further-out parts of Northland: Kaikohe, Kaitāia, marae-based programmes.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that NorthTec will cancel courses at its Kaikohe and Kaitāia delivery sites and its marae-based programmes as a result of the restructure.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NorthTec/Te Pūkenga transition programme schedules and any published change proposal outcomes for 2026-2027; true if courses at Kaikohe, Kaitāia or marae-based programmes are discontinued, false if the same programmes continue to be offered at those sites.

divination.statement: It’s going to see the closure of its main campus in Whangārei, as an example, to be relocated somewhere else.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that NorthTec's main Whangārei campus will close and its delivery be relocated to another site.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: NorthTec/NZIST announcements and Whangārei District Council records; true if the existing main Whangārei campus ceases teaching operations and delivery moves to another site, false if it remains NorthTec's operating main campus.

focus.statement: We see WelTec, Whitireia, UCOL, where we’re seeing a downsizing of courses and programmes available to learners in our most regional and remote communities.
focus.explanation: Names specific institutions and a specific policy outcome (reduced course availability in regional communities) rather than attacking the governing parties in general. This is scrutiny of a named consequence of the bill.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: My theory is that, if the chairperson and deputy chairperson are the ones who are supposed to be leading the council, it makes perfect sense for the Minister to consult the members of the ITP concerned on who their chairperson and deputy chairperson might be, because the members might know something about the person that the Minister might want to appoint as chairperson and deputy chairperson that she doesn’t necessarily know.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanism of a named provision — who appoints the chair and what consultation should precede it — with no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: That is inequitable, Minister. You’ve made a commitment to achieving better outcomes than Te Pūkenga did for those learners.
civility.explanation: Hard criticism directed at the outcome of the policy and at a commitment the Minister made in her official capacity; no attack on her as a person, no imputation of bad faith.
civility.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Online learning is not the only vehicle by which people engage in learning opportunities, and you haven’t offered the specificity that we need to assure us and give us confidence that this legislation is going to retain access for regional learners, actually going to have pūtea, money, available to invest in those learners, because you are committed to a 1:18 student ratio.
specificity.explanation: Carries one concrete, checkable anchor — the 1:18 student-to-tutor ratio — but the rest is a general complaint about missing assurance, with no figures for regional funding or programme numbers.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That is exactly why NorthTec will be receiving the largest amount of any of the polytechnics—$3.648 million a year over the next two years, to ensure that they can keep that important provision going, because I know how much we must ensure access in those regions.
specificity.explanation: A named institution, an exact dollar figure and a stated duration — a reader could check the allocation directly.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: My question is: in section 319(1), instead of using the word “must”, why does it use the word “may”?
specificity.explanation: Pinpoints a numbered subsection and the exact word at issue — as precise as a question can be, and directly checkable against the bill.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: While in Tokoroa, the Minister thinks she may have saved the campus, there’s still significant job losses and, as a result, over consecutive years we will see less learning opportunities in smaller communities like Tokoroa that have already been heavily impacted.
rigor.explanation: Offers a premise (staff losses at the Tokoroa campus) and draws a conclusion that tracks it (fewer courses available over time). The inference is reasonable but has a gap: keeping the campus open with fewer staff does not automatically entail cumulative reductions in learning opportunities, and no figure links the two.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But trying to get recognition of exactly that—and the member is completely correct: that is why in a place like Telford, you can’t put 18 students who are trying to learn how to shear a sheep or drive a four-wheeler in front of one tutor.
rigor.explanation: A concrete counterexample that genuinely supports the conclusion drawn: practical, safety-constrained training at Telford cannot run at a 1:18 ratio, therefore a uniform ratio needs flexibility. The example does the work the conclusion needs; no fallacy or appeal.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: My theory is that, if the chairperson and deputy chairperson are the ones who are supposed to be leading the council, it makes perfect sense for the Minister to consult the members of the ITP concerned on who their chairperson and deputy chairperson might be, because the members might know something about the person that the Minister might want to appoint as chairperson and deputy chairperson that she doesn’t necessarily know.
rigor.explanation: Premise (council members hold local information about candidates the Minister lacks) supports the conclusion (the Minister should consult them before appointing). The inference follows; it leans slightly on an unevidenced assumption about what members know, but nothing fallacious.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Look, it is described as “may”, but it is, effectively, mandatory because the chair will be appointed.
rigor.explanation: Near-circular: the conclusion that a discretionary 'may' is effectively mandatory is supported only by restating that a chair will be appointed, which is the very thing in question. It offers nothing about why the discretion could not be exercised otherwise.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: Centralisation, where all of the decisions had to be made by a central entity that was supposed to be in Hamilton but was actually in Auckland—allowing those sorts of decisions to be made locally is incredibly important.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Te Pūkenga's central decision-making entity, though nominally headquartered in Hamilton, in fact operated out of Auckland.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Te Pūkenga's registered/head office address in Companies Office and Crown entity records and its annual reports, plus the location of its executive leadership team; true if the head office or the bulk of executive decision-making sat in Auckland, false if it was located in Hamilton as constituted.

veracity.statement: That is exactly why NorthTec will be receiving the largest amount of any of the polytechnics—$3.648 million a year over the next two years, to ensure that they can keep that important provision going, because I know how much we must ensure access in those regions.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that NorthTec's strategically important provision funding is $3.648 million per year for two years and is the largest such allocation to any polytechnic.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tertiary Education Commission strategically important provision / strategic funding allocation tables for 2026 and 2027; true if NorthTec's allocation is $3.648m per year and exceeds every other ITP's, false if the figure differs materially or another polytechnic receives more.

veracity.statement: Nowhere is more important than in the Far North, where we’ve got the highest number of NEETs anywhere in the country.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Far North has the highest level of young people not in employment, education or training of anywhere in New Zealand.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ Household Labour Force Survey / MSD NEET statistics broken down by region or territorial authority; true if Northland/Far North records the highest NEET rate in the country, false if another region records a higher rate. (Note the literal wording says 'number', which absolute counts in Auckland would falsify; the criterion should be applied to the rate the speaker plainly means.)

veracity.statement: You’ll see, in the earlier section, 317, that she will be appointing up to half of the current polytech council.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the section inserted by clause 22 as section 317 empowers the Minister to appoint up to half of a polytechnic's council membership.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of new section 317 as inserted by clause 22 of the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill; true if the Minister's appointment power extends to up to half the council, false if the proportion in the enacted/current text differs.

focus.statement: Why are the interests of those regions not actually something that the Minister is required to take into account when she issues one of these orders. Why is there not, for example in paragraph (b), the requirement to consult, for example, local institutions, regional industry groups, local community organisations, iwi and hapū?
focus.explanation: Squarely on the substance of the measure before the committee: names new section 315, paragraph (b), and the specific consultees he says should be required. No party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Essentially in the main Education and Training Act, the main section 289(7) doesn’t apply but new section 341J does apply.
focus.explanation: Entirely about the mechanics of the measure before the committee — which Crown observer provision applies to polytechnics and which does not. No party content.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: What advice are you receiving around the actual costs and funding that you need to establish this particular model for the 10-plus other polytechnics?
focus.explanation: Direct scrutiny of a named policy — the establishment costs of the anchor-polytechnic model for the remaining institutions. Textbook opposition accountability, no party-bashing.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Why are the interests of those regions not actually something that the Minister is required to take into account when she issues one of these orders. Why is there not, for example in paragraph (b), the requirement to consult, for example, local institutions, regional industry groups, local community organisations, iwi and hapū?
specificity.explanation: Identifies the exact provision and enumerates the concrete classes of body he would have the statute require consultation with. A drafter could act on it directly; it stops short of proposing precise wording.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Treasury’s advice was interesting over the period of time. We got that advice at different periods of time, and over the last 18 months, things have changed as the institutions have got stronger and more viable.
specificity.explanation: Answering a direct request about Treasury's advice on costs, this carries no dates, no content of any piece of advice, no figures and no measure of 'stronger and more viable'. Almost nothing here could be checked or acted on.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Essentially in the main Education and Training Act, the main section 289(7) doesn’t apply but new section 341J does apply.
specificity.explanation: Pins the point to two exact statutory provisions in the parent Act and the bill, so the drafting asymmetry she is questioning can be verified against the text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: What advice are you receiving around the actual costs and funding that you need to establish this particular model for the 10-plus other polytechnics?
specificity.explanation: Names what is wanted (establishment costs and funding advice) and scopes it to the 10-plus remaining polytechnics, but does not pin it to a period, a document or a figure.
specificity.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: If I think about West Auckland, it’s a part of the city with very particular demographic characteristics. We have a young, largely working-class population. We have real transport challenges that create barriers for our young people to get access to jobs and education and training opportunities. I’m sure that if you look at any particular region, there would be particular characteristics. So why doesn’t section 315 require that?
rigor.explanation: Premise (regions have materially different demographic and transport circumstances) supports the conclusion (the establishment test should require regional interests to be weighed). The generalisation from one electorate to every region rests on assertion rather than evidence, which is the gap; he does flag it as an assumption.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ll be very brief because I think that, as the member has pointed out, new section 315(2)(b), added by clause 22, covers that very open “consult other persons or bodies that the Minister thinks fit;”. It opens the door to consult with all of those entities that the member brought forward.
rigor.explanation: The question was why regional consultation is not *required*; the answer establishes only that it is *permitted*. A discretionary power does not entail the outcome the objection sought, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I’ve seen this and thought that it’s wonderful to have early intervention, to have different stages of intervention, because the worst thing possible is to allow a polytechnic to keep going and getting itself more and more in trouble and racking up huge amounts of debt.
rigor.explanation: A reason is offered and the conclusion tracks it: if unchecked deterioration is the worst outcome, staged early intervention follows as the remedy. The premise that it is 'the worst thing possible' is asserted rather than supported, which is the weakness.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Surely there will be instances where the Minister has a firm view and there is nothing that the council can say to dissuade you that there needs to be some outside intervention into this council. I just want to ask if “consult” is the correct word.
rigor.explanation: A valid inference: if the Minister may proceed regardless of the council's response, then a duty labelled 'consult' misdescribes what the process actually is. The premise about the Minister's discretion is supposed rather than established from the clause, which is the gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

civility.statement: A number of submissions were made on that, and I wonder if the Rt Hon Chris Hipkins sometimes reflects and wishes he’d gone down that track.
civility.explanation: A pointed needle at a named opponent over a past policy choice. It edges toward the person — inviting the House to picture him regretting his own decision — without impugning his character, competence or good faith.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The federation model isn’t new; it’s used in a number of countries. It was actually suggested to the previous Government, when they set up Te Pūkenga, that the federation model would be a good model.
veracity.explanation: Asserts two matters of record: that a federation model for vocational education is in use in other jurisdictions, and that a federation model was put to the previous Government during the establishment of Te Pūkenga.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Submissions to the Education and Workforce Committee on the Education (Vocational Education and Training Reform) Amendment Bill 2019/2020, and the Reform of Vocational Education consultation submissions: true if one or more submissions proposed a federated/federation model as an alternative to the single-institution Te Pūkenga design, false if none did. For the first clause, identifiable federated vocational/polytechnic systems in named comparator countries.

veracity.statement: I acknowledge that Treasury has advised you against this, they’ve highlighted the risks financially for this particular structure.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Treasury advised against the proposed polytechnic structure and identified financial risks in it. He is asserting this as fact, not relaying it as someone else's contention.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Treasury's published advice on the vocational education reform — the Regulatory Impact Statement for the Education and Training (Vocational Education and Training System) Amendment Bill and proactively released/OIA'd Treasury reports to Ministers: true if Treasury recommended against the disaggregated/anchor-polytechnic structure or expressly flagged financial risks in it, false if Treasury's advice endorsed it without such warnings.

specificity.statement: Who’ll judge whether an action is detrimental to the interests of an anchor polytechnic? And is there a specific definition around what “detrimental” might mean in this context?
specificity.explanation: Pins the question to a named test in new section 328(1)(b) and asks for two concrete things — the decision-maker and the operative definition of "detrimental". A precise question is as checkable as a precise answer.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: When I looked at what examples there might be, I could think of, for example, that if there were polytechnics that wanted the anchor polytechnic to develop a particular course but it was going to cost the anchor polytechnic a lot of money and divert them from other development, this might come into play.

veracity.explanation: Asserts that the bill's strike-notice provision has no effect on the legal right to take industrial action, only on the notice period — a contested claim raised by submitters.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2) as reported back, read against the Employment Relations Act 2000 strike provisions: true if the bill's only change to strike provisions is the notice period and no clause restricts eligibility to strike or the lawfulness of any strike; false if any clause narrows the circumstances in which a lawful strike may be taken.

rigor.statement: We know that attending school is strongly linked to achievement, and, to support this, the bill requires all schools to have attendance management plans in place that consistently responds to and addresses the diverse underlying causes of non-attendance and return students to school.
rigor.explanation: A premise (attendance is linked to achievement) offered in support of a conclusion (mandating board-level attendance management plans). The link cited is associative, and nothing is offered to bridge from that association to the claim that a mandated plan will change attendance, so there is a real gap between what is shown and what is concluded — but the inference is not fallacious.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Another key proposal in this bill is increasing the amount of days’ notice that unions must provide before they strike from three days to “no less than seven days”.
specificity.explanation: Names the exact mechanism and both figures — a change from three days' strike notice to no less than seven. Directly checkable against the bill text.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: I want schools to focus on getting back to the basics and getting them right so that all learners have the knowledge, skills, and competencies they need to reach their full potential.
specificity.explanation: A slogan-level aspiration in a passage otherwise full of clause-level detail: "the basics", "full potential" — no subject, standard, figure, mechanism or timeframe that anyone could check or act on.
specificity.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Another key proposal in this bill is increasing the amount of days’ notice that unions must provide before they strike from three days to “no less than seven days”.
focus.explanation: Squarely about a specific clause of the measure before the House; no party framing at all.
focus.subject: speaker

civility.statement: I believe that New Zealand’s learners deserve to attend schools where their attainment and their educational achievement is the highest priority, and I acknowledge submitters’ concerns and understand that some may think that the focus on educational achievement may demote other objectives, but to meet their paramount objectives, schools must continue to meet the other essential and supporting objectives.
civility.explanation: The proposal was genuinely contested and critics could easily have been dismissed or characterised as ideological. Instead the objection is restated fairly and answered on its merits; nobody is disparaged.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: It took on a responsibility for coping with inflation driven to stratospheric levels of danger as a consequence of a failed fiscal policy prior to our arrival.
rigor.explanation: A causal conclusion (previous fiscal policy caused the inflation) is asserted with nothing offered to connect the two — no mechanism, no evidence, and no acknowledgement of the global inflation shock. Bare assertion standing in for an inference.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Well, given that the size of our economy is $440-odd billion, it takes a while to turn the super-tanker around.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to analogy: the nominal size of the economy is offered as the premise, but nothing connects GDP magnitude to the claim that recovery must be slow. The super-tanker metaphor does the work an argument should.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Our reforms are delivering better outcomes for students. Three out of four teachers report that structured literacy approaches have improved literacy for most students.
rigor.explanation: The premise is a perception survey; the conclusion is about actual outcomes. Self-reported teacher opinion is offered as though it established measured achievement gains, and no attainment data is supplied to close that gap.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They’re both correct, because what we do know is that we have a higher aspiration for young people, clearly, than the Opposition do.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur: the reason given (the Government's aspirations) has no bearing on the question of whether two conflicting factual claims can both be correct. The "because" connects nothing.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Does she think it is reasonable to cut jobseeker for young people when over 218 applications for one role at a Tank Juice bar show that there are simply no jobs available?
rigor.explanation: Hasty generalisation from a single anecdote: applications for one hospitality vacancy are offered as showing that "there are simply no jobs available" across the labour market.
rigor.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: But as my colleague Mr Bishop has said, over $60 billion has been put aside for infrastructure, including the construction sector, over the next four years.
specificity.explanation: Carries a figure ($60 billion) and a timeframe (four years), so it is checkable, but gives no breakdown, no mechanism and nothing tying it to construction employment.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: How can she stand by her statement that “We have invested more in public infrastructure.”, when there are 20,000 fewer people working in construction?
specificity.explanation: A precise figure (20,000) attached to a named sector and a named claim. A questioner's precision counts the same as a minister's.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Nearly 80 percent of primary teachers have accessed professional learning and development in delivering structured literacy, and ERO found that teachers who used the 1.1 million maths books, textbooks, workbooks, and teacher guides that we have delivered were four times more likely to change their teaching practice.
specificity.explanation: Three separate checkable quantities — an uptake percentage, a resource count, and an effect size — each attached to a named mechanism and a named source.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Very exciting announcement: three new charter schools announced this week so far, taking the total number to 14, with more to come later in the week.
specificity.explanation: Concrete counts — three this week, fourteen in total — that someone could check against the public register.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why we had 58 different applications for people to run new schools in this round, and I’m very much looking forward to announcing even more of these new schools as well as a growing number of State schools converting to charter status as the year completes.
specificity.explanation: One hard figure (58 applications in the round), but the rest — "even more", "a growing number", "as the year completes" — carries no counts or dates.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Because under their watch, the number of young people that went on to benefit under the age of 25—the duration increased to 18 future years on welfare, a 49 percent increase since 2017.
