rigor.explanation: Unfalsifiable framing: it treats disagreement as automatic confirmation of the conclusion, so no possible response from the Government could count against it. Nothing is offered to connect dismissal to being out of touch.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Here’s the problem: limited fee increases, but they haven’t increased funding to practices. Now, practices have just diversified the range of fees they’re charging.
rigor.explanation: A genuine mechanism argument: capping one fee without raising funding creates pressure that surfaces as new fee categories, and the speech supplies concrete instances (first-visit charges, screening charges, double-appointment fees) consistent with the conclusion. The inference is not fully closed — no evidence rules out other causes of the new charges — but it tracks what was offered.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: But the merger of the seven CRIs into three PROs has actually gone well—maybe because the actors were willing participants and willing actors, but regardless, I want to thank them for that effort.
rigor.explanation: The conclusion that the merger 'has gone well' rests on the speaker's own say-so plus a speculative cause ('maybe because the actors were willing'), with no measure of success offered — no cost, timeline, retention or output evidence. He also discards the comparison he had just set up against Health NZ and Te Pūkenga rather than drawing anything from it.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: It is Luxon’s fault that a visit in New Zealand now to the GP, a standard adult visit to the GP, can cost nearly $100.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that a standard adult GP consultation in New Zealand can now cost close to $100. The checkable core is the fee level; the attribution of blame to the Prime Minister is a political judgement and not part of the criterion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Published standard adult consultation fees at New Zealand general practices as at October 2025 (practice fee schedules, Health NZ / GP fee-review data, or media surveys of enrolled adult fees). True if at least one enrolled standard adult daytime consultation fee is at or near $100; false if the highest such published fees are materially below that.

veracity.statement: They repealed free prescriptions, a policy that kept people well and out of hospital.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the current government reversed the policy of free prescriptions. The second clause (that it kept people out of hospital) is a causal claim not covered by the criterion.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2024 decisions and the associated Pharmaceutical (co-payment) settings. True if the $5 prescription co-payment removed by the previous government was reinstated by this government; false if free prescriptions remained in place for the general population.

veracity.statement: Well, sadly, people, ambulances now cost 30 percent more too.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a roughly 30 percent increase in the cost to patients of an ambulance callout.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hato Hone St John / Wellington Free Ambulance published part-charge before and after the 2025 change. True if the emergency ambulance part-charge rose by approximately 30 percent; false if the increase is materially smaller or no increase occurred.

veracity.statement: Now one in six New Zealanders say they cannot afford to go to the doctor.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that about 16.7 percent of New Zealanders report being unable to afford a doctor's visit.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Health Survey (or comparable national survey) measure of adults reporting unmet need for a GP visit because of cost in the most recent year. True if the rate is approximately 16–17 percent; false if materially different.

veracity.statement: Well, I and 16,000 other New Zealanders have written an open letter to Christopher Luxon calling for healthcare to be more affordable.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific number of co-signatories to an open letter on healthcare affordability addressed to the Prime Minister.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The published open letter and its signature count as at 15 October 2025 (campaign page or Labour Party release). True if signatories number approximately 16,000; false if materially fewer.

veracity.statement: Exports in one year are up from $500 million to around $750 million.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific year-on-year rise in New Zealand video game export revenue, roughly a 50 percent increase.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: New Zealand Game Developers Association annual industry survey figures for export revenue in the two most recent years. True if reported exports rose from approximately $500 million to approximately $750 million year on year; false if either figure or the growth is materially different.

veracity.statement: We’ve merged seven Crown research institutes (CRIs) into three public research organisations (PROs), creating some of the biggest research and development thematic institutions in the world.
veracity.explanation: Two assertions in one sentence: the structural fact of a seven-into-three merger, and the comparative claim that the resulting bodies are among the world's biggest thematic R&D institutions. The second is the part most likely to fail.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Two parts. (a) Government science-reform decisions and the establishing legislation/orders: true if seven CRIs were amalgamated into three PROs. (b) Comparison of the new PROs' revenue or research headcount against major international research organisations (e.g. CSIRO, Fraunhofer, CNRS, TNO, VTT): true if any PRO ranks among the largest thematic R&D institutions internationally; false if they are an order of magnitude smaller than the recognised leaders.

veracity.statement: It was the first time in space ever that high temperature superconducting magnets have been bolted on to the outside of the space station.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a world first: that this New Zealand-built high-temperature superconducting magnet payload is the first such device mounted on the exterior of the International Space Station.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NASA/ISS external payload records and Robinson Research Institute publications for the referenced Falcon 9 / Cygnus resupply mission. True if no prior high-temperature superconducting magnet payload was externally mounted on the ISS; false if an earlier external HTS magnet experiment is documented.

specificity.statement: Now one in six New Zealanders say they cannot afford to go to the doctor.
specificity.explanation: Carries a definite, checkable proportion, though no source, period or population is named, so a reader would have to hunt for the underlying survey.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Labour can fix this. We will make care more affordable and make it easier to see a doctor and nurse when you need one in your community.
specificity.explanation: A commitment with no mechanism, no funding figure, no target and no timeframe — 'more affordable' and 'easier to see a doctor' commit to nothing checkable, and unlike the rest of the speech no surrounding detail supplies the how.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Through the Bioeconomy Science Institute, we’ve brought together Landcare Research New Zealand, AgResearch, Scion, Plant and Food Research; Earth Sciences New Zealand, National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research and GNS Science, and, of course, the Institute of Environmental Science and Research renamed as the New Zealand Institute for Public Health and Forensic Science.
specificity.explanation: Names every constituent institute and the new entity each sits within, so a reader can verify exactly which organisations moved where. Concrete institutional detail rather than a description of direction.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: If the Government wants to dismiss that this is a problem, that is only proof of how out of touch they are.
civility.explanation: Aimed at the Government collectively rather than any individual, so it is short of a personal attack, but it converts any disagreement into evidence of a character flaw ('out of touch'), which edges toward imputing indifference.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: They have prioritised tax cuts for landlords, tax cuts for tobacco companies, and not putting money into our health system.
civility.explanation: A hard attack on the Government's fiscal choices that names no individual and makes no claim about anyone's character or competence. The implication of serving landlord and tobacco interests is pointed, but it is directed at the decisions rather than the people making them.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: The third example I’d give is the naming rights, also by New Zealand firm PikPok, to the video game Clusterduck—carefully and eponymously representing in so many ways the collective Opposition parties that we see today, to which we give them Clusterduck.
civility.explanation: Sustained mockery — an elaborate joke whose point is that the Opposition parties are a shambles, with a barely-veiled expletive as the punchline. No individual member is insulted and no one's competence or character is directly attacked, which keeps it above the personal-attack band, but it is derision rather than engagement.
civility.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: The same people in this coalition Government who crashed the economy leading to 36,000 fewer jobs the day that they took office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific employment figure — that 36,000 jobs have been lost since the coalition took office in late 2023.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ monthly employment indicators (filled jobs) and the Household Labour Force Survey, comparing November 2023 with the most recent release before October 2025; true if the net fall is approximately 36,000, false if the fall is materially different or employment rose.

veracity.statement: Over in the National Party we have our environment Minister destroying the name of her job, sitting outside of Cabinet for the first time in 50 years, providing no input—none—on fast-track projects that will destroy our taio and our moana.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Minister for the Environment currently sits outside Cabinet, and that this is the first time in fifty years that the portfolio has been held outside Cabinet.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Ministerial List published by DPMC as at October 2025 for whether the Minister for the Environment is ranked outside Cabinet, plus ministerial lists from 1975 onward for whether any earlier Environment Minister sat outside Cabinet; true if outside Cabinet and no prior instance since 1975, false if either limb fails.

veracity.statement: Spending time lobbying councils to speed up water consents for the benefit of a handful of farms that include her own colleague.
veracity.explanation: Alleges the Minister contacted councils to expedite water consents, and that the consents in question benefit a small number of farms, one of which belongs to a fellow government MP.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Ministerial correspondence and council records (OIA/LGOIMA releases, council agenda papers) showing contact from the Minister to a council about accelerating water consents, and the consent applicants' ownership; true if such contact is documented and an applicant is a sitting coalition MP, false if no such contact exists or no MP has an interest.

veracity.statement: Earlier this year, 142 jobs were lost from Carter Holt Harvey’s Eves Valley sawmill.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 142 jobs were lost at Carter Holt Harvey's Eves Valley sawmill near Nelson during 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Carter Holt Harvey's own closure announcement and contemporaneous reporting on the Eves Valley sawmill in 2025; true if the announced job losses were approximately 142, false if the figure is materially different or the closure did not occur in 2025.

veracity.statement: In fact, when I asked Nicola Willis in the House last week what she was doing about this, she claimed Nelson should be happy with the Government because they’re giving us half a hospital.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that in the House in the week before 15 October 2025, Nicola Willis answered a question about Nelson job losses by pointing to the Nelson hospital investment, and that the investment covers only part of the rebuild.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Hansard for the sitting week of 6–10 October 2025 for the exchange between Rachel Boyack and Nicola Willis, plus Health NZ / Budget documents on the announced scope of the Nelson hospital rebuild; true if Willis gave that answer and the funded scope is less than the full rebuild, false if no such exchange occurred or the full rebuild is funded.

veracity.statement: That’s why, in Budget 2025, the Government committed $250,000 to support rural New Zealand’s grassroots work.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Budget 2025 contained a $250,000 commitment supporting grassroots rural organisations.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Budget 2025 appropriations (Vote Agriculture, Biosecurity, Fisheries and Food Safety, and Vote Women) and the accompanying Budget day press releases; true if a $250,000 commitment for rural grassroots/community work appears, false if no such appropriation exists or the amount differs materially.

veracity.statement: This year marks the centennial of Rural Women New Zealand, an organisation that stood the test of time by adapting to the evolving needs of rural women and their communities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Rural Women New Zealand reaches its hundredth year in 2025.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Rural Women New Zealand's founding date, as recorded by the organisation itself and by Te Ara / Archives New Zealand (it began as the Women's Division of the Farmers' Union); true if founded in 1925, false if founded in any other year.

civility.statement: Winston Peters and Shane Jones on the other side of the House gloat about ruining our oceans and our soils and our air and telling our people that this is the only way forward.
civility.explanation: Names two individual members and imputes malice to them personally — that they take pleasure in environmental destruction. This goes past criticising their policy positions to characterising their motives.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Over in the National Party we have our environment Minister destroying the name of her job, sitting outside of Cabinet for the first time in 50 years, providing no input—none—on fast-track projects that will destroy our taio and our moana.
civility.explanation: 'Destroying the name of her job' is directed at the Minister personally rather than at any decision she has made — an attack on her fitness for the role. The Cabinet-status point is legitimate substance, but it is carried inside a personal characterisation.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: It’s been two years since the election, when Christopher Luxon stood in front of voters in 2023 as an economic genius who declared that he would fix the cost of living and the economy, and he has failed to do so.
civility.explanation: The 'economic genius' framing is sarcasm aimed at a named individual's competence rather than at his policy. The underlying accountability point (a promise made and not met) is legitimate, which keeps this well short of abuse.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: National are tone deaf and out of touch and they just don’t care.
civility.explanation: Aimed at a party, not at any individual member, so it insults no one. Robust party-political language of this kind is ordinary debate; the tribalism it carries is Focus's problem, not Civility's.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: The Government say fast tracking environmental destruction is going to create jobs. What limited imagination and ambition they have for our country.
rigor.explanation: Restates the opposing position in loaded terms the Government would not accept ('fast tracking environmental destruction' rather than 'fast tracking consents'), then answers it with an appeal to ridicule rather than any counter-argument. Strawman plus appeal to ridicule; no premise connects fast-track consenting to poor job outcomes.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Christopher Luxon and Nicola Willis’ economic mismanagement is wrecking local communities, including my region of Nelson and Tasman.
rigor.explanation: Attributes a set of regional business closures to government economic management. The closures listed afterwards are real evidence of job losses, but no mechanism is offered connecting any government decision to any particular closure — the inference is post hoc, from coincidence in time to causation.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: National has a proud history of backing farmers and farming, and our significant cohort of rural MPs—men and women—is a testament to this.
rigor.explanation: Offers the number of rural MPs in the caucus as evidence of a record of supporting farmers. That is a non sequitur — how many rural MPs a party elects says something about where it wins seats, not about what it has done in office. No policy or outcome is offered in support.
rigor.subject: speaker

focus.statement: New Zealand First—more like “Trans-Tasman Resources First”, more like “OceanaGold First”, more like overseas corporations first, New Zealand last.
focus.explanation: A play on a party's name. Two companies are named, but nothing is said about any consent, permit condition or decision — the content is entirely a characterisation of what the other party is really about.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: National are tone deaf and out of touch and they just don’t care.
focus.explanation: No policy, measure, figure or outcome appears at all — it is a characterisation of what the other party is like. This is the case Focus exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: In fact, when I asked Nicola Willis in the House last week what she was doing about this, she claimed Nelson should be happy with the Government because they’re giving us half a hospital.
focus.explanation: Names a specific government investment — the Nelson hospital rebuild — and holds a Minister to account for the scope of it. Scrutiny of a named commitment, squarely on policy.
focus.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That's why, come 2026, the people can choose a Government that will put its hands back on the wheel of the economy and steer it where it actually needs to go instead of into a ditch of environmental destruction.
specificity.explanation: An extended steering metaphor with no mechanism, figure or named policy. 'Where it actually needs to go' commits to nothing checkable.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Earlier this year, 142 jobs were lost from Carter Holt Harvey’s Eves Valley sawmill.
specificity.explanation: A named employer, a named site, an exact headcount and a rough date. Anyone could go and check it.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Labour will focus on what matters most to people in New Zealand and Nelson: jobs, health, homes, and real action on the cost of living.
specificity.explanation: Four policy areas listed with no mechanism, no amount and no timeframe. 'Real action on the cost of living' commits to nothing that could be checked later.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: That’s why, in Budget 2025, the Government committed $250,000 to support rural New Zealand’s grassroots work.
specificity.explanation: An exact figure tied to a named Budget and a stated purpose. Checkable against the Budget documents.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It’s why we’re also backing the Agri-Women’s Development Trust and Dairy Women’s Network to deliver coaching and training for young and established rural women leaders.
specificity.explanation: Two named organisations and a stated deliverable (coaching and training), but no funding amount, no participant numbers and no timeframe.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: And then every day, as costs go up under Christopher Luxon’s Government and he’s not helping with the rising cost of living and he’s more interested in protecting the big banks and tax cuts for tobacco companies, Kiwis aren’t seeing any of that correction they were promised and they’re not seeing the growing economy that they thought they were going to get.
civility.explanation: Names the Prime Minister and imputes a motive to him personally — that he is 'more interested' in banks and tobacco companies than in households. That is an attribution of bad faith to an individual rather than criticism of a decision, which is the 0.5 band; it stops short of a direct insult.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Thankfully, they never became a coalition in this Government, on the Government benches, but they have proven beyond reasonable doubt that they are an unholy alliance; that they are the “uni-party”; that they are one thing on that side of the House.
civility.explanation: The target is parties, not individuals; no person's character, competence or worth is attacked. Party-level jabs pass Civility cleanly, which is why the tribalism here has to be caught by Focus instead.
civility.subject: speaker

civility.statement: Do you want Erica Stanford, who delivers results in education, or Willow-Jean Prime, who can’t manage her emails?
civility.explanation: A named individual is attacked on personal competence — the jibe is about her ability to do basic administration, not about any position she holds or decision she made. A clear personal attack, and the speaker's own conduct regardless of who it is aimed at.
civility.subject: speaker

focus.statement: And then every day, as costs go up under Christopher Luxon’s Government and he’s not helping with the rising cost of living and he’s more interested in protecting the big banks and tax cuts for tobacco companies, Kiwis aren’t seeing any of that correction they were promised and they’re not seeing the growing economy that they thought they were going to get.
focus.explanation: There is real policy content (bank regulation, tobacco excise, the cost-of-living correction), but a substantial part of the weight is on what the Prime Minister is 'interested in' rather than on the measures themselves.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: But instead of being clear with consumers about who will bear the cost of that, they have lumped it on to small businesses.
focus.explanation: Names a specific measure (the surcharge ban) and identifies who bears its cost. This is scrutiny of a policy's incidence, which is squarely on-policy and the job of an opposition MP — no party framing carries the point.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Thankfully, they never became a coalition in this Government, on the Government benches, but they have proven beyond reasonable doubt that they are an unholy alliance; that they are the “uni-party”; that they are one thing on that side of the House.
focus.explanation: Entirely about what the Opposition parties are 'really like' — an alliance, a uni-party. No policy, measure, figure or outcome is named anywhere in it. This is the content-free party framing the attribute exists to catch.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Do you want Erica Stanford, who delivers results in education, or Willow-Jean Prime, who can’t manage her emails?
focus.explanation: A choice framed entirely between personalities. 'Delivers results' names no policy, measure or figure, and the counterpoint is about email management rather than any education outcome.
focus.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Fuel and transport costs keep going up, not because of global events but because this Government has added on fees that are administrative costs to keep moving around your city and your region, and this Government won’t own up.
rigor.explanation: An inference is genuinely advanced — costs rise, therefore the cause is government-added fees — but the alternative explanation (global events) is dismissed by assertion alone, and no fee, amount or mechanism is offered to close the gap between the premise and the causal conclusion. False dichotomy plus an unsupported causal step.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: They tried to merge Health New Zealand; they tried to merge three waters; and now they’re trying to merge Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori.
rigor.explanation: A faulty analogy: the conclusion that a prospective political arrangement will fail is carried entirely by listing unrelated administrative mergers. Nothing is offered connecting institutional restructuring to coalition formation, so the inference does not follow even granting the premises.
rigor.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: They’re also not being upfront with things like the pricing rules, which they say is going to be a big market intervention on those large corporates, those monopolistic large corporates that they say they are going to focus on when in fact they have picked the one pricing intervention which makes it illegal to drop prices.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's chosen pricing intervention has the effect of making price reductions illegal. Standard predatory-pricing and below-cost-selling provisions restrict only anti-competitive discounting, so the characterisation appears to be an overstatement, but the specific rule referenced would settle it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Government's announced grocery/competition pricing rules (Commerce Act amendments or grocery sector pricing regulation announced in 2025). True if the intervention as drafted prohibits or restricts a supplier or retailer from lowering prices; false if it targets predatory or below-cost pricing, price-fixing or resale price maintenance rather than price reductions as such.

veracity.statement: Some 73,900 New Zealanders are hearing that message and have left—200 New Zealanders every day with no plan to get them back.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific annual count of New Zealand citizens departing, and a derived daily rate. The two figures are internally consistent (73,900/365 ≈ 202).
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ international migration statistics, departures of New Zealand citizens for the most recent 12-month period before 15 October 2025. True if departures of NZ citizens are approximately 73,900 (and the daily rate approximately 200); false if materially different.

veracity.statement: It has shrunk since the day they took office.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the size of the New Zealand economy is smaller now than when the Government took office. Ambiguous between total and per-capita GDP; the criterion above resolves it on the total-real-GDP reading, which is the harder test for the claim.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Stats NZ real GDP (production measure, seasonally adjusted level) for the quarter containing October 2023 compared with the latest quarter published before October 2025. True if the level of real GDP is lower in the later quarter; false if it is higher.

veracity.statement: It’s not just good enough to point to those young people as something of a problem when this Government has a target to get 50,000 people off jobseeker support.
veracity.explanation: Asserts the existence and size of a specific government welfare target. A single announced figure settles it.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The Government's published welfare targets (MSD / Minister for Social Development announcements). True if a target of reducing jobseeker support recipients by 50,000 has been set; false if no such target exists or the number differs.

veracity.statement: It's been two years since the election, and when you are focused on managing a merger like they are, you can’t actually get things done, but let me tell you what we’ve done in the last two years since the election: in law and order, we’ve reduced violent crime—29,000 victims less than on election day; ram raids are down 85 percent; police patrols are up 40 percent; bans on gang patches.
veracity.explanation: Three separate quantitative claims about crime and policing outcomes since October 2023. Each has an identifiable official source; the ram-raid and patrol figures depend heavily on the baseline period chosen.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: NZ Crime and Victims Survey victimisation counts for the two years to October 2025 versus October 2023 (for the 29,000 figure); NZ Police recorded ram-raid offence counts over the same period (for the 85% claim); Police reported patrol hours or deployment statistics (for the 40% claim). True if each figure matches the published series within rounding; false if any is materially overstated.

veracity.statement: In health, there’s 16,000 more elective surgeries that have happened, 33 new cancer treatments, and 33 more medicines.
veracity.explanation: Asserts three delivery figures in health since the Government took office. The identical '33' for both cancer treatments and additional medicines is the point most likely to be an overlap or a misstatement.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Health New Zealand elective/planned care volumes for the period since October 2023 (for the 16,000 figure) and Pharmac funding decisions over the same period (for the cancer treatment and medicine counts). True if the published counts match; false if the numbers are materially different or double-count the same funding announcement.

veracity.statement: Do you want law and order with a reduction in ram raids and up with the confidence, or Tamatha Paul, who wants to defund the police?
veracity.explanation: Attributes a specific policy position — defunding the police — to a named MP. Settled by what she has actually said and by her party's published policing policy.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Tamatha Paul's public statements and Green Party police policy as at October 2025. True if she has advocated reducing or removing police funding; false if her recorded position is redirecting some functions or criticising police practice without proposing a funding cut.

specificity.statement: Some 73,900 New Zealanders are hearing that message and have left—200 New Zealanders every day with no plan to get them back.
specificity.explanation: Carries an exact figure and a derived rate that anyone could look up against the migration series. Precise and checkable regardless of whether it turns out to be correct.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: It's been two years since the election, and when you are focused on managing a merger like they are, you can’t actually get things done, but let me tell you what we’ve done in the last two years since the election: in law and order, we’ve reduced violent crime—29,000 victims less than on election day; ram raids are down 85 percent; police patrols are up 40 percent; bans on gang patches.
specificity.explanation: Four concrete, checkable items — a victim count, two percentage changes and a named measure. Someone could go to the source series and verify each one.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: In health, there’s 16,000 more elective surgeries that have happened, 33 new cancer treatments, and 33 more medicines.
specificity.explanation: Three exact figures attached to named categories of health delivery. Precise enough to be checked directly against Health NZ and Pharmac reporting.
specificity.subject: speaker

divination.statement: Exactly, Minister Collins: they will never get that chance.
divination.explanation: Forecasts that the Opposition parties will not get the opportunity to form a government — an outcome outside the speaker's own control, and therefore a prediction rather than a promise. Not yet resolvable at the time of speaking.
divination.subject: speaker
divination.falsification_criterion: The composition of the government formed after the next New Zealand general election. False if Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori (in any combination sufficient to govern) form the government; true if they do not.

focus.statement: My key concern is how this central government “Coalition of Chaos” is undermining local government at every opportunity.
focus.explanation: A general attack on the governing parties as a bloc using a nickname; no specific policy, measure or outcome is named for the claim that local government is being undermined.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: So that’s probably the influence on this Government—Don Brash pushing through legislation in this House that isn’t asked for and isn’t necessary.
focus.explanation: There is a real policy point underneath (the change is unnecessary), but the weight of the sentence is on who is supposedly behind the bill rather than on what it does.
focus.subject: speaker

focus.statement: Here we are, with the Government focused on big ideas and slogans, but this is a mish-mash of a bunch of small things that really speak to influences, I think, of the minor parties set up in this Government.
focus.explanation: Nominally about the bill, but the content is coalition politics — slogans, minor-party influence — rather than any named provision, cost or effect.
focus.subject: speaker

veracity.statement: In many areas, turnout was below 40 percent, and in some communities, it dropped into the 30s, which is a reflection of a voting system that is confusing, outdated, and disconnected from the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that turnout in the October 2025 local elections was under 40 percent in many areas and in the 30s in some.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Official turnout figures for the 2025 New Zealand local authority elections published by councils / the Department of Internal Affairs; true if a substantial number of territorial authorities recorded turnout below 40% and some below 40% into the 30s, false if the great majority were at or above 40%.

veracity.statement: This directly contradicts the Prime Minister in Monday’s post-Cabinet press conference saying he’s discussing the Electoral Commission running the local elections with Minister Watts.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that at the post-Cabinet press conference on Monday 13 October 2025 the Prime Minister said he was discussing with Minister Watts having the Electoral Commission run local elections, and that this conflicts with the Minister of Local Government's September answer declining to consider such a change.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The transcript or recording of the 13 October 2025 post-Cabinet press conference, together with the Minister of Local Government's September 2025 answer to the question referred to; true if the Prime Minister described such discussions with Minister Watts and the Minister had declined the same proposal, false if either statement is absent or the two are consistent.

veracity.statement: In Mt Albert Library, people were waiting two hours to cast their special votes.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that voters queued for around two hours to cast special votes at the Mt Albert Library voting place during the 2025 local elections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Auckland Council / electoral officer records of special-voting queues at the Mt Albert Library site in October 2025, or contemporaneous news reports of wait times there; true if waits of about two hours are documented, false if recorded waits were materially shorter.

veracity.statement: Under-resourcing voting systems is a form of voter suppression, though less blatant than this Government’s Electoral Amendment Bill, which would roll back voter enrolment for general elections by 13 days.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Government's Electoral Amendment Bill closes enrolment 13 days earlier than the current law for general elections.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Electoral Amendment Bill as introduced in 2025 and its explanatory note; true if it moves the enrolment deadline forward by 13 days (ending late/election-day enrolment), false if the change is a different length or of a different kind.

veracity.statement: Private companies are not—however well meaning, however good the staff—subject to the Official Information Act.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the private companies administering local elections fall outside the Official Information Act 1982.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: Schedule 1 of the Official Information Act 1982 and Ombudsman guidance on contractors; true if private election-services companies are not listed agencies and are not directly subject to the Act, false if they are covered in their own right.

veracity.statement: Despite the attacks on te reo, Te Tiriti, and Māori customary rights by the coalition partners, a strong majority across the country—as of today, 520,113 voters—voted to keep Māori wards.
veracity.explanation: Asserts a specific national tally — 520,113 votes to retain Māori wards across the 2025 Māori ward polls — and that this was a majority of votes cast nationally, with a margin over 60,000.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The sum of 'keep/retain' versus 'remove' votes across all council Māori ward polls held with the October 2025 local elections, per official council results declarations; true if the retain total is about 520,113 and exceeds the remove total by roughly 60,000, false if the totals differ materially or the national majority runs the other way.

veracity.statement: That’s a huge step up from the first couple of decades of this century, when only Wairoa got through.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that Wairoa was the only council to establish and retain a Māori ward through a binding poll in roughly 2000–2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The record of binding Māori ward polls held under the Local Electoral Act 2001 between 2001 and 2020; true if Wairoa District Council was the only one where the Māori ward survived the poll, false if any other council also succeeded.

veracity.statement: The bill removes some of the key parts of the Act that aim to promote and protect the rights of our tamariki and young people, such as those rights under Te Tiriti o Waitangi and under the National Education and Learning Priorities.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2) removes the Te Tiriti o Waitangi provisions and the National Education and Learning Priorities obligations from the Education and Training Act 2020.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The text of the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2) as reported back from the Education and Workforce Committee; true if it repeals or narrows the Act's Te Tiriti clause and the NELP requirements on boards, false if those provisions are retained.

veracity.statement: Only 13 percent supported this bill in its totality—13 percent out of hundreds of submissions that were received.
veracity.explanation: Asserts that 13 percent of the several hundred submissions received on the bill supported it in full.
veracity.subject: speaker
veracity.falsification_criterion: The departmental report to the Education and Workforce Committee on the Education and Training Amendment Bill (No 2), which tallies submitter positions; true if roughly 13% of submitters supported the bill in its entirety, false if the tally is materially different.

specificity.statement: In many areas, turnout was below 40 percent, and in some communities, it dropped into the 30s, which is a reflection of a voting system that is confusing, outdated, and disconnected from the lives of everyday New Zealanders.
specificity.explanation: Carries checkable numeric bands (below 40 percent, into the 30s) though the areas are unnamed; the diagnosis attached to it is general.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Under-resourcing voting systems is a form of voter suppression, though less blatant than this Government’s Electoral Amendment Bill, which would roll back voter enrolment for general elections by 13 days.
specificity.explanation: Names a specific bill and a specific figure (13 days), though the under-resourcing claim beside it is unquantified.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Despite the attacks on te reo, Te Tiriti, and Māori customary rights by the coalition partners, a strong majority across the country—as of today, 520,113 voters—voted to keep Māori wards.
specificity.explanation: Gives an exact vote count and, in the following sentence, a stated margin — precise and directly checkable against the results.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: If we want to rebuild trust in local democracy, we need reform backed by the Greens, Labour, and National—and if any of the other smaller parties want to join us, that would be good.
specificity.explanation: Calls for cross-party 'reform' without naming a mechanism, a change to the Local Electoral Act, a cost or a timeframe; the only concrete content is which parties should be involved.
specificity.subject: speaker

specificity.statement: Only 13 percent supported this bill in its totality—13 percent out of hundreds of submissions that were received.
specificity.explanation: A precise proportion tied to a defined base (submissions to the select committee), checkable against the departmental report.
specificity.subject: speaker

civility.statement: This bill, in my view—and I lean heavily into the university tertiary education component—is an absolute Government overreach, no matter which way you look at it.
civility.explanation: Blunt, unqualified condemnation of the bill and the Government's approach to it, with no individual attacked or bad faith imputed to any person — hard criticism of a policy is the standard.
civility.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: Anyone that’s visited a school—and I know many MPs in this House visit schools—knows that every single school has attendance management systems online, that they look at their data, that they use that, and here we have a bill that enforces this to happen.
rigor.explanation: Appeal to anecdote and shared common knowledge: personal school visits are offered as grounds for a universal claim about 'every single school', and the conclusion that the statutory requirement is therefore redundant is not established by it.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: So that’s probably the influence on this Government—Don Brash pushing through legislation in this House that isn’t asked for and isn’t necessary.
rigor.explanation: Non sequitur by association: from the Minister citing one example involving Don Brash, the conclusion is drawn that Brash is the driving influence behind the legislation. Nothing offered connects a cited example to authorship or influence.
rigor.subject: speaker

rigor.statement: I know that between Otago, between Canterbury that I visited, between Massey, Auckland, and the Auckland University of Technology, every university encourages academic freedom of speech, but there’s also got to be safety in place to ensure that that academic freedom of speech doesn’t translate into free hate speech—into free hate speech—in this country that we know impacts those that are most vulnerable.
rigor.explanation: Generalises from a handful of personal visits to a claim about every university, and the move from 'freedom of expression' to 'free hate speech' is asserted rather than shown — no mechanism in the bill is linked to the harm claimed.
rigor.subject: speaker
